news.titleZh: 如何将AI代理应用于物流
news.summaryZh: 物流中AI代理利用机器学习和自然语言处理自主管理运输与供应链工作，无需人工触发每一步。当卡车在临近交付窗口时抛锚，AI代理可发现中断、与司机协调并在同一线程中更新客户，减少手动往返沟通。AI代理处理高量任务如货物跟踪、交付更新和异常处理，人类仍控制复杂案例。与传统自动化不同，AI代理能解读上下文并实时适应异常，而非失败或升级给人工。多数团队从一两个高量工作流开始，根据效果扩展。Gartner预计到2026年底40%的企业应用将集成任务特定AI代理，2025年不足5%。IBM商业价值研究院报告，62%的供应链领导者称AI代理加速行动速度。UPS在海关经纪中集成代理AI后，2025年3月约21%的每日1.3万件美国入境包裹无需人工干预清关，到2025年9月提升至90%的11.2万件。AI代理应用包括：货物跟踪与可见性、主动客户更新、异常处理、库存与补货、调度与司机协调，以及运费对账、退货和逆向物流、多语言沟通。选择AI代理平台需关注集成深度、监督控制、渠道覆盖、合规性和可衡量结果。起步时，审计当前对话、选择一个工作流、连接数据源、设置护栏并上线、测量并扩展。Heymarket提供共享收件箱和AI代理，集成Salesforce和HubSpot，内置10DLC、TCPA和SOC 2 Type 2合规。
news.bodyHtml:
A truck breaks down twenty minutes from a delivery window. That’s a logistics problem, but it becomes a dispatch problem fast: someone has to find a replacement driver, reroute the load, and notify the customer, all before the delay compounds. Most teams still do that manually, holding three separate conversations for one disruption.

AI agents for logistics use machine learning and natural language processing to manage shipping and supply chain work on their own without a person triggering every step.

Paired with a shared inbox built for logistics, dispatch AI agents can catch a disruption, coordinate with the driver, and keep the customer updated in one thread instead of three, cutting the manual back-and-forth out of the response.

Key takeaways about AI agents for logistics

  • AI agents handle high-volume logistics tasks like shipment tracking, delivery updates, and exception handling while humans remain in control of complex cases.
  • Unlike traditional automation, AI agents interpret context and adapt to exceptions in real time instead of failing or escalating every one to a person.
  • Most teams start with one or two high-volume workflows and expand based on what’s working.

This guide covers what AI agents in logistics do, how they’re not like the automations you already run, where they deliver the clearest returns, and how to put them to work.

What are AI agents in logistics?

An AI agent is a software system that takes a goal, decides the steps to reach it, acts across your connected systems, and adapts when something changes. All without waiting for your team members to start each move.

In dispatch and logistics, an agent can track a shipment, notice a delay, rebook or reroute it, and notify your customer in one continuous workflow.

These benefits are attracting attention from businesses big and small. Gartner expects 40% of enterprise applications to integrate task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5% in 2025. At the same time, Fortune reported, Uber Freight runs a platform of more than 30 AI agents managing roughly $20 billion in freight.

These numbers show that AI agents for logistics purposes are only going to be more popular in the coming years.

How AI agents differ from traditional logistics automation

AI agents handle what traditional logistics automation systems can’t. They interpret the current state of your operation, reason, and take action instead of waiting for the human’s assistance.

Traditional automation, such as dispatch triggers and status updates, relies on fixed rules. These systems work until an exception occurs, like an unexpected delay or a complex customer query, forcing the process to fail or escalate to a human.

This matters because exceptions are where the most time and money can be lost. A significant amount of volume falls outside of standard rules, which is exactly where scripted automation fails. AI agents take over that off-script work, allowing your team to stop managing constant interruptions and focus on more important decisions.

Benefits of using AI agents in logistics

AI agents in logistics deliver measurable benefits across speed, throughput, and team efficiency, with the strongest evidence coming from real deployments. Benefits of using AI agents for logistics management include:

  • Faster decisions: IBM’s Institute for Business Value reports that 62% of supply chain leaders say AI agents accelerate speed to action. This means quicker decisions, recommendations, and customer communications.
  • Higher straight-through processing: With AI agents, you can handle significantly more production volume. After integrating agentic AI into its customs brokerage, UPS went from clearing about 21% of 13,000 daily U.S.-bound packages without manual intervention in March 2025 to 90% of 112,000 by September 2025.
  • More throughput with the same team: The best logistics teams not only respond faster, but also move more freight without stretching the team thinner. AI agents take over repetitive coordination tasks so your team members can spend their time on the exceptions that need judgment.

Examples of AI agents for logistics management

Shipping and delivery are where most logistics teams find value first. Processes involved here are typically high-volume, repetitive work.

A closer look at each:

1. Shipment tracking and visibility

An agent monitors shipment data continuously, not on a schedule. When a delivery slips behind its window, it flags the exception, checks the cause across your tracking and dispatch systems, and decides whether to reroute, escalate, or message your customer before anyone asks where the order is.

2. Proactive customer updates

Paired with automated text workflows, an agent sends delivery confirmations, ETA changes, and delay notifications the moment a status changes. Your customer who texts “leave it at the loading dock?” gets a handled response instead of a dropped message, which cuts inbound customer service volume and builds trust.

3. Exception handling

A capable AI agent reads an email thread, checks shipment status, contacts the carrier, and drafts the resolution—escalating only the cases that genuinely need a person. That’s the difference between your team managing exceptions and drowning in them.

Beyond individual shipments, AI agents coordinate the moving parts that keep freight flowing.

4. Inventory and replenishment

Inventory agents watch demand and stock levels across facilities and act on what they see—triggering replenishment and moving stock between locations, heading off the overstock carrying costs and stockout expedite fees that come from waiting for a weekly review.

5. Dispatch and driver coordination

Dispatch runs on back-and-forth messaging—assignments, confirmations, route changes. An agent handles that traffic by text, keeping drivers and dispatchers in sync without a coordinator chasing each thread manually.

Other ways to use AI agents in logistics

Other ways to use AI agents in logistics include freight reconciliation, returns and reverse logistics, and multilingual communication across driver and customer channels:

  • Freight reconciliation: Agents match invoices against shipment records, flag discrepancies, and clear straightforward cases without manual review.
  • Returns and reverse logistics: Agents walk customers through return eligibility, generate labels, and confirm timelines, escalating only the exceptions.
  • Multilingual communication: AI texting tools with built-in translation let teams serve drivers and customers in multiple languages without separate queues.

What to look for in an AI agent platform for logistics

Look for five things in an AI agent platform for logistics: how deeply it integrates, how much control you keep, which channels it covers, whether compliance is built in, and how it measures results.

Here’s why these features are important:

  • Integration depth: An agent that can’t pull data from your TMS, CRM, or order management system gives generic answers. Check for native integrations with the tools you already run.
  • Supervised control: You should be able to decide what an agent does on its own and what needs human approval. Supervised modes let agents handle the routine while a person reviews edge cases.
  • Channel coverage: Logistics communication spans SMS, email, and more. Look for a platform that brings it together in a shared inbox where your team sees every conversation in one view.
  • Compliance: If agents are texting customers or drivers at volume, you need 10DLC registration, the U.S. carrier system for business texting, and A2P 10DLC handled correctly. Look for platforms with SOC 2 Type 2 and proper opt-in management.
  • Measurable outcomes: The right tool measures itself against real metrics: on-time delivery, response time, cost per shipment.

How to get started with AI agents in logistics

Most teams see the best results when they start with one or two high-impact workflows and build from there.

  1. Audit your current conversations: Look at your highest-volume inbound messages—delivery questions, dispatch confirmations, recruiting replies—and find the ones that follow a pattern. Those are your best candidates.
  2. Pick one workflow: Start with something predictable and high-volume, like automated delivery notifications, where an agent can deliver value fast without a complicated setup.
  3. Connect your data sources: Agents act on the systems they connect to. Integrate your TMS, CRM, and order management so the agent has accurate data to work with.
  4. Set guardrails and go live: Define what the agent can do autonomously and what it routes to a person, then test before launch.
  5. Measure and expand: Track response times, on-time delivery, and ticket volume. Use what you learn to refine workflows and add new use cases.

Bringing AI agents into your logistics operation

A good logistics experience hinges on stellar communication. Tracking updates, dispatch coordination, driver messages, delivery exceptions. For every step, there’s a conversation that has to reach the right person at the right time.

That’s where a platform like Heymarket fits in. Heymarket gives your team a shared inbox for SMS, email, and other channels, with AI agents that handle the repetitive messaging while your people stay in control of exceptions.

Because it works inside your Salesforce integration and HubSpot, every conversation keeps its context instead of disappearing when the text thread ends. And with 10DLC, TCPA, and SOC 2 Type 2 compliance built in, you can manage that messaging volume the right way.

With Heymarket, your team manages more shipments and conversations at scale without losing the personal touch that keeps customers and drivers loyal.

If you’re looking for a platform that brings AI-powered messaging, automation, and omnichannel support together for logistics teams, Heymarket can help. Book a demo to see how it works.

FAQs about using AI agents for logistics

AI agents in logistics is still a relatively new space, and it’s common to have questions about how they work and where to start. Here are answers to some of the most frequently asked.

How does agentic AI improve supply chain management?

Agentic AI improves supply chain management by acting on data continuously and handling exceptions on its own. Instead of running fixed rules and escalating anything unexpected, agents reason about the current state of your operation, make a decision, and execute it across connected systems.

What are the best AI tools for logistics optimization?

For routing and inventory, look at agents that integrate with your TMS and warehouse systems. For communication at scale, look for a messaging platform with AI agents and a shared inbox that connects to your CRM. The right tool fits your existing systems, keeps you in control of what runs autonomously, and proves its value through real operational metrics.

How are AI agents different from traditional logistics automation?

Traditional automation executes fixed rules and escalates anything outside them. AI agents interpret context, handle exceptions, coordinate across multiple systems, and adapt to new data in real time.

1. Shipment tracking and visibility An agent monitors shipment data continuously, not on a schedule. When a delivery slips behind its window, it flags the exception, checks the cause across your tracking and dispatch systems, and decides whether to reroute, escalate, or message your customer before anyone asks where the order is.

2. Proactive customer updates Paired with automated text workflows , an agent sends delivery confirmations, ETA changes, and delay notifications the moment a status changes. Your customer who texts “leave it at the loading dock?” gets a handled response instead of a dropped message, which cuts inbound customer service volume and builds trust.

3. Exception handling A capable AI agent reads an email thread, checks shipment status, contacts the carrier, and drafts the resolution—escalating only the cases that genuinely need a person. That’s the difference between your team managing exceptions and drowning in them.

Beyond individual shipments, AI agents coordinate the moving parts that keep freight flowing.

4. Inventory and replenishment Inventory agents watch demand and stock levels across facilities and act on what they see—triggering replenishment and moving stock between locations, heading off the overstock carrying costs and stockout expedite fees that come from waiting for a weekly review.

5. Dispatch and driver coordination Dispatch runs on back-and-forth messaging—assignments, confirmations, route changes. An agent handles that traffic by text, keeping drivers and dispatchers in sync without a coordinator chasing each thread manually.

Other ways to use AI agents in logistics Other ways to use AI agents in logistics include freight reconciliation, returns and reverse logistics, and multilingual communication across driver and customer channels:

Freight reconciliation : Agents match invoices against shipment records, flag discrepancies, and clear straightforward cases without manual review. Returns and reverse logistics : Agents walk customers through return eligibility, generate labels, and confirm timelines, escalating only the exceptions. Multilingual communication : AI texting tools with built-in translation let teams serve drivers and customers in multiple languages without separate queues. What to look for in an AI agent platform for logistics Look for five things in an AI agent platform for logistics: how deeply it integrates, how much control you keep, which channels it covers, whether compliance is built in, and how it measures results.

Here’s why these features are important:

Integration depth: An agent that can’t pull data from your TMS, CRM, or order management system gives generic answers. Check for native integrations with the tools you already run. Supervised control: You should be able to decide what an agent does on its own and what needs human approval. Supervised modes let agents handle the routine while a person reviews edge cases. Channel coverage: Logistics communication spans SMS, email, and more. Look for a platform that brings it together in a shared inbox where your team sees every conversation in one view. Compliance: If agents are texting customers or drivers at volume, you need 10DLC registration, the U.S. carrier system for business texting, and A2P 10DLC handled correctly. Look for platforms with SOC 2 Type 2 and proper opt-in management. Measurable outcomes: The right tool measures itself against real metrics: on-time delivery, response time, cost per shipment.

How to get started with AI agents in logistics Most teams see the best results when they start with one or two high-impact workflows and build from there.

Audit your current conversations: Look at your highest-volume inbound messages—delivery questions, dispatch confirmations, recruiting replies—and find the ones that follow a pattern. Those are your best candidates. Pick one workflow: Start with something predictable and high-volume, like automated delivery notifications , where an agent can deliver value fast without a complicated setup. Connect your data sources: Agents act on the systems they connect to. Integrate your TMS, CRM, and order management so the agent has accurate data to work with. Set guardrails and go live: Define what the agent can do autonomously and what it routes to a person, then test before launch. Measure and expand: Track response times, on-time delivery, and ticket volume. Use what you learn to refine workflows and add new use cases. Bringing AI agents into your logistics operation A good logistics experience hinges on stellar communication. Tracking updates, dispatch coordination, driver messages, delivery exceptions. For every step, there’s a conversation that has to reach the right person at the right time.

With Heymarket, your team manages more shipments and conversations at scale without losing the personal touch that keeps customers and drivers loyal.

Instead of running fixed rules and escalating anything unexpected, agents reason about the current state of your operation, make a decision, and execute it across connected systems.

news.titleEn: 31% of Law Firms Say AI Improves Profitability
news.titleZh: 31%的律所表示AI提升了盈利能力
news.summaryZh:
BigHand的一项新定价调查显示，31%的律所在仔细审查数据后发现，AI“提高了每项业务的盈利能力”。这大概是因为AI有助于减少非计费工作的时间，从而让每个客户项目实现更多利润。此外，在固定收费的业务中，AI加速带来了可观的“技术红利”。同时，30%的律所发现AI有助于推动业务处理量增加，对于能够从更快完成的项目中获益的律所而言，这同样是显著提振。一些律所可能未给出肯定答复，仅仅是因为它们没有追踪回答这些问题所需的数据。

然而，还有其他几个因素为一些律所描绘了更复杂的财务图景：某些任务的可计费工时减少了27%，对人工任务的依赖降低了31%。对于完全固守传统计费小时模式的律所来说，这些数字并不受欢迎。对于能够驾驭AI影响下新定价环境的律所而言，上述情况也是好消息。另一个问题是，即便现在，35%的合伙人仍对与客户讨论AI使用感到“不自在”。但可以理解，当客户可能因律所在其业务中部署AI而要求折扣时——而如今在大多数大型律所使用此类技术已是标准做法。人们也会猜测，采用固定收费并拥抱快速处理量的律所更愿意进行此类讨论。总体而言，这些数据对正在适应变化的律所是好消息，也表明AI如今已真正以有意义的方式嵌入大部分市场。
news.bodyHtml:
A new pricing survey by BigHand shows that 31% of law firms – which had scrutinised their data – found that AI had ‘improved profitability per matter’.

This is presumably because AI is helping to reduce time spent on non-billable work, allowing more profits to be realised for each client project. Plus, where a matter is on a fixed fee AI acceleration provides a healthy ‘tech dividend’.

Also, 30% of firms saw that AI is helping to drive increased matter throughput – again a notable boost to firms that are able to benefit from more rapidly completed projects.

However, there are several other factors here that paint a more complex financial scenario for some law firms:

  • There was also a reduction in billable hours for certain tasks – 27%
  • And a reduced reliance on manual tasks – 31%

For firms that are wholly wedded to the traditional billable hour model, then such figures are not that welcome. For those that can navigate the new AI-influenced pricing environment, then the above is also good news.

As AL has said before, the key to law firm success with AI is primarily around getting the business model right for a world where efficiency is now a core element of the end product for the client. You can either work with this new reality and reap the rewards, or stick to the former, primarily time-based approach and struggle to make AI as profitable as it could be.

— Advertisement —

—

One other wrinkle is that even now, 35% of partners were ‘uncomfortable’ discussing AI use with clients. But, one can understand that when clients might be asking for discounts because of AI deployment on their matters – at a time when using such technology across most large firms is now standard. One would also guess that firms using fixed fees and embracing rapid throughput are more open to such discussions.

Overall, the data is good news for law firms that are adapting and also shows that AI is now truly embedded in a meaningful way across much of the market.

news.titleEn: Clio Hires Bridget Mary McCormack
news.titleZh: Clio聘请布里奇特·玛丽·麦科马克
news.summaryZh: Clio已聘请前密歇根州最高法院首席大法官布里奇特·玛丽·麦科马克。她最近担任美国仲裁协会首席执行官，期间推动法律AI的应用。她将以总经理（司法）身份加入Clio，据称此举将加强Clio向法院扩张背后的领导团队。此前不久，Clio刚聘请帕布罗·阿雷东多担任高级副总裁（司法），他是Casetext的前联合创始人，该公司已被汤森路透收购。这两项任命都是Clio更加关注“在法院、司法官员和争议解决组织合作伙伴中实现增长”的一部分。其以显著的规模和广泛的法律基础进入法院；收购vLex为平台增加了权威研究、判例法、案卷和法院记录，该平台被130多个国家的40多万法律专业人士使用。司法机构是加强法律体系运作的最大机会之一，他们正以长期雄心为此建设；布里奇特对这个市场的理解达到了极少数人才能达到的水平，她领导过法院，在司法系统中工作过，知道如何赢得他们想要服务的机构的信任。数百万人在利害关系最大的时刻依赖法院，却往往没有有意义的法律支持；现在的机会是给这些机构更好的工具来履行这一责任。
news.bodyHtml:
Clio has hired Bridget Mary McCormack, a former Michigan Supreme Court Chief Justice, and most recently CEO of the American Arbitration Association (AAA), where she spearheaded a drive toward legal AI adoption.

She will join the legal tech company as General Manager, Judiciary, strengthening the leadership team behind Clio’s expansion into the courts, they said.

The move follows swiftly on from the hire of Pablo Arredondo as Senior Vice President, Judiciary, who is the former co-founder of Casetext, which was bought by Thomson Reuters.

Both moves are part of an increased focus on ‘growth across courts, judicial officers, and dispute resolution organizational partners’. To which end they noted that ‘Clio enters the courts with significant scale and a broad legal foundation. Its acquisition of vLex added authoritative research, case law, dockets, and court records to a platform used by more than 400,000 legal professionals in over 130 countries.’

Jack Newton, CEO and Founder of Clio, commented: ‘The judiciary represents one of the largest opportunities to strengthen how the legal system works, and we are building for it with long term ambition.

‘Bridget understands this market at a level very few people do. She has led courts, worked across the justice system, and knows what it takes to earn the confidence of the institutions we want to serve. This is part of a much bigger vision for Clio to help shape the infrastructure of modern legal work, across the profession and the institutions that support it.’

McCormack concluded: ‘Millions of people rely on courts at moments when the stakes are highest, often without meaningful legal support. The opportunity now is to give those institutions better tools to meet that responsibility. If we do this well, the impact won’t be about efficiency. It will be the strengthening of the public justice system’s service to the people who depend on it, and the corresponding growth in public trust.’

Is this a big deal?

Well, it’s not every day you hire a former judge – or the head of the AAA, so this is indeed a big move. And as noted above, Clio is set on expanding into the judiciary field, so the new hire and that of Arredondo are significant steps towards accomplishing this goal.

news.titleEn: Salesforce Rolls Out Legora For Legal Function
news.titleZh: Salesforce为其法务部门部署Legora
news.summaryZh: Legora已被Salesforce选中，为其遍布美国、欧洲和亚太地区的法务团队提供服务。此举值得关注，因为Salesforce一直公开表示其内部自行开发了许多法律科技应用，并曾在Legal Innovators California上谈及此事。AI正在重塑法律团队的运作方式，借助Slack和Agentforce，Salesforce正在构建一个AI原生、信任优先的法务部门，使团队能够更高效地工作，将时间集中在影响最大的地方。将Legora加入其转型组合，为团队提供了额外的法律工具，以支持研究、起草和其他工作流程，从而让他们能花更多时间在需要专业知识和判断力的工作上。Salesforce决定采用Legora反映了内部法律团队拥抱代理式AI的更广泛转变，这是他们运行全面法律工作流程所依赖的关键基础设施的一部分。对于一家一直以利用自身技术和AI能力为法务团队进行建设而自豪的公司来说，在全球范围内部署Legora——后者必然提供了许多他们已经设计的相同‘技能’——对这家总部位于斯德哥尔摩的公司来说是一次成功。此外，Salesforce规模庞大，与数千家其他公司有联系，因此这对Legora来说是一个坚实的胜利。
news.bodyHtml:
AL doesn’t usually do client wins, but this one is worth a mention. Legora has been picked by Salesforce for its legal teams across the US, Europe and APAC. It’s noteworthy as Salesforce has been vocal about building many of its own legal tech applications for internal use. In fact, they talked about this at Legal Innovators California.

Erica Swainson, VP, Legal Innovation & Strategic Initiatives, Salesforce, commented: ‘AI is reshaping how legal teams operate, and with Slack and Agentforce we’re building an AI-native, trust-first legal function that empowers our team to work more efficiently and focus their time where it can have the greatest impact.

‘Adding Legora to our transformation portfolio gives our team additional legal tools to support research, drafting, and other workflows, so they can spend more time on the work that requires their expertise and judgment.’

And, Max Junestrand, CEO and Co-Founder of Legora, added: ‘Salesforce’s decision to adopt Legora reflects a broader shift in how in-house legal teams are embracing agentic AI. It’s part of the critical infrastructure they depend on to run comprehensive legal workflows.’

Is this a big deal?

Well, as mentioned, for a company that has taken great pride in leveraging its own tech and AI capabilities to build for its legal team, the fact they’re doing a global roll out of Legora – which must be offering many of the same ‘skills’ they’ve already designed for – is a coup for the Stockholm-based company. Plus, Salesforce is huge – and connects to 1,000s of other companies. So, a solid win for them here.

news.titleEn: American Legal Technology Awards Announces 2026 Finalists Ahead of October Gala in Boston
news.titleZh: 美国法律科技大奖公布2026年入围名单，十月波士顿颁奖晚宴在即
news.summaryZh: 美国法律科技大奖于2026年9月10日在加拿大温哥华公布第七届年度奖项入围名单。本届共收到来自十个类别的234份提交，为该项目历史上规模最大、竞争最激烈的一届。获奖者将于2026年10月25日星期日在马萨诸塞州波士顿萨福克大学法学院举行的颁奖晚宴上揭晓。入围者由杰出评审团选出，评审团由备受尊敬的法律创新专家、思想领袖和实干家组成，其专业知识和洞察力确保每个奖项反映真实影响力和卓越表现。提名免费向所有人开放，并鼓励自荐，符合该项目独立和包容的设计。每年他都以为该领域已达到上限，但每年这些入围者都证明他错了；在竞相奔向人工智能的世界中，这个群体始终将技术指向最需要它的人，这些杰出人士所做的工作使法律更易获取、更可负担、更人性化。终身成就奖不列入入围名单，因为该类别仅表彰一位获奖者，其得主将在晚宴上首次揭晓。颁奖晚宴将于2026年10月25日星期日在波士顿萨福克大学法学院举行，当晚将设正式晚宴、美酒和颁奖仪式，由杰基·谢弗主持。联合创始人汤姆·马丁、卡特·穆恩和帕特里克·帕莱斯将同台颁奖。门票现已在 https://americanlegaltechnology.com/tickets 发售，早鸟价于2026年9月30日截止。大奖感谢今年的赞助商：Clio、Smith.ai、Practising Law Institute、ARAG Legal、8am、Cloud925、Palace Law、LawDroid、VAILL以及主办方萨福克大学法学院。
news.bodyHtml:
VANCOUVER, CANADA – September 10, 2026 – The American Legal Technology Awards today announced the finalists for its seventh annual awards program. This year the Awards received 234submissions across ten categories, the strongest and most competitive field in the program’s history. Winners will be revealed at the Awards Dinner Gala on Sunday, October 25, 2026, at Suffolk University Law School in Boston, Massachusetts. 

Finalists were selected by a distinguished panel of world-class judges representing a cross-section of the most respected legal innovation experts, thought leaders, and doers. Their expertise and insight ensure that each award reflects real impact and excellence. Nominations were free and open to all, and self-nominations were encouraged, consistent with the program’s independent and inclusive design.

“Every year I think the field has reached its ceiling, and every year these finalists prove me wrong,” said Tom Martin, co-founder of the Awards. “In a world racing toward AI, this group keeps pointing the technology at the people who need it most. These are remarkable humans doing the work that makes the law more accessible, more affordable, and more human.”

 

2026 FINALISTS (listed in alphabetical order)

Award Category      
A2J Frontline Justice Julio Oyhanarte / Immigration TV Stanford Rhode Center and Legal Design Lab
Court Austin Community Court’s Mobile Court Team Illinois Court Help LA County Courts/Stanford
Education David Colarusso Korin Munsterman Tracy L.M. Norton
Enterprise Benchly Epiq AI Harbor
Individual Aliza Shatzman Amanda Brown Claire Robinson
Journalism Jennifer Leonard Stephanie Everett and Zack Glaser Steven Lerner
Startup Project Fortress Skribe.ai Techtivist
Law Firm Baker, Donelson, Bearman, Caldwell & Berkowitz PC Evolve Family Law Terms.Law (Law Office of Sergei Tokmakov)
Artificial Intelligence Ashley Oborn / Lone Star Legal Aid Frontline Justice / Frontline Q OpenLaws

 

The Lifetime Achievement award is not listed among the finalists, as the category recognizes a single honoree. That recipient will be revealed for the first time at the Gala.

 

About the Gala
The Awards Dinner Gala takes place Sunday, October 25, 2026, at Suffolk University Law School in Boston. The evening will feature a formal dinner, fine wine, and a heartfelt ceremony honoring the winners in each category, hosted by Jackie Shafer. Co-founders Tom Martin, Cat Moon, and Patrick Palace will take the stage together to present the awards. Attendees can expect a vibrant evening of inspiration, networking, and celebration with fellow innovators, thought leaders, and legal visionaries.

 

Tickets are available now at https://americanlegaltechnology.com/tickets. Early bird pricing ends September 30, 2026.

 

The Awards gratefully acknowledge this year’s sponsors: Clio, Smith.ai, Practising Law Institute, ARAG Legal, 8am, Cloud925, Palace Law, LawDroid, VAILL, and Suffolk University Law School, which is hosting the event.

 

 

Media Inquiries Contact:
Tom Martin, Co-Founder, American Legal Technology Awards

Email: tom@lawdroid.com | Website: https://americanlegaltechnology.com

 

About the American Legal Technology Awards:
Founded in 2020, the American Legal Technology Awards is an independent initiative designed to celebrate excellence in the legal industry. By recognizing those who are building a better future through thoughtful and creative use of technology, the Awards seek to inspire innovation that serves the public good.

news.titleEn: One Plus One Equals More Than Two: Clio Lands McCormack to Join Arredondo in Judiciary Expansion
news.titleZh: 一加一大于二：Clio 聘请 McCormack 与 Arredondo 共同推进司法领域扩张
news.summaryZh: Bridget M. McCormack 的去向已确定。她现任美国仲裁协会总裁兼首席执行官，曾任密歇根州最高法院首席大法官。她此前表示新机会“无法拒绝”，并暗示涉及“专注于法官的构建机会”。两周前，Clio 宣布开发面向法官的技术，并聘请 Casetext 联合创始人 Pablo Arredondo 担任司法业务高级副总裁。今日 Clio 正式宣布聘请 McCormack 担任司法业务总经理，帮助构建法院技术的未来。Clio 通过这两项招聘推动法院业务扩张。McCormack 在司法系统创新方面的经历可追溯至其担任密歇根州首席大法官期间，并在美国仲裁协会推动 AI 采用及开发 AI Arbitrator 等产品。Arredondo 曾领导 Casetext 开发包括首个 GPT-4 AI 法律助手 CoCounsel 在内的产品，Thomson Reuters 于 2023 年以 6.5 亿美元收购 Casetext。司法领域是加强法律体系运作的最大机会之一，Clio 正以长期雄心为此构建，McCormack 对该市场的理解很少有人能及，她领导过法院、在司法系统中工作过，知道如何赢得目标机构的信任。McCormack 将于 10 月开始在 Clio 工作，负责领导司法业务的市场与商业战略，直接向 Newton 汇报。Arredondo 将领导司法部门的产品开发与战略方向，向 Clio 首席产品官 John Foreman 汇报。Clio 进军法院技术开发正值司法领域的关键时刻。
news.bodyHtml:
The mystery of Bridget M. McCormack’s destination has been solved.

Last week, I reported that McCormack, current president and CEO of the American Arbitration Association and former chief justice of the Michigan Supreme Court, was leaving her job for an undisclosed opportunity that, as she said at the time, “I could not turn down,” teasing only that it involved “the chance to build something focused specifically on judges.”

The timing seemed telling, as I noted then. Just two weeks earlier, Clio had announced its move into developing technology for judges and its hiring of Casetext cofounder Pablo Arredondo as senior vice president, judiciary, to lead that effort. Could her announcement, so soon after, be mere coincidence?

Turns out, it was not. Today, Clio made it official, announcing that it has recruited McCormack to join the company as general manager, judiciary, “to help build the future of court technology.”

Clio’s dual hirings of McCormack and Arredondo to drive its expansion into the courts is one of those situations where one plus one adds up to a whole lot more than two.

McCormack’s track record on justice-system innovation traces back to her time as chief justice in Michigan and carries through to her tenure at the AAA, where she spearheaded its adoption of AI and its development of products such as the AI Arbitrator. (Listen: An AI Arbitrator? The Latest Innovations from the American Arbitration Association, with CEO Bridget McCormack and CTO Diana Didia.)

Arredondo, who led Casetext’s development of a strong of innovative products, including CoCounsel, the first GPT-4 AI legal assistant, first turned his attention to the challenges facing the judiciary while at Thomson Reuters, which acquired Casetext for $650 million in 2023. (Listen: Why Legal AI Pioneer Pablo Arredondo Is Joining Clio to Build Technology for the Courts.)

“The judiciary represents one of the largest opportunities to strengthen how the legal system works, and we are building for it with long term ambition,” said Jack Newton, Clio’s CEO and founder.

“Bridget understands this market at a level very few people do. She has led courts, worked across the justice system, and knows what it takes to earn the confidence of the institutions we want to serve.”

Leading Market Strategy

When McCormack begins working at Clio in October, her role will be to lead the market and commercial strategy for Clio’s judiciary business. She will report directly to Newton.

Arredondo will lead product development and strategic direction for the judicial division. He will report to Clio’s chief product officer John Foreman.

Clio’s push into developing technology for the courts comes at a critical time for the judiciary.

For decades, courts have been suffocating under the pressure of weightier and weightier caseloads and inadequate funding for the staff and technology to manage those caseloads.

Driving those caseloads has been the steady increase in the numbers of self-represented litigants (SRLs), who, according to a 2018 study, make up 72 percent of all parties in state courts – meaning only a quarter of litigants are represented by lawyers.

The advent of AI has only exacerbated that problem, providing SRLs with the tools to more easily research legal issues and prepare legal filings.

Many believe the courts are ill-prepared for the AI era and that the need for technological solutions has never been greater.

On the Michigan Supreme Court for nearly a decade, including four as chief justice, McCormack saw that pressure firsthand, Clio said in its announcement of her hiring, and that experience has helped shape her view of where AI can have the greatest impact.

“Millions of people rely on courts at moments when the stakes are highest, often without meaningful legal support,” said McCormack. “The opportunity now is to give those institutions better tools to meet that responsibility.

“If we do this well, the impact won’t be about efficiency. It will be the strengthening of the public justice system’s service to the people who depend on it, and the corresponding growth in public trust.”

news.titleEn: AI is changing legal delivery – but law firm pricing isn’t keeping up
news.titleZh: AI正在改变法律服务交付方式，但律所定价未能跟上
news.summaryZh:
BigHand最新研究显示，AI正在改变法律工作的经济模式，但近三分之二律所仍依赖传统方法定价。《2026年BigHand法律定价与预算趋势分析》基于英国和北美800多名资深法律财务专业人士的回复，发现63%的律所在为事项定价时依赖熟悉的方法。35%表示律师最常默认采用标准小时费率，28%直接照搬此前事项的定价而不作调整，仅1%表示使用现有定价或预算工具中的预制模板。

超过半数（56%）律所报告客户对AI驱动的效率或AI使用透明度需求增加，但35%表示合伙人不愿与客户讨论AI，是主动沟通该技术的最常见障碍。历史事项数据仍非常重要，但不能把先前事项当作答案而非起点；如果工作交付方式正在改变，简单沿用相同的人员配置或定价假设可能无法带来正确结果。对于AI效率带来的财务收益应由谁获取，目前仍缺乏共识：30%律所维持现有定价并利用AI效率提升盈利能力，另有30%仍在评估这些效率应如何影响未来定价，四分之一受访者表示在客户允许使用AI时提供折扣。31%报告AI带来每事项盈利能力提升，同样比例报告减少了对人工或重复性工作的依赖。客户压力还延伸至AI之外：51%律所报告财务透明度需求增加，49%报告替代费用安排需求增加。律所已投资于定价专业知识，但这些洞察并不总能传达到定价或调价时的律师手中；如果洞察在决策之后才到达，律所已失去行动机会，利润空间暴露，客户获得的确定性降低，从而挑战持续的业务关系。
news.bodyHtml:
AI is changing the economics of legal work, but nearly two-thirds of law firms still rely on traditional methods when setting prices, according to new research from BigHand.

The 2026 BigHand Legal Pricing and Budgeting Trends Analysis, based on responses from more than 800 senior legal finance professionals across the UK and North America, found that 63% of firms rely on familiar approaches when pricing matters.

Advertisement

Some 35% said lawyers most commonly default to standard hourly rates, while 28% copy pricing from a previous matter without adjusting it. Just 1% reported using pre-made templates within an existing pricing or budgeting tool.

That reliance on historic pricing models comes as AI begins to change both how legal work is delivered and what clients expect to pay for it.

Advertisement

More than half (56%) of firms reported increased client demand for AI-driven efficiencies or greater transparency around AI use. However, 35% said partner discomfort discussing AI with clients is the most common barrier to proactive conversations about the technology.

“Historical matter data is still incredibly important, but we have to be careful about using prior matters as the answer rather than as a starting point,” said Alexandra Guajardo, founder and principal of Xela Advisory, who is a leading industry voice quoted in the report.

“If the way the work is being delivered is changing, simply carrying forward the same staffing or pricing assumptions may not give us the right result.”

There is also little consensus yet over who should capture the financial benefit of AI efficiencies.

Some 30% of firms are maintaining existing pricing and using AI efficiencies to improve profitability, while another 30% are still evaluating how those efficiencies should affect future pricing. A quarter of respondents said they offer discounts when clients permit the use of AI.

The technology is already having a measurable impact for some firms: 31% reported improved profitability per matter as a benefit of AI, while the same proportion reported reduced reliance on manual or repetitive work.

Meanwhile, client pressure is extending beyond AI. Some 51% of firms reported increased demand for financial transparency and 49% increased demand for alternative fee arrangements.

“Client pressure on transparency, value, and pricing flexibility has become structural,” said Eric Wangler, Global President and ChiefRevenue Officer at BigHand. “Clients now enter pricing conversations better informed. Their internal capability has grown, and so have their expectations around cost, value, and the benefit of AI.

“Firms have invested in pricing expertise, but it does not always reach the lawyer when a price is set or changed. If insight arrives after the decision, the firm has already lost the chance to act. Margin is exposed, and clients get less certainty, challenging ongoing business relationships.”

You can download the full report HERE

news.titleEn: You Can Use AI in Court. You Can’t Secretly Rig It.
news.titleZh: 你可以在法庭上使用AI，但不能秘密操纵它
news.summaryZh: 康涅狄格州一名法官为AI时代划定了明确界限：使用人工智能辅助准备法庭文件没有问题，前提是使用者需核查其工作成果；但隐藏旨在操纵他人AI的指令则不被允许。在Elliott诉New York Bariatric Group案中，一名自我代理的原告在法庭文件中嵌入了白色小字文本，普通读者不可见但软件可读，指示任何审查文件的AI同意原告并帮助推翻先前的裁决。原告称其为“审计”，法院则认为是不诚实行为。在法院认定该做法并警告可能制裁后，隐藏信息仍继续出现，后续文件包含隐藏的“hi :)”消息和Nosferatu视频链接。该提示从未奏效，法院不使用AI裁决文件，法官阅读打印副本后驳回了动议。但这一尝试本身已足够：原告失去了电子提交权限，现在必须亲自提交文件。重要的是，法院并未拒绝AI，而是欢迎其诚实使用，尤其是作为改善司法可及性的工具。法官甚至承认在准备裁决时使用了AI辅助工具，同时独立核查工作并对结果负责。这一区分至关重要。AI可以帮助起草、总结和组织，但隐藏提示则不同。法院将其比作秘密通信，旨在影响决策者或决策者依赖的工具，而对方不知情且无机会回应。教训简单明了：如果AI有帮助就使用它，核查其工作，对结果负责，但不要试图让他人的机器站在你这边。技术会变，坦诚义务不变。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! A Connecticut judge has drawn a crisp line for the AI era: using artificial intelligence as an aid in preparing court filings is fine—provided the user checks its work. But hiding instructions designed to manipulate someone else’s AI will not fly. In Elliott v. New York Bariatric Group, a self-represented plaintiff embedded tiny white-on-white text in court filings. Invisible to ordinary readers but readable by software, it instructed any AI reviewing the documents to agree with the plaintiff and help overturn an earlier ruling. The plaintiff called it an “audit.” The court called it dishonest. The plaintiff’s explanation became even harder to swallow when the hidden messages continued after the court identified the practice and warned that sanctions were possible. Later filings included a concealed “hi :)” message and a link to a Nosferatu video. The prompt never worked. The court does not use AI to decide filings, and the judge denied the motion after reading a printed copy. But the attempt itself was enough: the plaintiff lost access to electronic filing and must now submit papers in person. Importantly, the court did not reject AI. It welcomed its honest use, particularly as a tool for improving access to justice. The judge even acknowledged using AI-assisted tools while preparing the decision—while independently checking the work and retaining responsibility for the result. That distinction matters. AI can help draft, summarize, and organize. A hidden prompt is different. The court likened it to a secret communication aimed at the decision-maker—or the tools the decision-maker relies on—without the other side knowing or having a chance to respond. The lesson is refreshingly simple: use AI if it helps. Check its work. Own the result. But don’t try to make someone else’s machine take your side. Technology changes. The duty of candor does not.

news.titleEn: Nvidia-Groq AI Deal: If It Quacks Like a Merger and Acts Like a Merger …
news.titleZh: 英伟达与Groq的AI交易：如果它像合并一样嘎嘎叫，又像合并一样行动……
news.summaryZh: 美国司法部据报正在调查英伟达与AI芯片初创公司Groq的许可交易是否规避了重大收购通常所需的反垄断审查。路透社在《纽约时报》率先报道后称交易价值约170亿美元，其他公开报道则接近200亿美元。路透社报道，英伟达宣布获得Groq芯片技术的非独家许可，聘请了包括创始人Jonathan Ross在内的多名Groq高管，随后收到司法部的正式信息请求。Groq是由前谷歌工程师创立的私营AI基础设施公司，以开发加速AI推理的语言处理单元（LPU）著称。与OpenAI、Anthropic或xAI不同，Groq主要不开发面向消费者的AI模型，而是专注于使AI系统实时向用户输出答案、图像、代码的计算层。AI系统依赖训练和推理两种计算功能：训练通过大量数据构建模型，推理则让训练好的模型投入使用。Groq竞争于推理层，其业务与快速高效大规模运行训练模型所需的芯片、服务器和软件系统相关。这支持从模型开发、训练计算和推理计算等价值链层面看待AI竞争，但各层面是否构成法律上可认知的反垄断市场需详细分析。这种分层结构在半导体、云计算、互联网和媒体等行业也有类似情况。欧洲竞争机构也对“acqui-hires”和“隐形合并”提出担忧。英伟达与Groq的安排介于类别之间：并非直接收购，而是获得技术访问权并聘请关键人员，使司法部调查更关乎交易实际效果而非标签。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The U.S. Department of Justice is reportedly investigating whether Nvidia structured its licensing transaction with AI-chip startup Groq in a way that avoided the type of antitrust review typically associated with major acquisitions. Reuters, following reporting first published by the New York Times, put the transaction value at roughly $17 billion, while other public reports placed the figure closer to $20 billion. Reuters reported that Nvidia announced a non-exclusive license to Groq’s chip technology, hired several Groq executives, including founder Jonathan Ross, and later received a formal DOJ request for information about the arrangement. The reported investigation is significant because it spotlights a broader pattern Mogin Law has been tracking in our AI Deal Table: major technology companies are increasingly pursuing AI capabilities through licensing arrangements, talent transfers, infrastructure commitments, minority investments, and strategic partnerships rather than formal mergers. Mogin Law has been tracking transactions and investments inside the AI infrastructure space: data centers, chips, cloud capacity, energy, cooling, copper, and other physical inputs needed to develop and deploy advanced AI systems. That makes Groq important not only as another AI startup, but as a company positioned in the infrastructure layer that can determine how trained AI models reach users. Groq is a privately held AI infrastructure company founded by former Google engineers and known for developing the Language Processing Unit, or LPU, a specialized chip designed to accelerate AI inference. Unlike OpenAI, Anthropic, or xAI, Groq does not primarily develop consumer-facing AI models, but focuses on the computing layer that enables AI systems to deliver answers, images, code, and other outputs to users in real time. This is an important difference. AI systems generally depend on two different compute functions: training and inference. Training is the resource-intensive process of building a model by exposing it to large amounts of data so it can recognize patterns and generate useful outputs. Inference comes later, when the trained model is put to work. Each time a user asks a chatbot a question, prompts an image generator, writes code with an AI tool, or runs an AI-powered application, the system uses compute infrastructure to apply the trained model and produce a response. Put differently, the system uses the trained model to “infer” the most likely, useful, or appropriate output. It is not thinking like a person, but it is applying learned patterns to your prompt. Groq competes in this second layer. Its business is tied to the chips, servers, and software systems needed to run trained models quickly and efficiently at scale. This supports viewing AI competition across several related layers of the value chain: model development, training compute, and inference compute. Those layers are related, and they may overlap, but they raise different competitive questions. Whether any of those layers constitute legally cognizable antitrust markets would, of course, require detailed market-definition analysis. That layered structure has analogues in other technology industries. Semiconductor markets distinguish among chip design, fabrication, packaging, and distribution. Cloud computing separates infrastructure, platforms, and software applications. Internet and media markets distinguish among content creation, distribution infrastructure, user-facing platforms, and access points. AI may develop similar layers, with competitive pressure arising not only where models are built, but also where they are trained, deployed, and delivered to users. This not just a U.S. story. Concerns about acqui-hires and “stealth mergers” have also been raised by competition agencies in Europe. The Nvidia-Groq arrangement warrants study because it sits between categories. Rather than an outright purchase, Nvidia reportedly secured access to Groq’s technology while hiring key personnel associated with the company. That makes the reported DOJ inquiry less about the transaction’s label and more about the deal’s practical effects.
news.relevanceReason: The article discusses antitrust review of an AI chip company acquisition, which is related to legal technology and AI regulation, but not primarily about legal AI products or workflows.

news.titleEn: Checkbox Launches ‘First Pass’ AI Contract Review
news.titleZh: Checkbox推出‘First Pass’AI合同审查功能
news.summaryZh: Checkbox作为面向企业的法律前台，推出First Pass，首次对合同内容进行实质性AI审查，依据企业自有操作手册评分，而非仅路由和跟踪，标志着其进入合同审查领域。该上下文感知AI代理可审查合同、发票和传入的法律请求，减少常规工作，并将需关注事项路由至正确位置，甚至可分配给法律团队中工作量最轻的人。其理念是让合同等文本输入中的数据被First Pass利用，将智能向上游移动。Checkbox不试图取代CLM，First Pass是“第一遍阅读”，当合同到达现有工具时，常规工作已完成，真正问题已被标记。此举因法律团队被大量合同、发票和请求淹没，而CLM和电子账单平台仅在事项进入系统后管理，不提前过滤或分流。今年1月，Checkbox完成2300万美元A轮融资，联合创始人兼首席产品官James Han表示，融资将推动为法律工作构建智能系统，把日常请求转化为机构专业知识，助团队更快行动、更一致并减少对外部律师依赖。
news.bodyText: Checkbox, a legal front door for corporates, has launched First Pass, marking a move into contract review – and which builds upon its platform for inhouse teams. (See AL interview with Evan Wong, CEO, below.) The company said that this new capability will entail a ‘context-aware AI agent that reviews contracts, invoices, and incoming legal requests, to reduce routine work and route what needs attention to the right place’. They added that the idea is that all the data embedded in contracts and other text-based inputs into a legal team can be harnessed by First Pass, which moves that intelligence ‘upstream’. One nifty feature that AL noted is that as requests are analysed by the AI, matters can be sent to ‘whoever has the lightest workload’ on the legal team. In terms of the details of how it will operate, they explained: It’s worth adding that in January this year they raised a Series A round of $23m. At that time, James Han, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer at Checkbox, commented: ‘The Series A funding will fuel Checkbox’s vision to build a system of intelligence for legal work, turning everyday requests into institutional expertise. This institutional expertise can then be leveraged by AI to help teams move faster, deliver more consistent work, and reduce dependency on outside counsel.’ — And now the AL interview with CEO, Evan Wong. Contract review for Checkbox is totally new? Yes, First Pass is the first time Checkbox is doing substantive AI review of contract content – scoring it against your own playbook – rather than just routing and tracking it.We’re not trying to replace anyone’s CLM. First Pass is exactly what it sounds like – the first read. By the time a contract reaches the tools legal teams already run, the routine work is done and the real questions are flagged. Why now? Legal teams are buried in contract, invoice, and request volume. CLM and e-billing platforms manage work once it’s already in the system – they don’t filter or deflect it before it reaches a lawyer. Nobody was working on the moment it arrived – partly because it’s unglamorous, partly because until recently you couldn’t automate a first read without creating more work than it saved. Both of those changed. First Pass moves that intelligence upstream.
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要介绍法律科技公司Checkbox推出的AI合同审查产品First Pass，涉及法律工作流程自动化、合同审查和内部法务团队技术，属于核心法律AI/法律科技范畴。

news.titleEn: U.S. AI Law – 2026 Midyear State Update
news.titleZh: 美国人工智能法律——2026年中期州级动态更新
news.summaryZh:
本文是“美国数据法更新”三部分系列的第二部分，聚焦州层面人工智能系统开发与部署相关立法。第一部分关注州消费者隐私法趋严，本部分审视州人工智能法如何针对人工智能最具潜在危害的用途。在州立法机构于第一、二季度持续颁布新的及修订的消费者隐私法之际，人工智能及相关立法活动在5月至8月加速。

加利福尼亚州立法机构继续在引入和颁布人工智能相关法律方面领先各州。若干以危害为重点的新人工智能法律于2026年1月1日生效。德克萨斯州负责任人工智能治理法案（TRAIGA）也于同日生效，适用于在德克萨斯州开展业务、生产供该州消费者使用的产品或服务、或在德州开发或部署人工智能系统的私营实体，但并非真正的通用人工智能法。对过于宽泛的州人工智能法影响创新的担忧始于2024年首部通用州人工智能法——科罗拉多州人工智能法——颁布之时；州长Jared Polis在签署时向立法机构表达了对新法可能阻碍该州创新的保留意见。该法已被一部范围更窄、聚焦重大自动化决策的法律取代。TRAIGA最初草案于2024年12月提出，与最初的科罗拉多州人工智能法类似。一个月后，第14179号行政命令发布，优先放松监管和促进人工智能创新，以维持美国全球主导地位。德州立法机构于2025年6月颁布TRAIGA时，其中适用于私营部门部署人工智能的部分聚焦于最有害用途。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! In this second of a three-part series on US data law updates, we cover state laws related to development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems. In Part I, we focused on the trend of more restrictive state consumer privacy laws. In this Part II, we review how state AI laws are focused on the most potentially harmful uses of AI systems. While state legislatures enacted a steady stream of new and amended consumer privacy laws during Q1 and Q2, legislative activity on AI and AI-related laws accelerated during May through August. This Part II focuses on some of the more significant developments during this period. The California legislature continues to lead the states in introducing and enacting AI related laws. Several new harm-focused AI laws entered into force on January 1, 2026, including: The Texas Responsible AI Governance Act (TRAIGA) also went into force on January 1, 2026. The TRAIGA applies to the development or deployment of an AI system by private-sector entities that conduct business in Texas, that produce a product or service used by Texas consumers, or that develop or deploy an AI system in Texas. The TRAIGA is not, however, a true general AI law (like the EU AI Act). Concerns about the effects of overly broad state AI laws on innovation started in 2024 when the first general state AI law – “Concerning Consumer Protections in Interactions with Artificial Intelligence Systems” (CO Rev Stat §§ 6-1-1701 — 6-1-1707) (Colorado AI Act) – was enacted (read our 2024 coverage here). Concurrent with signing the Colorado AI Act, Governor Jared Polis (D) expressed “reservations” to Colorado’s legislature that the new law would hamper innovation in Colorado. As discussed below, the Colorado AI Act was replaced with a law with a narrower approach focusing on consequential automated decision-making. The original draft of TRAIGA, introduced in December 2024, was like the original Colorado AI Act. A month later, Executive Order 14179 (Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence, January 23, 2025) was issued and prioritized deregulation and the promotion of AI innovation as a means of maintaining U.S. global dominance. When the Texas legislature enacted the TRAIGA in June 2025, the parts of TRAIGA that apply to private sector deployment of AI were focused on the most harmful uses of AI. In its final form, the TRAIGA prohibits an AI system that is developed or deployed: The TRAIGA does not offer a private right of action but has stiff penalties: not less than $10,000 per curable violation up to $200,000 per day for a continuing violation. The TRAIGA also offers a rebuttable presumption that an entity subject to TRAIGA used “reasonable care” to comply (§ A552.105(c)). The TRAIGA also protects a defendant from liability for an AI system when a third party uses the AI system for a prohibited purpose under TRAIGA. (§ A552.105(e)). That is, the intent in developing and distributing an AI system, not how the AI system is used or misused, is determinative. Other states also enacted targeted AI laws that went into force on January 1, 2026, including for AI likenesses (e.g., Montana’s Property Right in Use of Names, Voices, and Visual Likenesses), civil rights and employment (e.g., Amendmentto Illinois’ Human Rights Act and Consumer Protection Law), healthcare (e.g., Oregon’s HB 2748 which prohibits use of medical professional titles in the name/description of an AI system), and political advertising (e.g., Nevada AI Political Advertising Law).
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要讨论美国各州人工智能立法动态，涉及人工智能治理、合规与监管，与法律和人工智能交叉领域相关，但并非专门聚焦法律人工智能技术或法律工作流程。

news.titleEn: Law Firm Workflow Automation: From Court Docket to Case Task
news.titleZh: 律所工作流自动化：从法院案卷到案件任务
news.summaryZh:
法院和案卷数据应转化为人身伤害律所的工作流，因为截止日期不是需要留意的信息，而是由指定人员在指定日期完成的工作。当案卷条目在案件档案内转化为任务、事件和通知时，工作得以完成；否则只会被报告。人身伤害诉讼不是任务清单，而是一连串依赖关系，法院截止日期是其中一环，而非日历上的一条线。律所工作流自动化并非取代判断，而是确保下一步行动存在、被分配且可见。法律技术市场已开始反映这一点，近期发展将法院和案卷信息更直接地连接到诉讼工作流。

工作流自动化是定义案件中发生某事时应采取的行动，然后由案件管理软件按规则执行，而非依赖人员记忆。截止日期输入后，准备任务出现并带有负责人和日期；阶段变化时，下一组行动被分配；文件到达时，正确人员收到通知。这不是AI对案件做决定，而是律所一次性定义流程，软件每次以相同方式运行，判断权留给律师，记忆移至系统。案卷数据应直线连接法院与执行工作的人员，无系统间遗漏。步骤包括：监控案卷并捕获条目，将其日期和要求归档至事项而非收件箱；计算截止日期并输入案件日历，包括从法院日期倒推的内部截止日期；按规则为每项工作创建任务，各有负责人和到期日；日历事件发送给相关人员；团队在事项中查看状态。
news.bodyHtml:
Court and docket data should become workflow in a personal injury firm because a deadline is not information to be noted. It is work to be done, by named people, by a date. When a docket entry becomes a task, an event, and a notification inside the case file, the work gets done. Elsewhere, it gets reported on. 

Key takeaways 

  • PI litigation is not a task list. It is a chain of dependencies, and a court deadline is a link in that chain, not a line on a calendar. 
  • A deadline recorded somewhere other than where the work happens is a deadline someone has to remember to look for. 
  • Law firm workflow automation is not about replacing judgment. It is about making sure the next action exists, is assigned, and is visible. 
  • The test of any calendaring approach is simple: when a filing lands, does something happen, or does someone have to notice? 

Why should court and docket data become workflow in a personal injury firm? 

Because every docket entry implies work. A scheduling order sets deadlines that each need a task, an owner, and a date. An opposing filing needs a response, and a response needs research, drafting, review, and filing, each with its own deadline counted back from the court’s. Recording the docket entry is not the job. Turning it into the work it implies, inside the case where that work will be done, is the job. 

The legal technology market has started to reflect this. Recent developments have connected court and docket information more directly to litigation workflows, on the premise that a deadline and the work it triggers belong together. That premise is right, and personal injury firms, with long cases and unforgiving statutes, have more riding on it than most. 

PI litigation is not a task list. It is a chain where the demand depends on the chronology, the chronology depends on the records, and the motion depends on the deadline the court set. When the software tracking that work and the people doing it sit apart, you get status reporting instead of execution. Docket data becoming workflow is the plainest example of the alternative. 

What is law firm workflow automation? 

Law firm workflow automation is the practice of defining what should happen when something occurs in a case, then having the case management software carry it out by rule rather than relying on someone to remember. A deadline is entered, and the preparatory tasks appear with owners and dates. A stage changes, and the next set of actions is assigned. A document arrives, and the right person is notified. 

It is worth being precise about what this is and is not. It is not AI making decisions about a case. It is the firm deciding, once, how its process should run, and the software running it the same way every time. The judgment stays with the attorney. The remembering moves to the system. 

How should docket data connect to case workflow? 

In a straight line from the court to the person doing the work, with nothing falling into a gap between systems. The sequence that holds up in practice: 

  • The docket is monitored and the entry is captured, with its date and what it requires, and filed to the matter rather than to an inbox. 
  • The deadline is calculated and entered on the case calendar, including the internal deadlines counted back from the court date. 
  • Tasks are created by rule for each piece of work the deadline implies, each with an owner and a due date. 
  • Calendar events go to the people involved, so the hearing, the deposition, or the filing date is on their schedule as well as the case’s. 
  • The team sees the status in the matter: what is due, who owns it, what is done. Nobody has to ask, and nobody has to remember to check. 

Every step in that sequence happens inside the case. That is the point. The docket entry starts as court data and ends as a completed task in the matter, and it never had to cross into a separate system where it could be overlooked. 

Why should court deadlines create tasks automatically? 

Because the alternative depends on a person noticing, and people are busiest exactly when the caseload is heaviest and the noticing matters most. A deadline that only exists on a calendar is a reminder to someone to figure out what needs doing. A deadline that creates its tasks is the work already laid out, assigned, and visible before anyone had to think about it. 

The difference compounds. One missed internal deadline is a scramble. A pattern of them is a malpractice exposure. And in a PI firm, where the statute of limitations is the one deadline no amount of skill can recover from, the case for making deadlines drive work rather than merely record it is not really a technology argument. It is a risk argument. 

What it costs to keep the docket in a separate system 

The cost is invisible on any single day and constant across the year. Someone checks the docket system, then updates the calendar, then tells the paralegal, then the paralegal creates the tasks. Four handoffs between the court and the work, and each one is a place for a date to be mistyped, a task to be forgotten, or a message to sit unread. Multiply by every active case and the firm is spending real staff time on translation between systems that should have been one system. 

There is a second cost. When the docket lives apart from the case, the partner asking for status gets an answer assembled from three places by someone who had to go and look. Status reporting, in other words, instead of a case file that already knows. 

Where docket workflow lives in CloudLex 

In the matter, alongside everything else about the case. In the CloudLex ecosystem, the Platform holds the case from accident to resolution, Lexee AI works inside it, and Paralegal Services carry the structured work in the same matters, all on one case object rather than copies passed between systems. Court dates and deadlines sit on the case calendar, matter tasks carry owners and due dates, and the firm configures workflow rules so that a deadline entered in the matter generates the tasks and calendar events it requires. The team sees what is due and who owns it without leaving the case. 

For the monitoring itself, Paralegal Services provides human-led court calendar management and docket monitoring: PI specialists track filings and court dates and enter them into the matter, so the docket-to-workflow sequence starts with a person who knows what a scheduling order means for a personal injury case. From there, the workflow rules the firm has set carry the work to the right people. 

For the calendaring specifics, the court calendar and matter task pages cover the details. This blog is about why the connection matters, because a firm convinced of that will get the details right. 

 

A deadline is a promise with a date on it 

Every court deadline is a commitment the firm has made to a client, whether or not anyone said it out loud. Keeping it depends less on diligence than on design: whether the deadline lives where the work happens, whether it creates the work it implies, and whether the people responsible can see it without being told. Get the design right and diligence has something to work with. 

If you would like to see how deadlines, tasks, and calendar events connect inside one case file, schedule a demo and we will walk through the workflow end to end. 

Frequently asked questions 

Why should court deadlines automatically create tasks? 

Because a deadline implies work, and work needs an owner and a date. When a deadline entered in the case generates its tasks by rule, the preparation is laid out and assigned before anyone has to notice. When it only sits on a calendar, someone has to remember to translate it into action, and that person is busiest when it matters most. 

What is law firm workflow automation? 

Defining what should happen when something occurs in a case, then having personal injury case management software carry it out consistently by rule. A deadline creates tasks, a stage change assigns the next actions, a document arrival notifies the right person. Judgment stays with the attorney; remembering moves to the software. 

How should docket information connect to a PI case? 

The docket entry should be captured to the matter, its deadline entered on the case calendar with internal deadlines counted back, tasks created with owners and due dates, calendar events sent to the people involved, and status visible in the case. Every step inside the case file, with no handoff to a separate system. 

What is the risk of managing court deadlines in a separate system? 

Every handoff between the docket system, the calendar, and the case is a place for a date to be mistyped or a task to be forgotten. In personal injury, where the statute of limitations cannot be recovered from, that is a malpractice exposure rather than an inconvenience. 

Does workflow automation mean AI is managing the case? 

No. Workflow automation runs on rules the firm defines, applied the same way every time. It does not make decisions about the case. It makes sure the next action exists, is assigned, and is visible, which is a different thing from deciding what that action should be. 

Who monitors the docket in a PI firm using CloudLex? 

CloudLex Paralegal Services provides human-led court calendar management and docket monitoring, with PI specialists tracking filings and court dates and entering them into the matter. From there, the firm’s workflow rules generate the tasks and events the deadline requires.

Every step in that sequence happens inside the case. That is the point. The docket entry starts as court data and ends as a completed task in the matter, and it never had to cross into a separate system where it could be overlooked.

Why should court deadlines create tasks automatically?

Because the alternative depends on a person noticing, and people are busiest exactly when the caseload is heaviest and the noticing matters most. A deadline that only exists on a calendar is a reminder to someone to figure out what needs doing. A deadline that creates its tasks is the work already laid out, assigned, and visible before anyone had to think about it.

The difference compounds. One missed internal deadline is a scramble. A pattern of them is a malpractice exposure. And in a PI firm, where the statute of limitations is the one deadline no amount of skill can recover from, the case for making deadlines drive work rather than merely record it is not really a technology argument. It is a risk argument.

What it costs to keep the docket in a separate system

The cost is invisible on any single day and constant across the year. Someone checks the docket system, then updates the calendar, then tells the paralegal, then the paralegal creates the tasks. Four handoffs between the court and the work, and each one is a place for a date to be mistyped, a task to be forgotten, or a message to sit unread. Multiply by every active case and the firm is spending real staff time on translation between systems that should have been one system.

There is a second cost. When the docket lives apart from the case, the partner asking for status gets an answer assembled from three places by someone who had to go and look. Status reporting, in other words, instead of a case file that already knows.

Where docket workflow lives in CloudLex

In the matter, alongside everything else about the case. In the CloudLex ecosystem, the Platform holds the case from accident to resolution, Lexee AI works inside it, and Paralegal Services carry the structured work in the same matters, all on one case object rather than copies passed between systems. Court dates and deadlines sit on the case calendar, matter tasks carry owners and due dates, and the firm configures workflow rules so that a deadline entered in the matter generates the tasks and calendar events it requires. The team sees what is due and who owns it without leaving the case.

For the monitoring itself, Paralegal Services provides human-led court calendar management and docket monitoring: PI specialists track filings and court dates and enter them into the matter, so the docket-to-workflow sequence starts with a person who knows what a scheduling order means for a personal injury case. From there, the workflow rules the firm has set carry the work to the right people.

For the calendaring specifics, the court calendar and matter task pages cover the details. This blog is about why the connection matters, because a firm convinced of that will get the details right.

A deadline is a promise with a date on it

Every court deadline is a commitment the firm has made to a client, whether or not anyone said it out loud. Keeping it depends less on diligence than on design: whether the deadline lives where the work happens, whether it creates the work it implies, and whether the people responsible can see it without being told. Get the design right and diligence has something to work with.

If you would like to see how deadlines, tasks, and calendar events connect inside one case file, schedule a demo and we will walk through the workflow end to end.

Why should court deadlines automatically create tasks?

Because a deadline implies work, and work needs an owner and a date. When a deadline entered in the case generates its tasks by rule, the preparation is laid out and assigned before anyone has to notice. When it only sits on a calendar, someone has to remember to translate it into action, and that person is busiest when it matters most.

What is law firm workflow automation?

Defining what should happen when something occurs in a case, then having personal injury case management software carry it out consistently by rule. A deadline creates tasks, a stage change assigns the next actions, a document arrival notifies the right person. Judgment stays with the attorney; remembering moves to the software.

How should docket information connect to a PI case?

The docket entry should be captured to the matter, its deadline entered on the case calendar with internal deadlines counted back, tasks created with owners and due dates, calendar events sent to the people involved, and status visible in the case. Every step inside the case file, with no handoff to a separate system.

What is the risk of managing court deadlines in a separate system?

Every handoff between the docket system, the calendar, and the case is a place for a date to be mistyped or a task to be forgotten. In personal injury, where the statute of limitations cannot be recovered from, that is a malpractice exposure rather than an inconvenience.

Does workflow automation mean AI is managing the case?

No. Workflow automation runs on rules the firm defines, applied the same way every time. It does not make decisions about the case. It makes sure the next action exists, is assigned, and is visible, which is a different thing from deciding what that action should be.

Who monitors the docket in a PI firm using CloudLex?

CloudLex Paralegal Services provides human-led court calendar management and docket monitoring, with PI specialists tracking filings and court dates and entering them into the matter. From there, the firm’s workflow rules generate the tasks and events the deadline requires.

policy.titleEn: 最高人民法院发布人民法院网络法治典型案例
policy.titleZh: 最高人民法院发布人民法院网络法治典型案例
policy.summaryZh: 2026年9月14日至20日国家网络安全宣传周期间，最高人民法院于9月16日发布人民法院网络法治典型案例，共4件。案例涉及网络暴力情形下人格权侵害禁令适用、带货主播侵害他人人格权责任认定、搜索引擎服务提供者侵权责任认定、为跨境赌博提供网络技术支持服务的定罪量刑。案例一明确适用人格权侵害禁令应综合考量侵权行为方式、信息传播速度和范围、损害是否难以弥补及禁令措施限度等因素，长春新区人民法院裁定侵权人停止侵害，禁令有效期6个月。案例二明确带货主播受电子商务经营者委托推广商品时故意使用侵害他人人格权素材构成侵权，委托人未尽审核义务存在过失的构成共同侵权，北京互联网法院判决某文化公司赔礼道歉并赔偿12万元。案例三明确使用检索增强生成技术的搜索引擎服务提供者应承担与算法、数据优势相匹配的注意义务，对算法合规负更重证明责任，未主动上传、编辑、推荐信息且知悉侵权后及时处理的，不构成侵权，上海知识产权法院二审维持驳回全部诉讼请求。案例四明确明知跨境赌博集团仍提供软件开发、技术支持等服务的构成开设赌场共同犯罪，重庆市第五中级人民法院二审维持原判。
policy.bodyText:
网络生态治理是网络强国建设的重要任务，事关国家发展和安全，事关人民群众切身利益。习近平总书记多次强调，要健全网络生态治理长效机制，持续营造风清气正的网络空间。网络法治是网络强国建设的重要保障，司法审判是网络法治实施体系的重要方面。近年来，人民法院深入学习贯彻习近平法治思想和习近平总书记关于网络强国的重要思想，坚持为大局服务、为人民司法，依法惩治电信网络诈骗、网络暴力等违法犯罪，依法审理涉人工智能、数据权益、网络虚拟财产等新类型案件，有力保障网络空间各类主体合法权益，积极融入和促推网络空间安全综合治理，携手有关部门做实“抓前端、治未病”，提升网络领域矛盾纠纷预防化解能力，依法惩治网络违法犯罪，助力提升网络空间法治化水平。
2026年9月14日至20日是国家网络安全宣传周，本届宣传周主题为“网络安全为人民，网络安全靠人民——智能时代 网安护航”。为认真贯彻落实党中央部署要求，进一步发挥司法裁判的示范引领作用，配合做好网络安全法治宣传，9月16日，最高人民法院发布人民法院网络法治典型案例。此次发布的4件典型案例，涉及发生网络暴力时的人格权侵害禁令适用、带货主播侵害他人人格权的责任认定、搜索引擎服务提供者的侵权责任认定、为跨境赌博提供网络技术支持服务的定罪量刑等内容，彰显了人民法院依法惩治网络违法犯罪、处理涉网矛盾纠纷，维护人民群众合法权益、维护网络空间秩序、促进数字经济健康有序发展的坚定立场和工作成效。
下一步，人民法院将深入贯彻习近平法治思想和习近平总书记关于网络强国的重要思想，进一步提升涉网案件审判工作质效，结合审判实践强化网络法治调研，以严格公正司法护航网络生态治理，为网络强国、数字中国建设提供高质量司法服务和保障。

案例二：明确带货主播侵害他人人格权的责任认定规则，强化网络空间人格权益保护——李某瑾诉某文化公司网络侵权责任纠纷案
案例三：厘清搜索引擎服务提供者的侵权责任边界，平衡技术创新与权利保护——某文化公司诉某网络科技公司侵害作品信息网络传播权纠纷案
案例四：依法惩处为跨境赌博提供技术支持服务的犯罪，维护网络空间安全——黄某等人开设赌场案
【案例一】明确适用人格权侵害禁令的考量因素，及时有效遏制网络暴力——李某申请人格权侵害禁令案
【基本案情】
李某与张某、胡某均为短视频平台自媒体博主，张某、胡某的网络账号共计有超2000万粉丝。2023年7月起，张某以李某“插足”其与男友情感为由，在网络平台公开发布针对李某的侮辱、诽谤言论，并联合胡某炒作相关话题，煽动粉丝对李某实施谩骂、攻击、举报等网络暴力行为。事件发生后，李某的部分商业合作方解除与李某的合作协议。2023年10月，李某提起名誉权侵权诉讼。案件审理过程中，张某、胡某仍煽动粉丝实施上述网络暴力行为。2024年3月，李某向人民法院申请人格权侵害禁令，请求责令张某、胡某立即停止在全平台社交媒体发布、传播侵害其名誉权的内容。
【裁判结果】
吉林省长春新区人民法院经审查认为，张某、胡某对李某实施了群体性网络暴力违法行为，且在案件审理过程中仍继续实施上述网络暴力行为、扩大损害结果。张某、胡某通过直播等形式在网络上传播侵权信息，案涉信息传播速度快、波及范围广、负面影响大，已对李某造成精神损害和经济损失，不及时制止将导致李某合法权益受到难以弥补的损害，符合人格权侵害禁令的适用条件。吉林省长春新区人民法院依法裁定张某、胡某立即停止侵权行为，禁令有效期限为6个月；如违反禁令，法院将依法视情节轻重予以罚款、拘留；构成犯罪的，依法追究刑事责任。
【典型意义】
网络文明是新形势下社会文明的重要内容，是建设网络强国的重要领域。网络暴力行为传播速度快、影响范围广、损害不可逆甚至造成难以弥补的后果，严重影响社会公众安全感。民法典第九百九十七条规定了人格权侵害禁令条款，目的是及时制止人格权侵权、防止损害发生和扩大。《最高人民法院关于依法审理涉人工智能纠纷案件的意见》亦对依法适用人格权侵害禁令制度作出规范。司法实践反映，人格权侵害禁令条款的适用条件，特别是“不及时制止将使其合法权益受到难以弥补的损害”不好把握，有必要进一步细化明确适用的考量因素。本案例明确，对于网络暴力情形下适用人格权侵害禁令的审查，应当综合考量侵权行为方式、信息传播速度和范围等因素，判断是否达到需要及时制止的紧迫性标准；综合考量被侵害人格权类型、侵害行为性质、事后赔偿等救济手段是否能够充分弥补申请人的损害等因素，审查损害是否难以弥补；综合考量被侵害人格权类型、侵权行为方式以及损害范围、程度等因素，裁定采取相应禁令措施，防止超出必要限度。本案中，网络自媒体博主在社交平台、直播间侮辱诽谤他人，煽动粉丝实施网暴行为。该侵权行为具有持续性，且张某、胡某二人粉丝量超2000万，案涉侵权信息传播速度快、波及范围广，已导致李某社会评价降低、商业利益受损，制止该侵权行为具有紧迫性，如不及时制止，受害人将面临难以弥补的损害，故人民法院认为本案符合人格权侵害禁令适用条件，依法予以支持。本案的处理，有利于及时制止人格权侵害行为，防止损害后果扩大蔓延，有效遏制恶意炒作、煽动网络暴力等乱象，对规范网络言行、净化网络空间、维护网络秩序具有规范引领意义。
【案例二】明确带货主播侵害他人人格权的责任认定规则，强化网络空间人格权益保护——李某瑾诉某文化公司网络侵权责任纠纷案
【基本案情】
2024年，某文化公司为推广销售家庭育儿类图书，与某带货主播订立协议，委托带货主播制作并发布短视频为其店铺进行网络宣传。该协议约定，带货主播发布的视频侵犯第三方合法权益的，委托方某文化公司应当承担责任。随后，前述带货主播在某网络平台的个人账号发布了多个宣传视频，使用了李某瑾公开演讲、授课的视频片段，并配以与李某瑾声音在音色、语调、发音风格上高度近似的AI合成音频。用户点击宣传视频一侧的按钮，可以直接跳转至某文化公司网络店铺购买相关图书。经查，案涉视频中的相关素材并未取得李某瑾的授权，某文化公司对案涉视频的素材来源、授权材料等未进行审核。李某瑾向法院提起诉讼，请求判令某文化公司赔礼道歉、赔偿经济损失及合理开支25万元。
【裁判结果】
北京互联网法院经审理认为，案涉视频未经李某瑾同意，擅自使用李某瑾肖像并结合使用与其声纹特征高度吻合的AI合成声音，案涉行为构成对李某瑾肖像权和声音权益的侵害。某文化公司未对视频素材的来源、视频素材是否获得李某瑾授权等事项进行审核，存在未尽合理审核义务的过失，构成共同侵权。2025年7月18日，北京互联网法院判决某文化公司向李某瑾赔礼道歉、赔偿经济损失及维权合理支出12万元。宣判后，双方当事人均未提起上诉，判决已发生法律效力。
【典型意义】
强化网络空间人格权益保护，是加强网络生态治理、营造清朗网络空间的重要内容。当前，带货主播擅自使用他人肖像、AI合成声音等实施“仿冒名人带货”的商业推广行为时有发生，破坏网络生态环境，侵害他人人格权益，应当依法予以规制。本案例明确，带货主播受电子商务经营者委托，通过制作发布视频等方式进行商品推广时，故意使用侵害他人人格权等权益的素材的，构成侵权；委托人电子商务经营者对宣传推广内容未尽到法律规定或者合同约定的审核义务，对损害结果发生存在过失的，与带货主播成立共同侵权，应依法承担连带责任。本案中，某文化公司与带货主播形成委托关系，案涉协议明确了某文化公司对推广内容的审核责任和管理权限。在案涉视频明显、大量使用知名人士李某瑾肖像和高度仿真的AI合成声音，侵权风险显而易见的情况下，某文化公司未对视频素材来源、视频素材是否获得李某瑾授权等事项进行审核，存在未尽合理审核义务的过失。该过失与带货主播的侵权故意相结合，共同造成了损害后果，应当认定构成共同侵权。本案的处理，有效规制“仿冒名人带货”违法行为，依法保护网络空间人格权益，促推电子商务经营者对宣传推广内容切实履行审核义务，进一步推进网络生态治理法治化。
【案例三】厘清搜索引擎服务提供者的侵权责任边界，平衡技术创新与权利保护——某文化公司诉某网络科技公司侵害作品信息网络传播权纠纷案
【基本案情】
某网络科技公司基于某大语言模型（已通过国家网信办的生成合成类算法备案），使用检索增强生成技术（使用外部知识源对搜索结果进行补充完善，以提供精准搜索服务）开发并运营某AI搜索引擎平台。某文化公司享有《某兵》《某花》两部电视剧的信息网络传播权。2024年11月28日，某文化公司在案涉搜索引擎平台分别搜索上述两部电视剧，首位搜索结果是第三方网盘分享链接，链接提供的视频内容与两部电视剧内容一致。2024年12月5日，某文化公司向某网络科技公司提出下架搜索结果等要求，某网络科技公司当日即删除了案涉搜索结果。某文化公司向法院起诉，请求判令某网络科技公司赔偿经济损失。
【裁判结果】
上海市徐汇区人民法院经审理认为，案涉网盘分享链接侵害了某文化公司对《某兵》《某花》两部电视剧的信息网络传播权，但某网络科技公司作为某AI搜索引擎平台的网络服务提供者，未主动上传案涉侵权视频的网盘分享链接，不构成直接侵权。由于某AI搜索引擎平台展示的是源自公共互联网网页的内容，在现阶段现有技术无法自动识别侵权信息，且某网络科技公司已履行模型算法的备案义务，在获悉侵权信息后及时作出有效处理，尽到了注意义务，亦不构成帮助侵权。2025年7月1日，上海市徐汇区人民法院判决驳回某文化公司全部诉讼请求。宣判后，某文化公司不服，提起上诉。2025年12月25日，上海知识产权法院作出二审判决，驳回上诉，维持原判。
【典型意义】
人工智能、大数据等新技术新应用不断涌现，给网络生态治理带来新挑战。人民法院依法办理涉新技术应用案件，既依法规范技术应用，也尊重技术发展规律，依法支持技术迭代发展，为数智化转型提供司法保障。本案是一起厘清使用检索增强生成技术的搜索引擎服务提供者侵权责任边界的典型案例。民法典第一千一百九十七条规定：“网络服务提供者知道或者应当知道网络用户利用其网络服务侵害他人民事权益，未采取必要措施的，与该网络用户承担连带责任。”《最高人民法院关于审理侵害信息网络传播权民事纠纷案件适用法律若干问题的规定》细化了认定网络服务提供者对网络用户侵害信息网络传播权的情形是否“明知或者应知”的考量因素。与一般搜索引擎的网络服务不同，使用检索增强生成技术的搜索引擎服务的检索结果精准性、个性化更强，人民法院在适用上述法律规定认定网络服务提供者侵权责任时应当考虑技术特点、服务模式、检索结果生成过程等因素。本案例明确，搜索引擎服务提供者应当依法承担与其算法、数据优势程度相匹配的注意义务，对检索增强生成技术的算法合规负有更重的证明责任；检索信息来源于互联网，搜索引擎服务提供者未主动上传、编辑、推荐该信息，不符合明知或者应知的主观状态，且在知悉侵权信息后及时作出有效处理的，不具有侵权过错，不构成侵权。本案的处理，有利于实现著作权人、技术创新者、社会公共利益三者之间的利益平衡，推动形成支持和规范网络领域科技创新的法治环境。
【案例四】依法惩处为跨境赌博提供技术支持服务的犯罪，维护网络空间安全——黄某等人开设赌场案
【基本案情】
菲律宾某跨境赌博集团开发、运营了14个赌博网站、6个第四方支付平台，组织、招揽我国公民参与网络赌博。2016年至2020年，被告人黄某等人根据菲律宾某跨境赌博集团安排，在中国成立某软件科技公司，为该赌博集团提供技术支持服务，包括网络赌博软件开发、编写服务器代码、对服务器和域名进行管理、维护赌博平台等。经查，黄某等人违法所得共计1216万余元。
【裁判结果】
重庆市綦江区人民法院经审理认为，被告人黄某等人根据赌博犯罪集团安排，为赌博犯罪活动提供软件开发等技术支持服务，构成开设赌场罪，判处黄某等人有期徒刑五年六个月至六个月不等，并处罚金。宣判后，部分被告人提出上诉，2023年12月6日，重庆市第五中级人民法院作出二审裁定，驳回上诉，维持原判。
【典型意义】
党中央高度重视打击治理跨境赌博犯罪。当前，技术供应链降低了赌博网站开发和运营成本，跨境赌博犯罪存在网络化趋势，人民群众对此深恶痛绝。本案即为人民法院依法严惩为跨境赌博提供技术支持犯罪的典型案例。本案中，被告人黄某等人根据赌博犯罪集团安排，组建网络赌博技术供应链团队，开发架构复杂、功能齐全的软件，为跨境赌博集团运营的赌博网站、支付平台提供技术支持服务，与跨境赌博集团事先通谋并形成了较为稳定的配合关系，人民法院依法认定被告人黄某等人构成开设赌场罪。本案例明确，行为人明知是跨境赌博集团，仍根据其安排提供软件开发、技术支持等服务的，构成开设赌场的共同犯罪，彰显了人民法院全方位全链条打击跨境赌博犯罪的鲜明立场，以严格公正司法助力营造清朗网络空间。
