policy.titleZh: 肯尼亚发布新的跨境数据传输指南：概念相似，但本地差异重要
policy.summaryZh:
2026年9月8日，肯尼亚数据保护专员办公室（ODPC）发布新的《跨境数据传输指南》，就个人数据出境规则的适用提供更详细指引。指南出台之际，肯尼亚与欧盟正推进充分性认定进程，2026年6月欧盟委员会对此表示欢迎，并称“迄今评估积极”，打算尽快完成。指南在充分性、适当保障措施、约束性公司规则（BCRs）、第三国法律评估及补充保障措施等方面与欧盟《通用数据保护条例》（GDPR）相似，但在敏感个人数据、数据本地化、正当利益和后续传输等方面存在重要差异。

指南新增操作细节，包括控制者到控制者、控制者到处理者的标准条款及BCR审批流程，但不同于欧盟2021年SCCs的四个模块，仅涵盖前两种关系，并鼓励组织将条款纳入法律文书并视情况调整。标准条款要求各方在依赖前评估传输是否符合《数据保护法》和《通用条例》，考虑传输性质和目的、数据类别、接收方法律框架、可能影响合规的法律或实践（包括有法律约束力的政府访问请求）及补充措施，评估须记录并在重大情况变化时复审。为提升运营效率、服务效果和便利性而将个人数据托管在肯尼亚境外云服务器等情形，可能构成“令人信服的正当利益”，与GDPR第49条下狭窄的剩余 derogation 不同。敏感个人数据方面，《数据保护法》第49条要求境外处理须获数据主体同意并确认适当保障措施，指南要求将其明确反映在合同和传输文件中，并加强技术、组织、行政和合同保障。
policy.bodyText:
Kenya Issues New Cross-Border Data Transfer Guidance: Familiar Concepts, but Important Local Differences

By Dan Cooper , Deon Govender & Ahmed Mokdad on September 16, 2026

Posted in Cross-Border Transfers , Data Privacy , Data Transfers , International

On September 8, 2026, Kenya’s Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (“ODPC”) published new Guidance Notes for Cross-border Data Transfers (“Guidance”), providing organizations with more detailed guidance on the application of Kenya’s rules governing transfers of personal data outside the country.

The Guidance arrives at an interesting time for Kenya’s data protection framework. Kenya and the European Union are currently engaged in an adequacy process, and in June 2026 the European Commission welcomed progress in that process, noting the “positive assessment so far” and its intention to conclude the process as soon as possible. Against that backdrop, several features of the Guidance will look familiar to organizations accustomed to the EU General Data Protection Regulation (“GDPR”), including its treatment of adequacy, appropriate safeguards, Binding Corporate Rules (“BCRs”), assessments of third-country laws, and supplementary safeguards. But the comparison only goes so far. The Guidance also illustrates several important differences between Kenya’s cross-border transfer framework and the GDPR, including in relation to sensitive personal data, data localization, legitimate interests, and onward transfers. For multinational organizations seeking to use global transfer frameworks across jurisdictions, those differences are important.

An Increasingly Familiar Transfer Architecture

Kenya’s Data Protection Act, 2019 (“DPA”) and Data Protection (General) Regulations, 2021 (“General Regulations”) already establish the basic architecture for transfers outside Kenya. Before transferring personal data, a controller or processor must establish that the transfer is based on appropriate data protection safeguards, an adequacy decision, necessity, or the consent of the data subject.

That structure has obvious parallels with Chapter V of the GDPR, which similarly distinguishes between adequacy decisions, appropriate safeguards (including Standard Contractual Clauses and BCRs), and specified derogations where those mechanisms are unavailable.

The Guidance adds considerably more operational detail to the Kenyan framework. Among other things, it includes separate Standard Clauses for Legal Instruments Containing Appropriate Safeguards for controller-to-controller and controller-to-processor transfers and an application process for the approval of BCRs. There are, however, differences even at this level. The EU’s 2021 SCCs use four modules, covering controller-to-controller, controller-to-processor, processor-to-processor, and processor-to-controller transfers. The Kenyan Guidance provides clauses for the first two relationships only. In addition, while the core text of the EU SCCs generally cannot be altered if the parties wish to rely on their pre-approved status, the Kenyan Guidance encourages organizations to incorporate its clauses into their legal instruments and adapt them where necessary to the circumstances of the transfer, subject to maintaining the required level of protection.

Transfer Assessments Bring Schrems II-Type Questions into the Kenyan Framework

Perhaps the clearest point of convergence with the EU approach is the Guidance’s treatment of third-country risk.

The Kenyan Standard Clauses require the parties, before relying on them, to assess whether a transfer can be carried out consistently with the DPA and General Regulations. That assessment should consider the nature and purposes of the transfer; the categories of data and data subjects involved; the legal and regulatory framework applicable to the recipient; laws or practices that may affect the recipient’s ability to comply, including legally binding government access requests; and whether supplementary technical, organizational, or contractual measures are required. The assessment must be documented and reviewed if material circumstances change.

That approach closely resembles the transfer impact assessment that has become familiar under the GDPR following the Court of Justice’s Schrems II judgment. Clause 14 of the EU SCCs similarly requires the parties to assess whether the laws and practices of the destination country may prevent the importer from complying with the SCCs and, where necessary, to implement supplementary measures. The practical point is that the Kenyan regime is moving away from a model in which signing a transfer agreement is, by itself, the compliance exercise. Organizations relying on contractual safeguards will increasingly need to understand and document the actual transfer, the recipient environment, relevant foreign law, government access risks, and the effectiveness of supplementary measures.

A Different Approach to “Necessity” and Legitimate Interest

There is also a less obvious difference that may be important for multinational organizations.

The DPA includes within transfers based on “necessity” a transfer necessary for compelling legitimate interests pursued by the controller or processor that are not overridden by the rights and freedoms of the data subject. The Guidance goes further in illustrating how the ODPC understands this route: it states that a compelling legitimate interest may arise, for example, where an organization hosts personal data on cloud servers outside Kenya to improve operational efficiency, service effectiveness, and convenience.

That is notably different from the GDPR. Under Article 49, compelling legitimate interests provide a narrow residual transfer derogation, available only where the transfer cannot be based on adequacy or appropriate safeguards and none of the other Article 49 derogations applies. The transfer must also be non-repetitive, concern only a limited number of data subjects, and satisfy additional safeguards and notification requirements. The Kenyan Guidance therefore appears to contemplate a potentially more practical role for compelling legitimate interests in supporting international data flows than the GDPR does. Organizations should nevertheless be cautious about treating this as a general cloud-transfer exemption: the DPA requires the interest to be “compelling,” and the General Regulations require necessity to be established in the circumstances of the particular transfer.

Sensitive Data Is an Important Point of Divergence

In other respects, the Kenyan regime is more restrictive.

Section 49 of the DPA provides that sensitive personal data may be processed outside Kenya only after obtaining the data subject’s consent and confirmation of appropriate safeguards. The Guidance reinforces this position and states that the consent and safeguards requirements should be reflected expressly in the relevant contract and transfer documentation, together with enhanced technical, organizational, administrative, and contractual safeguards.

This is not the approach taken by the GDPR. Special-category data transferred outside the EEA must satisfy both the GDPR’s rules on processing special categories of data under Article 9 and the applicable Chapter V transfer requirements, but the fact that the data is special-category data does not itself require explicit consent as the transfer mechanism. Article 9 provides several possible grounds for processing special-category data, of which explicit consent is only one.

For multinational organizations, an EU-compliant transfer arrangement therefore should not simply be assumed to satisfy the Kenyan requirements where the transfer involves health, biometric, genetic, or other sensitive personal data.

Data Localization Adds Another Layer

Kenya’s data localization rules create a further distinction.

The Guidance reiterates that processing relating to specified “strategic interests of the State” is subject to localization requirements. Under the General Regulations, these categories include, among others, civil registration, elections, certain public-finance systems, basic education, and the provision of primary or secondary healthcare in Kenya. In those circumstances, personal data must be processed through a server and data center located in Kenya, or at least one serving copy must be stored in a Kenyan data center. The GDPR does not impose an equivalent general localization requirement. For businesses operating global infrastructure, this means the transfer question in Kenya cannot always be answered simply by identifying a valid transfer mechanism. Organizations first need to determine whether an applicable Kenyan localization requirement constrains the architecture of the processing itself.

Remote Access, Cloud Services, and Onward Transfers Are Squarely in Scope

The Guidance is also explicit that a transfer is not confined to physically moving a database from Kenya to another country. It describes a cross-border transfer as including the transmission, access, or making available of personal data from Kenya to a recipient outside Kenya, and expressly states that processing personal data in a cloud environment with servers outside Kenya constitutes a cross-border transfer.

This approach is broadly consistent with the direction taken by European regulators in relation to international access to personal data, but it is particularly significant for businesses that may still map transfers primarily by reference to the location of data centers.

The Guidance also takes a detailed approach to onward transfers. It contemplates prior written authorization, an assessment of the onward recipient and jurisdiction, equivalent protection, transfer documentation, and continued responsibility of the initial recipient. Particularly noteworthy is the Guidance’s statement that onward transfers for the recipient’s own purposes, including analytics, profiling, product improvement, or marketing, are strictly prohibited.

That provision may deserve particular attention from organizations using technology and AI providers, where service-provider terms may permit data, telemetry, or related information to be used for secondary purposes.

Key Takeaways from the Guidance

The Guidance does not replace the DPA or General Regulations, and organizations should be careful to distinguish between statutory requirements and the ODPC’s guidance on how those requirements should be implemented. But it provides a considerably clearer indication of the ODPC’s expectations for international transfers.

For multinational organizations, the broader message is that an existing GDPR transfer program provides a useful starting point for Kenya, but not necessarily an end point. Transfer assessments, contractual safeguards, BCRs, controls on onward transfers, and supplementary measures will all be familiar concepts. However, Kenyan requirements concerning sensitive personal data, localization, compelling legitimate interests, and the documentation of transfers need to be considered separately.

The significance of that convergence, and those remaining differences, may increase further if the ongoing EU-Kenya adequacy process is successfully concluded.

news.titleEn: The 90% Code: When AI Augmentation Turns Into Human Deletion with Sonali Sharma
news.titleZh: 90%法则：当AI增强变成人类删除——对话Sonali Sharma
news.summaryZh:
当前几乎所有行业都有数十亿美元资金涌入人工智能。董事会庆祝即时生产力提升、自动化工作流和算法效率，但在炒作之下，一场静默的危机正在形成。组织采用原本为增强人类判断而构建的AI工具，却用它们来取代人类判断；被设计用于提示不确定性的系统，被当作绝对可靠的权威。当预期回报消失或劳动力能力退化时，高管们急于归咎于算法。但问题可能不在代码，而在于治理、管理和组织设计。

本期深入探讨“对齐鸿沟”，即AI设计方式与企业实际部署方式之间的危险分歧。内容探讨组织悄然成为“智能租用者”而非真正能力拥有者时会发生什么，以及领导者必须如何在AI时代改写权力规则。
news.bodyText:
Across virtually every industry today, billions of dollars are flowing into artificial intelligence. Boardrooms are celebrating instant productivity gains, automated workflows, and algorithmic efficiency. But underneath the hype, a quiet crisis is taking hold.

We are adopting AI tools originally built to augment human judgment, only to watch organizations use them to replace it. Systems designed to signal uncertainty are being treated as infallible authorities. When expected returns evaporate or workforce capabilities degrade, executives rush to blame the algorithm. But what if the code isn’t at fault, what if it’s in our governance, management, and organizational design?

Today, we are diving deep into the “Alignment Gap”, the dangerous divide between how AI is designed and how companies actually deploy it. We’re exploring what happens when organizations quietly become “renters of intelligence” rather than owners of true capability, and how leaders must rewrite the rules of power in the AI era. Okay, let’s dive in!

news.summaryZh:
Simmons & Simmons Solutions前董事总经理Ben McGuire已加入法律科技构建工作室Purple，担任风险合伙人。Purple由ThoughtRiver前创始人Tim Pullan与前Gowling WLG律师Dom Conte创立，专注于设计并构建定制化AI法律技术解决方案以帮助创收。McGuire曾任Simmons合伙人，协助该所客户开发能力、技能和技术以打造差异化服务。

Pullan和Conte所建公司可能缺乏在律所内部运营的经验，他作为风险合伙人将帮助律所把与其共同构建的产品和服务落地到自身场景中。他将协助解答合伙人为何应关注、资金从何而来、如何支付、前景与运营模式等问题，并指出这与他近十年在Solutions所做的工作基本一致。他还会帮助律所处理如何利用节省的时间并再投资于更盈利事项等问题。当前律所日益重视利用自身知识和知识产权构建专有解决方案，但许多律所仍受困于遗留基础设施项目。可以直接利用AI等技术创收，为变革提供资金，而不必让合伙人苦等五年。他补充，当前技术的一大优势是可策展提供给生成式AI的上下文质量，无需彻底重构文档管理系统，初期可能仅限小型垂直领域，但仍能通过工程化数据提供上下文，在该垂直领域产生高质量成果，从而帮助支付其他事项。这并非全部答案，因为仍有大型基础设施项目需要完成，但应提前布局，而非被数据问题拖累两三年。
news.bodyHtml:
Ben McGuire, the former managing director of Simmons & Simmons Solutions, has joined legal tech build studio Purple as a venture partner. Purple was founded by Tim Pullan (former founder of ThoughtRiver) and Dom Conte (ex Gowling WLG lawyer), who have built a company that designs and builds custom AI-powered legal technology solutions that help generate income.

McGuire, who was also a partner at Simmons, helped the firm’s clients to develop the capabilities, skillsets and technology to build differentiated offerings.

Advertisement

Speaking to Legal IT Insider, McGuire praised the company that Pullan and Conte have built, observing: “Maybe the gap is that they haven’t run it inside a law firm. The gap I’m filling really is to be a venture partner, which essentially means helping law firms actually make products and services that they’ve built with us inside their context.”

Questions that he will help to address include “why should partners be interested in this? Where’s the money going to come from? How are you going to pay for it? What does the outlook look like? What does the operating model look like?” And he points out, “Because that’s basically what I did with Solutions for nearly a decade.” He will also be helping law firms to process questions including how to leverage time saved and reinvest it, “doing more profitable things than they were before.”

Advertisement

There has been a strong emphasis recently among law firms on leveraging their own knowledge and IP to build proprietary solutions. While many firms are still battling with legacy infrastructure projects, McGuire observes: “I think you can do more than just worry and think to yourself, ‘right, we need partners to suck it up for five years while we sort this out before we get any benefit.’ Because you can do quite a lot to generate revenue directly using AI and other technologies and approaches, which will help to significantly pay for that change.”

He adds: “One of the great things about the technology we’re using now is you can curate the quality of the context that you’re giving to generative AI. And you can make sure that it has high-quality context without completely re-engineering your document management system or making sure that everything’s in place. And it might only be in small verticals initially, but you can still engineer data and give context to generative AI, which will produce a very high quality outcome in that small vertical, which will start to help you pay for other things. It’s not the whole answer, right? Because there are some big infrastructure projects that people need to do. But why not get ahead of the loop instead of thinking ‘I’ve got this ball and chain holding me back for the next two or three years while I make sure all my data is in the right place.’”

news.summaryZh: 2026年9月15日，位于波士顿的法律研究与智能平台Descrybe宣布，Susan E. Guthrie以战略顾问身份加入公司。Guthrie拥有超过35年作为律师、调解员、教育者和法律创新者的经验，职业生涯专注于帮助法律与争议解决专业人士应对变革。她曾任美国律师协会争议解决分会主席，培训超过25000名专业人士，是四届亚马逊畅销书作者。她创建并主持全球排名前1%的播客《Divorce & Beyond》，以及《The Practice Playbook Podcast》，其播客下载量超过300万次，近期还作为专家嘉宾做客《The Oprah Podcast》。Guthrie善于预见变革并帮助法律专业人士实际应对变革，AI正在改变法律工作的地点和方式，Descrybe正在为这一新环境构建法律智能层，Guthrie对技术转变和采用的人文层面均有理解。AI已经改变了法律实践，重要的是让法律专业人士获得可自信且负责任使用的可靠法律智能。Descrybe的技术将结构化美国初级法律与引证、后续处理、争点和来源智能相结合，帮助用户研究法律问题、分析权威、理解法律如何组合、验证来源并识别无依据主张。用户可通过Descrybe平台、集成于ChatGPT、Claude、Microsoft 365 Copilot Cowork和Perplexity等领先AI助手的Descrybe Legal Engine，或通过Descrybe Open Connector在自定义AI工具和工作流中使用。Descrybe成立于2023年，已从自力更生的初创公司成长为塑造品类的法律科技公司，服务数千用户。
news.bodyHtml:
Leading attorney, mediator, educator, and legal innovation thought leader joins Descrybe.

BOSTON, Sept. 15, 2026 — Descrybe, the legal research and intelligence platform for people and AI systems, today announced that Susan E. Guthrie has joined the company as a strategic advisor.

Guthrie brings more than 35 years of experience as an attorney, mediator, educator, and legal innovator, along with a career focused on helping legal and dispute resolution professionals navigate change. A past chair of the American Bar Association Section of Dispute Resolution, she has trained more than 25,000 professionals and is a four-time Amazon bestselling author. She is the creator and host of Divorce & Beyond, a top 1% podcast globally, and host of The Practice Playbook Podcast. Her podcasts have generated more than three million downloads, and she was recently featured as an expert guest on The Oprah Podcast.

“Susan has spent her career seeing change coming and then helping legal professionals actually navigate it,” said Kara Peterson, CEO and Co-Founder of Descrybe. “That matters enormously right now. AI is changing where and how legal work gets done, and Descrybe is building the legal intelligence layer for that new environment. Susan understands both the technology shift and the human side of adoption, and that combination is incredibly valuable to us.”

Guthrie joins Descrybe at a pivotal moment for the legal profession, as generative AI moves rapidly from experimentation into everyday professional workflows. Descrybe is building the legal intelligence layer for that shift, combining structured U.S. primary law with citation, subsequent treatment, issue, and source intelligence to help people and AI systems research legal questions, analyze authority, understand how the law fits together, verify sources, and identify unsupported claims.

“The question is no longer whether AI will change legal practice. It already has,” said Guthrie. “What matters now is giving legal professionals access to reliable legal intelligence they can use confidently and responsibly. Descrybe is doing something especially important by bringing that intelligence directly into the AI tools where professionals are increasingly working, while making sophisticated legal research accessible well beyond the largest firms and institutions. I’m delighted to join Kara, Rich, and the Descrybe team as they help shape what comes next.”

Descrybe can be used directly through the Descrybe Platform, through Descrybe Legal Engine in leading AI assistants including ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft 365 Copilot Cowork, and Perplexity, or through the Descrybe Open Connector, which brings its legal research and intelligence capabilities into custom AI tools and workflows. Its technology helps users research legal questions, assess which authorities matter, review subsequent treatment, check citations and quotations, verify source material, and surface unsupported claims.

Founded in 2023, Descrybe has grown from a bootstrapped startup into a category-shaping legal technology company, serving thousands of users while helping redefine how legal intelligence is accessed, delivered, and built into the AI tools people use.

###

  

About Descrybe

Descrybe is a legal research and intelligence platform for people and AI systems. Its technology combines extensive U.S. primary-law coverage with citation, subsequent treatment, issue, and source intelligence to help users move from finding law to understanding what matters. Descrybe can be used directly through the Descrybe Platform, through Descrybe Legal Engine in leading AI assistants, and through the Descrybe Open Connector in custom AI tools and workflows. Founded on the belief that legal professionals should not have to choose between sophisticated legal technology and fair, accessible pricing, Descrybe brings powerful, reliable legal research and intelligence wherever people work.

For more information, visit Descrybe.com.

Media Contact
Kara Peterson
Co-Founder & CEO
kara@descrybe.com

news.titleEn: From AI users to builders: Akerman hires first director of AI development
news.titleZh: 从AI用户到构建者：Akerman聘请首位AI开发总监
news.summaryZh: 美国律所Akerman任命了首位AI开发总监，从德克萨斯州律所Munck Wilson Mandala聘请了Charles Zerner。Zerner最初是诉讼律师，后转向AI领域，在新职位上将负责构建定制AI应用。Akerman已是AI的重度用户，部署了Harvey、TR CoCounsel、Copilot、Claude和ChatGPT等工具，但Zerner的任务是识别现有工具无法满足或定制工具可能更有效满足需求的领域。现成产品能满足一定数量的需求，但它们是面向大量客户设计的，模型能力与利用这些模型加速法律工作的实施之间存在巨大潜力和差距。律所对AI采取“整体”方法，涵盖数据、技术和确保AI安全部署所需的治理。Zerner的任命是在Akerman于8月聘请Michael Adler担任AI治理与数据保护总监之后进行的。Akerman近年来在AI上投入巨大，这已成为律所“最重要的预算分配”之一，且相对于历史支出增长快于其他领域。他预计今年AI支出占总预算的比例将再次增加，但表示“关键不在于花多少钱，而在于怎么花”。Akerman的方法一直是先确定哪些工作流程可以应用AI，然后再确定工具，而不是先购买或构建工具再想办法应用到工作中。吸引他加入Akerman的是共同愿景，即预见律师需求并努力填补空白、解决问题。他说，自己既是诉讼律师又是AI工程师的经历意味着他从独特视角看待这一角色。Zerner于2000年联合创立了一家神经网络初创公司，自2012年以来在法律实践中部署机器学习。在上一家律所，他设计并构建了生产级法律实践AI系统，包括一个完全在律所控制下运行、基于开源模型的文档审查平台。
news.bodyHtml:
By Joanne Harris

US firm Akerman has appointed its first director of AI development, hiring Charles Zerner from Texas firm Munck Wilson Mandala.

Zerner, originally a litigator before moving into AI, takes on a new role in which he will be responsible for building custom AI applications.

Advertisement

Akerman is already a heavy user of AI, deploying tools including Harvey, TR CoCounsel, Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT, but Zerner is tasked with identifying areas where a tool does not currently exist, or where a bespoke tool may do the job more effectively.

“You have the ability to fulfil a certain number of needs with off the shelf products, but at the same time off the shelf products are designed for a large number of clients. There’s an enormous potential and an enormous gap between what models can do and the implementation of those models to accelerate legal work,” Zerner told Legal IT Insider.

Advertisement

“Part of my job is to look for those specific needs that we have that are not going to be met by existing commercial platforms, or that we can do better; part of it is the long term understanding that models are evolving fast. What do we need to build out so that we’re ready when the models are that capable?”

Akerman chief executive officer Scott Meyers said the firm’s approach to AI was “holistic”, encompassing data, technology, and the governance required to ensure AI could be deployed safely. Zerner’s appointment followed Akerman’s August hire of Michael Adler as director of AI governance & data protection.

Meyers said Akerman had been investing heavily in AI in recent years, and it was now one of the firm’s “most significant budget allocations” as well as increasing faster than other areas relative to historic spend. He added that Akerman anticipated it would continue to increase its spend on AI as a proportion of total budget again this year, although he said: “It’s less about how much you spend and more about how you spend it.”

Meyers added: “Our approach has always been rather than to buy or build a tool and then figure out how to apply it to our work, to figure out what workflows we can apply to AI and then figure out the tool.”

Zerner said he was attracted to joining Akerman by the shared vision of anticipating lawyers’ requirements and working to fill gaps and solve problems. He said his experience both as a litigator and an AI engineer meant he was approaching the role from a unique perspective.

Zerner co-founded a neural-network startup in 2000 and has deployed machine learning in legal practice since 2012. At his previous firm he designed and built production-scale AI systems for legal practice, including a document review platform built on open-source models running entirely within the firm’s control.

“You can put a lot of investment into building things that don’t serve the lawyers’ needs because they don’t match the way that they work,” Zerner added. “That’s why having someone with a foot in both worlds is so important, and that’s where you can create value.”

Zerner will be part of Akerman’s information technology team under chief information officer Azfar Shamsi.

An increasing number of major international law firms are investing in building their own solutions in addition to buying from technology companies. Among the most significant announcements, in May this year, Kirkland said it would spend $500m over the next three to four years developing custom AI tools and services.

news.titleEn: ILTA and Thomson Reuters Release Second Installment in AI Guide Series: "AI Guide for Litigators"
news.titleZh: ILTA与汤森路透发布AI指南系列第二辑：《诉讼律师AI指南》
news.summaryZh: 国际法律技术协会（ILTA）与汤森路透于2026年9月14日在芝加哥宣布发布《诉讼律师AI指南》，这是其AI白皮书系列的第二辑。该指南旨在为诉讼律师在采用AI工具时提供实用指导，涵盖发现程序、案件策略、伦理义务和风险管理等独特考量。指南汇集了来自法律行业从业者、技术专家和思想领袖的专业知识。ILTA此前于2026年6月下旬发布了首部AI基础指南。本指南是ILTA计划中五部指南的第二部，后续将涵盖交易法（目标2026年10月下旬）、监管（目标2026年12月中旬）以及公益与司法可及性（目标在EVOLVE大会前两周发布）。主要合著者包括Farella Braun + Martel法律服务总监Gillian Glass、前AmLaw 100合伙人Brendan W. Miller、King & Spalding LLP顾问Kassi Burns、汤森路透高级生成式AI解决方案工程Doug McGhee以及Perfectense负责人Leonard Lee。ILTA团队包括内容副总裁Jannise Vinson、高级教育项目经理Brian Balistreri等。汤森路透团队包括思想领导力内容与战略关系高级总监Stephen Seemer等。作为前诉讼律师，他观察到AI对话常因术语而停滞，真正的变革管理依赖于从业者与技术专家之间的翻译，他自豪于参与创建这份将AI应用分解为实用且熟悉概念的指南。ILTA服务于超过27,000名国际法律技术专业人士，自1980年成立以来，致力于为其成员和法律技术行业取得成果。

New white paper equips litigation professionals with practical guidance for responsibly integrating AI into their practice

Chicago, IL — 14 September 2026 — The International Legal Technology Association (ILTA), in partnership with Thomson Reuters, today announced the release of AI Guide for Litigators , the second installment in its ongoing white paper series exploring artificial intelligence's impact across the legal profession. The publication follows ILTA's inaugural AI Foundational Guide, released in late June 2026, and continues the organization's commitment to equipping legal professionals with practical, sector-specific AI guidance.

AI Guide for Litigators addresses the unique considerations litigators face when adopting AI tools, from discovery and case strategy to ethical obligations and risk management. The guide draws on the expertise of a cross-section of practitioners, technologists, and thought leaders from across the legal industry.

"As a former litigator now working in legal innovation and technology, I've watched AI conversations stall the moment jargon enters the room. The real work of change management lives or dies on translation between practitioners and technologists. I'm proud to have helped create this guide that breaks AI use in litigation into practical and familiar concepts legal practitioners can use to foster understanding in their work," said Brendan W. Miller, J.D. , Legal Innovation & Practice Transformation Advisor, Former AmLaw 100 Partner.

Contributing Co-Authors

Gillian Glass, Director of Legal Services, Farella Braun + Martel

Brendan W. Miller, J.D., Legal Innovation & Practice Transformation Advisor, Former AmLaw 100 Partner

Kassi Burns, Counsel, King & Spalding LLP

Doug McGhee, Advanced GenAI Solutions Engineering, Thomson Reuters

Leonard Lee, Principal, Perfectense

ILTA Team

Jannise Vinson, VP of Content

Brian Balistreri, Senior Education Programs Manager

Kelly Thomas, Editor of Content and Publications

Rebecca Christensen, Creative Director

TJ Jones, Graphic Designer

Thomson Reuters Team

Stephen Seemer, Senior Director, Thought Leadership Content and Strategic Relations

Joseph Kubes, Director, Strategic Alliances, Thomson Reuters Legal

Bryce Engelland, Enterprise Content Lead for Innovation & Technology

AI Guide for Litigators AIGuideForLitigators by Rebecca Christensen - Flipsnack is the second of five planned guides in ILTA's AI series, with upcoming installments covering transactional law (target: late October 2026), regulation (target: mid-December 2026), and pro bono and access to justice (target: two weeks before EVOLVE).

About ILTA

The International Legal Technology Association (ILTA) serves the professional needs of more than 27,000 international legal technology professionals and their organizations. Since its founding in 1980, the association's focus has been to achieve results for its membership and the legal technology profession at large. Much of the value provided by the association comes from coordinated efforts with its global volunteer membership teams.

news.summaryZh: FINRA会员公司（“会员”）以及许多会员所属的企业组织，正在迅速部署公司批准的人工智能工具供其员工使用。随着采用速度加快，可用工具（以及员工使用它们的能力和意愿）将急剧增加。绝大多数员工将正确使用人工智能技术，就像他们使用先前技术一样。政策与程序将被制定并遵循，希望可以避免对客户造成损害。然而，与任何新技术一样，公司应始终注意，人工智能可能为滥用、规避既定控制措施或意外的合规问题创造机会。适当的治理、监督和监控仍然很重要。本GT Alert的目的是识别公司可能开始遇到的、涉及员工以造成客户损害或违反公司政策与程序的方式使用人工智能的各类问题。借鉴过去二十年内部审查中观察到的 misconduct 模式，并认识到员工不当行为的既定动机，本Alert识别了公司可能的几个领域。

Explore More Job Openings HB Ad Slot Internal Reviews Covering the Use of AI by FINRA Associated Persons by: John O. Lukanski, William B. Mack, Steven M. Malina, Greenberg Traurig, LLP  - Alerts Tuesday, September 15, 2026 Mail Download />i

FINRA member firms (“Members”), and the enterprise organizations in which many sit, are moving rapidly to deploy firm-approved artificial intelligence tools for use by their employees. As adoption accelerates, the available tools (and employees’ ability and willingness to use them) will increase dramatically.

The vast majority of employees will properly utilize AI technology, just as they have prior technologies. Policies and procedures will be written and followed, and hopefully customer harm can be avoided. Nevertheless, as with any new technology, firms should remain mindful that AI may create opportunities for misuse, circumvention of established controls, or unintended compliance issues. Appropriate governance, supervision, and monitoring remain important.

The purpose of this GT Alert is to identify categories of issues that firms may begin to encounter involving their employees’ use of AI in ways that cause customer harm or violate firm policies and procedures. Drawing on misconduct patterns observed in internal reviews conducted over the past two decades, and recognizing well-established motivations for employee misconduct, this Alert identifies several areas that firms may wish to consider for review.

Misconduct of Associated Persons and the Obligation to Undertake an Internal Review

Historically, internal reviews have often involved situations in which individuals acted outside firm policies for personal benefit, convenience, or to avoid perceived adverse consequences. When material issues arise in a firm’s business, including employee misconduct, the firm has a duty to scope those issues. See generally FINRA Rule 3110. That duty includes understanding both the root cause and the extent of the misconduct, as well as any resulting customer harm. Firms also have various reporting obligations. See e.g. FINRA Rule 4530, and Forms U4 and U5. Customer remediation issues also must be considered.

Some traditional internal review topics reflecting employee misconduct have included, but certainly are not limited to:

  • Improper Loans from Customers
  • Churning and Reverse Churning
  • Unapproved Outside Business Activities and Private Securities Transactions
  • Undisclosed Outside Accounts
  • Taking Time and Price Discretion and Unauthorized Trading
  • Outright Fraud (all varieties)
  • Selling Away
  • Customer Profiling, and Account Document Completion
  • Creation, Reliance Upon, and Distribution of Unapproved Sales Literature
  • Unapproved Communications with the Public
  • Failure to Report Customer Complaints
  • Gifts and Entertainment Issues

The motivations underlying misconduct do not change simply because an employee uses AI. Employees who are inclined to act improperly may continue to seek gain or attempt to avoid adverse consequences, regardless of the tools available to them.

Ongoing Efforts to Use AI at Broker-Dealers

Over the past several months, many firms have announced the rollout of new firm-approved AI tools for their employees and customers alike. AI has been touted as an amplifier of talent, enabling higher productivity. The tools include sophisticated platforms utilizing AI agents, and other basic tools such as ones that search and summarize information and explain workflows. Of course, these tools are distinct from the AI tools that employees may access outside firm-approved ones, such as personal versions of Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and similar products.

In order to capture and identify uses of AI for Members, FINRA has provided a number of useful publications and resources. Among other things, FINRA’s website has a section dedicated to AI (Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the Securities Industry | FINRA.org), and FINRA has produced a podcast (An Evolving Landscape: Generative AI and Large Language Models in the Financial Industry | FINRA.org), and has provided a chart identifying 14 areas in which Members are utilizing AI (How-Member-Firms-Use-GenAI.pdf). Those 14 areas are:

  • Summarization and Information Extraction
  • Conversational AI & Question Answering
  • Sentiment Analysis
  • Translation
  • Content Generation & Drafting
  • Classification & Categorization
  • Workflow Automation & Process Intelligence
  • Coding
  • Query
  • Synthetic Data Generation
  • Personalization & Recommendation
  • Analysis & Pattern Recognition
  • Data Transformation
  • Modeling & Simulation

FINRA also has issued Regulatory Notice 24-09 addressing AI, and FINRA has devoted a substantial section to AI in its 2026 Annual Regulatory Oversight Report. In that report, FINRA identified “Summarization and Information Extraction” as the most common AI use among Members.

Possible AI-Related Topics for Internal Reviews

At present, AI appears to be expanding the risk of employee misconduct in four primary areas: (i) unsanctioned creation of materials (and attendant recordkeeping violations), (ii) unsupported investment advice, (iii) outright fraud and other deliberate misconduct, and (iv) unapproved communications with the public. The risks are particularly acute when an employee uses an AI tool outside the firm’s environment to create work product that the employee then utilizes to interface with firm customers. Although such outside activity may fall outside the firm’s direct line of sight, the firm maintains its obligation to supervise how its employees interact with customers.

It is also worth noting that there continues to be a fair amount of recruiting and transition of employees between firms. That activity creates an additional risk – the acceptable AI practices of the prior firm may not align with the new firm’s practices. Therefore, firms should include AI practices as part of due diligence of new recruits.

1.  Unsanctioned Creation of Materials (and attendant recordkeeping violations)

There are multiple improper reasons why employees would want to create unsanctioned materials to provide to customers. Perhaps the employee views the firm’s reporting as ineffective or imperfect, and the employee believes they can use AI to generate something better. Perhaps the intention is more nefarious. With AI, the bad behavior becomes much easier. All of the following reflects employee misbehavior pre-AI, that could be repeated with AI:

  • An employee creates account reporting for a customer to massage bad performance.
  • An employee generates account reports to conceal fraud.
  • An employee plays stock guru by producing their own research or relies upon unvetted sources.
  • An employee, dissatisfied with a firm procedure or perceiving a gap in it, creates an ad hoc form and inserts it into the firm’s process.

The use of AI also introduces additional risk scenarios. For example, what happens when an employee loads customer data into an outside AI tool? Or when an employee determines that a firm-designated workflow is inefficient and uses AI to develop an alternative process?

These issues also create books & records problems, and probable surprises in litigation and regulatory enforcement.

2.  Unsupported Investment Advice

AI heightens the risk that employees of Members will formulate and offer their own unsupported investment advice, and will base investment recommendations to customers on research that has not been reviewed or approved by the firm. Most employees will follow established firm guidance and use conventional, approved sources. However, there will always be the risk of employees who do not.

Experience indicates that when employees develop and act on unsound investment strategies of their own design, problems can also exist in the completion of customer account profiling paperwork.

3.  Outright Fraud and Other Deliberate Misconduct

Firms conducting internal reviews have encountered situations in which an employee of a Member has operated an unapproved outside business, or even solicited customer investment into a fictitious outside business or fraudulent investment scheme. Scoping is particularly important in those situations because harm in such cases is rarely limited to a single victim. AI makes it easier for employees – and third parties – to establish and operate outside businesses and to generate supporting documentation, including materials designed to appear official or firm-issued, which can then be used to solicit investments from firm customers. Those businesses may be legitimate but unapproved by the firm, or they may be part of a fraudulent scheme. Even where customer investments are not involved, the efficiency that AI provides appears to increase the risk of employees establishing or participating in unapproved outside businesses.

4.  Unapproved Communications with the Public

There is a meaningful risk that employees will use AI to create and distribute to customers retail communications that require firm approval, filing, and retention under FINRA Rule 2210. AI also makes it easier for employees to develop seminar and presentation materials. Whether such materials would satisfy FINRA’s content standards is an open question that warrants attention.

There is also concern about practices that allow an employee to use AI to autonomously generate responses to customer emails. For example, what happens when a customer email contains a complaint that the employee is not authorized to respond to independently? Employees also may attempt to use AI to generate responses that appear to come from the firm but that the firm has no knowledge of or involvement in.

*****

Firms should consider proactively evaluating how AI use within their organizations may give rise to issues requiring internal review. The pace of AI development makes early attention to these questions advisable.

news.titleEn: Generative AI Is Coming to Medical Devices. FDA Is Already Thinking About What Comes Next.
news.titleZh: 生成式AI即将进入医疗器械领域，FDA已在思考下一步
news.summaryZh: 2026年8月，FDA数字健康卓越中心发布讨论文件，探讨医疗器械监管如何应对生成式人工智能等不断变化的技术。该文件并非指南，不施加新要求，而是提出FDA认为利益相关方在将这些技术安全可靠地部署于医疗场景前需解决的问题，并公开征求制造商、临床医生、研究人员等各方意见。生成式AI与传统软件不同，能针对广泛问题生成新内容，而非从固定应答中选取；同一问题因措辞和语境不同可能得到不同回答。许多产品还依赖其他公司提供的AI技术，该技术可能在医疗器械上市后更新。这些特性有助于临床医生解读医疗信息、识别潜在问题、与患者沟通并支持临床决策，但也增加了预测产品可能遇到的所有情况、确定测试充分性以及应对第三方AI技术变化的难度。FDA的核心关切在于：能影响治疗决策的AI工具与仅提供背景信息的工具面临不同的监管问题。推荐药物剂量、建议是否寻求急诊或自行采取临床行动的工具，若输出错误可能造成更严重后果。信息接收者同样重要：医疗专业人员更有能力识别可疑回答并与其他临床信息比对，而直接使用产品的患者可能更依赖该回答。传统医疗器械测试聚焦于产品在既定条件下是否按预期运行，这一方法可能无法充分评估能产生多种不同回答的系统。

Explore More Job Openings HB Ad Slot Generative AI Is Coming to Medical Devices. FDA Is Already Thinking About What Comes Next. by: Jennifer German, Womble Bond Dickinson (US) LLP  - Law Meets Science Tuesday, September 15, 2026 Mail Download />i

Imagine a medical device that can answer questions, summarize patient records, suggest next steps, and interact with users through a conversation that feels natural. Now imagine that the device does not always provide the same response twice and may continue changing after it reaches the market through software updates.

That is the challenge FDA is beginning to confront as generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) enters healthcare. In August 2026, FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence released a discussion paper exploring how medical device oversight might address these changing technologies. The paper is not guidance and does not impose new requirements, but it highlights the issues FDA believes stakeholders will need to address before these technologies can be deployed safely and reliably in healthcare settings. FDA released the paper to solicit feedback from manufacturers, clinicians, researchers, and other interested stakeholders as it considers potential approaches to regulating these technologies.

Why Generative AI Requires a Different Regulatory Approach

Generative AI operates differently from traditional software because it can respond to a wide range of user questions and generate new content rather than drawing from a fixed set of programmed responses. People can ask the same question in different ways and receive different responses based on wording and context. Many products also rely on AI technology supplied by another company, and that technology may be updated after the medical device is released.

These features may help clinicians interpret medical information, identify potential concerns, communicate with patients, and support clinical decision-making. They also make it harder to predict every situation a product may encounter, decide how much testing is enough, and respond when the underlying AI technology supplied by a third-party provider changes.

The Growing Influence of AI in Healthcare

FDA's basic concern is straightforward: an AI tool that can influence treatment decisions presents different regulatory concerns than one that simply provides background information. A tool that recommends a medication dose, advises whether to seek emergency care, or takes a clinical action on its own may create more serious consequences if its output is incorrect.

Who receives the information also matters. A healthcare professional may be better positioned to recognize a questionable response and compare it with other clinical information. A patient using the product directly may rely more heavily on the answer.

Practical compliance action: Companies should examine what each AI feature does, who receives its output, and whether the output merely informs a decision, recommends a specific action, or acts without further review.

Rethinking How AI-Enabled Devices Are Evaluated

Medical device testing has traditionally focused on whether a product performs as expected under defined conditions. That approach may not fully address a system capable of producing many different responses.

FDA is exploring whether developers should demonstrate that an AI-enabled device can reliably perform the tasks that matter to its intended use. Testing might examine whether the device recognizes urgent situations, stays within its stated purpose, explains uncertainty, uses clinical information correctly, and performs consistently for the patients expected to use it.

FDA is also considering how companies can show that development results carry over to healthcare settings. Depending on risk, this could involve reviewing responses to past patient information, operating the device without allowing its output to affect care, obtaining clinician review, or conducting a clinical study.

Practical compliance action: Companies should define in advance how they will measure success and develop a testing strategy that reflects how the device will actually be used in clinical practice.

How to Manage Performance Across the Product Lifecycle

Testing before launch may not tell the whole story. Medical devices often receive software updates, but generative AI presents a different challenge. Updates to the AI model may change how the device responds to users, interprets information, or generates recommendations. When a device relies on AI technology supplied by a third-party provider, changes to that technology could affect the device's performance even if the manufacturer did not make the update itself. FDA is considering whether manufacturers should repeat performance testing, review samples of real-world responses, and watch for signs that a product is becoming less reliable.

Third-party AI providers add another layer of complexity. If the company that supplies the underlying AI model changes that model, the manufacturer needs a way to understand the change and evaluate whether it affects the regulated product.

Practical compliance action: Companies should define when a change or performance concern will trigger reassessment and ensure that agreements with AI providers support timely notice and access to safety-related information.

Looking Ahead

Although FDA's discussion paper does not impose new requirements, it offers a useful roadmap. Companies developing GenAI-enabled healthcare products should consider:

  • Determining whether each AI-enabled function may be regulated as a medical device.
  • Evaluating how much users may rely on AI-generated information or recommendations.
  • Building testing around the product's intended use, its level of independence, and the possible harm from an incorrect response.
  • Planning evidence that addresses both development testing and performance in realistic clinical use.
  • Strengthening oversight of third-party AI providers, software changes, and performance after launch.

The medical device in our opening example may one day help a clinician review patient records, flag information that may require attention, and evaluate potential diagnostic or treatment options. FDA's discussion paper asks how a manufacturer can show that such a tool remains safe, effective, and reliable when its answers can vary and its technology can change. Companies that begin building that evidence and oversight now will be better prepared as FDA's approach develops.

Imagine a medical device that can answer questions, summarize patient records, suggest next steps, and interact with users through a conversation that feels natural. Now imagine that the device does not always provide the same response twice and may continue changing after it reaches the market through software updates.

That is the challenge FDA is beginning to confront as generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) enters healthcare. In August 2026, FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence released a discussion paper exploring how medical device oversight might address these changing technologies. The paper is not guidance and does not impose new requirements, but it highlights the issues FDA believes stakeholders will need to address before these technologies can be deployed safely and reliably in healthcare settings. FDA released the paper to solicit feedback from manufacturers, clinicians, researchers, and other interested stakeholders as it considers potential approaches to regulating these technologies.

Why Generative AI Requires a Different Regulatory Approach

Generative AI operates differently from traditional software because it can respond to a wide range of user questions and generate new content rather than drawing from a fixed set of programmed responses. People can ask the same question in different ways and receive different responses based on wording and context. Many products also rely on AI technology supplied by another company, and that technology may be updated after the medical device is released.

These features may help clinicians interpret medical information, identify potential concerns, communicate with patients, and support clinical decision-making. They also make it harder to predict every situation a product may encounter, decide how much testing is enough, and respond when the underlying AI technology supplied by a third-party provider changes.

The Growing Influence of AI in Healthcare

FDA's basic concern is straightforward: an AI tool that can influence treatment decisions presents different regulatory concerns than one that simply provides background information. A tool that recommends a medication dose, advises whether to seek emergency care, or takes a clinical action on its own may create more serious consequences if its output is incorrect.

Who receives the information also matters. A healthcare professional may be better positioned to recognize a questionable response and compare it with other clinical information. A patient using the product directly may rely more heavily on the answer.

Practical compliance action: Companies should examine what each AI feature does, who receives its output, and whether the output merely informs a decision, recommends a specific action, or acts without further review.

Rethinking How AI-Enabled Devices Are Evaluated

Medical device testing has traditionally focused on whether a product performs as expected under defined conditions. That approach may not fully address a system capable of producing many different responses.

FDA is exploring whether developers should demonstrate that an AI-enabled device can reliably perform the tasks that matter to its intended use. Testing might examine whether the device recognizes urgent situations, stays within its stated purpose, explains uncertainty, uses clinical information correctly, and performs consistently for the patients expected to use it.

FDA is also considering how companies can show that development results carry over to healthcare settings. Depending on risk, this could involve reviewing responses to past patient information, operating the device without allowing its output to affect care, obtaining clinician review, or conducting a clinical study.

Practical compliance action: Companies should define in advance how they will measure success and develop a testing strategy that reflects how the device will actually be used in clinical practice.

How to Manage Performance Across the Product Lifecycle

Testing before launch may not tell the whole story. Medical devices often receive software updates, but generative AI presents a different challenge. Updates to the AI model may change how the device responds to users, interprets information, or generates recommendations. When a device relies on AI technology supplied by a third-party provider, changes to that technology could affect the device's performance even if the manufacturer did not make the update itself. FDA is considering whether manufacturers should repeat performance testing, review samples of real-world responses, and watch for signs that a product is becoming less reliable.

Third-party AI providers add another layer of complexity. If the company that supplies the underlying AI model changes that model, the manufacturer needs a way to understand the change and evaluate whether it affects the regulated product.

Practical compliance action: Companies should define when a change or performance concern will trigger reassessment and ensure that agreements with AI providers support timely notice and access to safety-related information.

Although FDA's discussion paper does not impose new requirements, it offers a useful roadmap. Companies developing GenAI-enabled healthcare products should consider:

Determining whether each AI-enabled function may be regulated as a medical device.

Evaluating how much users may rely on AI-generated information or recommendations.

Building testing around the product's intended use, its level of independence, and the possible harm from an incorrect response.

Planning evidence that addresses both development testing and performance in realistic clinical use.

Strengthening oversight of third-party AI providers, software changes, and performance after launch.

The medical device in our opening example may one day help a clinician review patient records, flag information that may require attention, and evaluate potential diagnostic or treatment options. FDA's discussion paper asks how a manufacturer can show that such a tool remains safe, effective, and reliable when its answers can vary and its technology can change. Companies that begin building that evidence and oversight now will be better prepared as FDA's approach develops.

ILTA Releases 2026 Legal Technology Survey Results: Revealing the Year Ahead

By

ILTA News

posted

19 hours ago

Like

(Chicago, IL) 14 September 2026 — The International Legal Technology Association (ILTA) is proud to announce the release of its most anticipated annual publication: the 2026 Legal Technology Survey Results . This year's survey offers an unparalleled view into the evolving landscape of legal technology, drawing insights from 508 law firms, representing over 139,000 lawyers and approximately 275,000 total users across the globe.

In its latest edition, ILTA's Technology Survey remains the gold standard for benchmarking technology adoption, implementation strategies, and future planning in the legal sector. From cloud migration trends to AI integration, cybersecurity priorities to document management systems, the 2026 report reveals the key decision points shaping the industry.

“This survey is more than just data, it’s a strategic compass for legal professionals navigating rapid innovation,” said Joy Heath Rush, CEO of ILTA. “Each year, we see not only what firms are doing, but why, and this year’s results show that compass pointing squarely at AI adoption and how firms are putting it to responsible, practical use.”

Access the Full Report

The 2026 Legal Technology Survey Results are available now to ILTA members and subscribers, at the same pricing and access terms as last year. To download or learn more, visit www.iltanet.org/techsurvey26 .

About ILTA

The International Legal Technology Association (ILTA) serves the professional needs of more than 26,000 international legal technology professionals and their organizations. Since its founding in 1980, the association's focus is to achieve results for our membership and the legal technology profession at large. Much of the value we provide as an association occurs through the coordinated efforts with our global volunteer membership teams.

For more information about ILTA and its initiatives, please visit www.iltanet.org .

research.titleEn: Lexplorer: Navigating the Complexity of Legal Document Landscapes
research.titleZh: Lexplorer：驾驭法律文件景观的复杂性
research.abstractEn: As technological and social innovations create novel regulatory challenges, legal systems grow in complexity - increasing the need for interfaces that enable effective interactions with legal document collections. Through interviews with legal scholars (n=15), we find that supporting legal work requires going beyond retrieval-centered legal-information-system paradigms. Hence, we propose Lexplorer, a flexible interface for exploring, navigating, and analyzing legal documents, based on a taxonomy capturing user intents. Distinguishing text and data views for one, few, and many documents, Lexplorer enables context-sensitive interactions with evolving collections of interconnected legal texts, facilitating Adaptive Meaning Construction in law. We evaluate Lexplorer with legal scholars (n=20) in the context of European Union law, validating our elicited requirements, intent taxonomy, and prototype design. Resulting from a close collaboration between visual-analytics researchers and legal scholars, our work also provides nuanced insights into the process required to design interactive systems for expert domains driven by implicit methodological knowledge.
research.abstractZh: 随着技术和社会创新带来新的监管挑战，法律体系日益复杂——这增加了对能够有效与法律文件集合进行交互的界面的需求。通过对法律学者（n=15）的访谈，我们发现支持法律工作需要的不仅仅是以检索为中心的法律信息系统范式。因此，我们提出了Lexplorer，一个基于捕捉用户意图的分类法，用于探索、导航和分析法律文件的灵活界面。Lexplorer区分了针对一个、少数和多个文件的文本和数据视图，使得与不断演变的相互关联的法律文本集合进行上下文敏感的交互成为可能，促进了法律中的自适应意义构建。我们在欧盟法律的背景下，与法律学者（n=20）一起评估了Lexplorer，验证了我们引出的需求、意图分类法和原型设计。我们的工作源于可视化分析研究人员和法律学者之间的密切合作，还提供了对设计由隐性方法论知识驱动的专家领域交互系统所需过程的细致见解。

news.summaryZh: 9月9日，Consilio宣布与Legora正式建立合作伙伴关系，协助内部法律团队和律师事务所进行实施、治理、工作流、培训与采用。Consilio以电子取证服务闻名，同时提供文件审阅、灵活法律人才和转型咨询服务，年收入达10亿美元。在正式宣布前，该公司已与Legora合作超过一年。公司将帮助内部团队和律所将Legora整合到现有事务和工作流中，并提供工作流设计以及整合、治理和培训方面的协助，以帮助团队更快、更有效地采用。公司正在组建法律和技术人才团队以满足该领域需求。18个月前还能找到同时具备法律和技术技能的人，现在很难找到，因此正在组建两者兼备的团队。Consilio使用Legora交付客户工作已超过一年，熟悉其在研究、起草和文件审阅方面的全套能力。该关系并非独家：Consilio旗下的LOD与法律AI公司Wordsmith有正式合作。能够与客户就其使用的工具开展合作很重要，若走独家路线，约三分之二的客户会不满意。他估计此类整合工作占Consilio收入不到10%，但属于增长中的业务。谈及个人AI使用，Macdonald承认，如今使用AI工具的频率可能至少是1月份的50倍，但不确定自己是否更高效。这正是Consilio寻求在组织层面为客户解决的挑战，即确保工具得到恰当嵌入。
news.bodyHtml:
By Tom Saunders

Last week (9 September) Consilio announced a formal partnership with Legora, assisting in-house legal teams and law firms with implementation, governance, workflow, training and adoption.

Advertisement

Consilio, which is best known as an eDiscovery provider, also offers services including document review, flexible legal talent, and transformation consulting services. The company, which reports annual revenues of $1bn has been working with Legora for over a year prior to the formal announcement.

Andy Macdonald, CEO of Consilio, told Legal IT Insider that Consilio will help in-house teams and law firms integrate Legora into existing matters and workflows. The company will also provide workflow design and assist with integration, governance and training to help teams adopt faster and more effectively. The company is building teams of legal and technical talent to meet demand in this space, with Macdonald commenting, “Eighteen months ago, I could get someone who had the legal and tech skills in a single body but they’re hard to find now, so we’re building teams that have a little bit of both.”

Advertisement

Consilio has also been delivering client work using Legora for over a year, so is familiar with the full suite of its capabilities across research, drafting and document review. The relationship is not exclusive: LOD, which is owned by Consilio, has a formal partnership with legal AI company Wordsmith. For Macdonald, it is important to be able to work with clients on the tools they are using, and he says: “If I were to go exclusive, I would then have probably have two-thirds of my clients who would be unhappy with me.”

Macdonald estimates that this sort of integration work accounts for less than 10% of Consilio’s revenues, but it is a part of the business that is growing. Speaking about his personal AI use, Macdonald admits: “The amount of times I use AI tools today versus January, is probably at least 50 times more, but I don’t know that I’m any more efficient.” This is exactly the challenge Consilio is looking to solve for clients at an organisational level by making sure tools are embedded properly.

news.titleEn: Which AI Product Is Most Popular Among Law Firms? Findings of ILTA’s Tech Survey May Surprise You
news.titleZh: 哪款AI产品最受律师事务所欢迎？ILTA技术调查结果可能出乎意料
news.summaryZh: 国际法律技术协会（ILTA）近期发布2026年技术调查，覆盖500多家律所，从精品所到全球巨头，涉及12个国家、14万名律师。调查显示，94%的律所正在使用或探索生成式AI工具，高于去年的80%。然而，最受欢迎的AI产品并非法律AI供应商CoCounsel、Harvey或Legora，而是微软365 Copilot，76%的律所使用。排名第二的是Thomson Reuters CoCounsel（44%）、Harvey（43%）和Anthropic的Claude（44%）并列。Legora仅16%，低于Lexis+AI（26%）、ChatGPT Enterprise（22%）、iManage（22%）和Litera One（17%）。按律所规模细分，少于50名律师的律所中，Copilot仍居首（59%），Claude（42%）和CoCounsel（40%）次之，Harvey降至22%，Legora仅6%。在700名以上律师的大型律所中，Copilot（88%）与Harvey（84%）差距缩小，Claude仍达64%，高于Legora（47%）和CoCounsel（43%）。部署方面，仅两款产品在至少半数律所中全面部署：微软Copilot（52%）和Westlaw Advantage（50%）。律所正在测试或试点的产品中，iManage的Ask iManage（80%）和NetDocuments的ndMAX App Builder（58%）领先。AI主要用途包括起草文档初稿、会议记录和摘要、法律研究以及总结长文档。安全方面，生成式AI首次进入律所三大安全挑战名单，位列第二，仅次于用户行为。完整调查共489页，涵盖战略、新兴技术、实践管理等多个领域。
news.bodyHtml:
At the recent conference of the International Legal Technology Association, the big legal AI vendors CoCounsel, Harvey and Legora had outsized presences, with ginormous booths in the exhibit hall, major-name performers at their parties, and advertising so ubiquitous it even popped up in people’s Uber apps. (See: Have We Reached ‘Peak Legal Tech?’ Sure Felt That Way At ILTACON this Week.)

So which of those is the preferred choice of law firms? Turns out, the answer is “None of the above,” at least according to the findings of the just released 2026 technology survey.

The survey spanned over 500 law firms — all ILTA members — from small boutiques to global giants, representing a dozen countries and 140,000 lawyers.

Of them, the vast majority, 94%, say they are using or exploring generative AI tools, up from 80% last year.

But when ILTA asked the firms which tool they are using or exploring, the leader by a wide margin was Microsoft 365 Copilot, used by 76% of firms.

Second place was effectively a three-way tie between two of the leading legal AI products, Thomson Reuters CoCounsel (44%) and Harvey (43%), and one non-legal general AI product, Anthropic’s Claude (44%).

Legora came in much lower in the results, at 16%, behind products such as Lexis+AI (26%), ChatGPT Enterprise (22%), iManage (22%) and Litera One (17%).

Breaking that down by firm size shows interesting patterns. Among firms of fewer than 50 lawyers, Copilot retains its top position (59%), followed again by Claude (42%) and CoCounsel (40%), but Harvey drops to 22% and Legora to 6%.

At the other end of the size spectrum, among firms of 700 or more lawyers, the gap narrows between Copilot and Harvey, with Copilot seeing usage among 88% of firms and Harvey among 84%. But even among those large firms, Claude still gets 64% of usage, ahead of Legora (47%) and CoCounsel (43%).

Deployment vs. Piloting

It is one thing for a firm to say it is using one or more of these AI products, but it is another thing entirely to consider where these firms are in their AI deployment. Here again, the survey offers some revealing data.

Only two AI products in the survey have been fully deployed by at least half of respondent firms’ lawyers: Microsoft Copilot, with 52% of firms reporting full deployment among lawyers, and Westlaw Advantage, with 50% of firms reporting full deployment.

However, here is where the survey results get a bit confusing, as the Copilot that leads in deployment is not Microsoft 365 Copilot, which is a paid product, but, as the survey puts it, “Microsoft Copilot (formerly Bing Chat),” which would appear to be the free version included in Windows. But the survey also provides results for “Microsoft Copilot for Windows.”

Microsoft’s own website lists three versions with different names than those used in the survey: Copilot Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot (Basic) and Microsoft 365 Copilot (Premium).

Setting aside that discrepancy, the more interesting findings may be those relating to which products firms are currently testing or piloting. There, the two top products are both from iManage, and only nine products were listed by more than half of firms:

  • iManage AI Enrichment (91%).
  • Ask iManage (iManage AI Assistant) (80%).
  • Claude (68%).
  • Litera One / Lito (64%).
  • NetDocuments’ ndMAX App Builder (PatternBuilder MAX) (58%).
  • Clio’s Vincent AI (56%).
  • ChatGPT (55%).
  • Legora (51%).
  • Laurel (51%).

Also of interest is how firms are using AI. Perhaps not surprisingly, the top uses, all within the 73-79% range, are the ones you would expect: creating initial drafts of documents, meeting notes and summaries, legal research, and summarizing or analyzing long or complex documents or files.

 

Even as firms are using and testing AI, they also remain concerned about it, particularly from a security standpoint.

When asked, “What are your firm’s three biggest security challenges?” gen AI made the list for the first time — and it arrived in second place. As an executive summary put it:

“This year, GenAI appeared on the survey’s tracked ‘security challenge’ list for the first time – and immediately claimed second place, outranking malware, compliance, and every legacy threat except user behavior.”

Firms’ only greater security challenge, according to the survey, is user behavior — the perennial Achilles’ heel of any IT security system.

The findings about AI are just one segment of the full ILTA survey, which, at 489 pages, spans strategy, emerging technologies, practice management, business applications, document processing, collaboration and communication, infrastructure, computer hardware and operating systems, and security.

At the recent conference of the International Legal Technology Association, the big legal AI vendors CoCounsel, Harvey and Legora had outsized presences, with ginormous booths in the exhibit hall, major-name performers at their parties, and advertising so ubiquitous it even popped up in people’s Uber apps. (See: Have We Reached ‘Peak Legal Tech?’ Sure Felt That Way At ILTACON this Week .)

So which of those is the preferred choice of law firms? Turns out, the answer is “None of the above,” at least according to the findings of the just released 2026 technology survey .

The survey spanned over 500 law firms — all ILTA members — from small boutiques to global giants, representing a dozen countries and 140,000 lawyers.

Of them, the vast majority, 94%, say they are using or exploring generative AI tools, up from 80% last year.

But when ILTA asked the firms which tool they are using or exploring, the leader by a wide margin was Microsoft 365 Copilot, used by 76% of firms.

Second place was effectively a three-way tie between two of the leading legal AI products, Thomson Reuters CoCounsel (44%) and Harvey (43%), and one non-legal general AI product, Anthropic’s Claude (44%).

Legora came in much lower in the results, at 16%, behind products such as Lexis+AI (26%), ChatGPT Enterprise (22%), iManage (22%) and Litera One (17%).

Breaking that down by firm size shows interesting patterns. Among firms of fewer than 50 lawyers, Copilot retains its top position (59%), followed again by Claude (42%) and CoCounsel (40%), but Harvey drops to 22% and Legora to 6%.

At the other end of the size spectrum, among firms of 700 or more lawyers, the gap narrows between Copilot and Harvey, with Copilot seeing usage among 88% of firms and Harvey among 84%. But even among those large firms, Claude still gets 64% of usage, ahead of Legora (47%) and CoCounsel (43%).

It is one thing for a firm to say it is using one or more of these AI products, but it is another thing entirely to consider where these firms are in their AI deployment. Here again, the survey offers some revealing data.

Only two AI products in the survey have been fully deployed by at least half of respondent firms’ lawyers: Microsoft Copilot, with 52% of firms reporting full deployment among lawyers, and Westlaw Advantage, with 50% of firms reporting full deployment.

However, here is where the survey results get a bit confusing, as the Copilot that leads in deployment is not Microsoft 365 Copilot, which is a paid product, but, as the survey puts it, “Microsoft Copilot (formerly Bing Chat),” which would appear to be the free version included in Windows. But the survey also provides results for “Microsoft Copilot for Windows.”

Microsoft’s own website lists three versions with different names than those used in the survey: Copilot Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot (Basic) and Microsoft 365 Copilot (Premium).

Setting aside that discrepancy, the more interesting findings may be those relating to which products firms are currently testing or piloting. There, the two top products are both from iManage, and only nine products were listed by more than half of firms:

Ask iManage (iManage AI Assistant) (80%).

NetDocuments’ ndMAX App Builder (PatternBuilder MAX) (58%).

Also of interest is how firms are using AI. Perhaps not surprisingly, the top uses, all within the 73-79% range, are the ones you would expect: creating initial drafts of documents, meeting notes and summaries, legal research, and summarizing or analyzing long or complex documents or files.

news.summaryZh: Patlytics联合创始人兼CEO Paul Lee在播客中介绍，该公司为知识产权打造的AI平台正改变专利生命周期，支持专利撰写、现有技术分析、审查意见答复、组合管理、诉讼准备及权利要求对照表编制等工作流程。Lee透露，Patlytics目前与约55%的Am Law 100律所及数百家科技、生物技术、制药等专利密集型行业企业合作。Lee将公司起源追溯至其风险投资家经历及与专利律师的100多次对话，这些访谈揭示了从撰写详细专利说明书到构建诉讼权利要求对照表等昂贵且劳动密集的流程。他对苹果与三星专利大战、风投支持企业的知识产权支出以及与联合创始人Arthur Jen和前Latham & Watkins专利诉讼律师Bob Steinberg的交流也促成了公司创立。在讨论与USPTO审查员相关的工作时，Lee指出质量和审查积压是专业技术的两个重点领域，并将Patlytics与Harvey、Legora等通用法律AI平台区分，认为专利专业人士需要针对IP工作精度、技术细节和专门流程设计的工具。Lee强调人类判断仍处于核心地位，专利律师拥有工作成果、批准关键决策，并在AI生成分析不足时承担责任。客户期望不断提高，要求更快、更高质量和更低成本，而律所需要可持续利润率。Lee认为固定费用安排和更可预测的工作流程是分享“AI红利”的途径，企业内部团队也能获得更多能力进行侵权分析、并购中的专利组合审查、交叉许可策略和诉讼准备。
news.bodyHtml:
Paul Lee, co-founder and CEO of Patlytics, joins Greg Lambert to explain how an AI platform built specifically for intellectual property work is changing the patent lifecycle. Patlytics supports workflows spanning patent drafting, prior art analysis, office action responses, portfolio management, litigation readiness, and claim-chart preparation. Lee reports that the company now works with roughly 55 percent of the Am Law 100 and hundreds of corporations across technology, biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, and other patent-intensive industries.

Lee traces Patlytics’ origins to his experience as a venture capitalist and more than 100 conversations with patent attorneys. Those interviews exposed a practice filled with expensive, labor-intensive processes, from drafting detailed patent specifications to constructing claim charts for litigation. His interest also grew from the Apple and Samsung patent battles, the IP expenses faced by venture-backed companies, and conversations with Patlytics co-founder Arthur Jen and former Latham & Watkins patent litigator Bob Steinberg.

The conversation turns to Patlytics’ work involving USPTO patent examiners and the broader effect of placing AI on both sides of the examination process. While confidentiality limits the details Lee discusses, he identifies quality and the examination backlog as two areas where specialized technology offers meaningful assistance. He also contrasts Patlytics with broad legal AI platforms such as Harvey and Legora, arguing that patent professionals need tools designed for the precision, technical detail, and specialized workflows of IP practice.

Human judgment stays central to Lee’s vision. Patent attorneys still own the work product, approve key decisions, and remain responsible when an AI-generated analysis falls short. At the same time, client expectations continue to rise. Clients want faster work, higher quality, and lower costs, while law firms need sustainable margins. Lee sees flat-fee arrangements and more predictable workflows as one route toward sharing the “AI dividend” between clients and their outside counsel. In-house teams also gain more capacity for infringement analysis, patent-portfolio reviews during M&A, cross-licensing strategy, and litigation preparation.

Looking ahead, Lee describes a striking change in attitude among patent professionals, from widespread skepticism a year ago to broad optimism today. His crystal-ball concern is less about whether lawyers will adopt AI and more about whether its economics will hold together. As free experimentation gives way to consumption-based pricing, firms will need to measure the value of each workflow and avoid spending $50,000 in AI costs on a $5,000 matter. Token maxing had its moment. ROI gets the next meeting invitation.
