Hi TCPAWorld!

On September 10, 2026, Governor Gavin Newsom signed a sweeping package of new laws aimed at protecting children from the perceived dangers of social media and AI products. Instead of focusing only on the content children see online, the laws also address features designed to keep users scrolling and interacting.

At the center of the package are Assembly Bill 1709, which restricts addictive social media features for users under 16, and Senate Bill 1119, known as “Adam’s Law,” which establishes extensive safety requirements for AI companion chatbots used by minors.

AB 1709 Restricts Addictive Features for Users Under 16

AB 1709 prohibits a “covered platform” from providing “addictive features” to California users under the age of 16. Those features include autoplay and personalized feeds that recommend or prioritize user-generated content based on information associated with a user or the user’s device. Users under the age of 16 may still have social media accounts, but platforms must offer them an experience without the prohibited addictive features.

Before offering an addictive feature, platforms must verify a user’s age and take reasonable measures to prevent young users from accessing those features. If a platform cannot provide an account without addictive features, it must delete the underage user’s account and the personal information associated with it.

The potential penalties are significant. A knowing violation can carry a civil penalty of up to $50,000 per affected minor, while a negligent violation can result in a penalty of up to $25,000 per affected minor.

AI Chatbots Cannot Act Like a Child’s Best Friend

California is also placing guardrails around AI companion chatbots. These chatbots are systems designed to create human-like, personal interactions with users.

Senate Bill 1119, known as “Adam’s Law,” requires covered chatbot operators to evaluate and address potential harm to children. Beginning January 1, 2027, operators must determine users’ age or apply specified child-safety protections to everyone. For minors who use companion chatbots, the law requires parental control, age-appropriate disclosures, crisis-response protocols, and default usage limits. A child’s use must generally be limited to one continuous hour and two total hours per day unless a parent changes the settings. Push notifications and persistent conversational memory must also be disabled by default.

The law also contains provisions concerning what AI companions may say to children. For example, operators are required to take reasonable measures to prevent chatbots from encouraging emotional dependence on the chatbot, using excessive praise or flattery that is disproportionate to the context, or encouraging a child user to circumvent parental controls. In other words, a chatbot cannot be designed to make a child believe that it is a person or an irreplaceable emotional confidant.

Violations may expose operators to government enforcement, civil penalties, and, in certain circumstances, lawsuits brought on behalf of children who suffer actual harm.

A New Compliance Reality for Technology Companies

These laws mark a significant change in the online child-safety debate. Regulators are paying closer attention to how online products are designed, not just what appears on them.

As California continues to regulate how social media and AI products interact with children, companies should expect increased scrutiny of the features built into their platforms.

We’ll keep you updated as these new requirements take shape. Until next time, TCPAWorld!

research.titleEn: Legislating World-Model-Based Planning with Legal Reasoning
research.titleZh: 基于世界模型的规划与法律推理的立法
research.abstractEn: As robotic systems grow more general, legal norms are needed to integrate them into society. This paper extends the isomorphism problem of aligning legal source texts with their encodings, and measures two key challenges to robot normative control: (1) the \textit{grounding isomorphism gap}, where perception error grounds false atoms for legal reasoning, and (2) the \textit{ontological isomorphism gap}, where one legal conclusion admits many faithful translations into planning constraints. The paper introduces a legal planning stack that employs Defeasible Deontic Logic (DDL) to constrain a motion planner. The stack leverages learned world models to plan and to provide legal context, enabling \textit{ex ante} governance that intervenes before an illegal action is executed. It was deployed on a simulated robot arm pushing a cube across a $3\times3$ grid. The findings were (1) the legislated agent abided substantially more often than the non-legislated one, and modeling perception uncertainty lifted abidance even further, (2) the legal reasoning ran efficiently at runtime and its verdicts were auditable, and (3) the stack adapted to exogenous signals and endogenous rule changes. Both gaps were measured: (4) world model and probe error corrupted the factual input for the DDL reasoner, and (5) a single law admitted several faithful metric interpretations yielding drastically different abidance. Thus, \textit{ex ante} legislation functions as intended, and closing these gaps with a standardized mapping from the law to runtime constraints and improved fact grounding from perception will yield robust laws that align robot behavior with society's norms.
research.abstractZh: 随着机器人系统日益通用化，需要法律规范将其融入社会。本文扩展了法律源文本与其编码对齐的同构问题，并衡量了机器人规范控制的两个关键挑战：（1）基础同构差距，即感知错误为法律推理奠定错误原子；（2）本体同构差距，即一个法律结论可允许多种忠实翻译为规划约束。本文引入了一个法律规划栈，采用可废止道义逻辑（DDL）来约束运动规划器。该栈利用学习到的世界模型进行规划并提供法律背景，从而实现事前治理，在非法行动执行前进行干预。它被部署在一个模拟机械臂上，该机械臂在3×3网格上推动一个立方体。研究发现：（1）受立法约束的智能体比未受立法约束的智能体遵守规则的比例显著更高，且对感知不确定性建模进一步提高了遵守率；（2）法律推理在运行时高效运行，其裁决可审计；（3）该栈适应外生信号和内生规则变化。两个差距均被测量：（4）世界模型和探测错误破坏了DDL推理器的事实输入；（5）单一法律允许多种忠实的度量解释，导致遵守率截然不同。因此，事前立法按预期发挥作用，通过标准化从法律到运行时约束的映射以及改进感知的事实基础来弥合这些差距，将产生稳健的法律，使机器人行为与社会规范保持一致。

research.abstractZh: 随着机器人系统变得越来越通用，需要法律规范将其融入社会。本文扩展了将法律源文本与其编码对齐的同构问题，并衡量了机器人规范控制面临的两个关键挑战：（1）基础同构差距，即感知错误为法律推理提供了错误的事实原子；（2）本体同构差距，即一个法律结论可以有许多忠实的翻译转化为规划约束。本文引入了一个法律规划栈，采用可废止道义逻辑（DDL）来约束运动规划器。该栈利用学习到的世界模型进行规划并提供法律背景，从而实现事前治理，在非法行动执行之前进行干预。它被部署在一个模拟机械臂上，该机械臂在3x3网格上推动一个立方体。研究结果如下：（1）受立法约束的智能体比未受立法约束的智能体遵守规则的比例显著更高，并且对感知不确定性进行建模进一步提高了遵守率；（2）法律推理在运行时高效运行，其裁决可审计；（3）该栈能够适应外生信号和内生规则变化。两个差距均被测量：（4）世界模型和探测错误破坏了DDL推理器的事实输入；（5）单一法律允许多种忠实的度量解释，导致遵守率差异巨大。因此，事前立法按预期发挥作用，通过标准化的法律到运行时约束的映射以及改进的感知事实基础来弥合这些差距，将产生稳健的法律，使机器人行为与社会的规范保持一致。项目页面：https://dylanwaldner-cail.github.io/Legislated-Planner/。

DOJ and Education Department Find Berkeley Law Used Race in Admissions

by Bruno Queiroz

The Justice Department and Department of Education have announced a joint finding that UC Berkeley School of Law discriminated on the basis of race in its admissions process, marking a significant federal civil-rights enforcement action in the post- Students for Fair Admissions landscape. Although the announcement is not a final court judgment, it signals how aggressively federal agencies may scrutinize admissions practices at colleges and universities following the Supreme Court’s rejection of race-conscious admissions policies.

For Berkeley Law, the immediate stakes are obvious: a federal finding of noncompliance can trigger pressure to change admissions criteria, recordkeeping, training, and internal review procedures. But the broader significance extends well beyond one law school. The move suggests that federal enforcers are willing to investigate not only formal admissions policies, but also how schools operationalize application review, diversity goals, and evaluative factors that may be seen as proxies for race.

Legally, the matter is important because it reflects the government’s interpretation and enforcement of Title VI in the wake of the Supreme Court’s recent affirmative-action rulings. Those decisions reshaped the boundaries of lawful consideration of race in higher education, but left many institutions grappling with practical questions: what admissions language is still permissible, how essay prompts should be evaluated, and whether diversity-related initiatives create litigation or enforcement risk. This finding indicates that federal agencies are prepared to answer some of those questions through investigations, not just through courtroom precedent.

For litigators, the development is a useful indicator of where future disputes may arise. Expect more administrative investigations, more challenges to admissions frameworks, and more discovery fights over internal communications, training materials, statistical analyses, and applicant-review protocols. For in-house counsel and compliance teams at universities and other educational institutions, the announcement is a reminder that post- SFFA compliance cannot stop at revising written policies. Institutions should be reviewing committee guidance, holistic review standards, data retention practices, and audit mechanisms to ensure that day-to-day admissions decisions match formal legal commitments.

The enforcement action also has implications for private plaintiffs and advocacy groups. Even without a judicial merits ruling, a federal finding can influence litigation strategy, shape settlement discussions, and invite similar complaints against peer institutions. Law schools, graduate programs, and undergraduate admissions offices should all be watching closely.

In short, this is more than a headline about one elite law school. It is a signal that the next phase of affirmative-action enforcement will likely be driven by detailed agency review of how admissions systems function in practice—and legal teams advising educational institutions should plan accordingly.

research.titleEn: Building Legal Reward Models for Grounding and Abstention
research.titleZh: 构建用于依据与弃权的法律奖励模型
research.abstractEn: Large language models are increasingly used in high-stakes domains such as law, where systems must ground their reasoning in retrieved evidence and abstain when that evidence is insufficient. However, existing reward models are largely optimised for general preferences rather than contextual grounding, limiting their ability to evaluate these behaviours in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) settings. We introduce a framework for transforming existing legal QA datasets into contextual preference data and use it to construct LegalRewardBench (LRB), a benchmark for evaluating grounded legal generation under noisy and insufficient retrieval conditions. Across general and legal contextual evaluation, we find that contextual DPO improves grounded evaluation, but performance is sensitive to preference-data construction. Length-balanced augmentation substantially improves grounded legal evaluation, with the strongest configuration combining length-balanced legal and general contextual preference data and improving performance by up to $\mathbf{+25.6}$pp over baseline. We further find evidence of cross-jurisdiction transfer: models contextually refined primarily on Victorian criminal-law data improve grounded evaluation on external US legal benchmarks, including a $\mathbf{+16.2}$pp improvement on \textsc{Housing Statute QA}. Together, these results provide a reproducible foundation for constructing and evaluating grounded legal reward models in retrieval-augmented settings.
research.abstractZh: 大型语言模型越来越多地用于法律等高风险领域，在这些领域中，系统必须将其推理建立在检索到的证据之上，并在证据不足时弃权。然而，现有的奖励模型主要针对一般偏好进行优化，而非上下文依据，限制了它们在检索增强生成（RAG）设置中评估这些行为的能力。我们引入了一个框架，将现有的法律问答数据集转化为上下文偏好数据，并利用它构建了LegalRewardBench（LRB），这是一个用于评估在噪声和不足检索条件下基于依据的法律生成的基准。在一般和法律上下文评估中，我们发现上下文DPO改善了基于依据的评估，但性能对偏好数据的构建方式敏感。长度平衡增强显著改善了基于依据的法律评估，最强的配置结合了长度平衡的法律和一般上下文偏好数据，性能比基线提升了高达+25.6个百分点。我们进一步发现了跨司法管辖区迁移的证据：主要基于维多利亚州刑法数据上下文精调的模型，在外部美国法律基准上改善了基于依据的评估，包括在Housing Statute QA上提升了+16.2个百分点。总之，这些结果为在检索增强设置中构建和评估基于依据的法律奖励模型提供了可重复的基础。

news.summaryZh:
人工智能已从研究实验室进入实战部署的国防系统，包括自主ISR平台、战场决策支持引擎、预测性后勤工具、电子战优化软件及AI目标模块。对于与国防部合作的美国企业，关键问题已不再是硬件是否受出口管制，而是算法、训练数据、模型权重、仿真环境及工程协作流程是否构成《国际武器贸易条例》（ITAR）下的“技术数据”或“国防服务”。2026年，AI驱动的国防创新与原本为导弹、图纸和物理部件设计的监管结构发生碰撞，法律风险包括民事处罚、刑事责任、取消资格、声誉损害及并行制裁风险。

ITAR由美国国务院国防贸易管制局（DDTC）管理，管制美国军火清单（USML）所列国防物品及直接相关的技术数据。AI带来三类分类问题：AI模型本身是否为国防物品；源代码、模型架构或训练数据是否构成技术数据；训练或集成协作是否构成国防服务。若AI系统专为USML所列国防物品设计、开发、配置、改装或集成到受控武器平台，相关模型产物本身可能构成受控技术数据。自主无人机、巡飞弹、ISR系统及无人地面车辆通常属于USML第四、八、十二类等。若AI实现目标识别、武器制导、自主打击授权逻辑或电子战对抗优化，该AI层不太可能被视为可与国防物品商业分离。AI目标引擎若实质性贡献武器部署能力，可能构成ITAR受控技术数据；向外国人提供设计、优化、故障排除或集成协助，即使无正式文件传输，也可能构成国防服务。

Executive Summary

Artificial intelligence has moved from research laboratories into deployed defense systems: autonomous ISR platforms, battlefield decision-support engines, predictive logistics tools, electronic-warfare optimization software, and AI-enabled targeting modules.

For U.S. companies operating in this field, particularly startups collaborating with the Department of Defense, the key question is no longer whether hardware is export-controlled. The more complex inquiry is whether algorithms, training data, model weights, simulation environments, and engineering collaboration workflows constitute “technical data” or “defense services” under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (“ITAR”).

In 2026, AI-driven defense innovation is colliding with a regulatory structure originally designed for missiles, schematics, and physical components. The resulting legal exposure may include civil penalties, criminal liability, debarment, reputational harm, and parallel sanctions risk.

This article examines how AI-enabled defense technologies trigger ITAR jurisdiction, where enforcement exposure is emerging, and how companies should structure compliance frameworks in this evolving environment.

I. The ITAR Framework Applied to Artificial Intelligence

ITAR, administered by the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) within the U.S. Department of State, regulates:

  • Defense articles listed on the U.S. Munitions List (USML)
  • Technical data directly related to defense articles
  • Defense services

Historically, export-control analysis centered on tangible hardware: aircraft, missiles, armored vehicles, and avionics. AI disrupts this paradigm by introducing three recurring classification questions:

  1. Is the AI model itself a defense article?
  2. Does source code, model architecture, or training data constitute “technical data”?
  3. Does collaboration in training or integration constitute a “defense service”?

The analysis no longer focuses solely on physical exports. It turns on whether AI functionality enhances combat capability or supports USML-controlled systems.

II. When AI Becomes “Technical Data”

ITAR defines “technical data” broadly to include information required for the design, development, production, manufacture, assembly, operation, repair, testing, maintenance, or modification of defense articles.

In the AI context, this may include:


Practical Regulatory Reality

If an AI system is:

  • Specially designed, developed, configured, adapted, or modified for a USML-listed defense article; or
  • Integrated into controlled weapons platforms;

then associated model artifacts may themselves constitute controlled technical data.

A persistent misconception is that “software is not hardware.” Under ITAR, that distinction is irrelevant. Code may be export-controlled to the same degree as a physical weapons platform.

III. Autonomous Systems and USML Exposure

Autonomous drones, loitering munitions, ISR systems, and unmanned ground vehicles commonly fall within USML Categories IV, VIII, XII, or related categories depending on capability.

If AI enables:

  • Target identification
  • Weapons guidance
  • Autonomous strike authorization logic
  • Electronic-warfare countermeasure optimization

the AI layer is unlikely to be considered commercially separable from the defense article.

DDTC evaluations frequently turn on whether the AI functionality is:

  • Uniquely military in purpose
  • Optimized for battlefield deployment
  • Architecturally embedded at the systems level

The deeper the integration into weapons functionality, the stronger the ITAR nexus.

IV. Targeting Algorithms and Defense-Service Exposure

AI-driven targeting engines present heightened compliance risk.

Such systems may:

  • Fuse multi-sensor intelligence
  • Prioritize and rank potential targets
  • Recommend engagement options
  • Optimize strike parameters in real time

If the algorithm materially contributes to weapons deployment capability, it may qualify as ITAR-controlled technical data.

Additionally, furnishing assistance to foreign persons in designing, optimizing, troubleshooting, or integrating such targeting systems may constitute a defense service under ITAR even in the absence of a formal file transfer.

Virtual meetings, whiteboard sessions, and advisory guidance may carry export implications.

V. Cloud Computing, Git Repositories, and Deemed Exports

Modern AI development environments introduce structural compliance vulnerabilities, including:

  • Distributed cloud-based compute
  • Globally dispersed engineering teams
  • Foreign-national software developers
  • Git-based version-control access
  • Cross-border DevOps pipelines

Deemed Export Risk

ITAR treats disclosure of controlled technical data to a foreign person within the United States as a “deemed export.”

This may include:

  • Repository access granted to foreign-national engineers
  • Debugging sessions involving controlled code
  • Zoom-based system design discussions

Lawful immigration status does not eliminate deemed export exposure. Access controls, not employment classification, determine regulatory outcomes.

VI. AI Training Data: A High-Risk Blind Spot

Training datasets derived from controlled defense systems present a growing compliance exposure.

If a dataset:

  • Reflects performance specifications of U.S. Munitions List systems;
  • Encodes operational thresholds or targeting parameters;
  • Incorporates simulation outputs based on controlled mission scenarios;

it may constitute technical data subject to ITAR.

Classification is driven by informational content—not file type.

VII. ITAR vs. EAR Jurisdictional Analysis

Not all military-adjacent AI falls under ITAR.

Export jurisdiction depends on whether technology is:

  • Enumerated on the U.S. Munitions List (ITAR), or
  • Controlled under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), administered by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS).

Dual-use AI systems, such as predictive maintenance engines or satellite-image analytics tools, may fall under EAR rather than ITAR.

However, when AI is specially designed or modified for combat systems or integrated into weapons platforms, ITAR jurisdiction becomes more likely.

Commodity Jurisdiction (CJ) requests remain essential where ambiguity exists.

VIII. Enforcement Convergence and Parallel Risk

ITAR enforcement increasingly intersects with:

  • Criminal export investigations
  • Actions coordinated with the U.S. Department of Justice
  • Sanctions-based scrutiny administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control
  • National-security procurement reviews

Regulatory exposure frequently involves:

  • Unauthorized defense services
  • Technical-data exports without license
  • Misclassification
  • Inadequate technology control plans
  • Governance failures

For venture-backed defense startups, even informal inquiry may materially affect funding, M&A transactions, and government-contract eligibility.

IX. Recommended Compliance Architecture for AI Defense Companies

We recommend structured, proactive compliance measures, including:


Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Can AI source code be controlled under ITAR?

Yes. If it is specially designed or modified for a USML defense article, it may constitute controlled technical data.

Are AI model weights export-controlled?

They may be, if they reflect controlled system characteristics or operational capabilities.

Can granting Git repository access trigger an export?

Yes. Providing foreign persons access to controlled code may constitute a deemed export.

What constitutes a “defense service” in AI development?

Providing training, consulting, optimization, or integration assistance involving controlled defense articles may qualify, even absent data transfer.

Does a Department of Defense contract eliminate ITAR risk?

No. Government contracting status does not substitute for export authorization or compliance obligations.

Is open-source AI automatically exempt?

No. The public-domain exception is narrow and fact-specific. Improper disclosure may itself constitute a violation.

Conclusion

AI-enabled defense technologies fundamentally reshape export-control exposure.

Under ITAR:

  • Code can be technical data.
  • Consulting can be a defense service.
  • Remote collaboration can trigger deemed exports.
  • Cloud architecture can create licensing obligations.

Organizations operating at the intersection of artificial intelligence and national security must integrate export-control analysis at the earliest stages of product development.

For companies developing autonomous systems, targeting algorithms, or other military AI applications, export compliance is no longer peripheral –– it is structural.

Artificial intelligence has moved from research laboratories into deployed defense systems: autonomous ISR platforms, battlefield decision-support engines, predictive logistics tools, electronic-warfare optimization software, and AI-enabled targeting modules.

For U.S. companies operating in this field, particularly startups collaborating with the Department of Defense, the key question is no longer whether hardware is export-controlled. The more complex inquiry is whether algorithms, training data, model weights, simulation environments, and engineering collaboration workflows constitute “technical data” or “defense services” under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (“ITAR”).

In 2026, AI-driven defense innovation is colliding with a regulatory structure originally designed for missiles, schematics, and physical components. The resulting legal exposure may include civil penalties, criminal liability, debarment, reputational harm, and parallel sanctions risk.

This article examines how AI-enabled defense technologies trigger ITAR jurisdiction, where enforcement exposure is emerging, and how companies should structure compliance frameworks in this evolving environment.

I. The ITAR Framework Applied to Artificial Intelligence

ITAR, administered by the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) within the U.S. Department of State, regulates:

Defense articles listed on the U.S. Munitions List (USML)

Technical data directly related to defense articles

Historically, export-control analysis centered on tangible hardware: aircraft, missiles, armored vehicles, and avionics. AI disrupts this paradigm by introducing three recurring classification questions:

Is the AI model itself a defense article?

Does source code, model architecture, or training data constitute “technical data”?

Does collaboration in training or integration constitute a “defense service”?

The analysis no longer focuses solely on physical exports. It turns on whether AI functionality enhances combat capability or supports USML-controlled systems.

II. When AI Becomes “Technical Data”

ITAR defines “technical data” broadly to include information required for the design, development, production, manufacture, assembly, operation, repair, testing, maintenance, or modification of defense articles.

In the AI context, this may include:

Practical Regulatory Reality If an AI system is: Specially designed, developed, configured, adapted, or modified for a USML-listed defense article; or Integrated into controlled weapons platforms; then associated model artifacts may themselves constitute controlled technical data. A persistent misconception is that “software is not hardware.” Under ITAR, that distinction is irrelevant. Code may be export-controlled to the same degree as a physical weapons platform. III. Autonomous Systems and USML Exposure Autonomous drones, loitering munitions, ISR systems, and unmanned ground vehicles commonly fall within USML Categories IV, VIII, XII, or related categories depending on capability. If AI enables: Target identification Weapons guidance Autonomous strike authorization logic Electronic-warfare countermeasure optimization the AI layer is unlikely to be considered commercially separable from the defense article. DDTC evaluations frequently turn on whether the AI functionality is: Uniquely military in purpose Optimized for battlefield deployment Architecturally embedded at the systems level The deeper the integration into weapons functionality, the stronger the ITAR nexus. IV. Targeting Algorithms and Defense-Service Exposure AI-driven targeting engines present heightened compliance risk. Such systems may: Fuse multi-sensor intelligence Prioritize and rank potential targets Recommend engagement options Optimize strike parameters in real time If the algorithm materially contributes to weapons deployment capability, it may qualify as ITAR-controlled technical data. Additionally, furnishing assistance to foreign persons in designing, optimizing, troubleshooting, or integrating such targeting systems may constitute a defense service under ITAR even in the absence of a formal file transfer. Virtual meetings, whiteboard sessions, and advisory guidance may carry export implications. V. Cloud Computing, Git Repositories, and Deemed Exports Modern AI development environments introduce structural compliance vulnerabilities, including: Distributed cloud-based compute Globally dispersed engineering teams Foreign-national software developers Git-based version-control access Cross-border DevOps pipelines Deemed Export Risk ITAR treats disclosure of controlled technical data to a foreign person within the United States as a “deemed export.” This may include: Repository access granted to foreign-national engineers Debugging sessions involving controlled code Zoom-based system design discussions Lawful immigration status does not eliminate deemed export exposure. Access controls, not employment classification, determine regulatory outcomes. VI. AI Training Data: A High-Risk Blind Spot Training datasets derived from controlled defense systems present a growing compliance exposure. If a dataset: Reflects performance specifications of U.S. Munitions List systems; Encodes operational thresholds or targeting parameters; Incorporates simulation outputs based on controlled mission scenarios; it may constitute technical data subject to ITAR. Classification is driven by informational content—not file type. VII. ITAR vs. EAR Jurisdictional Analysis Not all military-adjacent AI falls under ITAR. Export jurisdiction depends on whether technology is: Enumerated on the U.S. Munitions List (ITAR), or Controlled under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), administered by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS). Dual-use AI systems, such as predictive maintenance engines or satellite-image analytics tools, may fall under EAR rather than ITAR. However, when AI is specially designed or modified for combat systems or integrated into weapons platforms, ITAR jurisdiction becomes more likely. Commodity Jurisdiction (CJ) requests remain essential where ambiguity exists. VIII. Enforcement Convergence and Parallel Risk ITAR enforcement increasingly intersects with: Criminal export investigations Actions coordinated with the U.S. Department of Justice Sanctions-based scrutiny administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control National-security procurement reviews Regulatory exposure frequently involves: Unauthorized defense services Technical-data exports without license Misclassification Inadequate technology control plans Governance failures For venture-backed defense startups, even informal inquiry may materially affect funding, M&A transactions, and government-contract eligibility. IX. Recommended Compliance Architecture for AI Defense Companies We recommend structured, proactive compliance measures, including: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) Can AI source code be controlled under ITAR? Yes. If it is specially designed or modified for a USML defense article, it may constitute controlled technical data. Are AI model weights export-controlled? They may be, if they reflect controlled system characteristics or operational capabilities. Can granting Git repository access trigger an export? Yes. Providing foreign persons access to controlled code may constitute a deemed export. What constitutes a “defense service” in AI development? Providing training, consulting, optimization, or integration assistance involving controlled defense articles may qualify, even absent data transfer. Does a Department of Defense contract eliminate ITAR risk? No. Government contracting status does not substitute for export authorization or compliance obligations. Is open-source AI automatically exempt? No. The public-domain exception is narrow and fact-specific. Improper disclosure may itself constitute a violation. Conclusion AI-enabled defense technologies fundamentally reshape export-control exposure. Under ITAR: Code can be technical data. Consulting can be a defense service. Remote collaboration can trigger deemed exports. Cloud architecture can create licensing obligations. Organizations operating at the intersection of artificial intelligence and national security must integrate export-control analysis at the earliest stages of product development. For companies developing autonomous systems, targeting algorithms, or other military AI applications, export compliance is no longer peripheral –– it is structural.

news.titleEn: Xapien raises $56m funding round
news.titleZh: Xapien完成5600万美元融资
news.summaryZh: 总部位于伦敦的人工智能原生尽职调查平台Xapien宣布完成一轮5600万美元的投资，由专注于风险与合规技术（包括World-Check和Verafin）的增长股权公司Spectrum Equity领投，现有投资者YFM Equity Partners也参与了本轮融资。这笔增长投资将用于拓展Xapien在美国的业务，该公司目前已有50%的收入来自美国市场，计划扩大波士顿办公室，并将首席执行官及其他高管迁至美国。Xapien上一轮融资为2024年的800万美元A轮融资。Xapien成立于2018年，由Dan Secretan和Shaun O'Mahony与2022年加入的首席执行官Chris Green共同创立，三人均曾任职于BAE Systems的金融犯罪和国家安全部门。该公司服务于跨国公司、律师事务所、私人银行以及领先的大学和非营利组织，并为领先的专业服务公司提供自动化支持。Xapien已实现快速市场采用，目前有15个国家的350个客户和合作伙伴使用其平台来提升尽职调查能力，代表性客户包括Greenberg Traurig、ABB、Dow Jones Risk & Compliance和KPMG。第三方尽职调查二十年来一直顽固地依赖人工操作，企业不得不将审查限制在少数关系上，并在入职时进行一次性检查，这使它们面临巨大风险。这笔资金将使Xapien能够为合规、法律和采购团队提供对每个交易对手的全天候全面可见性，帮助组织快速行动。
news.bodyHtml:
Xapien, an London-founded AI-native due diligence platform that investigates people and companies, has announced a $56m investment round led by Spectrum Equity, a growth equity firm that specialises in risk and compliance technology, including World-Check and Verafin.  Existing investor YFM Equity Partners also participated in the round. This growth investment will be used to build out Xapien’s U.S. presence, where it already generates 50% of its revenue, expanding its Boston office and relocating the CEO and other leaders. Xapien last raised an $8m Series A in 2024.

Business relationships are a key source of ongoing risk, yet budget and time constraints force organisations to reserve due diligence scrutiny for only a fraction of these counterparties, leaving them with significant blind spots. This gap in diligence coverage has consequences, as only 30% of organisations report having the bandwidth to assess even half of their business relationships.

Advertisement

“Third-party due diligence has remained stubbornly manual for twenty years,” said Chris Green, CEO of Xapien. “Hence, businesses have had to ration their scrutiny to a subset of relationships with one-off checks at the point of onboarding, leaving them massively exposed. This funding lets Xapien pursue its mission to give compliance, legal, and procurement teams full visibility on every counterparty, all the time, giving organizations the confidence to move at speed.”

Xapien was founded in 2018 by Dan Secretan and Shaun O’Mahony along with CEO Chris Green who joined in 2022, all three veterans of BAE Systems’ financial crime and national security divisions. The Company serves multinational corporations, law firms, private banks, and leading universities and nonprofits, as well as powering automation for leading professional services firms. The company has seen rapid market adoption, with 350 clients and partners in 15 countries now using Xapien to transform their due diligence capabilities. Representative clients include Greenberg Traurig, ABB, Dow Jones Risk & Compliance, and KPMG.

Advertisement

news.titleEn: Latham builds its own AI models with Nvidia GPU server investment
news.titleZh: Latham自建AI模型，投资Nvidia GPU服务器
news.summaryZh: 据英国《金融时报》9月11日报道，美国跨国律师事务所Latham & Watkins已购买Nvidia GPU服务器，并开始定制自己的AI模型。Latham是美国第二大律师事务所，去年营收达83亿美元。近年来，该公司购买了多台服务器，每台服务器配备多个GPU，这些强大的计算机芯片用于运行AI模型。此举的主要驱动力之一是能够将客户的敏感数据完全保留在自己的系统内。有时他们可能拥有非常敏感的信息，即客户信息，他们非常希望保护这些信息，不想将其交给任何云供应商。随着AI使用定价的消费成本即将到来，该所希望拥有“灵活性”。这一做法与大多数主要律师事务所采取的方法截然不同，后者主要依赖云基础设施和第三方法律AI平台（如Harvey和Legora），或者构建自己的应用程序，同时继续通过外部提供商消费底层模型和计算资源。Latham在技术栈上走得更深。通过拥有GPU基础设施并自行定制开放权重模型，该所可能在某些AI工作负载中无需将客户数据发送给法律AI供应商、模型提供商或超大规模云服务商。这使Latham在保密性、模型选择以及潜在成本方面拥有更大的控制权，尤其是随着供应商开始从补贴代币使用转向按消费计费。然而，这也带来了显著的权衡。内部运行GPU基础设施和模型需要大量的资本投资和专业技术专长，并将维护和确保基础设施安全的责任完全放在该所身上。更多细节敬请期待。
news.bodyHtml:
US multinational law firm Latham & Watkins has bought Nvidia GPU servers and started customising its own AI models, the Financial Times revealed yesterday (11 September).

Latham, the US’s second-largest law firm with $8.3bn in revenue last year, has in recent years purchased several servers, each of which holds multiple GPUs, the powerful computer chips that run AI models, the FT said.

Advertisement

One of the driving forces is the ability to keep clients’ sensitive data entirely within its own systems.

“Sometimes we may have information that is so sensitive, client information that we really want to protect, we don’t want to put it to any cloud vendor,” Rene Mendoza, the firm’s chief information officer, told the FT.He added that “with a lot of consumption costs coming” for how AI usage is priced, the firm wanted to have “flexibility”.

Advertisement

The approach is markedly different from that taken by most major law firms, which have largely relied on cloud infrastructure and third-party legal AI platforms such as Harvey and Legora, or built their own applications while continuing to consume underlying models and compute through external providers.

Latham is going further down the technology stack. By owning GPU infrastructure and customising open-weight models itself, the firm can potentially run certain AI workloads without sending client data to either a legal AI vendor, model provider or hyperscaler.

That gives Latham greater control over confidentiality, model choice and potentially cost, particularly as vendors begin to move away from subsidised token use to a consumption basis. It does come with a significant trade-off. Running GPU infrastructure and models in-house requires substantial capital investment and specialist technical expertise, and places responsibility for maintaining and securing the infrastructure squarely on the firm.

Keep an eye out for more details.

news.bodyHtml:
New online app experience and product enhancements help legal professionals improve writing
and verify what AI gets wrong before their work reaches a client, court or opposing counsel.

WASHINGTON, D.C., September 9, 2026 — BriefCatch, the legal writing and editing tool trusted by prominent law firms and both state and federal courts, today unveiled its transformation into a unified suite of tools for improving and verifying legal briefs. The launch debuts a new, fully self-serve online app, featuring a standalone writing and editing environment that works alongside Word and Outlook. The app also brings RealityCheck citation verification to general availability, adds new writing, learning and administrative capabilities and opens direct purchase for the first time to every legal professional, from individual attorneys and students to large firms and courts.

Generative AI has transformed how legal professionals research, draft and revise legal documents, dramatically accelerating many parts of the writing process. But that speed has introduced new risks. AI-generated work can appear polished and persuasive while containing fabricated citations, inaccurate quotations, misstated holdings or unsupported propositions. If one of these errors makes its way into a court filing, the consequences can include sanctions, reputational damage and malpractice exposure. Yet neither general-purpose AI tools nor most legal technology products are designed to catch these problems, which often turn on subtle questions of legal context that automated tools struggle to assess but that are critical to a brief’s accuracy and credibility. These tools are optimized to produce a faster first draft, not to verify and contextualize the authorities supporting it.

With its expanded suite, BriefCatch closes this critical reliability gap by making citation verification and sharper writing recommendations standard on every plan, and by putting that protection within reach of every legal professional, not just the largest firms. Attorneys can also use BriefCatch to easily catch errors in opponents’ briefs to gain competitive advantage and prevent unreliable statements of law from slipping through and misleading the court.

“This isn’t just a product update – it’s a reintroduction of BriefCatch. Clear, persuasive, credible legal writing shouldn’t require a tradeoff between speed and accuracy. Nor should it be something only the largest firms can access,” said Ross Guberman, founder and CEO of BriefCatch and a leading legal writing expert. “With the new BriefCatch, we’re giving all legal professionals the tools to produce stronger, more accurate work today, while becoming better writers and reviewers over time.”

What’s New Across the Suite

  • BriefCatch Online App: Sign up, manage your account and access the Learning Hub, then edit with the full BriefCatch suite, including Writing Assistant, CiteCheck and RealityCheck, through BriefCatch’s secure online environment or in Word and Outlook – whichever fits your workflow best.
  • RealityCheck, standard on every plan: Out of beta and available to every user, RealityCheck reads the cases you cite and checks whether the opinion supports your brief’s quotations, holdings, dispositions and propositions. It flags altered quotes, misstated holdings and unsupported citations, tells you to manually verify any case it can’t confirm across three case-law sources and scans documents for concealed text such as white-on-white type, hidden formatting and zero-width characters. Unlike a traditional citator, which tells you whether an authority is still good law, RealityCheck tells you whether that authority actually supports the sentence it is cited for.
  • Upgraded writing engine: Sharper recommendations across five specific dimensions (engagement, concision, flow, punch and clarity), each with a plain-English explanation and before-and-after examples from top legal writers.
  • Online Learning Hub: Integrated directly into the online experience, Ross Guberman’s complete four-course legal-writing curriculum includes 90 self-paced modules and five AI-focused webinars drawing on techniques Guberman has used to train federal judges and legal professionals at more than 300 law firms and 80 courts. Formerly offered exclusively through costly live, in-person workshops, this training reinforces core principles behind BriefCatch’s recommendations to turn every edit into a lasting skill.
  • Self-serve administration: Manage seats, access and AI credit allocation instantly in the online app, with transparent credit tracking and organization-wide usage management.
  • Scalable, flexible plans: BriefCatch offers Individual, Pro and Enterprise plans. Individual legal professionals—including solo practitioners, law students, judicial clerks and public interest lawyers—can now subscribe directly without firm affiliation. New online app experience and product enhancements help legal professionals improve writing and verify what AI gets wrong before their work reaches a client, court or opposing counsel.

WASHINGTON, D.C., September 9, 2026 — BriefCatch , the legal writing and editing tool trusted by prominent law firms and both state and federal courts, today unveiled its transformation into a unified suite of tools for improving and verifying legal briefs. The launch debuts a new, fully self-serve online app, featuring a standalone writing and editing environment that works alongside Word and Outlook. The app also brings RealityCheck citation verification to general availability, adds new writing, learning and administrative capabilities and opens direct purchase for the first time to every legal professional, from individual attorneys and students to large firms and courts. Generative AI has transformed how legal professionals research, draft and revise legal documents, dramatically accelerating many parts of the writing process. But that speed has introduced new risks. AI-generated work can appear polished and persuasive while containing fabricated citations, inaccurate quotations, misstated holdings or unsupported propositions. If one of these errors makes its way into a court filing, the consequences can include sanctions, reputational damage and malpractice exposure. Yet neither general-purpose AI tools nor most legal technology products are designed to catch these problems, which often turn on subtle questions of legal context that automated tools struggle to assess but that are critical to a brief’s accuracy and credibility. These tools are optimized to produce a faster first draft, not to verify and contextualize the authorities supporting it.

With its expanded suite, BriefCatch closes this critical reliability gap by making citation verification and sharper writing recommendations standard on every plan, and by putting that protection within reach of every legal professional, not just the largest firms. Attorneys can also use BriefCatch to easily catch errors in opponents’ briefs to gain competitive advantage and prevent unreliable statements of law from slipping through and misleading the court.

“This isn’t just a product update – it’s a reintroduction of BriefCatch. Clear, persuasive, credible legal writing shouldn’t require a tradeoff between speed and accuracy. Nor should it be something only the largest firms can access,” said Ross Guberman, founder and CEO of BriefCatch and a leading legal writing expert. “With the new BriefCatch, we’re giving all legal professionals the tools to produce stronger, more accurate work today, while becoming better writers and reviewers over time.”

BriefCatch Online App : Sign up, manage your account and access the Learning Hub, then edit with the full BriefCatch suite, including Writing Assistant, CiteCheck and RealityCheck, through BriefCatch’s secure online environment or in Word and Outlook – whichever fits your workflow best.

RealityCheck, standard on every plan: Out of beta and available to every user, RealityCheck reads the cases you cite and checks whether the opinion supports your brief’s quotations, holdings, dispositions and propositions. It flags altered quotes, misstated holdings and unsupported citations, tells you to manually verify any case it can’t confirm across three case-law sources and scans documents for concealed text such as white-on-white type, hidden formatting and zero-width characters. Unlike a traditional citator, which tells you whether an authority is still good law, RealityCheck tells you whether that authority actually supports the sentence it is cited for.

Upgraded writing engine : Sharper recommendations across five specific dimensions (engagement, concision, flow, punch and clarity), each with a plain-English explanation and before-and-after examples from top legal writers.

Online Learning Hub: Integrated directly into the online experience, Ross Guberman’s complete four-course legal-writing curriculum includes 90 self-paced modules and five AI-focused webinars drawing on techniques Guberman has used to train federal judges and legal professionals at more than 300 law firms and 80 courts. From Innovation Labs to Embedded Intelligence: How AI Is Reshaping Big Law

By

Damian Priamurskiy

posted

2 days ago

Like

Please enjoy this blog post co-authored by Damian Priamurskiy, Legal Project Manager, Lowenstein Sandler LLP and Julianne Kasprzyk Crowley, Paralegal Manager, Investment Management, Lowenstein Sandler LLP.

For much of the past century, the organizational chart of large law firms has had one shape: a pyramid, partners at the apex, associates below climbing toward partnership one billable year at a time. That pyramid is no longer the only structure in the building. Firms are now building a second one alongside it, with its own budget line running into hundreds of millions of dollars. In May 2026, Kirkland & Ellis disclosed a commitment of $500 million and approximately 180 technology professionals to building its own AI platform. Scroll the careers page of a top Am Law 100 firm today and, next to “Associate, Mergers & Acquisitions,” the reader will find postings unheard of a decade ago: “Director of Artificial Intelligence,” “Legal Engineer,” “Data Scientist, Applied Intelligence.” The firm hiring for these roles isn't Big Tech — it’s Big Law. The industry is building the equivalent of an internal tech department from scratch, at a scale and speed with no real precedent in the profession's history

Image 1. Pyramid law firm model [1].

From Buying Tools to Building Departments

In 2022, Reed Smith created an Innovation Lab — a virtual space for discovering, incubating and accelerating creative ideas at the firm and alongside clients [11], Reed Smith’s Innovation Lab offered an early marker for Big Law’s tech-forward approach to reimagining its organizational structure. The label “lab” can imply separation from practice, but Reed Smith’s announced structure was explicitly integrated — built to work with the firm’s own internal technology subsidiary, GravityStack™. That template — durable, integrated, and built to connect legal ops and technical staff rather than separate them — is the one larger firms have since scaled up considerably:

Kirkland & Ellis — $500 million committed, 180 in-house tech professionals, a platform built from 250 lawyers’ know-how. Firm-owned IP, not licensed.

Cleary Gottlieb’s acquisition of Springbok AI — a team of 10 data scientists and AI engineers folded directly into the firm.

Linklaters’ Applied Intelligence — lawyers and data scientists in a front-office team on live matters.

Three different strategies — proprietary build, acquisition, embedded team — and no firm has settled on a single playbook. But each path or combination forces the same unresolved question underneath it: Is building this capability in-house justified, or whether licensing an external platform gets the job done at a lower cost?

The Math Behind the Bet: Build vs. Buy, and What Clients Will Pay

Generally, licensing an outside platform is an entry point with less initial investment. Based on industry estimates, some of the popular subscription-based legal AI tools targeted at law firms come at $1,000–$2,000 per seat per month for mid-market firms, dropping to $100–$200[PD9.1] per seat at Am Law 100 scale — a palpable investment, but nothing close to the outlay that building such a tool internally requires [12].

On the other hand, building internal “labs” at Kirkland & Ellis’ scale, has meant a $500 million commitment — a figure that dwarfs any licensing spend, not just an internal productivity tool. That $500 million compares with an estimated $7.46 million a year for a firm of Kirkland’s size to license outside tools instead — roughly 4,145 attorneys at $150 per seat per month. Substantial, but still far below a $500 million multi-year build commitment.

Figure 2. Reduction in the prevalence of the billable hour and AI trends [2].

The real tension to name: The economic distinction here is not simply between buying and building AI. It’s between building a tool for a single use case and building an institutional capability. A bespoke tool developed for one narrow task carries its full development and maintenance cost on a single workflow. A capability reused across clients, practices, and matters spreads that same fixed cost over a much larger base of work. At that point, AI stops being a technology expense and starts functioning as firm infrastructure — infrastructure that requires a new era of specialists to run.

The Hiring Curve and the Changing Docket

Beyond the headline numbers is a quieter story. This shift is not about the budget — it's about the roster. Tech hiring is visibly accelerating: Legal-AI job postings are reportedly up roughly 340 percent between January 2024 and January 2026, and 78 percent of Am Law 200 firms have created at least one AI-focused position. Traditional hiring has not been keeping the same pace — first-year associate classes are down at Am Law 100 and 200 firms in recent cycles. SurePoint Technologies’ 2026 Law School Hiring Report found new-associate hiring remained roughly flat over the prior three years despite strong revenue growth. It is too early to attribute that decline to AI alone; some of it predates generative AI at scale, and the evidence is better read as a change in hiring mix than a clean substitution rate.

Kirkland offers a live version of that mix inside a single firm: 180 technology professionals now sit alongside a platform built from the know-how of 250 lawyers, including 100 partners — a real, present-day ratio of technical to legal headcount inside one AI build-out. Linklaters shows a smaller but more deliberate version of the same shift: It launched Applied Intelligence, reportedly staffed at a ratio of three lawyers to three data scientists rather than the traditional model of assigning associates in proportion to a matter’s size.

The composition of the firm’s head count is shifting rapidly: more technical and specialist hires, a flatter, but still growing associate base.

Who Gets Cut — or Who Gets Hired?

Reed Smith’s 2022 appointment of anthropologist Dr. Madeline Boyer to lead its Innovation Lab is particularly revealing. Dr. Boyer’s academic background includes research on organizational culture and history of work, not primarily legal technology. That hire uniquely highlights innovation as a discipline of human behavior, organizational design, and collaboration, not simply a matter of software selection pipeline.

The traditional pyramid, for example, a large first-year class conducting document review, billed by the hour, is now compressing because AI removes that routine work. Similarly, on the business-services side, Baker McKenzie's cut of an estimated 600–1,000 business-services roles in February 2026, explicitly citing AI, is the largest AI-attributed cut in the legal industry to date.

The frame to land on is not necessarily fewer people but fewer types and more specialized roles. Fewer first-year associates and more AI-fluent paralegals, knowledge professionals, product managers, data scientists, and legal-operations specialists who operate and validate AI output. The new emerging architecture is not a replacement for legal talent, but a brand-new structure built around it. The old advantage was talent. The new advantage is talent combined with architecture. Firms that build the right team win the client.

From Technology Investment to Operating Model

These developments share a common direction: Competitive advantage is beginning to move beyond individual lawyers and the traditional partnership pyramid toward firm-owned workflows, proprietary technology, and interdisciplinary teams. Whether those investments become durable assets or expensive bets will depend on scale, reuse, and whether client pricing captures the value they create.

What is already clear is that the internal AI function is no longer a support function. As embedded teams move into the place where matters are scoped and delivered, practice management and legal operations move with them — helping select matters, assemble teams, price work, and convert one-off solutions into reusable infrastructure. This evolution is increasingly organizational, not merely technological. The question is no longer whether firms use AI, but how they are reorganizing around it.

news.bodyHtml:
Founded in August 2026 by former lawyer Brig Ricks, SaaS Tracker helps legal and operations teams keep on top of changing software terms, privacy policies and online contracts, using AI to identify, track and explain the changes that matter. Here’s the founder with more.

How would you describe your company to a friend?

SaaS Tracker is like a smoke detector and filing cabinet for online contracts. It keeps copies of the terms, privacy policies, and other online legal documents for the software a business uses, watches for changes, and explains what changed and why it might matter.

Advertisement
And to a techy?

SaaS Tracker is a multi-tenant change-intelligence platform that monitors online legal documents, normalizes and versions their content, detects meaningful changes, and uses AI to summarize their potential legal and operational impact. It combines automated retrieval, immutable evidence, document diffs, alerts, assignments, deadlines, audit history, and team workflows in one system.

When were you founded?

August 2026

Advertisement
By who?

Brig Ricks (https://www.linkedin.com/in/brigricks/)

Who are your key managers/senior execs?

Brig Ricks

Who are your target clients?

Lean legal teams, outside general counsel, and operations leaders at SaaS/software companies.

What is your plan (growth strategy)?

Position Saas Tracker as “legal change intelligence,” not merely website monitoring. The distinction is archived evidence, meaningful version comparisons, AI-assisted impact analysis, assignments, deadlines, and team workflows.

Key achievements?

The biggest achievement has been turning a recurring problem I saw in legal practice into a working production platform. From a concept in my head, to a prototype, to a pilot release, to a limited public release, now a full public release. Each step in the process was both challenging and fulfilling, fueling me for the next step.

Have you received investment?

Bootstrap.

Have there been any key changes in direction since you were founded?

No.

What are the key challenges in your market?

1. The problem is largely invisible – Business may not recognize the risk until a consequential change is missed.

2. The value is event-driven – A customer may receive no significant alerts for months and question the subscription’s value.

3. Category confusion – Prospects may compare ST to inexpensive webpage monitoring or very expensive contract management systems. ST falls between those categories.

Tell us something people don’t already know about the company? 

I named my AI agent, “SaaSy.”

news.summaryZh: 关于AI对律师影响的讨论往往聚焦于高薪律师，却忽视了行政人员、律师助理、市场部及账单催收人员等基层员工。这些岗位正是AI供应商宣称可被削减和消除的，而律所也在通过大规模裁员来降低成本，同时以超过40万美元的年薪招聘法律工程师或AI总监。文章引用Tom's Guide中Elton Jones的报道，援引Tenet的数据称，到2030年全球约有9200万个工作岗位可能被AI取代，未来十年美国47%的劳动者面临自动化风险。Jones让ChatGPT、Gemini、Claude和Perplexity列出最可能被AI取代的十大职业，各模型一致认为客服代表首当其冲，其他包括数据录入员、销售代表、簿记员、初级内容写手以及律师助理和法律研究员。这些岗位的共同点是可预测性，即依赖结构化规则、数据检索、标准文本生成或常规交易。作者批评AI客服体验糟糕，并强调法律行业本质上是客户服务行业，客户遇到棘手或情感问题时更愿意与有同理心的人类接待员沟通。此外，基层员工往往是律所文化的最佳传承者，拥有机构记忆，能帮助年轻律师避免触怒合伙人。律所面临律师短缺，律师助理可像医师助理一样承担更多无需法律学位的工作，但律所却急于裁撤他们。最后，作者呼吁律所应承担对员工的责任，通过再培训保留人才，而非简单抛弃，因为AI没有灵魂，无法真正关怀他人。
news.bodyHtml:
Neal Page: Sir, excuse me. I know this is your cab, but I’m desperately late for a plane, and I was wondering if I could appeal to your good nature and ask you to let me have it.

Lawyer getting into cab: I don’t have a good nature.

Planes, Trains and Automobiles, 1987.

There’s a lot of hand-wringing these days about the impact AI is going to have on the poor lawyer. You know the one. The guy who brought home over $5 million in compensation last year. Poor baby.

But what isn’t talked about is the impact AI will have down below. The administrative staff. The paralegals. Those in the marketing department. Those who labor in billing and collections to make sure Mr. Big gets his $5 million. All these people slave away in internal offices for peanuts with no clout or status. These are the jobs and the costs the AI vendors merrily trumpet can be eliminated and reduced. These are the people who can least afford to be marginalized.

And what are the firms doing about this issue? Eliminating these positions to cut costs. Conducting massive layoffs of staff. And hiring fancy legal engineers. Searching for directors of AI sometimes at salaries of over $400,000.

Who’s Really at Risk?

A recent article in Tom’s Guide brought this home. It was written by Elton Jones, who writes about AI for a living. He cites some statistics from Tenet that some 92 million jobs could be replaced by 2030 worldwide. 47% of US workers are at risk of being automated away in the next 10 years.

So Jones, being curious, asked ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Perplexity to rank the 10 most likely jobs to be replaced by AI. Now granted, the bots had some self-interest here since the more jobs they can replace, the more valuable they are. (AI can’t think like humans? Right).

Oh great. The bots we hate dealing with the most are going to take over customer service

The job they all agreed on: customer service representatives. Oh great. The bots we hate dealing with the most are going to take over customer service. Jones quoted Perplexity as to why: “Chatbots and voice agents can answer routine FAQs, check order status, reset accounts, schedule appointments, process simple returns, and triage tickets around the clock.”

Except they often can’t: if these are the jobs most likely to be replaced by a bot, why can’t the bot do something besides tell me to push one. Or two. Or something novel, like answer the fucking question I’m asking. I’ve been trying to get my dermatologist appointment rescheduled for a week now, dealing with a bot that can’t seem to grasp the fact that I am already a patient. Jones puts it best: “I’d much rather deal with a human who fulfills such a role.” I’m with you, Elton.

But look at some of the other jobs the bots put on the endangered list: data entry people, inbound sales reps, bookkeepers and accounting types. Writers for entry-level content. All folks who labor in the bowels of law firms. And here’s one that really hits home: paralegals/legal assistants and researchers.

 Jones quotes Perplexity’s answer to why all this is so: “The common factor across all these roles is predictability. Roles reliant on structured rules, data retrieval, standard text generation, or routine transactions are being automated.”

Whew. Mr. Big is safe. 

Remember Customer Service? I Do

But here’s the thing. Just like when you can’t get ahold of a human to solve your routine customer service issue, something is lost when all those people that help a law firm serve its clients are gone. Does anyone really think someone who calls a law firm with a thorny or emotional legal problem, like my husband just left me, would rather speak to a bot that starts by saying listen carefully, because our menu options have recently changed? Or would they rather speak to a human receptionist who is empathic, friendly, and actually helpful?

Will clients be happier when a bot calls them to remind them last month’s bill hasn’t been paid? Do you think your chances of getting hired are better when the potential client reads AI generated marketing slop?

What happens to quality when all that work is done by a bot?

And those paralegals. You know, the humans who are often charged with doing things like checking cites or making sure the factual references are correct. What happens to quality when all that work is done by a bot? Not to mention the interface that, in my experience, paralegals often have with clients.

Let’s face it, we are in a customer service industry. But are we being too eager to jettison the very people that help provide customer service? I fear in the rush to embrace AI and save costs (gotta pay for that AI investment some way, right?), that’s what’s going to happen.

Here’s A Thought

There’s another reason we might want to think long and hard about what we are doing. Many of those people who serve in non-legal roles are the very employees who have been around the longest. (Let’s face it, there’s not much of a lateral market for a law firm billing clerk). 

They are the people who know the firm’s culture the best. The admin assistant who has been sitting outside a partner’s office for 22 years, for example. And in an age when lawyers lateral back and forth between firms willy-nilly, it is these people who are the very ones who have institutional knowledge that others don’t. They are the ones who can tell a young associate working on a project for a partner that the style in which the associate is writing is one the partner detests. I know. That happened to me, and the admin saved my scalp from a partner known to rip associates to shreds if he didn’t like something.

More than that, many of those people know how the law works. They know the stresses lawyers are under. They understand client relationships. They respect the profession and those with whom they work. I had an admin once who cared so much about the work that she suggested how I might more efficiently handle the massive number of files I was trying to juggle. That wasn’t in her job description. No lawyer thought of that or bothered to care.

Lots of law firms are having trouble finding enough associates to do the work that needs to get done. Yet paralegals can help fill in the gap

And when it comes to paralegals, there’s a practical reason to keep them and utilize them properly. Lots of law firms are having trouble finding enough associates to do the work that needs to get done. Yet paralegals can help fill in the gap by doing lots of tasks for which having a law degree is not a prerequisite. Work that requires skill, judgment, and familiarity with the law and clients. 

Think of the physician assistant in the medical context: medicine didn’t respond to a shortage of doctors by firing everyone else. It expanded their roles. And paralegals are even more needed in the age of AI, not less. 

But blinded by the shiny AI lights and aided by vendors and consultants, firms are quick to can these folks. They are quick to hire expensive so-called experts to help. Ever think of retraining what you already have? It may not be as sexy, but it might be cheaper and get you a better product long term.

So yes, AI can do a lot. But it can’t take care of people. It has no soul

What Does It Profit?

What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul?

Which brings me to a final point, and one lawyers aren’t well known for: responsibility for our fellow man. Respecting those who have been loyal and worked in the trenches day and night. Looking for ways to keep them by retraining them and finding new roles instead of dumping them on the street. These people don’t make $5 million per year. They don’t have well-funded 401ks. They rely on the firm for basics like health insurance. 

So yes, AI can do a lot. But it can’t take care of people. It has no soul. It doesn’t know what good nature is.  And if we aren’t careful, we soon won’t either.

news.titleEn: ILTACON Included A Sobering Memorial to 9/11, with Video Interviews Of Some Who Were There (Including Me). Now, ILTA Has Posted the Full Interviews
news.titleZh: ILTACON 包含对 9/11 的沉痛纪念，并播放了亲历者（包括我）的视频采访；如今 ILTA 已发布完整采访
news.summaryZh: 今年 ILTACON 周三上午的主题演讲以对 9/11 事件 25 周年的沉痛而感人的致敬开场。ILTA 播放了一部由其制作的 30 分钟影片，其中包含对当天在曼哈顿的 ILTA 成员和朋友的采访，随后进行了长时间的默哀，屏幕上滚动着所有遇难者的名字。本文作者当时担任《国家法律杂志》主编，也是受访者之一，此前曾多次回忆当天的经历。如今，在 9/11 事件 25 周年之际，ILTA 已在 YouTube 上发布了纪念活动中播放的视频，其中包括经过剪辑的采访以及每位出镜者的完整采访。除作者外，受访者还包括现任 Porzio, Bromberg & Newman 网络安全总监的 Brian Clarke、现任 ILTA 首席执行官的 Joy Heath Rush、现任 ILTA 高级项目经理的 Laura Murphy，以及现任 Relativity 发现顾问和法律教育总监的 David Horrigan。此外还有一段 David 与作者共同接受的采访，因为两人曾在《国家法律杂志》共事。ILTA 首席体验官 Dawn Hudgins 因远见卓识促成了此事，并在 ILTACON 期间完成了大量工作。采访于 ILTACON 开始前的周六拍摄，并在周三纪念活动前剪辑成最终视频。
news.bodyHtml:
Wednesday morning’s keynote session at ILTACON this year opened with a sobering and moving 25th anniversary tribute to 9/11. ILTA showed a 30-minute film it produced with interviews of ILTA members and friends who were in Manhattan that day, followed by an extended moment of silence as the names of everyone who lost their lives scrolled across the screen.

I was among those interviewed. I was editor-in-chief of The National Law Journal at the time, and I have previously recounted some of my memories of that day, here and here and here.

Today, on this 25th anniversary of that awful day, ILTA has posted the video it showed at the ILTACON memorial, which contained edited interviews, as well as the full interviews of each person who appeared in that video.

You can find them all here on YouTube. I’ll also drop them in below.

Besides myself, those who were interviewed were:

  • Brian Clarke, who is now cybersecurity director at Porzio, Bromberg & Newman.
  • Joy Heath Rush, now the CEO of ILTA.
  • Laura Murphy, now senior project manager at ILTA.
  • David Horrigan, now discovery counsel and legal education director at Relativity.

There is also an interview of David and me together, as David and I had a shared experience as colleagues at the NLJ.

A special shout out is much deserved for Dawn Hudgins, chief experience officer at ILTA. Not only did Dawn have the foresight to pull this all together, but she did much of the work during ILTACON, in what I have to believe is already the busiest week of her year. The interviews were filmed on the Saturday of the weekend that ILTACON started, and they were edited into the final video in time for the memorial on Wednesday.

news.titleEn: Best AI for Generating Medical Chronologies in PI Cases
news.titleZh: 人身伤害案件中生成医疗时间线的最佳AI
news.summaryZh: Lexee AI Medical Summaries被认为是人身伤害案件中生成医疗时间线的最佳AI，因为它直接利用已存储在CloudLex案件中的医疗记录，无需上传至第三方系统或单独登录供应商平台，并在交付前经过专家审核。对于希望全流程外包的原告律所，CloudLex的Paralegal Services可负责从供应商处获取记录、构建时间线，并将完成的工作返回至同一案件文件。医疗时间线是索赔要求的前提，没有时间线就无法提出索赔或达成和解。评估AI的关键不在于其生成质量，而在于其能访问哪些数据；仅基于上传导出的工具无法知晓最近到达的记录。专家审核是将草稿转化为可提交给理赔员文件的关键，输出位置同样重要，自动归档至案件文件比手动下载和归档更高效。医疗时间线是诉前阶段最大的时间消耗点，因为复杂案件涉及多个供应商、不同格式、重叠日期、重复页面及账单记录，需人工整理成时间线并识别诊断和程序。多律师律所同时处理数百件案件时，时间线队列成为瓶颈，每延迟一周都会延长和解时间并推迟应急费用收入。评估工具时应关注五个标准：专家审核、数据是否离开系统、是否同时生成摘要和时间线、输出是否自动归档、是否专门针对人身伤害记录训练。Lexee AI在CloudLex内运行，与Matter Manager和文档管理集成，输出直接进入案件文件，并支持后续的索赔包起草和案件问答。CloudLex的Paralegal Services提供端到端服务，包括记录获取、时间线构建、专家审核和交付，全程不离开平台。
news.bodyHtml:
The best AI for generating medical chronologies in PI cases is the AI that already has the records. Lexee AI Medical Summaries generates AI-assisted medical summaries and treatment timelines from records that are already inside your CloudLex matter, with expert review before delivery, so there is no upload to a third-party system and no separate vendor login. For plaintiff-side firms that want the full workflow handled, CloudLex’s Paralegal Services retrieves the records from providers, builds the chronology, and delivers the completed work back into the same case file.

Key takeaways

  • Medical chronologies are the prerequisite for the demand. No chronology, no demand, no settlement.
  • The evaluation question is not how good the AI is, but what the AI can see. A tool working from an uploaded export cannot know about the records that arrived last week.
  • Expert review is the difference between a draft and something you can put in front of an adjuster.
  • Where the output lands matters as much as how it was made. A PDF you have to download and file is administrative work nobody counts.

Why medical chronologies are the biggest time drain in PI pre-litigation

Every demand rests on a chronology, and every chronology rests on records that arrive when providers feel like sending them. That dependency makes the chronology the single most reliable bottleneck in pre-litigation.

The work itself is genuinely demanding, which is why it resists shortcuts. A complex case brings records from several providers in different formats, with overlapping dates, duplicate pages, and billing records that have to be reconciled against treatment notes. Someone has to order all of it into a timeline, identify each diagnosis and procedure, and document gaps in care before opposing counsel does it for them. Ask any PI paralegal how long that takes on a difficult file and the answer is measured in days of available working time.

Now scale it. A multi-attorney firm running several hundred active cases may have dozens sitting in the pre-litigation and demand stage at any moment. Each one needs the same treatment. That is a standing queue of paralegal hours, and it does not clear itself, because new cases enter the demand stage at roughly the rate the team clears them.

The consequence is measured in weeks. Every week a case waits in the chronology queue is a week before the demand can go out, which extends the settlement timeline and delays contingency revenue on costs the firm has already advanced. Our guide to reducing a demand backlog covers that economics in more detail.

What makes good medical chronology software, and what most tools get wrong

Most evaluations of AI chronology tools focus on output quality, which is the wrong first question because every tool demos well on a clean file. Five criteria matter more.

1. Expert review, not just accuracy claims

A chronology is read by an adjuster and, if the case does not settle, by opposing counsel. AI output without human verification carries real risk in that document, and accuracy percentages published by vendors are not verifiable by you. Look for human review inside the delivery workflow rather than described in the fine print as an option.

2. Whether your records leave your system

Uploading client medical records to a third-party AI platform raises a data question you will have to answer, both to yourself and potentially to a client. Protected health information belongs to people who did not choose to become data. The lower-risk architecture is AI that operates on records already inside your personal injury case management software, so the question never arises.

3. Summary or chronology, and whether you get both

These are different documents. A medical summary is a condensed narrative of what happened. A chronology is a date-ordered timeline of every medical event. A PI demand typically needs both, the chronology as the factual spine and the summary as the narrative for the adjuster. Confirm which one a tool actually produces before assuming.

4. Where the finished work lands

If the completed chronology arrives as an emailed PDF, someone at your firm downloads it, renames it, and files it to the right matter, every time, for every case. That is not a rounding error at volume. Ask whether the output appears in the case file automatically.

5. Whether it understands PI records specifically

General legal AI is not trained on the patterns that matter in personal injury: treatment timelines, gaps in care, causation documentation, and the damages narrative. Those are the parts of a chronology that carry weight in a negotiation, and they are the parts a generic tool handles least well.

news.titleEn: Look What You Made Me File: Taylor Swift Turns to Trademark Law to Fight AI Deepfakes
news.titleZh: Look What You Made Me File: Taylor Swift Turns to Trademark Law to Fight AI Deepfakes
news.summaryZh: 泰勒·斯威夫特于2026年4月24日向美国专利商标局提交三件申请，寻求注册两个声音商标和一个图像商标：以她本人声音说出的“Hey, it's Taylor Swift”（序列号99784980）和“Hey, it's Taylor”（序列号99784979），以及一张她在Eras Tour舞台上穿亮片紧身衣、持粉色吉他表演的照片（序列号99784977）。申请属于国际第041类（娱乐服务），基于至少可追溯至2011年的商业使用，并附有来自Amazon Music和Spotify的样本。这些申请似乎针对AI生成的深度伪造。声音可作为商标，一旦具有显著性，能让听众将其与单一来源联系起来。2025年12月，美国专利商标局批准了马修·麦康纳的八件商标申请，涵盖其声音、形象和口头禅。名人已拥有形象权这一工具，但形象权完全属于州法层面。联邦商标注册可全国适用。NO FAKES Act于2026年6月22日从参议院司法委员会一致通过。莱昂内尔·里奇于2026年6月提交了自己的声音和形象申请，后街男孩同月提交了“hi, we're the Backstreet Boys”的声音商标申请。商标注册有实际限制：训练模型不属于商标法范围，仅声音相似而未使用注册短语的合成片段也在此之外。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Is a pop star’s voice a trademark? Taylor Swift’s legal team is betting yes. On April 24, 2026, she filed three applications with the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) seeking federal registration of two sound marks and one image mark: the spoken phrases “Hey, it’s Taylor Swift” (Serial No. 99784980) and “Hey, it’s Taylor” (Serial No. 99784979), both spoken in Swift’s own voice, and a photograph of her performing on the Eras Tour stage in a sequined bodysuit with a pink guitar (Serial No. 99784977). The applications are filed in International Class 041 (entertainment services), rest on use in commerce dating back to at least 2011, and are supported by specimens pulled from Amazon Music and Spotify. Unlike Swift’s prior trademark work protecting album titles and lyrics, these filings are not about merchandise or lyrics. They appear to be aimed squarely at AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic audio and video that can now convincingly mimic a celebrity’s voice and image without copying a single frame or note of anything she actually recorded. Registering a sound isn’t a new trick. MGM’s roaring lion, NBC’s three-note chime, and Intel’s audio bong have all held federal registration for years, and under the Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure § 1202.15, a sound qualifies as a mark once it is distinctive enough that a listener connects it to a single source rather than treating it as background noise or pure information. The bar climbs higher for anything commonplace (e.g. an alarm beep or a ringtone), which needs proof of acquired distinctiveness under Section 2(f) before the USPTO will register it. Zippo cleared that bar for the click-flip-click of its lighter by showing years of sales figures and advertising spend tied specifically to that sound. What’s novel here is the subject matter — not a jingle, but a celebrity’s own spoken voice, introducing herself by name. That raises a real examination question, is “Hey, it’s Taylor Swift” functioning as a source identifier for entertainment services, or is it just Taylor Swift talking? Even if the mark registers, what is genuinely untested is whether it does any practical work against an AI-generated clip that merely sounds like her without reproducing the registered phrase word for word. The deeper doctrinal questions run further still. Courts have not worked out how to analyze likelihood of confusion when the allegedly infringing content comes from an algorithm rather than a person copying a phrase, or how liability might reach a platform or model developer that never itself displays the mark. Swift isn’t the test case, though. In December 2025, the USPTO approved eight trademark applications from actor Matthew McConaughey covering his voice, image, and his signature catchphrase, “alright, alright, alright,” registered down to the pitch pattern of each syllable. McConaughey’s team was candid that their goal was to give him standing to sue in federal court over AI-generated content that mimics his voice or likeness, whether or not anyone is selling a product with it. If McConaughey’s registrations hold up, they are a strong signal the USPTO is willing to register these marks. The harder question is what they will actually be worth in an infringement fight. Celebrities already have a tool for unauthorized use of their name, image, and voice — the right of publicity. Bette Midler used it successfully against Ford in 1988 after the automaker hired her former backup singer to imitate her distinctive voice in a commercial (Midler v. Ford Motor Co., 849 F.2d 460 (9th Cir. 1988)), and Tom Waits won a similar case against Frito-Lay a few years later (Waits v. Frito-Lay, Inc., 978 F.2d 1093 (9th Cir. 1992)). The catch is that right of publicity lives entirely at the state level. Coverage, remedies, and even whether the claim exists at all shift depending on which state’s law applies, and the doctrine grew up around human impersonators, not a model that can generate a synthetic voice on demand. A federal trademark registration sidesteps that patchwork. It applies nationwide and comes with causes of action built for exactly the kind of consumer confusion a convincing AI-generated “endorsement” would create. Registering these marks does not retire a right-of-publicity claim; it adds a federal option that can run alongside it. Congress may soon add a third layer. The NO FAKES Act, which would create a federal property right against unauthorized AI-generated digital replicas of a person’s voice and likeness, advanced unanimously out of the Senate Judiciary Committee on June 22, 2026. If it passes, it will give artists (and everyone else) a federal statutory claim to sit alongside trademark and state right-of-publicity theories. It is tempting to read this as pop-star news and move on, but the underlying problem is a business problem, not just an entertainment one. Companies build recognizable voices and images into their brands too, and those signals are just as exposed to synthetic imitation as Swift’s are. Disney didn’t wait for a celebrity test case to make this argument. In December 2025 it went straight after Google, demanding that the company stop its Gemini AI tool from generating images of copyrighted Disney characters, and Google reportedly took the material down within a day of receiving the letter. And Swift and McConaughey are not operating in isolation. Lionel Richie filed his own voice-and-likeness applications in June 2026, and the Backstreet Boys filed a sound mark for “hi, we’re the Backstreet Boys” that same month. What started as one artist’s novel filing is starting to look like a standard defensive playbook. That playbook has real limits worth understanding before anyone assumes trademark registration solves the AI-impersonation problem outright. Training a model on existing recordings does not fall within trademark law’s reach. It’s not a commercial “use” of a mark in the sense the statute requires; it’s internal computation. A synthetic clip that merely sounds like someone, without using her actual registered phrase, sits outside the registration too. It is also only as strong as the paper trail behind it. Swift’s filings rest on a signed consent to register and a decade of documented use pulled from actual streaming specimens. And because no single doctrine covers the whole problem, the more durable answer tends to be a layered one: trademarks alongside state right-of-publicity law, contract terms addressing AI use, and, if the NO FAKES Act clears Congress, a federal statutory claim on top of all of it.
