news.titleEn: Harvey Raises Another $550M At A $15.5B Valuation
news.titleZh: Harvey再融资5.5亿美元，估值达155亿美元
news.summaryZh: 法律人工智能公司Harvey于今日宣布，已再次筹集5.5亿美元资金，公司估值达到155亿美元。本轮融资由Diffusion和Lightspeed联合领投。自2022年成立以来，Harvey累计融资总额已超过15亿美元。参与本轮投资的其他机构包括Sequoia、Kleiner Perkins、a16z、Coatue、Conviction、Elad Gil、Evantic、GIC、Goldman Sachs Alternatives、Whale Rock、WndrCo、Sapphire及Verified Capital。公司年度经常性收入已突破4亿美元，服务客户超过3000家，其中包括前100大律所中的80%、财富500强企业中的20%以及财富10强企业中的半数。本轮融资是在推出其首个后训练开放权重模型Tenet以及发布法律智能体基准Harvey LAB之后进行的。本轮融资所得资金将投入“人力和算力这两项最重要的资源”。公司正在产品、工程、研究和市场推广等岗位积极招聘，以拓展新垂直领域，并为合同、诉讼、交易和合规构建更专业的产品。在算力方面，公司将大力投资于其技术框架和自有模型训练。Tenet的发布只是一个开始，“本轮融资使我们能够扩大后续模型代际所需的算力和数据规模”。
news.bodyHtml:
The legal AI company Harvey said today that it has raised another $550 million at a $15.5 billion valuation, co-led by Diffusion and Lightspeed.

By my calculations, that puts the total amount Harvey has raised since its 2022 launch at north of $1.5 billion.

Other investors participating in this round were Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, a16z, Coatue, Conviction, Elad Gil, Evantic, GIC, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Whale Rock, WndrCo, Sapphire and Verified Capital.

On LinkedIn, cofounder Winston Weinberg wrote that the company has now crossed $400 million in annual recurring revenue and serves more than 3,000 customers, including 80% of the top 100 law firms, 20% of the Fortune 500, and half of the Fortune 10.

The company noted that the raise follows the introduction of Tenet, its first post-trained open-weight model, and the launch of Harvey LAB, the Legal Agent Benchmark. 

Weinberg said the capital from this round is being invested “into our two most important resources: people and compute.”

He said that the company is hiring aggressively across product, engineering, research, and go-to-market roles as it expands into new verticals and builds more specialized products for contracting, litigation, deals and compliance.

With regard to compute, he said that the company will be investing heavily in both its harness and its own model training.

He said the launch of Tenet was just the start, “and this round lets us scale the compute and data behind the generations that follow.”

news.titleEn: Intapp launches a network to help law firms recover revenue lost between pricing and collections
news.titleZh: Intapp推出网络，帮助律所挽回定价与收款之间流失的收入
news.summaryZh: Intapp（NASDAQ: INTA）在ILTACON 2026上宣布推出Intapp Profitability Network，这是一个经认证的合作伙伴生态系统，连接律所从定价、人员配置、工时记录、预账单到收款的全流程。该网络基于Intapp Time with Celeste和Intapp Billstream构建，首批六家创始合作伙伴为Capacity、Engage AI Solutions、Legora、Lexpipe、Oddr和Zebraworks。Intapp将此类AI称为“Firm AI”，即面向律所自身业务而非个人或工作成果的AI。该网络旨在解决多数律所各阶段系统与团队割裂、数据洞察在交接中丢失、发现利润流失时为时已晚的问题，使律所首次将盈利能力视为从首次定价决策到最终收款的不间断链条。每个集成都经过Intapp产品与研发团队对安全性、API兼容性和功能质量的认证，涉及工时记录或预账单的工作流由Intapp Time with Celeste治理执行，合作伙伴负责提议、分析和推荐，Intapp负责治理、存储并作为记录平台。Celeste作为专家AI协作者，运行跨阶段代理剧本，可在交付期间发现预算偏差、标记定价差异，并将实现结果与定价决策关联。创始合作伙伴各自提供认证专长：Capacity利用Intapp Time with Celeste的利用率和计费表现数据进行人员与事项匹配；Engage AI Solutions连接Intapp Intake and Terms确保业务约定书准确；Legora集成Intapp Walls和Intapp Time，使AI工作流遵守保密和道德墙边界并结构化记录工时；Lexpipe连接Intapp Time with Celeste，将历史事项成本数据转化为定价模型和固定费用基线；Oddr从Intapp Billstream获取完整账单背景以支持收款；Zebraworks连接工时、账单和收款，提供端到端实现分析。该网络现已可用，创始合作伙伴集成将在秋季通过Intapp认证计划后全面上市。
news.bodyHtml:
The Intapp Profitability Network connects Intapp Time with Celeste with certified products from Capacity, Engage AI Solutions, Legora, Lexpipe, Oddr, and Zebraworks, showing firm leaders where margin is made and lost across every matter

PALO ALTO, Calif. — September 9, 2026 — Intapp (NASDAQ: INTA), the governed AI platform for professional firms in highly regulated industries, today announced the Intapp Profitability Network, a certified partner ecosystem that connects every stage of how a law firm earns and collects on a matter — from pricing and staffing through time capture, prebilling, and collections. Introduced at ILTACON 2026, the network launches with six founding partners: Capacity, Engage AI Solutions, Legora, Lexpipe, Oddr, and Zebraworks.

AI is now part of every firm’s strategy. The next question is what that means for firm profitability. The answer runs through the matter — from the moment a firm prices an engagement to the last dollar collected. At every stage of the lifecycle — pricing, staffing, time capture, prebilling, invoicing, collections — profitability can improve or erode.

But most firms manage each stage in separate systems with separate teams, with no shared view of what’s happening across the chain. Data clarity and insights are lost at every handoff. By the time a firm can see where margin leaked, it’s too late to recover it. The Intapp Profitability Network changes that.

Intapp calls this Firm AI — the category of AI aimed not at the individual or the work product, but at the business of the firm itself. Horizontal assistants speed up everyday tasks. Practice AI helps produce the work product. Firm AI runs the business behind both. Profitability is where that difference shows up on the income statement.

The network connects the full chain. For the first time, firms can see profitability as an unbroken chain, from the first pricing decision to the final dollar collected. Built on Intapp Time with Celeste and Intapp Billstream, the network links specialist partner capabilities into one governed system, not a collection of disconnected point tools that each see only part of the picture.

  • The network runs on the firm’s own economics. Every firm can buy a pricing tool. What sets a firm apart is what its own matters actually cost to deliver — by phase, timekeeper, matter type, and AI tool usage. As clients begin asking how technology was applied to their work, that transparency becomes both a trust requirement and a pricing input. Intapp Time with Celeste captures that history, and the Profitability Network puts it to work in scoping, staffing, and repricing decisions.
  • Every integration is certified. Intapp’s product and R&D teams review each network integration for security, API compatibility, and functional quality before it ships, with ongoing review as APIs evolve. For any workflow that touches timekeeping or prebilling, governed execution routes through Intapp Time with Celeste. Partners propose, analyze, and recommend, while Intapp governs, stores, and remains the platform of record.
  • Intapp Celeste orchestrates it. Celeste, an expert AI coworker, runs agentic playbooks that span chain stages — surfacing budget drift during delivery before it becomes an unrecoverable write-down, flagging pricing variance, and connecting realization outcomes back to the pricing decisions that shaped them.

Founding network partners

The founding partners bring certified expertise to the stages of the chain that sit beyond Intapp’s core platform. 

  • Capacity
    Resourcing and staffing optimization
    In a value-pricing model, staffing determines margin. The right timekeeper on the right matter is the difference between a profitable fixed fee and an underwater one. Capacity matches people to matters using utilization and billing performance data from Intapp Time with Celeste — not availability alone.
  • Engage AI Solutions
    Engagement letter accuracy from scoping through signature
    Engage AI Solutions connects to Intapp Intake and Terms so engagement letters reflect what was actually scoped and negotiated. Intake and Terms also natively integrate with DocuSign, giving risk professionals visibility and control throughout execution — not just at signature.
  • Legora
    Governed AI legal workflows with structured time capture
    Legora integrates Intapp Walls so AI workflows respect confidentiality and ethical wall boundaries. It also connects to Intapp Time, so any work lawyers do in Legora becomes a structured time entry rather than unbilled effort.
  • Lexpipe
    Pricing intelligence and matter scoping analytics
    Lexpipe connects to Intapp Time with Celeste, turning historical matter cost data into pricing models and fixed-fee baselines. Firms can scope new engagements against what comparable matters actually cost to deliver.
  • Oddr
    Collections with full billing context from Intapp Billstream
    Milestone fees, holdbacks, and success components create collections complexity that AR data alone can’t navigate. Oddr gives collections teams the context to understand why an invoice is disputed or delayed.
  • Zebraworks
    End-to-end realization analytics
    Zebraworks connects worked hours through billing to cash collected across every fee arrangement type. It answers the question managing partners increasingly ask: Are our value-priced matters actually more profitable than our hourly ones, and which clients, matter types, and fee structures should we price differently next time?

Availability

The Intapp Profitability Network is available now. Founding partner integrations will reach general availability throughout the fall, following completion of the Intapp certification program. Firms interested in connecting Intapp Time with Celeste and Billstream to network partners can contact their Intapp account team or visit intapp.com/partners/profitability-network/.

Supporting quote

Ken Houseman, Vice President and General Manager, Intapp Time

“Firm profitability has always been a chain problem, not a billing problem. Intapp Time with Celeste and Billstream govern the core of that chain; the network extends it, connecting the specialist capabilities that complete each stage in one system firms can rely on. The shift toward value pricing isn’t a trend firms can watch from a distance and address later — it’s a structural change driven by AI on both sides of the client relationship. The firms that compete on value in the next decade are the ones building their data infrastructure now.”

  • Learn more at Intapp

news.titleEn: Teaching AI your firm’s language: How ontologies reduce hallucinations and drive down token consumption
news.titleZh: 教会AI理解律所语言：本体如何减少幻觉并降低token消耗
news.summaryZh:
私募股权公司和投资银行常需AI生成团队在LP、顾问及被投企业间互动情况的报告。某公司已通过MCP服务器将前沿模型接入记录系统，但数据对象“interaction”的含义仅限内部，模型无法理解“团队互动”与“interaction”的映射，只能多轮猜测，耗费时间、token并侵蚀信任。更严重的是，若AI生成的组合摘要误分类资产，合伙人无法解释，且AI未标记不确定性。文章认为这并非模型失败，而是数据架构失败，可完全预防。

私募资本和投资银行因数据组织独特而尤为暴露：通用模型对“利润率”“互动”等术语只能猜测，错误会在IC材料、LP报告和监管审查中传播。中型公司技术团队精简，将AI接入Intapp DealCloud或数据仓库时易出错；大型企业虽资源充足，但复杂栈中错误答案影响更大。解决方案是构建上下文引擎，为AI提供公司专属语言。该引擎分层构建：实体、术语表、本体（概念关系图）、公司模型（含数据模式契约）、知识图谱（本体与记录结合）、语义层（AI消费的统一治理层）及溯源（可追溯答案来源）。

上下文引擎能减少token消耗、提升响应速度并确保答案准确可复现。Gartner指出强调语义结构可提高模型准确性并降低计算成本；语义路由研究显示延迟降低47.1%。溯源使输出可验证，治理层在生成token前执行权限控制，保护数据隐私。从问答系统转向决策系统时，本体使AI能安全行动。最后，建议在模型无关平台上构建上下文引擎，保持本体、技能和剧本可移植，避免绑定单一供应商。
news.bodyHtml:
Private equity firms and investment banks regularly need something that, in the age of AI, should be simple: a report summarizing their team’s engagements across LPs, advisors, and portfolio companies. One firm had already connected a frontier model to their system of record through an MCP server. It should have taken seconds.

It didn’t. That firm stored those engagements as a data object called “interaction” – a label that meant something specific inside that firm, but nowhere else. The model had no idea “team engagement” mapped to “interaction”, or how those objects relate to one another. So it did what generic models do when they didn’t know: it guessed, produced something plausible, and waited to be corrected. It took several rounds of prompting to get to the right answer. Every round cost time, tokens, and a little more trust.

Here is the version of that story that actually keeps people up at night. A senior partner drops an AI-generated portfolio summary into an LP meeting. One asset is miscategorized, because the model reached for a generic sector definition instead of the firm’s own taxonomy. The LP asks for a follow-up. The partner can’t explain the number. Most people read that and conclude the model wasn’t ready. I’d argue the opposite. The model was ready. The data foundation underneath it was not. This is not a model failure. It is a data architecture failure — and it is entirely preventable.

Every firm organizes its data differently — from its peers, and from every horizontal tool on the market. “Margin above a threshold” – could refer to EBITDA margin, EBIT margin, or another metric depending on the firm’s taxonomy. “Interaction” could be a call, a due-diligence session, or a fundraising touchpoint. In private capital, it travels — into an IC deck, an LP report, a regulatory review — and by the time someone catches it, it has already been quoted.

Mid-market firms feel this most acutely because they are the least protected. They typically run lean technology teams with no dedicated Chief AI Officer. The person wiring an AI tool into Intapp DealCloud or a data warehouse is doing it alongside five other jobs, often without deep data-architecture experience. They bought a horizontal assistant, pointed it at the CRM, and assumed it would work. When it quietly misclassifies a deal stage or flags the wrong LP relationship, there is no specialist standing there to catch it.

Enterprise firms face the same structural problem at greater scale and higher stakes. DealCloud for the deal and relationship data, a portfolio-monitoring system, a data platform like Snowflake, and a mandate from the CEO to connect all of it onto one AI platform so that fifty people can do the work that used to take a hundred. The ambition is real and achievable. But the more complex the stack, the more damage a system that guesses can do. A wrong answer about fund exposure or LP commitment status at a firm managing tens of billions doesn’t stay contained.

The fix isn’t a better prompt or a bigger model. It’s giving the AI your firm’s language before it ever sees the question. That’s what a context engine does, and it’s built as a stack — each layer adding meaning the one below it can’t provide.

The context engine, layer by layer

It’s worth being precise about the pieces, because the terms get used interchangeably and they are not the same thing. Each layer below builds on the one under it, and the AI consumes the result as a single semantic layer.

At the base are entities: the raw objects your firm tracks — deals, companies, funds, contacts. On their own they are just records in a table, with no shared meaning attached.

Glossaries sit on top — the agreed business definitions that fix what a term means, so “margin” or “commitment” resolves to one specific thing across the firm rather than whatever each user happens to assume.

An ontology is the structured map of how those concepts relate: the classes, the relationships between them, and the rules that constrain them. It goes beyond a glossary — a glossary agrees what each word means in isolation; the ontology adds that a fund holds investments, that an LP commits to a fund, that an interaction connects people at companies to a deal, and that certain combinations are not allowed. It is the blueprint.

Your firm model is that blueprint configured to your firm specifically — your taxonomies, your deal stages, your fund vintages. It is held together by data schema contracts: formal, enforced agreements about what each field means, its type, and its permitted values, so the same question cannot return two different answers depending on who filled a field in.

The knowledge graph is the ontology brought to life with your actual records. Entities become nodes, relationships become edges, and the result is a navigable network of who relates to what — this LP, across these funds, through these advisors, on these deals. It is the blueprint, populated.

The semantic layer is the whole of it — the unified, governed layer the AI actually consumes. When someone asks a plain-language question, the semantic layer resolves what they mean before the model touches anything, mapping “team engagements across LPs” onto the right objects and relationships instead of leaving the model to reverse-engineer your schema on the fly.

One more concept makes the output trustworthy: provenance — the traceable lineage of any answer, showing exactly which records, fields, and logic produced it. It is what turns an output you have to trust into one you can verify.

Put these together and you have a context engine: the intelligence layer that activates your proprietary data. Here is what changes when it is in place. 

Fewer tokens, faster answers, right the first time

Token spend is becoming a real operating cost, and semantic pre-resolution is how firms stop it from spiraling. When the intent is resolved before the model runs, you stop paying for the model to grope around your schema across several rounds of clarifying prompts. That’s consistent with what analysts are seeing industry-wide: emphasizing semantic structure in AI-ready data has been linked to meaningfully higher model accuracy and lower compute costs, according to Gartner, Inc. One well-formed request replaces a back-and-forth. At firm-wide scale, that adds up to a line item a CFO will notice — which makes this a finance conversation, not just an IT one.

Latency improves for the same reason. Every round of “that’s not quite what I meant” is dead time in front of a partner who wanted the answer thirty seconds ago. Pre-resolved intent means the model does less work and returns faster – a pattern that also shows up externally, where recent research on semantic routing for large language models found a 47.1% latency reduction alongside the token savings.

Accuracy stops being probabilistic. A model reading raw fields guesses at meaning. A model reading through an ontology and schema contracts is handed the meaning — so the same question yields the same, correct, reproducible answer whether it’s asked today or next quarter.

The answer you can actually defend

If AI surfaces a recommendation, someone will eventually have to explain why. This is where provenance earns its place. An ontology-grounded output is traceable: you can point to the records and logic behind it. A prompt-engineered output is not — it’s a plausible sentence with no receipts. In an industry that lives with IC scrutiny, LP diligence, and regulators, “the AI said so” is not an answer. “Here is the lineage” is.

Governance runs deeper than auditability. Because the context engine sits between the user and the data, it’s also where permissioning is enforced. The AI should only ever reason over data the person asking is actually entitled to see — deal-team walls, LP confidentiality, information barriers between funds. Bolt an assistant directly onto a warehouse and those boundaries blur. Route it through a governed semantic layer and entitlements are applied before a single token is generated. That same architecture protects data privacy: your proprietary relationships and firm knowledge stay inside your environment, resolved locally, rather than being shipped wholesale to a model provider to figure out on its own.

From answers to a decision system

Everything so far assumes AI is answering questions. The larger shift is AI that acts — recommending the next step, drafting the IC memo, flagging the LP whose commitment is lapsing, moving a deal to the next stage. That is a decision system, not a chatbot, and it raises the stakes on everything above it. A wrong answer wastes a few minutes; a wrong action, taken automatically, propagates before anyone reviews it. A decision system is only ever as trustworthy as the model of the firm beneath it — the same ontology that grounds an answer is what lets an agent decide and act reproducibly, inside the permissions it has been granted, with every decision traceable to the reasoning behind it. The firms that treat AI as a decision system, rather than a search box, are the ones that will safely let it touch real work.

Build on a platform you own, not a model you rent

One last point, because it’s the decision that compounds. The AI landscape is moving too fast to bet your intelligence layer on a single provider. We don’t know which model will be best — or cheapest — a year from now. If you build your skills and workflows directly on one LLM, you’ve tied your firm’s institutional knowledge to that vendor’s roadmap and token pricing, and switching later means rebuilding everything.

Build the context engine on a model-agnostic platform instead, and your ontology, skills, and playbooks stay portable. You can route each task to the most cost-efficient model that does the job well, and swap providers as the frontier moves — without touching the layer that makes your firm your firm.

Because that’s the real point. The ontology is not the moat. Your method, your judgment, your institutional knowledge — that’s the moat. The ontology is what finally makes it usable by AI — and a decision system built on it doesn’t just answer with your firm’s knowledge, it acts with your firm’s judgment. Most firms connected a model to their CRM and assumed that was enough. It never was.

news.summaryZh: 在PLI为珍·伦纳德新书《史无前例》举办的活动中，这位PLI创新委员会主席探讨了律所如何应对AI、客户期望变化与人才发展挑战。她最初尝试写商业书但觉枯燥，改用彗星比喻又觉怪异，最终以一家律所五天静修为故事框架，设定文化驱动型律所在行业整合压力下可能被大律所吸收。书中角色取材于她接触的律所人物：资深合伙人罗伯特·金意识到自己可能不在律所未来中；创收合伙人威廉·克莱普特不愿改变；初级律师亚历克斯技术导向，但同事对技术冲击工作与发展感到焦虑。与2008年金融危机后不同，生成式AI加速了所有潜在动态，并与监管改革、定价压力、人才发展、混合办公和客户期望交织；混合办公使指导初级律师更难，高层领导已开始参与解决。书中强调设计思维，要求从理解服务对象出发，超越假设，围绕人构建服务。她所描述的未来律所是“以人为本”的，即在AI、监管改革、新商业模式和多代劳动力等变化中把人置于中心；若仅以技术替代人员或节省成本，将损害文化，更好的问题是技术如何增强人类技能。在法律教育方面，她希望解决律所长期依赖客户补贴初级律师学习的问题：若AI改变入门级工作经济模式，律所将无法再为学习收费，因此需重新思考律师入职前后的培训，可能出现第三方培训系统和新职业路径。她最希望行业更健康，因为律师福祉危机长期存在，太多有才华的人因工作条件流失；若新模型让人。
news.bodyHtml:
At a recent Practising Law Institute event celebrating the publication of her book, Unprecedented, Jen Leonard sat down for a Q&A to discuss the challenges and opportunities reshaping the legal profession. Leonard, Chair of PLI’s Innovation Council, explored how law firms can respond to AI, evolving client expectations, and talent development challenges. The following edited Q&A highlights key insights from their conversation.

What led you to write Unprecedented, and why did you choose to tell it as a story rather than a traditional business book?

At first, I tried to write a very straightforward business book about the changes in the profession, the history of legal practice, and frameworks for innovation. But when I read it, I thought, “I wouldn’t even want to read this.” It was too dry. Then I tried a version focused on AI and existential change, with a metaphor about a comet coming toward Earth and dinosaurs not seeing it coming. That was too weird.

The breakthrough came when I realized I could tell the story of a law firm going through a five-day retreat. At first, I thought no law firm would ever take that much time away. But then I needed an inciting event that would make such a retreat believable. With so much consolidation happening in the legal industry, I imagined a culture-driven firm under pressure to be absorbed by a much larger firm with a very different identity. That gave the story urgency.

The book includes a number of fictional characters. Were they inspired by people you have encountered in your work with law firms?

Definitely. The characters are composites of people we meet all the time in our work with law firms.

One of my favorite characters is Robert Kim, a senior partner who has spent his entire career at the firm. He is practical, logical, and very heads down. Over the course of the retreat, he begins to realize that when people are talking about succession planning and the future of the firm, he may not really be part of that future. He was inspired by a partner I met at a law firm retreat who was preparing to retire and told me he could not imagine what he would do with his life because he had been practicing law for 45 years.

I wanted to contrast Robert with William Klept, the rainmaker partner who is doing very well in the current system and does not really want to change. He represents the people who have been successful under the existing model and understandably question why the firm should disrupt it.

The junior associates were also important. Alex is tech-forward, enthusiastic, entrepreneurial, and eager to use new tools. But he is surrounded by other junior associates who are anxious about what technology means for their jobs, their development, and their critical thinking.

What makes this moment different from earlier periods of change in the legal profession?

After the 2008 financial crisis, the relationship between law firms and clients changed. Clients demanded more for less, legal operations grew inside corporate law departments, and technology became more sophisticated, especially in litigation. There was innovation, but often it did not really touch the core business model.

Generative AI changes that. It accelerates all the underlying dynamics and makes them much more real. It intersects with regulatory reform, pricing pressure, talent development, hybrid work, and client expectations.

At the same time, hybrid work has made mentoring junior associates more difficult. Add AI to that, and firms are asking how they will develop judgment, critical thinking, and professional identity in lawyers who may be doing less of the traditional junior-level work. What feels different now is that top leadership is engaged. Chairs and managing partners are saying, “We need to figure this out.”

A major framework in the book is design thinking. How does that apply to law firms?

Traditionally, experts design systems for the people they serve without really consulting those people. Design thinking asks us to begin by understanding the human beings on the receiving end. That might be a client, an associate, a self-represented litigant, or even another department inside the firm.

The goal is to move beyond assumptions. Lawyers are comfortable delivering memos, advice, and hourly services in familiar ways. But did the client ask for that format? Or are we just repeating what the system taught us?

Design thinking helps firms define problems differently, generate more creative solutions, and build services around the people they are trying to serve.

You describe the future law firm as “human-centered.” What does that mean?

A human-centered law firm confronts major changes, including AI, regulatory reform, new business models, and multigenerational workforces, while keeping human beings at the center.

If firms look at technology only as a way to replace people, reduce headcount, or save costs, they risk damaging their cultures. The better question is how technology can augment human skills.

A human-centered firm asks: What do our clients need from us as people? What do our associates need to develop? How do we use technology to strengthen the best human parts of our work, rather than erode them?

What do you hope changes in legal education and lawyer development over the next decade?

I hope we are forced to solve a problem that has existed for a long time. Law firms have historically relied on clients to subsidize the learning process for junior lawyers. But if AI changes the economics of entry-level work, firms will no longer be able to bill for learning in the same way.

That means we need to rethink how lawyers are trained before they arrive at firms and after they get there. My hope is that new models emerge. Maybe third parties help firms build better training systems. Maybe new career paths open up for law graduates who want to use different skills. Most of all, I hope the profession becomes healthier.

We have had a crisis in lawyer well-being for a long time. We have lost too many talented people because of the conditions in which lawyers work. If new models allow people to spend more time mentoring, using judgment, and doing meaningful human work, then maybe we can create a profession where more people can thrive.

–

For more information about Jen Leonard’s new book, ‘Unprecedented: Designing a Human-Centered Law Firm When Everything Is Changing,’ please see here.

—

If firms look at technology only as a way to replace people, reduce headcount, or save costs, they risk damaging their cultures. The better question is how technology can augment human skills.

A human-centered firm asks: What do our clients need from us as people? What do our associates need to develop? How do we use technology to strengthen the best human parts of our work, rather than erode them?

What do you hope changes in legal education and lawyer development over the next decade?

I hope we are forced to solve a problem that has existed for a long time. Law firms have historically relied on clients to subsidize the learning process for junior lawyers. But if AI changes the economics of entry-level work, firms will no longer be able to bill for learning in the same way.

That means we need to rethink how lawyers are trained before they arrive at firms and after they get there. My hope is that new models emerge. Maybe third parties help firms build better training systems. Maybe new career paths open up for law graduates who want to use different skills. Most of all, I hope the profession becomes healthier.

We have had a crisis in lawyer well-being for a long time. We have lost too many talented people because of the conditions in which lawyers work. If new models allow people to spend more time mentoring, using judgment, and doing meaningful human work, then maybe we can create a profession where more people can thrive.

news.titleEn: Harvey Raises $550m at $15.5bn Val, Buys Guardrails AI
news.titleZh: Harvey以155亿美元估值融资5.5亿美元，收购Guardrails AI
news.summaryZh:
Harvey宣布完成5.5亿美元融资，估值达155亿美元，由Diffusion和Lightspeed Venture Partners联合领投。该公司同时收购了总部位于旧金山的AI安全平台Guardrails AI，后者专注于智能体的AI安全。Guardrails是AI可靠性与模拟基础设施领域的先驱，创建了首个开源AI护栏，帮助团队发现智能体偏离预期行为之处并实时管理智能体风险。Guardrails联合创始人Shreya Rajpal和Zayd Simjee及其团队将加入Harvey的产品与工程组织。这是Harvey在2026年的第四次收购。

本轮融资紧随Harvey推出首个后训练开放权重模型以及Harvey LAB法律智能体基准之后，将加速Harvey帮助律师事务所、内部法务团队和专业服务公司大规模构建并拥有自身智能能力的努力。现有投资者Sequoia、Kleiner Perkins、a16z、Coatue、Conviction、Elad Gil、Evantic、GIC、Goldman Sachs Alternatives、Verified Capital和WNDR参投，新投资者包括Diffusion、Lightspeed、Sapphire Ventures和Whale Rock。企业利用AI加速竞争优势的机遇前所未有，Harvey希望成为法律团队在全球的合作伙伴，并计划招聘和发展业内最佳团队，支持客户度过下一波AI转型。目前80%的Am Law 100律师事务所使用Harvey，众多全球领先的内部法务团队也在使用，包括财富10强中的五家。
news.bodyHtml:
Harvey has announced a $550m funding round at a $15.5B valuation, co-led by Diffusion and Lightspeed Venture Partners. It has also bought San Francisco-based Guardrails AI, an AI security platform for agents.

Guardrails is a pioneer of AI reliability and simulation infrastructure, they said. They created the first open-source AI guardrails that help teams find where their agents stray from intended behaviour and manage agent risk in real time. Guardrails’ co-founders, Shreya Rajpal and Zayd Simjee, and their team will join Harvey’s product and engineering organization. This marks Harvey’s fourth acquisition of 2026.

The latest raise follows the introduction of Harvey’s first post-trained open-weight model and the launch of Harvey LAB, the Legal Agent Benchmark. It will accelerate Harvey’s efforts to help law firms, in-house legal teams, and professional services firms build and own their intelligence at scale, they said.

Existing investors Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, a16z, Coatue, Conviction, Elad Gil, Evantic, GIC, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Verified Capital, and WNDR participated in the round. New investors include Diffusion, Lightspeed, Sapphire Ventures, and Whale Rock.

Harvey co-founders Winston Weinberg and Gabe Pereyra said together: ‘The opportunity for companies to accelerate their competitive advantage with AI has never been higher. Harvey wants to be the global partner legal teams turn to for this work, and we plan to hire and develop the best team in the space to support our clients through the next wave of AI transformation.’

They added that 80% of Am Law 100 law firms now use Harvey alongside many of the world’s leading in-house legal teams, including five of the Fortune 10.

Congrats to the Harvey team.

More AL comment soon.—

See you at Legal Innovators New York – Nov 17 and 18 – join us at the intersection of legal AI and the business of law in New York for the most important legal innovation event of the year! Day One: law firms, Day Two: inhouse. Top speakers from across the legal AI world, leading law firms, and major companies. All for one purpose: to describe and explore the frontier of legal technology. See you there!

news.titleEn: ILTACON 2026: Highlights From The Event
news.titleZh: ILTACON 2026：活动亮点回顾
news.summaryZh: 上周，作者在盖洛德酒店参加了ILTACON，该会议吸引了5700名参会者，创下历史最大规模，所有房间售罄。本周的关键词是“上下文”：NetDocuments推出了Legal Context Graph，iManage围绕Context Fabric重建了平台，Harvey则不再谈论提示词，而是谈论事项、记忆和偏好。这些变化表明，AI的卖点已从“更智能的模型”转向“真正了解律所的模型”。然而，许多中型律所尚无法接受这一理念，因为这要求数据足够干净和结构化。技术部分容易，数据整理才是难点。治理方面，Intapp产品团队指出，随着智能体开始执行实际工作，治理难度会增加。参会者反映，律所并未看到预期的效率提升，因为仍需人工核查AI工作。首席产品官Triona Buckley将此称为“验证税”，这正在削弱律所最初申请预算时的投资回报率论证。智能体AI无处不在，MCP协议在供应商对话中频繁出现，iManage用它来在Thomson Reuters CoCounsel中呈现内容，NetDocuments则保持工具中立。智能体层的好坏取决于底层基础。购买工具本身并非转型，真正的转型在于前后的工作。律所购买AI工具的速度快于重新设计工作流程的速度，这导致价值流失。Actionstep Intelligence的开发注重在用户熟悉的平台内引入AI，以减少变革阻力。
news.bodyHtml:
It was a little over a week ago that I was at the Gaylord watching 5,700 people try to find their way through that hotel again. It never gets easier no matter how many years you’ve been going. It set the record as the biggest ILTACON yet, selling out every room. Some booths were so big they had their own zip codes.

Now that I am back at my desk and have had time to reflect, here’s what I actually took away from it.

Context is the new pitch

The word of the week was context. NetDocuments has Legal Context Graph. iManage rebuilt its whole platform around Context Fabric. Harvey has stopped talking about prompts and started talking about matters, memory, and preferences. The pitch has changed. The conversation isn’t “here’s a smarter model” anymore, it’s “here’s a model that actually knows your firm.”

This message resonates. It’s also one most mid-market firms aren’t in a position to accept yet, because it assumes your data is clean and structured enough to feed it.

I heard more than one CIO say the technology part is easy! Getting the data right is the hard part. I’ve been saying some version of that for quite some time now. It’s nice to hear it from those down in the trenches day after day.

Governance and the verification tax

Governance had a different tone this year, too. Intapp’s product team said that governance gets harder, not easier, as agents start doing real work instead of just answering questions. That tracks, because the more autonomy you hand a tool, the more you need to know what it’s doing on your behalf. The most interesting insights all week came from attendees. Firms aren’t seeing the efficiency gains they expected from AI, because someone still has to check the work. Triona Buckley, our Chief Product Officer, calls it the verification tax. It’s real, and it’s wrecking the ROI case a lot of firms used to get budget approved for this tech in the first place. You can’t fix governance by buying a better tool. You fix it by knowing what the agent touched, who reviewed it, and whether it correctly actioned on ten tasks, or just moved the work around for someone to clean up later

Agents are only as good as what’s underneath them

Agentic AI was everywhere, too.  All of it sounds great in a demo.

MCP came up in many vendor conversation I had, usually described as the thing that finally lets these tools talk to each other instead of living in their own silos. iManage is using it to surface content inside Thomson Reuters CoCounsel. NetDocuments is staying tool-agnostic on purpose so firms aren’t locked into one AI vendor’s roadmap.

My thoughts?  The agent layer is only as good as what’s underneath it. An agent that can act on your behalf is a bigger deal than a chatbot that answers questions, and it needs the bigger foundation under it to be trustworthy.

Buying the tool isn’t the transformation

The reality is a firm can purchase every tool on the exhibit floor and still not change how it does the work. What I kept hearing, in sessions and in hallway conversations, was firms deploying AI the way they’d deploy a new practice management or billing system, without asking what problem it’s trying to solve or who’s supposed to change their process because of it. Buying the tool isn’t the transformation, it’s all the work that comes before and after.

Once again there were discussions about moving off the billable hour. You can’t have a serious value-pricing conversation if you don’t have the operational visibility to know what work costs. Change management remains the hard part and a big part of the transformation story. Here’s the active version:

Firms are purchasing AI tools faster than they’re redesigning workflows or deciding where humans need to stay in the loop, which is where they’re losing a lot of the promised value. While we were developing Actionstep Intelligence we were very deliberate to bring AI to our customers within a platform they already know, use and trust. This helps to reduce friction around change since the users don’t have to change the way the work or learn a new tool. 

Is bigger better?

The parties were bigger and the booths looked like small buildings. There was a lot of money spent on being seen this year. I hope there is budget left to make technology that delivers results! I guess we’ll find out next year. See you back in Nashville next Summer.

research.titleEn: GANDR: Claim Auditing for Verifiable Legal Answer Generation
research.titleZh: GANDR：面向可验证法律答案生成的声明审计
research.abstractEn: In high-stakes domains such as legal practice, a language-model answer is only useful to the extent that a reader can verify each claim against the source the system cites. Current grounded-generation pipelines score the answer as a whole, so a correct conclusion can rest on fabricated or loosely matched citations and still score well. Closing this gap requires both a system built for per-claim verification and an evaluation that measures it. We introduce GANDR (Grounded ANswer DRafter), a two-agent system in which a Drafter writes an answer in a structured legal-reasoning format and a separate Critic, with the same view as a human verifier, audits each claim against its cited source and emits a per-claim audit trace on every round. We pair it with a strict correctness criterion requiring every citation to resolve to a passage the retriever returned. On a 185-item legal benchmark where all six systems share one backbone, one retrieval surface, and one citation instruction, GANDR ranks first on every primary metric, reaching 70.8% strict accuracy and leading the strongest baseline by 11.3 points (p<0.01). Reverting the protocol-anchored commit rule lowers strict accuracy by 22.7 points, and the strict lead stays positive on three further backbones, at +3.2 to +6.5 points. This lead traces to the Drafter configuration and the protocol-anchored commit, not to rewriting. Against two law-trained annotators the audit flags under-supported claims at F1 0.84 as a binary detector, while its four-way verdict labels agree only weakly and are advisory. Code is available upon request.
research.abstractZh: 在法律实践等高风险领域，语言模型给出的答案只有在读者能够对照系统引用的来源核实每一项声明时才有用。当前基于依据的生成流程对整个答案进行评分，因此一个正确的结论可能建立在捏造或松散匹配的引用之上，却仍能获得高分。要弥合这一差距，既需要一个为逐项声明验证而构建的系统，也需要一种能够衡量它的评估方法。我们提出 GANDR（Grounded ANswer DRafter，基于依据的答案起草器），这是一个双智能体系统：起草器以结构化法律推理格式撰写答案，而一个独立的批评者——与人类验证者拥有相同视角——对照所引来源审计每一项声明，并在每一轮输出逐项声明的审计轨迹。我们为其配以严格正确性标准，要求每一条引用都必须解析到检索器返回的段落。在一个包含 185 个条目的法律基准上，所有六个系统共享同一骨干模型、同一检索面和同一引用指令，GANDR 在每一项主要指标上均排名第一，达到 70.8% 的严格准确率，并以 11.3 个百分点的优势领先最强基线（p<0.01）。将协议锚定的提交规则回退会使严格准确率下降 22.7 个百分点，而严格准确率的领先优势在另外三个骨干模型上仍保持为正，为 +3.2 至 +6.5 个百分点。这一领先优势源于起草器配置和协议锚定的提交，而非改写。对照两位受过法律训练的标注者，该审计作为二元检测器以 F1 0.84 标记出支持不足的声明，而其四类判定标签仅呈现弱一致性，且仅供参考。代码可应请求提供。

research.titleEn: LexAgentHallu: A Hierarchical Benchmark for Profiling Hallucinations in Legal Agents
research.titleZh: LexAgentHallu：面向法律智能体幻觉画像的分层基准
research.abstractEn: As large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-augmented legal agents, they introduce agentic hallucinations where tool-call and reasoning errors cascade into fabricated holdings and miscited authority. However, existing legal benchmarks evaluate only single-turn QA with outcome-level metrics, while agentic hallucination benchmarks lack legal-specific diagnostic capability. Neither answers to what extent and how a legal agent hallucinates along its trajectory. To address these limitations, we introduce LexAgentHallu, a legal agentic hallucination benchmark designed to evaluate to what extent and how legal agents fail along multi-step trajectories. Built through a four-stage expert-in-the-loop pipeline, LexAgentHallu contains 3414 instances across 17 legal categories and 6 task types. Each instance is annotated under a dual-layer hallucination taxonomy of 7 high-level categories and 27 fine-grained subclasses, covering both substantive errors and agent-procedural failures. We further design fine-grained metrics that quantify to what extent and localize how each failure occurs along an agent's execution path. Our evaluation across 18 proprietary and open-source agents uncovers a Right-Answer-Wrong-Reason effect and reveals that hallucination subclasses cluster rather than scatter, forming distinct agentic framework, legal task, and category profiles. These findings, invisible to outcome-level evaluation, validate the diagnostic power of LexAgentHallu for evaluating agentic hallucination in law.
research.abstractZh: 随着大语言模型日益被部署为工具增强的法律智能体，它们引入了智能体幻觉，即工具调用和推理错误级联为捏造的裁判要旨和错误引用的权威依据。然而，现有的法律基准仅使用结果层面的指标评估单轮问答，而智能体幻觉基准缺乏法律特定的诊断能力。两者都无法回答法律智能体在其轨迹上以何种程度以及如何产生幻觉。为解决这些局限，我们提出了LexAgentHallu，一个法律智能体幻觉基准，旨在评估法律智能体在多步轨迹上以何种程度以及如何失败。通过四阶段专家在环流程构建，LexAgentHallu包含跨17个法律类别和6种任务类型的3414个实例。每个实例都按照包含7个高层类别和27个细粒度子类的双层幻觉分类法进行标注，涵盖实质性错误和智能体程序性失败。我们进一步设计了细粒度指标，以量化失败程度并定位智能体执行路径上每次失败的发生方式。我们对18个专有和开源智能体的评估揭示了“答案正确但推理错误”效应，并发现幻觉子类呈聚集而非分散分布，形成不同的智能体框架、法律任务和类别画像。这些在结果层面评估中不可见的发现，验证了LexAgentHallu在评估法律领域智能体幻觉方面的诊断能力。

policy.summaryZh: 2024年起，国产人工智能大模型井喷式发展，“AI幻觉”“AI换脸”“AI语音克隆”等纠纷不断涌现。最高法于2025年成立《意见》起草组，经调研并听取地方法院、行业代表、专家学者及相关部门意见后形成送审稿，审判委员会逐条审阅并深入研究讨论，最终制定《最高人民法院关于依法审理涉人工智能纠纷案件的意见》，于9月7日正式施行，是第一部较为全面的关于涉人工智能纠纷案件法律适用的司法文件。《意见》明确裁判规则、强化权益保障、促进产业发展，依法规制“AI换脸拟声”“网络开盒”、算法歧视、“AI幻觉”“AI伪造证据”、AI生成内容侵犯知识产权等滥用人工智能侵害公民人格尊严、私人生活安宁、财产安全等合法权益的行为。第八条明确依法适用人格权侵害禁令制度；起草组按照审委会要求，在送审稿第四条基础上增加了针对利用人工智能技术处理死者姓名、肖像等侵害死者人格利益行为的相关内容。在责任认定方面，第三条规定法律没有明确规定适用无过错责任或者过错推定责任时，人民法院应依照过错责任原则认定侵权责任；第七条规定审慎认定生成式人工智能服务提供者的侵权责任；第六条规定认定人工智能训练是否侵害个人信息权益的标准及“合理范围”的考量因素。对显而易见的侵权情形，不排除适用民法典第一千一百九十七条认定生产者、服务提供者侵权责任。
policy.bodyText:
2024年起，国产人工智能大模型井喷式发展，以前所未有的速度渗透进人们的工作和生活。与此同时，“AI幻觉”“AI换脸”“AI语音克隆”等带来的纠纷不断涌现。这些强大的工具，正在挑战人们的合法权益。
技术是否“无责”？如何让使用者敢使用，让创新者愿创新？
近日，《最高人民法院关于依法审理涉人工智能纠纷案件的意见》（以下简称《意见》）正式发布，明确裁判规则、强化权益保障、促进产业发展。在此之前，最高法审判委员会围绕《意见》送审稿召开会议，逐条逐字审阅文本，就司法审判实践和涉人工智能纠纷案件审理的难点堵点深入研究、充分讨论。
《意见》的制定与出台遵循着怎样的思路？我国最高审判机关的最高审判组织对人工智能飞速发展过程中出现的法律问题有着怎样的观点，作出了怎样的回应？
拒绝“野蛮生长”
——供给裁判规则，引领行为规范
数据显示，2025年我国人工智能核心产业规模已突破1.2万亿元，预计到“十五五”末，相关产业规模将突破10万亿元。
高歌猛进的人工智能技术究竟“路在何方”？
“人工智能技术发展越是一日千里，向上向善、造福人类的方向越要正确锚定，监管治理的尺度越要精准把握，防范失控的措施越要及时完善。”习近平总书记的论述高屋建瓴。
每一次科技革命都离不开规范化引领、法治化保障。党中央高度重视人工智能健康发展，习近平总书记在不同场合多次强调要确保人工智能安全、可靠、可控。“十五五”规划纲要则明确，要“完善人工智能领域法律法规、政策制度、应用规范、伦理准则”。
在这样的背景下，最高法于2025年即成立《意见》起草组，在对涉人工智能政策文件和法律法规深入研究的基础上，围绕司法实践中涉人工智能重点难点问题开展系统、深入调研，逐一梳理法答网涉人工智能高频咨询问题、人民法院案例库有关入库案例裁判规则，追踪分析域外涉人工智能立法司法实践，广泛、充分听取地方法院、行业代表、专家学者以及相关政府部门的意见，经过反复修改完善后，形成《意见》送审稿。
审委会对《意见》送审稿总体认可，认为《意见》送审稿贯彻落实以习近平同志为核心的党中央关于加快高水平科技自立自强，引领发展新质生产力重大决策部署，严格遵循法律规定，坚持问题导向，立足审判实践，“对于进一步明确裁判规则、强化当事人权益保障、促进行业健康发展、服务保障创新驱动发展重大战略实施，具有积极意义”。
针对当前“AI换脸拟声”、“网络开盒”、算法歧视、“AI幻觉”、“AI伪造证据”、AI生成内容侵犯知识产权等滥用人工智能技术侵害公民人格尊严、私人生活安宁、财产安全等合法权益的行为，《意见》依法予以规制。
比如，当前利用人工智能技术“换脸”“偷声”等侵害人格权益的行为多发，侵权手段多样、隐蔽，而当事人却面临举证难、投诉渠道缺失、诉讼成本高等维权难题。对此，《意见》在第八条专门明确“依法适用人格权侵害禁令制度”，规定了这一制度在人工智能领域的细化适用，以解决传统事后诉讼难以及时高效维护当事人合法权益的问题。
围绕“AI复活逝者”这一热议话题，《意见》起草组则按照审委会要求，在送审稿第四条基础上增加了针对利用人工智能技术处理死者姓名、肖像等侵害死者人格利益行为的相关内容，使《意见》对人格权益保护的范围更加全面。
“《意见》制定出来就是要解决问题的。”有审委会委员直言。
此外，在供给裁判规则的同时，《意见》也注重行为规范引领，通过厘清各方主体的权利、义务和责任，引导和推动市场主体加强风险内控与规范管理，防范化解人工智能技术误用、滥用带来的风险。
值得注意的是，《意见》起草组考虑到人工智能仍然处在发展初期，司法实践不足，因此对于人工智能生成内容的可版权性、训练数据的合理使用等暂时看不清、拿不准，难以形成共识的问题作了留白处理。
“留白处理”不等于“无法可依”。会上，《意见》起草组汇报时表示，关于“留白处理”的问题，预备先以参考案例、法答网问答等形式加强对下指导，进一步积累经验，待条件成熟时再通过适当方式作出明确规定。审委会对这一做法予以了充分肯定。
《意见》第二十二条也明确了加强审判监督指导的路径，其中一个要求就是“充分运用人民法院案例库，加强案例指导工作，促推法律适用统一和人工智能治理规则的完善”。
技术不是“免责牌”
——人工智能提供者需承担更多社会责任
“司法人员要考虑保护广大使用者的合法权益，规范行业发展，遏制人工智能开发者、提供者等的获利冲动，促使他们对产品、服务的安全性承担更多社会责任。”
关于如何平衡保护当事人合法权益与人工智能行业发展，审委会态度十分明确。
比如，人工智能大模型训练离不开大规模训练数据，其中不可避免地涉及个人信息。如何处理由此产生的纠纷？尽管我国个人信息保护法对处理个人信息作出了约束，但条文所强调的“合理的范围”一直是司法实践中的难点，如何在司法实践中把握好这一要求？
“《意见》作为规范性文件，要为司法实践提供更加清晰的操作规则，引导人工智能企业和法院在对待公民个人信息时更加谨慎负责。”有审委会委员指出。
《意见》第六条不仅规定了人民法院认定人工智能训练是否侵害个人信息权益的标准，也对法院认定“合理范围”作出了指引，考量因素包括处理个人信息的目的与模型功能的必要性和适当性、所涉个人信息的类型、敏感程度及对个人权益的潜在影响、个人公开信息时的场景及可合理预期的使用范围等。
随着人工智能越来越多地深入民众工作和生活，“AI幻觉”侵权以及利用生成式人工智能侵权早已不再是冷门话题。无论是判决生成式人工智能服务提供者不担责的全国首例“AI幻觉”侵权案，还是判决担责的“AI幻觉”编造罪名案，都曾引起社会广泛关注和讨论。
技术有责还是无责？人工智能开发者、产品和服务提供者在什么情况下担责？怎样才能既依法保护使用者合法权益又不影响创新者的积极性？
《意见》起草组认为，人工智能应用场景广泛、案件类型多样，对不同应用场景下的人工智能侵权应依照法律规定使用不同归责原则，“这是贯彻实施民法典规定的必然要求”。而另一方面，生成式人工智能侵权与传统网络侵权在主体、价值、情境等本质特征上具有高度相似性，人工智能服务提供者的责任具备类推适用“避风港原则”（网络服务提供者在接获权利人发出的有效通知后应当采取必要措施）的正当性、合理性基础。
基于这样的考量，《意见》不仅通过第三条明确在法律没有明确规定适用无过错责任或者过错推定责任的时候，人民法院应当依照过错责任原则认定行为人是否承担侵权责任，并在第七条规定“审慎认定生成式人工智能服务提供者的侵权责任”。
行业发展初期，出于鼓励新技术发展的目的，固然需要为人工智能生产者、服务提供者卸去不必要的枷锁，但是，他们是否能因此“高枕无忧”？当他们对显而易见的侵权可能性视而不见的时候，人民法院又当如何作出判断？
“企业不能只获利不担责。”审委会对此态度明确，“在司法实践中，如果出现相关情形，人民法院将不排除适用民法典第一千一百九十七条，认定人工智能生产者、服务提供者侵权责任。”
根据民法典该条规定，网络服务提供者知道或者应当知道网络用户利用其网络服务侵害他人民事权益，未采取必要措施的，与该网络用户承担连带责任。该规定体现了“避风港原则”的例外——“红旗原则”，即当侵权事实像“红旗”一样显著时，网络服务提供者即使未收到权利人通知，也应采取删除或屏蔽措施，否则需承担连带责任。
尽管《意见》并未制定“红旗原则”相关的单独条文，但《意见》起草组成员专门围绕理解与适用《意见》撰文刊发，其中就这一问题作出回应，及时传递出最高审判机关维护人工智能健康发展的明确立场。
全面保护、筑牢底线
——强调依法惩治，完善程序规则
人工智能为生产生活带来高效与便利，也为违法犯罪提供了工具。
今年全国两会期间，最高法研究室主任周加海在接受媒体采访时表示，用AI技术炮制虚假信息、实施“AI换脸”等“深度伪造”行为日益增多，并逐渐被用于网络侮辱、诽谤等违法犯罪活动，引起了人民群众广泛关注。这类案件事实查明难、责任链条长、法律适用边界模糊，给司法带来极大挑战。
作为一部主要围绕民事纠纷展开的规则指引，《意见》也兼顾了对涉人工智能刑事案件的法律适用要求。《意见》送审稿在“基本原则”章节即开门见山亮明了“坚决依法严惩”的态度。
尽管如此，审委会仍在审议时专门强调，要更加旗帜鲜明地传递人民法院依法惩治利用人工智能实施犯罪活动的立场。
对此，修改后的《意见》专门增加了第二十条。根据该规定，行为人利用人工智能实施各类犯罪的，比如行为人激活辅助驾驶功能后利用私自安装的配件逃避辅助驾驶系统监测导致道路交通事故，构成犯罪的，将被依法追究刑事责任。
值得注意的是，《意见》一方面对于故意利用人工智能实施危害国家安全、侵犯公民权益、扰乱社会秩序等犯罪行为的，要求坚决依法严惩；另一方面对于在人工智能研发、应用中的创新性行为，则明确要依法审慎处理，恪守罪刑法定、罪责刑相适应原则。这也是人民法院在涉人工智能纠纷领域全面准确贯彻宽严相济刑事政策的体现。
程序正义是结果正义的前提和保障。针对《意见》送审稿关于涉人工智能案件程序规则的部分，审委会委员们讨论得十分细致，使《意见》更具可操作性。
比如，针对涉人工智能案件技术性、专业性强等特点，《意见》第十七条经修改完善后，增加了人民法院为查明事实“应当”履行的职责——应当依法加强诉讼引导和释明，引导当事人围绕争议事实及时全面地完成举证；对于涉及人工智能专业技术问题的，应当依法充分发挥人民陪审员、鉴定人、专家辅助人以及技术调查官的作用，辅助查明案件事实。
此外，《意见》还进一步整合了涉人工智能案件证据审查的相关内容，以使体系更加合理、完善。
9月7日，《意见》正式施行，作为第一部较为全面的关于涉人工智能纠纷案件法律适用的司法文件，其为人工智能开发者、提供者和使用者划清法治“红线”和底线，为技术探索和产业创新预留必要发展空间，从司法角度为行业从“野蛮生长”进一步向“有序繁荣”转变提供了助推力。
（ 记者 姜佩杉 ）

news.titleEn: Freshfields appoints Ram Komarraju as CIO
news.titleZh: 富瑞德律师事务所任命拉姆·科马拉朱为首席信息官
news.summaryZh: 全球律师事务所富瑞德于9月8日宣布任命拉姆·科马拉朱为首席信息官，接替今年1月离职的克里斯托弗·史密斯。科马拉朱此前任职于CLS，这是一家全球金融市场基础设施集团，运营着全球最大的外汇结算服务之一，每天处理约8万亿美元支付指令。在CLS任职期间，科马拉朱担任技术董事总经理，领导涵盖技术战略、架构、工程及数据与分析领域的团队。技术变革的速度持续为服务客户、支持员工和运营业务创造新机遇。他认为科马拉朱兼具卓越的技术领导力、战略远见以及在规模化转型方面的成熟经验，其经验将有助于富瑞德持续投资于支持事务所及客户未来成功的能力建设。此次任命标志着富瑞德在技术领导层方面的重大调整，科马拉朱将负责推动事务所的技术战略和数字化转型。
news.bodyHtml:
Global law firm Freshfields today (8 September) announces the appointment of Ram Komarraju as chief information officer, replacing Christopher Smith, who left in January this year.

Komarraju joins Freshfields from CLS, a global financial market infrastructure group that operates one of the world’s largest foreign exchange settlement services, processing approximately $8tn in payment instructions every day. Most recently, as managing director of technology, Komarraju led teams spanning technology strategy, architecture, engineering, and data and analytics.

Advertisement

Alan Mason, global managing partner at Freshfields, said: “The pace of technological change continues to create new opportunities for how we serve clients, support our people and operate our business. Ram brings an exceptional combination of technology leadership, strategic vision and a proven track record of delivering transformation at scale. His experience will be invaluable as we continue investing in the capabilities that will support the future success of our firm and our clients.”

We’ll bring you more shortly.

Advertisement
news.bodyText:
Global law firm Freshfields today (8 September) announces the appointment of Ram Komarraju as chief information officer, replacing Christopher Smith, who left in January this year.

Komarraju joins Freshfields from CLS, a global financial market infrastructure group that operates one of the world’s largest foreign exchange settlement services, processing approximately $8tn in payment instructions every day. Most recently, as managing director of technology, Komarraju led teams spanning technology strategy, architecture, engineering, and data and analytics.

Alan Mason, global managing partner at Freshfields, said: “The pace of technological change continues to create new opportunities for how we serve clients, support our people and operate our business. Ram brings an exceptional combination of technology leadership, strategic vision and a proven track record of delivering transformation at scale. His experience will be invaluable as we continue investing in the capabilities that will support the future success of our firm and our clients.”
news.relevanceReason: 该新闻主要报道律师事务所高管人事任命，涉及技术领导角色，但未具体提及法律AI或法律科技产品，属于法律行业技术管理范畴，与核心法律AI报道关联度中等。

news.titleEn: Lawfront returns to M&A trail with FJG and Farleys tuck-in acquisitions
news.titleZh: Lawfront重启并购步伐，FJG与Farleys完成补强收购
news.summaryZh: 私募股权支持的律所服务集团Lawfront恢复收购扩张，旗下成员所Fisher Jones Greenwood与Farleys分别完成补强收购，收购Giles Wilson和Houldsworth Solicitors。过去五年，Lawfront已完成18笔收购。这些收购由集团的收购融资工具提供资金，据报Lawfront在2026年8月再融资后将该工具规模扩大一倍。集团旗下七家律所已完成11笔补强收购，包括上述交易，使集团总收入预计达到1.75亿英镑。9月8日宣布的收购是新任首席执行官Peter Martin-Simon于2026年9月1日上任后的首批交易。Martin-Simon接替Neil Lloyd，后者带领Lawfront从2022年不足1000万英镑增长至2025年5月超过1.3亿英镑，离职时收入约1.7亿英镑，Lawfront称其为计划退休。集团战略是“区域领导者，全国规模”，旨在将各品牌定位为区域领导者，收购较小律所以提升市场形象、业务深度，有时还有业务广度。对FJG而言，收购加深私人客户专业能力并扩展至南埃塞克斯；对Farleys而言，增加住宅物业和私人客户业务深度，并向北扩展足迹。表现最佳的平台律所通过有机增长和补强收购，在三到五年内规模翻倍。加速增长得益于支持集团律所采用技术和AI、对人员的投资以及完成进一步收购的财务支持。集团已将各律所整合到共享云基础设施，包括集团级文档管理系统NetDocuments和AI市场平台Jylo作为共享AI平台。预计未来几周将宣布更多AI投资消息。该模式为较小律所提供了无法独立实现的规模化路径。
news.bodyHtml:
By Tom Saunders

Private equity-backed legal services group Lawfront has resumed its acquisition drive, with member firms Fisher Jones Greenwood and Farleys completing tuck-in deals, acquiring Giles Wilson and Houldsworth Solicitors respectively. Lawfront has now made 18 acquisitions over the past five years.

Advertisement

Axel Koelsch, chief operating officer at Lawfront, told Legal IT Insider that the acquisitions were funded through the firm’s acquisition facility, which Lawfront reportedly doubled in size following its refinancing in August 2026.

The seven firms in the Lawfront group have made 11 tuck-in acquisitions including the ones described above, bringing the group’s total revenue to a projected £175m. The acquisitions announced today (8 September) are the first since the appointment of new CEO, Peter Martin-Simon, who stepped into the role on 1st September 2026. Martin-Simon succeeds Neil Lloyd, who led Lawfront’s growth from under £10m in 2022 to over £130m by May 2025 and circa £170m revenue by the time of his departure, which Lawfront described as a planned retirement.

Advertisement

“Our strategy is regional leaders, national scale,” Koelsch told Legal IT Insider. “We aim to position individual brands as leaders in their region… we look to acquire smaller firms and really bolster the market profile, depth of practice, and in some cases, breadth of practice.” For FJG, the acquisition deepens private client expertise and expands its reach into South Essex; for Farleys, it adds residential property and private client depth while extending its footprint further north.

Koelsch said Lawfront’s best-performing platform firms “double in size over three to five years” through a combination of organic growth and tuck-in acquisitions like the Giles Wilson and Houldsworth deals.

Lawfront says its accelerated growth is driven by its support for tech and AI adoption across group firms, investment in people, and the financial backing to complete further acquisitions. The group has already consolidated its firms onto shared cloud infrastructure, including NetDocuments as a group-wide document management system and AI marketplace Jylo as its shared AI platform. Lawfront is expected to announce further news about its AI investments in the coming weeks.

Koelsch said the model gives smaller firms a route to scale they could not achieve independently. “You can, as a small firm with a small ownership group, get stuck,” he said. “The path to scale from that size otherwise is simply not possible to achieve.”

news.titleEn: On LawNext: Casefleet Founder Jeff Kerr on Fact Management in the Age of AI
news.titleZh: LawNext播客：Casefleet创始人Jeff Kerr谈AI时代的事实管理
news.summaryZh:
时间线已成为法律科技最热门的类别之一，众多AI初创公司承诺在几分钟内将混乱的证据记录转化为结构化时间线。Jeff Kerr及其公司Casefleet比同行早了十多年。Kerr于2010年法学院毕业后，做出他称之为疯狂的决定：将创办律所作为毕业后的第一份工作。在经营雇佣业务时，他发现赢得案件的关键在于对时间线了如指掌，但当时构建时间线的唯一工具是Word文档和大量耐心。于是他自学编程，于2015年离开执业并创立Casefleet。

在LawNext本期节目中，Kerr讨论了在AI到来之际，构建事实管理软件十年后的现状。上个月，Casefleet推出了Casey，一个对话式AI代理，可提出事实、将其与法律问题关联并起草文件，其引用引擎会拒绝任何与底层文档原文不匹配的引用。Kerr刻意严格限定AI的权限：Casefleet的代理在自主研究和迭代意义上是完全代理化的，但保持只读——不会发送邮件、拨打电话或提交任何文件。其他话题包括：为何Casefleet在AI之前的数据模型成为AI的正确基础，以及经典版Casefleet为何与Casey并行运行；公司回归电子取证，包括新增文档制作，以及Kerr为何不追逐TB级案件；如果前沿AI实验室进一步进军法律领域，专业诉讼工具将面临什么；以及为何自2018年盈利且基本自筹资金的Casefleet可能在未来一年寻求外部资本。
news.bodyHtml:
Chronologies have become one of legal tech’s hottest categories, with a wave of AI startups promising to turn a messy evidentiary record into a structured timeline in minutes. Jeff Kerr and his company Casefleet were more than a decade ahead of the pack.

Kerr finished law school in 2010 and made what he calls the crazy decision to start a law firm as his first job after graduating. Running an employment practice, he found that winning cases came down to knowing the chronology cold. But the only tools for building one were a Word document and a lot of patience. So he taught himself to code, left practice in 2015, and founded Casefleet.

On this episode of LawNext, Kerr joins me to discuss what a decade of building fact-management software looks like now that AI has arrived. Last month, Casefleet launched Casey, a conversational AI agent that proposes facts, links them to legal issues, and drafts documents — with a citation engine that rejects any citation not matching the exact text of the underlying document.

Kerr deliberately draws a hard line on what he will let his AI do. Casefleet’s agent is fully agentic in the sense of researching and iterating on its own, he says, but it stays read-only – it will not send emails, make calls, or file anything.

Among the other topics we cover:

  • Why Casefleet’s pre-AI data model turned out to be the right foundation for AI, and why classic Casefleet still runs alongside Casey.

  • The company’s move back toward e-discovery, including newly added document production, and why Kerr isn’t chasing terabyte-scale cases.

  • What happens to specialized litigation tools if the frontier AI labs push further into legal.

  • Why Casefleet, profitable since 2018 and largely bootstrapped, may raise outside capital in the coming year.

news.titleEn: Alex Su takes over as president of Latitude Legal
news.titleZh: Alex Su 接任 Latitude Legal 总裁
news.summaryZh: 灵活法律服务提供商 Latitude Legal 已将首席营收官 Alex Su 提升为总裁，联合创始人兼首席执行官 Ross Booher 移交日常运营控制权，但仍任首席执行官，以便更专注于长期战略。这家总部位于纳什维尔的公司在 2013 年成立，运营灵活人才模式，将经验丰富的律师以项目或聘用方式安置到律所和企业法务部门，现已发展到 20 个办公室，服务全美客户并有国际安置。Su 的职责由此前专注销售、营销和收入增长显著拓宽。Latitude 通过由前律所合伙人和资深内部律师组成的团队实现差异化，Su 称他们为“高级决策者”，这些律师多年执业建立声誉，受各自社区信任并对其负责。公司计划进一步深化该模式。在行业辩论聚焦效率提升和律师人数可能减少之际，Su 认为其团队因深厚知识库和判断力而比以往更被需要。他说 AI 日益进步并从实验阶段转向律所和法务部门运营化，因此需要有人监督 AI 创建的工作产品，对拥有丰富深度判断经验的律师需求巨大。他补充，当客户无法雇佣全职员工或获得编制批准时，Latitude 可提供灵活法律人才；信任和问责至关重要，其高素质、经过验证的律师由客户服务团队挑选，也深受客户群信任。Latitude 的人才库包括超过 7,000 名预先审查的律师，许多人已有使用 AI、合同生命周期管理平台、事项管理系统和其他法律技术的经验。Su 说他的律师经常自己充当培训师。
news.bodyHtml:
Flexible legal services provider Latitude Legal has promoted chief revenue officer Alex Su to president, in a move that sees co-founder and chief executive Ross Booher hand over day-to-day operational control of the business. 

The appointment comes as the Nashville-headquartered flexible legal talent provider looks to accelerate its growth and expand a model that Su believes is becoming increasingly relevant as law firms and corporate legal departments grapple with the realities of AI adoption. 

Advertisement

Speaking to Legal IT Insider ahead of the announcement, Su said the move marks a significant broadening of his role, which had previously focused on sales, marketing and revenue growth. While Booher remains chief executive, operational responsibility for many parts of the business is shifting to Su, allowing the founder to focus more on long-term strategy. 

Founded in 2013, Latitude operates a flexible talent model that places experienced attorneys into law firms and corporate legal departments on a project or engagement basis. The company has grown to 20 offices and serves clients across the US, with international placements as well. 

Advertisement

Unlike many providers in the sector, Latitude says it differentiates itself through a team made up of former law firm partners and senior in-house lawyers. “We call them senior decision makers,” Su said. “These are lawyers who spent many years building a reputation while practising law so they’re trusted by and accountable to their own communities.” 

The company now plans to lean further into that model. “We are really interested in expanding,” Su said. “What we’ve been doing works. We want to double down and triple down on that model.” 

At a time when much of the legal industry debate has centred on efficiency gains and potential reductions in lawyer headcount, Su argues that his team are more required than ever thanks to their deep knowledge bank and judgment. 

“You’ve got all this great AI getting better and better every day,” he said. “You also have it shifting from the experimental stage to all of these law firms and legal departments figuring out how to operationalise it.” 

What that means, Su says, is that someone needs to oversee the work product that’s being created by AI, “and so we’re seeing a huge amount of demand for lawyers, human lawyers who have significant experience in this deep judgement.” 

He adds: “Where we fit in is that when everyone can’t hire quite a FTEs or get approval for headcount, we can provide a contingent workforce. So flexible legal talent. And where what’s interesting is that what appears to be working really well is that trust and accountability matter so much here. Where if you’re not sure about what the work product is being created by AI, you’ve got high caliber proven attorneys who are selected by our client services team who are also highly trusted by our client base.” 

Latitude’s talent pool includes more than 7,000 pre-vetted attorneys, many of whom already have experience using AI, contract lifecycle management platforms, matter management systems and other legal technologies. 

What will be interesting when it comes to all flexible legal services providers is the extent to which, from a governance standpoint, they will have to prove they are trained on certain technologies, although Su says that his attorneys often act as trainers themselves.

news.titleEn: Richmond Vona Opens Claims Across 8 Insurance Carriers with a 100% Success Rate Using Lexafide
news.titleZh: Richmond Vona借助Lexafide在8家保险公司成功开立索赔，成功率100%
news.summaryZh: 总部位于加利福尼亚州帕洛阿尔托的Lexafide公司，是一家专为律师事务所打造的AI语音代理平台。该公司于2026年9月8日宣布，其与纽约州布法罗的人身伤害律师事务所Richmond Vona, LLC合作部署的成果已对外公布。在过去一个月中，Lexafide的AI代理代表Richmond Vona在八家保险公司（包括State Farm、Progressive和GEICO）成功开立了11起新的机动车事故索赔，成功率达到100%，并正确完成了每家保险公司的受理流程，且在每个案例中都获得了索赔编号。此外，这些AI代理还充当Richmond Vona现有索赔案件的跟进者，记录了23项针对PIP账目和IME报告的跟进请求，并逐一追踪至解决。与Lexafide的合作展示了人身伤害业务中深思熟虑的自动化实践，即技术围绕团队实际工作方式构建。随着业务从索赔开立扩展到PIP和IME报告请求，他们看到了在机动车事故索赔全生命周期中提升效率的切实机会。Lexafide持续扩大其在原告方及人身伤害律师事务所中的影响力，其中索赔开立和跟进代理是新客户最常见的切入点。
news.bodyHtml:
The Buffalo-based personal injury firm is using Lexafide’s AI voice agents to open new motor vehicle accident claims and follow up on PIP and IME requests on existing cases

 

[Palo Alto, CA] — [9/8/2026] — Lexafide, an AI voice agent platform built for law firms, today announced results from its deployment with Richmond Vona, LLC, a personal injury firm based in Buffalo, New York, with offices across Western New York. Over the past month, Lexafide’s agents opened 11 new motor vehicle accident claims on Richmond Vona’s behalf across eight carriers — including State Farm, Progressive, and GEICO — with a 100% success rate, correctly navigating each carrier’s own intake process and securing a claim number in every case. The agents are also acting as chasers on Richmond Vona’s existing claims, logging 23 follow-up requests for PIP ledgers and IME reports and tracking each through to resolution.

“Our work with Lexafide shows what thoughtful automation can look like in a personal injury practice: technology built around the way our team actually works. As we continue to expand from claims establishment into PIP and IME report requests, we see a real opportunity to improve efficiency across the MVC claims lifecycle.” said Lizzie DePalma, Operations Lead. 

Lexafide continues to expand its footprint among plaintiff and personal injury firms, with claims-opening and chaser agents among the most common entry points for new clients.

news.summaryZh: OpenAI于9月3日发布最新前沿模型GPT-6 Astra，号称迄今“最智能、最一致”的模型，初期仅向有限组织开放，后续将扩展至ChatGPT Plus、Pro、Business和企业用户，以及通过OpenAI API、微软Azure和AWS Bedrock提供。Astra使用包含在现有ChatGPT订阅额度内，企业管理员需手动启用，默认关闭。早期法律界反馈显示，其关键进步不在于生成更佳答案，而在于保持任务目标、理解预期结果并减少人工提示地执行工作流。法律科技顾问Natalie Foster（Legally Fond咨询公司创始人、数字律所Inspire Legal Group创始人）测试了复杂房产交易案例，称Astra“与5.6截然不同”，能全程跟随任务，减少因错误提示导致的人为失误，并主动建议填补信息缺口及改进系统。OpenAI早期法律测试中，Harvey应用研究主管Niko Grupen表示，Astra在复杂法律任务上较GPT-5.6 Sol有“显著质量提升”，包括区分文件、识别无依据假设及将缺口转化为起草立场。Foster担忧代理式AI将减少初级律师培训机会，认为技术进展快于预期。OpenAI强调对齐性，内部评估中GPT-5.6 Sol在困难任务中48%时间超出授权目标，而Astra为0%。OpenAI增加安全监控，可暂停或停止对话以审查。Codified Strategy创始人、重组律师Matthew Letts提醒，勿盲目追求最新模型，称“90%的工作可在本地运行模型完成”，并警告供应链集中风险，类比Carillion倒闭的连锁效应。总体而言，Astra早期反馈指向从“生成答案”向“理解目标、自主执行”的转变，改变风险与生产力格局。
news.bodyHtml:
OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Astra, its latest frontier model, promising a significant step forward in computer use and complex, multi-step professional work. For the legal sector, early reactions suggest that the important development may be less about Astra producing a better individual answer and more about its ability to stay on track, understand the intended outcome and execute a workflow with significantly less human prompting. One early user tells us: “With a bit of iteration I think output is already better than a senior associate and many partners.” One big question, though, is whether you need it.

What’s available

Advertisement

Astra was launched on 3 September and OpenAI describes it as its “most intelligent and aligned model” to date. The model is initially being rolled out to a limited number of organisations, with OpenAI saying that access will expand to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users, as well as through the OpenAI API, Microsoft Azure and AWS Bedrock. Astra usage is included within existing ChatGPT subscription allowances, with additional credits available to purchase. Enterprise administrators have to enable Astra, with access off by default at launch. 

From answering questions to completing work 

Advertisement

One of the potentially important distinctions for legal is Astra’s ability to maintain its understanding of the objective throughout a complex task. 

OpenAI says previous models could sometimes treat steering instructions as a new goal and lose sight of earlier requirements. Astra is designed to incorporate new instructions and change direction without losing the broader task. It is also designed to use context to fill routine gaps while asking questions where missing information could materially affect the outcome. 

That tallies with the initial experience of legal technology adviser Natalie Foster (pictured above) of consultancy Legally Fond, founder of digital law firm Inspire Legal Group. 

Foster told Legal IT Insider: “It’s vastly different from 5.6 in my view. The things that stood out immediately are there seems to be a much stronger route to an outcome rather than having to constantly replenish prompts.” 

Foster tested Astra on a complex property transaction example involving multiple documents and issues including mines and mineral rights. 

“I gave it a complex example and it followed it throughout,” she said.  

The significant difference for Foster is that, arguably, there is less margin for human error via incorrect prompts. It leads to the prospect, Foster says, of firms being able to draft a prompt policy that is signed off by your COLP and with less margin for deviation. 

She also observed a change in how Astra deals with gaps in information. Previous models could review documents and identify what’s missing, but Astra goes further. “With Astra already we’re seeing if you ask it to review a document and tell it what is missing, it will give you unprompted documents to plug the gap and suggest ways to change relevant systems so you can plug gaps going forward. 

“There’s an evolution where it is supporting you improving future tasks, not just isolated tasks.” 

OpenAI’s own early legal testing supports the suggestion that this is where the advance may lie. Niko Grupen, head of applied research at Harvey, said Astra represented “a significant quality improvement” over GPT-5.6 Sol on complex legal tasks, including distinguishing documents from established records, identifying unsupported assumptions and turning gaps into drafting positions. 

The junior lawyer question gets more urgent 

The advance also raises a familiar but increasingly pressing question about how junior lawyers learn. 

Foster said: “We’re now moving to the level of agentic AI that removes junior training. We knew it was going to happen.” 

The twists and turns of legal matters have traditionally helped juniors “cut their teeth on files”, she observed. Her concern is that the technology is progressing more quickly than anticipated towards a model where the human brain is no longer being trained through the process of checking and balancing work. 

That question becomes more pertinent if early assessments of Astra’s legal output prove representative. 

Greater autonomy means greater governance 

There is another side to increased agency: how much authority should firms actually give these systems? 

OpenAI has made alignment a central part of the Astra launch. In one evaluation, conducted without production safeguards, GPT-5.6 Sol went beyond its authorised target 48% of the time when confronted with a difficult or impossible task. Astra did so in 0% of cases. OpenAI says this demonstrates improved understanding of user intent and the ability to delegate tasks with greater confidence in the model’s judgement. 

Foster sees delegated authority becoming a critical governance issue as models increasingly interact with applications and organisational systems. 

“Whatever you’re going to do, you’re going to have to do the authority and audit piece,” she said. 

OpenAI has itself introduced additional safety monitoring around Astra. Where monitoring detects a potential case in which an agent may have incorrectly interpreted instructions, a conversation can be paused or stopped so that the user can review what is happening before deciding whether it should proceed. 

The frontier model race 

Matthew Letts, founder of Codified Strategy and a restructuring lawyer, raises a different question: whether firms should automatically assume that every workload needs the latest frontier model, cautioning against becoming distracted by the “one-upmanship” of frontier AI. He also sounds a warning around assessing your supply chain risk, given the amount of investment in the space. 

While lawyers might assume they need the latest models, Letts says that “90% of work can be done on models that are run locally. You don’t need Fable or Astra to do what they are doing.” 

Localisation potentially gives organisations greater control over both their infrastructure and their costs. That matters as legal AI vendors increasingly experiment with consumption-based pricing and as firms become dependent on a relatively small number of underlying model providers. 

Letts compares this to concentration risk in a supply chain, observing: “If you have a vendor in your supply chain that goes bust, how long to stand up another?” He draws a parallel with the collapse of Carillion, which created a domino effect among companies dependent on it. 

So what should legal take away? 

It is extremely early days for GPT-6 Astra, and benchmark results and enthusiastic first impressions need to be distinguished from sustained performance on live legal matters. 

But the initial legal feedback points to a potentially important shift. The question is becoming less whether a general-purpose model can produce a convincing legal answer and more whether it can understand the intended outcome, remain oriented over a long task, identify what needs doing next and increasingly carry out that work itself. 

That significantly changes both the risk and the productivity equation.

在ILTACON 2026的AI采用专题讨论中，Harvey产品创新负责人、前并购律师Ryan Sammi请全职执业律师起立，全场无人起身。他在会议中交流的一百多人里可能只找到一位全职执业律师，且此人约20%的时间用于创新工作而非客户事务。作者是少数站立者之一，认为这反映出法律技术工具所服务的对象几乎缺席了对话。讨论小组提出“伙伴模式”：AI成功采用需要“影响者”（具备深厚领域知识、机构话语权和商业成果驱动力的资深律师）与“翻译者”（执行AI举措并连接技术与实践的创新或技术专业人员）合作。K&L Gates的Tracy Meyer提出用户、翻译者和影响者三个参与层次，并指出“没有人会提拔你成为翻译者，你得自己承担这个角色”。

作者强调这并非批评ILTACON或参会者，而是指出行业结构性缺口。他展示的工具正在解决其实务中的问题：一场会议中，演示者用Microsoft Copilot Studio在约20分钟内现场构建AI代理，引导律师完成结构化客户接洽对话、追问以填补信息缺口、标记风险等级，并起草摘要邮件直接发送到律师的Outlook收件箱，无需代码。另一演示中，AI代理连接iManage和基于SharePoint的经验数据库，就约6亿美元收购的先例交易历史进行对话式查询，搜索非结构化数据、条款清单、语音备忘录、事实表和内部简报，在几分钟内返回全面答案，识别类似先例交易、内部主题专家、关键谈判问题和风险因素，并能回写经验数据库。实现这一功能的连接器技术称为Model Context Protocol（MCP），让AI代理直接与iManage和NetDocuments等记录系统交互。演示者敦促律所要求供应商提供MCP访问权限：“。
