California AI Rules for Lawyers and Arbitrators Move to Newsom’s Desk

by Bruno Queiroz

California is on the verge of becoming one of the first states to directly regulate how generative AI may be used by attorneys and arbitrators in legal practice. A bill that cleared the state legislature now awaits action by Gov. Gavin Newsom, putting the legal industry on notice that AI governance is moving beyond ethics opinions and court standing orders into statute.

While courts and bar regulators around the country have already warned lawyers about AI-related risks — including hallucinated citations, confidentiality concerns, and inadequate supervision of automated work product — this measure is significant because it would create a state-level framework specifically aimed at participants inside the legal system. That makes it more than a general AI policy debate. It is a legal operations issue for anyone practicing in California.

For litigators, the practical implications are immediate. Generative AI is now routinely used for research summaries, drafting assistance, document review, and internal case analysis. A California law focused on attorney use of AI could affect disclosure obligations, diligence standards, and the extent to which lawyers must review or verify machine-generated output before relying on it in pleadings, briefs, discovery responses, or settlement discussions. Even if the bill does not prohibit AI use, it signals that unsupervised or opaque use will face closer scrutiny.

The inclusion of arbitrators is especially notable. Arbitration has often moved faster than courts in adopting technology, but with less public visibility. Regulating AI use by neutrals raises questions about fairness, transparency, and whether parties should know when AI tools influence procedural decisions, legal analysis, or award drafting. Companies that rely heavily on arbitration clauses may want to watch this closely, particularly if they manage large volumes of employment, consumer, or commercial disputes in California.

For in-house counsel and compliance teams, the bill is another reminder that enterprise AI policies must account for legal-specific workflows. It may no longer be enough to have a broad corporate AI policy. Legal departments may need separate rules governing approved tools, human review requirements, confidentiality protections, vendor diligence, and documentation of how AI-assisted work is created and checked.

If signed, the legislation would likely influence policy discussions well beyond California. Other states, bar regulators, and courts are watching the same issues, and California often serves as an early model for technology regulation. Legal professionals should treat this development as a sign that AI governance in law is entering a more formal phase — one where internal guardrails, training, and defensible review practices may become just as important as the tools themselves.

news.titleEn: Europe’s draft cloud rule would put vendor ownership in the audit file
news.titleZh: 欧洲云规则草案将供应商所有权纳入审计文件
news.summaryZh: 《云与人工智能发展法案》是一项欧洲法规草案，其审计附件要求审计师收集供应商的股东信息直至最终所有者、股权结构表、战略决策机构、决策所需多数、持有5%及以上资本或投票权的所有主体，以及通过商业或财务联系施加的任何影响。该审查适用于保证级别2及以上，不适用于级别1。该法案为提案，尚未成为法律，欧盟委员会于2026年6月3日发布，未设定通过日期。欧洲央行研究提供背景：美国风险基金总规模约9300亿欧元，欧盟约1500亿欧元，后期阶段差距扩大；两家机构未将各自工作相互关联，文章称关联为自身观点。买方无需等待法案通过即可借用附件问题，审计标准现可作为问卷使用，需观察买方是否采用。该法规草案针对公共买方，触发条件是公共部门活动被认定有助于维护公共秩序，而非行业标签，这将所有权从尽职调查移入审计文件。数据位置是基础设施事实，谁决策是股东、董事会和投票门槛的事实，采购部门可能在其变化时不知情。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: The Cloud and AI Development Act, a draft European regulation, asks a question many vendor questionnaires may not reach: who actually decides. Its audit annex would tell an auditor to collect the shareholders up to the ultimate owners, the cap table, the bodies that take strategic decisions, the majorities those decisions need, everyone holding 5 percent or more of capital or votes, and any influence running through commercial or financial links. That examination would attach at assurance level 2 and above, not at level 1.

The act is a proposal, not adopted law. The Commission published it on June 3, 2026, and no adoption date is set. European Central Bank research supplies context for why the ownership question may matter: a total fund size of approximately 930 billion euros for venture funds located in the U.S. against roughly 150 billion euros for funds located in the EU, a gap that widens at later stages. Neither institution connects its work to the other; the article says the connection is its own.

Buyers need not wait for adoption to borrow the annex’s questions. The audit criteria can function as a questionnaire now. Watch whether buyers do.

News Analysis – Data Privacy and Protection Beat

Europe’s draft cloud rule would put vendor ownership in the audit file

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

A draft European regulation would ask who controls a cloud provider, and the annex explaining how control is assessed would tell an auditor to ask for the cap table. Among the public buyers it covers, what triggers it is the work rather than the sector label: a public sector activity identified as contributing to the preservation of public order. That moves ownership out of due diligence and into an audit file. Where data sits is a fact about infrastructure. Who decides is a fact about shareholders, boards and voting thresholds, and procurement may not hear when it changes.

news.bodyText:
Lawyers spend more than half their day on paperwork from calls and meetings.

After every client conversation, there's a file note to write, emails to send, and documents to draft. On top of all that, most of you have to record every single minute of your day.

Now, you don’t have to.

If you already use VXT, you know it turns your phone calls into notes and time entries that save to your legal software .

Today, we're launching VXT Meet , which does exactly that for your meetings too.

Here’s what VXT Meet can do:

During your meetings, VXT takes the notes, so you can focus on your client and still have an accurate record of everything that was said. VXT tracks your time during conversations and creates a time entry after every meeting, so you can bill for work that used to go untracked. After your meetings, VXT summarizes and saves your AI notes and time entry straight to the right matter in the legal software you already use. VXT drafts a follow-up email based on what was said during the conversation, ready to review and send in seconds. ‍

Our next chapter

With this news, VXT can now cover every type of conversation you have and give you back around 10 minutes after every call and meeting.

We can’t wait to show you what’s next.

If you already use VXT, VXT Meet is available today, here’s how to start using it.

If you're new here, you can download the app or book a demo to see how VXT works.

news.titleEn: The Innovators – ‘Conference’
news.titleZh: 创新者——‘会议’
news.summaryZh:
Katie在Smyth & Marmalade担任创新主管。Project Rubicon（自建AI系统）成为公关灾难，合伙人之间爆发内战，物业主管Sara Keating与弱势的管理合伙人Timothy Marks对立。Katie收到加入反对Tim的邀请后，生活归于平静。某日，The Spot agency联合创始人Freddy Freeman到访，称管理合伙人Tim授权其协助新AI战略。Freddy表示AI本质是营销，目标是获取声望而不做实质改变。计划重启Rubicon，以最小成本、最大公关价值进行，预算来自The Spot的公关费用，约5000英镑，一个月内完成，赶在颁奖季前展示。Katie不满但无奈。

数日后，Katie飞往旧金山参加Legal AI Summit。航班上，她意外被升级至头等舱，发现Sara Keating在邻座，Sara问Katie是否加入其阵营。抵达后，Katie假装不认识Sara。她入住公司安排的破旧酒店，随后乘Waymo前往The Battery酒店，以‘Mr Smith’名义会见Sara。Sara介绍她认识西海岸律所Spender & Blume的主席Cornelius Strang和创新主管Zack Petulis。Sara离开前耳语Katie是‘人类测谎仪’。Zack透露该所正进行合并谈判，并阐述其AI驱动律所改革的理念：合伙人相信AI，客户支持变革，测试显示PEP上升，计划全球扩张。Katie印象深刻。两人饮酒交谈，分享法律AI经验。Katie因时差告辞，下楼见Sara等候，此时Harry Harmer出现，对Sara眨眼，对Katie说‘欢迎加入团队’。
news.bodyHtml:
Recap: After the summer break, Katie’s adventures as head of innovation at Smyth & Marmalade continue. Project Rubicon – to build their own AI system – was a PR disaster, with Katie now stumbling into the middle of a civil war between the partners that has set Head of Property, Sara Keating, against weakened managing partner, Timothy Marks. Which side will Katie pick? And will trouble shooter Harry Harmer end her career before anything happens?

–

After the invitation to join the coup against managing partner Tim, Katie’s life returned to a strange quietness. She didn’t dare reach out to Sara, as she assumed – correctly – that Harmer had her under surveillance. Meanwhile, everyone seemed to be busy and absorbed in their work. Life, despite everything that had happened recently, seemed to just carry on.

One morning, just when she was starting to believe that the world was once again ‘normal’, there was a knock on the door of her new and far larger office. A smart young man, sporting a yellow tie and slicked back hair, let himself in. Katie eyed her diary and saw an entry that simply said: ‘Marketing strategy meeting’.

She had expected the usual internal team to show up, but not so. This was Freddy Freeman, co-founder of ‘The Spot’ agency, which was apparently the new, cool, PR outfit in the City of London that all the top firms were turning to.

He made his introductions, complimented her on the view from her corner office, and explained that managing partner Tim had given him great leeway to help with the new AI strategy. He then proceeded to tell her what would be happening next.

‘Fundamentally, all this AI stuff is a marketing exercise. After the…er….how can we say….recent challenges around Project Rubicon, the rather unfair characterisation of you as a member of the living puppet realm, and the hard work done to smooth things over with the press and your clients…..it’s been decided that The Spot will be looking after things now,’ he explained with an overly-assured tone that grated painfully.

‘From our perspective, AI is simply a PR message. A means to gain client attention and remain in the conversation. But, when people take it too seriously things go astray, as demonstrated recently.’

‘The goal is to gain as much kudos as possible while not actually changing anything substantive at all. Are you with me?’

Katie nodded unwillingly. She already hated him.

‘So, this is the plan. We restart Rubicon, but we do it in a way that it will have maximum PR value, but won’t upset anyone.’

‘We will?’

‘Yes, and I should remind you, I have the full confidence of the managing partner in this operation.’

‘OK. So, you want us to do innovation theatre?’

‘Exactly. Tim said you’d understand. Now, what would be something very, very…how can we say….harmless, that we could do?’

‘Like Rubicon, but minuscule? Well, I guess we could pick a very narrow area of work, maybe like fund formation, and build something around that, take an open weights model, build something we can show off, I suppose. If that’s what you mean?’

‘Excellent. And how much would it cost?’

‘It depends,’ Katie replied with a hard smile.

‘Well, the budget for this has to come out of whatever The Spot and the firm have agreed for our remuneration for this engagement. So, what’s the absolute minimum spend?’

‘The AI project is coming out of your PR budget?’ Katie asked in shock, sitting back.

‘Indeed. I was thinking maybe £5,000? How about that?’

‘I don’t know. But, if we keep things very, very small. Barely a wireframe, really.’

‘Perfect, if you can get it all done in about a month, with something nice to show off just before awards season, that would be perfect,’ Freddy stated. ‘I’ll tell my admin team to release the funds.’

‘I look forward to working with you,’ he concluded without a shred of sincerity, and then departed as smoothly as he had arrived. 

—

Katie was still fuming days later as she boarded the flight to California to attend the Legal AI Summit in San Francisco. What was worse, they’d only given her Premium Economy on what was an 11-hour flight. She knew she would not sleep a wink.

She dragged out her laptop ready to do some non-sensitive work, just as a couple with two screaming babies arrived and sat directly behind her.

It was getting dark outside and an attendant on the British Airways flight was making her way down the aisle suggesting that people close their blinds and prepare for the lights to go off. As she reached Katie’s row the attendant leaned over and asked her name. Apparently there was a seat free ahead in First Class and she was welcome to an upgrade if she wanted it.

You bet she wanted it, she replied, and didn’t wait to hear a reason for why this was happening.

She’d never flown First and the spacious cubicle with lie-flat bed looked great. As she was arranging her things, she couldn’t help but have a look around – hoping to perhaps see someone famous. Who she saw though was not a tech bro, or a pop star, but Sara Keating grinning right back at her, sitting in the adjoining cubicle, a glass of champagne in her hand.

‘Sorry, thought this was the best way to have a little chat.’

Katie gulped.

‘So, have you decided yet? You with us or against us?’

–

After landing at SFO, Katie did as she had been advised and pretended she didn’t know who Sara was. In any case, Sara zoomed through a fast-track doorway and was gone. Katie remained with the rest of the flight and stood for about an hour, then managed to get a taxi to a place a little bit too close to the Tenderloin for her liking. The slightly dilapidated hotel had been chosen by the firm.

It was late afternoon in California, but deep into the night for her body clock. She really needed some sleep, not the least because she was sitting on one of the first panels of the morning at the conference tomorrow and needed to get her head clear. But, that was not going to happen, not tonight. Not after her ‘chat’ with Sara about the planned palace coup.

She showered quickly, grabbed some fresh – but crumpled – clothes and rushed out again, leaving her phone on the bed. Katie took a self-driving Waymo to a much fancier hotel called The Battery about a mile away, closer to Embarcadero.

Inside it looked like an artists’ collective, with a super-cool vibe that was a huge change from the rather shabby place she was in. As set out by Sara, Katie went to reception, and told them she was meeting a ‘Mr Smith’.

She couldn’t decide if Sara’s cloak and dagger act was a bit too much, or in fact rather exciting. Katie concluded that as long as it involved cool hotels and better plane seats, then she could put up with it.

The receptionist led her up a flight of stairs and to a long corridor of plush meeting rooms. At door 23 she was left on her own. Inside she could hear Sara’s laughter and a deep booming voice. She knocked with trepidation.

–

She was introduced to the Chairman of Spender & Blume, one of the leading West Coast law firms. Katie had heard of them, they were big in the tech and VC world. The Chairman, Cornelius Strang, introduced her in turn to Zack Petulis, head of innovation. They all shook hands and left her with Zack.

As she was departing, Sara paused and whispered in her ear: ‘Remember, you’re my human lie detector.’

Zack was friendly, but seemed quite tense. He poured a glass of wine for her from an open bottle on the table, which she drank down way too quickly.

‘So,’ he began hesitantly, ‘apparently we’re in merger talks.’

‘Yes, so I’ve been told.’

‘And you’re here to grill me?’ he added, the nervous smile now fading from his angular face.

‘Also apparently,’ Katie replied. ‘Shall we begin?’

Zack laid it all out. Strang and team were ‘believers’. The partners spent most of their time advising companies on the cutting edge of the AI boom. What might seem like normality to most of Big Law, now looked like something out of a history book to them, he explained. The clients were ready to get behind a law firm that truly changed.

A great shift was coming, that was Strang’s prediction and they wanted to be at the ‘tip of the spear’. They wanted to really get ahead of the pack. They’d built the financial models to support radical redesign and through testing had found that PEP went up, not down, based on the new AI-driven approach. The next step was to then expand like crazy, to build a global winner and reshape the Big Law world.

Katie was impressed. They seemed to be travelling down the same road her firm had been trying to traverse…but had then suddenly abandoned. The key difference was that they knew what they were doing. They also sounded like they had the confidence to see things through.

They then shared war stories about the legal AI world and discussed how they were approaching things like open weights, picking platforms, and how to hire the best staff. Zack impressed her on every aspect of the discussion.

She had another glass of wine, which she drank more slowly, and they moved to softer subjects: how they arrived in legal tech, families, a shared love of California’s wilder spaces. She looked at her watch just as they were on the topic of Death Valley and realised that for her it was 5AM London time.

Katie excused herself and headed out. To her lack of surprise, Sara was waiting for her downstairs. She was just formulating in her mind how to suggest that they talk later as she really needed to get some sleep, at least two hours if possible, when Katie saw a fiercely focused bald man marching towards them across the lobby.

‘Oh no!’ Katie uttered out loud and froze in her tracks.

‘Hello, Katherine,’ said Harry Harmer, as he stopped abruptly in front of her, then turned to give an unsettling wink to Sara. ‘Welcome to the team.’

–

news.bodyText:
Recap: After the summer break, Katie’s adventures as head of innovation at Smyth & Marmalade continue. Project Rubicon – to build their own AI system – was a PR disaster, with Katie now stumbling into the middle of a civil war between the partners that has set Head of Property, Sara Keating, against weakened managing partner, Timothy Marks. Which side will Katie pick? And will trouble shooter Harry Harmer end her career before anything happens?

After the invitation to join the coup against managing partner Tim, Katie’s life returned to a strange quietness. She didn’t dare reach out to Sara, as she assumed – correctly – that Harmer had her under surveillance. Meanwhile, everyone seemed to be busy and absorbed in their work. Life, despite everything that had happened recently, seemed to just carry on.

One morning, just when she was starting to believe that the world was once again ‘normal’, there was a knock on the door of her new and far larger office. A smart young man, sporting a yellow tie and slicked back hair, let himself in. Katie eyed her diary and saw an entry that simply said: ‘Marketing strategy meeting’.

She had expected the usual internal team to show up, but not so. This was Freddy Freeman, co-founder of ‘The Spot’ agency, which was apparently the new, cool, PR outfit in the City of London that all the top firms were turning to.

He made his introductions, complimented her on the view from her corner office, and explained that managing partner Tim had given him great leeway to help with the new AI strategy. He then proceeded to tell her what would be happening next.

‘Fundamentally, all this AI stuff is a marketing exercise. After the…er….how can we say….recent challenges around Project Rubicon, the rather unfair characterisation of you as a member of the living puppet realm, and the hard work done to smooth things over with the press and your clients …..it’s been decided that The Spot will be looking after things now,’ he explained with an overly-assured tone that grated painfully.

‘From our perspective, AI is simply a PR message. A means to gain client attention and remain in the conversation. But, when people take it too seriously things go astray, as demonstrated recently.’

‘The goal is to gain as much kudos as possible while not actually changing anything substantive at all. Are you with me?’

Katie nodded unwillingly. She already hated him.

‘So, this is the plan. We restart Rubicon, but we do it in a way that it will have maximum PR value, but won’t upset anyone.’

‘Yes, and I should remind you, I have the full confidence of the managing partner in this operation.’

‘OK. So, you want us to do innovation theatre?’

‘Exactly. Tim said you’d understand. Now, what would be something very, very…how can we say…. harmless , that we could do?’

‘Like Rubicon, but minuscule? Well, I guess we could pick a very narrow area of work, maybe like fund formation, and build something around that, take an open weights model, build something we can show off, I suppose. If that’s what you mean?’

‘Excellent. And how much would it cost?’

‘It depends,’ Katie replied with a hard smile.

‘Well, the budget for this has to come out of whatever The Spot and the firm have agreed for our remuneration for this engagement. So, what’s the absolute minimum spend?’

‘The AI project is coming out of your PR budget?’ Katie asked in shock, sitting back.

‘Indeed. I was thinking maybe £5,000? How about that?’

‘I don’t know. But, if we keep things very, very small. Barely a wireframe, really.’

‘Perfect, if you can get it all done in about a month, with something nice to show off just before awards season, that would be perfect,’ Freddy stated. ‘I’ll tell my admin team to release the funds.’

‘I look forward to working with you,’ he concluded without a shred of sincerity, and then departed as smoothly as he had arrived.

Katie was still fuming days later as she boarded the flight to California to attend the Legal AI Summit in San Francisco. What was worse, they’d only given her Premium Economy on what was an 11-hour flight. She knew she would not sleep a wink.

She dragged out her laptop ready to do some non-sensitive work, just as a couple with two screaming babies arrived and sat directly behind her.

It was getting dark outside and an attendant on the British Airways flight was making her way down the aisle suggesting that people close their blinds and prepare for the lights to go off. As she reached Katie’s row the attendant leaned over and asked her name. Apparently there was a seat free ahead in First Class and she was welcome to an upgrade if she wanted it.

You bet she wanted it, she replied, and didn’t wait to hear a reason for why this was happening.

She’d never flown First and the spacious cubicle with lie-flat bed looked great. As she was arranging her things, she couldn’t help but have a look around – hoping to perhaps see someone famous. Who she saw though was not a tech bro, or a pop star, but Sara Keating grinning right back at her, sitting in the adjoining cubicle, a glass of champagne in her hand.

‘Sorry, thought this was the best way to have a little chat.’

‘So, have you decided yet? You with us or against us?’

After landing at SFO, Katie did as she had been advised and pretended she didn’t know who Sara was. In any case, Sara zoomed through a fast-track doorway and was gone. Katie remained with the rest of the flight and stood for about an hour, then managed to get a taxi to a place a little bit too close to the Tenderloin for her liking. The slightly dilapidated hotel had been chosen by the firm.

It was late afternoon in California, but deep into the night for her body clock. She really needed some sleep, not the least because she was sitting on one of the first panels of the morning at the conference tomorrow and needed to get her head clear. But, that was not going to happen, not tonight. Not after her ‘chat’ with Sara about the planned palace coup.

She showered quickly, grabbed some fresh – but crumpled – clothes and rushed out again, leaving her phone on the bed. Katie took a self-driving Waymo to a much fancier hotel called The Battery about a mile away, closer to Embarcadero.

Inside it looked like an artists’ collective, with a super-cool vibe that was a huge change from the rather shabby place she was in. As set out by Sara, Katie went to reception, and told them she was meeting a ‘Mr Smith’.

She couldn’t decide if Sara’s cloak and dagger act was a bit too much, or in fact rather exciting. Katie concluded that as long as it involved cool hotels and better plane seats, then she could put up with it.

The receptionist led her up a flight of stairs and to a long corridor of plush meeting rooms. At door 23 she was left on her own. Inside she could hear Sara’s laughter and a deep booming voice. She knocked with trepidation.

She was introduced to the Chairman of Spender & Blume, one of the leading West Coast law firms. Katie had heard of them, they were big in the tech and VC world. The Chairman, Cornelius Strang, introduced her in turn to Zack Petulis, head of innovation. They all shook hands and left her with Zack.

As she was departing, Sara paused and whispered in her ear: ‘Remember, you’re my human lie detector.’

Zack was friendly, but seemed quite tense. He poured a glass of wine for her from an open bottle on the table, which she drank down way too quickly.

‘So,’ he began hesitantly, ‘apparently we’re in merger talks.’

‘And you’re here to grill me?’ he added, the nervous smile now fading from his angular face.

‘Also apparently,’ Katie replied. ‘Shall we begin?’

Zack laid it all out. Strang and team were ‘believers’. The partners spent most of their time advising companies on the cutting edge of the AI boom. What might seem like normality to most of Big Law, now looked like something out of a history book to them, he explained. The clients were ready to get behind a law firm that truly changed.

A great shift was coming, that was Strang’s prediction and they wanted to be at the ‘tip of the spear’. They wanted to really get ahead of the pack. They’d built the financial models to support radical redesign and through testing had found that PEP went up, not down, based on the new AI-driven approach. The next step was to then expand like crazy, to build a global winner and reshape the Big Law world.

Katie was impressed. They seemed to be travelling down the same road her firm had been trying to traverse…but had then suddenly abandoned. The key difference was that they knew what they were doing. They also sounded like they had the confidence to see things through.

They then shared war stories about the legal AI world and discussed how they were approaching things like open weights, picking platforms, and how to hire the best staff. Zack impressed her on every aspect of the discussion.

She had another glass of wine, which she drank more slowly, and they moved to softer subjects: how they arrived in legal tech, families, a shared love of California’s wilder spaces. She looked at her watch just as they were on the topic of Death Valley and realised that for her it was 5AM London time.

Katie excused herself and headed out. To her lack of surprise, Sara was waiting for her downstairs. She was just formulating in her mind how to suggest that they talk later as she really needed to get some sleep, at least two hours if possible, when Katie saw a fiercely focused bald man marching towards them across the lobby.

‘Oh no!’ Katie uttered out loud and froze in her tracks.

‘Hello, Katherine,’ said Harry Harmer, as he stopped abruptly in front of her, then turned to give an unsettling wink to Sara. ‘Welcome to the team.’

news.titleEn: The Next Wave of AI Regulation- What Employers Should Know About State-Level Activity
news.titleZh: AI监管的下一波浪潮——雇主应了解的州级动态
news.summaryZh: 本期《We Get AI》播客中，Jackson Lewis律所AI团队负责人Eric Felsberg与Joe Lazzarotti讨论了美国各州AI立法的最新进展及其对跨州雇主的影响。各州AI法律日益碎片化，使得多州雇主在维持一致的招聘实践、满足通知、透明度和治理要求方面面临更大挑战。近期最显著的发展是科罗拉多州对其先前全面而广泛的AI法律进行了大幅缩减，但雇主仍需履行某些义务。与此同时，康涅狄格州通过了新的法律，涵盖就业、伴侣机器人、聊天机器人、涉及儿童的问题等多个领域。过去一年中，纽约市、伊利诺伊州、科罗拉多州、加利福尼亚州和康涅狄格州等司法辖区相继出台AI相关法规，纽约市作为地方司法辖区，在就业领域AI使用监管方面被视为先行者，其要求包括偏见审计和发布相关通知。各司法辖区虽然关注相似主题，但具体做法有所不同。早期如科罗拉多州等地曾侧重于分析就业工具输出中的偏见证据，而当前各州立法呈现多样化趋势，雇主需密切关注并适应这一不断演变的监管环境。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The growing patchwork of AI laws makes maintaining consistent hiring practices and complying with notice, transparency and governance requirements more challenging for multi-state employers. In this episode, We Get AI co-hosts Eric Felsberg and Joe Lazzarotti address how the latest AI laws in Colorado and Connecticut fit into the broader employment regulatory landscape. Eric FelsbergPrincipal, Long Island Welcome to the We Get AI podcast. My name is Eric Felsberg, and I'm joined by my colleague Joe Lazzarotti. Joe and I are the leaders of the AI group at Jackson Lewis. We're happy to be with you as we try to demystify a lot of the AI developments that we're all experiencing; this is a rapidly moving area. The goal of this podcast is to ensure that we take some of those developments and break them down into easy-to-understand segments. If it goes well, offer you some practical tips on how to navigate this evolving area. Joe LazzarottiPrincipal, Tampa Hey, good to be with you, Eric. Today we want to try to touch on some recent developments. There was a significant change in Colorado. They had come out with a comprehensive, expansive AI law that required developers and deployers to take several steps, and it looks like that's been pretty scaled back, although there are still some things that have to be done. Connecticut more recently passed its own law that touched on a whole range of areas, obviously including employment, but also companion bots, chat bots, AI with children, issues with children, and a whole range of other issues. A good place to start is to touch on the Connecticut law and tell us what the key issues are and what businesses should be thinking about. Felsberg Those have been the two most recent developments. It's helpful to provide some context to the landscape of AI laws that are now joined by this updated Colorado law, as you mentioned, of course, Connecticut. We have seen laws pop up pretty consistently over the last year or so in different jurisdictions. We have New York City, of course, Illinois, Colorado, you mentioned, Joe, and you're going to cover. Colorado has this take two, if you will. California and Connecticut – these states are all popping up. In the case of New York, New York City as a local jurisdiction is coming up with its own methods for enforcing AI. It's challenging for employers because each of these jurisdictions is getting at the same themes. They're just going about it a little bit differently. The other thing that I find interesting is New York City, at least with respect to regulating use of AI in the employment context, has been seen as the leader here. You may recall New York City has a bias audit requirement. There's a publication requirement of the bias, or of course there's a notice piece. For a while, in places like Colorado, there seemed to be an emphasis on analyzing the output from some of these tools that we use in the employment context for evidence of bias. That seemed to be the emphasis early on.
news.relevanceReason: 内容聚焦于AI在就业领域的监管法律，涉及雇主合规、偏见审计等法律科技议题，属于法律AI监管范畴。

news.titleEn: SpaceX–Reflection Deal Moves the AI Compute Debate Deeper into Infrastructure
news.titleZh: SpaceX与Reflection交易将AI算力之争推向基础设施深层
news.summaryZh:
SpaceX于2026年6月与开源AI初创公司Reflection AI达成协议。据CNBC和TechCrunch报道，Reflection每月将支付约1.5亿美元，到2029年总额约63亿美元，以获取托管在SpaceX旗下Colossus 2数据中心的高性能英伟达GB300芯片及相关基础设施的使用权。该合同使Reflection立即获得稀缺的下一代训练算力。英伟达是Reflection的投资方之一，英伟达据报在投资该公司的同时，Reflection正付费获取由SpaceX收购并运营的英伟达硬件，这使英伟达既是该AI开发商的财务支持者，也是其增长所依赖的稀缺芯片的间接供应方。

该交易并非孤立事件。据CNBC报道，SpaceX今年早些时候完成与埃隆·马斯克旗下人工智能公司xAI的合并，合并后企业估值约1.25万亿美元，将发射能力、卫星基础设施与AI模型开发整合于同一公司架构。Colossus数据中心最初为支持内部AI业务而建，如今日益向包括谷歌和Anthropic在内的外部客户开放。该协议表明SpaceX正将大规模算力基础设施这一资本密集型能力转化为经常性收入来源，也反映出AI生态系统中先进模型开发对高端GPU等专用硬件的依赖及供应限制。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The agreement shows how control over frontier compute, data centers, chips, and related infrastructure may shape which AI developers can compete at scale. SpaceX’s June 2026 agreement with open-source AI startup Reflection AI underscores a broader shift Mogin Law has tracked in prior analysis of AI chokepoint deals: control is moving down the stack, from models to compute. According to CNBC and TechCrunch, Reflection will pay approximately $150 million per month—up to roughly $6.3 billion through 2029—for access to high-performance Nvidia GB300 chips and related infrastructure housed in SpaceX’s Colossus 2 data center. The contract gives Reflection immediate access to scarce, next-generation training capacity, a constraint that increasingly defines the frontier of AI development. The Nvidia connection adds another layer to the competitive picture. Later reporting described Reflection as having Nvidia among its backers, and noted that Nvidia reportedly invested in the company while Reflection is now paying for access to Nvidia hardware acquired and operated by SpaceX. That structure makes Nvidia both a financial supporter of the AI developer and an indirect supplier of the scarce chips on which the developer’s growth depends. The deal is not an isolated transaction. It reflects a deliberate effort by SpaceX to position itself as a central supplier of AI compute capacity, not merely as a participant in model development. Earlier this year, SpaceX completed its merger with Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI in a transaction that valued the combined enterprise at approximately $1.25 trillion, according to CNBC reporting. That deal consolidated launch capability, satellite infrastructure, and AI model development within a single corporate structure. The Reflection agreement shows how SpaceX is now monetizing a key byproduct of that integration: large-scale compute infrastructure. This fits reporting on AI infrastructure transactions. Capital is flowing into the physical and operational layers needed for AI systems to scale. Originally built to support internal AI efforts, the Colossus data centers are increasingly being opened to outside customers, including major AI developers such as Google and Anthropic. That model also echoes the competitive questions raised by major AI compute and cloud arrangements, including Mogin Law’s analysis of the AWS–OpenAI deal. This strategy resembles earlier platform shifts in technology markets. Control over critical infrastructure—whether operating systems, cloud platforms, or semiconductor fabrication—has often solidified durable competitive advantages. Here, the relevant input is not software distribution or chip design, but access to the compute resources required to train and run large language models. (Control over infrastructure is even into literal power itself, as big deals are being cut for electricty generation.) The importance of the Reflection deal lies less in its size and more in what it signals about constraints in the AI ecosystem. Advanced AI development depends on access to specialized hardware, particularly high-end GPUs. Supply remains limited, and the costs associated with building and operating large-scale data centers—including power, cooling, and real estate—are substantial. By aggregating these resources at scale, SpaceX is effectively converting a capital-intensive capability into a recurring revenue stream.

news.titleEn: Negotiating HR Vendor Agreements in the Age of AI: Key Provisions and Considerations
news.titleZh: 人工智能时代下人力资源供应商协议谈判：关键条款与考量因素
news.summaryZh: 人工智能正迅速改变人力资源运营，雇主日益依赖产品基于或由AI驱动的第三方供应商，涵盖招聘筛选、入职、绩效预测、生物识别身份验证及ERISA福利计划管理等。劳动与就业律师需重新审视供应商协议谈判。尽管大多数州尚未颁布AI专项就业立法，但各州法律拼凑成形，联邦机构正将现有框架扩展至AI，供应商所在州义务也可能影响合同。协议应清晰定义所购服务，涵盖明确以AI营销的产品及任何包含、整合或基于AI的服务，包括生成式AI和自主行动的代理式AI系统；同时应要求供应商书面披露AI使用性质和范围，标记或识别含AI的交付物，并应要求全面披露AI服务使用情况。协议还应明确雇主对内容、提示、输入及生成输出的所有权，并禁止供应商未经批准用雇主数据训练、再训练或改进AI模型。算法偏见是AI决策的头条风险：纽约市AEDT法要求招聘或晋升前一年内完成独立偏见审计并公布结果摘要；加州民权部门法规虽无明确审计要求，但承认反偏见测试证据与抗辩相关；康涅狄格州新AI法也有类似规定。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming human resources operations. From AI-powered recruiting platforms that screen résumés and rank candidates, to onboarding tools that personalize new-hire experiences, performance management systems that predict attrition, identity verification solutions using biometrics, and platforms administering ERISA-governed benefit plans, employers are increasingly relying on third-party vendors whose products are built on or enabled by AI. For labor and employment lawyers, this shift demands a fresh look at how we negotiate and structure vendor agreements. While most states have not yet enacted AI-specific employment legislation, all employers deploying such technologies should pay careful attention to the terms in their AI vendor agreements. A patchwork of state laws is emerging across the country, federal agencies are actively extending existing frameworks to AI, and even a vendor’s home-state obligations can shape the contractual landscape. This article offers a high-level overview of several key issues practitioners should consider when negotiating agreements with HR technology vendors that use AI. Define What You’re Buying Vendor agreements should clearly define service provided under the agreement, capturing not only products explicitly marketed as AI but also any service that includes, incorporates, or is based upon or enabled by artificial intelligence, including generative AI, and agentic AI systems that autonomously act and make decisions in response to prompts and other actions. Equally important is defining the vendor’s obligation to disclose the nature and extent of its use of AI. Require that the vendor mark or otherwise identify for Customer in writing all deliverables that incorporate or derive from AI, and provide upon request, a full disclosure of the use of AI services in connection with the preparation of any deliverables. Similarly, consider requiring the vendor to notify the employer of a new AI use case, particularly when the current services do not involve AI. Without this transparency, employers cannot assess their own compliance obligations under emerging state and federal laws. Data Ownership and Restrictions on Training HR data is among the most sensitive information an organization holds. Vendor agreements should unambiguously establish employer ownership of all content, prompts, inputs, and—critically—all generated output, meaning results or derivative works created by the AI using the employer’s data. Perhaps most important, the agreement should expressly prohibit the vendor from using employer data to train, retrain, or improve its AI models without approval. This is not a theoretical concern—HR data used to train a general-purpose model could expose the employer to claims under data privacy laws and compromise confidential workforce information. Bias Testing and Anti-Discrimination Protections The risk of algorithmic bias is the headline issue for AI-driven decision making, particularly in certain areas including health care, housing, financing, and, of course, employment. A growing number of jurisdictions are imposing affirmative obligations on employers who deploy these tools. New York City’s Automated Employment Decision Tool (AEDT) law, for example, requires employers to ensure an independent bias audit was conducted within the past year before using an AEDT for hiring or promotion decisions, and to publish a summary of the audit results. California’s Civil Rights Department regulations do not have an express bias audit requirement, but recognize that evidence of anti-bias testing or similar proactive efforts to avoid unlawful discrimination is relevant to defending a claim. A similar rule is present in Connecticut’s new AI law.
news.relevanceReason: 文章聚焦于AI在人力资源领域的应用及供应商协议谈判，涉及法律合规和就业法律，但核心是人力资源技术合同，而非直接的法律AI或法律技术产品。

research.titleEn: KhatianDoc: A Human-Verified Benchmark Diagnosing Multimodal LLM Failure on Bengali Legal Land Records
research.titleZh: KhatianDoc：一个人类验证的基准，用于诊断多模态大语言模型在孟加拉法律土地记录上的失败
research.abstractEn: Land ownership in Bangladesh is recorded in Ana-Ganda-Kora-Kranti-Til, a base-16 positional fraction system with dedicated Unicode glyphs, no mainstream font, and no coverage in any OCR pipeline or tokenizer. The handwritten records that carry these fractions, RS Khatians, are the authoritative title record for millions of parcels and a frequent subject of civil litigation, yet no benchmark has asked whether a machine can read one. We introduce KhatianDoc, a four-task benchmark built from 107 real RS Khatian records from the Vumi (land) Office of Munshiganj, Bangladesh: symbol recognition, base-16-to-decimal conversion, structured field extraction, and legal document question answering over 1,634 QA pairs. Ground truth was transcribed by hand, verified by a land-law practitioner to full agreement, and anonymized through positional tokens that keep the referential distinctions multi-hop questions depend on. We evaluate six multimodal LLMs (8B to 72B+, open and closed) under a fixed zero-shot protocol. Five QA categories, 39.3% of our stratified set, return zero correct answers from every model; on the arithmetic task, every model that emits a number does worse than a constant-mean baseline, with exact- and near-match scores coinciding: decorrelation, not approximation. Auditing our own metrics surfaced two artifacts in opposite directions: we correct a refusal-scoring bug and report the fixed scores beside the originals, and flag an inflated metadata metric as an upper bound. KhatianDoc documents not a performance gap but the absence of a capability, with verified ground truth for future systems. Code and data, with a redacted image release, are publicly available.
research.abstractZh: 孟加拉国的土地所有权记录在Ana-Ganda-Kora-Kranti-Til中，这是一种基数为16的位置分数系统，拥有专用的Unicode字形，没有主流字体，且在任何OCR流程或分词器中均无覆盖。承载这些分数的手写记录，即RS Khatians，是数百万地块的权威所有权记录，也是民事诉讼的常见主题，然而尚无基准测试询问机器是否能读取其中一份。我们引入了KhatianDoc，一个由孟加拉国Munshiganj的Vumi（土地）办公室的107份真实RS Khatian记录构建的四任务基准：符号识别、基16到十进制转换、结构化字段提取，以及针对1,634个问答对的法律文档问答。真实标签由手工转录，经土地法律从业者验证完全一致，并通过位置标记进行匿名化，这些标记保留了多跳问题所依赖的指代区分。我们在固定的零样本协议下评估了六个多模态大语言模型（8B至72B+，开源和闭源）。五个问答类别，占我们分层集的39.3%，从所有模型返回零正确答案；在算术任务上，每个输出数字的模型都比常数均值基线表现更差，精确匹配和近似匹配分数重合：去相关，而非近似。审计我们自己的指标发现了两个方向相反的伪影：我们修正了一个拒绝评分错误，并在原始分数旁报告修正后的分数，同时将一个虚高的元数据指标标记为上限。KhatianDoc记录的不是性能差距，而是能力的缺失，并为未来系统提供了经过验证的真实标签。代码和数据，以及经过脱敏的图像发布，均已公开可用。

news.titleEn: Filevine Takes On Shepard’s and KeyCite With Its Own AI Case Law Citator and Hallucination Checker
news.titleZh: Filevine推出自有AI判例引证工具及幻觉检测功能，对标Shepard's与KeyCite
news.summaryZh: 法律科技公司Filevine在LOIS平台推出AI原生引证工具及配套简报审查工具，性能媲美或优于LexisNexis和Thomson Reuters的领先产品。引证工具可检查简报中的幻觉引用、篡改引文和错误描述权威，并允许用户高亮判决段落以验证其是否仍为有效法律。反幻觉工具本周首次发布。传统黄金标准Shepard's和KeyCite常对案件有效性意见不一，引用研究显示三者一致率仅15%，失败率分别为33%、38%和72%；Westlaw和Lexis的重叠率仅约三分之一。简报审查工具提取分析引用后，报告命题、系统发现、状态及严重程度。演示中，工具识别出简报错误引用“100%治愈”保单和Knight案中的引文问题。引证工具通过遍历引证图和语义相似性搜索，发现隐性冲突，并生成综合论文。评估显示，在2,073条引用中，LOIS验证61.8%，标记38.2%供审查，8.4%为严重，包括捏造案例、错误引文和错误描述权威。Filevine使用CourtListener库，计划添加法规。Anderson承认工具不能完全替代人工审查。
news.bodyHtml:
The legal technology company Filevine has launched an AI-native citator and a companion brief-checking tool inside LOIS, its Legal Operating Intelligence System AI platform, that its CEO says perform as well as or better than the leading legal citators from LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters.

The citator has two core features. One checks a filed or draft brief for hallucinated citations, altered quotations, and mischaracterized authority. The other checks whether a proposition is still good law by letting a lawyer highlight a specific passage in an opinion and find out whether later courts have undercut the holding expressed in the passage.

Although Filevine had previously announced the citator in June as part of its new LOIS Legal Research offering, which provides access to millions of opinions from U.S. federal and state courts, CEO Ryan Anderson, in a briefing this week, told me the company had not heavily promoted the citator until it believed the product was fully ready for customers to use.

The company had not previously announced the anti-hallucination tool, which is being released for the first time this week.

As Filevine described the citator in its June release: “While legal verification tools rely on explicit citation relationships and apply treatment signals to entire opinions, LOIS Legal Research operates at the user-selected passage level.” This enables legal professionals to verify the exact rule they plan to rely on in their argument.

The Challenge Of Citators

I have previously written that developing a strong citator tool is the Holy Grail of a legal research platform. Among companies to have succeeded in developing their own in recent years were vLex and Paxton, Descrybe, and Midpage, and if you read those linked articles, you will see that each of them took distinct approaches to the problem. (My Midpage article only teased its forthcoming citator, which it has since released.)

But it is not an easy task. In fact, in my briefing with Filevine this week, John Rizner, the product manager who led the development of the citator, pointed out something that most law librarians will know but that may be news to almost everyone else, which is that the two citators lawyers have long considered to be the gold standard routinely disagree with each other about whether a case is still good law.

He pointed to a 2018 study in the Law Library Journal by Paul Hellyer, a librarian at William & Mary Law School, who reviewed 357 citing relationships that at least one of Shepard’s, KeyCite or BCite had labeled negative.

All three citators agreed that the treatment was negative only 53 times, meaning that in 85% of the relationships in Hellyer’s sample, the three citators did not agree that a negative treatment had occurred.

Hellyer also examined whether the flags that did appear were correct. Counting relationships the citators omitted or mislabeled as positive or neutral, together with those labeled negative but incorrectly described, he found overall failure rates of 33% for Shepard’s, 38% for KeyCite and 72% for BCite.

Rizner also cited a second line of research, from Susan Nevelow Mart, the former director of the law library at the University of Colorado, whose 2013 examinations of digest and citator results found that the overlap between the Westlaw and Lexis citator systems on relevant results was small – only about a third.

As the abstract of Mart’s article put it: “Neither algorithm is doing a very good job of finding all the relevant results; the overlap between the two citator systems is not that large.”

Ahead of our briefing, Rizner ran his own test. He pulled Freedom Mortgage Corp. v. Engel on both platforms and filtered each down to negative treatment in reported opinions. Westlaw found 28 and Lexis found 13. The overlap between the two sets, by his count, was about 41%.

“If my law firm happens to have Lexis, I might be missing opinions because I don’t have Westlaw, or vice versa,” Rizner said.

What that means, Anderson said, is that even though the legacy citators have been best in class up until now, that does not mean that they do not make mistakes.

Citators As An Essential Tool

At this point, you may be thinking: “Sure, but what does this all have to do with Filevine, which is not a legal research platform?”

In my opinion, it has everything to do with Filevine and every other legal platform in which legal professionals are using AI to draft legal documents that rely on legal citations.

Thanks to concerns about AI accuracy and rampant hallucinations, the role – or maybe I should say the place – of the citator is evolving.

For most of their history, citators were legal research products – the last step before you wrapped up your research. But, as Anderson argued in our briefing, citation validation is now a required step in any legal workflow that produces a document relying on case law.

“Usually you’re taking facts, applying them to law and drafting,” he said. “That is the day-to-day shoe leather work of a lawyer.”

Filevine already held the facts, he said, but the missing pieces were a case law corpus and a way to confirm that what the corpus returns is still good law.

“And I think now there’s another step,” he said, “which is make sure nothing you’ve looked at is hallucinated.”

Earlier this year, at a meeting of roughly 20 large firms that Filevine convened, Anderson heard the same anxiety about hallucinations expressed repeatedly. One litigator said his top-10 firm now requires three separate sign-offs before any filing goes out, with the briefing associate required to attest that the associate had checked every citation and every holding.

Filevine’s Answer to This Need

So what is Filevine’s answer to this need? In our briefing this week, Anderson and Rizner demonstrated how the brief auditor and citator work.

For the brief auditor, after It ingests a document, it extracts and analyzes every citation, and then reports four things in a side-by-side chart:

  • The proposition the brief says the authority supports.
  • The citation given.
  • What the system found in the opinion.
  • The status, which can be verified, unverified, suspect, ambiguous, mischaracterized or wrong case name.

Using briefs pulled from PACER in matters where courts had already found problems, Anderson showed me examples. In one, a brief asserted that the 11th Circuit had squarely held that “100% healed” policies violate the ADA. The tool reported that the phrase appears in the opinion only in the plaintiff’s own request to return to full duty.

In another, drawn from Knight v. Baptist Hospital of Miami, the brief cited a passage for the proposition that disparate discipline of similarly situated employees is evidence of pretext. The tool flagged that the quoted sentence does not appear in the opinion and that the court’s reasoning runs the other way, having found the comparator not similarly situated.

“It’s really quite remarkable how subtle these hallucinations can be even when the case itself is not hallucinated,” he said. He noted that fabricated support often turns up in a dissent or in a recitation of case history rather than in the holding.

A Different Kind Of Citator

The citator works differently from a traditional one. Rather than starting from a case and examining its citation graph, the user highlights the specific language at issue.

Filevine then runs two passes – a traversal of the citation graph and a semantic similarity search – across its corpus for opinions using comparable reasoning. Opinions that come up as likely candidates are handed to LLMs, which distill the conflicts.

The output is a report keyed to the highlighted passage, with a severity rating and a written treatment for each authority.

In the results, a second tab generates what Rizner described as a synthetic treatise – a narrative discussion of the doctrinal tension, structured like a secondary source but built around the specific issue the user selected.

Because the semantic pass does not depend on one court citing another, Rizner said, it surfaces sub silentio conflicts, such as, for example, a 1985 decision and a 2005 decision that squarely contradict each other but never cite each other. This would be invisible to any citator built on a citation graph alone.

Evaluating the Results

Filevine gave me access to an as-yet unpublished paper evaluating its anti-hallucination tool.

According to the paper, Filevine’s evaluation team started with a database of 1,314 actual matters in which a judge had identified potentially hallucinated citations tied to admitted or suspected use of gen AI. It narrowed that pool to federal filings and then to filings submitted by attorneys rather than pro se litigants. That left 103 cases, of which 68 had records available for full analysis.

For each of the 68 matters, Filevine pulled the court’s order and the offending brief, ran the brief through LOIS using an identical prompt, and compared the output against the order. LOIS worked only from its own case law corpus, blocking general web search to keep it from finding news coverage or blog abouts about the cases.

Across 2,073 citations, LOIS verified 61.8%, flagged 38.2% for attorney review, and marked 8.4% as severe, meaning they were mischaracterized holdings or citations pointing to the wrong or a non-existent case. Every document in the sample produced at least one flag. Among the highest-citation filings, the cleanest still had roughly 9% of its citations flagged, while the worst had 76%.

Specifically, LOIS was instructed to look for three categories of hallucinated cases: fabricated case law, false or misattributed quotations, and mischaracterized authority.

For fabricated case law, LOIS found them in multiple matters. The report gave the example of Renschler v. Yosh, 909 F. Supp. 2d 1197, a citation LOIS flagged because no case by that name appeared anywhere in the reporter database.

For altered quotations, it also found multiple examples. The paper points to a Rule 37 sanctions argument that quoted the 2nd Circuit case of Shcherbakovskiy v. Da Capo Al Fine, Ltd. as requiring fault “of the sanctioned party,” when the court actually wrote “of the deponent.”

Filevine said the third category, mischaracterized authority, yielded “the exercise’s most critical observation,” which was the high number of instances when the citation appeared legitimate, but it did not stand for the proposition asserted, did not contain the argument attributed to it, or contained citations that LOIS could not access to confirm the authority.

In one filing, a brief cited Watson v. State of California for the proposition that California Government Code § 845.6 imposes an affirmative duty to summon medical care, when the opinion holds the statute confers broad immunity and the Watson plaintiff lost.

In another, Nai v. National Asset Mortgage, LLC, in the Western District of Michigan, counsel quoted RESPA’s limitations provision, 12 U.S.C. § 2614, as running from the “first” occurrence of the violation. The word “first” is not in the statute, meaning its insertion converted an occurrence-based trigger into a first-occurrence trigger, which counsel used to argue two tax years of claims were time-barred.

Notably, the report says, in matters where the bad citation had already been flagged by a court, LOIS caught the same defect, and it identified authorities cited for propositions that contradicted the underlying argument.

A Few Other Notes

As I noted above, the citator bases its analysis on the text highlighted by the user. Given that, I asked Rizner whether it was possible that a lawyer who validates one holding in a long, multi-issue opinion would not necessarily learn that the case was reversed on an unrelated holding.

He confirmed that is possible, though he said the system’s severity ratings are designed to explain when a citing case engaged with the opinion but not with the issue at hand. Anderson suggested that a direct query, or highlighting the full opinion, would likely catch it, but acknowledged the company had not tested that.

As for the source of Filevine’s case law corpus, it is using the CourtListener library, supplemented by licensed material that provides reporter citations and pagination for cases where they are lacking from the CourtListener collection.

The collection does not currently include statutes or regulations, although Filevine plans to add them in the future.

Bottom Line

I have not yet directly tested Filevine’s citator and anti-hallucination tools, although I hope to do that soon.

However, I think that this will prove to be of significant value to Filevine’s customers, many of whom are law firms with significant litigation practices.

By integrating within its AI platform both a corpus of case law and the ability to check citations against that corpus, Filevine is providing customers with an important safety check against hallucinations.

Of course, as Anderson pointed out, none of that replaces the need for lawyers and legal professionals to validate their own work.

“I don’t think it completely solves the problem,” he said. “A human still has to take a look. But at least we’re going to point you in the right direction.”

news.titleEn: 15% of Large Firm Lawyers ‘Now Dependent on AI’
news.titleZh: 调查：大型律所15%律师“现在依赖AI”
news.summaryZh: LexisNexis在英国开展的一项调查发现，大型律所中15%的律师“现在依赖AI”完成工作，企业内部律师的这一依赖比例也达到13%，表明法律AI已真正嵌入整个行业，且这些数字只会继续上升。在500多名受访律师中，34%表示每天使用AI工具处理法律工作，32%表示每周使用多次，约三分之二的律师频繁使用AI。调查显示，排名前三的使用场景为起草、法律研究和文件审阅。绝大多数受访者仍担忧AI工具可能产生幻觉和错误，许多人青睐能围绕准确性和使用经过验证的来源提供保障的AI系统，而大型法律数据提供商可以做到这一点。调查还发现，多数人认为AI的使用正导致公众及其自身客户对法律问题产生错误理解。调查表明，法律AI已成为许多律师生活中的关键部分，相当数量的律师离开它便无法工作。这些数字只会上升，意味着法律人才可能流向支持高水平AI使用的律所。这对法律AI公司而言也是天赐良机，其客户不会流失，且还会增多；尽管控制市场份额的竞争可能激烈，但市场似乎只会更广更深。大量使用AI的一个副作用是token成本，该领域仍在变化，但显然总得有人为token使用付费；这或许并非致命问题，而是市场成熟的标志。总体而言，这对法律AI领域非常有利，尽管有些人可能会担忧越来越多律师不愿在没有AI辅助的情况下工作，另一些人则可能认为这在意料之中，就像许多律师需要Microsoft Word、电脑、桌子和椅子一样。
news.bodyHtml:
15% of lawyers at large law firms are ‘now dependent on AI’ to do their job, a survey by LexisNexis in the UK has found. For inhouse this dependency also stood at a notable 13% – indicating that legal AI has well and truly become embedded now across the profession. Plus, those numbers will only increase.

Moreover, 34% of the 500-plus lawyers surveyed said that they used AI tools for legal work every day, and 32% ‘multiple times per week’. So, around two-thirds of lawyers are really using AI frequently.

They also surfaced that the top three use cases are: drafting, legal research, and document review, which is to be expected.

Understandably, the vast majority were still concerned about a potential risk for hallucinations and errors from AI tools, and equally understandably many favoured AI systems that could provide reassurance around accuracy and the use of verified sources – something that the major legal data providers can do.

One other survey finding was that the majority also felt that AI use is leading to the general public, and their own clients, getting an incorrect understanding of legal issues – something that connects to yesterday’s survey by Justice about the wider use of chatbots.

What does this tell us?

It shows – especially on the usage and dependence points – that legal AI has become a critical part of many lawyers’ lives, in fact so much so that a notable number could not do their work without it.

Those numbers will only rise, meaning that legal talent will likely gravitate to those firms that support high levels of AI usage.

It also is manna from heaven for the legal AI companies, i.e. their customers are not going anywhere – and there will be more of them. There may be intense competition to control market share, but that market is only growing wider and deeper, it appears.

One side effect of heavy AI use is token costs. This area is still in flux, but quite clearly someone, somewhere has to pay for the token usage. Although, this is perhaps not a killer problem – and is a sign of a maturing market.

Overall, all very promising for the field of legal AI – although some may of course be concerned that an increasing number of lawyers would not want to do their work without AI in a supporting role. Others may say that this is to be expected, the same as many lawyers would want to have Microsoft Word, a computer, a desk and a chair….! Technology moves on, and so do expectations of what is normal to have.

You can find the LexisNexis survey and report here.

—

Come and join us in London this November 4th + 5th at Legal Innovators! The conference at the intersection of legal AI and the business of law. Day One: law firms, Day Two: inhouse.

Legal Innovators UK – London, Nov 4 and 5

Those numbers will only rise, meaning that legal talent will likely gravitate to those firms that support high levels of AI usage.

It also is manna from heaven for the legal AI companies, i.e. their customers are not going anywhere – and there will be more of them. There may be intense competition to control market share, but that market is only growing wider and deeper, it appears.

One side effect of heavy AI use is token costs. This area is still in flux, but quite clearly someone, somewhere has to pay for the token usage. Although, this is perhaps not a killer problem – and is a sign of a maturing market.

Overall, all very promising for the field of legal AI – although some may of course be concerned that an increasing number of lawyers would not want to do their work without AI in a supporting role. Others may say that this is to be expected, the same as many lawyers would want to have Microsoft Word, a computer, a desk and a chair….! Technology moves on, and so do expectations of what is normal to have.

You can find the LexisNexis survey and report here .

Come and join us in London this November 4th + 5th at Legal Innovators ! The conference at the intersection of legal AI and the business of law. Day One: law firms, Day Two: inhouse.

Legal Innovators UK – London, Nov 4 and 5

news.titleEn: What Does the AWS Deal with OpenAI Mean for Competition?
news.titleZh: AWS与OpenAI达成协议对竞争意味着什么？
news.summaryZh: OpenAI于2026年4月修改与微软的独家云安排，其最先进模型、Codex编码工具和托管AI代理现可通过AWS的Bedrock平台供企业客户使用。据亚马逊和OpenAI公告，亚马逊将向OpenAI投资至多500亿美元，并提供2吉瓦基于Trainium加速器的计算容量；OpenAI则承诺向AWS投入数百亿美元云支出用于训练和推理。微软Azure此前多年是OpenAI模型的独家商业云提供商，该独家性现已结束。2026年4月下旬宣布的修订允许OpenAI在包括AWS在内的多个云平台部署和销售模型，同时保留微软作为主要合作伙伴的地位，微软保留OpenAI知识产权长期许可、技术可行时对新模型的优先访问权，以及到2030年的上限收入分成安排；除非Azure无法支持必要能力，OpenAI产品仍将首先在Azure发布。这一重组反映AI基础设施需求规模增长，而非双方关系破裂。据OpenAI高管，企业客户日益需要多云可用性、区域灵活性和冗余。据亚马逊，OpenAI模型现可通过Amazon Bedrock获得；AWS还推出了Bedrock Managed Agents，使企业能在AWS基础设施内部署OpenAI驱动的代理。据AWS，推理和代理操作在客户AWS环境中运行，解决数据控制、可审计性和监管合规担忧。从竞争角度看，AWS在寻求基于OpenAI的AI服务时与Azure大致平等。据Synergy Research Group等，AWS约占全球云基础设施支出30%，微软Azure约20-22%，谷歌云约13%，三家合计约占全球收入三分之二，但无单一提供商超过多数份额。2026年4月前，获得OpenAI模型是Azure在企业采购中的差异化特征；一旦OpenAI模型在可比治理和安全条件下通过AWS提供，这一差异化因素便减弱。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! OpenAI’s expanded partnership with Amazon Web Services marks a significant shift in the relationship between major AI developers and hyperscale cloud providers. With OpenAI’s April 2026 decision to amend its exclusive cloud arrangement with Microsoft, OpenAI’s most advanced models are now available to enterprise customers through AWS’s Bedrock platform, alongside new OpenAI-powered agent services and jointly developed infrastructure tools. According to announcements from Amazon and OpenAI, the partnership brings OpenAI’s frontier models, Codex coding tools, and managed AI agents into AWS’s enterprise AI ecosystem. The partnership comes with substantial financial and infrastructure commitments. Amazon has agreed to invest up to $50 billion in OpenAI and to supply two gigawatts of compute capacity, using AWS’s Trainium accelerators. Separately, OpenAI has committed tens of billions of dollars in cloud spend to AWS for training and inference workloads. For several years, Microsoft Azure was the exclusive commercial cloud provider for OpenAI’s models, a relationship both companies credited with accelerating the commercial adoption of generative AI. That exclusivity is now over. According to OpenAI and Microsoft, amendments announced in late April 2026 permit OpenAI to deploy and sell its models on multiple cloud platforms—including AWS—while preserving Microsoft’s status as OpenAI’s primary partner. Microsoft retains long-term licenses to OpenAI intellectual property, preferential access to new models where technically feasible, and a capped revenue-sharing arrangement through 2030. OpenAI products will continue to ship first on Azure unless Azure cannot support necessary capabilities. This restructuring reflects the growing scale of AI infrastructure requirements rather than a breakdown in the Microsoft–OpenAI relationship. According to statements by OpenAI executives, enterprise customers increasingly require multi-cloud availability, regional flexibility, and redundancy—demands that are difficult to satisfy under exclusive cloud arrangements. AWS has moved quickly to fill the gap left by the end of OpenAI’s Azure exclusivity. According to Amazon, OpenAI models are now available through Amazon Bedrock, AWS’s managed platform for deploying foundation models under unified security, governance, and billing controls. AWS has also launched Bedrock Managed Agents, allowing enterprises to deploy OpenAI‑powered agents entirely within AWS infrastructure. According to AWS, inference and agent operations run inside the customer’s AWS environment, addressing common enterprise concerns about data control, auditability, and regulatory compliance. From a competition perspective, this places AWS on substantially equal footing with Azure for customers seeking OpenAI-based AI services. Despite its scale, AWS does not control a majority of the global cloud infrastructure market. According to Synergy Research Group and other industry analysts, AWS accounts for approximately 30 percent of worldwide cloud infrastructure spending, compared with roughly 20–22 percent for Microsoft Azure and about 13 percent for Google Cloud. Collectively, these three providers account for roughly two thirds of global cloud infrastructure revenue, but no single provider exceeds a majority share. This market structure helps explain why OpenAI’s shift to multi-cloud deployment is competitively significant. Prior to April 2026, access to OpenAI’s models served as a differentiating feature for Azure in enterprise procurement decisions. According to customer and analyst commentary, that differentiator diminished once OpenAI models became available through AWS under comparable governance and security conditions.

news.titleEn: Compliance used to be a cost center. The best firms are running it like a competitive advantage.
news.titleZh: 合规曾是成本中心，顶尖律所正将其转化为竞争优势
news.summaryZh:
客户会注意到律所受理新业务的速度差异：三小时与三天的差距并非人员配置问题，而是流程问题，并已成为竞争问题。过去二十年，合规与业务受理被视为必要但令人暗自抵触的职能，冲突分析师埋首搜索结果、受理请求停滞在队列中、聘用函来回往复，每家律所都面临同样的摩擦，却无人寻求更优方案。如今这一假设不再成立。AmLaw 100律所需管理复杂的外部律师指南，要求记录冲突审查流程、依据特定义务审核聘用条款，并在工作开始前配置道德墙。手动、大规模、不增加人手地满足这些要求，问题不会自行解决，反而随客户关系复杂化和监管预期收紧而恶化。行动最快的律所并未通过招聘解决，而是重建了该职能。

文章解释“代理式AI”的具体变化：新业务进入时，完整受理工作流自动运行，包括冲突检索与分类、外部律师指南匹配与例外审查、聘用条款起草、道德墙配置。合规专业人员看到业务时，常规工作已完成，呈递的是真正需要人类判断的例外。代理完成工作后交由专业人员决策，合规团队未被取代，而是被释放以专注于最重要案件。速度是可见收益，更不可见的是长期积累：每笔业务强化冲突检索逻辑、优化指南匹配、增加可搜索的机构知识，形成竞争对手无法构建的竞争护城河。文章警告，运行本地基础设施的律所面临风险，每季度停留在遗留系统，云端原生律所就在机构知识上扩大领先。
news.bodyHtml:
There is a firm in your market that accepted a new matter in three hours. Yours took three days. The client noticed and filed that away.

That gap is not a staffing problem. It’s a process problem. And it’s now a competitive one.

The first three pieces in this series made the case for why the firms pulling ahead are running the business side of law with the same rigor they bring to the practice side: growing on better relationship intelligence, protecting revenue before it disappears at billing. This is where that argument lands. Because none of it compounds the way it should if the front door is slow. A firm that wins the relationship but takes three days to onboard the matter is losing ground to a firm that closes in three hours.

Compliance and business acceptance aren’t separate from growth and revenue protection. They’re the function that either accelerates both or quietly constrains them.

For most of the last two decades, compliance and business acceptance were functions firms managed around. Necessary, respected in principle, quietly resented in practice. The conflicts analyst buried in search results. The intake request stalled in someone’s queue. The engagement letter going back and forth while the client waited to get started. Every firm dealt with the same friction. Nobody had a better option, so nobody asked whether there was one.

That assumption no longer holds.

The cost of slow intake

The economics of business acceptance have always been straightforward. A matter your firm can’t onboard in time is a matter your competitor onboards instead. What’s changed is the speed at which clients form that comparison and how quickly a pattern of slow intake compounds into a structural relationship disadvantage.

AmLaw 100 firms manage complex outside counsel guidelines that require documented conflict-check processes, engagement terms reviewed against specific obligations, and ethical walls configured before work begins. Meeting those requirements manually, at volume, without adding headcount, is not a problem that works itself out. It’s a problem that gets worse as client relationships grow more complex and regulatory expectations keep tightening.

The firms moving fastest have not found a way to hire their way out of it. They’ve rebuilt the function.

What agentic compliance actually means

The phrase “agentic AI” earns skepticism in most firms, and rightly so. A decade of technology promises has taught legal and compliance leaders to tune out the abstractions and ask what, specifically, changes.

Here is what specifically changes. This isn’t another technology layer on top of the work; it’s a fundamental shift in how the work gets done and who does it.

The moment a new matter comes in, the full acceptance workflow runs automatically. Conflicts are searched and triaged. Outside counsel guidelines are pulled, matched against the specific matter, and reviewed for exceptions. Engagement terms are drafted. Ethical walls are configured where required. By the time a compliance professional sees the matter, the routine work is done. What lands on their desk is the exception that genuinely needs them: the complex conflict, the unusual OCG requirement, the high-risk engagement that warrants human judgment.

Agents do the work and bring it back to your professionals for the decisions that actually require them. The compliance team isn’t displaced; they’re freed to focus on the cases that matter most, at scale.

The compounding advantage

Speed is the visible benefit. The less visible one compounds over a longer horizon.

Every matter that flows through an agentic system strengthens the conflict-check logic, refines OCG matching, and adds to searchable institutional knowledge that competitors running manual processes cannot build. That accumulated intelligence becomes the firm’s competitive moat. The gap it creates is structural and doesn’t close.

The firms most at risk are the ones currently running on-premises infrastructure and treating migration as a future-year decision. On-premises technology is a competitive problem. Every quarter spent on legacy systems is a quarter the cloud-native firms are extending their lead on the institutional knowledge that only accumulates in the cloud.

Where Intapp Celeste fits

Intapp Celeste is the AI platform purpose-built for the work that runs a professional firm, on your own data, under your own rules. Compliance with Celeste deploys agents across conflicts clearance, new business intake, and client obligations management: the three functions that together determine how fast and how cleanly a firm can onboard new business.

In practice, that means an agent that constructs conflict search strategies, matches corporate trees for every party, and runs the search automatically. An agent that creates and prepopulates intake forms using emails shared by requestors, validates data before submission, and flags enhancements before the request goes through. An agent that ingests outside counsel guideline documents, matches them to client records, and auto-populates key information into a central repository that enforces compliance in downstream systems.

Compliance with Celeste doesn’t replace the compliance professional. It removes the work that should never have required one.

To see how Compliance with Celeste runs agentic intake and conflicts workflows, register for the Compliance with Celeste: First Look webinar on September 29.

The window

The firms running manual intake processes are falling behind relative to firms that have already automated the routine. That gap is real and measurable. A firm that onboards in three hours wins business; a firm that takes three days does not. A firm whose compliance team spends its time on genuine risk decisions retains better talent and makes better calls than one where analysts are absorbed in search logistics.

This series has argued that the firms pulling ahead are operating on better information across three dimensions: growing on relationship intelligence, protecting revenue through engagement intelligence, and running compliance as a function that compounds in their favor rather than slows them down. Each of those shifts matters individually. Together, they describe a firm that is structurally different, not just more efficient, but harder to compete with in ways that don’t reverse.

The window to close that gap is narrowing. Every quarter spent on legacy systems is a quarter the cloud-native firms are extending a lead that doesn’t shrink on its own.

The firms that move now won’t just be more compliant. They’ll be faster, leaner, and running a business that the firms still waiting simply cannot match.
