news.bodyText:
New partnership will connect Legora with Intapp Walls for AI compliance and Intapp Time for automated AI-driven time capture, establishing a foundation for joint agentic innovation spanning the business and practice of law

NEW YORK, N.Y. — August 25, 2026 — Intapp (NASDAQ: INTA), the governed AI platform for professional firms in highly regulated industries, and Legora , the collaborative AI platform for lawyers, today announced a strategic partnership to deliver governed, AI-native workflows for the world’s leading law firms. The partnership will bring Intapp Walls for AI governance to Legora, while Legora will provide enriched data to Intapp Time for better time entry and profitability insights. This new partnership will establish a foundation for joint agentic innovation spanning the business and practice of law.

Legal and professional services firms need AI that operates within their existing ethical walls and permissions governance while connecting easily to the compliance and time capture platforms they already use. Legora and Intapp are partnering to address both at once.

The partnership spans three areas:

Governed AI through Intapp Walls for AI: Legora will integrate with Intapp Walls for AI so that AI-powered legal work in Legora respects a firm’s ethical walls, confidentiality obligations, and regulatory requirements. This means every workflow on Legora — from legal research and contract review to document drafting, due diligence, and extraction of insights — operates within the access controls defined under Intapp’s compliance framework.

Automated AI-driven time capture with Intapp Time: A differentiated integration with Intapp Time automatically captures structured usage data from work done in Legora and generates time entries in Intapp Time. Lawyers benefit from highly accurate, AI-driven time capture generated directly from the work they do in Legora, reducing leakage, and administrative burden without changing how they work.

Joint agentic innovation between Legora Agent and Intapp Celeste: The companies will co-innovate on native agentic workflows that combine the capabilities of the Legora Agent with Celeste, Intapp’s expert AI coworker that runs the business of the firm. An initial version will enable mutual customers to trigger Celeste capabilities within Legora, and Legora capabilities within Celeste.

One partnership across the business and practice of law

The partnership is designed for firms that want to scale AI across their organization without compromising on governance or operational rigor. With Intapp Walls for AI, firms can extend the ethical walls and information governance controls they already rely on to every AI interaction in Legora. With Intapp Time, the work lawyers do in Legora can drive accurate, AI-assisted time capture. And through joint agentic innovation via a Legora Agent–Intapp Celeste integration, the two companies intend to bring new governed agentic use cases to market over time.

Legora and Intapp will deliver the integrations in phases, with further details and availability coming soon to mutual customers.

Max Junestrand, Co-founder and CEO, Legora

“Firms want to put AI to work across both the practice of law and the business of law, but never at the expense of the controls their clients rely on. Integrating Legora with Intapp lets them do exactly that. They can deploy AI broadly with the assurance that every step stays within their existing ethical walls and permissions.”

John Hall, Chairman and CEO, Intapp

“Professionals are entrusted with their clients’ most sensitive matters, and that trust has to extend to every tool they use, including AI. Legora’s capabilities for the practice of law complement Intapp Celeste’s agentic solutions for the business of law. By bringing them together with Intapp Walls for AI and Intapp Time, we’re helping firms adopt AI that is governed, accountable, and connected to how their business actually runs.”

news.summaryZh: 在ILTACon第一天，变革管理、分类法、AI和文档管理等多场会议呈现共同主题：律所在增加更多技术之前，需先做好基础工作——明确要解决的问题、确定参与人员、确保信息结构足以支持目标，并评估工具是否真正契合工作流程。变革管理会议上，Michael Best & Friedrich LLP的Harriet Joubert-Vaklyes指出，应在决定新工具前先提出问题。现场民调显示，同行倡导者被视为推动采用的最有效方式，优于自上而下的指令或单纯培训。许多律所承认，变革管理规划仍发生在律师预期使用新工具前不久。结构良好的数据可提高AI效率，包括减少LLM需消耗的上下文量，并建议就术语含义达成一致，如股票购买协议与股份购买协议的区别及决策者，同时警告设计AI分类法时“多未必好”。图书管理员是律所内现有专业知识的来源，他们理解信息应如何协同工作。尽管代表法律技术生态的不同部分，发言者在数据结构、治理和复用重要性上表现出显著一致。分类法正成为AI讨论中更核心的部分。
news.bodyText: By Special Correspondent, Will Seaton at Draftwise. Missed day one at ILTACon? Across sessions on change management, taxonomy, AI, and document management, a common theme emerged: before firms add more technology, there’s some groundwork to do. What problem are you solving? Who needs to be involved? Is your firm’s information structured well enough to support what you want to do? And is the tool you’re evaluating actually built for the workflow you have in mind? Here are the key takeaways from day one. 1. Talk openly about the problem you’re solving In a session on change management, Harriet Joubert-Vaklyes of Michael Best & Friedrich LLP put it simply: ‘You need to start with questions long before you decide that a new tool is necessary.’ A live audience poll found that peer champions were seen as the most effective way to drive adoption, ahead of top-down mandates or training alone. At the same time, many firms acknowledged that change management planning still happens shortly before lawyers are expected to start using a new tool. The takeaway: Start the adoption work early. Understand the problem, involve the people who will use the technology, and give them a role in shaping the decision. 2. Get your own language straight Heath Harris of NetDocuments made the case that well-structured data can make AI more efficient, including by reducing the amount of context an LLM needs to consume. His practical advice was straightforward: agree on what things mean. Is it a stock purchase agreement or a share purchase agreement? Who decides? When designing taxonomies for AI, Harris cautioned that ‘more is not better’. Ivy Grey of iManage pointed to librarians as an existing source of expertise inside firms: ‘They understand how information is supposed to work together.’ Despite representing different parts of the legal technology ecosystem, the speakers showed notable alignment around the importance of data structure, governance, and reuse. Taxonomy is becoming a much more central part of the AI conversation.

news.bodyText: As predicted by AL, another tech giant has joined the legal world. Google Cloud has unveiled Gemini Enterprise for Legal, an ‘enterprise-grade, purpose-built agentic AI solution engineered for the complex requirements and workflows of the legal industry’. It now joins OpenAI and Anthropic in having a dedicated legal offering. Legora has also announced that they will become a partner, and that ‘approved mutual customers will be able to utilise some Legora capabilities from within Gemini Enterprise, receiving responses and answers to queries that link back to the relevant Legora thread, where citations, source grounding and permissions remain in place’. They’re also going to market with consultants and ALSPs, from Deloitte and Accenture, to Factor Law. But back to the main Gemini offering. They explained: ‘The solution includes specialized skills for lawyers, connectors to specialized legal systems, an expanding partner ecosystem of third-party agents [i.e where Legora and others would fit], and the foundational Gemini Enterprise platform. Initially available in preview for the legal industry, Gemini Enterprise for Legal debuts with launch customers including legal teams from Cleary, Freshfields, Weil, and Williams & Connolly.’ Gemini Enterprise for Legal and Financial Services are the first in a series of specialized, packaged industry solutions built on top of the secure, fully-governed Gemini Enterprise platform. Each industry solution delivers out-of-the-box, domain-specific, purpose-built AI capabilities, which may include tailored agents, specialized skills that provide simple shortcuts to manage a variety of workflows, data connectors, and model optimizations tailored for a specific industry, they added. Although Google has dabbled in legal, this appears to be the first fully operational legal AI offering for the wider market. They describe it this way: ‘Gemini Enterprise for Legal is a legal plugin inside the Gemini Enterprise app, not a separate application your team logs into.’ However, this massively expands upon what most people would regard as a ‘plugin’ – this is a plugin the size of Texas! — (Advertisement) — Legal Innovators New York conference – Nov 17 and 18. — Gemini Enterprise for Legal ‘delivers an integrated, secure environment configured for rapid deployment with four core components’:

research.titleEn: Beyond Accuracy: A Dual-Judge Evaluation Protocol for Vision-Language Models in Legally Grounded Tasks
research.titleZh: 超越准确性：法律基础任务中视觉-语言模型的双法官评估协议
research.abstractEn: AI systems are increasingly evaluated for legally accountable settings, where correct outputs must also be justifiable against an applicable legal standard. Existing legal-AI benchmarks and LLM-as-judge protocols provide important infrastructure for measuring task performance and open-ended response quality. We contribute one additional evaluation signal: a dual-judge protocol that pairs a standard 0-10 quality judge with a strict binary semantic-equivalence judge against a human-curated reference.   We study a controlled, visually grounded regulatory task - UK traffic-sign interpretation, whose meaning is a codified question with a known reference for every input - and measure not merely whether the two judges disagree (by construction they must) but how much and where. On 4,680 evaluations under seven visibility levels and two occlusion modes, the two judges are moderately associated (point-biserial r = 0.644), while revealing an asymmetric Type II pattern affecting 8.0% of all evaluations.   Its distribution is instructive: the marginal rate peaks at high visibility (14.2% at v = 0.8) simply because high-scoring answers are common there, but conditioned on the answer already scoring above 7, the rate is highest under heavy occlusion (54-63% at v <= 0.3), so a high quality score is least trustworthy when the input is most degraded.   We are explicit that the signal is a property of this judge and reference: a 49-row human check shows the 0-10 judge aligns closely with everyday-reader judgement (Pearson r = 0.81; r = 0.80 with the LLM accuracy sub-score), while the equivalence judge is fairly but one-directionally stricter. The protocol adds one LLM call per evaluation and surfaces a signal single-judge protocols do not report. We release the prompt template, occluded variants, and full evaluation results.
research.abstractZh: 人工智能系统越来越多地被用于法律问责环境中，在这些环境中，正确的输出还必须能够根据适用的法律标准进行辩护。现有的法律人工智能基准和LLM作为法官的协议为衡量任务性能和开放式回答质量提供了重要基础设施。我们贡献了一个额外的评估信号：一个双法官协议，将标准的0-10质量法官与一个严格的二元语义等价法官配对，并与人工策划的参考进行比较。我们研究了一个受控的、视觉基础的监管任务——英国交通标志解释，其含义是一个编码问题，每个输入都有已知的参考——并不仅衡量两个法官是否不同意（按构造它们必须不同意），而且衡量它们不同意的程度和位置。在七种可见性水平和两种遮挡模式下的4,680次评估中，两个法官中度相关（点二列相关系数r = 0.644），同时揭示了影响所有评估8.0%的不对称II型模式。其分布具有启发性：边际率在高可见性时达到峰值（在v = 0.8时为14.2%），仅仅因为高分答案在那里很常见，但以答案已经得分高于7为条件，该率在重度遮挡下最高（在v ≤ 0.3时为54-63%），因此当输入最退化时，高质量分数最不可信。我们明确指出，该信号是此法官和参考的属性：一个49行的人工检查显示，0-10法官与日常读者判断紧密一致（Pearson r = 0.81；与LLM准确性子分数r = 0.80），而等价法官虽然公平但单向更严格。该协议每次评估增加一次LLM调用，并揭示了单一法官协议未报告的信号。我们发布了提示模板、遮挡变体和完整评估结果。

news.titleEn: From Search Rankings to Vibe Coding: How Best Lawyers Is Rebuilding for the AI Era
news.titleZh: 从搜索排名到氛围编程：Best Lawyers如何为AI时代重建自身
news.summaryZh:
Best Lawyers首席执行官Phillip Greer和高级副总裁Elizabeth Petit介绍了公司的内部AI转型。传统搜索正在变化，Google AI Overviews和ChatGPT等答案引擎越来越多地直接提供答案，而不引导用户点击蓝色链接。SEO仍然重要，但律所现在需要考虑生成引擎优化（GEO），以及AI系统在决定信任哪些来源时使用的信号。结构化数据、模式标记、实质性内容和第三方验证都成为因素。Best Lawyers长期积累的同行评审排名数据，可能被AI系统视为独立信号。Petit介绍了Smithy AI，该系统帮助律师和律所营销人员基于Best Lawyers的结构化信息和现有律师内容生成个人资料内容初稿，再由人工编辑。随着生成系统使通用法律内容生产变得容易，独特的专业知识、声音和可信的第三方信号将更有价值。

Greer还推动了一项不寻常的AI采用计划。在构建连接SQL数据库、HubSpot、Gong、Google Analytics和会计数据的安全数据层后，他创建了内部Best Lawyers App Store，员工用自然语言基于公司数据构建应用。最初约30%的员工进行氛围编程，现已增长到约40%。Petit描述了在非软件工程背景下构建研究和KPI仪表板。过去需要Excel公式、Power BI报告和数周等待的项目，现在有时从9:30的提问到10:30就能生成可用的内部应用。这一转变也改变了软件工程师的角色，他们更专注于架构、数据基础设施、性能和治理。Greer描述了将部分数据架构转向Elasticsearch，并开发内部代理AI团队成员“Bestie”。Petit和Greer还提到“AI吸血鬼”效应，即即时反馈鼓励人们持续工作。Best Lawyers在2026年版《美国最佳律师》中引入了人工智能法律作为正式实践领域。Greer和Petit预计AI不会一夜之间取代计费小时，但客户会更多询问付费内容。
news.bodyHtml:
What happens when a 40-year-old legal data company decides its employees should start building their own software? This week on we talk with Best Lawyers CEO Phillip Greer and Senior Vice President of Research and Product Strategy Elizabeth Petit about an internal AI transformation that reaches far beyond adding ChatGPT to the corporate toolkit. Best Lawyers is experimenting with generative engine optimization, internal agentic systems, vibe coding, and an AI development environment where employees across research, finance, marketing, and other departments build applications around the company’s data.

Greer begins with a challenge facing every law firm marketing team: traditional search is changing. Google AI Overviews and answer engines such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini increasingly give users answers without sending them to the familiar list of blue links. Greer argues that SEO still matters, but law firms now need to think about Generative Engine Optimization, or GEO, and the signals AI systems use when deciding which sources deserve trust. Structured data, schema markup, substantive content, and third-party validation all become part of the equation. For Best Lawyers, its long history of peer-reviewed rankings offers an interesting advantage. The company’s data serves as an independent signal that AI systems might weigh differently from content produced by a firm’s own marketing department.

Petit explains how Best Lawyers is applying the same thinking to legal marketing through Smithy AI, a system designed to help attorneys and law firm marketers develop profile content without endlessly copying the same biography across websites. Smithy draws from Best Lawyers’ structured information and existing lawyer content to produce a starting point that attorneys and marketers then edit. The larger goal is authenticity. As generative systems make producing generic legal content almost effortless, Greer argues that distinctive expertise, voice, and credible third-party signals become more valuable rather than less.

The conversation then moves inside Best Lawyers, where Greer has taken a far more unusual approach to AI adoption. After building a secure data layer connecting systems including SQL databases, HubSpot, Gong, Google Analytics, and accounting data, he created an internal Best Lawyers App Store where employees use natural language to build applications against company data. What began with roughly 30 percent of the workforce vibe coding has grown to around 40 percent, according to Greer. Petit describes building research and KPI dashboards despite coming from a research rather than software engineering background. Projects that once required Excel formulas, Power BI reports, development queues, and weeks of waiting now sometimes move from a question at 9:30 to a working internal application by 10:30.

That shift also changes the role of professional software engineers. Rather than spending their time building another reporting screen or internal form, Best Lawyers’ engineers increasingly concentrate on architecture, data infrastructure, performance, governance, and the guardrails surrounding employee-built applications. Greer describes moving parts of the company’s data architecture toward Elasticsearch and developing “Bestie,” an internal agentic AI team member. Yet speed introduces another problem. Petit and Greer describe an “AI vampire” effect, where instant feedback encourages people to keep working because the machine never gets tired, goes home, or stops responding. Human judgment includes knowing when the human needs to stop.

The discussion closes with what these changes mean for legal practice itself. Best Lawyers introduced Artificial Intelligence Law as a formal practice area in the 2026 edition of The Best Lawyers in America, reflecting how AI work has spread across technology, intellectual property, privacy, employment, compliance, litigation, and counseling. Looking further ahead, Greer and Petit do not expect AI to erase the billable hour overnight. They do expect clients to ask harder questions about what they are paying for, how legal work was produced, where AI contributed, and where the lawyer’s judgment created value. If AI makes routine production dramatically faster, the economic question for law firms becomes less about how many hours technology saves and more about how firms explain, price, and defend the value of human expertise.

What happens when a 40-year-old legal data company decides its employees should start building their own software? This week on we talk with Best Lawyers CEO Phillip Greer and Senior Vice President of Research and Product Strategy Elizabeth Petit about an internal AI transformation that reaches far beyond adding ChatGPT to the corporate toolkit. Best Lawyers is experimenting with generative engine optimization, internal agentic systems, vibe coding, and an AI development environment where employees across research, finance, marketing, and other departments build applications around the company’s data.

Greer begins with a challenge facing every law firm marketing team: traditional search is changing. Google AI Overviews and answer engines such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini increasingly give users answers without sending them to the familiar list of blue links. Greer argues that SEO still matters, but law firms now need to think about Generative Engine Optimization, or GEO, and the signals AI systems use when deciding which sources deserve trust. Structured data, schema markup, substantive content, and third-party validation all become part of the equation. For Best Lawyers, its long history of peer-reviewed rankings offers an interesting advantage. The company’s data serves as an independent signal that AI systems might weigh differently from content produced by a firm’s own marketing department.

Petit explains how Best Lawyers is applying the same thinking to legal marketing through Smithy AI, a system designed to help attorneys and law firm marketers develop profile content without endlessly copying the same biography across websites. Smithy draws from Best Lawyers’ structured information and existing lawyer content to produce a starting point that attorneys and marketers then edit. The larger goal is authenticity. As generative systems make producing generic legal content almost effortless, Greer argues that distinctive expertise, voice, and credible third-party signals become more valuable rather than less.

The conversation then moves inside Best Lawyers, where Greer has taken a far more unusual approach to AI adoption. After building a secure data layer connecting systems including SQL databases, HubSpot, Gong, Google Analytics, and accounting data, he created an internal Best Lawyers App Store where employees use natural language to build applications against company data. What began with roughly 30 percent of the workforce vibe coding has grown to around 40 percent, according to Greer. Petit describes building research and KPI dashboards despite coming from a research rather than software engineering background. Projects that once required Excel formulas, Power BI reports, development queues, and weeks of waiting now sometimes move from a question at 9:30 to a working internal application by 10:30.

That shift also changes the role of professional software engineers. Rather than spending their time building another reporting screen or internal form, Best Lawyers’ engineers increasingly concentrate on architecture, data infrastructure, performance, governance, and the guardrails surrounding employee-built applications. Greer describes moving parts of the company’s data architecture toward Elasticsearch and developing “Bestie,” an internal agentic AI team member. Yet speed introduces another problem. Petit and Greer describe an “AI vampire” effect, where instant feedback encourages people to keep working because the machine never gets tired, goes home, or stops responding. Human judgment includes knowing when the human needs to stop.

The discussion closes with what these changes mean for legal practice itself. Best Lawyers introduced Artificial Intelligence Law as a formal practice area in the 2026 edition of The Best Lawyers in America , reflecting how AI work has spread across technology, intellectual property, privacy, employment, compliance, litigation, and counseling. Looking further ahead, Greer and Petit do not expect AI to erase the billable hour overnight. They do expect clients to ask harder questions about what they are paying for, how legal work was produced, where AI contributed, and where the lawyer’s judgment created value. If AI makes routine production dramatically faster, the economic question for law firms becomes less about how many hours technology saves and more about how firms explain, price, and defend the value of human expertise.

So it is a fun time to get yourself absorbed in what’s happening new in legal tech.

Marlene Gebauer (02:46) Yeah, serendipity is definitely part of the ILTACON experience, but this is great advice in terms of using the Legal Technology Hub directory because it can be overwhelming, and this will allow you to focus on the vendors and people that you definitely need to talk to before you leave.

Marlene Gebauer (03:14) Welcome to The Geek in Review, the podcast focused on innovative and creative ideas in the legal industry. I’m Marlene Gebauer.

Greg Lambert (03:21) And I’m Greg Lambert, and today we are exploring how a legacy data institution is completely rearchitecting itself from the inside out for the generative AI era.

Marlene Gebauer (03:34) We are thrilled to welcome Phillip Greer, CEO of Best Lawyers, and Elizabeth Petit, Senior Vice President of Research and Product Strategy. Phillip and Elizabeth have been leading a radical internal and external transformation at Best Lawyers, turning the organization into a pioneer for agentic workflows, vibe coding, and generative engine optimization. Elizabeth and Phillip, welcome to The Geek in Review.

Phillip Greer (03:58) Thank you so much for having us. We’re quite excited to be here today.

Greg Lambert (04:03) Right. Well, Phillip, I’m excited about this because I think a lot of us have been hearing about SEO for years, and now recently, with all the AI, we’re hearing more about generative engine optimization, or GEO.

Greg Lambert (04:20) Last year you noticed that there was a massive drop in traditional web traffic due to all of these AI overviews that you see with Google and others, to where people are getting answers rather than getting links out to the websites and then going and finding the answer themselves.

So you talk about your pivot away, or, well, I’m sure you still use SEO, but you’re also having to implement this new generative engine optimization, and that differs a lot from the SEO that a lot of us here at law firms have grown up on and realized, in order for us to get high up on the Google rankings, we need to be good at that.

So how does GEO differ from traditional SEO? And why is it that these third-party reviews or peer reviews are becoming the primary, what you call a trust signal, that keeps firms from being compressed out of the AI search answers that we need to get involved in?

Phillip Greer (05:26) Yeah, so I think it’s helpful to give a little bit more context. You started that process.

We’ve all been chasing SEO for over two decades, right? Google came out, and then, how do we get to the top of that Google ranking so that our customers and new clients can see the work that we’re doing? And we did that through so many things, backlinking efforts, keywords, thought leadership pieces, marketing associations, marketing partnerships with different types of organizations, et cetera, et cetera.

It’s been popular to say that SEO is dead. So first off, I don’t think SEO is dead. Traditional SEO is still important, and it’s the foundation of AIO.

So a few years ago, Google changed their search engine, and when you started searching, all of a sudden the middle of the funnel, or that blue-links world, started to go away, and you were using that Google Gemini. So you would say, “Hey, I need to find a lawyer for an issue I’m having,” and then it would give you a summary.

And then what was happening was so many law firms, and any type of business, were losing 15, 20, 30 percent of their web traffic because the blue links aren’t being clicked anymore. The users are going in, they’re getting that overview, they’re getting what they need, and they’re kind of moving on.

Well, those original AIO types of overviews were being fed from those SEO efforts.

Phillip Greer (06:51) The shift that we did over the last couple of years is, first, make sure that our content is structured in a way that, when these LLMs such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini or Claude are coming to our website and looking at our data in traditional SEO forms, we’re tagging it and presenting it in ways that are helpful.

So you think about SEO stuff you used to do. It was all about meta descriptions, keywords, page titles, and then, again, we talked about some of the backlinking techniques. Those things were structuring it so that, when the crawlers are finding your website, they know how to get that data.

Well, that’s kind of amped up with AIO and then eventually what we’ll talk about with GEO. You not only needed the meta descriptions, you needed to have good schema markup. You need to describe sections on the page, to be able to ask questions, answer questions, so that when the AI engines were gathering data, it wasn’t only finding it, they could start to interpret it, because that interpretation is what becomes a little more important when you think of things like ChatGPT or Google Gemini.

It has to take the structured data, and then it has to interpret it and create insights and say, okay, now you can start showing up in these overviews.

The latest shift, and I think it’s the biggest shift, is this GEO, and that was your opening question.

Phillip Greer (08:14) The generative engine optimization approach. And that is making these AI systems not only get your data, but understand that they can trust your data. And so, how do you trust data?

Data has to come from quality places, things that are not produced by a marketing staff. So we’ve all gamed the SEO world. Every year, Google changed the algorithm again. What do we do? How do we get to the top? We spend more dollars. We make sure that we have more content. We flood the internet with it. We do backlink strategies, right?

That would work for SEO, and then it would work until they changed the next algorithm again.

With GEO, you have these AI systems that have some insight and intellect in the sense that it knows whether or not the content is being produced by you, your law firm, putting more information out there, or are you reading a service like Best Lawyers that’s known for producing peer review surveys and, ultimately, lists of lawyers? It’s an annual process. It’s been around for 40 years. It’s got a strong standing, a big domain authority. It is a trusted source. It’s third party to the industry that is putting out their data, right?

Marlene Gebauer (45:41) Not unless you

Marlene Gebauer (45:42) create an agent to remind you.

Greg Lambert (45:44) Yeah, exactly.

Elizabeth Petit (45:44) Yeah, exactly.

Phillip Greer (45:46) And that runs into, you mentioned earlier, the AI vampire. That’s what it is. It’s feeding off of you, you’re feeding off of it, and you have to recognize, okay, I get to walk out in the sunlight. So I need to go do that some.

Marlene Gebauer (46:01) Tear my eyes away from the screen, yes.

Greg Lambert (46:04) Yeah, well, I always say when somebody asks me what’s the addictive game that I’m playing on my phone, I say it’s my $200-a-month Claude account. I’m on it all the time.

Phillip Greer (46:15) Yeah, yeah.

Elizabeth Petit (46:16) Yeah. Yeah.

Greg Lambert (46:18) So yeah, you’re right.

Elizabeth, before we start wrapping up, I know that AI, of course, isn’t only affecting how we manage engineers, how we manage managers, and how we all become vibe coders. It’s becoming a part of Best Lawyers content as well.

Do you mind talking about what that encompasses, how you came up with it, and what you found?

Elizabeth Petit (47:00) Yep. So, you know, it is always our goal to help connect clients in need of legal services, whether that’s professional or personal, with the right attorney for their case.

And so about three years ago, we started to see that law firms were adding AI practice groups. And so we added this and started researching AI as its own practice area.

Now, when this first started, I envisioned this would be sort of a subset of emerging tech.

And we have technology law, and that this would kind of,

Greg Lambert (47:51) This is what the blockchain lawyers morphed into, right?

Elizabeth Petit (47:54) Yeah, exactly. This is sort of what I thought this would evolve into.

Phillip Greer (47:54) Yeah. Yeah.

Elizabeth Petit (47:57) But as AI is so dynamic and evolving so quickly, the definition of an AI lawyer is quite nebulous.

Are you counseling AI corporations? Are you focused on data privacy? Are you looking at government issues? Even labor and employment. I mean, AI is truly touching everything.

And so because of that, it started off more as a subset of technology. But we will have to evolve with AI in our awards as this industry evolves so rapidly to make sure that it is reflective of how legal is addressing AI and the needs of clients.

Greg Lambert (48:49) Are you thinking about

Phillip Greer (48:49) We didn’t even get it.

Greg Lambert (48:52) an AI-native law firm category? That seems to be the big buzz phrase these days.

Elizabeth Petit (49:01) Yeah. We are getting ready to evaluate adding new practice areas for next year. So look for that webinar series coming up soon.

Phillip Greer (49:10) Yeah, and whether or not we have AI law firms that we recognize, that’s currently not on the horizon.

But it is the question, when do I have my work done by AI and AI Inc.?

Greg Lambert (49:29) All right. Well, before we get to our crystal ball question and we start looking at the future, I want to ask you guys to look back in the past. And I think I know where this is going based on our conversation.

Phillip and Elizabeth, what’s something that’s true today that wasn’t necessarily true for you and Best Lawyers a year ago? What’s changed in that year?

Greg Lambert (49:52) What’s changed in that year?

Phillip Greer (49:53) I mean, the biggest thing, it’s everything we talked about, that we have non-builders, and they’re taking their data and they’re solving their own problems.

We have a decent engineering team as far as size because our company is research and tech. We use a lot of tech to build rankings and recognitions in over 76 countries.

And so we always built a lot of custom software, and we’ve always been able to do dynamic things for each department. But there was always a process. You got in line, got queued up, and then it handed off to the engineering team.

Phillip Greer (50:30) And now that’s changed greatly because everybody is handling the majority of their own needs internally.

We’re still externally using our engineers. We’re not developing any software. All software that’s hitting our customers is still handled by our engineering team because that’s the right way to handle it.

But for all our internal needs, everyone’s a builder. So that was a big change I’ve seen. That is different now.

Elizabeth Petit (50:59) I think the surprise that has come out of this is, I’ve been with Best Lawyers for over 15 years now, and I did not expect this career development opportunity.

Elizabeth Petit (51:15) So I thought that I would continue to grow in leadership or other traditional career development paths, but all of a sudden to have an entire skill set that I did not have last year, that’s pretty amazing.

And I’m grateful to have been given that opportunity.

Marlene Gebauer (51:37) All right, we’ve looked a little bit at the past, and now it’s time to look in the future.

If you would gaze into your crystal ball and look ahead a few years, as autonomous agents and vibe coding become standard inside both data organizations and law firms, what’s the single biggest shift you see coming for the legal profession’s economic model, specifically regarding the billable hour?

Phillip Greer (52:03) Hmm. So I don’t think the billable hour is going to disappear overnight, right? But it will shift.

People are going to have more scrutiny of how you’re backing up the value of what’s coming from the work product.

And there’ll be more questions about how did you derive that actual result set.

It was already the question, you hire the partner and you ask yourself, am I getting the partner’s hours or am I getting the junior associate? That’s already been on the table for a long time. And some clients have been wanting to know that. And they want to know, I am paying for the partner’s time.

I think there’s going to be a lot of questions that more clients are going to be asking. I want you to break down the justification. Am I paying for the senior partner’s time, or how much am I paying for the AI’s time?

I don’t know what that’s going to look like as far as how it wants to be shown in transparency, but I think that’s going to be a big question.

Marlene Gebauer (53:01) How about Elizabeth?

Elizabeth Petit (53:04) I agree. I don’t think that this is, legal doesn’t revolutionize overnight. We’ve all been in this industry for a minute.

But a lawyer is not going to become twice as productive with AI. They’re not going to bill twice as many hours a day. That’s not possible.

And so figuring out that balance between what is the appropriate use for AI, but still what requires that human judgment that AI will never replace.

Marlene Gebauer (54:18) Yeah, thank you.

Phillip Greer (54:18) Yeah, thank you so much for having us.

Elizabeth Petit (54:19) Thank you for having us.

news.titleEn: Newcode raises Series A, bringing 2026 funding to $20M
news.titleZh: Newcode完成A轮融资，2026年累计融资达2000万美元
news.summaryZh: 总部位于挪威的法律AI公司Newcode于8月24日宣布完成A轮融资，使其2026年迄今的融资总额达到2000万美元。Newcode未公开本轮A轮融资的具体金额，但该公司今年3月已获得650万美元的种子轮融资。本轮A轮融资由OnDean Forward领投，The LegalTech Fund（也是种子轮投资者）大力参与，同时还有Antiportfolio Ventures、Relativity的投资部门Rel Labs以及其他现有投资者参投。这笔资金将帮助Newcode拓展美国市场。AI革命对律师事务所而言最终是好事，但法律市场需要控制力和灵活性才能转型为AI原生，公司的使命是帮助律所构建真正属于自己的AI能力。Newcode提供多个MCP连接器，并构建了专有的智能检索系统，可在整个律所及其文档中情境化信息。用户可以通过跨数据源构建工作流，或通过前沿模型访问Newcode，从而为客户创建独特的工作成果。该技术为律所提供了一条拥有自身AI技术栈的路径，并帮助他们在法律实践和业务中加速AI应用。Newcode在2026年增长显著加快，目前为欧洲和美国的60多家律所及政府机构提供服务。过去12个月，年度经常性收入增长超过两倍，新增客户遍布欧洲、AmLaw 200强律所、不断增长的美国部署客户群以及爱尔兰律师协会（该协会为全国超过2150名出庭律师提供支持）。他们与律所领导和企业法务负责人交流时，客户一致希望AI平台能适应他们的运营方式，而不是强迫他们去适应平台，Newcode已证明能满足这一需求。
news.bodyHtml:
Norway-founded legal AI company Newcode today (24 August) announced Series A funding round that brings its total funding so far in 2026 to $20m. While Newcode hasn’t stated publicly the value of this Series A, in March this year it raised $6.5m in seed funding.

The Series A, which will help Newcode expand into the US, was led by OnDean Forward with significant participation from The LegalTech Fund (also a seed investor), alongside Antiportfolio Ventures, Relativity’s investment arm Rel Labs, and other existing investors. 

Advertisement

“The AI revolution is ultimately a great thing for law firms,” said Maged Helmy, founder and CEO of Newcode. “But to transform to AI-native, the legal market needs control and flexibility. Our mission is to help firms build AI capabilities that are truly their own.”

Newcode comes with multiple MCP connectors and has built a proprietary agentic retrieval system that contextualises information across the firm and its documents. Users can create unique work product for their customers by building workflows across data sources, or by accessing Newcode through a frontier model.

Advertisement

“We’re excited to work with Maged and the team at Newcode,” said Andrew Sieja, Relativity founder and principal partner at OnDean Forward. “The tech gives law firms a path to own their AI stack and helps them accelerate the use of AI across the practice and business of law.”

Newcode’s growth has accelerated sharply in 2026. The company now serves more than 60 law firms and government agencies across Europe and the United States. Annual recurring revenue has more than tripled in the last 12 months, with new customers added across Europe, the AmLaw 200, a growing base of U.S. deployments, and The Bar of Ireland, which provides support to more than 2,150 barristers across the country.

“We spend a lot of time with law firm leaders and heads of in-house legal teams,” said Zach Posner, managing partner at The LegalTech Fund. “They are consistent on one point: they want AI platforms that adapt to how they operate, not platforms that force them to adapt. Newcode has proven it can meet that demand, and we’re excited to support their continued growth.”

news.titleEn: Exclusive: Jigsaw set to move into entity management in major product expansion
news.titleZh: 独家：Jigsaw 将进军实体管理领域，进行重大产品扩展
news.summaryZh:
视觉智能与公司图表平台 Jigsaw 将进军端到端实体管理领域，利用其与交易各阶段实体（从律师事务所到企业和金融机构客户）的关系。Jigsaw 于2020年在英国由前投资基金律师 Stephen Scanlan 和前魔术圈律师转银行家 Travis Leon 创立，帮助律师可视化交易，并已发展为项目管理工具。2024年完成1500万美元 A 轮融资。收入仍主要来自法律行业，但近年已扩展至会计师事务所，与包括四大在内的前十大事务所全部建立关系，进而与这些领域的大型企业客户合作。

过去约一年半，Jigsaw 一直在增长企业和金融机构客户。客户希望交易建模后成为活生生的现实，将公司结构图维护为嵌入数据的实体管理系统。企业希望一个平台覆盖各垂直领域：客户端维护、跟踪、合规、KYC 和申报日期；顾问（律所或四大等）进行建模和起草拟议结构。Jigsaw 正在推出实体生命周期管理平台。Jigsaw 独特地拥有律所和四大的分销渠道以及建模和数据能力。现有实体管理巨头没有法律客户。Jigsaw 有详细的权限控制，确保律所只能访问其参与的事项，防火墙是核心部分。企业侧受益于所有顾问集中一处，而非手动更新 PowerPoint 或 PDF。Jigsaw 已签约四个大型设计合作伙伴，将于9月开始工作。
news.bodyHtml:
Visual intelligence and corporate diagramming platform Jigsaw is set to move into the end-to-end entity management arena, leveraging its relationships with entities across every stage of a deal, from law firms to corporate and financial institution customers, we can reveal. 

Founded in the UK in 2020 by former investment funds lawyer Stephen Scanlan and former magic circle lawyer-turned-banker Travis Leon, Jigsaw, helps lawyers to visualise transactions and has also evolved into a project management tool. It raised a $15m Series A in 2024.

Advertisement

While its revenue still largely comes from the legal sector, in recent years it has expanded into working with accountancy firms, notching up relationships with all ten of the top 10 firms, including the ‘Big Four’. That in turn has led to working with large corporate customers of both of those verticals. 

Speaking to Legal IT Insider about the genesis of the entity management concept, Scanlan said that clients of Jigsaw’s clients “started receiving our diagrams and our steps papers, so a major corporate would get a diagram from our client, Gibson Dunn, for example. And they’ll say, ‘well, that’s interesting. Where do you get that? What can we do with it? Can we put data behind it?’” 

Advertisement

As a result, for the past circa year and a half, Jigsaw has been growing its corporate and financial institutions customers and Scanlan said: “They came to us and said, ‘you’ve historically been great at the modelling side, the blueprinting side, but what could a corporate structure look like? What could the entities look like in terms of if I want to make a fund launch or I want to do a corporate restructure?’ 

“What they wanted was for that transaction, once it had been modelled, to become a living reality. They wanted to then maintain the corporate structure chart as an entity management system that itself embedded data.” 

While very few law firms use entity management software, most corporates do and Scanlan says: “They are looking for a tool that can become one platform across each vertical. So there’s the client side, the corporate financial institution side, where they want to maintain and track and do compliance and KYC and filing dates on the living structure. But they also want their advisors, whether that’s a law firm or a Big Four or beyond, to come in and do the modelling and the drafting of proposed structures.  

“That’s a virtuous ecosystem where they don’t want to have some teams in Excel, some teams in Athennian, some teams in PowerPoint, some teams in Jigsaw, some teams in some of our competitors. They want one tool where the whole entity lifecycle management and ELM, entity life cycle management, is the platform that we are launching.” 

It’s very early days in terms of product development but Scanlan says the demand is there and so is the rare access to all buyers across the deal cycle. 

“As of today, we are really uniquely positioned to make this play because no one else has a distribution across the law firms and the Big Four and the product capabilities on both the modelling and the data side.” 

While there are enormous entity management players in the market, Scanlan says: “They have zero legal clients. So that means that they can’t get that cycle working, that entity life cycle working.”  

In terms of governance and ensuring that firms only access the matters they are working on, Scanlan says: “We have very, very detailed permissions control. So if you are a big private equity house and you are the relevant administrator, you see everything. You see your panel of 40 law firms. From your perspective, you don’t really care where the modelling has come from, as long as you can aggregate it into your one big bucket. What you don’t want is other law firms seeing other law firms deals with proposals. So that firewalling is a very core part of the product.” 

He adds: “From the corporate side, it’s actually a benefit that you can finally have all your advisors in one place as opposed to all your advisors sending you PowerPoint or PDF files from time to time, which you then have to manually update your records with. It’s all just there.” 

Scanlan says Jigsaw has signed up four large design partners to start work in September. 

“We’re not the biggest company or the most profitable company or the fastest growing company, but weirdly, we are the only company in the world that can do this product this year,” he says.

news.titleEn: LexisNexis Unveils ‘Legal Intelligence Engine,’ Rebuilding Protégé Around Dynamic Agentic Orchestration
news.titleZh: LexisNexis推出“法律智能引擎”，围绕动态代理编排重建Protégé
news.summaryZh: LexisNexis Legal & Professional发布新一代Lexis+ with Protégé，推出新的代理能力，让法律专业人士在一个直观的AI体验中从初步想法推进到可供审阅的工作成果。该版本被命名为LexisNexis法律智能引擎，核心是新的编排层或“harness”，它根据用户描述的任务动态选择并协调AI模型、代理、技能和内容来源，而非像此前平台那样通过预定义工作流路由请求。用户可以描述想要完成的任务，并在Microsoft Word、Excel或PowerPoint中收到可供审阅的输出，系统在后台决定应用哪些模型、工具和来源，同时将上下文从一个事项步骤延续到下一步。与先前代理平台的关键变化是harness架构：此前工作流预先脚本化，而新平台可引入额外工具和信息，检查工作并在输出未完全满足请求时循环重做。系统在执行计划前向用户展示计划，允许修改，并逐步展示工作过程。harness可调用LexisNexis组合中的内容，如Lex Machina的法官分析、Intelligize的SEC相关研究和Law360的新闻，以及公司超过2000亿份文档和客户文档管理系统中的文档。法律搜索和网络搜索已统一，系统还会验证网络结果中的引文，消除了多来源工作此前需要的工具切换。新能力包括Shepard's Verify，将引文服务扩展到起草工作流，除确认引案准确且仍为有效法律外，还验证其与当前任务的相关性。当被问及律师能否将对方即决判决动议交给系统并返回完成的答辩状时，Smyth表示现实“介于两者之间”，用户仍需审阅结果，因为监管机构表示用户仍需对所提交内容负责。
news.bodyHtml:
LexisNexis Legal & Professional today announced what it is calling the next generation of Lexis+ with Protégé, its generative AI legal assistant, unveiling new agentic capabilities designed to enable legal professionals to move from an initial idea to review-ready work product in one intuitive AI experience.

Branding it the LexisNexis Legal Intelligence Engine, the release centers on a new orchestration layer, or “harness,” that dynamically selects and coordinates AI models, agents, skills and content sources based on the task a user describes, rather than routing requests through predefined workflows as the platform previously did.

The practical effect, the company says, is that a legal professional can describe what they want to accomplish and receive review-ready output in Microsoft Word, Excel or PowerPoint, with the system deciding behind the scenes which models, tools and sources to apply, all while carrying context forward from one step of a matter to the next.

“It’s really creating an ecosystem bringing together all of our content, all of our capabilities, and the customer data, with a much more intelligent engine, which is why we call it the Legal Intelligence Engine, because it seamlessly brings all of this together,” Jeff Reihl, executive vice president and chief technology officer, told me in a briefing last week.

A Dynamic Harness

The key change in this new release from the company’s prior agentic platform is the harness architecture, Reihl said. In the platform’s prior version, workflows were scripted in advance.

“The agentic capabilities we had before were much more predefined,” Reihl said. “So if you’re going to create a brief, it followed very specific steps that were predefined.”

The new platform, he said, “can bring in additional tools, it can bring in additional information, and it can check its work and then loop back and redo it” if it determines the output does not fully answer the request.

Before executing a plan, the system presents it to the user, allowing the user to modify it, such as by correcting a jurisdiction adding or removing data sources. It then shows its work at each step, indicating what data it is drawing on and where each piece of a drafted document comes from.

The harness can draw on content from across the LexisNexis portfolio without requiring the user to switch products. The system can, for example, pull in judge analytics from Lex Machina, SEC-related research from Intelligize, and current news from Law360.

Of course, it also draws from the company’s core body of more than 200 billion documents and can draw from a customer’s own documents in a connected document management system.

Legal search and web search, which were previously separate functions, are now unified, with the system also validating citations returned from web results.

In our briefing last week, Alexandra Smyth, executive vice president and general counsel of LexisNexis, said the change eliminates the tool-switching that previously characterized multi-source work.

“If I’m working on something around the SEC, in the past I would have done drafting in one bit, done some research in Intelligize, and put it back,” she said. “Now it all does it in the one place. … It knows to jump between the two on its own.”

Among the new capabilities Reihl described is Shepard’s Verify, which extends the company’s long-standing citation service into the drafting workflow. Beyond confirming that a cited case is accurate and still good law, Reihl said, the feature also validates that the case is relevant to the specific task at hand.

When I asked whether a lawyer could now hand the system an opponent’s summary judgment motion, go get a cup of coffee, and return to a finished responsive brief, Smyth said the reality is “somewhere between the two.”

A user can set the system off on the task, she said, but must still review the result. “Every regulator in the world that’s commented on this has said you’re still responsible for what you file,” she said.

Reihl added that a user could first direct the system to analyze the opposing brief, assessing the strength of its arguments and validating its citations, before prompting it to draft a response.

Skills and Memory

The platform now includes several hundred skills, which are packaged instructions for specific document types, briefs and client communications. Reihl said LexisNexis has also incorporated skills from Anthropic’s Claude Legal offering.

Firms can customize the default skills and will soon be able to create their own skills and workflows.

This new version also introduces memory, meaning that the system remembers the context of what happens during a session.

“So if you look at Lex Machina, and you bring that forward and you look at a particular judge, it remembers that and it can bring that into later parts of the conversation,” Reihl said.

In later versions of the platform, Reihl said, it will be able to remember even more, including documents you have created in the past and your preferences.

“It knows that you’ve worked on a case similar to this three months ago, that you’ve used other cases related to this particular legal area and it’ll remember and bring that stuff in,” he said.

As to the LLM models underlying all this, the company says that Lexis+ with Protégé applies the model best suited for each task by default, while allowing users to select a preferred model.

The company also said that it will preview its own models later this year. In our briefing, Reihl offered some context on that effort.

In the past, he said, the company fine-tuned models, including a fine-tuned version of Mistral, and invested substantially in reinforcement learning with Anthropic as early as 2023, with results that “didn’t move the dial” relative to the cost.

With better base models and the new harness architecture, he said, the company is “going to take another shot at it,” describing the current work as evaluation and testing.

“We’re pretty certain we’ll have some customized models,” he said, “but just how far we go with the reinforcement learning and using our content” remains to be seen.

news.titleEn: Thomson Reuters launches proprietary legal LLM “Thomson”
news.titleZh: 汤森路透推出专有法律大语言模型“Thomson”
news.summaryZh: 汤森路透推出专有法律大语言模型Thomson。该模型基于开放权重模型构建，旨在让公司对产品内智能拥有更多控制权，改善经济性，减少对他人路线图的依赖，并在技术训练和部署上获得更大自主权。在强大模型获取日益商品化的背景下，拥有更多智能具有战略重要性。Thomson表明，控制权与前沿能力并非互斥。其难以复制之处不在于开源基础，而在于数据、训练方法、领域专业知识、偏好数据及评估基础设施。目前仅使用不到10%的汤森路透内容，未来将识别能提升性能的内容并转化为高质量训练数据。Thomson为CoCounsel提供可控智能，公司可在最佳任务上使用Thomson，在第三方模型更优时使用第三方模型，目标是让CoCounsel为正确工作使用正确智能，同时改善经济性和控制力。Thomson表明，律所或专业组织不必在能力与主权之间二选一。汤森路透对直接授权Thomson持开放态度，对象包括律所、企业法务部门、开发团队等。Thomson最初作为汤森路透的基础设施构建，现可能成为他人的基础设施，提供底层智能。
news.bodyHtml:
Why did Thomson Reuters build its own model?

“We built Thomson first and foremost for ourselves. We wanted more control over the intelligence inside our products: to make them better, improve the economics, reduce our dependence on someone else’s roadmap and give ourselves greater sovereignty over how that technology is trained and deployed. As access to powerful models becomes increasingly commoditised, we think owning more of that intelligence becomes strategically important.”

Why build on an open-weight model rather than continue relying entirely on frontier providers?

“Historically there has been a trade-off. You could use the most capable closed models and accept the dependency that comes with them, or you could take greater control with an open model and accept some distance from the frontier. What Thomson demonstrates is that those things do not have to be mutually exclusive. We can have control and sovereignty while still building a model that competes at a very high level.”

What makes Thomson difficult for someone else to replicate?

“The open-source foundation is the starting point, not the moat. The difficult part is everything that happens after that: the data, the training methodology, the domain expertise, the preference data and the evaluation infrastructure required to know whether the model is actually getting better at professional work. Thomson Reuters has spent decades building the corpus and expertise behind that system, and our research team has spent years working on how to translate those assets into model performance.”

Why did you only use about 10% of Thomson Reuters content?

“Less than 10% so far. And what comes next is not simply feeding the model more data. It is identifying which content will actually improve performance, turning that content into high-quality training data, and validating the results with the same expert-led process we have used to date. The fact that we have reached this level of performance using a relatively small portion of the content available to us gives us a lot of runway to keep improving Thomson across more tasks and workflows.”

What does Thomson mean for CoCounsel and Thomson Reuters products?

“Thomson gives us another form of intelligence that we control and can optimise around the work our customers actually do. We can use Thomson where it is the best model for the task, use third-party models where they are better, and keep evaluating that mix as the technology changes. The goal is not to force every problem through our model. It is to give CoCounsel the ability to use the right intelligence for the right work while improving the economics and control behind the system.”

Does Thomson mean customers have to choose between capability and sovereignty?

“That is one of the most important things we think Thomson demonstrates. A law firm or another professional organisation should not necessarily have to choose between the capability of a frontier model and the security, control and sovereignty advantages of owning more of its AI stack. We have shown there is a path to both. That creates a very different set of choices for organisations thinking seriously about their long-term AI strategy.”

Could law firms or other organisations eventually license Thomson directly?

“Yes. We built Thomson to make our own products better, but in doing that we have created a lot of optionality. There are law firms, corporate legal departments, development teams and other organisations that want to take more direct ownership of their AI strategy. They may want greater control over deployment, more sovereignty over their technology stack or the ability to build directly on a model designed for professional work. We are very open to working with those organisations and to Thomson being licensed directly.”

How big could that opportunity become?

“We built Thomson as infrastructure for Thomson Reuters. What we are beginning to see is that it could also become infrastructure for others. A lot of organisations today are deciding which models are best for which work. Thomson gives us the opportunity not only to be the company building applications on top of AI, but potentially to provide some of the underlying intelligence as well for companies making those model choices. That was not the primary reason we started the project, but it is a very interesting opportunity that comes from what the team has built.”

news.titleEn: LexisNexis adds context-carrying harness to Lexis+ with Protégé
news.titleZh: LexisNexis为Lexis+推出Protégé，新增上下文保持型智能体框架
news.summaryZh: 8月24日，LexisNexis Legal & Professional宣布为Lexis+ with Protégé推出新功能，引入“智能体框架”（agentic harness），使法律专业人士能够在同一工作流中调用多种工具，并集成于可保留上下文的Legal Intelligence Engine中。该引擎整合了公司各项功能，核心创新在于上下文保持能力，使研究和起草不再分离，用户可同时获取最新法律信息并生成客户文件。研究嵌入起草过程，无需分两步操作；该框架整合了Intelligize和Lex Machina等工具，用户提问后系统自动选择合适数据源，并可将答案直接导入Word、PowerPoint或Excel。引擎可基于用户自身政策、先例和风险偏好进行定制，结合LexisNexis语料库及RELX内部资料，确保输出可信且可核查，附有引用链接以防幻觉。上下文按案件隔离，防止客户信息泄露；系统作为“完全智能体框架”，会通过Shepard's引文数据库校验输出，而非仅依赖底层模型，因为即使最优秀的智能体也可能出错，必须通过框架加以约束。
news.bodyHtml:
LexisNexis Legal & Professional today (24 August) unveiled new capabilities for Lexis+ with Protégé, introducing an ‘agentic harness’ that enables legal professionals to leverage multiple tools in one workflow within a Legal Intelligence Engine that now retains context.

Speaking to Legal IT Insider, Greg Dickason, executive vice president and chief technology officer at LexisNexis, said: “We’re packaging up all the ways in which we’re working into the LexisNexis Legal Intelligence Engine, but the piece that I think is probably net new is that context, the ability to carry context forward.”

Advertisement

The new functionality means that research and drafting no longer have to happen as separate steps: Dickason said: “You can say to the agent, find out what the latest law is about this and draft me a document for my client. And it’ll do both at the same time.”

Alexandra Smyth, executive vice president and general counsel for the LexisNexis Legal added: “I think the benefit of this is the research is embedded within drafting. So you don’t have to separately do research and then turn around and draft it using the research. You can just do it all in one spot. So if you’re drafting something that requires research, it’s now no longer two steps.

Advertisement

“In the past, if I wanted to ask a question about the SEC, I would go into Intelligize and look it up there. If I wanted to ask a question about what a judge had done in the past, I look in Lex Machina. Whereas now this harness brings it all together. So I can just ask it a question and it knows which one to call on. It gives me the answer and then it allows me to put that answer into Word, PowerPoint, Excel, whatever, without having to do all of that separately.”

Smyth points out that you can ground the new engine in your policies, precedents and risk appetite, commenting: “We’ve got the LexisNexis corpus, which is fantastic, but we’ve also got what the RELX policies are or what we’ve done previously. So you can tailor it to your own bespoke way of using it.

“What I really care about is getting a piece of output that I can actually trust and not worrying about whether it’s been hallucinated. We’ve seen that loads of times, I think, not with our products, but with lawyers in general, being burnt by legal AI. And so what I like about our product is you can easily check everything it gives you. There’s links to the citations.”

Dickason was clear that context is walled off by matter, so work done for one client cannot leak into another. He described the system as “a fully agentic harness” that checks its own output against LexisNexis’s Shepard’s citation database rather than relying on the underlying model alone: “It doesn’t matter how good your agent is, it can always make up something. You’re never going to get to 100% non-hallucination. So you’ve got to put the harness around it.”

news.titleEn: Thomson Reuters Launches Thomson, Its Own Proprietary LLM Trained on Westlaw and Practical Law Content
news.titleZh: 汤森路透推出自研大语言模型Thomson，基于Westlaw和Practical Law内容训练
news.summaryZh:
汤森路透正式发布自研大语言模型Thomson，该模型完全由公司拥有和控制，开发成本远低于ChatGPT和Claude等前沿模型。Thomson基于汤森路透数十年的专有内容、技术及领域专业知识训练而成。Thomson展示了另一条路径：从强大基础出发，针对重要工作进行深度专业化，即可构建高效且完全可控的智能。汤森路透在过去两年中为开发Thomson投入约4000万美元，涵盖人才和算力，最终训练运行成本仅为45万美元。

Thomson将首先部署于即将发布的CoCounsel Legal中，驱动其表格分析功能，并作为该功能的默认模型，管理员可通过后台切换至其他模型。CoCounsel将保持多模型策略，在最具优势的场景应用Thomson。公司计划最终将Thomson模型扩展至其法律和税务产品组合。Thomson 1.0是Thomson系列模型中的首个，基于开源模型Qwen 3.5训练，过程包括价值观对齐、使用Westlaw、Practical Law、Checkpoint和路透社的专有内容继续训练，以及与汤森路透研究工具的直接集成。数百名内部专家参与了训练目标制定、高质量答案示例创建及盲测评估。训练数据不包含客户数据。汤森路透已聘请第三方安全公司验证模型托管、服务和安全性。公司还开始与大型律所和企业就模型直接访问进行初步对话，包括希望用自身数据微调模型的机构。汤森路透将发布技术报告，并已向学术研究者提供模型评估，同时在Hugging Face上以非商业学术许可发布小型开放权重版本。
news.bodyHtml:
It certainly has been no secret that Thomson Reuters has been building its own proprietary large language model. In fact, in my June interview with TR’s CEO Steve Hasker, he talked openly about it, and just a few weeks ago, I reported on TR’s release of preliminary benchmarking data that showed impressive results comparable to the best general-purpose AI models.

But today TR makes it official, launching Thomson, an LLM that TR emphasizes was developed at a fraction of the cost of the frontier LLMs such as ChatGPT and Claude and that TR fully owns and controls.

More importantly – at least when it comes to positioning within the legal market – TR highlights the fact that Thomson was trained and built using its own proprietary content built up over decades, as well as its own technology and, as it says, “domain expertise no other company can match.”

Joel Hron, TR’s chief technology officer, says this is an achievement that could change the economics of professional AI.

“For years, the AI industry has treated scale as the answer: bigger models, more compute, more money,” he says. “Thomson shows there is another path.

“Start with a strong foundation, specialize it deeply for the work that matters, and you can build intelligence that is highly capable, far more efficient and entirely under your control.”

Compared to the billions spent to develop models such as ChatGPT and Claude, TR says it has invested some $40 million into developing Thomson over the past two years, covering both talent and compute. And during a media briefing last week, Hron revealed that the final training run for the version launching today cost just $450,000.

“This $450,000 number I think is indicative of what we were able to do with our data and content on top of world-class open source models,” Hron said.

To Be Deployed in CoCounsel

Thomson will get its first deployment in an upcoming release of CoCounsel Legal, driving its Tabular Analysis functionality. TR says this is “exactly the kind of high-volume, structured document review where a purpose-built model’s advantage shows up immediately.”

Thomson will be the default model for Tabular Analysis, Hron said, although administrators will be able to switch the feature to another model through CoCounsel Legal’s admin settings.

Overall, CoCounsel will remain multi-model, tapping into whichever LLM is best suited for the task at hand. TR says it will apply Thomson “where it delivers the clearest advantage” and other models elsewhere.

Over time, Hron said, he expects Thomson to take “a bigger and bigger share of the tokens” and of the work CoCounsel is doing, and the company says it plans eventually to extend Thomson models across its portfolio of legal and tax products.

“Thomson does not need to keep pace with the frontier of general intelligence across all dimensions,” he said. “Thomson needs to set the frontier of intelligence for legal.”

Beyond its own products, TR has begun early conversations with large law firms and corporations about direct access to the model, Hron said, including firms interested in fine-tuning it with their own data as they look to bring greater sovereignty to their own knowledge and expertise.

“We are very open to working with those organizations and to Thomson being licensed directly,” Hron said in a Q&A document TR provided to media, adding: “We built Thomson as infrastructure for Thomson Reuters. What we are beginning to see is that it could also become infrastructure for others.”

How Thomson Was Built

The model launching today is formally Thomson 1.0, the first in what Hron described as a family of models that will carry the Thomson name.

Rather than build a model from scratch, TR started with an existing open-source model and trained it to become a legal specialist. Although the models it used changed over the course of the project, the most recent was Qwen 3.5.

Jonathan Schwarz, TR’s head of foundational research, said during the media briefing that the process involved TR first aligning the model’s values and behavior with its own, and then continuing to train it exclusively on TR’s proprietary content from Westlaw, Practical Law, Checkpoint and Reuters. The final step was to train it to work directly with TR’s own research tools.

Central to that process were TR’s subject-matter experts – the armies of lawyers and tax professionals it employs. Andrew Bean, who heads TR’s evaluations team, said hundreds of experts helped decide what the model should be trained to do in the first place, created many thousands of examples of high-quality answers, and then judged the model’s outputs in blind, head-to-head comparisons against frontier models.

None of that training data comes from customers. “We do not use customer data at all in that process,” Hron said in response to a question about governance. Rather than mining customer data for training signals, TR replicates the relevant tasks with its own experts.

He also said TR has engaged several third-party security firms to validate the hosting, serving and security controls around the model.

Because open-source models keep improving, TR built the process to be repeatable. Hron said TR has swapped out its open-source starting point close to half a dozen times over the life of the project as better models have emerged.

“The bigger finding here is less the individual model and more the model factory we built,” Schwarz said.

The result, Schwarz said, is a model that gained deep capability in legal and tax work without losing the general abilities – writing, math, reasoning over long documents – that narrowly fine-tuned models often sacrifice.

Putting It To the Test

TR says its internal testing of Thomson has shown strong results.

One evaluation described during the briefing was an in-house benchmark TR calls Deep Research, built around legal research queries drafted by its experts based on the work they would do in practice. For each query, the experts also supplied the criteria a good answer should contain.

Answers were scored on two dimensions: completeness, meaning whether the answer contained all the elements of a right answer, and factuality, meaning whether the citations provided actually supported the claims being made.

“You can have a model that provides a correct answer,” Bean said, “but more importantly, you can have a model that provides a correct answer with proof that it is correct.”

Using that benchmark, TR compared Thomson against GPT 5.4 and Claude Sonnet 5, scoring each model twice – once with access only to web content and once with access to TR content.

You can see the results in the image below. While Thomson performed respectably in the web-only test – “within the scope of the other models, but certainly not the leader yet,” as Bean put it – it did much better in the test using TR content, outscoring both of the other LLMs.

 

“The last column really shows that there’s a big uplift that comes from being able to train on and practice with your own tools,” Bean said. “And that’s the sort of specialization that we think is a real value of having our own in-house model.”

In response to my question during the briefing about whether TR would release more detailed benchmarking, Schwarz said TR will publish a technical report this week with a comprehensive set of evaluations, including results on standard public AI benchmarks, legal-specific benchmarks and human testing.

TR has also begun making the model available to a group of legal and AI academics for their direct evaluation, and it is making a “small” version available as an open-weight model on Hugging Face, under a non-commercial academic license, to broaden the evaluation.

Hron said TR sees the open-weight release “as a mechanism for really anybody in the world to pick it up and critique and validate or invalidate any aspects of what we’re saying.”

One of those academics, Jonathan H. Choi, at Washington University School of Law, in a statement provided by TR, said that he tested Thomson against ChatGPT and Claude using what he considered to be some of the more challenging questions students have asked in his Corporate Tax class.

“All three models answered the questions correctly, but I preferred Thomson’s responses overall. I especially appreciated the links to treatises, which made its responses more transparent and useful for legal work.”

TR is also building a developer portal that will eventually allow outside parties to access the model directly, with API keys, configurable parameters and sample documentation. Hron demonstrated an early version during the briefing, but cautioned that it is “still very early at the moment.”

Early Days

While emphasizing Thomson’s training on its “decades of authoritative content,” TR says the model has so far been trained on less than 10% of that content.

“What comes next is not simply feeding it more data,” the company says. “It is continued discovery of new kinds of specialization and understanding, made possible only by building on decades of proprietary content and editorial expertise.”

In its announcement of the launch, the company casts Thomson as a turning point:

“The launch of Thomson marks a new chapter for Thomson Reuters. The company has always owned the content, the expertise, and the tools professionals rely on every day. Now it owns the model too. Thomson Reuters is no longer only integrating the world’s best content, technology and expertise. It is building intelligence that will power the future of professional work.”

news.titleEn: Harvey and PacerPro Announce Partnership To Connect Docket Data with AI Litigation Workflows
news.titleZh: Harvey与PacerPro宣布合作，将案卷数据与AI诉讼工作流连接
news.summaryZh: 法律AI公司Harvey与法院数据公司PacerPro宣布建立集成合作伙伴关系，使在Harvey中工作的诉讼团队能够访问其律所的完整诉讼记录，包括律所此前处理事项及当前在案卷中的案件文件与案件背景。PacerPro在州和联邦法院文件及其基础文件发布时即进行抓取，将每份文件与其案件和案卷历史关联，并按事项整理为持续更新的律所诉讼记录。尽管这些信息驱动着诉讼团队的工作，但往往存在于律师用于研究、起草和分析的工具之外；此前连接这些内容通常需要律师检索新文件、重建相关案件历史、在律所文档管理系统中搜索先前工作，并在实质性工作开始前整合背景。通过PacerPro与Harvey，文件成为起点：法院事件触发工作，事项记录提供背景，律所诉讼历史提供经验。该合作旨在支持诉讼团队日常使用案卷数据的方式，包括州和联邦案卷监控、诉讼工作流自动化及实时文件提醒，PacerPro作为法院数据和工作流基础设施支持集成。法院记录的真正价值不在于案卷条目告知发生了什么，而在于提交了什么，这是法律与事实相遇之处。PacerPro在诉讼团队中的往绩使其成为将法院数据引入Harvey的直接选择，文件本身、其背景及与律所自身事项的关联为Harvey的诉讼工作提供了强大基础。两家公司举例说明：当处分性动议到达时，PacerPro提供该动议及背后的事项背景，包括有效诉状、先前简报、先前裁决和程序历史，Harvey可帮助律师理解论点、识别记录中的关键内容并借鉴律所此前相。
news.bodyHtml:
The legal AI company Harvey and the court data company PacerPro have announced an integration partnership that gives litigation teams working in Harvey access to their firm’s complete litigation record, including the filings and case context from matters the firm has previously handled and those currently on the docket.

PacerPro captures state and federal court filings and their underlying documents as they post, connecting each filing to its case and docket history, and organizing that activity into a continuously updated record of the firm’s litigation, matter by matter.

Even though this is the information that drives the work of litigation teams , it often lives outside the tools lawyers use to research, draft, and analyze.

Until now, the companies say, connecting those things has often required lawyers to retrieve a new filing, reconstruct the relevant case history, search the firm’s document management system for prior work, and assemble the context before substantive work can begin.

With PacerPro and Harvey, the filing becomes the starting point: the court event triggers the work, the matter record supplies the context, and the firm’s litigation history supplies the experience.

The companies say that their partnership is designed to support the ways litigation teams already use docket data on a daily basis, including state and federal docket monitoring, litigation workflow automation, and real-time filing alerts, with PacerPro serving as the court data and workflow infrastructure enabling the integration.

“We started PacerPro because the real value of the court record isn’t a docket entry telling you that something happened,” said Gavin McGrane, CIO and cofounder at PacerPro. “It’s what was filed. That’s where law meets fact — where lawyers make arguments and courts decide them. … With Harvey, a filing that arrives today can be understood in the context of the case behind it and the firm’s experience before it.”

How does this work? The companies gave these examples:

  • A dispositive motion arrives. PacerPro provides the motion together with the matter context behind it — the operative pleadings, earlier briefing, prior rulings and procedural history. Harvey can help the lawyer understand the argument, identify what matters in the record, and draw on relevant work the firm has done before.
  • An order issues. The team can understand the ruling in the context of the arguments that preceded it and determine what comes next. When a new legal question arises, the firm’s prior matters provide a record of how its lawyers have applied law to fact before: the arguments they made, the authorities they relied on, how opponents responded and what courts ultimately did.

“When we looked at how to bring court data into Harvey, PacerPro’s track record with litigation teams made it a straightforward choice,” said Megan McMillin, legal innovation partner at Harvey. “The filings themselves, the context around them, and the connection to the firm’s own matters give Harvey a powerful foundation for litigation work. Lawyers can work from what is happening in the case now while putting their firm’s prior experience to use.”

If you are at ILTACON this week, Harvey and PacerPro will demonstrate the integration live tomorrow, Aug. 25, at the Harvey booth. A joint webinar will follow the conference; registration details will be available at pacerpro.com.

[DISCLOSURE: I serve in a paid capacity on PacerPro’s board of advisors.]

news.titleEn: How to use AI for multilingual customer support
news.titleZh: 如何利用AI提供多语言客户支持
news.summaryZh:
多语言客户支持指在客户偏好的语言环境中，通过短信、电子邮件、聊天和社交消息等渠道提供服务，结合人工客服、翻译和AI，使团队能够用西班牙语、法语、中文等语言回复客户。CSA Research调查了29个国家的8709名消费者，发现76%的消费者偏好使用自己语言提供信息的产品，40%的消费者永远不会从其他语言的网站购买。多语言支持不仅影响购买决策，还影响客户留存和问题解决速度。

多语言支持并非逐字翻译，而是传递语气、语境和意图，使回复读起来自然。AI翻译和AI代理让小型团队无需为每种语言招聘专职双语代表即可覆盖更多语言。最佳实践包括：按语言训练和测试AI、保持清晰的人工交接、在统一平台管理所有对话，以及在受监管领域确认平台符合HIPAA和SOC 2 Type 2认证。传统翻译服务依赖人工翻译或机构，适合法律、医疗等高风险内容，但速度慢、按字计价；AI翻译则实时进行，适合日常支持。两者结合是最佳方案。Heymarket提供内置翻译的共享收件箱，支持英语、西班牙语、法语和中文，并可通过AI代理处理常规问题。
news.bodyHtml:
When your team receives a message in a language they don’t speak, they have to switch between translation tools or ask for help, slowing down response times. Serving customers in their own language keeps support fast and personal, even as your customer base grows.

Multilingual customer support answers customers in their preferred language across the channels they already use, like SMS, email, chat, and social messaging. It combines human agents, translation, and AI so your team can answer in Spanish, French, Chinese, or whichever language your customer writes in.

This guide covers the benefits of multilingual support, examples of how it works across different support channels, how AI and automation can improve efficiency, and more.

Key takeaways about multilingual customer support
