news.titleEn: What is AI data enrichment?
news.titleZh: 什么是AI数据增强？
news.summaryZh: AI数据增强是利用人工智能（包括机器学习、自然语言处理和大语言模型）自动改进和扩展现有业务数据的过程。它通过实体匹配、缺失属性推断、情感与意图分析、分类与评分等流程，自动清理、连接和扩展数据，使团队无需手动研究即可获得完整、可操作的客户记录。与数据扩充不同，数据扩充是创建合成数据来训练机器学习模型，而AI数据增强则改善真实业务记录。销售、营销、医疗、物流和零售等团队使用数据增强AI来个性化外联并保持客户记录准确。挑战包括外部数据质量、隐私合规以及随着记录变化而持续验证的需求。例如，在医疗场景中，患者发短信预约，AI代理可解析对话，提取姓名、医生偏好、地点和保险信息，自动记录到CRM，并即时个性化回复。AI数据增强与传统方法不同，它不只是从购买的列表中追加静态数据，而是学习模式、处理非结构化信息并持续更新记录。选择AI数据增强方法时，需考虑CRM和平台集成、实时与批量处理、隐私合规（如GDPR、CCPA、HIPAA）以及数据质量验证。保持数据准确性需要持续运行，并标记过时记录。
news.bodyHtml:
Your sales rep opens a lead record, finding a name and email address but nothing about the company, their role, or the context around what the person actually needs. So your rep opens LinkedIn in another tab, cross-references the company website, guesses at the job title, and types it all in manually. Multiply that by fifty new leads a week, and your team is spending hours piecing together contact info and data entry. Now, AI data enrichment makes it possible to gain complete, actionable customer records without the constant back-and-forth research.

AI data enrichment is the process of using artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models, to automatically improve and expand your existing business data. Instead of manually updating contact records or cross-referencing spreadsheets, AI runs in the background to identify gaps, infer missing details, and add context to the information you already have. The result is cleaner, more complete data that your team can actually act on, rather than fragments they have to piece together.

Using AI for data enrichment: key takeaways

  • AI data enrichment uses machine learning to fill in missing CRM fields, standardize records, and add context like sentiment or intent, all without manual effort from your team.
  • It differs from data augmentation, which creates synthetic data to train ML models rather than improving real business records.
  • Teams in sales, marketing, healthcare, logistics, and retail use data enrichment AI to personalize outreach and keep customer records accurate.
  • Challenges include data quality from external sources, privacy compliance, and the need for ongoing validation as records change over time.

What is AI data enrichment, and why use it?

If you’ve ever inherited a CRM full of half-filled contact records, you already know the problem AI data enrichment solves. It takes the data you have and makes it useful without needing you or your team to spend time reviewing and updating it.

Data enrichment AI connects your existing datasets, like CRM records, marketing lists, or customer databases, to intelligent models that analyze, match, and expand that information automatically. This process helps your team get complete records without manual research, and your campaigns get better targeting without guesswork.

How does AI data enrichment work?

AI data enrichment works by running your records through a series of intelligent machine learning and NLP processes that clean, connect, and expand them. It takes the process that your team would normally take time doing and turns it into an automated workflow.

Here’s what the process might look like:

  1. Entity matching: AI compares records across systems to identify duplicates and link related entries. If the same contact appears in your CRM with slightly different formatting (“Robert Smith” vs. “Bob Smith, Acme Corp”), the model resolves these into a single accurate record.
  2. Inferring missing attributes: When a contact record is missing key fields like job title, company size, industry, or location, AI can infer these based on patterns in your existing data and publicly available information. A lead who fills out a form with just an email and company name can have their record expanded with role, department, and firmographic details.
  3. Sentiment and intent analysis: AI reads unstructured text, things like support conversations, email replies, and form submissions, and tags records with sentiment scores or purchase intent signals. If a lead’s recent messages suggest an unhappy experience or high buying interest, the model attaches that context to their profile automatically.
  4. Classification and scoring: Models can categorize contacts by lifecycle stage, score leads based on engagement patterns, or tag conversations by topic. These enriched fields feed directly into your routing rules, campaign triggers, and segmentation.
  5. Lead enrichment from conversations: Some data enrichment platforms with AI go further by extracting enrichment data from live conversations. For example, Heymarket’s AI agent feature captures details like name, provider preference, and location directly from inbound messages, then logs them to your connected CRM automatically. If a patient texts that they need a follow-up with a specific doctor in Raleigh, the agent picks that up and uses it to personalize the next reply.

Unlike older enrichment methods, AI doesn’t just append static data from a purchased list. It learns patterns, processes unstructured information, and updates records continuously as new data flows in.

What does a data enrichment AI feature look like in action?

Say a new patient texts your clinic: “Hi, I need to schedule a follow-up appointment with Dr. Patel. I’m in the Raleigh area and my insurance is Blue Cross.”

Before AI data enrichment, that patient’s record in your system might contain a phone number and nothing else. Your front desk staff would need to manually log the name, note the provider preference, confirm the location, and verify insurance details before they could even start scheduling. That’s several minutes of admin work, all for a single reply.

With a platform that has data enrichment AI features running in the background, here’s what happens instead:

  1. The lead enrichment agent parses the conversation: It picks up that the patient is requesting a follow-up, prefers Dr. Patel, is located in Raleigh, and has Blue Cross insurance. Those details get logged to the CRM record automatically.
  2. Missing profile fields get filled in: Based on the contact’s phone number and existing records, AI appends their full name, date of birth, and any prior visit history already in the system.
  3. The conversation gets personalized instantly: Because the agent captured the patient’s provider preference and location, the next message can be tailored right away: “Hi Maria, I can see you’re looking for a follow-up with Dr. Patel at our Raleigh office. We have openings next Tuesday and Thursday. Would either of those work?”
  4. The record is tagged and routed: AI classifies the inquiry by type (follow-up appointment, returning patient) and routes it to the appropriate scheduling queue so your team can prioritize accordingly.

All of that happens in seconds, without your staff toggling between tabs or typing anything into your CRM. The conversation moves forward with context, and your patient records stay clean from the first interaction.

AI data enrichment vs. data augmentation

These terms get mixed up a lot, but they solve very different problems.

AI data enrichment improves real business records by adding missing context. Think: appending a company’s industry to a lead record, or tagging a conversation with a sentiment score. You’re working with actual customer and prospect data, making it more complete and useful for sales, marketing, and operations.

Data augmentation creates synthetic data to expand a training dataset for machine learning models. If you’re building a model to detect spam messages but only have 500 examples, augmentation generates thousands of variations, so the model trains more effectively. It doesn’t add real-world information to your records.

Enrichment matters more for most teams that heavily rely on CRMs in their workflows. Your marketing team, for example, needs accurate contact records so your drip campaigns reach the right people with relevant messaging.

How is AI data enrichment used across industries?

AI data enrichment helps any team that depends on accurate, up-to-date records to personalize outreach and operations.

Enriched records with accurate lifecycle stages and engagement history also help your marketing team run more relevant patient outreach. Automated messages and email workflows for wellness check reminders or seasonal flu shots reach the right patients, instead of blasting a generic message to your entire list.

2. Logistics and delivery operations

Logistics teams deal with high volumes of time-sensitive customer data, from shipping addresses to delivery preferences. AI data enrichment keeps those records clean across systems, so your team can send accurate tracking updates, route delivery notifications to the right contact, and catch address errors before they cause failed shipments.

3. Retail and e-commerce

Retailers enrich purchase and browsing data with inferred preferences and predicted intent. AI can identify which customers are likely to churn, which are ready for an upsell, and which segments respond best to specific messaging channels. Platforms with AI-powered sales tools combine enriched data with automated outreach for faster pipeline movement.

What to look for in an AI data enrichment approach

Your data enrichment setup should match how your team’s lead management actually works, which might take some trial and error.

Here are a few areas to think about when it comes to your needs, compliance requirements, and overall workflow:

  1. CRM and platform integration: Your enrichment process needs to connect directly to the systems your team already uses, whether that’s your Salesforce CRM, email, a messaging channel like Instagram, or a marketing automation tool. If enriched data sits in a separate warehouse and never makes it back to the tools where your team works, it won’t change outcomes. Look for bidirectional sync so enriched fields appear where reps and marketers actually see them.
  2. Real-time vs. batch processing: Some use cases need enrichment to happen the moment a new lead enters your system, while others are fine with nightly batch runs. Consider which records need immediate context (like inbound leads hitting a routing rule) versus which can wait (like quarterly database cleanup).
  3. Privacy and compliance: Any AI data enrichment process that pulls external data or processes customer conversations needs to respect regulations like GDPR, CCPA, and HIPAA. Confirm how the tool you’re researching handles consent, data residency, and PII minimization, especially if you’re enriching records in healthcare or financial services.
  4. Data quality validation: AI enrichment requires data from an accurate source. Low-quality third-party data or outdated models can degrade your records rather than improve them. Keep your data clean with confidence scoring, human review for edge cases, and ongoing monitoring to catch drift over time.

Tools that combine data enrichment with AI features for conversation analysis, like extracting intent from customer texts or summarizing support threads, add another layer of context that static data providers can’t match.

Keeping enriched data accurate over time

AI data enrichment isn’t a one-time project. Information always needs to be updated because people change jobs, companies get acquired, and customers move. The data enrichment process needs to run continuously by flagging outdated records and re-enriching them as it notes changes.

Platforms that combine enrichment with AI texting tools can close the loop even faster, using enriched data to personalize automated messages while feeding conversation outcomes back into the enrichment model. Your process might need updating over time as you start seeing how it handles real customer data.

  2. Schedule periodic backtests where you compare enriched data against known ground truth.
  3. Monitor for model drift—if the accuracy of inferred fields starts declining, it’s time to retrain or swap data sources.

news.bodyHtml:
What does the future of AI look like for professional firms?

Sebastian Hartmann

One thing is clear — the future won’t belong to firms that standardize on AI from a single technology partner — things are moving too quickly for that. To get the most value from AI, firms are increasingly turning to multiple vendors for specialized tools that excel at different tasks. For instance, a firm might have one tool for research, another for drafting, and another for financial analysis, depending on their various practice groups or service lines.

The most successful firms will be the ones that can make these tools work together in a way that optimizes outcomes for the firm, their professionals, and their clients. Firm AI will make this happen by connecting to tools and data sources within firm-specific workflows.

Instead of deciding which tool to use for each task, professionals will describe what they need in natural language through a single platform. Firm AI will route each request to the right tool or capability, then return the result through the platform while enforcing the firm’s compliance rules.

AI is also changing how firms differentiate themselves. Work that used to scale with headcount — research, review, drafting, analysis — can now scale with AI coworkers — so productivity is becoming table stakes. And all firms now have access to the same AI models.

So, what will set firms apart is not how hard their professionals work or what AI models they use, but how they use AI to surface actionable intelligence from their institutional knowledge and client relationships in ways that are compliant and aligned with how they operate.

Western intelligence alliance Five Eyes has issued a strong warning to business leaders: AI-driven transformation of cyber risk is already here, and the time to act is now. The alliance, comprising of domestic cyber security agencies from Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States of America, published a joint statement calling on boards and executives to treat cyber resilience as a core business priority rather than a technical consideration. The shift in the threat landscape is attributed to increasingly capable AI models, which can rapidly detect vulnerabilities in cyber security infrastructure. While this benefits defenders, it equally enables malicious actors to exploit those vulnerabilities and simultaneously lowers the technical barrier to entry. Five Eyes recommends the following while noting that these are urgent, but not novel priorities: For organisations, the Five Eyes statement is a timely reminder to review cyber resilience and ensure protection. Controls need to be appropriately tested, response plans need to be up-to-date and cyber security needs to be incorporated into core business strategy. And as the timeline being measured in months rather than years, there is little room for delay, and significant risk in waiting. You can read the full report here. news.summaryZh:
AI正加速法律工作，起草周期压缩，法律研究从数小时缩短至数分钟，律所和内部团队在交易与诉讼领域逐步实现效率提升。但速度本身不等于进步。AI暴露了大型及全球律所多年来的挑战：推动案件和交易的大部分工作仍在相互孤立的系统中进行。这些系统分别存储文件、处理案件启动和跟踪时间，但没有任何一个能在一处掌握案件的全部背景，包括事实、法律、经济、历史及客户意图。AI只是暴露了这种系统脱节，而非治愈它。工作成果生成加速，但围绕它的系统难以跟上。案件团队仍需在决策前从不同系统提取财务、人员和程序信息来重建背景。新工具减少起草时间，却增加验证和协调的工作量。律师行动更快，但花更多时间确保一切对齐。问题不在于速度，而在于精力最终流向何处：起草时间下降，审查和协调时间上升；个体收费人员可能更快，但组织未必更早冲过终点线。当组织在碎片化系统基础上加速工作时，压力不会消失，只会转移。

连贯性是缺失的要素。任何法律事项都是事实、问题、法律、程序、利益相关者及其目标之间活生生的连接群，由案件团队的战略和战术判断塑造。当这种状态分散在互不连接的系统时，律师需用经验和记忆来补偿，团队通过会议、邮件和非正式交接来同步。若脱节系统间的连贯性是制约因素，答案就是平台思维。根据Clio与Neuro-Insight的2025年神经分析研究，使用单一集成平台的律师报告认知负荷下降25%。
news.bodyText: By Dan Hoadley, Clio. AI is speeding up legal work in increasingly visible and practical ways. Drafting cycles are compressing. Legal research that once took hours now takes minutes. And, law firms and in-house teams are incrementally realising efficiency gains across an expanding range of practice areas that span the transactional and litigation divide. Work is getting done faster. But speed alone does not equate to progress. AI is exposing a challenge that law firms, particularly large and global firms, have grappled with for years: most of the work to drive matters and deals is still conducted across disconnected systems. These systems store documents, handle matter inception and track time, but none of them individually hold the full context of a matter (the facts, the law, economics, history, and client intent) in one place. To date, AI has merely served to expose this dislocation of systems rather than curing it. The generation of work-product may be accelerating, but the system around it is struggling to keep up. In large firms, matter teams still need to reconstruct context before making decisions, pulling financial, staffing, and procedural information from different systems. New tools reduce drafting time, but they increase the amount of work required to verify and coordinate. Lawyers move faster, but they spend more time making sure everything lines up. The issue isn’t speed, it’s where the effort ends up. Drafting time goes down, but review and coordination time go up. Individual fee earners may be moving faster on some activities, but organisations do not necessarily cross the finish line sooner. When organisations accelerate work on a fragmented foundation of systems, the strain doesn’t disappear. It just moves. Coherence is the missing ingredient It is trite to say that legal work is document-centric. We all know that. But, the obviousness of this obscures the reality: any legal matter, no matter how simple it may be, is a living swarm of connections between facts, issues, law, procedure, stakeholders (and their objectives), all being shaped and mastered by the strategic and tactical judgment of the matter team. With that state distributed across disconnected systems, lawyers need to compensate with experience and memory. Teams synchronise through meetings, email threads, and informal handoffs. It works, but operationally it’s far from ideal. If coherence and cohesion between dislocated systems is the constraint, the answer is platform-thinking. The tooling is advancing rapidly, and the productivity gains they yield are real: lawyers using a single integrated platform report a 25% decrease in cognitive load, according to Clio’s 2025 neuroanalytics research with Neuro-Insight. We’ve seen this pattern before. Early cloud adoption digitised workflows. The real transformation came when organisations stopped stitching tools together and built coherent operating platforms instead. A platform isn’t just “integrated software.” It’s an environment where information, workflow, and decision-making state are connected enough that the organisation can operate with clarity under pressure, retain institutional memory through change, and scale without amplifying friction. To realise the full benefit of AI tools and transform business outcomes, firms must situate those tools in a coherent, integrated platform. That means building environments where the state of a matter is visible in the present, carries forward over time, and can be governed as work evolves. When a lawyer opens a matter, they should see the full context and dive into their tasks, not waste time trying to reconstruct it. When teams change, knowledge should persist, not walk out the door. When AI is deployed, it should operate inside real guardrails informed by the actual state of the work, not generate fluent output in isolation. Context that travels with the work
news.relevanceReason: 文章聚焦法律AI对律所工作流程的影响，讨论AI工具在提高速度的同时暴露的系统集成问题，并提出平台化解决方案，属于法律技术核心议题。

news.titleEn: Cem Ucan, Ex-Legoran, Launches a16z Speedrun-Funded NewMod
news.titleZh: 前Legora高管Cem Ucan推出获a16z Speedrun加速器投资的新模式律所NewMod
news.summaryZh: Cem Ucan曾在贝克·麦坚时律师事务所工作，于2024年加入Legora，现已离职并创立新模式律所Athena，获得a16z Speedrun加速器及基金的投资前种子轮支持。Ucan担任该律所技术板块的联合创始人兼首席执行官。a16z Speedrun是风险投资公司安德森·霍洛维茨推出的为期12周的密集加速器项目，投资额最高可达100万美元。与其他采用MSO安排的新模式律所一样，Athena设有技术部门和独立的法律部门。Kieran Keenan曾与Ucan同在Legora共事，现为技术板块的联合创始人。Kieran从零开始构建了Legora的评估基础设施，并致力于大语言模型质量提升，在Athena负责律所律师所使用的技术和评估系统。这家总部位于加利福尼亚州的律所，其律师联合创始人为Karen Abesamis和Juan Soto。Abesamis曾任摩根路易斯律所的公司与并购合伙人，后担任Superhuman（前身为Grammarly）的公司与合规主管。Soto曾任洛温斯坦·桑德勒律所的顾问律师，主导风险融资、并购及其他国内和跨境交易。Athena是众多进入市场的新模式律所之一，业务涵盖并购、风险投资融资和房地产领域。目前正在大规模招聘。他们创建这家律所旨在将AI带来的效率提升直接传递给客户。尽管律所已采用AI，但客户仍按小时付费，面临费用上限被突破以及重要工作排队等待的问题。Kieran和Ucan在Legora为律师构建技术时发现了这一差距：法律工具的能力显著增强，但围绕其的经济模式和运营模式并未改变。
news.bodyText: Cem Ucan, who previously worked at Baker McKenzie before joining Legora in 2024, has now moved on to launch a NewMod law firm, Athena, with the pre-Seed backing of the a16z Speedrun accelerator and fund, (see AL interview below). He becomes the co-founder and CEO of its tech element. a16z Speedrun is an intensive 12-week accelerator program by venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) that invests up to $1m. As with other NewMods using an MSO arrangement, it has a tech side and a separate legal part. Kieran Keenan, who was also at Legora, is Cem’s co-founder for the tech bit. Ucan told this site that ‘[Kieran] built Legora’s evaluation infrastructure from the ground up and worked on LLM quality. At Athena, he leads the technology and evaluation systems used by the law firm’s attorneys’. Meanwhile, the California-based NewMod’s lawyer co-founders are Karen Abesamis and Juan Soto. Abesamis was a Corporate and M&A partner at Morgan Lewis and later Head of Corporate and Compliance at Superhuman, formerly Grammarly. Soto was counsel at Lowenstein Sandler, where he led venture financings, M&A and other domestic and cross-border transactions. It’s one of many NewMod law firms coming to market, in this case covering M&A, VC funding and real estate. And in relation to the last area, they are now ‘on a hiring spree’ they told this site. AL Interview with Cem Ucan Tell us about Athena We built a law firm designed to pass the efficiency gains of AI directly to clients. Law firms have adopted AI. Yet clients are still paying by the hour, blowing through fee caps and waiting for important work to reach the top of someone else’s queue. Has the technology made any noticeable difference to your bill, timetable or experience? Kieran (see above) and I saw this gap while building technology for lawyers at Legora. Legal tools became dramatically more capable, but the economics and operating model around them remained unchanged.
news.relevanceReason: 文章聚焦于一家利用AI技术提升效率的新模式律所，涉及法律科技应用、AI在律所运营中的角色，以及法律行业的技术创新，属于核心法律AI领域。

news.titleEn: LexisNexis Picks Document Drafter for Automated Docs
news.titleZh: LexisNexis 选定 Document Drafter 实现文档自动化
news.summaryZh: LexisNexis 在评估多个平台后，选定丹麦公司 Document Drafter 为其全球客户提供自动化文档服务。Document Drafter 还开发了一个转换器，成功迁移了 LexisNexis 庞大的模板库。该模板库历经数十年积累，涵盖主要司法辖区，包含超过 25,000 个模板。此次合作中，Document Drafter 不会单独品牌化，但意义重大。律所将直接在 LexisNexis 平台内使用该功能，选定模板后，Document Drafter 将接管后续流程直至文档生成。LexisNexis 客户将获得与 Document Drafter 客户相同的体验，且过程无缝衔接，用户不会察觉平台切换。他们构建了 100% 自动化的转换器，耗时一年多完成，并称这是有史以来规模最大的遗留文档自动化平台迁移。目前转换已完成，由 Document Drafter 驱动的新产品将在未来几周内逐步向客户推出。此外，文章还预告了今年十一月在伦敦和纽约举行的 Legal Innovators 大会，分别于 11 月 4 日至 5 日和 11 月 17 日至 18 日举办，涵盖律所日与法务日。
news.bodyText: LexisNexis has selected Denmark-based Document Drafter to deliver its automated documents to customers globally after an evaluation of multiple platforms. The startup also built a converter that handled the migration of the huge LexisNexis template library. Although there will be no separate branding of Document Drafter for this feature, it’s a big deal because the LexisNexis library of automated templates has been built up over decades and includes more than 25,000 templates across key jurisdictions. In terms of how it will work, law firms will use this directly within LexisNexis. Once a template is selected, Document Drafter ‘takes over the experience through to the generation of the document. LexisNexis customers will get the same experience as a Document Drafter customer – although this will feel completely seamless and they will not notice any platform shift’. Michael Bjerg Hansen, Co-founder & CEO, told Artificial Lawyer: ‘This was done by building a 100% automated converter and took a little more than a year to complete. I believe this is the largest migration out of a legacy document automation platform ever done. ‘The conversion now has been completed, and the new offering powered by Document Drafter is rolling out to customers gradually over the next few weeks.’ Congrats to Michael and team. — Two Major Legal Innovators Conferences this November Come and join us in New York and London this November at Legal Innovators! Legal Innovators UK – London, Nov 4 and 5 And, then Legal Innovators New York – Nov 17 and 18. After another fantastic Legal Innovators California, where we had speakers from OpenAI, Y Combinator, Google, Meta, and many more pioneering organisations; and our stellar inaugural event in Paris this June, we are now looking forward to the landmark conferences in London and New York, both in November, and both across two days: Law Firm Day, and Inhouse Day.
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要报道法律科技公司 Document Drafter 被 LexisNexis 选中用于自动化文档生成，涉及法律文档自动化平台、模板库迁移及律所工作流程，属于核心法律科技内容。

news.titleEn: DeepJudge + Legora Form ‘Bidirectional Partnership’ – Updated
news.titleZh: DeepJudge与Legora建立“双向合作伙伴关系”——更新
news.summaryZh: 知识管理先驱DeepJudge与Legora建立双向合作伙伴关系。这是深度合作，Agent Handoff Protocol（AHP）是其中一部分，但合作超出Legora单纯采用该协议。这家瑞士公司最初似乎暗示此举超越了与Harvey和TR通过AHP的合作方向，后澄清方向非常相似，只是Legora与DeepJudge的连接不止于使用AHP。更大的转变是DeepJudge的机构智能被引入Legora体验中。在Legora工作的律师可在工作流程中调用由DeepJudge呈现的律所自身先例、过往工作、经验和知识；且是双向的：Legora中创建的新工作通过DeepJudge回流至律所机构知识，使知识持续累积并影响未来工作。AHP是实现互操作性的赋能层，Legora合作是这一理念成为实际产品体验及公司间更深关系的例证。这紧密关联上周AHP报道，但是下一章：不仅商定AI产品如何互通，而是将机构知识带入律师工作流程，并确保新知识成为律所未来智能的一部分。过往工作影响后续工作，新工作增加组织经验，为律师和AI代理创造持续更丰富的智能来源。随着Thomson Reuters、Harvey及如今Legora采用AHP，法律AI生态系统正走向更连接的用户体验。关键方面包括：从知识到工作产品，律师可在DeepJudge中搜索分析组织集体知识，并将选定文件直接发送至Legora进行谈判、审查和起草，可从Legora或DeepJudge平台操作。
news.bodyText: KM pioneer DeepJudge and Legora have formed a bidirectional partnership. A spokesperson told this site: ‘It’s a deep level of engagement. The Agent Handoff Protocol (AHP) – (see AL article from last week) – is part of the story, but the partnership goes beyond Legora simply adopting the protocol.’ The Swiss company initially appeared to suggest that this move went beyond where they were going with Harvey and TR via the AHP, which had both agreed to use the protocol, but then later today sought to clarify their message and explain that it was in fact a very similar direction, it was just that the Legora and DeepJudge connection would be more that just using the AHP. The company’s spokesperson continued: ‘The bigger shift is that DeepJudge’s institutional intelligence is being brought into the Legora experience. — (Advertisement) — — ‘A lawyer working in Legora can draw on their firm’s own precedent, prior work, experience and knowledge surfaced by DeepJudge as part of the workflow. And it’s bidirectional: the new work created in Legora flows back into the firm’s institutional knowledge through DeepJudge, so that knowledge continues to compound and can inform future work. ‘AHP is an enabling layer for that interoperability. The Legora partnership is an example of what it looks like when that idea becomes an actual product experience and a deeper relationship between the companies. ‘In short, it’s very much connected to the AHP story covered last week, but it’s the next chapter: not just agreeing on how AI products can talk to each other, but actually bringing institutional knowledge into the workflows where lawyers are doing their work, and ensuring the new knowledge created there becomes part of the firm’s intelligence going forward.’ And, they added that ‘past work informs what comes next, and new work adds to the organization’s experience, creating a continuously richer source of intelligence for lawyers and AI agents to draw on’.So, there you go. They also added that ‘with Thomson Reuters, Harvey, and now Legora adopting AHP, we’re moving toward a more connected user experience across the legal AI ecosystem’. And here’s a summary of the key aspects: From knowledge to work product: Lawyers can search and analyze their organization’s collective knowledge in DeepJudge and send the selected documents directly to Legora for negotiation, review, and drafting, from either the Legora or DeepJudge platforms.
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要报道法律科技公司 DeepJudge 与 Legora 的合作，涉及法律 AI 产品集成、知识管理和工作流程，属于法律 AI 生态的核心内容。

news.titleEn: South Korea Opens the Door to Copyright Registration of AI-Assisted Works
news.titleZh: 韩国开放AI辅助作品的版权登记
news.summaryZh: 韩国音乐著作权协会（KOMCA）撤销了此前对AI辅助音乐作品的登记禁令，于2026年8月4日发布通知公布修订后的登记标准，修订规则立即生效。新标准取代了2025年3月24日生效的“零百分比”政策，该政策要求创作者确认作品完全由人类创作贡献完成、无AI参与。根据修订后的制度，当人类创作者作出实质性且主导性的创作贡献时，KOMCA将登记AI辅助作品；依据2026年8月3日更新的登记表，这意味着人类创作参与占创作过程的一半以上。但KOMCA明确禁止仅靠提示词生成，申请人必须确认作品并非仅由提示词产生。申请人须指出并确认作品中哪些部分涉及AI、所使用的AI工具、各工具的使用方式，以及歌词、作曲、编曲等各相关部分的人类创作贡献，而非笼统声明“使用了AI”。登记还要求登记者对每项AI相关陈述与保证单独同意，包括作品保留了基于人类实质性且主导性创作选择与表达的人类创作。KOMCA将登记与可验证的人类参与证明挂钩，指示创作者保留支持创作过程的材料（如数字音频工作站项目文件、修订历史、乐谱和提示词日志）及相关修订历史，KOMCA可要求提供，申请人须及时提供。通知还描述了针对存疑登记的审查轨道，KOMCA可进行技术检查或内部审议，以核实AI使用、检验披露真实性及评估人类贡献是否构成实质性且主导性。通知强调虚假申报将依据协会规则和合同条款承担直接后果，措施包括扣留版税、追回不当所得、施加合同处罚及终止信托协议。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! South Korea’s largest music copyright collective, the Korea Music Copyright Association (“KOMCA”), has reversed its prior ban on registering AI-assisted musical works. The change expands what can be registered, but it comes with stricter disclosure requirements and more explicit enforcement tools. KOMCA announced the revised registration standards in a notice dated August 4, 2026, and the amended rules took effect immediately. KOMCA’s new approach replaces its earlier “zero percent” policy, which took effect March 24, 2025. Under that prior rule, creators were required to confirm that a work was made solely through human creative contributions, with no AI involvement. Under the revised system, KOMCA will register AI-assisted works when a human creator made a substantial and leading creative contribution, which, according to KOMCA’s copyright registration form, updated as of August 3, 2026, means that human creative involvement accounts for more than half of the creative process. However, KOMCA draws a bright line against prompt-only generation. In practice, the applicant must confirm that the work did not result solely from prompts. Applicants must now identify and affirm which parts of a work involved AI, the AI tools used, how each tool was used, and the human creative contribution for each relevant part, including lyrics, composition, and arrangement. This is not framed as a general “AI was used” statement. Rather, disclosure requires a detailed account of where AI was involved and what the human creator contributed. Additionally, registration of an AI-assisted work requires the registrant’s individual consent to each AI-related representation and warranty, including that the work retains a human-created work based on substantial and leading creative choices and expression by a human. KOMCA also ties registration to verifiable proof of human involvement. The notice instructs creators to keep materials that support the creative process (e.g., digital audio workstation project files, revision histories, sheet music, and prompt logs), and to retain related revision history. KOMCA may request these materials, and applicants are expected to promptly provide supporting documentation when asked. The notice also describes a review track for registrations that raise questions. KOMCA may conduct technical checks or use an internal deliberation process to verify AI use, test the truth of the disclosure, and/or assess whether the human contribution qualifies as substantial and leading. KOMCA’s notice highlights direct consequences for false filings under its association rules and contract terms. Those measures include holding royalty payments, recovering improperly received amounts, imposing contractual penalties, and terminating the trust agreement. In other words, the disclosure and verification requirements are backed by remedies that can affect both cash flow and ongoing participation in KOMCA’s system. KOMCA also tightened procedural rules for common filing structures. For agent-filed applications, KOMCA now expects written authority signed by the principal that expressly covers AI-related reporting, confirmation, representation, warranty, and pledge; nevertheless, the representations and warranties regarding the substantial and leading creative contribution by human and no prompt-only generation shall be made in the name of the principal. For joint works, a co-author may file and confirm the filer’s own contribution, and may report other co-authors’ contributions based on information received. KOMCA provides a seven-day objection window after notice.
news.relevanceReason: 文章聚焦韩国音乐版权机构对AI辅助作品的登记政策，涉及AI在创作中的法律与合规问题，属于法律与AI交叉领域，但主要针对版权登记实务，而非广义法律AI技术或法律行业应用。

news.titleEn: Inhouse Embraces AI…And Does Little With It
news.titleZh: 内部法务拥抱AI……却鲜有作为
news.summaryZh: LegalOn新调查显示，内部法务团队虽已基本引入AI工具，但使用水平极低、影响甚微。92%的团队使用AI，但市场仍不成熟，多数处于最早采用阶段：54.9%仍在实验阶段，探索提示词和工具，没有共享工作流程或标准；标准化提示词和工作流程（26.5%）可领先约三分之二市场；实现连接知识（8.8%），即AI基于自身行动手册和政策而非通用提示词，可进入前11%；仅2.0%（n=2）描述了覆盖受理、分诊、合同工作和签署后洞察的完整工作流程支持。换言之，仅2%真正充分利用内部法律AI平台。虽有内部团队拥抱AI并大幅削减外部法律支出的轶事，但数据显示这些仍是异常值。为何故事惊人而数据仅约2%？答案在于规模：仅美国估计就有超过12,000家员工超1000人的公司，可能设有内部律师和显著法律需求，其中少数分享出色举措即可填满一场会议，但仍只占整体极小比例，全球范围更甚。这是“牵马到水边”的挑战：内部律师乐于在局部范围用AI获得快速胜利和即时效率提升，但要真正改变整个团队工作方式以充分利用当前LLM能力，要求很高。许多公司尚未具备支持AI工具有力部署的组织结构或文化，合同“属于所有人”，记录系统分散，缺乏整体变革战略。
news.bodyText: A new survey by LegalOn has found empirical data that supports what Artificial Lawyer is hearing on the legal tech street, namely that while inhouse teams have now largely onboarded AI tools, their use level remains minimal and it’s having little meaningful impact. As the graph below shows, and as LegalOn explained: ‘Despite 92% of teams using AI, the market remains immature, with the majority of these teams still in the earliest stages of adoption.’ They added: ‘Ordered left to right, from least-to-most advanced (Laggards to Innovators), the shape is telling: more than half of respondents (54.9%) are still in the experimentation phase, exploring prompts and tools without shared workflows or standards. ‘Standardizing prompts and workflows (26.5%) puts you ahead of roughly two-thirds of the market. Reaching connected knowledge (8.8%), where AI is grounded in your own playbooks and policies rather than generic prompts, puts you in the top 11%. A single-digit handful (n=2, 2.0%) describe full workflow support across intake, triage, contract work, and post-signature insight.’ In short, only 2% are really using inhouse legal AI platforms to their full extent. And yet AL has also heard a few great anecdotes about how some inhouse teams have really embraced AI, and some have even massively cut outside legal spending…..but, these are the outliers for now, as the data shows. But, things will change. Meanwhile, one may ask: how can we hear such amazing stories about substantive change, and yet the data says it’s only about 2% of companies doing this? The answer is all about scale. For example, it’s estimated that there are over 12,000 companies – just in the US – with more than 1,000 staff. I.e. companies that probably have inhouse lawyers and notable legal needs. Of those, we only need a handful to share some great initiatives and you could fill a conference with wonderful stories of change. Yet, it would remain a tiny proportion of the whole. Then, when you look globally, the scale issue extends. Thus, we have a long way to go. What Does This Mean? It’s the old ‘you can lead a horse to water’ challenge. Inhouse lawyers are happy to use AI tools that give them some quick wins and immediate efficiency gains in a very localised way, but moving to a scenario where they really have to change how they work – across the whole team – to get the most out of what LLMs can do now, is a big ask. As explored yesterday – see here – many companies just don’t have the organisational structure or culture in place yet to support really powerful deployment of AI tools. Contracts ‘belong to everyone’, systems of record are divided, and there is no overall strategy for change.

news.titleEn: Next Gen ‘Harvey II’ Launches with Memory at Its Core
news.titleZh: 下一代“Harvey II”发布，以记忆功能为核心
news.summaryZh: Harvey推出下一代法律AI平台，以Memory能力为核心，同时具备偏好设置、上下文共享，并能从律所律师及其客户的需求中学习。此次重大更新被命名为Harvey II。Harvey一直在演进，这是产品的重大转变，重点聚焦上下文和Memory，以及如何利用Memory并保护道德墙。这或许类似于高端酒店的做法，即不断学习并响应客人的偏好，以提供最定制化的体验。这凸显了Harvey所能带来的价值，即它正在尽可能超越任何LLM所能提供的能力，无论模型多么复杂。它使其应用层与你的工作方式、数据、先例、工作风格以及客户偏好紧密交织，从而打造一种让人愿意不断回归的“体验”。因此，大型LLM制造商可以推出任何模型——Harvey当然也会利用它们——但它们无法提供这种级别的连接性和个性化，至少在AL看来，这一战略似乎如此。此外，在这种情况下，Memory不仅仅是一个通用术语，而是Harvey自今年早些时候以来与客户携手开发的一种特定学习能力。Memory的核心在于学习你的偏好的能力——你的用词选择、起草风格、工作结构。如果Harvey随后做出判断，它可以基于这些定制偏好给出答案。这将扩展到特定事项上的客户偏好，而这又与每个事项的上下文相关联——Harvey将其链接起来。这进而延伸到Shared Spaces——它提供的客户与律所之间的协作论坛。最终结果是，“Harvey使用得越多就变得越好。你可以部署的代理也会变得更好。所以，这是一个游戏规则改变者”，Drumright总结道。总体而言，这一战略非常合理。
news.bodyText: Harvey is launching the next generation of the legal AI platform with its Memory capability at its core, alongside preference setting, context sharing, and learning from both what a law firm’s lawyers and their clients want. The major refresh is branded as Harvey II. Anique Drumright, CPO, told Artificial Lawyer: ‘Harvey has been on an evolution and this is a big shift in the product. There is a major focus on context and Memory, and how we can leverage Memory and protect ethical walls.’ Artificial Lawyer suggested that this is perhaps similar to the approach of a high-end hotel, where the guests’ preferences are continually learned and responded to in order to provide the most customised experience. One could then add that this accentuates the value that Harvey can bring. I.e. it’s doing as much as possible above and beyond what any LLM can provide, no matter how complex the model. It’s making its application layer so intertwined with how you work, with your data, your precedents, with working styles and also that of your clients’ preferences, that the ‘experience’ is one that you want to keep coming back to. The giant LLM makers therefore can roll out whatever models they want – and of course Harvey will tap them as well – but they won’t be able to offer you this level of connectedness and personalisation, or at least that’s how the strategy appears to AL. Plus, in this case, Memory is not just a general term, but rather a specific learning capability that Harvey has been developing since earlier this year, hand-in-hand with customers. Here’s a short video about this: And here’s a quick overview of what Harvey II is all about: Drumright continued: ‘Memory is all about the ability to learn your preferences – your choice of words, your drafting style, the structure of the work. If Harvey then makes a judgment call it can give answers based on those tailored preferences.’ She then noted that this will extend to client preferences on certain matters and that in turn connected to the context of each matter – which Harvey links to. And then in turn this runs to the Shared Spaces – the collaborative forum – that it offers between a client and law firm. The net result is that ‘Harvey gets better and better the more you use it. The agents [that you can deploy] get better. So, this is a game changer’, Drumright concluded. Overall a strategy that makes a lot of sense.

news.titleEn: The Rules of Evidence Are AI-Resilient
news.titleZh: 证据规则对人工智能具有韧性
news.summaryZh: 生成式人工智能使合成音频、视频和图像的制作变得容易且逼真，显著增加了法官作为证据守门人的难度，也加大了伪造证据扭曲司法的风险。合成证据带来两类威胁：伪造证据可能被误认为真实，真实证据也可能被无端质疑为伪造，二者都会侵蚀公众对法院辨别真伪能力的信任。但现有可采性学说并未因此失效，最有效的应对是借助教育和制度支持，让法官掌握当前人工智能的能力与局限，在现有框架下可靠地裁定证据。证据规则只提供框架，并不足以让法官评估人工智能生成和检测合成证据的能力。仅需一分钟清晰音频，市售软件即可克隆声音并生成任意内容的音频。历史上，DNA证据的引入并未要求专门规则，而是通过Frye标准及后来的《联邦证据规则》第702条、Daubert案，逐步提升法官的守门人职能；第901条则一般适用于认证。法律一贯通过提高可采性门槛、要求更多可靠性与真实性证明，并由法官作初步事实认定，来将现有标准适用于新证据类型。这一历史路线图将指导司法系统应对人工智能时代的证据可采性问题。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! A victim reports receiving a series of threatening voicemail messages left by a former partner. The victim sends the recordings to police by email. The call logs from the victim’s phone show the threatening calls originated from a blocked number. The victim's original phone is no longer available. The defendant denies making the calls and claims the recordings are deepfake imitations of his voice. In the criminal trial for threats, the prosecutor seeks to admit the recordings as evidence. The defendant objects, challenging their authenticity. Before the jury hears the audio evidence, the judge must decide if it is admissible. Generative AI has significantly increased the practical difficulty of carrying out the judge's role as evidentiary gatekeeper. As the ability to create convincing synthetic audio, video, and images becomes widely accessible, the risk of fabricated evidence distorting the administration of justice grows more pressing by the day. Yet, the rapid evolution and growing accessibility of generative AI do not diminish the continued applicability of existing admissibility doctrines. As a result, the most effective response today is to ensure judges are equipped, through education and institutional support, to apply existing principles to evidence as generative AI becomes commonplace. The rules of evidence provide a framework for deciding admissibility, but they alone do not equip judges to assess the capabilities and limitations of AI to produce and detect synthetic evidence. With as little as one minute of clear audio as a sample, commercially available software can clone a person's voice and generate audio saying anything the creator types into a prompt.1 Never has the fabrication of evidence been so easy and the outcome so convincing. Our system of justice depends on judges and juries applying procedures designed to maximize the likelihood of finding the truth. Public confidence in verdicts rests on the historic reliability of those procedures. The existing rules and doctrines of evidence have proven reliable over generations at separating truth from fabrication, and the public trusts outcomes because the process that produces them has earned that trust. Synthetic evidence threatens that foundation in two distinct ways. First, fabricated evidence may be credited as genuine. Second, genuine evidence may be challenged as fabricated without any basis for the claim. Each failure carries the potential consequence of a verdict resting on something other than the truth. The cumulative risk is that repeated failures of either kind would erode the public's confidence that courts can distinguish real evidence from manufactured evidence, and ultimately their ability to find the truth. The advent of AI has made the core function of a judge, to apply law to facts, more difficult as the authenticity of those facts is now harder to verify. Questions of evidence admissibility and authenticity are not new; judges make them every day. But the tools available to help them are increasingly insufficient, and given the trajectory of technological advances since deepfakes emerged as a recognized phenomenon in 2017,2 it is unlikely that deepfake identification tools will outperform deepfake creation ones anytime soon.3 That makes it critical that judges be well-versed in current AI capabilities, so they can reliably make evidentiary rulings under the existing frameworks. In 1988, before DNA evidence was introduced by expert testimony for the first time in a U.S. criminal trial, a Florida court in Andrews v. State held an evidentiary hearing and considered application of a standard set in 1923. There, the court pondered the applicability of the Frye4 standard to determine the admissibility of DNA evidence as a case of first impression. In doing so, Andrews built upon Frye and affirmed "…relevancy as the linchpin of admissibility…" when considering novel evidence.5 The Frye standard was developed sixty years earlier to determine the relevancy of the systolic blood pressure deception test, a precursor to the modern-day polygraph. The introduction of DNA evidence did not require a bespoke rule upon which to determine admissibility. Instead, it relied on the practical evolution of then-existing principles. The Frye standard eventually gave way fully to Rule 702 of the Federal Rules of Evidence. In Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc.,6 the Supreme Court further elevated the "gatekeeper" function of the judge in its interpretation of Rule 702. While those standards apply to scientific evidence specifically, Rule 901 applies to authentication generally. It is under Rule 901 that the judge's gatekeeper function is tested by synthetic evidence. It is through the application of law to facts under Rule 901 that a judge with accumulated experience and understanding of the technology can separate the irrelevant from the relevant evidence before it makes it to a jury. The law has historically applied, and later adapted, existing standards to new evidence types through the imposition of high bars to admissibility by requiring an increased demonstration of the reliability and authenticity of evidence, and assigning the preliminary fact determination to the judge. This is the historical roadmap that will guide the judicial system as it navigates evidence admissibility in the AI era.

research.titleEn: CoAL-RAG: A Complexity-Aware Legal Retrieval-Augmented Generation Method
research.titleZh: CoAL-RAG：一种复杂度感知的法律检索增强生成方法
research.abstractEn: Legal consultation questions exhibit multi-level complexity. A single retrieval strategy often leads to over-reasoning for simple questions and poor interpretability for complex ones, making it difficult to meet the requirements for both answer quality and efficiency in high-risk scenarios. To address this issue, this paper proposes CoAL-RAG, a complexity-aware legal retrieval-augmented generation method, which constructs a multi-dimensional evaluation mechanism based on ``question essence'' and ``retrieval consistency'' to enable adaptive routing of retrieval strategies. First, the reasoning demand is quantified according to the logical structure of the question. Then, the discrepancy between semantic retrieval and keyword retrieval is utilized to indirectly reflect problem complexity, thereby selecting the most appropriate retrieval strategy and dynamically filtering contextual information. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms baseline models not only on Chinese legal benchmarks (SocialLawQA, LawBench) but also demonstrates strong cross-jurisdictional generalization on English datasets (LexGLUE, CaseHold). Specifically, on Chinese datasets, the BLEU score improves by 42.5\% and ROUGE-L reaches 3.6 times that of knowledge graph-based methods. On English benchmarks, CoAL-RAG maintains highly competitive accuracy, achieving an optimal balance between generation quality, deep logical reasoning, and system efficiency across different legal systems.
research.abstractZh: 法律咨询问题呈现出多层次复杂性。单一的检索策略往往导致简单问题的过度推理和复杂问题的可解释性差，难以满足高风险场景下对答案质量和效率的双重要求。针对这一问题，本文提出了CoAL-RAG，一种复杂度感知的法律检索增强生成方法，该方法基于“问题本质”和“检索一致性”构建了多维评估机制，以实现检索策略的自适应路由。首先，根据问题的逻辑结构量化推理需求。然后，利用语义检索与关键词检索之间的差异间接反映问题复杂度，从而选择最合适的检索策略并动态过滤上下文信息。实验结果表明，所提出的方法不仅在中国法律基准（SocialLawQA、LawBench）上显著优于基线模型，而且在英文数据集（LexGLUE、CaseHold）上展现出强大的跨法域泛化能力。具体而言，在中国数据集上，BLEU分数提高了42.5%，ROUGE-L达到基于知识图谱方法的3.6倍。在英文基准上，CoAL-RAG保持了极具竞争力的准确性，在不同法律体系下实现了生成质量、深度逻辑推理和系统效率之间的最佳平衡。

news.titleEn: Guest Post: AI means legal tech project plans are no longer fit for purpose
news.titleZh: 客座文章：AI意味着法律科技项目计划已不再适用
news.summaryZh:
采用生成式AI工具的方式需要改变。过去引入法律科技解决方案需多团队确定需求并全面市场调研，该方法已不再适用。更有效的做法是选择几个有改进潜力的领域，用现有或可快速采购的工具进行实验，然后聚焦交付高影响力的成果，提升团队熟悉度、信心和参与度。这一迭代过程可能浪费资源，但AI市场变化太快，传统方法完成时技术已过时。实验和教育能让团队更好发现机会并快速行动，长期收益将超过早期实验成本。

内部法律团队常问应投资法律专用AI工具还是通用模型。目前Copilot等通用工具在后勤和组织任务上表现超出预期，但法律专用AI在严肃法律工作中仍更优。Anthropic和微软等公司的进展令人瞩目，但竞争结局尚早，不能成为不作为的借口。选择方案时，除产品外还需考虑供应商领导力、资金、客户和未来计划。采用率低通常不是技术问题，而是需要开始使用、建立熟悉度、破除迷思和培养信任。快速变化带来焦虑，律师天生怀疑，过度乐观的鼓吹者加剧问题。必须提醒人们潜在收益真实且显著，等待市场发展而竞争对手前进不是选项。快速行动意味着不等待、不追求完美，当前学习比可衡量收益更重要，实际影响比站在前沿更重要。
news.bodyHtml:
By Ben Williams, Pinsent Masons Vario

The way we look at adopting generative AI tools needs to change.

Advertisement

Cast your mind back just five years, the process of introducing a new legal technology solution would start with multiple teams sitting down together and pinpointing exactly what their requirements were before carrying out an exhaustive market review to find the best possible solution. That approach is no longer fit for purpose.

Pilots in key areas more effective

Across the in-house legal teams that we work with, we’re finding that it’s now much more effective to pick a few areas where you feel there’s real potential for improvement and start experimenting; ideally with a tool that you either already have available or can procure very quickly and without vast expenditure.

Advertisement

After all, one of the benefits of generative AI is the tools being incredibly quick to introduce and accessible for the mainstream workforce.

Then, once you have these in place, we recommend focussing on delivering practical, high impact wins across your focus areas. This will hopefully improve familiarity, confidence and buy-in from the legal teams that you work with and highlight where further gains may be made.

Of course, this is an iterative process and I’m constantly finding new areas where I feel generative AI could make a real difference for clients.

Speed of market change outpacing traditional project timelines

Of course, this approach does mean that you might spend time and money on solutions which turn out not to work as you’d hoped.

My response to that challenge would be to say that’s fine, and in the nature of experimentation. The AI market is moving so quickly that by the time you have completed a more traditional approach, you face the same risks anyway; the technology will have changed and made your work obsolete.

Having experimentation and education as your primary focus will leave your team better equipped to spot the right opportunities and move fast themselves, which will in turn open up more significant opportunities. In time, the benefits that you realise will outweigh the cost of early experimentation.

Being hyper-focussed on what your problems are and finding pragmatic, if imperfect, solutions today will stand you in good stead in the longer run.

Legal-specific AI solutions better for serious legal work

One of the questions we’re often asked by in-house legal teams is whether they need to invest in a legal-specific AI tool or should introduce a general-purpose model.

At the moment, you can do more that you’d expect with general-purpose tools like Copilot, especially logistical and organisational tasks, but legal-specific AI tools are still outperforming general-purpose solutions when it comes to serious legal work.

A lot of ink has already been spilled over whether legal-specific AI tools will eventually be made obsolete by the likes of Anthropic and Microsoft making serious plays in the space. There’s no doubt that they’re beguilingly impressive, and will have an impact, but it’s still too early to say exactly what this will be. There is a long way for this race to run and the winners are unclear, but that cannot be an excuse for inaction.

On choosing solutions, thinking beyond the product to whether a vendor company has good leadership, solid funding, real clients and a clear plan for the future can help you select a tool with real longevity.

Reminding users of potential gains crucial

When in-house legal teams tell us that they’re struggling with low solution adoption, we find that the issue is rarely the technology itself.

Adoption is about making a start, building familiarity, debunking myths and developing trust. The sheer pace of change that we’re seeing does create anxiety, as does a perceived lack of transparency and accountability; lawyers are trained to be sceptical after all!

Many evangelists also exacerbate these issues when their claims turn out to be overly optimistic. We have to remind people that the potential gains are real and significant; waiting to see how the market develops while your competitors move forward isn’t an option.

Learning and real impact more important than perfection

Moving quickly can mean buying a tool, or indeed several tools, setting up a working group, or meeting lots of vendors.

We’re still really early on this journey. For me, moving quickly means not waiting and not aspiring to perfection. Experiment, try things. Right now, learning is more important than measurable gains and real impact is more important than being right at the cutting edge.

Ben Williams is head of consulting and technology at  Pinsent Masons Vario. He has previously held senior management roles at KPMG, Elevate, and Allen & Overy Peerpoint. 

Unlike many other publications, we don’t charge for guest posts or any written editorial content – if you have something interesting to say, message us. caroline@legaltechnology.com

news.titleEn: Patrick Forquer on Legora’s Agentic AI, Legal Engineering, and Consumption-Based Pricing
news.titleZh: Patrick Forquer 谈 Legora 的代理式 AI、法律工程与基于用量的定价
news.summaryZh:
法律 AI 正从实验转向日常工作。Legora 大量投资于法律工程师，即具有执业经验的律师，他们与客户合作推进采用、工作流设计、提示与上下文工程及变革管理。其收购战略旨在拓宽法律工作覆盖面，同时深化诉讼、商业房地产、监管监测和法律研究；近期收购 Wexler、Cadastral 和 Graceview 将专业能力整合进更广泛的代理平台。Legora 自身 13 天的收购流程，展示了并购尽职调查、文件审查、起草和分析如何通过共享 AI 环境完成。

Forquer 区分了传统工作流自动化与代理式 AI：工作流遵循预定步骤，代理则接收目标、收集上下文、制定计划、调用工具，并在人工审查下处理更长期任务。上下文工程因此更为重要，事项数据、律所知识、权限、法律技能及通过 MCP 等工具与系统的连接都影响代理工作质量，并购尽职调查是长期代理流程获得关注的领域。Legora 通过代理操作系统 aOS 描述相同架构。在经济学方面，Greg 提到 Crowell & Moring 报告的 91% 律师采用率和近 70% 周使用率，Forquer 认为登录数和激活许可证只能说明部分情况；Legora 跟踪日常活动与功能使用深度，包括 Tabular Review、技能、剧本和提取模板。Agent Pro 转向基于用量的定价，信用与使用量挂钩，并提供仪表板、支出控制和项目级归因。Forquer 指出数据层是成功代理式 AI 的核心问题之一，安全访问文档、事项级权限、治理、律所知识和结构化上下文决定代理在复杂法律工作中的进展；人才与基础设施同样重要，这引出了法律工程师和跨越法律、AI、知识管理与数据治理的新混合角色。
news.bodyHtml:
In this episode of The Geek in Review, we talk with Patrick Forquer, Chief Revenue Officer at Legora, about legal AI’s move from experimentation into daily legal work. Forquer explains why Legora has invested heavily in legal engineers, lawyers with practice experience who work alongside clients on adoption, workflow design, prompt and context engineering, and change management. The conversation also explores an emerging career path for lawyers who pair substantive legal knowledge with AI fluency, especially as firms search for people able to translate practice needs into working systems.

Legora’s acquisition strategy provides another lens on the company’s ambitions. Forquer describes a strategy aimed at building breadth across legal work while adding depth in litigation, commercial real estate, regulatory monitoring, and legal research. Recent acquisitions such as Wexler, Cadastral, and Graceview bring specialized capabilities into a broader agentic platform. Legora’s own 13-day acquisition process also serves as an example of how M&A diligence, document review, drafting, and analysis are beginning to move through shared AI environments.

A major portion of the discussion focuses on the difference between traditional workflow automation and agentic AI for legal work. Forquer draws a line between prebuilt automation and agentic systems: workflows follow predetermined steps, while agents receive a goal, gather context, form a plan, call tools, and work across longer tasks with human review. Context engineering therefore becomes increasingly important. Matter data, firm knowledge, permissions, legal skills, and connections to systems through tools such as MCP all shape the quality of agentic work. M&A due diligence already represents one area where longer-horizon agentic processes are gaining traction. Legora describes the same architecture through its agentic operating system, or aOS.

The discussion then turns to economics, pricing, and proof of adoption. Greg points to Crowell & Moring’s reported 91 percent attorney adoption and nearly 70 percent weekly usage, while Forquer argues login counts and activated licenses tell only part of the story. Legora tracks daily activity and depth of feature use, including tools such as Tabular Review, skills, playbooks, and extraction templates. Agent Pro’s shift to consumption-based pricing introduces another measurement challenge, with credits tied to usage alongside dashboards, spending controls, and project-level attribution. For law firms, a broader question follows: when AI compresses hours while increasing speed, scope, and output quality, traditional measures of efficiency and value start pulling in different directions.

The episode closes with a look at what law firm innovation leaders should prepare for next. Forquer identifies the data layer as one of the central issues behind successful agentic AI. Secure access to documents, matter-level permissions, governance, firm knowledge, and well-structured context determines how far agents progress into complex legal work. Talent matters alongside infrastructure, which brings the conversation back to legal engineers and new hybrid roles spanning law, AI, knowledge management, and data governance. The episode leaves innovation and KM leaders with a practical agenda: improve data governance, build legal engineering skills, align stakeholders around risk and outcomes, and measure value through work product, adoption depth, and client impact.

LINKS

  • Legora
  • Legora aOS, Agentic Operating System
  • Legora Introduces Consumption-Based Pricing for Agent Pro
  • Crowell & Moring Marks Six Months of Legora Integration
  • Measuring the Impact of AI on Law Firms, Ari Kaplan and Legora
  • Legora Acquires Wexler
  • Legora Acquires Cadastral
  • Legora Acquires Graceview
  • How Legora Uses Its Platform to Close M&A Deals in Days
  • Legora Series D Funding Announcement
  • Legaltech Hub
  • ILTACON 2026
