Grow as a Leader Beyond Your Day Job

By

Raquel Lewis

posted

27 days ago

Like

Please enjoy this blog authored by Raquel Lewis, Technical Program Manager, Intapp.

Leadership development doesn't require a title. It doesn't require a promotion, a direct report, or a seat at the executive table. For many legal technology professionals, some of the most meaningful leadership growth happens outside the office, through professional associations, nonprofit boards, volunteer committees, employee resource groups, and industry organizations.

I know this firsthand. Over the course of my career, I've served on the LMA Southwest board, rising to president. I've spoken at ILTA conferences as a CRM subject matter expert. I've co-chaired an employee resource group at my company. I've served on the LMA Education Advisory Council, co-chaired the LMA Marketing Technology SIG, and volunteered for ILTA's Content Coordination Teams, among others. Each of those experiences shaped how I lead, how I think about my career, and how I show up at work.

What I've noticed looking back is that my reasons for saying yes evolved significantly over time. Early on, I took on outside roles largely because I was asked, and because I recognized they would help me build visibility and credibility in a field I was still finding my footing in. There's nothing wrong with that. Career development is a legitimate motivator, and being strategic about how you invest your time outside of work is smart, not cynical. But somewhere along the way, something shifted. The roles I sought out later weren't ones I took because they would look good or get my name out there. They were roles I genuinely wanted… work I loved, in an industry I cared about, alongside people who shared my interests. The visibility and networking became a byproduct of doing work that mattered to me, rather than the goal itself.

That shift is worth paying attention to, because it changes everything about how you show up.

Where Leadership Opportunities Exist Outside of Work

For legal technology professionals, the landscape of outside leadership opportunities is broader than it might initially seem. Professional associations like ILTA and LMA are obvious starting points, but the range extends to nonprofit boards, civic leadership programs, employee resource groups, mentorship networks, and community organizations of all kinds.

My own entry point came through a relationship. A colleague and friend asked if I'd be interested in joining the LMA Southwest board. I said yes, partly because I trusted her judgment, and partly because I thought it would be good for my career. I was appointed treasurer, and a couple years later, became president. That single conversation, that one relationship, opened a door I didn't even know to knock on.

Relationships have been the connective tissue across nearly every outside leadership role I've taken on since. I was asked to speak at ILTA because of connections I'd built around CRM. I was asked to co-chair WIN (Intapp’s Women’s Interest Network) because of relationships I'd developed internally at my company. My work on the LMA Education Advisory Council led directly to an invitation to serve as Marketing Technology SIG co-chair. Even my decision to join ILTA's Content Coordination Team was informed by years of knowing what that community valued and who was doing interesting work in it.

The pattern isn't unique to me. Opportunities find people who are already present, already engaged, already known.

“Outside of my role at Benchly, I've stayed active in ILTA's NextGen Legal Innovators, which I recently applied to volunteer for. What keeps me coming back is the mentorship side of the NGLI community, which helps young professionals in legal tech build the relationships and perspective they need early in their careers, while also learning from those further along in their own careers. Investing in others that way has made me a better leader than I would have become on my own.”

Haydn Jones, Vice President, Strategy, Benchly

“Serving as the co-chair of WIN (Intapp’s Women’s Interest Network) has been a rewarding area of involvement for me. Supporting and advocating for women is something I will never tire of. Leadership in this context is getting involved in something that provides meaning to myself and others to create a structure that can be sustained and benefits our work community. It’s a way to continue to learn and grow while also giving back to those who are starting out.”

Alexa Pothier, Senior Growth Director, Intapp

What Outside Leadership Actually Teaches You

There are skills you can develop in a structured corporate environment and skills that are much harder to build there. Influencing without authority. Leading people who have no obligation to follow you. Navigating ambiguity without a playbook. Building consensus among people with competing priorities and limited time. These are the skills that outside leadership roles develop almost by necessity, because the conditions that force them are built into the work.

For me, the most significant shift came from my time in WIN and LMA leadership roles. Those experiences made me think more strategically about my own visibility and surfaced something I'm still working on: learning to advocate for myself. It doesn't come naturally to me, and I suspect I'm not alone in that. But in volunteer and association roles, you earn your standing by showing up, contributing, and making your value visible. That practice has slowly changed how I think about doing the same at work. Because in those spaces, no one hands you credibility. You build it.

“Serving in leadership roles through organizations like ILTA and LMA taught me that leadership isn't about having all the answers-it's about creating opportunities for people to connect, contribute, and learn from one another. That perspective has shaped how I approach my work throughout my career, and today it influences how I lead cross-functional initiatives, encourage technology adoption, and help bridge the gap between people, processes, technology, and intelligence at Barnes & Thornburg.”

Myisha Aldridge, Business Intelligence Analyst, Barnes & Thornburg

“Leading volunteer teams through ILTA, and eventually founding LegalSEC, meant leading without formal authority, so real influence had to be practiced, not assumed. Several volunteering leadership roles also taught me that networking is an invisible control for your leadership, reducing blind spots and stress-testing assumptions. That shows up concretely in the following way: before any major strategy or risk finding goes to a board or client, I may run it through trusted peers first, they consistently add value such as asking the one question I missed. I explore this further in my book, Cyber Executive By Design, in the section "The Power of Networking: Your Invisible Security Control."

Carlos Rodriguez, CEO & vCISO, CA2Security

How to Get Started

The most common barrier isn't lack of opportunity; it's not knowing where to look, or waiting for the "right" moment that never quite arrives.

My advice is simple: start with what you love. Think about the work that energizes you, the problems you find yourself gravitating toward, the conversations you never get tired of having. If you're not doing enough of that in your day job, go find the organizations that need those skills. They exist. They are looking for people exactly like you.

The legal technology community in particular, through ILTA, LMA, and the many adjacent organizations that serve this space, is full of entry points for professionals at every stage of their career. You don't need to start as a board chair or a committee co-chair. You can start by showing up, raising your hand, and being useful. The relationships and opportunities tend to follow.

“Your title on your business card shows your role at the firm on a baseline level. It does not dictate the potential breadth of influence you can have. Networking with individuals both inside and outside the legal technology industry will expand that sphere of influence. It will also open you to ideas that you might not have access to at a firm level.

In addition, everyone has something they are passionate about in the industry, whether or not it is role specific. Each of us has at least one idea that can benefit at least one other person. We have to be willing to share it. Literally reaching out to a vendor of your firm can create an avenue for your ideas to gain a larger audience online.

In short, be willing to put yourself out there. Many people are looking for someone like you to help them. You won’t ever know if you don’t ask.”

Brady Johnson, Learning & Development Specialist, McAfee & Taft

“If you want to grow as a leader, step outside your comfort zone and volunteer. The best leadership lessons rarely come from a job description. They come from working with people who think differently than you, solving problems without formal authority, and learning to earn trust rather than rely on a title. That is exactly what ILTA has given me. From volunteering to coordinating conference teams and now serving as the incoming ILTACON Conference Co-Chair, every opportunity has stretched me in ways that directly improved how I lead. It has expanded my perspective, strengthened my network, and reminded me that leadership is ultimately about serving others and helping people succeed together.”

Ceyda Sydney Tocsoy, Organizational Strategist & Legal Technology Consultant

Your Next Step

Looking across everything I've described… the boards, the committees, the speaking engagements, the volunteer roles, what connects it all isn't strategy or ambition, even though both played a role at various points. It's relationships.

Every significant outside leadership opportunity I've had, came through or led to a meaningful professional relationship. And those relationships, more than any title or credential, are what have shaped my career and my growth as a leader.

If you're a legal technology professional looking to grow beyond your current role, ILTA is a natural place to start. The Content Coordination Teams, committees, and volunteer opportunities within this organization exist precisely because members show up and do work they care about. That's the whole model… and it works.

Start somewhere. Start with something you love. The rest tends to take care of itself.

Where to Get Involved: A Resource Guide

The opportunities for legal technology professionals to lead beyond their day job span a wide range of organizations and formats. Here are some places to start exploring.

Professional Associations in Legal Technology and Legal Marketing

• ILTA — International Legal Technology Association — Content Coordination Teams, committees, and peer communities across practice areas

• LMA — Legal Marketing Association — Regional boards, Special Interest Groups, and the Education Advisory Council

• CLOC — Corporate Legal Operations Consortium — Councils, committees, and regional groups focused on legal operations

Broader Legal and Business Professional Associations

• ALA — Association of Legal Administrators — Leadership and management roles for legal operations and business professionals

• ABA — American Bar Association — Committees and leadership opportunities across practice and technology areas

• SHRM — Society for Human Resource Management — For professionals with an HR or people leadership focus

Nonprofit Board Service

• BoardSource — Resources for finding and preparing for nonprofit board roles, including a certificate program for corporate employees

• V olunteerMatch — Search for volunteer and board opportunities by location and interest area

Civic and Community Leadership Programs

• Many cities have civic leadership programs that place professionals in community projects and government-adjacent roles — search for "[your city] leadership program" or "[your city] civic fellows" to find local options

Mentorship and Peer Networks

• MentorCity — Structured mentorship platform used by professional associations

• Internal ERGs (employee resource groups) at your firm/company— often an underutilized starting point that builds influence close to home

news.titleEn: Work Done In Harvey Now Creates Time Entries In Aderant’s iTimekeep, Thanks To New Integration
news.titleZh: Harvey与Aderant iTimekeep集成：在Harvey完成的工作自动生成计时条目
news.summaryZh: Harvey与Aderant于今日宣布推出新集成，使法律专业人士在Harvey中完成的工作能够自动在Aderant的iTimekeep中生成草稿计时条目。该集成面向同时使用Harvey和iTimekeep的律师事务所，允许他们将两个产品连接起来，从而让Harvey中的工作被计时系统捕获。据两家公司介绍，时间捕获功能包括事项背景、持续时间以及AI生成的叙述，律师可以随后进行审查、编辑和提交。这种集成正是他执业时所希望拥有的连接体验，并指出录入时间很痛苦，而这是解决该问题的第一步。该集成对律师和律所均有优势：对律师而言，减少了重建时间的麻烦，并提供更丰富、更全面的草稿叙述；对律所而言，草稿计时条目更准确、更详细，意味着更少的编辑和更快地将已完成工作转化为收入。去年12月，Harvey和Aderant宣布了一项被称为“市场定义级”的合作，旨在弥合法律业务软件与法律实践软件之间的差距。今日的公告基于此前宣布的合作。Harvey已经理解客户律师每天所做的工作，将该知识直接集成到iTimekeep中，为律所创建了更互联的生态系统，使用户无需改变计费流程即可实现更准确的时间捕获。
news.bodyHtml:
Perform legal work in Harvey, get a draft time entry created automatically in Aderant’s iTimekeep.

That is the upshot of a integration announced today by the two companies.

With the integration, law firms that are customers of both Harvey and iTimekeep can connect the two products so that work done in Harvey is captured by the timekeeping system.

The companies say that the time capture includes matter context, duration, and an AI-generated narrative, which lawyers can then review, edit and submit.

“This integration is exactly the kind of connected experience that I would have loved when I was practicing,” Matthew Guillod, senior product manager at Harvey, said in a statement provided by the companies. “Entering time is painful, and this is the first step towards solving that pain.”

The companies say the integration offers advantages for both lawyers and firms:

  • For lawyers, it reduces the hassle of reconstructing their time and provides them with richer, more comprehensive draft narratives.
  • For firms, draft time entries are more accurate and detailed, meaning fewer edits and faster conversion of completed work into revenue.

In December, Harvey and Aderant announced a partnership they described as “market-defining” for the way it would bridge the gap between software for the business of law and software for the practice of law.

Today’s announcement builds on that previously announced partnership.

“Harvey already understands the work our clients’ attorneys are doing every day,” said Lisa Erickson, SVP of product management and AI at Aderant. “Integrating that knowledge directly into iTimekeep creates a more connected ecosystem for firms, enabling users to achieve more accurate time capture without requiring any changes to their billing process.”

news.titleEn: OUTPUT v. INPUT- Copyright Ownership Challenges in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
news.titleZh: 输出与输入——人工智能时代的版权归属挑战
news.summaryZh: 人工智能可快速创作音乐、绘画、书籍、剧本及计算机程序，但现行版权法既不支持“AI产出全归用户”，也不支持“所有基于版权材料训练的系统均违法”。版权保护以人类作者为前提，侵权判定则取决于复制内容、获取方式、使用方式、系统产出及是否损害现有或合理预期市场，属事实密集型问题。近期判决开始划定界限，但上诉法院尚未提供生成式AI的全面框架。《版权法》保护固定于有形媒介的“原创作品”，长期要求人类作者。在Thaler诉Perlmutter案中，哥伦比亚特区巡回法院维持版权局拒绝登记由“创造力机器”自主生成图像的决定，最高法院于2026年3月2日拒绝复审。但AI辅助作品并非一概不受保护。人类作者可就其在AI辅助作品中贡献的原创表达获得保护，包括创意选择、协调、编排、修改或最终作品中可感知的人类创作材料，但保护仅延及人类创作元素。提示词本身通常不足以确立对输出的作者身份。Zarya of the Dawn案中，版权局保留人类撰写文本及创意编排的登记，但排除AI生成图像；Théâtre D’opéra Spatial案中，审查委员会维持按提交内容拒绝登记，同时承认Allen可寻求仅限其人类修改部分的登记；SURYAST案中，委员会认定Sahni创作了原始照片，但未创作RAGHAV为生成所主张衍生图像而添加的表达元素。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Artificial intelligence can now compose music, generate paintings and photographs, draft books and screenplays, and write computer programs in seconds. That speed has created an understandable temptation to treat the legal issues as equally binary: either everything produced by AI belongs to the user, or every system trained on copyrighted material is unlawful. Current copyright law, however, supports neither conclusion. The more accurate answer is that copyright follows human authorship, while infringement turns on what was copied, how it was obtained, how it was used, what the system produces, and whether the use harms an existing or reasonably likely market. Those are fact-intensive questions. Recent decisions have begun to draw the lines, but the appellate courts have not yet supplied a comprehensive framework for generative AI. Under the Copyright Act, protection extends to “original works of authorship” fixed in a tangible medium. 17 U.S.C. § 102(a). The phrase has long been understood to require a human author. In Thaler v. Perlmutter, 130 F.4th 1039 (D.C. Cir. 2025), the D.C. Circuit affirmed the Copyright Office’s refusal to register an image identified as having been created autonomously by a computer system called the Creativity Machine. The applicant listed the machine as the sole author and sought ownership as the machine’s owner. The court held that the Copyright Act requires a work to be authored in the first instance by a human being. The Supreme Court denied review on March 2, 2026, leaving that holding intact. Thaler answers the easiest version of the question: a machine cannot be the author, and a purely machine-generated work is not copyrightable. It does not mean that every work made with AI assistance is unprotected. Cameras, word processors, digital editing programs, and other tools do not disqualify human expression, and neither does AI merely because it participated in the process. The Copyright Office’s January 2025 report, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability, applies that same distinction. A human author may obtain protection for original expression the person contributes to an AI-assisted work, including creative selection, coordination, arrangement, modification, or the use of human-authored material that remains perceptible in the final work. Protection, however, extends only to the human-authored elements, not to material generated by the system without sufficient human control. Prompts present the difficult middle. The Copyright Office concluded that, with generally available technology, prompts alone are unlikely to establish authorship of the output. A prompt may be detailed and may itself contain copyrightable expression, but it ordinarily operates as an instruction: the system determines many of the final expressive details, and identical prompts may generate materially different results. Repeated prompting also does not necessarily solve the problem. Copyright rewards authorship, not effort or “sweat of the brow.” This analysis may change as tools give users more direct and predictable control over expressive elements. The current registration cases and agency decisions sharpen the human-authorship rule. They also expose the line that Thaler did not decide – how much human control over an AI-assisted output is enough. Thaler involved a work identified as autonomously created by a machine. The D.C. Circuit expressly declined to decide the harder case in which a human claims authorship using AI as a tool. The Copyright Office first confronted a mixed human-and-AI work in Zarya of the Dawn (Feb. 21, 2023), a graphic novel containing human-written text and Midjourney-generated images. The Office maintained registration for the author’s text and for her creative selection, coordination, and arrangement of the text and images, but excluded the individual AI-generated images. The decision illustrates that a work may be registrable as a whole even though some constituent elements receive no protection. The Office reached the opposite result for the claimed images in Théâtre D’opéra Spatial (Sept. 5, 2023) and SURYAST (Dec. 11, 2023). Jason Allen used more than 600 prompts to create Théâtre D’opéra Spatial with Midjourney and made additional edits, but refused to disclaim the Midjourney-generated material. The Review Board therefore affirmed refusal of the claim as submitted, while recognizing that Allen could seek registration limited to his human-authored modifications. In SURYAST, Ankit Sahni supplied his own photograph and a style image to the RAGHAV Artificial Painting App. The Board concluded that Sahni authored the original photograph, but not the expressive elements added by RAGHAV to produce the claimed derivative image.

news.titleEn: AI Is Fundamentally Changing When, Why, and How Companies Build Legal Teams
news.titleZh: AI正在从根本上改变公司组建法律团队的时机、原因和方式
news.summaryZh: 多年来，构建内部法律团队的模式相当可预测：创始人先招聘工程师，随后是销售团队，产品扩张，法律职能通常较晚才设立，往往等到合同变得复杂、监管机构开始问询或外部律师费用过高时。这一顺序已不再适用于AI公司。过去一年，法律职能已从被动招聘转变为最早的策略性投资之一，公司从一开始就组建法律团队以推动增长，而非应对增长带来的挑战。历史上，许多风投支持的公司可以等到规模显著扩大后再进行首次内部法律招聘。如今，许多AI企业在A轮或B轮融资前后便招聘经验丰富的法律顾问，有时甚至更早。原因在于AI公司并非仅仅推出另一个SaaS平台，它们同时面临日益增加的监管审查、复杂的数据许可问题、知识产权关切、企业采购要求、网络安全义务和投资者期望。法律职能已变得过于重要，不能留待以后处理。增长最快的公司认识到，首位法律招聘不是为了解决昨天的问题，而是为了帮助业务扩展至明天的机遇。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! For years, the playbook for building an in-house legal team was fairly predictable. Founders hired engineers first. Sales teams followed. Product expanded. Legal came later, usually once the company reached a point where the contracts became more complicated, regulators started asking questions, or outside counsel became too expensive to rely on. That sequencing no longer applies to AI companies. Over the past year, I've watched legal move from being a reactive hire to one of the earliest strategic investments businesses are making. Rather than responding to the challenges of growth, companies are building legal teams to enable it from the outset. That's a fundamental shift, and one I don't think the market has fully appreciated yet. Historically, many venture-backed companies could comfortably delay their first in-house legal hire until they reached significant scale. Today, many AI businesses are hiring experienced counsel around Series A or Series B funding, sometimes even earlier. The reasons are obvious when you look at the environment they're operating in. AI companies aren't simply launching another SaaS platform. They're facing increasing regulatory scrutiny, complex data licensing questions, intellectual property concerns, enterprise procurement requirements, cybersecurity obligations, and investor expectations all at once. Legal has become too important to leave until later, in summary. The companies growing fastest are recognizing that the first legal hire isn't there to solve yesterday's problems. They're there to help the business scale into tomorrow's opportunities.

news.titleEn: Is Someone Recording? Managing the Workplace Risks of Portable AI Notetakers
news.titleZh: 有人在录音吗？管理便携式AI笔记工具的工作场所风险
news.summaryZh: AI笔记工具正在改变工作方式，例如可吸附在手机背面的“AI助手”能即时完成会议记录、摘要和跟进事项，减轻行政负担并让员工专注对话。此前虚拟笔记工具会作为参会者出现在视频会议中，便于批准或移除，组织也可限制公司设备上的应用安装或连接公司系统。但便携式AI笔记工具可录制面对面谈话和电话通话，离线存储后同步生成文字记录、摘要和行动项，部分小到可放入口袋或附着手机，无需加入虚拟会议、运行于组织网络或安装在公司电脑上。员工控制的设备可能在组织不知情下录制会议室讨论、面试、电话或非正式对话，并将信息发送给第三方AI服务。这虽有益处，却带来隐私、安全、雇佣和诉讼风险。联邦和州法律可能限制录制电话和其他通信：多数州只需一方同意，其他州通常要求所有各方同意，参与者跨州或跨国时分析尤为复杂。便携设备还扩大了问题场景，包括求职面试、客户通话、工作场所调查、便利安排会议及涉及患者或访客的对话。即使参与者同意被录制，该同意未必授权将录制及信息分享给第三方AI供应商，参与者可能不了解服务会接收其声音和陈述，用于创建文字记录、识别说话者、总结讨论并生成额外记录。许多组织已实施控制措施，如阻止AI会议机器人、限制浏览器扩展、阻止软件安装或限制公司设备访问公共AI平台，但便携式AI录音设备可绕过这些控制。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! AI notetakers illustrate how artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing how people work. For example, there are now “AI Assistants” that snap onto the back of cell phones like a wireless battery pack. Instead of taking detailed notes during a meeting, preparing a summary, and identifying follow-up items, employees can use an AI notetaker to complete these tasks almost instantly. These tools can reduce administrative burdens, improve follow-up, and allow employees to focus on a conversation rather than on taking notes. An assistant, wrapped in a small, inconspicuous package. Until recently, many AI notetakers were relatively easy to identify. A virtual notetaker, for example, might appear as a participant in a videoconference, which gives the meeting organizer and other attendees an opportunity to approve its use or remove it from the meeting. Organizations could also restrict which applications employees installed on company devices or connected to company systems. But what if the AI notetaker does not appear on the meeting’s participant list? What if it is already sitting on the conference-room table, or in an employee’s pocket? Portable AI notetakers can record in-person conversations and telephone calls, store recordings while offline, and later synchronize the recordings to generate searchable transcripts, summaries, action items, and other AI-enabled content. Some are small enough to fit in a pocket or attach to a cell phone. As a result, an AI notetaker no longer needs to join a virtual meeting, operate on an organization’s network, or be installed on an organization-issued computer. An employee-controlled device may be able to record a conference-room discussion, interview, telephone call, or informal workplace conversation and later send that information to a third-party AI service without the organization’s knowledge. While portable AI notetakers may provide meaningful benefits, they can also expose organizations to significant privacy, security, employment, and litigation risks. Federal and state laws may restrict the recording of telephone calls and other communications. In most states, the consent of one party to the conversation is sufficient. Other states generally require the consent of all parties. The analysis can become particularly complicated when participants are located in different states or countries. Additionally, portable devices expand the settings where the issue may arise, including job interviews, customer calls, workplace investigations, accommodation meetings, and conversations involving patients or visitors. Even when participants consent to being recorded, that consent alone may not authorize the recording and associated information to be shared with a third-party AI vendor. Participants may not understand that the service will receive their voices and statements and use that information to create a transcript, identify speakers, summarize the discussion, and generate additional records. Many organizations have implemented controls to prevent employees from using unapproved AI tools on their systems. An organization might block AI meeting bots, restrict browser extensions, prevent software installations, or limit access to public AI platforms from company devices. Portable AI recorders can bypass these controls. An employee may be able to record a workplace conversation without installing software on an organization’s computer or connecting the recorder to its network, then upload the recording through a personal device or account. This is a practice known as “shadow AI”: technology used without organizational approval or oversight. The organization may not know which tools are being used, what information is collected, where it is sent, which third parties process it, or how long it is retained. Workplace conversations frequently include information that should not be disclosed outside the organization. A discussion may concern an employee’s medical condition, a workplace complaint, customer or patient data, business strategy, or trade secrets. A portable recorder may capture incidental information that would never appear in formal meeting notes, such as an employee discussing a family member’s health, a trip to a place of worship, or another personal matter unrelated to the purpose of the meeting.

news.titleEn: Are ChatGPT Records Subject to FOIA?
news.titleZh: ChatGPT记录是否受《信息自由法》约束？
news.summaryZh: 联邦机构日益使用ChatGPT等生成式AI，政府雇员的提示、回复和对话历史是否受《信息自由法》（FOIA）约束成为新的透明度问题。目前尚无联邦上诉法院判决直接处理该问题，但现有判例提供了可行框架。FOIA要求机构披露非豁免的“机构记录”。在司法部诉税务分析师案中，最高法院确立两部分测试：机构须创建或获取所请求材料，并在请求提出时控制该材料。分析不取决于信息载体是纸质备忘录、电子邮件、数据库、浏览器历史还是AI对话，法院关注机构能否使用或处置材料、人员是否依赖它、它是否融入机构文件。在Cause of Action Institute诉管理和预算办公室案中，哥伦比亚特区巡回法院裁定，政府计算机上自动生成的浏览器历史若未被机构使用、依赖或整合，且雇员基本控制其保留或删除，则不属于机构记录。ChatGPT对话可能不同：雇员若故意要求AI分析法规、总结评论、准备草案或比较政策选项并在官方工作中使用回复，可能支持机构记录地位。最强情形是机构管理或企业AI环境中的记录，机构可访问、使用或控制信息；若机构维护使用日志、设定保留规则或能检索、导出对话，则倾向于支持机构控制。一旦雇员将AI输出保存到机构驱动器、复制到邮件、分发给同事、附于报告或纳入机构决定，机构即已独立获取并保留信息。个人ChatGPT账户问题更复杂。在竞争企业研究所诉科技政策办公室案中，哥伦比亚特区巡回法院驳回了仅因工作相关邮件位于私人账户就超出FOIA的绝对论。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! As federal agencies increasingly use ChatGPT and other generative artificial intelligence tools, a new transparency question is emerging: Are government employees’ AI prompts, responses, and conversation histories subject to the Freedom of Information Act (“FOIA”)? There is not yet a reported federal appellate decision squarely addressing ChatGPT conversation histories under FOIA. Existing precedent, however, provides a workable framework. In many circumstances, AI records are likely to qualify as “agency records”—particularly when an agency creates or obtains the information and exercises control over it. FOIA generally requires federal agencies to disclose nonexempt “agency records.” In U.S. Department of Justice v. Tax Analysts, the Supreme Court established a two-part test: an agency must have either created or obtained the requested material, and it must control the material when the FOIA request is made.1 The analysis does not depend on whether the information appears in a paper memorandum, email, database, browser history, or AI conversation. Instead, courts look to factors such as whether the agency can use or dispose of the material, whether agency personnel relied upon it, and whether it became integrated into agency files.2 A useful analogy is Cause of Action Institute v. Office of Management and Budget, which involved automatically generated browser histories on government computers. The D.C. Circuit held that those histories were not agency records where the agencies did not use, rely upon, or integrate them into their records systems and employees largely controlled whether the histories were retained or deleted.3 ChatGPT conversations may present a different situation. An employee might deliberately ask an AI system to analyze a regulation, summarize comments, prepare a draft, or compare policy alternatives and then use the response in official work. Those facts could support agency-record status under the traditional control analysis. The strongest case involves records maintained in an agency-managed or enterprise AI environment where the agency has access to, uses, or controls the information. If an agency maintains usage logs, sets retention rules, or can retrieve or export conversations, those circumstances weigh in favor of agency control. The argument becomes even stronger once an employee saves an AI output to an agency drive, copies it into an email, circulates it to colleagues, attaches it to a report, or incorporates it into an agency decision. At that point, the agency has independently obtained and retained the information. Personal ChatGPT accounts present a closer question. In Competitive Enterprise Institute v. Office of Science and Technology Policy, the D.C. Circuit rejected the categorical argument that work-related emails were beyond FOIA simply because they were located in a private email account.4 Accordingly, the physical or digital location of a record is not by itself dispositive. Applied to AI, a personal ChatGPT conversation may still be subject to FOIA if it was used for agency business and is retained and retrievable for agency purposes. But where the agency never obtained, used, relied upon, or controlled the conversation, the case for agency-record status is weaker.

news.titleEn: INVITED PARTICIPANT OR THIRD-PARTY EAVESDROPPER?- Court Holds That Otter.ai Is A Third-Party Eavesdropper Because It Uses The Recordings For Its Own Benefit
news.titleZh: 受邀参与者还是第三方窃听者？法院裁定Otter.ai因将录音用于自身利益而构成第三方窃听者
news.summaryZh: 美国加州北区联邦地区法院在In Re Otter.AI Priv. Litig.案中部分批准、部分驳回Otter的驳回动议。法院认定，Otter的AI会议助手“Otter Notetaker”作为“沉默参与者”加入虚拟会议，实时录制并转录所有发言，且保留录音、转录文本和声纹，用于训练其自动语音识别和机器学习模型。因此，Otter独立收集、保留并将通信用于自身商业目的，构成《加州侵犯隐私法》第631条下的第三方窃听者，而非会议主持人的“受邀参与者”或录音工具。法院还认定，仅称通信“私密”或“敏感”而不提供具体事实细节，不足以根据第632条主张机密通信。七名来自加州、伊利诺伊州和华盛顿州的原告提出CIPA、ECPA、BIPA、不当得利和UCL等索赔。法院支持原告的Article III standing，并将本案与Popa v. Microsoft Corp.区分，认为录制与医疗和金融专业人士的私人通信内容不同于记录宠物用品网站上的鼠标移动等会话回放技术。CIPA、ECPA、BIPA、不当得利和UCL索赔全部存活；CFAA、CDAFA和华盛顿隐私法索赔以及除一名原告外的普通法隐私索赔被驳回。Otter不仅转录对话，还保留录音并用于训练自身模型，因此“扩展理论”不能使其免责。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Ever wondered how CIPA applies to the AI Notetakers that now show up uninvited in all the meetings on your calendar? In In Re Otter.AI Priv. Litig., No. 25-CV-06911-EKL, 2026 WL 2351237 (N.D. Cal. Aug.13,2026) United States District Court for the Northern District of California granted in part and denied in part Otter’s motion to dismiss. The CIPA, ECPA BIPA, unjust enrichment, the UCL claims survived in full. The CFAA, CDAFA, and the Washington Privacy Act claims were dismissed, as well as the common law privacy claims of every plaintiff except one. The Court holds that (1) Otter is a third-party eavesdropper under Section 631 because Otter independently collects, retains, and uses communications for its own commercial purposes and that (2) it is not enough to call your communication “private” or “sensitive” without giving additional factual detail regarding the substance of those communications to plausibly allege confidential communications under Section 632. The situation is familiar to anyone who has ever sat through a Zoom or Microsoft Teams call. Seven plaintiffs from California, Illinois, and Washington allege that Otter’s AI meeting assistant, the “Otter Notetaker,” joins virtual meetings as a “silent participant” and records and transcribes everything said in real time without the consent of all participants. The Plaintiffs allege that Otter then keeps the recordings, including transcripts and voiceprints, and uses that material to train its automatic speech recognition and machine-learning models. The conversations allegedly included communications with a doctor regarding “deeply personal and private medical information”, calls with financial professionals, sensitive business discussions, strategic planning sessions, confidential project meetings, performance reviews, discussions with clients and finally professional opportunities discussions. On Article III standing the Court distinguishes Popa v. Microsoft Corp., 153 F.4th 784 (9th Cir. 2025) on which Otter principally relies, saying that using sessionreplay technology to record a user’s interactions with a pet supply website, including information such as computer mouse movements, clicks, keystrokes, and pages visited is similar to “a store clerk’s observing shoppers”. Recording the content of the private communications with medical and financial professionals is completely different. The Court said the alleged conduct is closer to concrete injury alleged in Campbell where private Facebook messages were intercepted. So, Plaintiffs do have standing. Now CIPA claims: Otter’s main defense to the Section 631(a) claim was that the Notetaker is an “invited participant” and functions as the meeting host’s own recording tool, which would make it a party rather than an eavesdropper. That works under Graham v. Noom, Inc., 533 F. Supp. 3d 823 (N.D. Cal. 2021), where a software provider that acts only as an extension of its client is not a third-party interceptor, because a party to a communication may record it. However, Otter does not just participate in meetings, it retains the recordings of the conversations and uses them to improve its own machine-learning models and services. The Court held that Otter is a third-party eavesdropper who collects, retains and uses communications for its own commercial purposes. That is the main difference: Otter is not just a tool that transcribes the conversation and hands it back to the participants, but an independent party who uses the recordings to train its models for its own benefit. On Section 632 the Court held that Plaintiff Theus plausibly alleged confidential communication because he alleged a call with a medical professional involving “deeply personal medical information”. Plaintiffs Brewer and Ryan, by contrast, alleged only that their conversations were “private” or “sensitive,” saying nothing about the substance. Those labels were held “conclusory and insufficient”. For the same reason Brewer’s and Ryan’s intrusion upon seclusion and California constitutional privacy claims were dismissed. Washington plaintiff’s claims failed as well. As for pen register theory, the plaintiffs withdrew their Section 635 and Section 638.51 claims. On the ECPA claim, Otter unsuccessfully argued the party exception under 18 U.S.C. § 2511(2)(d). The Plaintiffs invoked the tortious purpose, alleging that Otter used their conversations to train its systems for its own pecuniary gain. Otter’s response was that its purpose was commercial. The Court said that “committing a tort and seeking a profit are not mutually exclusive.” Otter had no chance with BIPA. Voiceprints are biometric identifiers, and the plaintiffs alleged enough about Otter’s speaker tagging and speaker identification profiles to support an inference that the voiceprints can identify them. Otter’s reading of Zellmer v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 104 F.4th 1117 (9th Cir. 2024), was rejected as too broad. Because a Section 15(b) violation was plausibly alleged, standing followed for the Section 15(a). The extraterritoriality defense was rejected, since the plaintiffs alleged they were Illinois residents and they were physically located in Illinois when Otter collected their data during the meetings. Despite all, Otter had success with CFAA theories. The allegation that Otter accesses participants’ computers was conclusory under Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021), with no facts about how the Notetaker reaches any file, folder, or database. The Section 1030(a)(4) claim failed for want of a cognizable loss, since lost data value and emotional distress fall outside the statute’s narrow definition. See Andrews v. Sirius XM Radio Inc., 932 F.3d 1253 (9th Cir. 2019). The CDAFA claim went the same way under Cottle v. Plaid Inc., 536 F. Supp. 3d 461 (N.D. Cal. 2021). The important takeaway here is that the party status of an AI tool under Section 631 depends more on what the tool does with the recorded information. Companies using meeting assistants should ask their vendors only one question: does the vendor retain and reuse customer conversation content for model training? If the answer is yes, the “extension theory” will not save them. Big lesson for Plaintiffs is that vague pleading can cost you claims. Conclusory pleadings like “private” and “sensitive” are not enough to allege confidential communications.

news.titleEn: AI in Hiring- A Regulated Employment Practice, Not Just a Technology Purchase
news.titleZh: 招聘中的人工智能——受监管的雇佣实践，而非单纯的技术采购
news.summaryZh: 人工智能在雇主招聘流程中日益主流化，筛选简历、分析视频面试、预测候选人成功率及优化排班的工具已成为HR技术供应商的常见产品。但快速采用可能忽视相关法律框架。雇主应将AI招聘工具视为受监管的雇佣实践，而非单纯的技术采购，其带来诉讼风险。AI招聘工具易引发联邦和州反歧视法下的差别影响索赔，即使微小算法偏见也可能产生系统性不利影响。历史训练数据可能复制或放大先前歧视性招聘模式。Mobley诉Workday案和EEOC与iTutorGroup的和解表明，AI相关就业歧视索赔正被积极诉讼和执法。根据ADA，雇主仍需确保第三方AI工具不非法筛除残疾人，依赖供应商“ADA合规”保证不免除独立法律义务。许多AI工具是专有“黑箱”，决策逻辑透明度有限，但雇主而非供应商对歧视性结果负责。供应商保证不足，雇主需获取验证研究、不利影响分析和审计文档，并能解释招聘决定。联邦、州和地方各自独立监管AI招聘，要求零散且联邦统一指南不确定，雇主须监控自身使用并关注法律更新。使用或考虑AI招聘工具的雇主应考虑实际合规步骤。AI招聘工具的效率便利收益真实，法律暴露风险亦然。最安全使用结合可解释性、监督和文档。雇主通过理解工具运作、建立治理结构并将合规视为设计要求，可捕获效率收益并管理诉讼风险。将AI招聘视为采购决策而非受监管举措者，可能面临执法行动或集体索赔。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! What Employers Need to Know as Legal Requirements Try to Catch Up with Algorithmic Hiring Tools. Artificial intelligence is becoming more mainstream in employers’ hiring workflows. Tools that screen resumes, analyze video interviews, predict candidate success, and optimize scheduling are often standard offerings from HR technology vendors. But rapid adoption of these tools can overlook the legal frameworks governing them. Employers should approach AI-powered hiring tools not as just technology purchases but as regulated employment practices that carry litigation risks, including the following. Disparate Impact and Algorithmic Bias. AI hiring tools are susceptible to disparate impact claims under federal and state anti-discrimination laws. Even small algorithmic biases arising from biased training data, flawed model design, or so-called “proxy” variables like zip code, educational institution, or commute distance can produce selection ratios that may systematically disadvantage protected groups without any discriminatory intent on the part of the employer or tool developer. Historical data used to train the AI tool may replicate or amplify prior discriminatory hiring patterns, making bias a systemic rather than incidental risk. As we have previously written, cases like Mobley v. Workday and the EEOC’s settlement with iTutorGroup demonstrate that AI-related employment discrimination claims are actively being litigated and enforced. Disability Accommodation. Under the ADA, employers remain responsible for ensuring that third-party AI tools do not unlawfully screen out individuals with disabilities. When an AI assessment method disadvantages applicants with disabilities, employers may need to provide alternative assessment methods. Reliance on a vendor’s assurance that the tool is “ADA-compliant” does not relieve the employer of its independent legal obligations. Black-Box and Vendor Issues. Many AI hiring tools operate as proprietary “black boxes” with limited transparency into their decision-making logic. Yet employers, not vendors, bear responsibility when these tools produce discriminatory outcomes. Vendor assurances alone are insufficient; employers need access to validation studies, adverse impact analyses, and audit documentation. Ultimately, if a hiring decision is challenged, employers should be able to explain why they made it. Patchwork Federal, State, and Local Requirements. Federal, state, and local jurisdictions are each moving independently to regulate AI hiring, as we have previously written about. Given the patchwork of requirements and uncertainty regarding uniform federal guidelines, employers must both monitor their own usage of AI in hiring and stay apprised of updates to federal, state, and local laws and regulations. Practical Compliance Checklist for Employers. Employers using or contemplating AI hiring tools should consider the following steps: While the efficiency and convenience gains of AI hiring tools may be genuine, so are the legal exposure risks. The safest use of AI in hiring combines explainability, oversight, and documentation. Employers will be positioned to capture the efficiency benefits of AI while managing litigation risk by understanding how their tools work, building governance structures around them, and treating compliance as a design requirement for them. Those that treat AI hiring as a procurement decision rather than a regulated initiative may find themselves on the wrong end of an enforcement action or class claim. More Upcoming Events

news.titleEn: Claude’s Watermarks and their Legal Sector Impact
news.titleZh: Claude水印及其法律行业影响
news.summaryZh: Anthropic公司推出的Claude模型将采用一种新型水印技术，该技术通过在文本生成过程中嵌入隐蔽标记，使AI生成内容可被识别。根据欧盟《人工智能法案》要求，所有在欧盟运营的大语言模型提供商必须提供某种形式的标识，以告知用户和当局输出内容是否由AI生成。Anthropic作为OpenAI的竞争对手，已迅速明确其立场并保持高度透明。其水印机制并非传统意义上的可见水印，而是将信号伪装成页面上的正常词汇。大语言模型逐词生成文本，每次选择下一个词时，会从候选词列表中挑选最合理或最可能的选项。例如，在句子“今天天气寒冷且”中，下一个词不太可能是“甜的”，但很可能是“阴天”或“灰色”。在多数情况下，读者对模型选择哪个词并不敏感，句子含义基本相同，此时选择由随机数决定。水印技术利用这些低风险选择，在生成的文本中留下模式，该模式对读者不可见，但持有密钥的人可以检测。当启用水印时，选择仍是随机的，但随机源不同，使用密钥和前面的几个词来决定模型应选择的词。因此，Claude选择的词仍是随机的，但可以检查词序列是否与使用密钥时Claude的选择一致，从而判断文本是否由Claude生成。该方法基于Google DeepMind在2024年论文中提出的SynthID-Text方法。将很快提供水印检测API，目前正在制定实施细节。
news.bodyText: How will Claude’s watermarks work and how will they impact the legal world? Artificial Lawyer explores. Anthropic – and all other LLM makers operating within the EU – will have to provide some form of identification that tells a user and authorities whether an output is AI-generated. This is because of the EU AI Act. The rival to OpenAI has been both quick to set out its stall and has been very transparent. First, how they work. Essentially what Claude will do is insert certain words where there is a choice of options, in a way that it matches a key designed to reveal whether text is AI-manufactured or not. I.e. there is no actual ‘watermark’ as such, at least in the document, rather one could say the signal is ‘camouflaged’ as part of the normal words on the page. Claude gives a great explanation: ‘Large language models like Claude work by generating one word at a time. Each time the model decides on the next word, it chooses among a list of potential candidates, ultimately selecting the most sensible or likely based on the preceding text. ‘Take the sentence “The weather today was cold and…”. The next word is very unlikely to be “sugary.” But it is quite likely to be “overcast” or “grey.” ‘Under most circumstances, it doesn’t matter much to the reader which of these latter two words the model ultimately chooses, the meaning of the sentence is largely the same either way. In cases like this, the choice is settled by a random number…. ‘Watermarking uses low-stakes choices…., which occur many times over a piece of generated text, to leave a pattern in Claude’s responses. That pattern is undetectable to the reader, but is detectable to anyone who has a key that encodes it. ‘When watermarking is used, choices are still made at random, but the source of the randomness is different. Instead of using an arbitrary random number generator to pick the next word, watermarking uses the key and a few words that come before to settle what word the model should pick. ‘That is, the words that Claude picks are still random, but now, one can check the sequence of words and see if it’s consistent with the choices Claude would make if it was using the key. If it is, one can assign a probability that the text was generated by Claude.’ It truly is ingenious and builds upon the SynthID-Text approach published by Google DeepMind in a paper in 2024. They added that: They also noted that: ‘We will soon be offering a watermark detection API. We’re in the process of working out the details of its implementation.’

news.titleEn: Culture Still Eats AI For Breakfast – Workday Survey
news.titleZh: 文化仍比AI更“难吃”——Workday调查揭示法律AI落地困境
news.summaryZh: Workday对10个国家7000名律师及企业员工进行的一项大型调查显示，合同管理混乱问题依然普遍存在，仅有37%的企业内部律师认为“自己负责商业协议的签署后管理”。此外，超过半数受访者表示，他们仍然缺乏集中化的合同管理系统。调查表明，企业文化仍是阻碍法律AI充分发挥效益的主要因素。尽管这一结果可能令人意外，但Artificial Lawyer指出，十多年来类似统计数据屡见不鲜，说明尽管技术有所进步，核心的人类行为和企业文化并未发生太大变化。调查还显示，即便在律师群体中，也只有37%的人认为追踪合同是“自己的责任”，而企业其他员工中仅25%认为这是律师的工作。更令人担忧的是，26%的员工认为合同应由“最相关的”团队负责，这种模糊的归属感导致合同管理缺乏明确责任人。调查还发现，到2026年，情况依然令人惊讶。总体而言，当前面临的挑战与十年前相同，即使AI承诺带来巨大改进，合同仍“散落各处”，缺乏集中控制和监控，“所有权”似乎属于当天觉得最重要的人。法律AI若无法解决合同可见性和责任归属问题，便难以帮助企业全面掌握义务、加快流程或降低风险。
news.bodyText: A major survey by Workday of 7,000 lawyers and other enterprise staff across 10 countries has found that contract chaos persists, with only 37% of inhouse lawyers believing ‘they are responsible for post-signature management’ of business agreements. Moreover, over half of those surveyed said that they still lack a centralized contract system. In short, corporate culture is still dominant in preventing the full benefits of legal AI. While this may sound surprising, the reality is that Artificial Lawyer has been hearing statistics like this for over a decade – indicating that although the tech has improved, core human behaviours and enterprise culture has not changed that much. Moreover, despite the promise of legal AI tools, if most large companies are not even sure who is responsible for contract management, nor have moved to implement some form of cross-business contract system, then there is only a little that can be done to improve things. As the table below shows: Even among lawyers only 37% felt it was ‘their responsibility’ to track contracts, while for the rest of the staff in an enterprise only 25% thought it was the lawyers’ job. And that perhaps would not be a problem if at least someone did claim that role. However, the survey shows that 26% of staff felt contracts should belong to whichever team seemed to be ‘most relevant’. And then they also found that: And that amazingly in 2026: Plus they also found: In short, the overall challenge today is the same as it was 10 years ago, even if AI promises great improvements. Contracts are literally ‘all over the place’; there is little central control and monitoring; and ‘ownership’ seems to belong to whoever feels it matters most to them on the day. How is legal AI meant to make a dent in this? How can AI help a business to be on top of all of its obligations and help to speed things along, or reduce risk, if the contracts themselves are out of sight and out of mind, as it were, for many of the key people – and AI systems – that might be relevant?

news.titleEn: The real cost of building your own compliance
news.titleZh: 自建合规平台的真实成本
news.summaryZh: 多数律所并非有意自建合规平台，而是从通用AI工具、脚本和电子表格起步，直到人员离职、脚本失效才暴露问题。通用AI缺乏律所合规所需的数据模型，无法编码真实利益冲突、案件受理逻辑、客户义务及跨司法辖区规则，直接使用只会产生无审计轨迹、不可辩护的输出。将律所术语、义务和方法编码到通用代理中需从零开始数年，而Intapp已基于AmLaw 100中97家律所、二十年积累完成这一工作。自建还面临持续维护负担：客户指南变更、新AI模型发布、律师协会规则更新，均需内部人员更新、测试、验证并记录理由，形成永久开销。治理风险不体现在项目预算中：通用AI供应商无法回答如何尊重道德墙、避免幻觉、不暴露错误数据并生成可辩护的审计轨迹。通用AI保留文档内容却剥离元数据，而元数据正是合规态势所在——哪些合伙人被隔离、哪个交易团队掌握MNPI、哪些文档处于诉讼保留，剥离标签等于制造泄露。此外，通用AI将文档复制到律所保留规则和访问控制之外的新存储，可能面临取证请求却无保留计划。目前33%的律所已全所使用AI，高于2025年的17%，但76%的专业人员仍使用未经批准的工具，自建工具反而扩大这一差距。机会成本是决定性因素：Intapp Compliance with Celeste部署代理起草受理请求、构建冲突搜索策略、匹配公司树并摄取外部律师指南，吸收常规工作。律所每花一个季度自建，竞争对手就扩大一个季度差距，并损失自上线之日起累积的能力优势。
news.bodyHtml:
Most law firms don’t set out to build a compliance platform. It starts with a general-purpose AI tool pointed at conflicts, a script someone wrote to help with intake, a spreadsheet that tracks outside counsel guidelines. None of it feels like a platform decision. Until two years pass and a senior analyst leaves, the script breaks, and nobody is sure who owns fixing it.

General-purpose AI doesn’t know what a true conflict is

Conflicts clearance, matter intake, and client obligations management run on a data model that general-purpose AI doesn’t have. That model encodes what counts as a true conflict for your firm, why a matter was passed, which relationships carry institutional weight, and how your rules apply when a new matter touches three jurisdictions and a prior lateral hire. A general-purpose model has none of that context. Pointing it at your compliance data doesn’t give it the legal compliance model — it gives you confident-sounding output with no audit trail and nothing defensible underneath it. Encoding a firm’s vocabulary, obligations, and methods into a general agent is years of work from scratch. That work is already done.

Every change to regulations, client requirements, or AI models becomes your team’s problem

Assume the build goes well on day one. The maintenance problem starts immediately. Client guidelines change. New AI model versions ship. Bar rules update. Every one of those changes requires someone inside the firm to own the update, test the logic, validate the output, and document the rationale for when a regulator or client asks. That’s permanent overhead — staffed by people whose time is almost certainly better spent on higher-value work.

97 of the AmLaw 100 run on Intapp. That installed base represents two decades of exactly this work: building and maintaining the compliance data model, the legal-specific architecture, the workflow integrations. Firms choosing to build instead are spending time and engineering resources to get to where the category already is, while bearing the maintenance burden indefinitely after arrival.

The governance risk doesn’t show up in a project budget

Every firm leader eventually has the same conversation about a firm-wide compliance agent: “How do I know it will respect the ethical walls, not hallucinate, not surface the wrong data, and produce an audit trail I can defend to a court or a partnership vote?” General AI vendors can’t answer those questions, because the answers require an architecture the firm runs on — not a model with a wrapper around it.

General AI keeps the content of a document and strips the metadata around it. In a firm, the metadata is the compliance posture. Which partner is walled off? Which deal team has MNPI? Which documents are on litigation hold? Strip those tags and you haven’t built an assistant — you’ve built a breach. There’s also a second exposure in the same approach: to make a firm’s documents usable, general AI copies them into a new store outside the firm’s retention rules and access controls. A discovery request reaches it. A retention schedule does not. 33% of firms now use AI firmwide, up from 17% in 2025. In that environment, 76% of professionals still use AI tools their firm hasn’t sanctioned. A homegrown tool built on general AI doesn’t close that gap. It widens it in a different direction.

The opportunity cost is what closes the argument

Intapp Compliance with Celeste deploys agents that draft intake requests, construct conflicts search strategies, match corporate trees, and ingest outside counsel guidelines — absorbing the routine work that rising volume used to demand more people for. Every quarter a firm spends building is a quarter a competitor widens that gap.

The build decision doesn’t just cost time and engineering. It costs the compounding capacity advantage that starts the day a competitor goes live.

research.titleEn: Can LLMs Reason in a Legally Meaningful Manner? A Small-scale Study on European Court of Human Rights Cases
research.titleZh: LLM能否以具有法律意义的方式进行推理？一项关于欧洲人权法院案件的小规模研究
research.abstractEn: Reasoning has become a standard technique and feature for contemporary LLMs; however, its application and quality in the context of demanding legal-oriented tasks, such as legal case forecasting, remain under explored. We investigate how LLMs reason in the context of legal case forecasting, using legal cases from the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) as a testbed. We evaluate OpenAI GPT 5.4, a recent top-tier LLM, by exploring alternative prompting strategies that are more or less suggestive of what counts as legally meaningful reasoning in the context of ECtHR jurisprudence. We present our findings derived from assessing the model's responses with both human and LLM evaluation. We find that the examined model scores far from ideal in legal reasoning, the model produces structurally complete but substantively shallow analyses, and that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators are internally consistent yet align only weakly with our trained annotators, i.e., reliable but not a valid substitute for human evaluation. Overall, the expert-curated prompt leads to more comprehensive reasoning, which does not result in more accurate predictions compared to the other examined settings. Based on our findings, we urge the community not to rely solely on automated LLM-based evaluation and to avoid using task accuracy as an appropriate proxy for reasoning quality.
research.abstractZh: 推理已成为当代LLM的标准技术和特征；然而，在诸如法律案件预测等要求较高的法律导向任务中，其应用和质量仍未得到充分探索。我们以欧洲人权法院（ECtHR）的法律案件为测试平台，研究LLM在法律案件预测背景下的推理方式。我们评估了OpenAI GPT 5.4（一款最新的顶级LLM），通过探索在ECtHR判例背景下，哪些提示策略或多或少地暗示了具有法律意义的推理。我们通过人工和LLM评估来评估模型的响应，并展示了我们的发现。我们发现，所检查的模型在法律推理方面得分远非理想，模型产生的分析结构完整但实质浅薄，并且LLM作为评审者的评估在内部一致，但与我们的训练有素的标注者仅弱对齐，即可靠但并非人工评估的有效替代品。总体而言，专家策划的提示导致更全面的推理，但与其他检查设置相比，并未导致更准确的预测。基于我们的发现，我们敦促社区不要仅依赖基于LLM的自动化评估，并避免将任务准确性作为推理质量的适当代理。

news.titleEn: DOJ’s $3.2 Million Settlement With OpenAI and Statsig Signals Heightened Hiring-Discrimination Scrutiny
news.titleZh: 美国司法部与OpenAI及Statsig达成320万美元和解，释放加强招聘歧视审查的信号
news.summaryZh:
美国司法部民权司宣布与OpenAI OpCo LLC及Statsig Inc.达成320万美元和解，以解决有关两家公司歧视美国工人的指控。该和解不仅因涉及大型AI公司而引人注目，也凸显了政府在移民法、招聘与劳动力合规交叉领域持续关注雇佣实践。民权司在此类调查中通常审查雇主是否通过招聘渠道、职位广告、筛选标准或担保相关做法，非法偏向签证持有者或其他非美国工人，而非可用的合格美国工人。

对法律专业人士而言，此案具有实际意义。内部法律顾问与合规团队应重新审视人才招聘流程，尤其在移民担保常见或招聘高度集中之处。表面上中立的政策，若招聘人员、招聘经理或自动化工具系统性地不利于美国工人，仍可能产生风险。文件记录、审计轨迹与培训在监管机构调查时至关重要。对诉讼律师而言，该和解可能标志着执法优先事项，政府审查可引发后续风险，包括私人雇佣索赔、举报人活动、董事会治理关切及声誉影响。此案也凸显更广泛趋势：AI公司成熟过程中，正面临与其他大型雇主相同的监管压力，但受关注度更高，合规职能可能需扩展至产品与隐私之外，包括更严格审查招聘运营、移民相关雇佣决定及招聘中使用的分析或软件。

DOJ’s $3.2 Million Settlement With OpenAI and Statsig Signals Heightened Hiring-Discrimination Scrutiny

by Bruno Queiroz

The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division has announced a $3.2 million settlement with OpenAI OpCo LLC and Statsig Inc. over allegations that the companies discriminated against U.S. workers. The resolution is notable not only because it involves a major AI company, but also because it underscores the government’s continued focus on employment practices at the intersection of immigration law, recruiting, and workforce compliance.

While the public attention around AI companies often centers on data use, intellectual property, and product liability, this matter is a reminder that hiring practices remain a significant enforcement risk. Civil Rights Division investigations in this area typically examine whether employers unlawfully favor visa holders or other non-U.S. workers over available and qualified U.S. workers, including through recruiting pipelines, job advertising, screening criteria, or sponsorship-related practices. A multimillion-dollar settlement in that context sends a clear message: fast-growing technology companies are not insulated from traditional employment enforcement.

For legal professionals, the significance is practical as much as symbolic. In-house counsel and compliance teams should view this as a prompt to revisit talent-acquisition workflows, especially where immigration sponsorship is common or recruiting is highly centralized. Policies that appear neutral on paper can still create risk if recruiters, hiring managers, or automated tools systematically disadvantage U.S. workers. Documentation, audit trails, and training will matter if regulators come calling.

For litigators, the settlement may also be a useful marker of enforcement priorities. Government scrutiny of hiring discrimination can generate follow-on exposure, including private employment claims, whistleblower activity, board-level governance concerns, and reputational fallout. Even where a matter resolves without protracted litigation, the investigative burden alone can be substantial, particularly for companies scaling quickly and hiring across multiple jurisdictions.

The case also highlights a broader trend: as AI companies mature, they are increasingly encountering the same regulatory pressures as other large employers, but with added visibility. That means compliance functions at technology companies may need to expand beyond product and privacy issues to include more rigorous review of recruiting operations, immigration-related employment decisions, and the use of analytics or software in hiring.

Bottom line: this settlement is a high-profile warning that DOJ remains active in policing alleged discrimination against U.S. workers, and that headline-grabbing AI companies are squarely within that enforcement lens. For companies operating in competitive hiring markets, this is the kind of development that should move employment compliance higher up the legal risk agenda.

2026年8月14日，专利审判与上诉委员会（PTAB）收到新的IPR2026-00413请愿书，程序标题中列明Luxottica of America Inc.。对于关注眼镜、零售、消费品或品牌技术领域的专利从业者，此案值得关注。目前公开案卷仅确认程序名称、提交日期和PTAB案卷编号，被挑战的专利号、请愿人与专利权人的完整当事人关系，以及依据35 U.S.C. §§ 102和/或103主张的具体无效理由等关键细节，可能随请愿书及随附文件加入案卷而逐渐清晰。

此次提交本身意义重大。多方复审请愿常是专利执法或防御策略的关键时刻，尤其涉及知名商业主体时。若Luxottica或其关联实体被直接牵涉，法律顾问将关注被挑战权利要求是否涉及产品设计、零售系统、智能眼镜、镜片技术、电子商务工作流等商业重要类别，以及现有技术参考文献的身份和请愿书是否依赖印刷出版物、专利参考文献或两者组合。此程序可能提供实际启示：洞察当事人在消费者导向创新与品牌差异化交叉领域如何构建PTAB挑战；立案决定可能揭示委员会对权利要求解释立场和组合动机理论的看法；与同一专利族相关的平行地区法院诉讼或ITC活动可能使此IPR具有超出委员会的战略重要性。专利权人和请愿人均应监控案卷中的请愿书、强制通知、实际利益方披露及早期程序性动议，以评估禁反言风险、自由裁量驳回论点和更广泛的商业利益。

New PTAB Challenge Filed in IPR2026-00413 Involving Luxottica of America

by Bruno Queiroz

A new petition at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, IPR2026-00413 , was filed on August 14, 2026 , and names Luxottica of America Inc. in the proceeding caption. For patent practitioners tracking activity in the eyewear, retail, consumer products, or branded technology spaces, this is a matter worth watching as the record develops.

At this early stage, the publicly available docket information identifies the proceeding title, filing date, and PTAB docket number, but key details that practitioners will want—most notably the patent number being challenged , the full party alignment between petitioner and patent owner, and the specific invalidity grounds asserted under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and/or 103—will likely become clearer as the petition and accompanying papers are added to the docket.

That said, the filing itself is significant. An inter partes review petition is often a pivotal moment in a broader patent enforcement or defensive strategy, especially where a prominent commercial player is involved. If Luxottica or an affiliated entity is directly implicated, counsel will be watching for whether the challenged claims relate to product design, retail systems, smart eyewear, lens technology, e-commerce workflows, or another commercially important category. The identity of the prior art references—and whether the petition relies on printed publications, patent references, or a combination of both—will also shape how this case is evaluated by PTAB regulars.

For IP counsel, this proceeding may offer several practical takeaways. First, it could provide insight into how parties are framing PTAB challenges in sectors where consumer-facing innovation intersects with branding and product differentiation. Second, the institution decision, if issued, may reveal how the Board views the petition’s claim construction positions and motivation-to-combine theories. Third, any parallel district court litigation or ITC activity tied to the same patent family could make this IPR strategically important beyond the Board itself.

Patent owners and petitioners alike should monitor the docket for the petition, mandatory notices, real-party-in-interest disclosures, and any early procedural motions. Those filings typically supply the context needed to assess estoppel risk, discretionary-denial arguments, and the broader business stakes behind the challenge.

research.titleEn: Gated Against One Model, Open to the Next: Option-Only Solvability in Legal Multiple-Choice Benchmarks
research.titleZh: 对一种模型设防，对下一种模型敞开：法律多项选择基准中的仅选项可解性
research.abstractEn: Multiple-choice benchmarks are graded on whether a model picks the right option, not on whether it needed the question. Measuring that gap takes care: a model answering A to most items scores above chance wherever the key sits at A, and reads as recognition when it is not. We measure it on UA-JudgeExam: 11,990 four-option items with official keys, published by Ukraine's Higher Qualification Commission of Judges.   Shown the options and no question, Claude Haiku 4.5 scores 0.383 against chance, and the leak is concentrated: 11.8% of items are answered blind on all eight option orders, against 0.2 items expected by chance. It is not quotation: search over 280,059 editions of Ukrainian legislation recovers 0.128. Gating those out retains 8,128 items, on which the gating model itself now scores 0.204, and GPT-5.6, which took no part in the selection, still answers 0.515 of them with the question hidden. Scoring twelve held-out models on the whole set and subtracting each one's answer-position habit, only two keep an excess: GPT-5.6 at +0.265, Sonnet 4.6 at +0.081. Without it the ranking misleads: Llama 3.1 8B scores 0.292 blind, above every model but those two, purely by answering A to 92% of items.   The gate does select something real: on the items it rejected, eleven of twelve models score 0.518-0.789, every interval clear of what the same model scores on the items it kept. But that signal is one model's, and filtering on it does not transfer upward. Neither is visible on a 400-item sample, where nine models read as "statistically at chance". Rewriting distractors instead overshoots to 0.168, below chance and as exploitable. The same probe on LEXam returns chance: every option there points into the stem, none longer than 33 characters. Item format decides whether the problem can arise; capability decides how much is extracted. We release the corpus, the predictions and the harness.
research.abstractZh: 多项选择基准的评分依据是模型是否选择了正确的选项，而非其是否需要问题。衡量这一差距需要谨慎：一个对大多数题目回答A的模型，在正确答案位于A的情况下，其得分会高于随机水平，而当并非如此时，则会被视为识别。我们在UA-JudgeExam上对此进行了测量：该基准包含由乌克兰法官最高资格委员会发布的11,990道四选项题目，并附有官方答案。在仅显示选项而无问题的情况下，Claude Haiku 4.5的得分为0.383（随机水平之上），且泄漏集中：11.8%的题目在所有八种选项顺序下均被盲答，而随机预期仅为0.2题。这并非引用：对280,059个乌克兰立法版本进行搜索，仅恢复0.128。将这些题目排除后，保留8,128题，此时筛选模型本身的得分为0.204，而GPT-5.6（未参与筛选）在隐藏问题的情况下仍能答对其中0.515的题目。对十二个保留模型在整个集合上进行评分，并减去每个模型的答案位置习惯后，仅有两个模型保持超额：GPT-5.6为+0.265，Sonnet 4.6为+0.081。若无此调整，排名将产生误导：Llama 3.1 8B的盲测得分为0.292，高于除这两个模型外的所有模型，这纯粹是因为它对92%的题目回答了A。该筛选确实选择了某种真实的东西：在被其拒绝的题目上，十二个模型中有十一个的得分在0.518至0.789之间，每个区间都明显高于同一模型在保留题目上的得分。但该信号仅属于一个模型，基于此进行筛选并不能向上迁移。在400题的样本上，两者均不可见，其中九个模型被统计为“处于随机水平”。改写干扰项反而过度，达到0.168，低于随机水平且同样可利用。同样的探针在LEXam上返回随机水平：那里的每个选项都指向题干，且长度均不超过33个字符。题目格式决定了问题是否可能出现；能力决定了能提取多少。我们发布了语料库、预测结果和测试工具。

research.titleEn: Time as Structure: Temporal Dependency Graphs for Verifiable Deadline Computation over Legal Documents
research.titleZh: 时间即结构：用于法律文件可验证截止日期计算的时间依赖图
research.abstractEn: Miss a filing deadline by one day and the claim is barred, however strong the case. Computing that deadline is rarely simple: the period runs from a triggering event, is counted by a statutory convention, and may be suspended by a mandatory conciliation window. We ask whether a language model should answer such questions directly, or read the document and leave the arithmetic to code. We extract dated facts and their dependencies into a temporal dependency graph and compute deadlines from it with a calendar-correct engine. On UK Employment Appeal Tribunal judgments the engine reproduces six of seven timeliness rulings, and matches the judges' own dates to the day. The strongest of four language models, asked the same cases, gets the arithmetic right and the answer wrong: in six of twenty-one responses its stated verdict contradicts its own thinking, and every contradiction runs the same way, calling a late claim timely. To test the systems at scale we move the dismissal date across the statutory boundary, generating 427 cases whose answers are computed rather than annotated. On the cases both systems answer, the pipeline is right 90.2% of the time against 61.2% for direct answering. The limit is extraction: on contracts the errors are almost never in the arithmetic, but in choosing which event the period starts from.
research.abstractZh: 错过提交截止日期一天，无论案件多么有力，索赔即被禁止。计算该截止日期通常并不简单：期限从触发事件开始计算，按法定惯例计数，并可能因强制调解窗口而中止。我们探讨语言模型是否应直接回答此类问题，还是阅读文件并将计算留给代码。我们将带日期的事实及其依赖关系提取到时间依赖图中，并使用日历正确的引擎从中计算截止日期。在英国就业上诉法庭的判决中，该引擎再现了七项时效裁定中的六项，并与法官自己的日期精确到日。四个语言模型中最强的一个，在回答相同案件时，算术正确但答案错误：在二十一个回答中，有六个其陈述的裁决与其自身推理相矛盾，且每个矛盾都以相同方式出现，即将迟交的索赔称为及时。为了大规模测试系统，我们将解雇日期移至法定边界，生成427个案例，其答案由计算而非注释得出。在两个系统都回答的案例中，流水线在90.2%的情况下正确，而直接回答为61.2%。限制在于提取：在合同上，错误几乎不在算术，而在于选择期限从哪个事件开始。

news.titleEn: DoorDash AI inquiry turns model selection into a governance test
news.titleZh: DoorDash 的 AI 调查将模型选择变成治理考验
news.summaryZh:
美国众议院两个委员会要求 DoorDash 在今日之前提供七类记录，涉及中国人工智能。要求涵盖自 2025 年 1 月 1 日起，DoorDash 或其子公司评估或使用的、来自中国或受中国控制开发者的所有模型，包括开发、测试、预发布或生产环节，并延伸至基准测试、安全测试、风险评估、成本、AI 治理政策，以及公司对 Moonshot AI 蒸馏指控所知情况的时间线。该信函并非传票，本身不强制提交文件或出席。

值得法律与合规团队关注的细节是简报人员名单：主席要求 AI 基础设施、软件安全、模型评估、采购以及法律或合规审查负责人参与，这是本次调查中首次点名具体职能。调查源于 7 月 6 日 DoorDash 联合创始人兼首席技术官 Andy Fang 在 X 上的发帖，称公司 AI 代码审查器将较低级工作交给北京 Moonshot AI 的开源权重模型 Kimi K2.6，将更难任务交给美国前沿模型 Anthropic 的 Fable，内部基准测试显示这种分工质量更好、成本更低且不降低代码质量。25 天后，众议院中国问题特别委员会和国土安全委员会主席致函 DoorDash 联合创始人兼首席执行官 Tony Xu，要求 8 月 14 日前提交文件、8 月 21 日进行当面简报。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: Congressional scrutiny of Chinese AI models has found its operating rhythm, and it runs through the records a company keeps about its own engineering choices. Two House committees asked DoorDash for seven categories of documents by today, starting with every model from a PRC-based or PRC-controlled developer the company has evaluated or used since Jan. 1, 2025, in development, testing, staging or production, and running through its benchmarking, its security testing, its risk assessments, its costs, its AI governance policies and a timeline of what it knew about the distillation allegations against Moonshot AI. The letter is not a subpoena and does not itself compel production or attendance. The detail worth the attention of legal and compliance teams is the briefing roster: the chairmen asked for personnel responsible for AI infrastructure, software security, model evaluation, procurement, and legal or compliance review, the first time in this investigation that any function has been named.

Watch whether the Aug. 21 briefing happens on schedule. The nearer question is what your own answer would look like if the same seven categories arrived tomorrow.

Industry News – Artificial Intelligence Beat

DoorDash AI inquiry turns model selection into a governance test

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

Today is the requested deadline for DoorDash to provide two House committees with seven categories of records concerning Chinese artificial intelligence.

That request begins with every model from a PRC-based or PRC-controlled developer that DoorDash or a subsidiary has evaluated or used since Jan. 1, 2025, in development, testing, staging or production.

The DoorDash inquiry followed a July 6 post, though the investigation it belongs to had been underway since April. That day, Andy Fang, DoorDash’s co-founder and chief technology officer, wrote on X that the company’s AI code reviewer sends lower-level work to Kimi K2.6, an open-weight model from Beijing-based Moonshot AI, and routes more difficult tasks to an American frontier model, Anthropic’s Fable. Internal benchmarking, Fang wrote, showed the split delivered better quality at lower cost without degrading code quality.

Twenty-five days later, the chairmen of the House Select Committee on China and the House Homeland Security Committee sent a joint letter to DoorDash co-founder and Chief Executive Tony Xu. Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan and Rep. Andrew Garbarino of New York, both Republicans, asked for the documents by Aug. 14 and an in-person briefing by Aug. 21. The select committee’s announcement leaned into the company’s line of business, closing its headline with the words “A Recipe for Risk.”

news.summaryZh: 在纳什维尔ILTACON倒计时之际，DeepJudge、DISCO、Spellbook及工作场所技术提供商Korbyt本周发布一系列公告。瑞士法律AI公司DeepJudge推出Agent Handoff Protocol（AHP），该开放协议旨在让用户在不同AI平台间切换时不丢失工作上下文。MCP等协议虽能实现系统间信息交换，但律师切换AI工具时常丢失宝贵上下文，被迫重建提示、重新上传文档并重新分析。新协议不仅传输信息，还传输目标、对话历史和支持材料。Harvey是首批实施该协议的供应商之一，测试版集成将于本月推出，Thomson Reuters也宣布支持。这反映出法律技术市场日益普遍的观点：没有单一AI平台能主导法律工作的所有方面，需要专业系统间更强的互操作性。诉讼技术提供商DISCO全面推出新的Advanced Research能力。该代理式AI工具通过多步推理处理复杂事实调查和证据分析，自动审查自身发现、识别缺口并启动额外搜索以优化结果。DISCO称该工具可帮助诉讼团队从大量证据集中快速生成时间线、调查备忘录和证言提纲。早期用户报告显著生产力提升，早期访问计划期间客户参与度增加一倍以上。这标志着eDiscovery提供商正从传统文档搜索转向日益自主的调查工作流。Spellbook在其Associate平台内推出AI文档编辑器，将Word体验引入Associate，允许律师在不切换应用的情况下审阅、修改和定稿文档。供应商称用户可指示Spellbook从一个地方对多个相关文档进行数百处更改，然后手动审阅和优化结果。Korbyt表示将AI引入其工作场所和会议室管理平台。
news.bodyHtml:
A series of announcements this week from DeepJudge, DISCO, Spellbook and workplace technology provider Korbyt is worth noting as things start to heat up in the countdown to ILTACON in Nashville.

Perhaps the most strategically significant announcement comes from Swiss legal AI company DeepJudge, which has introduced the Agent Handoff Protocol (AHP), an open protocol designed to allow users to move between AI platforms without losing the context of their work. While protocols such as MCP enable systems to exchange information, DeepJudge says lawyers frequently lose valuable context when switching between AI tools, forcing them to rebuild prompts, re-upload documents and recreate analysis.

Advertisement

The new protocol aims to solve that problem by enabling AI systems to transfer not only information but also objectives, conversation history and supporting materials. DeepJudge says Harvey is among the first vendors to implement the protocol, with a beta integration launching this month, while Thomson Reuters has also announced support. The move reflects an increasingly common view in the legal technology market that no single AI platform will dominate every aspect of legal work, requiring greater interoperability between specialist systems.

Elsewhere, litigation technology provider DISCO has made its new Advanced Research capability generally available. The agentic AI tool is designed to tackle complex fact investigations and evidence analysis through multi-step reasoning, automatically reviewing its own findings, identifying gaps and launching additional searches to refine results.

Advertisement

DISCO says the tool can help litigation teams rapidly develop timelines, investigation memos and deposition outlines from large evidence collections. Early users report significant productivity gains, with customer engagement more than doubling during the early access programme. The launch is another example of eDiscovery providers moving beyond traditional document search towards increasingly autonomous investigative workflows.

Also this week, Spellbook launched an AI document editor within its Associate platform. The new functionality brings the Word experience into Associate, allowing lawyers to review, amend and finalise documents without switching between applications. The vendor says users can instruct Spellbook to make hundreds of changes across multiple related documents from one place, before manually reviewing and refining the results.

Last but not least, Korbyt this week said it is bringing AI to its workplace and meeting room management platform. Ahead of ILTACON, the company unveiled new booking capabilities including ConciergeAI, a natural language assistant that enables lawyers and staff to reserve desks and meeting rooms through Microsoft Teams, Outlook or the Korbyt platform. Korbyt says the system automatically applies firm booking rules and availability constraints before presenting options, with the goal of reducing administrative friction and helping firms better utilise office space.
