news.titleEn: Powerful Tool, but Not an Attorney: Massachusetts Court Rejects Work Product Protection for AI-Generated Documents
news.titleZh: 强大工具但非律师：马萨诸塞州法院拒绝为AI生成文件提供工作成果保护
news.summaryZh: 马萨诸塞州高等法院商业诉讼庭在首例裁决中认定，AI工具生成的材料不受工作成果原则保护，除非为律师或应律师指示而准备。在Shealy诉Seaside Investments案中，法院指出向非律师（包括AI工具）披露的信息可能面临开示风险。该案源于2025年1月购买协议和本票引发的商业投资纠纷。2025年5月，Earl Wade Shealy, Jr.收到Seaside关于潜在违约的函件后，将函件及交易文件发给恋爱对象Debbi Fields，让其用ChatGPT分析并准备回复。Fields上传文件及提示词，并将AI输出发回Shealy。尽管Shealy在交易中有律师代理，但二人均未咨询律师。诉讼后，Shealy提交经编辑的通信并主张工作成果保护。法院驳回，理由为：Fields和ChatGPT均不符合工作成果原则中“代表”的定义，马萨诸塞州不承认恋爱对象为“代表”，ChatGPT工具本身也不是Shealy的“代表”。法院区分了Morgan诉V2X和Warner诉Gilbarco等联邦案例，这些案例将保护扩展至无律师代理当事人使用AI生成的输出和提示词，因其反映当事人思维印象；但Shealy有律师代理且未按律师指示行事，故不适用。法院强调AI是工具而非人，ChatGPT生成内容不披露律师或其他代表的思维印象、结论、意见或法律理论，因此不能获得意见工作成果的高度保护。法院还类比2026年2月United States诉Heppner案，该案中受律师代理的刑事被告自行使用AI工具，不受特权或工作成果保护。裁决表明，实体和个人不能将AI查询外包给非律师并期望结果免于开示；要使AI工具使用受保护，必须由律师指示，否则AI输出及提示词可能成为开示对象。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! In a decision of first impression in Massachusetts, a judge in the Business Litigation Session of the Superior Court ruled that material generated by an artificial intelligence tool, or “AI output,” is not protected under the work product doctrine unless performed for or at the direction of counsel. Shealy v. Seaside Investments, LLC, serves as a cautionary example of courts analyzing AI-generated materials through the lens of established attorney-client privilege and work product frameworks and deciding that information disclosed to a non-attorney, including an AI-powered tool, potentially exposes those materials to discovery. The underlying dispute in Shealy v. Seaside Investments, LLC developed from a commercial investment relationship between sophisticated partners who executed a purchase agreement and promissory note in January 2025. After receiving correspondence from Seaside in May 2025 concerning a potential default under the promissory note, Earl Wade Shealy, Jr. sent Seaside’s correspondence and related transaction documents to his romantic partner, Debbi Fields, to have ChatGPT analyze and prepare a response letter. Fields then uploaded the documents to ChatGPT along with instructions or “prompts” and sent the AI-generated output back to Shealy. Notably, neither Shealy nor Fields consulted with an attorney during this process even though Shealy was represented by counsel in the transaction at issue. When the dispute escalated to litigation, Shealy produced redacted correspondence between himself and Fields, claiming that the correspondence and resulting AI output was protected as work product. Work product protection shields from discovery the mental impressions, conclusions, and legal theories that an attorney or representative prepares in anticipation of litigation. In ruling on Seaside’s motion to compel unredacted communications, the court rejected Shealy’s contention that the AI-generated materials were protected by the work product doctrine on multiple grounds. First, the court determined that neither Fields nor Chat-GPT qualified as a “representative” within the meaning of the work product doctrine, which protects materials prepared by or for certain representatives, including attorneys, consultants, agents, and insurers. Massachusetts does not recognize romantic partners as “representatives” for purposes of work product protection, and the trial court declined to extend the doctrine to include them in this instance, ultimately concluding that exchanges between Shealy and Fields were subject to disclosure. The court further determined that the ChatGPT tool itself was not Shealy’s “representative” for purposes of extending the work product protections to the AI output. In reaching this conclusion, the court distinguished recently-decided cases around the U.S. where certain courts have held that material prepared by ChatGPT and similar AI programs was protected as work product. For example, in Morgan v. V2X, Inc. and Warner v. Gilbarco, Inc., federal courts in Colorado and Michigan extended the work product doctrine to shield AI-generated output and prompts utilized by pro se litigants as such material reflected the mental impressions, opinions, and theories of the pro se litigants acting in the role of counsel. The Morgan court specifically noted the policy interest of leveling the playing field between represented and unrepresented parties. However, in Shealy, the Court found those cases inapposite because Shealy was represented by counsel at the time he and Fields utilized ChatGPT to generate the output, and acted without counsel’s direction. Shealy decided entirely on his own initiative to use AI through a non-attorney third party, without consulting counsel about how the tool would be used. The court further emphasized a critical consideration underlying its analysis, and stated: “[n]or does the output from ChatGPT constitute opinion work product. AI is a tool not a person. Nothing about what ChatGPT produces discloses the ‘mental impressions, conclusions, opinions, or legal theories of an attorney or other representative of a party concerning the litigation.’” (emphasis added). Absent attorney direction or input, the AI-generated output did not reflect an attorney’s or qualified representative’s strategic thinking or mental impressions. Consequently, the output cannot qualify for the heightened protection afforded to opinion work product. The Massachusetts trial court analogized the case to the February 2026 decision in United States v. Heppner, where a represented criminal defendant’s independent use of an AI tool without counsel’s direction fell outside the scope of privilege or work product protection and was subject to disclosure to the opposing party. The decision in Shealy v. Seaside Investments provides important guidance as AI tools become increasingly prevalent across commercial operations and decision-making, including those related to litigation. Entities and individuals, including those represented by counsel, cannot simply outsource AI queries to non-attorneys and expect the results to be shielded from discovery. For AI tool use to receive protection, counsel must direct it; otherwise, the AI output and the prompts used to generate it may be fair game for discovery. This ruling reflects a growing trend in which courts apply traditional privilege doctrines to AI-generated materials without modification, holding that the technology itself does not warrant departing from established frameworks. The takeaway is clear: once litigation becomes anticipated, involving counsel in any analytical work, AI-assisted or otherwise, is essential to shield a party’s mental impressions, theories, and strategies from discovery.

research.titleEn: How Much Do Legal RAG Systems Still Hallucinate?
research.titleZh: 法律RAG系统仍然会产生多少幻觉？
research.abstractEn: Hallucination is a major challenge for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in the legal domain, where ungrounded answers can lead to serious consequences. To better understand this problem, we conduct a fine-grained analysis of hallucination behavior in eight legal RAG systems across two legal corpora, the GDPR (in English) and a national civil law (in French). Using claim-level and answer-level evaluation, we report on hallucination density and severity, analyze performance across question categories and user personas, and validate our findings on an independent set of 142 legal-expert-authored questions. Our results show that hallucinations remain pervasive, ranging from less than 10% of responses for the best-performing systems to nearly half in the worst case. We further find that false-premise questions, containing incorrect assumptions that must be rejected, produce high hallucination rates on the manually-drafted questions.
research.abstractZh: 幻觉是法律领域检索增强生成（RAG）系统面临的主要挑战，因为无根据的答案可能导致严重后果。为了更好地理解这一问题，我们对两个法律语料库（英文的GDPR和法文的国家民法）中的八个法律RAG系统进行了细粒度的幻觉行为分析。通过声明级和答案级评估，我们报告了幻觉密度和严重程度，分析了不同问题类别和用户角色的表现，并在142个由法律专家撰写的问题的独立集上验证了我们的发现。结果表明，幻觉仍然普遍存在，从表现最好的系统中不到10%的回答到最差情况下近一半的回答。我们进一步发现，包含必须拒绝的错误假设的虚假前提问题，在手工起草的问题上产生了较高的幻觉率。

news.titleEn: CosmoLex Launches AI Intake, a Breakthrough Feature That Automates Client Onboarding for Law Firms From First Click to First Consultation
news.titleZh: CosmoLex推出AI Intake突破性功能，实现律所从首次点击到首次咨询的客户引导自动化
news.summaryZh:
CosmoLex于2026年8月13日宣布推出以AI Intake为首的一系列AI功能。AI Intake利用人工智能即时生成定制引导表单，并将现有PDF和Word旧表单转换为可提交的数字化在线表单。表单提交后，CosmoLex自动将数据映射至正确的联系人和潜在客户记录，消除手动重新录入并降低错误风险。提交后自动化工作流随即触发，自动处理文件交付、咨询预约和后续沟通，使新客户提交表单后关键的24小时无需人工分诊。该功能解决每家律所都熟知的问题，即新线索进入后24小时内的混乱，通过自动生成正确表单、首次即正确映射数据并在提交时启动跟进，律所可将引导流程转变为优势。

该发布还包含更广泛的AI功能：AI引导表单构建器允许律所提供描述所需信息、格式、分区和必填字段的书面提示，AI完成约95%的工作，生成可审查、调整和发布的表单，无需CosmoLex更强大的CRM附加组件；文档摘要内置于原生文档存储中，可快速了解文档内容、呈现关键数据点并生成要点大纲；AI驱动的自然语言过滤允许用户直接输入自然语言查找所需内容。上述功能自2026年8月13日起向CosmoLex客户提供。CosmoLex是面向北美中小型律所的端到端法律实践管理解决方案，隶属于ProfitSolv。
news.bodyHtml:
New suite of AI-powered capabilities, including AI Intake, document summarization, and natural-language search, eliminates manual data entry and gives firms back the first 24 hours of every new client relationship

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. —Aug 13, 2026 — CosmoLex, a leading cloud-based legal practice management platform, today announced a new set of AI-powered features headlined by AI Intake, a transformational capability that captures clean client data and automatically moves every intake forward without anyone touching it. 

Client intake is the first, and often most costly bottleneck in a law firm’s client relationship. Manually built forms, re-keyed data, and disconnected follow-up processes routinely delay a firm’s response to new leads and create the risk of losing prospective clients in the shuffle. CosmoLex’s AI Intake is designed to remove that friction entirely, turning what has historically been a time-consuming, error-prone manual process into a seamless, connected experience, all within a single platform and without the need for a separate, third-party intake tool.

AI Intake: The Premiere Feature of the Release

At the center of the launch is AI Intake, which uses artificial intelligence to instantly generate custom intake forms and convert existing legacy PDF and Word forms into digitally intuitive online forms that users can submit. Once a form is submitted, CosmoLex automatically maps the data to the correct contact and lead records, eliminating the need for manual re-keying and reducing the risk of costly errors.

From there, CosmoLex’s automated post-submission workflows take over. Triggered the moment a form is submitted, the platform can automatically handle document delivery, consultation booking, and follow-up communications, often the critical first 24 hours after a prospective client submits an intake form runs without anyone needing to manually triage it.

“AI Intake is the feature we’re most excited to bring to market, because it solves a problem every single law firm knows intimately: the chaos of the first 24 hours after a new lead comes in,” said Kelley Castell, CEO at CosmoLex. “By automatically generating the right forms, mapping the data correctly the first time, and kicking off follow-up the moment a form is submitted, firms can finally treat intake as a strength rather than a source of lost time and lost clients.”

A Full Suite of AI-Powered Capabilities

AI Intake is joined by a broader set of AI features designed to reduce administrative work across the firm, including:

AI Intake Form Builder — Building the right intake form for each case type has traditionally been an overwhelming task, even though the right questions are critical to reducing back-and-forth and administrative follow-up. With CosmoLex’s new AI builder, firms can simply provide a written prompt describing the information they want to collect, along with formatting, sections, and required fields. The AI form builder does approximately 95% of the work, generating a ready-to-use form that firms can review, adjust, and publish — all without requiring CosmoLex’s more robust CRM add-on.

Document Summarization — Built directly into CosmoLex’s native document storage, this feature allows users to quickly understand what a document is about, surface key data points, and generate a bulleted outline — a highlight reel for even the longest documents. For document-heavy firms, this capability can eliminate hours of administrative review time.

AI-Powered Natural-Language Filtering — Rather than manually scouring through filters to find what they need, users can simply type in natural language what they’re looking for and let CosmoLex’s AI do the work of surfacing the right results.

“Firms already come to CosmoLex because they want one login and one connected view of their matters, billing, and accounting,” added Kelley Castell. “These AI features extend that same philosophy to the front end of the client relationship and to the everyday administrative work inside the platform, so firms spend less time on data entry and searching, and more time practicing law.”

Availability

AI Intake, the AI Intake Form Builder, Document Summarization, and AI-powered natural-language filtering will be available to CosmoLex customers beginning August 13, 2026. 

About CosmoLex

CosmoLex is a leading end-to-end legal practice management solution trusted by thousands of small to mid-sized law firms across North America. CosmoLex connects intake, calendaring and tasks, document management, billing, trust accounting, and firm accounting in one modern, compliant platform, giving firms a single login and a complete view of their matter and firm data, and reducing the need for additional tools and integrations. CosmoLex is part of ProfitSolv, a collection of best-in-class software solutions for professional services firms. For more information, visit www.cosmolex.com.

Media Contact

Karen Dixon/CMO

Email: PR@ProfitSolv.com

With CosmoLex’s new AI builder, firms can simply provide a written prompt describing the information they want to collect, along with formatting, sections, and required fields. The AI form builder does approximately 95% of the work, generating a ready-to-use form that firms can review, adjust, and publish — all without requiring CosmoLex’s more robust CRM add-on.

Document Summarization — Built directly into CosmoLex’s native document storage, this feature allows users to quickly understand what a document is about, surface key data points, and generate a bulleted outline — a highlight reel for even the longest documents. For document-heavy firms, this capability can eliminate hours of administrative review time.

AI-Powered Natural-Language Filtering — Rather than manually scouring through filters to find what they need, users can simply type in natural language what they’re looking for and let CosmoLex’s AI do the work of surfacing the right results.

“Firms already come to CosmoLex because they want one login and one connected view of their matters, billing, and accounting,” added Kelley Castell. “These AI features extend that same philosophy to the front end of the client relationship and to the everyday administrative work inside the platform, so firms spend less time on data entry and searching, and more time practicing law.”

AI Intake, the AI Intake Form Builder, Document Summarization, and AI-powered natural-language filtering will be available to CosmoLex customers beginning August 13, 2026.

CosmoLex is a leading end-to-end legal practice management solution trusted by thousands of small to mid-sized law firms across North America. CosmoLex connects intake, calendaring and tasks, document management, billing, trust accounting, and firm accounting in one modern, compliant platform, giving firms a single login and a complete view of their matter and firm data, and reducing the need for additional tools and integrations. CosmoLex is part of ProfitSolv, a collection of best-in-class software solutions for professional services firms. For more information, visit www.cosmolex.com .

news.titleEn: amicable applies to SRA to launch “tech-forward” law firm
news.titleZh: amicable向SRA申请成立“技术驱动型”律师事务所
news.summaryZh: 获奖离婚与分居服务提供商amicable已向律师监管局（SRA）提交申请，计划成立一家新的独立律师事务所，服务英格兰和威尔士。该所将独立接受监管，从而能够提供amicable作为未受监管企业所无法提供的法律服务和代理。amicable同时启动招聘，寻找协助创建该所的律师。创建amicable是因为相信应有更友善的离婚方式，但共同协作并非适用于所有情况，此前无法直接帮助这些人；新所正是为他们而设，将基于相同价值观以及让服务更优的技术与创新，并寻找认同这一愿景、希望从第一天起参与塑造律所的家事和产权转让律师。十多年来，amicable已帮助数千对夫妇以合作而非对立方式分手。新所将服务amicable目前无法直接帮助的人群，并承接amicable现有客户已需要的受监管律所工作。除家事法业务外，新所还将为分居或离婚后需转移财产的人提供产权转让服务，专注于分离夫妇将家庭住房转入一方名下的权益转移及相关再抵押，规模小而聚焦。有意加入创始团队的律师可发送邮件至alex.woolley@amicable.co.uk了解详情。
news.bodyHtml:
amicable, the award-winning divorce and separation service, has submitted its application to the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) to launch a new, separate law firm serving England and Wales. Alongside that, it’s opening the search for the solicitors who will help build it.

The new firm will be regulated in its own right, allowing it to offer legal services and representation that amicable itself, as an unregulated business, does not provide.

Advertisement

Pip Wilson, CEO of amicable, said: ‘We started amicable because we believed there had to be a kinder way to divorce. But working with couples together isn’t always possible for every situation, and until now we haven’t been able to help those people ourselves. The new firm is for them. It will be built on the same values, and on the technology and innovation that let us do things in a better way. We’re looking for family and conveyancing solicitors who share that ambition and want to help shape the firm from day one.’

For more than a decade, amicable has helped thousands of couples separate together rather than on opposing sides. The new firm will work with the people that amicable can’t currently help directly, as well as carrying out some of the work amicable’s own customers already need from a regulated firm.

Advertisement

Alongside the family law work, the new firm will provide conveyancing services for people who need to transfer property following separation or divorce. It will be a small, focused service covering transfers of equity and related remortgages, when a separating couple moves the family home into one name.

Solicitors interested in joining the founding team can find out more by emailing alex.woolley@amicable.co.uk .

news.titleEn: DeepJudge Releases an Open Protocol for Passing Users – and Their Context – Between AI Products, with Harvey and Thomson Reuters On Board
news.titleZh: DeepJudge发布开放协议，实现用户及其工作上下文在AI产品间无缝传递，Harvey与汤森路透已加入支持
news.summaryZh: 总部位于苏黎世的企业搜索公司DeepJudge近日推出“Agent Handoff Protocol”（AHP）开放协议，旨在让用户能够在不同AI产品之间切换时保留完整的工作上下文。Harvey已宣布正在构建集成该协议的方案，并计划于本月进入测试阶段；汤森路透则表示将在其法律产品CoCounsel for Legal中支持该协议，但具体实施细节和时间尚未公布。DeepJudge开发AHP是为了解决用户在不同AI产品间切换时需重建上下文的问题。现有协议如Anthropic开发的Model Context Protocol（MCP）虽能实现系统间信息交换和操作执行，但无法将工作目标、支持材料、对话历史及已完成的分析等更广泛的上下文随用户迁移。AHP则允许AI平台将用户及其继续工作所需的上下文从一个系统传递至另一个系统。律师在DeepJudge中研究先例问题后，可直接带着相关上下文进入Harvey，无需重新上传材料或重建分析。该协议的技术文档已发布在agenthandoffprotocol.org，用户操作仅需点击一个按钮。协议规定传递的上下文内容由实施方自行决定，例如Harvey可能传递对话历史，而DeepJudge作为搜索引擎更可能传递用户找到的文档。AHP基于MCP构建，并非替代MCP，而是提供不同的用户体验。DeepJudge发布的是协议规范而非实现代码，无许可费用，旨在鼓励其他厂商采用。该协议不限于法律领域，DeepJudge希望其他垂直行业也能采纳。
news.bodyHtml:
DeepJudge, the Zurich-based enterprise search company that describes itself as the institutional intelligence platform for legal AI, today introduced the Agent Handoff Protocol, an open protocol designed to let users move from one AI product into another – and, in some cases, back again – while retaining the full context of their work.

Harvey has already announced that it is building an integration implementing the protocol, which will enter beta this month, and Thomson Reuters says it will support it in CoCounsel for Legal, with details on its implementation and timing still to come.

“The most capable legal workflows will draw on more than one specialized system,” said Siva Gurumurthy, chief technology officer at Harvey. “Agent Handoff Protocol lets a user move from Harvey into a partner’s product and back without losing the thread of their work, while leveraging both products to their full potential.”

DeepJudge developed AHP to address the increasingly common problem of having to move between different AI products and experiences – such as from Harvey to DeepJudge – to get work done.

While existing protocols such as the Model Context Protocol developed by Anthropic let systems exchange information and perform discrete actions, they do not allow the broader context of the work – the objective, the supporting materials, the conversation history, the analysis already done – to travel with the user from one product to another.

“The Agent Handoff Protocol addresses this challenge by enabling AI platforms to transfer the user and the context needed to continue work from one system to another,” DeepJudge says. “Rather than rebuilding context each time they switch products, users can move between AI experiences while preserving the information and progress that led to the current point.”

In its announcement, DeepJudge gives the example of a lawyer researching a precedent question in DeepJudge, who can then move into Harvey with the relevant context already in place, without re-uploading materials, recreating prompts, or rebuilding prior analysis.

“No single AI experience will be the right one for every task,” Yannic Kilcher, DeepJudge’s CTO and co-founder, said in the announcement. “People should be able to use the AI tool that’s best for what they need to do and take their context with them.”

How It Works

For those wanting to dive in deeper, the technical documentation for the protocol can be found at agenthandoffprotocol.org. But in an interview yesterday, Kilcher told me that, for users, the actual mechanism of the handoff is a simple button. The user clicks it and says, in effect, I want to continue this work in this other application.

“In the background we take care of bringing that context along,” Kilcher said. “There’s multiple things that have to happen in the background. We have to authenticate you, so the whole transfer is secure and scoped to you as a user.”

The GitHub page describes it this way: “AHP gives two independently operated agent applications one shared action: Continue this user’s task over there, with this objective, this selected conversation context, and these resources.”

In terms of what context gets carried over, the protocol leaves that open so it is up to the vendor implementing the protocol to make that decision.

“The protocol itself has no opinion on that,” Kilcher said. “We feel it is the job of the individual partners in the ecosystem to decide what an appropriate context is.”

Harvey might decide the user’s conversation history is the right thing to pass, for example, whereas DeepJudge, as a search engine, is more likely to pass back the documents the user found.

As currently written, the specification describes one application handing off to another, and then the other possibly handing back.

Kilcher said the hand-back is optional for developers to adopt. A user who starts in DeepJudge, collects documents, and moves into CoCounsel to finish a drafting workflow may have no particular reason to return, he noted.

Handoffs among multiple applications are conceivable but not specified, Kilcher said. “We’re just trying to keep it really simple for now.”

Not an MCP Replacement

When asked how AHP differs from MCP, Kilcher said AHP is built on top of MCP and is not intended to replace it.

For simple retrieval, MCP works well, he said. For example, a lawyer using a firm’s Claude Enterprise deployment who asks whether the firm has done a particular kind of deal before can get an answer from DeepJudge through MCP without ever needing to leave Claude.

But for more complex tasks, it is sometimes preferable to work directly within the connected application’s full user interface.

“There is a reason products have different user interfaces, because we built these products to serve very particular needs,” Kilcher said. “There was no good way of delivering that via MCP, because all you get is basically the bit of text you send back and forth.”

The GitHub page puts it this way:

MCP connects an LLM application to external context and capabilities. Its core architecture has hosts, clients, and servers; servers expose resources, prompts, and tools through JSON-RPC over transports such as stdio and Streamable HTTP. A host can use those capabilities while keeping the user in the host application.

AHP connects two complete, independently operated agent applications. It transfers an explicit objective, a selected conversation sample, resources, and continuity identifiers, then returns a URL for a prepared experience in the receiving application. The user and the task cross the product boundary; tools, credentials, and execution privileges do not.

AHP reuses a good deal of MCP’s machinery, including how messages are structured. “It’s really about providing a different user experience than MCP, but it’s compatible and complementary to MCP,” Kilcher said. “This is not a replacement.”

He notes that MCP connectors often come with restrictions. A vendor will allow you to connect to its MCP server, but it may allow you to do only limited functions.

“With this, we’re voluntarily passing the user to the other product,” Kilcher said. “Philosophically, this is an ecosystem. The different players fulfill different roles, and if we make the user experience great, everyone profits.”

An Open Protocol

DeepJudge is publishing the specification, not an implementation. There is no license fee and no reference code, and Kilcher said the point of releasing it openly is to remove any question about whether other vendors can build on it.

“We wanted to make it so that there is no danger of us being like, ‘Hey, this is ours,’” he said. “We’re not releasing the implementation anyway. This would be useless today – you can just give this protocol spec that we released to an LLM. It will do a fine job at implementing it.”

The spec covers what each side of the handoff must implement – message structure, transfer mechanism, how resources are represented – and Kilcher said it documents what DeepJudge has already built with its partners, so it is not aspirational.

“This is a full description of what we have implemented with our partners. So we know that this works.”

Nothing about the protocol is legal-specific, and Kilcher said DeepJudge would be happy to see it picked up in other verticals. Asked whether anything comparable already exists, he said the team found individual projects but no standard.

“Professionals will increasingly work across specialized AI experiences, and those systems need to work together without sacrificing the context, trust, and expertise required for high-stakes work,” said Joel Hron, chief technology officer at Thomson Reuters. “Open standards like Agent Handoff Protocol can help enable that interoperability.”

To my mind, the premise of AHP makes perfect sense. There are some things you can do well via an MCP connector to an application and some things you can do well only by directing engaging with the application and its full user experience. But you do not want that context switching to lose the context of your work.

As for whether AHP becomes a widely used standard, time will tell. Kilcher is modest about that. “This is how we’re doing it,” he said. “It’s a suggestion from us to the industry.”

news.titleEn: Opus 2 once again selected as Best Places to Work honoree by the Kansas City Business Journal
news.titleZh: Opus 2 再次入选《堪萨斯城商业期刊》最佳工作场所
news.summaryZh: 2026年8月12日，堪萨斯城——领先的法律技术提供商Opus 2连续第二年被评为《堪萨斯城商业期刊》2026年度最佳工作场所。该年度奖项旨在表彰堪萨斯城大都会区营造卓越职场文化和员工敬业度的公司。为团队感到自豪，并期待继续在堪萨斯城发展和投资；再次获得认可尤其有意义，因为该奖项完全基于员工反馈，反映了团队的凝聚力、才华和活力。公司总部位于伦敦，近年来扩大了美国业务，在堪萨斯城地区增加了营销、销售、运营和客户成功团队成员。Opus 2在员工人数10至50人的超小型企业类别中获奖，提名者根据保密的员工调查进行评估和排名，员工在工作满意度、领导诚信以及文化是否支持健康与福祉等方面对雇主进行评分。此外，Opus 2近期还荣获SaaS Awards法律与法律服务最佳SaaS解决方案奖、三年内第二次获得CODiE最佳法律解决方案奖，以及三项美国商业奖金奖：最佳法律公司（大型）、最佳法律解决方案和最佳法律解决方案人民选择奖。公司还获得了Legalweek科技法律领袖奖和A.I. Awards的认可。Opus 2成立于2008年，开发屡获殊荣的AI赋能软件，解决法律实践中最紧迫的问题。其一流解决方案对商业争议生态系统至关重要，受到全球最成功律师事务所的信赖，用于处理关键事务。这些解决方案构建在灵活强大的平台上，帮助律所创建智能法律解决方案，赢得业务、深化客户参与并简化全所工作流程。
news.bodyHtml:
Recognition of the growing Kansas City team reflects the leading legal technology company’s people-focused values and collaborative culture 

 

KANSAS CITY – August 12, 2026 – Opus 2, a leading legal technology provider, has been named a 2026 Best Place to Work by the Kansas City Business Journal for the second year in a row. The annual awards celebrate companies in the Kansas City metropolitan area that foster exceptional workplace cultures and employee engagement. 

“We’re proud of the team we’ve built here, and we’re excited to continue growing and investing in Kansas City,” said Beau Wysong, Chief Marketing Officer at Opus 2. “Being recognized as a Best Place to Work again this year is especially meaningful because it’s entirely based on employee feedback and reflects the alignment, talent, and energy of our team.” 

Although headquartered in London, the company has expanded its U.S. presence in recent years, adding marketing, sales, operations, and client success team members in the Kansas City area. 

Opus 2 was recognized in the extra-small category for companies with 10–50 local employees. Nominees were evaluated and ranked based on confidential employee surveys. Employees ranked their employers in areas such as job satisfaction, leadership integrity, and whether the culture supports their health and well-being.  

In addition to this victory, Opus 2 recently won Best SaaS Solution for Law and Legal Services in the SaaS Awards, the CODiE Award for Best Legal Solution for the second time in the last three years, and three Gold American Business Awards® for Best Legal Company (Large), Best Legal Solution, and People’s Choice for Best Legal Solution. The company was also recognized in the Legalweek Leaders in Tech Law Awards and the A.I. Awards. 

 

About Opus 2 

Founded in 2008, Opus 2 develops award-winning, AI-enabled software that solves the most pressing problems facing the practice of law. The company’s best-in-class solutions are essential to the commercial disputes ecosystem and trusted by the world’s most successful law firms for their critical matters. Those solutions are built on a flexible, powerful platform that helps firms create intelligent legal solutions that win business, deepen client engagement, and simplify workflows firmwide. To learn more, visit Opus2.com.

The annual awards celebrate companies in the Kansas City metropolitan area that foster exceptional workplace cultures and employee engagement.

“We’re proud of the team we’ve built here, and we’re excited to continue growing and investing in Kansas City,” said Beau Wysong, Chief Marketing Officer at Opus 2. “Being recognized as a Best Place to Work again this year is especially meaningful because it’s entirely based on employee feedback and reflects the alignment, talent, and energy of our team.”

Although headquartered in London, the company has expanded its U.S. presence in recent years, adding marketing, sales, operations, and client success team members in the Kansas City area.

Opus 2 was recognized in the extra-small category for companies with 10–50 local employees. Nominees were evaluated and ranked based on confidential employee surveys. Employees ranked their employers in areas such as job satisfaction, leadership integrity, and whether the culture supports their health and well-being.

In addition to this victory, Opus 2 recently won Best SaaS Solution for Law and Legal Services in the SaaS Awards , the CODiE Award for Best Legal Solution for the second time in the last three years, and three Gold American Business Awards® for Best Legal Company (Large), Best Legal Solution, and People’s Choice for Best Legal Solution. The company was also recognized in the Legalweek Leaders in Tech Law Awards and the A.I. Awards .

Founded in 2008, Opus 2 develops award-winning, AI-enabled software that solves the most pressing problems facing the practice of law. The company’s best-in-class solutions are essential to the commercial disputes ecosystem and trusted by the world’s most successful law firms for their critical matters. Those solutions are built on a flexible, powerful platform that helps firms create intelligent legal solutions that win business, deepen client engagement, and simplify workflows firmwide. To learn more, visit Opus2.com.

news.titleZh: TalkingTech播客：AI在法律领域最大的挑战不是技术，而是数据
news.summaryZh: 生成式AI在法律行业从试验走向实施之际，律所的数据基础是否足以支撑AI成为持续讨论的焦点。Legal IT Insider编辑Caroline Hill与Morae Global首席战略官Mathew Crocker在最新TalkingTech播客中，结合Crocker与客户的交流，解读Morae关于AI采用的最新研究。研究显示，在行业高速推进AI的进程中，存在严重的数据完整性障碍和治理缺口。Crocker是业内知名人士，曾在Morae工作多年，并担任2019年被Morae收购的Phoenix Business Solutions的首席执行官兼联合创始人。多数律所专注于法律AI解决方案，却较少考虑这些方案所依赖的数据。双方探讨了数据战略以及引发信任和采用挑战的数据问题；缺乏信任会产生“验证税”，侵蚀投资回报率。调查显示，律所面临来自客户要求快速行动的压力，同时也非常担心数据被滥用，双方讨论了律所面临的多重竞争压力。展望未来，讨论涉及基于消费的定价模式、代币驱动的成本及其对律所预算的影响。对于困惑于AI采用为何仍具挑战的律所，本期播客对法律市场的真实状况以及领导者下一步需要做什么，提供了务实而坦率的评估。TalkingTech播客属于Legal IT Insider的商业服务系列，欲了解更多信息请联系helen@legaltechnology.com。可在Spotify收听完整播客，或在YouTube观看完整视频。
news.bodyHtml:
As generative AI moves from experimentation to implementation, one question continues to dominate conversations in the legal sector: are law firms’ data foundations strong enough to support it?

In our latest TalkingTech podcast, Legal IT Insider’s editor Caroline Hill sits down with Morae Global’s chief strategy officer Mathew Crocker to unpack Morae’s latest research into AI adoption, set against the conversations that Crocker is having with customers.

Advertisement

The new research from Morae shows that in the industry’s high speed AI journey, there is a serious data integrity barrier and a governance gap, among many other findings that we dive into during the discussion.

Crocker is a well-known figure in the industry from both his many years at Morae but also his time as CEO and co-founder of Phoenix Business Solutions, acquired by Morae in 2019.

Advertisement

We chat about the fact that most law firms are focusing on legal AI solutions, with less thought given about what those solutions are being fed. We look at data strategies and the data issues that are causing trust and adoption challenges. Without trust, there is a “verification tax” that is eating ROI.

The pressure on law firms to move quickly is coming from clients  but they are also (the survey shows) really worried about their data being misused. We discuss some of the competing pressures that law firms are under.

Looking ahead, we discuss the emergence of consumption-based pricing models, token-driven costs and the implications for law firm budgeting.

For firms wondering why AI adoption remains challenging, this podcast offers a practical and refreshingly candid assessment of where the legal market really stands, and what leaders need to do next.

news.titleEn: How Law Firms Should Plan for AI: Start with Strategy, Not Software
news.titleZh: 律师事务所应如何规划AI：从战略开始，而非软件
news.summaryZh: 人工智能正迅速成为法律行业最受关注的技术之一，从文件审查、法律研究到合同起草和证词摘要，AI有望提升效率并减少行政工作。但许多律所问错了问题：不应先问“该买哪种AI工具”，而应先问“AI在哪里能为律所创造最大价值，同时保护客户、数据和声誉”。美国律师协会2024年法律技术调查报告显示，生成式AI在法律行业的采用加速，企业客户也开始期望外部律师利用技术提高效率而不牺牲质量或安全。律所管理着各行业中最机密的信息，若无明确计划，引入AI可能带来客户保密、数据隐私、道德义务、监管合规、影子AI、不准确或“幻觉”法律信息、治理与可审计性等新问题。部署AI前应制定路线图：第一步，审视团队在何处浪费时间，通过审查计费数据、内部时间跟踪、服务台请求和工作流报告，寻找手动文件准备、重复客户沟通、行政审批、信息检索、intake流程等模式，并询问律师和员工哪些任务重复、耗时过长，观察实际工作流以发现重复数据输入、手动审批、多版本文件、冗长邮件链和不必要上下文切换等瓶颈。第二步，优先高影响、低风险用例，如文件摘要、法律研究辅助、起草初稿、知识管理和行政自动化。第三步，在扩展前建立AI治理，明确批准的平台、可输入AI的客户信息、人工审查要求、数据保留政策、安全控制、用户权限、审计日志和员工培训。第四步，确保基础设施AI就绪，评估敏感客户数据保护、现代身份控制、设备管理、数据备份与恢复、远程安全访问、AI。
news.bodyText:
Artificial intelligence is quickly becoming one of the most talked-about technologies in the legal industry. From document review and legal research to drafting contracts and summarizing depositions, AI promises to improve efficiency and reduce administrative work.

But many firms are asking the wrong question.

Instead of asking, “Which AI tool should we buy?” , law firms should first ask:

“Where can AI create the greatest value for our firm while protecting our clients, data, and reputation?”

The firms that see the biggest return on AI won’t necessarily be the ones with the most software; they’ll be the ones with the best strategy.

AI Is Becoming a Competitive Advantage

According to the American Bar Association’s 2024 Legal Technology Survey Report, generative AI adoption has accelerated across the legal profession, with firms increasingly experimenting with AI for legal research, drafting, summarization, and administrative tasks. Meanwhile, corporate clients are beginning to expect their outside counsel to leverage technology that improves efficiency without compromising quality or security.

The opportunity is significant, but so are the risks.

Law firms manage some of the most confidential information in any industry. Client communications, litigation strategies, financial records, intellectual property, and privileged documents all require the highest levels of security and governance.

Without a clear plan, introducing AI can create new concerns around:

Client confidentiality

Data privacy

Ethical obligations

Regulatory compliance

Shadow AI (employees using unauthorized AI tools)

Inaccurate or “hallucinated” legal information

Governance and auditability

Before deploying AI across the organization, firms should build a roadmap.

Step 1: Look at Where Your Team Wastes Time

The best AI opportunities often aren’t the most glamorous, they’re the most repetitive.

Before evaluating vendors or purchasing licenses, take a step back and identify where your attorneys and staff spend time on work that doesn’t create strategic value.

Ask questions like:

Which tasks are repetitive?

What slows people down every day?

Where do attorneys lose billable time?

What work could be automated without sacrificing quality?

There are several practical ways to identify these opportunities.

Watch How Time Gets Spent

Review billing data, internal time tracking, service desk requests, and workflow reports.

Look for patterns such as:

Manual document preparation

Repetitive client communications

Administrative approvals

Information retrieval

Intake processes

These activities often take hundreds of hours every year.

Look for Repeated Requests

If your IT team or legal operations staff repeatedly receives the same questions or requests, that’s a strong indicator that automation may help.

Examples include:

Password resets

Document location requests

Matter status updates

Template requests

Standard policy questions

Client onboarding paperwork

AI-powered assistants can often handle many of these interactions automatically.

Ask Your People

One of the simplest and most overlooked approaches is simply talking to attorneys and staff.

Ask questions like:

What part of your day feels repetitive?

What takes longer than it should?

If you could eliminate one task every week, what would it be?

The people closest to the work usually know exactly where efficiency can improve.

Observe Real Workflows

Sometimes the biggest inefficiencies never appear in reports.

Sit with attorneys, paralegals, legal assistants, and administrative staff while they complete routine work.

Watching actual workflows often uncovers:

Duplicate data entry

Manual approvals

Multiple document versions

Excessive email chains

Unnecessary context switching

These workflow bottlenecks frequently become excellent candidates for AI-assisted automation.

Step 2: Prioritize High-Impact, Low-Risk Use Cases

Not every AI project needs to transform the firm overnight.

Many successful firms begin with narrowly focused use cases that deliver measurable value.

Examples include:

Document Summarization

AI can summarize lengthy pleadings, contracts, depositions, and case files, allowing attorneys to review key information more quickly.

Legal Research Assistance

Modern AI tools can help organize research, identify relevant authorities, and accelerate early-stage legal analysis while attorneys remain responsible for validating the results.

Drafting First Versions

AI can generate initial drafts of:

Engagement letters

Internal memos

Client communications

Standard contracts

Policies

Meeting summaries

This reduces administrative work while keeping attorneys in control of final review.

Knowledge Management

Many firms possess years of valuable internal knowledge that is difficult to search for.

AI can help organize internal precedents, policies, templates, and historical work products, making institutional knowledge easier to access.

Administrative Automation

AI can also streamline:

Scheduling

Intake

Conflict checks

Client follow-ups

Internal help desk requests

Meeting summaries

Workflow routing

These improvements often produce immediate productivity gains across the firm.

Step 3: Build AI Governance Before Scaling

Technology alone doesn’t reduce risk.

Every law firm should establish clear AI governance policies before broad adoption.

A governance framework should define:

Which AI platforms are approved

What client information may be entered into AI systems

Human review requirements

Data retention policies

Security controls

User permissions

Audit logging

Employee training

Without governance, employees may unknowingly expose confidential information through consumer AI applications that were never intended for legal workloads.

Step 4: Ensure Your Infrastructure Is AI-Ready

Even the best AI platform depends on the underlying IT environment.

Law firms should evaluate whether their infrastructure can support AI securely by asking:

Is sensitive client data properly protected?

Are users authenticated with modern identity controls?

Are devices consistently managed?

Is data backed up and recoverable?

Can remote users securely access applications?

Are AI workloads isolated from sensitive systems when appropriate?

Is the environment monitored for unusual activity?

An AI initiative is only as secure as the infrastructure that supports it.

Step 5: Measure Business Outcomes – Not AI Adoption

The goal isn’t to say your firm uses AI.

The goal is to improve measurable business outcomes.

Successful firms track metrics such as:

Attorney productivity

Reduction in administrative hours

Faster client response times

Improved document turnaround

Lower support ticket volume

Reduced operational costs

Higher employee satisfaction

Better client experience

When AI initiatives are tied to business objectives, firms can prioritize investments that produce meaningful returns.

AI Should Enhance Legal Professionals -Not Replace Them

The legal profession depends on judgment, experience, ethics, and client relationships. AI is not a substitute for those qualities.

Instead, AI should handle repetitive, time-consuming work, so legal professionals can focus on higher-value activities that require expertise and strategic thinking.

Firms that approach AI thoughtfully starting with process improvement, governance, and secure infrastructure will be better positioned to deliver faster service, improve operational efficiency, and meet evolving client expectations without compromising confidentiality or compliance.

How IronOrbit Helps Law Firms Build an AI Foundation

Successful AI initiatives require more than software. They require secure infrastructure, governance, reliable performance, and expert guidance.

IronOrbit helps law firms prepare for AI by delivering secure cloud desktops, managed IT services, cybersecurity, backup and disaster recovery, Microsoft 365 management, and strategic IT consulting designed for highly regulated environments. Built on IronOrbit’s private cloud infrastructure, these services are backed by seven consecutive years of SOC 2 Type II compliance with no exceptions , giving law firms confidence that the infrastructure supporting their AI initiatives meets rigorous standards for security, availability, and operational excellence.

Whether your firm is evaluating its first AI use case or developing a long-term AI roadmap, building a secure, compliant IT foundation helps ensure AI becomes a competitive advantage, not a security risk.

As AI continues to reshape legal services, the firms that invest in strategy before technology will be best positioned to succeed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best way for a law firm to start using AI?

The best way for a law firm to begin using artificial intelligence is by identifying repetitive, time-consuming tasks before selecting any AI software. Start by evaluating where attorneys, paralegals, and administrative staff spend the most non-billable time, such as drafting standard documents, summarizing case files, conducting legal research, or responding to routine client inquiries. Once these opportunities are identified, firms should establish AI governance policies, ensure sensitive client data is protected, and train employees on the responsible use of AI. A strategic, phased approach allows firms to improve efficiency while maintaining client confidentiality, regulatory compliance, and ethical obligations.

How can law firms use AI without compromising client confidentiality?

Law firms can use AI securely by implementing strong governance and security controls before deploying AI tools. Firms should use approved AI platforms that offer enterprise-grade security, restrict what client information can be entered into AI systems, require human review of AI-generated content, and maintain audit logs for compliance. Multi-factor authentication, encryption, secure cloud infrastructure, and endpoint protection are also critical for protecting confidential legal data. Establishing clear AI usage policies helps reduce the risks associated with unauthorized or “shadow AI” applications used by employees.

What are the most valuable AI use cases for law firms?

Some of the highest-value AI use cases for law firms include document summarization, legal research assistance, contract drafting, meeting transcription, document classification, knowledge management, client intake automation, and administrative workflow automation. AI can also help IT departments automate repetitive help desk requests and improve internal knowledge sharing. Rather than replacing attorneys, these tools reduce repetitive work, so legal professionals can spend more time on strategic legal analysis, client relationships, and billable activities.

Does my law firm’s IT infrastructure need to be upgraded before adopting AI?

In many cases, yes. AI applications perform best when supported by secure, modern IT infrastructure. Before expanding AI initiatives, firms should evaluate whether their environment includes secure cloud desktops, identity and access management, reliable backup and disaster recovery, endpoint security, encrypted data storage, and continuous monitoring. An AI strategy built on a secure infrastructure helps protect sensitive client information, improves performance, simplifies compliance, and creates a scalable foundation for future AI initiatives. Investing in the underlying technology first allows firms to adopt AI with greater confidence and lower risk.

news.titleEn: FTC Issues Proposed Policy Statement on AI Accuracy and Output Steering
news.titleZh: FTC发布关于AI准确性与输出引导的拟议政策声明
news.summaryZh:
2026年7月1日，美国联邦贸易委员会（FTC）发布拟议政策声明，聚焦将AI输出导向未披露意识形态目标的做法，认为其可能损害准确性并违背消费者合理预期。该声明紧随第14365号行政令，该命令要求FTC澄清《FTC法》第5条如何适用于AI模型及各州新兴AI监管法律。

消费者通常期望AI力求准确并忠实执行请求，但开发者可能暗中“引导”输出以推进意识形态、回避争议或限制法律风险等目标。声明特别提及科罗拉多州《人工智能法》，该法规定企业可能因客户使用其产品产生的歧视性输出而担责；企业为遵守该法及其他州类似法律也可能损害准确性，若未充分披露，可能违反第5条。声明对披露设定高标准：不能埋在服务条款中，一次性披露后藏于细则也不够，必须清晰显著地消除系统旨在给出最佳答案的观念。遵守州要求不自动消除联邦欺骗担忧，州法律强制修改输出有时可能与联邦消费者保护原则冲突。声明未提供正式优先规则，但反映当前政府推动更统一国家AI监管框架的兴趣，并为FTC未来分析AI治理、透明度和内容控制提供初步路线图。利益相关者应审查营销传播和公开声明，评估AI训练与内容审核治理流程，并处理州AI与隐私法律及国际法律（如欧盟AI法案）与FTC立场之间的潜在脱节。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! On July 1, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) issued a proposed policy statement focusing on AI models that steer outcomes toward undisclosed ideological objectives. According to the FTC, this practice may compromise accuracy and be contrary to reasonable consumer expectations about how AI models work. The proposed policy statement follows Executive Order 14365, which specifically directs the agency to clarify how § 5 of the FTC Act applies to both AI models and emerging state laws that regulate those models. According to the proposed policy statement, consumers generally expect AI systems to strive for accurate responses and faithfully carry out consumer requests, subject to ordinary technological limitations. These expectations are reasonable, the FTC contends, due to the inherent nature of AI systems and explicit or implied representations that companies have espoused for years about those systems. Unbeknownst to consumers, however, AI developers may engage in “steering” the output, the FTC says, by deliberately configuring AI systems to advance objectives other than accuracy (e.g., achieving ideological goals, avoiding controversial topics, or attempting to limit legal exposure). To illustrate this point, the proposed policy statement specifically points to Colorado’s recently enacted Artificial Intelligence Act, which provides, among other requirements, that companies can be held liable for discriminatory AI model outputs resulting from customers’ use of those products. The FTC asserts that even a company’s efforts to comply with this statute (and similar laws in other states) could compromise accuracy and be contrary to consumers’ reasonable expectations about how AI models work. In the FTC’s view, failure to sufficiently disclose this to consumers may violate § 5 because deception under the FTC Act includes “implied misrepresentations, half-truths, and instances where only a ‘significant minority’ of consumers are misled.” The proposed policy statement appears to set a high bar as to what constitutes an adequate disclosure on outcome steering, noting that the disclosure cannot be buried in the terms of service, and a one-time disclosure “subsequently hidden away in fine print” is unlikely to suffice. Instead, the disclosure must “clearly and conspicuously dispel the notion that the system is designed to give the best answer possible.” Additionally, the FTC clarifies that the more the disclosure cuts against the reasonable expectations that users would take away from other contexts, the more persistent and prominent the disclosure would need to be. In the proposed policy statement, the FTC considers how emerging state laws on AI, including the Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act, may require AI developers to alter, constrain, or otherwise influence AI outputs to achieve particular public policy objectives. The FTC takes the position that compliance with a state requirement does not automatically eliminate potential federal deception concerns if consumers are not adequately informed about how those requirements affect outputs. The proposed policy statement also suggests that state laws compelling modifications to AI outputs could, in some instances, conflict with federal consumer protection principles. Although the proposed policy statement does not provide a formal preemption rule, its discussion of emerging states AI laws seems to reflect the current administration’s interest in promoting a more uniform national framework for AI regulation. The proposed policy statement provides a tentative roadmap to how the FTC may analyze questions involving AI governance, transparency, and content controls in the future. Stakeholders should consider reviewing the content of their marketing communications and other public-facing statements — not only for explicit claims about AI products, but also for implied representations or potentially relevant information that has been omitted. Companies should consider assessing governance processes for AI model training and content moderation, given the FTC’s apparent scrutiny of intentional design choices. They should also consider how to address the potential disconnect between state AI and privacy laws (and international laws, such as the EU AI Act, where relevant) and the FTC’s position. news.titleEn: Privacy Tip #503 – Read This Before You Upload Medical Information into an AI Tool
news.titleZh: 隐私提示#503——在将医疗信息上传至AI工具前请阅读本文
news.summaryZh: 当前将医疗信息上传至生成式AI工具的人数统计令人震惊，许多人并未意识到其中的风险。今年早些时候，OpenAI宣布推出专门帮助个人管理健康记录的聊天机器人版本。无论将医疗信息分享给ChatGPT还是其他聊天机器人，都存在风险。《美国医学会杂志》文章《当患者与AI聊天机器人分享一切——大型语言模型的风险与机遇》概述了将电子健康记录未经筛选上传至大型语言模型的潜在益处，以及隐私侵犯、歧视和健康差距加剧等风险。这些风险包括：健康信息一旦分享给商业公司便不受HIPAA保护；共享信息可能作为输出被其他人的其他提示披露；结果可能不准确、有偏见或具有歧视性；信息可能根据公司隐私政策被分享给其他第三方。上传任何医疗信息前，必须彻底阅读公司隐私政策，了解风险，尽量减少上传实际医疗记录，并谨慎过度依赖结果。有研究表明，从AI工具接收诊断或治疗信息时应谨慎。已有数人起诉AI开发者，指控误诊造成伤害。一人起诉ChatGPT及其CEO，声称“ChatGPT的医疗建议几乎害死他”。OpenAI条款规定个人不应依赖其提供医疗建议。遗憾的是，很少有人深入阅读隐私政策。结论是：分享信息前阅读隐私政策非常重要，即使它们很长。花时间阅读，这是了解公司如何使用和披露你最敏感信息的唯一途径。同样重要的是要明白，与第三方分享医疗信息时它不受保护。保护最敏感的信息，在分享给商业实体或依赖AI机器人结果之前了解风险。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The current statistics on how many people upload their medical information into a generative AI tool are staggering. It is clear to me that people are unaware of the risks of doing so, and if you are contemplating sharing your medical information with a generative AI tool, like ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude, please read this first. Earlier this year, OpenAI announced the launch of a version of the chatbot dedicated to assist individuals with navigating their health records. Whether you are contemplating sharing your medical information with ChatGPT, or another chatbot, there are risks of doing so that have been outlined in the article “When Patients Share Everything With an AI Chatbot – Risks and Opportunities of Large Language Models” published in the Journal of the American Medical Association. The article outlines the “potential benefits and discuss the attendant risks of privacy violations, discrimination, and the exacerbation of health disparities that may accompany the unfiltered upload of EHRs” into large language models. These risks include the fact that once the health information is shared with a commercial company, it is not protected by HIPAA, the federal law that protects health information that is created or maintained by medical providers. In addition, the shared information could be disclosed as output for other prompts by other people. Further, the results could be inaccurate, biased, or discriminatory. Finally, the information can be shared with other third parties as outlined in the company’s privacy policy. It is imperative that prior to uploading any medical information, you read the company’s privacy policy thoroughly, understand the risks, minimize uploading the actual medical records, and be cautious about relying too heavily on the results. There are studies that show that caution should be used when receiving diagnosis or treatment information from an AI tool. Several individuals have sued AI developers for misdiagnosis that allegedly caused them harm. One individual is suing ChatGPT and its CEO alleging that “ChatGPT’s medical advice nearly killed him.” OpenAI’s terms state that individuals should not rely on it for medical advice. Unfortunately, it is well-known that it is rare for individuals to read privacy policies in depth. The takeaway? As we have said before, it is really important to read privacy policies before you share your information, even if they are long. Take the time, as that is the only way you will find out how companies are using and disclosing your most sensitive information. It is similarly important to understand that your medical information is not protected when you share it with a third party. Protect your most sensitive information, and know the risks before you share it with a commercial entity or rely on the results of an AI bot. More Upcoming Events
news.relevanceReason: 文章聚焦于AI工具在医疗信息处理中的隐私风险，涉及法律合规（HIPAA）和AI使用风险，与法律AI相关但主要面向医疗场景。

news.titleEn: The Copyright Battle That Could Push AI Out of Reach
news.titleZh: 版权之战或将使人工智能变得遥不可及
news.summaryZh: 一场围绕生成式人工智能训练中版权材料合理使用权的重大法律诉讼正在美国展开。数十位作者（包括乔治·R·R·马丁）及多家主要新闻机构联合起诉OpenAI，指控其未经许可使用受版权保护的材料训练大型语言模型。案件的核心争议点在于“合理使用”原则，该原则自美国内战前便已存在，并在50年前由国会写入《版权法》，允许在创作全新且不同作品时使用受版权保护的材料，前提是新作品不替代原作。原告方要求法院下令开发者撤回现有生成式AI模型，直至其仅使用授权材料重新训练。其使用方式符合合理使用原则，因为训练材料未被复制、存储或转售，而是被转化为一种新工具，并非替代任何特定书籍或文章。他们还援引最高法院及上诉法院的判例，指出多功能产品的制造商通常不对他人利用该产品侵犯版权的行为负责。若法院大幅限制AI训练的合理使用范围，将导致训练所需的海量数据需购买或租赁，成本极其高昂，对初创企业而言几乎不可行，并可能影响课堂、实验室、初创公司、图书馆、市场及工作场所等广泛领域，对每个人产生至少四个方面的负面影响。该案的核心法律问题预计将于今年秋季进入关键阶段，并可能于明年初在纽约市联邦法官面前进行辩论。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Restricting fair use for AI training would raise costs, suppress competition, and widen the knowledge divide. For more than two years, opposing armies have been massing and digging in as they prepare for a battle royale to decide the future of their respective domains. No, the Iron Throne doesn’t hang in the balance, but the future of generative AI, and its potential to better the lives of literally everyone everywhere, does. Those are the stakes in a massive consolidated copyright legal case against OpenAI brought by dozens of authors, including George R.R. Martin and major news organizations. After years of preliminary jousting by lawyers and experts, the central legal issue will come to a head in the fall and is expected to be argued early next year before a federal judge in New York City. The key issue is “fair use,” a cornerstone of American copyright law since before the Civil War and written into the Copyright Act by Congress 50 years ago this fall. It expressly allows copyrighted works to be used without the prior permission of their owners to create something fundamentally new and different, provided the new work does not substitute for the original itself. Ironically, authors and news outlets regularly rely on “fair use” of copyrighted material to write their own books and articles. Yet that hasn’t stopped many of them from going to court to stop generative AI developers from using copyrighted material, much of it from the open internet, to initially train large language models like ChatGPT. Plaintiffs are asking in many cases for court orders that would force developers to pull their existing gen AI models off the market entirely until they can be retrained using only licensed material. Developers like OpenAI push back with a different reading of the law. They argue that their use of copyrighted material is a textbook case of fair use under decades of precedent, because the material on which gen AI models are trained isn’t copied, stored or resold – it’s transformed into a new kind of tool, not a substitute for any specific book or article. They also cite a clear line of Supreme Court and appellate rulings that the maker of a multi-purpose product isn’t usually on the hook when someone else uses that product to violate copyright law. For most of the general public, this may sound like an obscure legal fight between powerful companies over money, but it’s much bigger than that. If courts dramatically narrow fair use for AI training, the consequences would reach every classroom, laboratory, startup, library, marketplace and workplace that increasingly relies on generative artificial intelligence. That could negatively affect every one of us in at least four important ways: Today’s leading AI models require enormous amounts of information during training. Instead of using fair use material, the alternative would be to buy or lease that material. It sounds simple enough, but the volume of material required is astronomically large and would be astronomically expensive. That’s a non-starter for start-ups. Worse yet, the cost and mechanics of simply identifying and negotiating for the huge amount of data necessary would itself be prohibitive for all but the biggest existing developers.

news.titleEn: Neota Rolls Out New AI Governance Strategy
news.titleZh: Neota推出全新AI治理策略
news.summaryZh: Neota Logic以“法律团队的AI治理层”为定位，推出AI编排能力，允许律师将自选大语言模型引入受治理的工作流：每次调用均被记录、对照团队规则检查并路由至人工签核。该公司起源于2010年，曾是首批“无代码”法律工作流自动化公司之一，如今聚焦生成式AI，尤其是内部团队和合规团队的应用。新治理产品是其多项AI能力中的第一项，均遵循同一标准：法律团队应以AI速度推进工作，同时不丧失为工作辩护的能力。该编排将模型置于工作流内，仅用于提取、摘要、分类等擅长任务，规则、路由和人工签核仍由团队控制。工作流决定输出处理：合同可由模型读取，依据公司自身操作手册评估后自动路由，低风险事项直接通过，重大事项升级给相应律师。调用可链式进行，在下一步前检查上一模型输出，置信度下降时立即升级人工审查。每次运行产生完整审计追踪：AI被问及什么、返回什么、运行了哪个模型及谁签核。模型集中审批，默认不调用任何模型，团队通过自有账户与Anthropic、OpenAI、Azure OpenAI、Google、开源及AWS Bedrock等已用提供商合作。公司重申人工将检查最终输出。客户在AI上投入更多，但不想失去使法律和合规流程运作的规则与控制，希望将已选模型引入可信赖的工作流。随着LLM兴起，全球“无代码”规则型工作流自动化公司都面临重大挑战，因为简单自然语言提示即可执行复杂文本任务，而LLM中的代理和推理能力只会加剧这一点。
news.bodyText: Neota Logic, which is now going to market as ‘the AI governance layer for legal teams’, has launched an AI orchestration capability which lets lawyers bring their own choice of large language models into governed AI workflows. This means that ‘every AI call [to an LLM] is logged, checked against the team’s own rules, and routed for human sign-off’. This is a big change from what many of you will remember Neota doing in the past, which was one of the first ‘no code’ legal workflow automation companies. Neota, which can trace its roots back to 2010, is now very much focused on generative AI use, and in particular how inhouse teams and compliance groups are using the technology. They added that the new AI governance offering is ‘the first of several AI capabilities the company is bringing to market, all built to a single standard: legal teams should be able to move at the speed of AI without giving up the ability to defend the work’. But, back to the governance part. How does it work? This is how they explain it: ‘Calling a large language model is straightforward, and most tools stop at that: they return an answer and leave the user to catch what is wrong. Neota Logic’s AI orchestration places the model inside a workflow instead. It is called only for the tasks it does well, such as extraction, summarization, and classification, while the rules, the routing, and the human sign-off around it stay under the team’s control. ‘The workflow decides what happens to the model’s output. A contract can be read by the model, assessed against the firm’s own playbook, then routed automatically: low-risk matters cleared, anything material escalated to the right lawyer before it moves. Calls can be chained so one model’s output is checked before the next step runs, and a workflow can escalate to human review the moment confidence drops. ‘Every run produces a full audit trail: what the AI was asked, what it returned, which model ran, and who signed off. Models are approved centrally, no model is ever invoked by default, and legal teams work with the providers they already use, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Google, Open Source and AWS Bedrock, through their own accounts.’ And they reiterated that they are working on the basis that a human will check the final output. Vinay Varma, Chief Customer Officer at Neota Logic, commented: ‘Our customers are investing more in AI, but they do not want to lose the rules and controls that make their legal and compliance processes work. They want to bring the models they have already chosen into workflows they can trust and stand behind.’ Is this a big deal? Well, all of the ‘no code’ rules-based workflow automation companies across the world faced a major challenge once LLMs took off. This was because you easily could ask such AI systems to perform complex text-based tasks with just a simple, natural language prompt. Agents and better reasoning within LLMs only accentuated this.
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要介绍法律科技公司 Neota 推出的 AI 治理功能，旨在为法律团队提供受控的 AI 工作流，属于法律 AI 领域的直接报道。

news.titleEn: Anthropic Will Embed Watermarks in AI Outputs
news.titleZh: Anthropic将在AI输出中嵌入水印
news.summaryZh: Anthropic本周宣布，自2026年8月2日起发布的所有Claude产品将在其AI生成内容中加入机器可读标记，但旧版Claude模型的水印部署期限为2026年12月2日。此举旨在遵守欧盟《人工智能法案》第50(2)条，该条款要求生成合成音频、图像、视频或文本内容的AI系统提供商确保输出以机器可读格式标记并可被检测为人工生成或操纵。Anthropic保证水印不可见，不影响大语言模型输出的质量或可读性。水印可置于输出文本中，或出现在音频、图像、视频的元数据中。Anthropic确认将协助用户及第三方检测作品是否含水印，但尚未详细说明具体机制。该功能将在全球范围推出，而非仅限于欧盟，被视为欧盟法律“布鲁塞尔效应”影响全球标准的例证，类似GDPR的全球推广。Anthropic也指出新功能的局限：用户可能通过重新保存和格式化输出从元数据中提取水印；使用Claude进行校对、翻译和摘要时，若摘要文本被复制粘贴，水印仍可能出现；水印缺失并不 definitive 表明AI未参与创作。欧盟《人工智能法案》承认，若AI系统仅执行标准编辑的辅助功能或未实质性改变部署者提供的输入数据，则义务不适用。第99条规定，违反第50条可能面临最高1500万欧元或上一财年全球年营业额3%的行政罚款（取较高值）。其他AI公司如Google DeepMind已开发SynthID工具，可在图像、音频和文本中嵌入不可见水印。自愿性《AI生成内容透明度行为准则》已获190多个组织签署，包括Google、Meta、OpenAI和Microsoft。
news.bodyText: By Donna Carpenter. This week, Anthropic announced that all of its Claude products released from 2 August 2026 onwards will now include machine readable marking in all of its AI generated content. However, the company has until 2 December 2026 to roll out watermarking for older Claude models. This change has been implemented in order to comply with the EU AI Act (specifically Article 50(2)). Under the Act, ‘providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.’ The EU AI Act was adopted to ‘promote trustworthy artificial intelligence’, and to support technological advancements while at the same time ensuring the protection of fundamental rights as set out in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (CFREU). Anthropic has assured its users that the watermark will be invisible and shall not affect the quality or readability of the LLMs output. The watermark can either be placed in the text of the output that has been produced, or it will appear in the metadata of audio files, images, or videos. However, Anthropic has confirmed that it will assist its users and other parties to detect whether a piece of work contains a watermark. Although the company has yet to elaborate further on this, it will be interesting to see how the system will work in practice. This move could also potentially have wide-ranging ramifications for the legal and other industries where confidentiality, accountability, and data provenance are of paramount importance. Perhaps surprisingly, Anthropic has confirmed that this new feature will be rolled out globally and not just within the confines of the European Union. This is a prime illustration of how EU law and the ‘Brussels Effect‘ can influence global standards and practices. This can easily be compared with the adoption of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR); whereby some multinational companies adopted higher data privacy and protection standards on a global scale rather than just the European Union, as maintaining different systems would prove inefficient and expensive. As part of their announcement, Anthropic flagged that there are certain constraints to the newly developed feature. For example, it is possible for users to extract watermarks from metadata. This could potentially be done through resaving and reformatting the output material. Furthermore, many people use Claude to assist with proofreading, translating, and summarising documents. In this context, Claude has not generated the original text, although a watermark might still appear if for example a summarised text has been copied and pasted. Additionally, the absence of a watermark does not definitively signal the fact that AI has not been involved in the production of certain work. However, the EU AI Act has recognised that ‘this obligation shall not apply to the extent the AI systems perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer’. Article 99 of the EU AI Act sets out the penalties for non-compliance with the Act. Depending on the nature of the infringement, if an entity does not strictly adhere to Article 50 of the Act it could potentially result in administrative fines of up to €15 million or up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year (the highest value will apply). Other AI companies such as Google DeepMind have developed a tool called ‘SynthID’ that also embeds invisible watermarks into various mediums such as images, audio, and text. Also interestingly, the voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content was developed to complement the legal obligations as set out in Article 50 of the Act. As it stands, over 190 organizations have signed. This includes many key market players such as Google, Meta, OpenAI, and Microsoft. —

news.titleEn: DeepJudge Launches Agent Handoff Protocol, Harvey + TR Adopt
news.titleZh: DeepJudge推出Agent Handoff Protocol，Harvey与汤森路透采纳
news.summaryZh: 知识管理先驱DeepJudge推出“Agent Handoff Protocol”（AHP），这是一个开放系统，使用户能够在不同AI平台之间切换而无需从头开始，并携带继续工作所需的上下文。Harvey和汤森路透均已决定参与。最强大的法律工作流将利用多个专业系统，AHP让用户从Harvey进入合作伙伴产品再返回，不会丢失工作线索，同时充分发挥两个产品的潜力。人们应该能够使用最适合其需求的AI工具，并随身携带上下文。专业人士将越来越多地跨专业AI体验工作，这些系统需要协同工作，而不牺牲高风险工作所需的上下文、信任和专业知识；AHP等开放标准有助于实现这种互操作性。DeepJudge解释，随着更多律师在不同AI产品之间切换，尽管已有MCP（模型上下文协议）允许系统交换信息和执行特定操作，但其灵活性不足以满足当今需求。律师工作需要更广泛的上下文来继续任务，包括目标、支持材料、对话历史和先前工作。AHP通过使AI平台能够将用户和继续工作所需的上下文从一个系统转移到另一个系统来解决这一挑战。例如，律师在DeepJudge中研究先例问题后，可以进入Harvey，相关上下文已就位，无需重新上传材料、重新创建提示或重建先前分析。Harvey宣布将于本月以测试版推出AHP。汤森路透也支持AHP，有关其实施和时间的更多细节将在未来公告中公布。
news.bodyText: KM pioneer DeepJudge has launched an ‘Agent Handoff Protocol’ or AHP, which is an open system that ‘enables users to move between AI platforms without starting fresh, carrying the context needed to continue their work’ – which is handy. Thomson Reuters and Harvey have both decided to get involved. Siva Gurumurthy, Chief Technology Officer at Harvey, commented: ‘The most capable legal workflows will draw on more than one specialized system. Agent Handoff Protocol lets a user move from Harvey into a partner’s product and back without losing the thread of their work, while leveraging both products to their full potential. We’re glad to be among the first to implement it.’ While Yannic Kilcher, CTO and Co-Founder of DeepJudge, added: ‘People should be able to use the AI tool that’s best for what they need to do and take their context with them. That is the experience we built Agent Handoff Protocol to enable.’ And Joel Hron, Chief Technology Officer at TR, concluded: ‘Professionals will increasingly work across specialized AI experiences, and those systems need to work together without sacrificing the context, trust, and expertise required for high-stakes work. Open standards like Agent Handoff Protocol can help enable that interoperability, which is why Thomson Reuters is excited to support this effort and help shape what comes next.’ All well and good, but why do this? DeepJudge explained that as more lawyers move ‘between different AI products and experiences to complete their work’ that although we have MCP (the Model Context Protocol) that allows systems to exchange information and perform specific actions, that it’s not sufficiently flexible to meet today’s needs. They underlined that in a lawyer’s work ‘a broader context [is] required to continue a task—including objectives, supporting materials, conversation history, and prior work’. The AHP addresses this challenge by ‘enabling AI platforms to transfer the user and the context needed to continue work from one system to another. Rather than rebuilding context each time they switch products, users can move between AI experiences while preserving the information and progress that led to the current point’. For example, they noted that a lawyer researching a precedent question in DeepJudge can now move into Harvey with the relevant context already in place, allowing the work to continue without re-uploading materials, recreating prompts, or rebuilding prior analysis. In terms of their legal tech peers, Harvey has announced it will roll out AHP in beta this month. While Thomson Reuters is also supporting AHP, with additional details on their implementation and timing to follow in future announcements. Overall, a nice move, and one that makes a lot of sense. In particular this is quite a coup for DeepJudge, given that they appear to be leading on this. The Agent Handoff Protocol specification and implementation resources are here.
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要介绍法律科技公司 DeepJudge 推出的智能体交接协议，旨在改善法律工作流中 AI 工具的互操作性，并获 Harvey 和汤森路透等法律科技公司采纳，核心内容围绕法律 AI 应用。

research.titleEn: Credible, Not Always Correct: How Reddit Users Verify AI-Generated Legal Advice
research.titleZh: 可信，而非总是正确：Reddit用户如何验证AI生成的法律建议
research.abstractEn: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by laypeople to resolve real legal problems, against a backdrop of persistent access-to-justice deficits. This article presents evidence that the practical force of AI-generated legal advice depends not on its accuracy but on the social production of its credibility. While existing research has assessed the accuracy of legal AI, less is known about how machine-generated guidance is verified and made credible enough for lay users to act on. Drawing on a dual-method analysis of 153 Reddit narratives and 5,341 community reactions, this article maps a spectrum of verification practices. At one end, a minority of users verify AI-generated legal advice by triangulating across models, and some submit AI-generated guidance to platform communities for evaluation before acting, a configuration we term distributed counsel. Far more commonly, however, narratives are silent on verification. AI-generated legal advice is acted on the strength of its lawyer-like form and emotional reassurance alone. These findings show that AI-assisted legal self-help operates within an emerging informal infrastructure which redistributes the work of verification to those least equipped to bear it.
research.abstractZh: 大型语言模型（LLMs）越来越多地被非专业人士用于解决实际法律问题，而这是在持续存在的司法服务获取不足的背景下发生的。本文提供的证据表明，AI生成的法律建议的实际效力并不取决于其准确性，而取决于其可信度的社会建构。虽然现有研究评估了法律AI的准确性，但对于机器生成的指导如何被验证并使其足够可信以供非专业人士采取行动，我们知之甚少。通过对153个Reddit叙事和5,341个社区反应的双重方法分析，本文描绘了验证实践的谱系。在谱系的一端，少数用户通过跨模型三角验证来验证AI生成的法律建议，有些用户在采取行动前将AI生成的指导提交给平台社区进行评估，我们将这种配置称为“分布式咨询”。然而，更常见的是，叙事中对验证保持沉默。AI生成的法律建议仅凭其类似律师的形式和情感安慰就被采纳。这些发现表明，AI辅助的法律自助在一个新兴的非正式基础设施中运作，该基础设施将验证工作重新分配给那些最不具备承担能力的人。

news.titleEn: LawNext: LexisNexis CTO Greg Dickason On Building Legal AI In Real Time with Customers in Its New Innovation Lab
news.titleZh: LawNext：LexisNexis首席技术官Greg Dickason谈在新创新实验室与客户实时共建法律AI
news.summaryZh: 本周，LexisNexis宣布在纽约市开设客户创新实验室，这是一个实体空间，法律专业人士、LexisNexis工程师以及OpenAI和亚马逊网络服务等AI公司同处一室，实时共同构建法律AI。该公司称这是法律AI开发和交付的新模式：客户将痛点带入实验室，工程师现场针对这些痛点编写代码，通过验证的原型可在数周内集成到Lexis+ with Protégé中。本期嘉宾是领导该项目的LexisNexis Legal & Professional首席技术官Greg Dickason。他于2019年加入LexisNexis，此前曾负责公司亚太业务，并在该地区推出了Lexis+ AI。在加入LexisNexis之前，他曾担任CoreLogic的首席技术官。在与主持人Bob Ambrogi的对话中，Dickason解释了实验室内部工程师与客户实时协作编码的具体情况，以及这与LexisNexis一贯宣称的客户驱动产品开发有何不同。他们还讨论了实验室已产出的成果，包括一个多媒体Protégé Vault，允许律师查询视频证词；为何法律起草是实验室的首要任务；以及Dickason如何看待智能体重塑法律工作。本期节目由Paradigm、Briefpoint、CosmoLex和Ajax等赞助商支持。
news.bodyHtml:
This week, LexisNexis announced the opening of its Customer Innovation Lab in New York City — a physical space where legal professionals, LexisNexis engineers, and AI companies such as OpenAI and Amazon Web Services sit in the same room and build legal AI together, in real time.

The company is calling it a new model for how legal AI gets built and shipped: Instead of developing products internally and asking customers to validate them afterward, customers bring their pain points into the lab, engineers code against them on the spot, and prototypes that pass muster can move into Lexis+ with Protégé in a matter of weeks.
