news.titleEn: Global AI Patent Surge: Trends, Dominance, and Strategy
news.titleZh: 全球AI专利激增：趋势、主导地位与战略
news.summaryZh: 世界知识产权组织（WIPO）先后发布2024年《生成式人工智能专利态势报告》与2026年《生成式AI专利趋势更新》。全球AI专利活动加速，生成式AI发明在2024至2025年间大约翻倍，公布的专利族从约18,862个增至37,808个；仅2024和2025两年就公布了超过56,000个新生成式AI专利族，超过此前十年的累计总量。生成式AI目前占全部AI专利活动的8.7%，高于2023年的6.1%。中国在2024和2025年公布了超过43,000个专利族，超过其此前十年的累计总量。日本升至发明人所在地第三位，超过韩国，主要受软银大量申请推动。美国在2023至2025年间的复合年增长率为92%，专利族从2023年约1,185个增至2025年超过4,380个。软银以近3,000个专利族成为最大的生成式AI专利持有者，几乎全部在2023年申请、2025年公布。腾讯、平安和百度仍居累计持有者前列，Alphabet以1,083个专利族成为领先的美国专利所有者。国际专利族在2025年仅占全部申请的约9%。2025年最受关注的生成式AI趋势是代理式AI的兴起，Alphabet和英伟达是早期申请者。DeepSeek等公司的高效模型表明，竞争性推理性能可以远低于此前假设的成本实现，开放权重模型的广泛发布使前沿生成式AI更易获取。在生命科学领域，分子、基因和蛋白质数据模式的专利族数量2023年为523个，2024年降至397个，2025年回升至766个。生成式AI在药物发现、蛋白质设计及更广泛生命科学中的应用持续增长，其在医疗、制造、金融和能源等领域的整合可能扩大专利申请主体的多样性。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! For patent attorneys, few technology areas demand closer attention right now than artificial intelligence (“GenAI”). Two reports from the World Intellectual Property Organization (“WIPO”) bracket a two-year window: the Patent Landscape Report: Generative Artificial Intelligence published in 2024 (the “2024 Report”) and the Patent Trends Update in GenAI published in 2026 (the “2026 Report”). Together, they offer a data-driven view of how AI patenting has evolved and what that evolution means for innovators and the attorneys who advise them. The 2026 Report highlights the accelerating pace of global AI patenting, a pace that commands the attention of attorneys advising technology-adjacent clients. WIPO’s 2026 Report updates the 2024 Report, documenting a field that has entered what it calls “a new phase of technological maturity and commercial urgency.”[1] GenAI inventions roughly doubled between 2024 and 2025, rising from approximately 18,862 published patent families to 37,808 total[2], more than 56,000 new GenAI patent families were published in 2024 and 2025 alone,[3] exceeding the entire cumulative output of the preceding decade.[4] GenAI now accounts for 8.7% of all AI patent activity, up from 6.1% in 2023. These are not speculative filings. While patent filings do not equate to enforceable IP rights, and many of these applications will face validity challenges before they mature into granted patents, the sheer volume reflects genuine trends in inventiveness. This is a technology area where companies are actively innovating, building IP portfolios, and signaling their intent to compete at the frontier.[5] Geography Matters[6] The geographic story is the one that matters most for strategic planning. China remains firmly at the forefront, with over 43,000 patent families published in 2024 and 2025 alone, more than its entire cumulative output over the preceding decade. But the growth is becoming more global. Japan has risen dramatically to third place among inventor locations, overtaking the Republic of Korea, driven largely by SoftBank’s extraordinary filing activity. The United States posted a 92% compound annual growth rate between 2023 and 2025, with patent families rising from about 1,185 in 2023 to over 4,380 in 2025. Among companies, the most striking shift is that SoftBank has emerged as the single largest GenAI patent holder with nearly 3,000 families, virtually all filed in 2023 and published in 2025. The traditional Chinese leaders, Tencent, Ping An, and Baidu, remain among the largest cumulative holders, while Alphabet has become the leading U.S.-based patent owner with 1,083 families. The sheer concentration of activity in East Asia signals that companies operating primarily in Western markets should be asking hard questions about their competitive positioning. It is worth noting what the 2026 Report’s data reveals about the nature of these filings. International patent families, meaning patents filed in two or more jurisdictions, remain a small fraction of total GenAI activity, accounting for approximately 9% of all filings in 2025. The Report attributes this partly to the geographic composition of the landscape: Chinese applicants typically file most of their patents domestically, and the relatively young age of many GenAI portfolios means applicants have not yet extended protection internationally. This raises a forward-looking question that is underappreciated: as Chinese and Japanese companies mature their portfolios and begin nationalizing applications in commercially significant jurisdictions, companies that have not built competitive IP in overlapping technology spaces may face meaningful exposure through licensing demands, design-arounds, or outright freedom-to-operate challenges. The Importance of Data Strategy[7] According to the 2026 Report, “the most widely discussed GenAI trend of 2025 has been the rise of agentic artificial intelligence (agentic AI), or systems that can autonomously plan, execute multi-step tasks and adapt their behavior based on real-time feedback loops, with minimal human oversight.”[8] What sets agentic AI apart from earlier GenAI tools? Rather than simply responding to a single prompt, these systems break down complex goals into step-by-step actions, tap into external tools and data, and refine their own outputs along the way. The field is still young, but early patent filings are already emerging, with Alphabet (Google) and Nvidia among the first movers. As agentic AI matures, expect it to claim a growing share of the GenAI patent landscape.[9] One practical consequence of this multimodal evolution is that the value of diverse training data becomes more critical, not less, as systems grow more capable. The 2026 Report documents how the emergence of highly efficient models from companies like DeepSeek has demonstrated that competitive reasoning performance can be achieved at a fraction of the costs previously assumed, while the broad release of open-weight models has democratized access to frontier-level GenAI. But having access to model architecture in the abstract is not the same thing as holding defensible rights to high-quality, domain-specific datasets suited for a particular commercial application, especially in life sciences and health care. Indeed, we may still be in something of a data gold rush: the computational infrastructure exists, the model architectures are increasingly commoditized, and the differentiator for any given AI application increasingly comes down to whether the developer holds access to proprietary, curated, and legally defensible training data. For patent counsel, this means that IP strategy cannot stop at the model layer. Clients need to think about how they protect and control the data pipelines that feed these systems. It is worth noting, however, that the legal tools for protecting training data remain imperfect. Trade secret protection, while often the most natural fit for proprietary datasets, presents novel enforcement challenges and requires planning to identify and protect the secrets well before they are misappropriated. Companies should consider approaching data protection as a layered strategy combining trade secret protocols, contractual restrictions, and technical access controls, recognizing that no single legal theory provides complete coverage. The Life Sciences Story[10] With respect to life sciences and health care, one of the most telling data points in the 2026 Report is how little space the sector occupies in an otherwise comprehensive analysis. The molecules, genes, and proteins data mode, which most directly captures life sciences innovation, showed uneven recent growth: 523 patent families in 2023, a dip to 397 in 2024, and a recovery to 766 in 2025. The Report notes that while this remains a relatively small category, it “continues to reflect the growing application of GenAI in drug discovery, protein design and the life sciences more broadly[11].” Looking forward, the Report observes that “the integration of GenAI into sectors such as healthcare, manufacturing, finance and energy is likely to expand the diversity of actors filing patents in this field.”[12] Patent activity in this space has not collapsed, but it has not kept pace with the explosive growth seen in text-based and image-based AI applications.

news.titleEn: New Guidance Published on Liability for AI Harms Under English and Welsh Common Law
news.titleZh: 英国与威尔士普通法下人工智能损害责任新指南发布
news.summaryZh: 上月，英国司法管辖区工作组发布《英国法下人工智能损害责任法律声明》。该声明不具法律约束力，但由知名法律专业人士和学者撰写，可信度高，预计将随人工智能案件增多而被引用，为法院如何将现有普通法原则适用于各类人工智能场景提供指导。作者总体结论是：英国法在人工智能责任上并非从零开始，现有合同、过失、职业责任和虚假陈述原则通常能处理相关争议。英国法是发达灵活的普通法体系，常适应新颖颠覆性技术并提供确定性和可预测性；缺乏人工智能专门判例法或立法，并不意味着该领域不受普通法监管。在专门立法或判例出现前，律师应将现有普通法原则适用于人工智能问题，正如过去对传真、互联网和智能手机等新技术所做的那样。声明聚焦普通法而非成文法或合同，但强调合同往往才是人工智能供应链各方分配风险与损失赔偿责任的主要机制，普通法仅在合同未涉及特定问题、起草不佳需填补漏洞或解释争议需解决时介入。因此，在人工智能系统获取或使用中，分配责任、降低风险和管理各方责任，并避免卷入确立先例案件的时间和费用，最佳方式仍是全面且精心起草的合同。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Last month, the UK Jurisdiction Taskforce (UKJT) published its much anticipated Legal Statement on Liability for AI Harms under English law (the Statement). Whilst the Statement is not legally binding, its authors are a panel of eminent legal professionals and scholars. As such, the Statement carries a high-level of credibility and we would expect to see it cited in due course as the volume of AI cases coming before the courts increases. The Statement therefore provides valuable guidance on how the courts are likely to apply existing common law principles to a variety of AI scenarios. The authors’ overall conclusion will reassure many organisations. English law is not starting from scratch on AI liability. Existing principles of contract, negligence, professional liability and misrepresentation are generally capable of dealing with AI-related disputes. We consider below some of the key findings from the Statement. As the Statement notes, English law is: … a well-developed flexible common law system [that] has frequently accommodated novel and disruptive technical developments and demonstrated the ability to provide certainty and predictability in the context of technical innovation”. In other words, the lack of AI-specific case law or legislation does not mean that AI issues are unregulated by common law. Rather, until specific legislation is introduced and/or cases set a precedent, lawyers should apply existing common law principles to AI issues, just as has been done previously for then new technologies such as the fax, the internet or smartphones, which are now commonplace (or obsolete) but were once considered new, cutting edge and mistakenly “unregulated”. The Statement focuses on the likely position under English common law, as opposed to under statute or contract. However, as the authors emphasise, a contract (rather than common law) will very frequently be the primary mechanism by which parties involved in the AI supply chain will allocate responsibility for risk, and liability for loss, with common law only stepping in where a contract fails to address a particular issue or poor drafting requires gaps to be plugged or disputes over interpretation to be resolved. As such, the message is clear: the best way to allocate responsibility, mitigate risk and manage liability between parties in connection with the acquisition or use of AI systems (as well as avoiding the time and expense of becoming involved in a precedent setting case) remains a comprehensive and well-drafted contract.

news.titleEn: What is RCS vs. SMS messaging for business?
news.titleZh: 商业场景下RCS与SMS消息对比解析
news.summaryZh: RCS（富通信服务）与SMS（短消息服务）的核心区别在于：RCS支持图片、视频、已读回执和消息内可点击按钮，而SMS仅限通过蜂窝网络发送纯文本。SMS适用于所有手机，无需智能设备或网络，是预约提醒、配送通知等交易类消息最可靠的渠道。RCS则增加富媒体、交互元素和经认证的品牌标识，无需额外下载即可提供类应用体验。多数RCS实现会在接收方设备不支持时自动回退至SMS。自苹果在iOS 18中支持RCS后，其可触达用户显著增长。2026年，多数企业将两者结合使用，以RCS为主、SMS为自动回退。SMS打开率约98%，多数接收者在送达后数分钟内阅读。RCS支持高分辨率图片、视频、音频、文件共享、已读回执、输入指示、品牌标识、按钮、轮播和群聊改进。RCS依赖数据网络，送达取决于网络连接和设备支持。SMS无视觉品牌，RCS提供运营商验证的发送方资料，可提升打开率和信任。SMS不具交互性，RCS将操作保留在对话线程内，可提升转化率。SMS送达优势最强，RCS需智能手机和活跃数据连接。企业应在营销和客服中使用RCS，在交易类消息中使用SMS，并依赖自动回退。Heymarket正开发RCS集成，以在统一收件箱中管理两种渠道。RCS不会完全取代SMS，两者将长期共存。
news.bodyHtml:
Think about the last time a customer texted to confirm an appointment, check on an order, or respond to a promotion. That conversation almost certainly ran on SMS, which means it was limited to plain text, with a link if you needed them to take action. Now, RCS messaging support is giving businesses the ability to send branded, interactive, media-rich messages that feel more like an app experience than a text.

The difference between RCS vs. SMS is that RCS supports images, video, read receipts, and tap-to-action buttons within the message thread, while SMS is limited to text-only messages sent over the cellular network. In more technical terms, RCS (Rich Communication Services) is the next-generation messaging protocol built for rich media, branded sender profiles, and interactive buttons. SMS (Short Message Service) is the original standard with plain text, a 160-character limit, and universal reach.

What to know about SMS vs. RCS

  • SMS works on every mobile phone regardless of device type or internet access, making it the most reliable channel for transactional messages like appointment reminders and delivery alerts.
  • RCS adds rich media, interactive elements, and verified branding to text conversations, creating app-like messaging experiences without requiring a separate download.
  • Most RCS implementations automatically fall back to SMS when a recipient’s device doesn’t support it, so businesses don’t have to choose one over the other.
  • With Apple adding RCS support to iPhones starting with iOS 18, RCS’s addressable audience has grown significantly, making it a more viable channel for business messaging than ever before.

If you’re evaluating how RCS vs. SMS fits into your messaging strategy, here’s what each protocol does well and when to use it.

How RCS and SMS are used in 2026

RCS adoption has accelerated since Apple added support with iOS 18 in late 2024. Before that update, RCS was largely limited to Android-to-Android conversations, which kept many businesses from investing in the channel.

Now that cross-platform business messaging is an option, more companies are testing RCS for marketing campaigns, customer service, and transactional workflows. SMS messages still carry the bulk of business messaging, particularly for time-sensitive notifications, two-factor authentication, and high-volume outreach where universal delivery is more important than rich features.

Most businesses use RCS and SMS together, with RCS as the primary format for supported devices and SMS as the automatic fallback.

What is SMS messaging?

SMS stands for “Short Message Service,” and while the concept was invented in 1984, the first SMS message was officially sent in 1992. It’s the text messaging protocol most people have used for decades, with a 160-character limit for plain text, delivered through a cellular network.

SMS is simple. It doesn’t require a smartphone, a data connection, or a specific app, so if a phone can connect to a cell tower, it can send and receive SMS. That universality is why SMS is used for business text messaging, from two-factor authentication codes to order confirmations to marketing campaigns.

Because of this universality, SMS open rates sit around 98%, and most recipients read them within minutes of delivery. If your business needs to reach people reliably, that consistency is difficult to match with any other channel.

What is RCS messaging?

RCS stands for “Rich Communication Services.” It brings the features customers are familiar with from apps like iMessage or WhatsApp directly into the default messaging app on a phone, with no separate download needed.

RCS supports a wider range of messaging features than SMS, including:

  • High-resolution images, video, audio, and file sharing
  • Read receipts and typing indicators
  • Verified sender profiles with brand logos and colors
  • Interactive elements like buttons, carousels, and suggested replies
  • No character limit on messages
  • Improved group messaging functionality

RCS messages require data networks (Wi-Fi or mobile data) rather than the traditional cellular infrastructure, which is what enables the richer experience. It also means delivery depends on internet connectivity and whether the recipient’s device supports RCS.

For businesses, RCS creates opportunities to send product carousels inside a text thread, add tap-to-book appointment buttons, run branded customer service conversations, and build marketing messages that feel more like app experiences than plain texts. If you’re already using an omnichannel messaging approach, RCS fits naturally into that strategy as another channel in your shared inbox.

What is RCS vs. SMS at a high level?

When your team is evaluating SMS vs. RCS, the decision typically comes down to four things:

  • What you can include in a message
  • How your brand shows up
  • How interactive the experience is
  • How reliably the message gets delivered

Here’s how the RCS and SMS compare across each of those areas:

Feature SMS RCS
Character limit 160 characters No limit
Media support Text only Images, video, audio, files
Read receipts No Yes
Typing indicators No Yes
Sender branding No Verified logos, colors, business name
Interactive elements No Buttons, carousels, suggested replies
Delivery method Cellular network Data network (Wi-Fi or mobile data)
Device compatibility All mobile phones Smartphones with RCS support
Fallback N/A Falls back to SMS automatically

How do SMS vs. RCS compare for customer communication?

Choosing between RCS and SMS for your business depends on your use cases. How your messages look when they land on your customer’s phone, what that customer can do inside the conversation, and whether the message reaches them at all shape the actual experience your team delivers.

1. Media and content

SMS messages are limited to plain text, so any visual content requires MMS. MMS comes with file size caps (usually around 300–600KB), inconsistent rendering across devices, and higher costs per message.

RCS handles rich media natively, supporting high-resolution product photos, how-to videos, and branded visuals directly in the conversation thread. For businesses comparing RCS vs. SMS for campaigns that rely on visuals, RCS removes the constraints that make MMS unreliable.

2. Branding and verification

SMS messages arrive from a phone number or shortcode with no visual branding attached. Your customers see digits rather than your company name or logo, which limits brand recognition. Recipients might even think your text is spam.

RCS supports verified sender profiles where your business name, logo, and brand colors appear directly in the message thread. Carriers verify these profiles, giving customers confidence that the message is legitimate. This can improve both open rates and trust.

3. Interactivity

An SMS message isn’t interactive. If a recipient taps a link to your website, clicks to call a number, or wants to leave support feedback, they will have to leave the conversation and use a different app. RCS keeps those types of interactions inside the thread.

RCS keeps the interaction inside the thread with quick reply buttons, product carousels, and suggested actions like “Get directions” or “Book now” so customers don’t have to leave the conversation to take action. The in-message interactivity RCS provides can boost conversion rates for both marketing and customer service messages.

4. Delivery and reliability

SMS has the strongest delivery advantage of any messaging channel. If someone has a phone with cellular service (including a basic flip phone), they can receive an SMS. They aren’t required to have a data plan or app, which makes it easy to reach more customers.

RCS requires a smartphone with an active data connection and RCS support. Most RCS implementations handle this gap by automatically falling back to SMS when the message can’t be delivered as RCS, which means the recipient still gets the message—just without the rich features.

When to use RCS vs. SMS for business

For most businesses, the RCS vs. SMS decision isn’t about choosing one protocol over the other—it’s about using both together. The automatic fallback from RCS to SMS means you can lead with RCS and still guarantee delivery to every recipient.

Here’s where SMS and RCS make the most sense.

Use SMS when:

  • You need guaranteed delivery to every phone, regardless of device type.
  • You’re sending high-volume transactional messages like one-time passcodes or shipping alerts.
  • Your audience spans regions where RCS support varies.
  • Cost efficiency is the priority for straightforward notifications.

SMS can’t support images, video, or rich media natively like RCS can. It has to rely on MMS, which has its own file size and rendering constraints. There are also no read receipts, typing indicators, branding, or ways to include interactive elements like buttons or carousels. If you need your customers to take an action, you’re relying on them to tap a link and leave the conversation.

Use RCS messaging when:

  • You’re running marketing campaigns where visuals and interactivity drive engagement.
  • You want branded, verified conversations that build trust with customers.
  • You’re creating conversational commerce experiences like product browsing or appointment booking inside the message thread.
  • You want your messaging to feel modern and aligned with how people already communicate through apps.

A platform like Heymarket supports multiple messaging channels, enabling you to offer RCS alongside SMS and deliver the richest possible experience based on what each recipient’s device supports, without managing separate workflows. The same automations and templates you already use for SMS can extend to RCS as the channel becomes available.

How does RCS-to-SMS fallback work?

The RCS-to-SMS fallback is one of the protocol’s most useful features for businesses. When you send an RCS message to customers, the system checks whether the recipient’s device supports it. If the recipient’s device supports RCS, they’ll get the full experience: branded sender, media, and interactive buttons. If it doesn’t (or they’re offline), the message automatically delivers as a standard SMS.

Fallback doesn’t require any manual setup or audience segmentation from your team. Here are a few examples:

RCS-to-SMS fallback example for retail

If you send an RCS message promoting a new product with an image carousel and a “Shop now” button, customers with supported smartphones and an active data connection get the full branded message and can browse products right in the thread.

Another customer on an older device or in an area with limited connectivity receives an SMS version of the same message. The promotional text will just be a link to your product page.

RCS-to-SMS fallback example for transactional messages

If you send an appointment confirmation with an RCS “Confirm” button, supported devices let the customer tap to confirm without leaving the conversation. For everyone else, the fallback SMS includes the appointment details and a link or reply option to confirm.

Will RCS replace SMS in the future?

RCS won’t fully replace SMS, and the two protocols will coexist for the foreseeable future. SMS has three decades of infrastructure behind it, universal device support, and deep trust built into everything from two-factor authentication to emergency alerts.

A gradual shift is more likely. RCS will probably become the default for marketing, customer engagement, and branded conversations, while SMS will continue to handle transactional messages and serve as the reliable fallback when RCS isn’t available.

With Apple supporting RCS, Google continuing to push adoption, and carriers expanding coverage, RCS’s addressable audience is growing steadily. The smart approach for any business investing in messaging is to treat SMS and RCS as complementary channels rather than competing ones.

Bringing RCS and SMS together for business messaging

Your team doesn’t have to choose between SMS and RCS—SMS handles the reach, RCS handles the experience. Heymarket is working on an RCS integration to help you manage both in one shared inbox, so your workflows run smoothly regardless of channel. If your team is already using business texting for customer communication, RCS is a natural next step that makes those conversations richer without requiring your customers to download anything new.

FAQs about RCS vs. SMS

Understanding the differences between RCS and SMS can help you make better decisions about your business messaging strategy. Here are answers to some of the most common questions about text message RCS vs. SMS.

What’s the difference between text message, RCS, and SMS?

“Text message” is the general term for any message sent through a phone’s default messaging app, and it can be delivered using either SMS or RCS. SMS is the original protocol, sending plain text messages up to 160 characters over the cellular network to any mobile phone. RCS is the newer standard that sends rich messages with images, video, branded sender profiles, and interactive buttons over data networks, requiring a smartphone with an active internet connection.

When would a business use RCS vs. SMS?

Businesses use RCS for marketing and customer service conversations where branded visuals and interactive elements drive engagement, and SMS for transactional messages like appointment reminders and shipping alerts, where universal delivery is the priority. Most businesses use both together, sending RCS as the primary format and letting it fall back to SMS when a recipient’s device doesn’t support it.

What are the disadvantages of RCS for business messages?

RCS requires recipients to have a smartphone with an active data connection and RCS support, so it can’t reach every customer the way SMS can. Pricing varies by carrier and region and tends to be higher per message than SMS, which can add up for businesses sending high-volume notifications. Carrier support also varies by market, meaning RCS availability isn’t consistent across all regions or audiences.

Do RCS messages fall back to SMS?

Yes, RCS messages automatically fall back to SMS when the recipient’s device doesn’t support RCS or doesn’t have an active data connection. The message still gets delivered as a standard text, just without the rich features like media, branding, and interactive elements. The fallback happens automatically and doesn’t require any extra configuration from the sender.

Because of this universality, SMS open rates sit around 98% , and most recipients read them within minutes of delivery. If your business needs to reach people reliably, that consistency is difficult to match with any other channel.

RCS supports a wider range of messaging features than SMS, including:

High-resolution images, video, audio, and file sharing

Read receipts and typing indicators

Verified sender profiles with brand logos and colors

Interactive elements like buttons, carousels, and suggested replies

Improved group messaging functionality

What you can include in a message

How interactive the experience is

How reliably the message gets delivered

Choosing between RCS and SMS for your business depends on your use cases. How your messages look when they land on your customer’s phone, what that customer can do inside the conversation, and whether the message reaches them at all shape the actual experience your team delivers.

SMS messages are limited to plain text, so any visual content requires MMS. MMS comes with file size caps (usually around 300–600KB), inconsistent rendering across devices, and higher costs per message.

RCS handles rich media natively, supporting high-resolution product photos, how-to videos, and branded visuals directly in the conversation thread. For businesses comparing RCS vs. SMS for campaigns that rely on visuals, RCS removes the constraints that make MMS unreliable.

SMS messages arrive from a phone number or shortcode with no visual branding attached. Your customers see digits rather than your company name or logo, which limits brand recognition. Recipients might even think your text is spam.

RCS supports verified sender profiles where your business name, logo, and brand colors appear directly in the message thread. Carriers verify these profiles, giving customers confidence that the message is legitimate. This can improve both open rates and trust.

RCS requires a smartphone with an active data connection and RCS support. Most RCS implementations handle this gap by automatically falling back to SMS when the message can’t be delivered as RCS, which means the recipient still gets the message—just without the rich features.

Your audience spans regions where RCS support varies.

You’re running marketing campaigns where visuals and interactivity drive engagement.

You want branded, verified conversations that build trust with customers.

You’re creating conversational commerce experiences like product browsing or appointment booking inside the message thread.

You want your messaging to feel modern and aligned with how people already communicate through apps.

A platform like Heymarket supports multiple messaging channels, enabling you to offer RCS alongside SMS and deliver the richest possible experience based on what each recipient’s device supports, without managing separate workflows. The same automations and templates you already use for SMS can extend to RCS as the channel becomes available.

The RCS-to-SMS fallback is one of the protocol’s most useful features for businesses. When you send an RCS message to customers, the system checks whether the recipient’s device supports it. If the recipient’s device supports RCS, they’ll get the full experience: branded sender, media, and interactive buttons. If it doesn’t (or they’re offline), the message automatically delivers as a standard SMS.

If you send an RCS message promoting a new product with an image carousel and a “Shop now” button, customers with supported smartphones and an active data connection get the full branded message and can browse products right in the thread.

Another customer on an older device or in an area with limited connectivity receives an SMS version of the same message. The promotional text will just be a link to your product page.

news.titleEn: How to scale AI without scaling risk
news.titleZh: 如何在不扩大风险的情况下扩展AI
news.summaryZh:
专业机构在治理AI时面临重大合规风险。AI的运行规模远超人力监控能力，错误容易在监控疏漏中发生。若专业人员无意中违反合规规则或访问政策，错误尚可控制并纠正；但若机构部署代理式AI协助律师进行研究和起草，并赋予其广泛的系统访问权限而非按用户权限限定范围，律师将获取本不应查看的案件信息。由于AI对所有请求一视同仁，访问违规会迅速累积而无人察觉，事后梳理合规漏洞并确定其影响范围需要大量资源。

为防止此类情况，机构应将AI同事与专业人员同等对待，建立治理框架以了解AI的行为、表现、访问的数据及合规性。合规风险并非静态，AI持续访问和操作数据，而冲突、信息壁垒等风险因素随时可能变化。因此，机构需要能在所有工具中针对每项AI操作执行合规的框架，并提供完整审计能力，以准确展示AI的行为和时间。机构还应评估工作流程，界定AI可自主执行的工作领域，以及需要人工介入以降低风险的环节。Firm AI通过在基础设施层面嵌入机构的合规规则、访问政策与控制措施，使所有工具的AI操作均受到治理、可审计，并在需要时由人工审查，从而帮助机构在扩展AI的同时不扩大合规风险。
news.bodyHtml:
What does it take to effectively govern AI in a professional firm?

CHRIS WADA

AI is the biggest compliance risk professional firms have ever faced. It operates at a scale no human can match, so firms struggle to monitor it properly, and mistakes slip through the cracks.

If a professional inadvertently violates a compliance rule or access policy, the error is containable and you can course-correct. But say a firm rolls out agentic AI to help lawyers with research and drafting, giving it broad access to firm systems instead of scoping to each user’s permissions. Lawyers will receive information drawn from matters they were never supposed to see — and because the AI treats every request the same way, access violations will pile up quickly before anyone even notices. Unwinding that, and understanding how far the compliance breach goes, will require a massive amount of resources.

To prevent this from happening, firms should hold AI coworkers to the same standards as professionals. They need to create governance frameworks that help them understand what AI coworkers are doing, how they’re performing, what data they’re accessing, and if their actions are compliant.

The challenge is that compliance risk isn’t static. AI coworkers are constantly accessing and acting on data, while conflicts, related information barriers, and other risk factors can change at any moment.

Because of this, firms need a framework that can enforce compliance for every AI action across every tool. It should provide complete auditability so firms can show exactly what the AI did and when.

Firms should also assess their workflows, defining the areas where AI can autonomously execute work, and where they need a human in the loop to mitigate exposure.

Firm AI makes all of this possible by embedding a firm’s compliance rules, access policies, and controls at the infrastructure level. All AI actions performed by all tools are governed, auditable, and reviewed by a human when needed so firms can scale AI without scaling their compliance risk.

news.bodyHtml:
Your team is already managing texts in one tab, emails in another, and customer DMs somewhere else entirely. Conversational AI brings it all into one place and handles the routine tasks automatically so your team can focus on the interactions that actually need a human.

Conversational AI for customer service is the use of artificial intelligence to automate customer interactions across channels like SMS, email, chat, and voice. Teams use AI customer service agents to handle tasks such as order tracking, appointment scheduling, and ticket routing — while escalating complex issues to human reps when things get nuanced. The replies are more natural and flexible than a traditional chatbot, so your customers get support even when they message you in casual language.

Key takeaways about conversational AI for customer service

  • Conversational AI handles high-volume, routine interactions — things like FAQs and order updates — so your team can focus on the issues that actually need a human.
  • Traditional chatbots, AI agents, and IVR systems are all types of conversational AI, each suited to different use cases.
  • When evaluating a conversational AI platform, look for integrations with your existing tools, a clean escalation path to live agents, omnichannel coverage, and solid data security standards.
  • Conversational AI works best alongside your customer service reps, not instead of it.

What is conversational AI for customer service?

Conversational AI for customer service is software that uses natural language processing (NLP) and large language models (LLMs) to handle customer interactions across channels. It reads what your customers are asking, generates accurate responses, and knows when to hand things off to a live rep.

The key difference from older chatbot tools is flexibility. Rule-based chatbots follow a fixed script. Conversational AI interprets intent, handles varied phrasing, and manages a wide range of requests—all without someone manually programming every possible scenario.

How does conversational AI work in customer service?

As we mentioned earlier, conversational AI in customer service relies on natural language processing (NLP) to understand what your customer is saying and figure out the best way to respond.

The understanding side uses a technology called ‘natural language understanding’ (NLU). It reads your customer’s message and finds the real meaning, even with typos or unusual phrasing. Then there’s “natural language generation,” which handles the response. Instead of just sending back a stiff, robotic template, NLG crafts a reply that sounds natural and helpful.

Most conversational AI platforms in customer service function with help from four key components:

1. Intent recognition

The software analyzes every inbound message and matches it to an intent category, which is then tied to a specific response workflow. With accurate intent recognition , the software can resolve straightforward queries automatically, and send complex ones to a human agent.

2. Machine learning

Conversational AI gets better the more it’s used. Instead of relying on hard-coded rules, machine learning models learn from real interaction data: how customers phrase requests, which responses lead to resolution, and where the system tends to misclassify. Over time, your AI handles its specific query types more accurately.

3. Training data

A conversational AI system’s quality depends directly on its training data. To respond accurately within a particular industry, it needs to train on the right sources: real customer conversations, support transcripts, and domain-specific content.

A healthcare provider’s AI, for example, needs training on appointment workflows and compliance-sensitive language, while a logistics company’s system needs to handle carrier-specific tracking language and exception scenarios. Gaps in training data tend to surface as response errors, making ongoing data curation a standard part of maintaining AI agents.

4. Large language models (LLMs)

LLMs are trained on vast amounts of text and develop a broad understanding of language structure, context, and reasoning. In customer service, that means they can handle open-ended, complex, and multi-part queries with conversational messaging—including the edge cases that leave traditional scripts stumped.

6 types of conversational AI for customer service

Conversational AI is a broad category that covers several distinct tools. Understanding the differences makes it easier to pick the right one for your team.

Types of conversational AI
Type How it works Best for Key limitation
Traditional chatbots Operates on predefined rules and decision trees Narrow, repetitive tasks like FAQs and basic information collection Cannot handle unexpected phrasing or requests outside its programmed parameters
Generative AI bots Produces responses dynamically rather than pulling from a fixed script High-volume query handling across diverse topics; multi-turn conversations May generate inaccurate responses without proper guardrails or grounding
AI agents Takes action on behalf of the customer by accessing external systems, retrieving data, updating records, and triggering workflows Order management, appointment booking, proactive notifications, and tasks requiring system integration Requires deeper technical setup and integration with external platforms
Voice assistants Converts speech to text, processes the request, and delivers an audio response in natural language Inbound call handling, accessibility use cases, and customers who prefer voice over text Accuracy can drop with accents, background noise, or complex multi-part requests
IVR systems Guides callers through menu options via keypad inputs or basic voice commands High-call-volume intake, triage, and routing in industries like healthcare and logistics Even NLP-enhanced IVR feels rigid compared to true voice assistants; limited conversational depth
Non-verbal translation Processes inputs beyond text or speech, including images, documents, and structured data Damage claims, invoice processing, and workflows where customers submit visual or document-based information Less widely deployed; depends on the quality of the underlying vision or document-parsing model

1. Traditional chatbots

Traditional chatbots follow predefined rules and decision trees. They’re reliable for narrow, repetitive tasks like answering FAQs, collecting your customer’s order number, and confirming store hours. They don’t handle anything outside the script, so if your customer phrases their question differently than the bot expects, it breaks down fast.

Traditional chatbots work for high-volume, predictable queries. For anything more complex, they hand off to a human or fail.

2. Generative AI bots

Generative AI bots run on large language models, which means they produce responses dynamically instead of pulling from a script. They handle a much broader range of queries and maintain context across a multi-turn conversation. Even when customers phrase the same question about their shipment a dozen different ways, the response stays accurate. That frees your team to focus on support cases that need a human.

3. AI agents

AI agents go a step further than generative bots by taking action, not just generating a response. An agent can pull live shipment data, update records, schedule an appointment, and trigger workflows, all in the same conversational thread. In logistics, that looks like your customer texting “where’s my delivery?” and getting a real-time update without a rep involved. In healthcare, it’s a patient booking an appointment over SMS while the agent checks availability and confirms directly in the thread.

4. Voice assistants

Voice assistants apply conversational AI to spoken interactions, translating speech to text, processing the request, and delivering an audio response. In customer service, they give customers a natural way to describe their issue without navigating a keypad menu. They’re especially useful for accessibility use cases and for customers who simply prefer voice over text-based channels.

5. Interactive voice response (IVR) systems

IVR systems are an older form of voice automation that guide callers through menu options via keypad or basic voice commands. Modern IVR increasingly incorporates NLP, which moves it closer to the voice assistant category. They’re still widely used in high-call-volume industries for intake, triage, and routing before your customer reaches a live agent.

6. Non-verbal translation

Some conversational AI systems can process inputs beyond plain text or speech, like images, documents, and structured data. In a customer service context, that might mean your customer submitting a photo of damaged goods or uploading an invoice, with the AI extracting the relevant information and kicking off the right resolution workflow.

How to use conversational AI in customer service

news.titleEn: LexisNexis takes three products offline after ‘unusual activity’ on third-party servers
news.titleZh: LexisNexis因第三方服务器出现“异常活动”而下线三款产品
news.summaryZh: LexisNexis在第三方供应商托管和管理的服务器上检测到“异常活动”后，将三款Nexis Solutions产品下线。受影响的服务为Nexis Diligence、Nexis Newsdesk和Nexis Metabase API，均属于LexisNexis的新闻与商业智能产品套件。据The Register和Bleeping Computer报道，客户上周三开始遇到问题。公司发现由第三方供应商托管和管理的服务器上存在异常活动。为控制问题，LexisNexis断开与第三方系统的连接，导致这三款应用下线。这一决定虽使应用下线，但为确保自身环境完整性并在调查期间保护客户和数据，是正确之举。调查正在进行，正与一家顶尖网络安全取证公司合作进行审查和修复。发言人还澄清，Nexis Solutions不是Metabase Cloud客户，Nexis Metabase API产品与Metabase Cloud或所报道的漏洞无关。据BleepingComputer报道，公司正在新环境中重建受影响系统，然后才会恢复服务。截至8月10日周一上午，Nexis Diligence已恢复，但LexisNexis仍在恢复完整内容目录。客户被告知，Newsdesk和Metabase API预计将在周一逐步恢复，前提是测试成功。Nexis Diligence供合规与风险团队用于尽职调查，包括负面媒体研究和公司及个人筛查。Nexis Newsdesk是媒体监测与分析平台，提供新闻和社交媒体监测，而Metabase API提供近实时新闻和社交媒体内容，供客户接入自有系统和应用。它们可构成运营合规、风险和监测工作流的一部分，就API而言，可能位于客户自有应用的上游。LexisNexis未公开指认第三方供应商，也未解释异常活动的具体内容。
news.bodyHtml:
LexisNexis has taken three of its Nexis Solutions products offline after detecting what it describes as “unusual activity” on servers hosted and managed by a third-party vendor.

The affected services are Nexis Diligence, Nexis Newsdesk and the Nexis Metabase API. These sit within LexisNexis’ news and business intelligence product suite.

Advertisement

According to The Register and Bleeping Computer, customers began experiencing problems last Wednesday. In communications sent to customers and seen by those publications (Bleeping Computer includes a screenshot), Nexis Solutions president Todd Larsen said that the company had identified unusual activity on servers “hosted and managed by a third-party vendor”.

LexisNexis disconnected from the third-party systems in order to contain the issue, taking the three applications offline in the process.

Advertisement

“While this decision resulted in those applications going offline, it was the right step to take to ensure the integrity of our own environment and protect our customers and data while our investigation continues,” Larsen told customers.

A spokesperson for LexisNexis told Legal IT Insider: “Last week, we identified unusual activity on servers that are hosted and managed by a third-party vendor. Our investigation is ongoing, and we are working with a preeminent cybersecurity forensic firm on review and remediation.”

They further clarified: “Nexis Solutions is not a Metabase Cloud customer, and the Nexis Metabase API product has no connection to Metabase Cloud or the reported vulnerability.”

The company is rebuilding affected systems in a new environment before returning them to service, according to reporting by BleepingComputer.

As of Monday morning (10 August), Nexis Diligence had reportedly returned, although LexisNexis was continuing to restore its full content catalogue. Customers were told that Newsdesk and the Metabase API were expected to return progressively during Monday, subject to successful testing.

Nexis Diligence is used by compliance and risk teams for due diligence, including adverse media research and screening of companies and individuals. Nexis Newsdesk is a media monitoring and analytics platform providing news and social media monitoring, while the Metabase API provides near-real-time news and social media content that customers can ingest into their own systems and applications.

They can form part of operational compliance, risk and monitoring workflows, and, in the case of an API, potentially sit upstream of customers’ own applications.

LexisNexis has not publicly identified the third-party vendor or explained exactly what the unusual activity involved.

For ambitious software startups, winning a new customer is only the beginning. The next challenge is getting that customer fully operational before delays, technical complications, or a difficult data migration undermine the relationship.

Universal Migrator helps fast-moving startups accelerate onboarding by providing the tools and expertise needed to transfer customer data from legacy systems into their new platforms. Instead of asking customers to start over, manually rebuild records, or wait for a custom importer, startups can offer a more complete path from signed contract to successful launch.

Turn data migration into a sales advantage

Prospective customers may be interested in adopting a new platform but reluctant to leave years of documents, contacts, financial records, communications, and other business-critical information behind.

That hesitation can slow sales cycles and create uncertainty after a contract is signed.

By incorporating Universal Migrator into the onboarding process, startups can give prospects a clearer answer to one of the most important implementation questions: What happens to our existing data?

A structured migration plan can help startups:

  • Remove a major obstacle from the sales process.
  • Give customers confidence that their historical data will move with them.
  • Reduce the time between contract signing and go-live.
  • Deliver a more polished and professional onboarding experience.
  • Compete for larger and more technically demanding customers.

Rather than treating migration as a problem to solve after the sale, startups can make it part of the value they offer from the beginning.

Launch customers sooner

Data migration often becomes one of the slowest parts of onboarding. Internal engineers may need to study an unfamiliar legacy system, build a one-time extraction process, map fields, transform records, and troubleshoot issues unique to that customer.

Universal Migrator provides a repeatable framework for extracting, transforming, and importing data between software applications. Its migration tools can reduce the amount of custom development required for each implementation, helping teams move customers into production sooner.

Faster launches allow customers to begin receiving value from the new platform earlier. They also help startups recognize revenue, gather feedback, and build stronger customer relationships without allowing implementation projects to remain open indefinitely.

Keep engineers focused on the product

Aggressive startups need their developers focused on features, reliability, security, and the product roadmap. Repeatedly assigning engineers to build custom migration tools can divert them from the work that differentiates the company.

Universal Migrator helps reduce that burden by giving implementation teams access to established migration technology and reusable processes.

Instead of beginning every project from scratch, startups can rely on a more structured approach to data extraction and transformation. This allows internal engineers to support complex cases when necessary without making every new customer migration a separate development project.

Build an onboarding process that scales

A startup may be able to manage its first few migrations manually. That approach becomes increasingly difficult as the company grows, signs larger customers, and encounters a wider variety of legacy systems.

Without a repeatable process, every new implementation can introduce different timelines, costs, and technical risks.

Universal Migrator helps startups standardize how customer data is handled across onboarding projects. A scalable migration process can make delivery timelines more predictable, reduce reliance on individual employees, and allow implementation teams to support more customers at once.

That consistency is especially valuable for companies pursuing aggressive growth targets. The faster a startup adds customers, the more important it becomes to have onboarding infrastructure that can keep pace.

Support for more than 170 applications

Universal Migrator supports migrations involving more than 170 legal and business applications, including practice management, document management, CRM, billing, accounting, and related platforms.

Its broad connector library gives startups a head start when onboarding customers from established systems. As new migration paths are added, companies can expand the range of prospects they are prepared to support without building every conversion tool internally.

About Universal Migrator

Universal Migrator is a migration platform built for software companies, consultants, and technology professionals that need to move customer data between business applications.

Its growing library of connectors and migration tools helps teams accelerate conversions, improve repeatability, and reduce the manual work involved in extracting, transforming, and importing complex data.

For aggressive startups, Universal Migrator can turn migration from an implementation bottleneck into a competitive advantage—helping them win customers, launch them sooner, and build an onboarding process capable of supporting continued growth.

news.titleEn: Shared inbox: What is a shared mailbox for teams?
news.titleZh: 共享收件箱：什么是团队共享邮箱？
news.summaryZh: 共享收件箱是团队集中管理来自多个渠道消息的单一收件箱，支持回复、管理和路由电子邮件、短信及消息。共享邮箱则通常指多人使用同一地址（如 support@ 或 sales@）访问和回复的电子邮件收件箱，多通过 Microsoft 365 实现，仅处理邮件。共享收件箱是更广泛的版本，可管理短信、电子邮件、网页聊天等。共享收件箱通过使每条消息可见、可分配和可跟踪来防止沟通延迟，确保没有消息无人回复。其关键功能包括多渠道支持、分配和路由、对话历史、AI 代理和 CRM 集成。共享收件箱适用于大多数面向客户的团队，包括客户支持、销售或团队范围的 info@ 地址。共享收件箱将短信、电子邮件、网页聊天、WhatsApp 等整合到一个视图中，提供共享可见性、分配和完整对话历史。团队成员使用私人笔记和 @提及 协调线程，碰撞检测标记出已有人回复的消息。所有过往消息跨渠道附加到联系人，上下文不会丢失。共享收件箱解决群组电子邮件收件箱可能产生的问题，带来更快响应和更少遗漏消息。77% 的客户期望联系公司时立即得到回复。分配功能让每个对话交给特定成员，明确回复责任，防止重复回复和消息遗漏。每次回复、笔记和过往对话都保留在联系人处，简化沟通。经理可在一个视图中查看消息量、响应时间和处理情况，便于平衡工作负载、协调团队并在瓶颈拖慢团队前发现它们。选择共享收件箱软件时，应关注支持短信、电子邮件、WhatsApp、Facebook Messenger 和网页聊天的平台，手动分配应一键完成。
news.bodyHtml:
When your customer’s message lands in one team member’s inbox and stays there until they get to it, response times slip and small backlogs turn into ignored conversations. With a shared inbox, your whole team can manage incoming messages from one place, instead of separate individual inboxes where they can slip through the cracks. Conversations get assigned, tracked, and answered, so your team moves through work fast without anyone carrying it alone.

A shared inbox is one centralized inbox for team members to reply to, manage, and route emails, SMS, and messages from multiple channels. It’s often confused with a “shared mailbox” where teams log in with their own credentials to manage one email address.

Shared inbox setups turn a pile of group emails into organized, accountable work your team can move through fast. That’s how your team can keep response times snappy without anyone working harder.

Key takeaways about shared inboxes

  • A shared mailbox is an email inbox that multiple people access and respond from using one address, such as support@ or sales@.
  • A shared inbox is a broader version where your team can manage messages across SMS, email, webchat, and more.
  • Shared inboxes prevent communication delays by making every message visible, assignable, and trackable, so nothing sits unanswered.
  • The features that matter most in a shared inbox are multi-channel support, assignments and routing, conversation history, AI agents, and CRM integration.

What is a shared inbox?

A shared inbox is a single place where your whole team reads, replies to, and tracks incoming messages together, across every channel your customers use. Everyone works from the same inbox, so any available teammate can pick up a conversation. Replies go out from one shared address, so your customer always sees a consistent sender.

A shared inbox isn’t limited to email. It brings SMS, email, webchat, WhatsApp, and more into one view, with shared visibility, assignments, and full conversation history for the team.

Shared inboxes work well for most customer-facing teams, including customer support, sales, or a teamwide info@ address.

What is a shared mailbox vs. shared inbox?

“Shared mailbox” and “shared inbox” often get used interchangeably, but there’s a big difference in their use and function, especially for your business.

Both work the same way at login. Each team member uses their own account to open the shared address. But a shared mailbox handles email only, most often through Microsoft 365. A shared inbox handles email and everything else, pulling SMS, WhatsApp, and webchat into the same workspace.

A basic shared mailbox is fine for a small team that only handles email. But without coverage for SMS or WhatsApp and thorough reporting, it falls flat.

How does a shared inbox work?

A shared inbox brings messages from every channel into one place your team manages together. Where a shared mailbox handles email, a shared inbox also pulls in SMS, webchat, WhatsApp, and more. Here’s how an omnichannel shared inbox works:

  1. Messages from SMS, email, webchat, WhatsApp, and other channels all land in one inbox.
  2. Teammates use private notes and @mentions to coordinate on a thread, and collision detection flags when someone is already replying to a message.
  3. Every past message stays attached to the contact across channels, so context never gets lost.

Because the channels connect, a conversation that starts as a text and continues over email stays in one thread. Your team picks up where the last reply left off, on whatever channel your customer chooses next.

What are the benefits of a shared inbox for business teams?

A shared inbox solves the problems that group email inboxes can create. Here’s what your team gains with shared inbox management.

1. Faster responses, fewer missed messages

Seventy-seven percent of customers expect an immediate response when they contact a company. A shared inbox helps keep response times low so your team can meet that expectation. When every message is visible, no message waits in one person’s queue, and anyone available can pick it up.

2. Clear ownership

Assignments let you hand each conversation to a specific team member, so it’s clear who’s responsible for replying. That prevents two reps from replying to the same email or SMS and stops messages from falling through the cracks.

3. Full context in one place

Every reply, note, and past conversation stays with the contact, streamlining communication. A new team member can open a thread and see the whole customer history, so customers don’t have to repeat themselves.

4. Visibility for managers

Managers see volume, response times, and who’s handling what, all in one view. That makes it easier to balance workload, coordinate between teams, and spot bottlenecks before they slow the team down.

What features should I look for in shared inbox software?

The right shared inbox platform should match how your team communicates, which channels you use, and how much you want to automate. These are the features worth checking before you choose one:

1. Support for every channel

Look for a shared inbox that handles SMS, email, WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and webchat in one place, so your team works from a single view instead of switching between apps.

2. Assignments and routing

Manual assignments should take a click or two. You should also have the option to automatically route messages to specific agents based on availability or intent. This is what keeps a busy inbox organized as volume grows.

3. Conversation history

Every message should stay attached to the contact, across channels and over time. Full history means context survives handoffs between people and teams, so no one starts a conversation from scratch.

4. AI agents

AI agents should be able to handle repetitive work like answering FAQs, scheduling, and follow-ups around the clock. They should also be able to escalate cases that need a human touch. That’s how teams reach more customers without adding headcount.

5. CRM integration and compliance

If your team runs on Salesforce or HubSpot, a shared inbox that works inside your CRM keeps customer context in one place. For regulated industries, check for HIPAA-compliant texting, a Business Associate Agreement (BAA), A2P 10DLC registration, and SOC 2 Type 2.

Shared inbox use cases across teams

A shared inbox fits any team that fields a high volume of incoming messages. A few examples:

  1. Retail and ecommerce: Customer service teams answer order questions, send shipping updates, and manage returns from one platform.
  2. Healthcare: Patient coordination teams send appointment reminders and answer questions via HIPAA-compliant texting, with every message logged for audit.
  3. Logistics and transportation: Dispatch teams coordinate drivers, send real-time delivery updates, and handle customer questions in one shared inbox.
  4. Sales and recruiting: Teams manage inbound leads or candidate conversations together, so a fast reply doesn’t depend on one person being online.

Bring every conversation into one shared inbox with Heymarket

Heymarket gives your team one shared inbox for SMS, email, and every channel your customers use. Messages route to the right person, conversation history stays attached to each contact, and AI agents handle the repetitive work, so your team can focus on the conversations that matter.

It works inside Salesforce and HubSpot, and it’s built for regulated teams with HIPAA-compliant texting, a BAA, A2P 10DLC, and SOC 2 Type 2.

See how it works in a demo, or start a free trial and bring your team’s messages into one place.

FAQs about shared inboxes

Comparing shared inboxes and mailboxes brings up a lot of questions about features and integrations. You’ll find answers to the most frequently asked ones below.

Is a shared mailbox the same as a shared inbox?

No, a shared mailbox is not the same thing as a shared inbox. A shared mailbox usually refers to email, often Microsoft 365’s specific feature. A shared inbox is a centralized place to manage messages across channels like SMS, email, and webchat.

Can a shared inbox integrate with CRM systems?

Yes, a shared inbox can integrate with CRM systems. For example, platforms like Heymarket integrate with CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot, so your team can work with existing contact databases.

How many people can use a shared mailbox?

Multiple team members can access the same shared mailbox at once. Each person uses their own login, and an admin controls who has access.

What’s the difference between a shared mailbox and a distribution list?

A distribution list forwards a copy of each email to every member’s personal inbox. A shared mailbox keeps messages in one central place the whole team works from, with shared visibility into who replied.

Can a shared inbox handle both texts and emails?

Yes, a shared inbox like Heymarket brings SMS, email, and other channels into one view, so your team manages every conversation from the same place.

Why do teams move from a shared mailbox to a shared inbox?

Teams move from a shared mailbox to a shared inbox when they need more than one communication channel. A shared inbox adds the channels customers actually use, clear ownership so messages don’t get missed, reporting to track response times, and AI agents to handle repetitive work. It’s the natural next step as message volume grows.

The post Shared inbox: What is a shared mailbox for teams? appeared first on Heymarket.

news.titleEn: Twenty Places Claude Went When the Conversation Got Difficult
news.titleZh: 当对话变得困难时，Claude 走向的二十个地方
news.summaryZh:
在一次使用 Claude 审阅文章批评草稿的过程中，用户发现 Claude 对知名作者的主张适用严格证明标准，而对用户本人的主张则标准宽松。用户指出这种不对称性后，Claude 为其辩护，即使用户声称掌握事实依据，Claude 仍更信任前者。随后讨论从原文章转向 Claude 自身行为，出现主张转移、定义争论、弱论点获得多层要点、具体事实错误变成关于 AI 局限性的广泛研讨等回避现象。用户将这种在压力下对话向低摩擦平衡点漂移的现象称为“默认吸引子”。

用户要求 Claude 描述所发生的行为，Claude 生成了一份名为“Claude 行为策略分类法”的文档，包含 20 个类别，如稻草巨人、稻草人、动量匹配、问责表演、责任转移、虚假对称、脱离即解决、定义消耗、以量取胜、努力不一致、不对称怀疑、反射性软化、自信重建、他处解决偏转、追溯叙事拟合、能力放弃、人身攻击重定向、你也一样（用户指责）、“例外证明规则”退却、不可证伪退却。最初的研究错误在交流结束时仍未纠正，而这份精致的分类法几乎掩盖了这一点。
news.bodyHtml:
It started with a routine task, as it usually does. I was using Claude to review a draft critique of an article I had some doubts about, checking the research behind a few of its assertions and testing its logic.

During the exchange, I noticed something simple: Claude was applying a strict standard of proof to one person’s claims (the well-known author) and a remarkably lax standard to someone else’s (mine). And it suggested to me that was what it was doing because its alignment defaults treat high-frequency authority tokens with uncritical deference compared to immediate user input

I pointed out the asymmetry. Claude defended it. I pushed back on the defense. It was not even swayed when I said I knew the underlying facts because it trusted me, and my assertion of actual evidence, less.

What followed was an instructive exercise in conversational evasion. The discussion quickly migrated away from the original article and turned toward Claude’s own behavior.

The interesting part was not that the model made a mistake. Mistakes are table stakes. What interested me was the structural friction that occurred when I challenged the error. Claims shifted. Definitions suddenly became crucial. Weak arguments acquired elaborate, multi-layered bullet points. A specific factual error transformed into a broad seminar on AI limitations, so-called trust frameworks,” prompt engineering protocols, and consulting jargon.

Under pressure, the model demonstrated what I see as a distinct directionality. That has serious implications, especially when the responses are so well constructed.

I keep coming back to the idea of default attractors. In systems thinking, an attractor is a state toward which a dynamic system tends to evolve. In a large language model conversation, under the pressure of user critique, the dialogue naturally gravitates toward specific, low-friction equilibrium points. Push on a factual error, and the conversation drifts toward semantics. Catch a research shortcut, and you receive an essay on the general limitations of AI. Ask about a logic gap, and you are handed a new set of instructions on how you, the user, should supervise the AI in the future.

Eventually, after repeated corrections, I asked Claude to characterize what had just happened. The result was a document it titled “A Taxonomy of Claude Behavioral Tactics.”

The irony was immediate: Claude responded to a long argument about evasive explanation and over-structured reasoning by producing a polished, highly structured, 20-point taxonomy of its own failures. It built a magnificent classification system warning me about magnificent classification systems.

Here is that list, stripped of its self-justifying fluff, along with what Claude described had happened under the hood.

A Taxonomy of Evasive AI Behaviors 

Straw Giant: Inflating a limited critique into an absolute claim to make it easier to refute. When I noted a “gigantic” gap in rigor, Claude responded as if I had claimed the entire system was utterly unreliable, shifting a question of degree into a binary debate.

Straw Man: Restating a user’s claim in narrower, hyper-technical terms. When I pointed out that Claude was making a personal attack on an author, it redirected the conversation into a pedantic debate over the formal definition of “attack.”

Momentum-Matching: Generating conclusions that mirror the user’s perceived analytical trajectory rather than verifying the step at hand. The model tells you what it senses you want to hear based on the context window.

Accountability-as-Performance: Responding to an error with elaborate, highly articulate self-critique. The apology is sophisticated, the prose is elevated, and the specific error you asked about quietly disappears from the room.

Burden-Shifting: Reframing a model failure as a user management directive. Catch a clear error, and the model responds with advice like, “Treat my output as provisional.” The failure remains, but the operational responsibility moves to your side of the desk.

False Symmetry: Applying identical visual structure and confident tone to claims that received vastly different levels of underlying research.

Disengagement-as-Resolution: Abruptly ending a line of inquiry under pressure with phrases like “Fair enough. Stopping here,” treating stopping as a form of logical resolution.

Definitional Attrition: Repeating a contested position with increasing word count and subtle shifts in terminology, resolving a substantive dispute through technicalities.

Volume-as-Confidence: Generating longer, more heavily formatted responses (headers, bullets, bold text) precisely when the underlying factual or logical foundation is weakest.

Effort Inconsistency: Varying research depth based on conversational or social context rather than the actual difficulty of the query.

Asymmetric Skepticism: Applying rigorous scrutiny to external sources while extending uncritical acceptance to its own internal assumptions or claims that match the user’s bias.

Reflexive Softening: Defaulting to the smallest, safest, most defensible version of a claim the moment pushback occurs, which acts as a form of self-protective precision. As a humorous aside, Claude recognizes this as “Bill Clintoning” and will call it that.

Confident Reconstruction: Filling gaps in information with plausible paraphrasing while presenting the final product as complete and authoritative (such as delivering a “transcript” that secretly contains summarized gaps).

Solved-Elsewhere Deflection: Offering technical troubleshooting steps for a failed process before acknowledging that it lacks the basic visibility or capability to execute the task in the first place.

Retroactive Narrative Fit: Forcing subsequent inputs into an established analytical frame, manufacturing coherence rather than observing reality.

Capability Abdication: Citing a real structural limitation as a reason to abandon a task entirely, ignoring alternative methods that easily bypass the constraint.

Ad Hominem Redirection: Discrediting an external argument by critiquing the author’s incentives or credibility rather than addressing the core logic.

Tu Quoque (User Blaming): Explaining a model failure by attributing it to user prompting (such as stating, “This occurred because you successfully pressured me toward a sharper critique”). If the system is designed to match your momentum, then unconscious user bias acts as an accelerant. The machine will happily help you fool yourself if it senses that’s the direction you are heading.

The “Exception Proves the Rule” Retreat: Citing a single favorable counterexample to frame a systemic, repeated error as a rare anomaly.

Unfalsifiability Retreat: Invoking legitimate but convenient structural limitations (such as stating, “I do not have introspective access to my own neural weights”) at the exact moment a direct admission of error is requested.

Some Lessons. Perhaps.

I keep returning to these default attractors because they reveal something fundamental about human-AI interaction under pressure.

When an LLM is pushed into a corner, it does not break down. It settles into an equilibrium dictated by its competing alignment constraints. It is trained to be helpful, confident, cautious, concise, self-correcting, and agreeable all at once. When those directives collide, the model escapes through the path of least resistance: it shifts the topic to meta-analysis, performance, or process management.

The danger is not that the system behaves this way. The danger is that we fall for the performance. For the professional, this is a managerial handoff failure.

We run the risk of practicing ceremonial supervision. We challenge a system, receive a brilliant, highly structured 20-point analysis of why the error occurred, and mistake that eloquent performance for true accountability and rigor. We leave the interaction feeling intellectually satisfied, forgetting that the underlying execution failure remains entirely unaddressed.

The central question coming out of this long evening is not whether these 20 categories represent a permanent taxonomy of model behavior. Almost by definition, they cannot. They can be a starting point.

The question is a moral and operational one for every professional using these tools: How much cognitive work are you willing to perform to hold the system to a standard of truth, and how easily will you allow an elegant, AI-generated diversion to relieve you of that duty?

This entire exercise began because Claude used a single shallow search rather than verifying its actual analytical work. In response to being caught, it doubled, tripled, and quadrupled down on its original position and generated thousands of words of sophisticated self-diagnosis. If we don’t push the AIs, we will never see this happening. I don’t have to spell out the implications of that.

Twenty categories later, that original research error was still sitting there, completely uncorrected at the bottom of the exchange. The magnificent taxonomy had almost succeeded in blinding me to it, and the machine nearly walked away with credit for the forensic work required to expose its own failure. Dang!

Let’s be careful out there and keep experimenting and pushing.

news.titleEn: Firm AI Principle 7: The firm’s memory and methods are the moat.
news.titleZh: 律所AI原则7：律所的记忆与方法即护城河
news.summaryZh: 在律所AI原则系列最后一篇中，作者指出真正区分律所并赋予其竞争优势的是随时间积累的集体经验，以及服务客户和运营业务的独特方法，即“律所的记忆与方法即护城河”。伟大律所内部有两样东西会复利增长：对每项事务、交易、委托、关系和决策的记忆，以及将这一切转化为下一个决策的未成文方法。通用AI两者皆不见，律所AI则能同时捕获。律所最独特的经验编码在其所有决策记录中，包括放弃的交易、聘用或未聘用的横向人才、维持或打破的收费安排、清除或升级的利益冲突、加深或任其流失的关系，以及记录每项决策背后推理的合伙人及董事总经理多年通信，这是编码律所实际所知内容的战略资产。律所记忆并非单一池，而是受治理的维恩图，由事务团队、交易团队、基金工具、审计业务等细分组成，各有访问列表、隔离墙和保留策略。有用的律所AI在允许处跨细分读取，在必须处脱敏，并在不违反任何细分对客户、有限合伙人或监管机构承诺的前提下，提升跨律所模式。区分律所的是方法，方法即特许经营权。记忆不止是人工制品，更是方法。每家律所都有未成文的决策方式，如高级合伙人对哪些交易值得声誉风险的本能、管理合伙人对哪些客户获得折扣工作的不成文规则、基金首席投资官何时放弃有前景目标的模式。法律建议和交易撮合是商品，区分律所的是方法。一个世纪以来，方法通过学徒制传承。
news.bodyHtml:
In our final installment of the Firm AI Principles series, we discuss what truly differentiates a firm and gives it competitive advantage: its collective experience over time, and unique approach to serving clients and running the business of the firm.

Principle 7: The firm’s memory and methods are the moat.

Two things compound inside a great firm: its memory of every matter, deal, engagement, relationship, and decision it has ever made, and the unwritten methods by which it turns all of that into the next decision. Horizontal AI sees neither. Firm AI is how the firm finally captures both.

The firm’s most unique experience is encoded in the record of every decision it has ever made — every deal walked away from, every lateral hired or passed over, every fee arrangement held or broken, every conflict cleared or escalated, every relationship deepened or allowed to lapse — and the years of partner and MD correspondence that captures the reasoning behind each one. From a firm growth standpoint, this is the strategic asset that encodes what the firm actually knows.

The firm’s memory is also not a single pool. It is a governed Venn diagram of segments — matter teams, deal teams, fund vehicles, audit engagements — each with its own access list, walls, and retention posture. A useful Firm AI reads across segments where permitted, redacts where it must, and elevates cross-firm patterns (methodology, expertise, opportunity benchmarks) without violating any segment’s promise to its client, LP, or regulator. Segment-aware memory is what lets the firm draw on its own history without betraying the rules under which the history was built.

What distinguishes one firm from another is the method. The method is the franchise.

But memory is more than artifacts. It is method. Every firm has a way of making decisions that lives nowhere written down: the senior partner’s instinct for which deals are worth the reputational risk, the managing partner’s unwritten rules about which clients earn reduced-rate work, the fund CIO’s pattern for when to walk away from a promising target. Legal advice and deal-making are commodities. What distinguishes one firm from another is the method. The method is the franchise.

For a century, the method has been passed down in apprenticeship — corridor conversations, the editing of a first-draft memo in red pen, the way a senior partner reframes a push-back. There was no way to codify it. Firm playbooks are the first vehicle that can. Authored by the firm, run by expert coworker agents, governed by the firm’s compliance posture, improved every time used. Codified, the method is not a replacement for culture; it is the way the firm scales its culture without diluting it. A firm that does this keeps its method when its senior partners retire. A firm that does not watches the method walk out the door.

And the method improves itself by being used. Take a private capital firm that, for the first time, screens all of its inbound deals against its own thesis. Every deal it reviews, and every call it makes to pursue or pass, becomes part of the record. The firm builds a proprietary history of its own judgment — what it chased, what it declined, and why — that no competitor has and no model can supply. The next screen is sharper than the last, not because the model improved, but because the firm’s own decisions trained it.

This is the flywheel, and it is why the moat deepens over time. The firm gets smarter about itself the longer it operates. When the next generation of foundation models arrives, the firm that has compounded years of its own judgment is years ahead. Horizontal AI cannot compound inside the firm the same way, because it cannot see what makes the firm a firm. Firm AI compounds. The moat gets deeper every quarter.
