news.titleEn: White House Moves Toward Voluntary AI Model Review Framework
news.titleZh: 白宫推进自愿性AI模型审查框架
news.summaryZh: 白宫正逐步推进一项自愿性框架，要求AI公司在公开发布最先进模型前将其提交给联邦政府。据报道，白宫国家网络主任办公室已向OpenAI、Anthropic和Google分发了该框架草案，这些公司联合提交了修改意见。审查流程细节尚未公开，但联邦政府对前沿AI模型发布前审查的持续兴趣，延续了此前关于为先进AI系统设立类似FINRA的监管机构的讨论。对企业而言，关键要点是：即使正式法律授权尚未确定，自愿性AI治理正日益成为实际期望。开发、部署或采购AI工具的公司应准备好记录模型治理、风险评估、测试、安全控制、数据来源、隐私考量及人工监督，以经受监管机构、客户、投资者和董事会的审查。即使初始联邦框架最直接适用于主要AI模型开发商，下游用户也应预期这些规范将通过供应商尽职调查、合同条款、审计权、采购问卷和企业AI政策传导。商业客户应利用当前时机整顿AI治理：清点AI系统和供应商，对高风险用例进行分类，更新AI工具的隐私和安全审查，并在推出新工具前建立清晰的内部审批流程。对于购买AI产品的公司，合同应涵盖测试、透明度、网络安全、数据使用限制、保密性、模型训练权利、监管合作、事件通知以及工具产生有害或不合规输出时的责任分配。当前的实际步骤不是等待最终联邦规则，而是建立可辩护的治理记录，反映对风险的深思熟虑评估、合理的决策过程以及清晰的监督和AI系统管理解释。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The White House is moving closer to a voluntary framework under which AI companies would submit their most advanced models to the federal government before public release. The White House’s Office of the National Cyber Director reportedly circulated the draft framework by to OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, and those companies jointly submitted edits. Although the review process details are not yet public, the continued federal interest in pre-release review of frontier AI models follows earlier discussion of a possible FINRA-like watchdog for advanced AI systems. For businesses, the key takeaway is that voluntary AI governance is increasingly becoming a practical expectation, even where formal legal mandates remain unsettled. Companies developing, deploying, or procuring AI tools should be prepared to document model governance, risk assessment, testing, security controls, data provenance, privacy considerations, and human oversight in a way that can stand up to regulator, customer, investor, and board scrutiny. Even if the initial federal framework applies most directly to major AI model developers, downstream users should expect those norms to flow through vendor diligence, contract terms, audit rights, procurement questionnaires, and enterprise AI policies. Business clients should use this moment to get their AI governance house in order: inventory AI systems and vendors, classify higher-risk use cases, update privacy and security reviews for AI-enabled tools, and build clear internal approval processes before rolling out new tools . For companies buying AI products, contracts should address testing, transparency, cybersecurity, data use restrictions, confidentiality, model training rights, regulatory cooperation, incident notice, and responsibility allocation if the tool produces harmful or noncompliant outputs. The practical step now is not to wait for a final federal rule, but to establish a defensible governance record that reflects a thoughtful assessment of risks, sound decision-making processes, and clear oversight and explanations of AI system management. news.titleEn: Harbor Seeks To Counter General LLM FDEs
news.titleZh: Harbor 寻求对抗通用大语言模型的前沿部署工程师
news.summaryZh:
法律科技咨询公司 Harbor 推出面向法律 AI 需求的“Deploy”服务，将在客户内部嵌入专业团队，包括前沿部署工程师（FDE）。该服务将与近期推出自有 FDE 团队作为关联咨询服务的通用大语言模型厂商展开竞争。Harbor 提到，OpenAI、Anthropic 和微软均已推出专门业务，在客户组织内部嵌入工程师，但随后补充称：“Harbor Deploy 专为一个行业打造：法律。

通用大语言模型公司及其 FDE 团队均在横向建设，同时覆盖所有行业，且多数与自身模型绑定。法律行业的运作方式不同于其他经济领域，工作流程、保密义务、治理以及律师事务所或法律部门内部的运行和管理方式都足够特殊，通用部署部门无论资金多么充足，都无法像法律原生团队那样深入其中，这正是 Harbor Deploy 要填补的空白。Harbor 拥有超过 900 名专业人员的全球团队，与超过 80% 的 Global 200 律师事务所和近 600 个公司法务部门合作。
news.bodyText: Legal tech consultancy Harbor has launched ‘Deploy’ for legal AI needs, which will see them ‘embed specialist teams, including forward-deployed engineers (FDE), inside clients’. They noted it will compete versus the general LLM makers which have recently launched their own FDE teams as part of a linked consultancy service. In short, this is a battle of specialist consultants vs generalists. Harbor mentioned that ‘OpenAI, Anthropic, and Microsoft have each launched dedicated businesses built to embed engineers inside client organizations’, but they then added: ‘Harbor Deploy is built for one [industry]: legal.’ That suggests they may be getting a bit nervous that they could miss out on the piles of lovely consulting cash if customers start to look to the FDE teams of the mega-LLM makers and their now closely allied consulting companies. Rudy DeFelice, Global Head of AI Strategy at Harbor, continued with the theme that you need a specialised legal tech consultancy to help with legal AI, with the following comment: ‘Each of [the general LLM companies and their FDE teams] is building horizontally, across every industry at once, and in most cases tied to their own model. ‘Legal doesn’t work like the rest of the economy. The workflows, the confidentiality obligations, the governance, and the way each is run and governed inside a law firm or a legal department are specific enough that a general-purpose deployment arm, however well-funded, can’t get inside them the way a legal-native team can. That’s the gap Harbor Deploy exists to close.’ Is this a big deal? What stands out is that they’re taking aim at the LLM giants and treating their consulting efforts as competition. This tells us something important: that OpenAI and Anthropic’s efforts are having an impact, otherwise Harbor and others would not need to make such pitches. This is especially relevant as both are also – at varying stages – rolling out legal specific capabilities. In short, Harbor could get outflanked here if it’s not careful. Hence the arrival of a newly branded Deploy and the new spiky marketing message. And as they noted, they have ‘a global team of over 900 professionals and work with more than 80% of Global 200 law firms and close to 600 corporate law departments,’ so if the LLM FDE teams start to eat away at the legal sector, then such a large super-focused business could struggle to feed so many consultants. — Two Major Legal Innovators Conferences this November Come and join us in New York and London this November at Legal Innovators!

news.titleEn: Must ‘Claude For Legal’ Head Be A Lawyer?
news.titleZh: ‘Claude法律版’负责人必须是律师吗？
news.summaryZh: Anthropic推出法律垂直领域能力Claude for Legal，最初是一组“技能”（即复杂提示集），并持续扩展。该业务此前由副总法律顾问Mark Pike领导，现正式任命Robert Mahari为Claude for Legal负责人。此举表明这家大语言模型巨头认真对待法律行业增长，该职位对Anthropic与法律界联络、开发律师所需功能至关重要。Mahari主要任职于学术界，拥有MIT法律AI博士学位，并担任斯坦福著名法律科技小组Codex的研究员。他拥有哈佛JD学位，但据其简历，仅在律所短期工作：2020年在Orrick暑期实习2个月，2016年在瑞士律所实习2个月。Artificial Lawyer通过Richard Tromans发布的社交媒体帖子已获全球超过470个点赞。然而，一些律师评论称：“所以他们雇了一个从未在律所工作过的人？”以及“奇怪的是，他们聘请了一位从未在法律行业有过实际工作的Claude for Legal负责人。”AL也听到过类似批评——总是来自律师——针对法律科技公司创始人，有时因为他们离开律所创业时只是助理，或甚至未达到该职位。这些评论的潜台词是，若未在律所或内部法律团队工作多年，就无法真正理解律师工作，因此其创业公司或其他产品不值得成功，且可能不会成功。这种观点99%的情况下是错误的。
news.bodyText: Some have criticised Anthropic’s choice of Robert Mahari as its ‘Head of Claude for Legal’ for not having worked long-term as a lawyer. But, does it matter? In fact, isn’t this an advantage? Artificial Lawyer explores. First, some background. Anthropic has launched its own legal vertical capability: Claude for Legal. It started as a group of ‘skills’ (i.e. a set of complex prompts), but is steadily expanding. Although it’s been helmed by Associate GC, Mark Pike, they’ve now hired a formally designated Head of Claude for Legal. This matters as it suggests the LLM giant is serious about growing in the legal sector. Plus, that role will be vital for Anthropic in terms of liaising with the legal world to help to develop what lawyers want. The hire, which AL shared on Friday, is Robert Mahari, who has primarily worked in academia, with a doctorate in legal AI from MIT and has the position of Fellow of Stanford’s famous Codex legal tech group. Although he has a JD from Harvard, which is no small thing, according to his CV he has only worked in law firms for a short time: for 2 months as a summer intern back in 2020 at Orrick, and before that for another 2 months also as an intern at a Swiss law firm in 2016. As of today, AL’s social media post (via Richard Tromans) about the Anthropic hire has garnered over 470 likes from across the world. However, a couple of lawyers made the following comments: ‘So they hired someone who’s never worked at a law firm?’ And, ‘Weird that they hired a head of Claude for Legal who’s never had an actual job in law.’ Meanwhile, AL has heard similar criticisms – always from lawyers – about the founders of legal tech companies, sometimes because they were only an associate when they left a law firm to create their startup, or perhaps didn’t even get to that point. Either way, the subtext of all such comments, here and elsewhere in the legal tech sector, is that ‘if you’ve not worked for many years inside a law firm or inhouse legal team, then you cannot really understand what lawyers do, and thus your startup (or other offering) doesn’t deserve to succeed and probably won’t’. And of course, they are wrong 99% of the time. The Lawyer Whisperers There are two main arguments as to why the ‘you must be an experienced lawyer to be a legal innovator’ is a bogus thesis.
news.relevanceReason: 文章聚焦于Anthropic的法律AI产品Claude for Legal及其负责人任命，讨论法律科技领域的人才标准，属于核心法律AI报道。

news.titleEn: 4 Legal Techs Join Y Combinator Summer ‘26
news.titleZh: 四家法律科技公司入选Y Combinator 2026年夏季班
news.summaryZh: 传奇创业孵化器兼投资机构Y Combinator已接纳四家法律科技公司进入其2026年夏季班。Perceptron ML为律所构建AI系统，基于各律所自身案件训练，并在其环境中私有部署，功能涵盖计时、案件接收与监控、研究、证据开示和起草。其“接地引擎”在模型引用前会对照原始来源核实每项事实，因此律所信任其处理现成法律AI常出错的工作。Erinys自称正在构建首个AI原生的原告方诉讼律所网络，利用先进技术更快、更实惠地向更多人提供高质量法律代理。Osmaura的智能体扫描网络，为律所合伙人提供新的客户与交叉销售机会，客户每天登录平台查看该联系谁、为何现在联系以及该说什么。Y Combinator的夏季班历来是创业公司获得资金和指导的重要渠道，此次入选凸显了法律科技领域持续升温的趋势。
news.bodyText: Legendary startup incubator and investor, Y Combinator, has accepted four legal tech companies into its summer 2026 cohort. Artificial Lawyer takes a look: Perceptron ML They build AI systems for law firms, trained on each firm’s own matters and deployed privately in their environment: timekeeping, intake and matter monitoring, research, discovery, and drafting. The ‘grounding engine verifies every fact against a primary source before a model can cite it, which is why firms trust us with work that off-the-shelf legal AI keeps getting wrong’, they said. AL comment: this is a smart move, and is tapping the current zeitgeist for law firms to try and crystallise their own knowledge with AI systems that they can control. Erinys ‘Erinys is building the first AI-native plaintiff-side litigation law firm network. We use sophisticated technology to deliver high-quality legal representation faster, more affordably, and to more people.’ AL comment: they’re tapping several themes at once here – the surge in interest on the plaintiff side of the market to use AI tools (because in no win-no fee cases, any cost reduction on the work done is an important business gain); the rise and rise of NewMod / AI-native law firms; and the fact that many smaller firms, or solo lawyers want to use AI, but don’t have the time to build out their own personalised AI-based platforms. AL would add: why stop at just plaintiff firms? P.S. the mention of a network is not really developed by the founders. AL really likes the idea of a real network of NewMods, but it doesn’t seem as if this is what they’re doing here, at least not yet. As noted, it’s more about offering lawyers the AI platform to operate more effectively. Osmaura ‘Our agents scan the web to deliver new client & cross-selling opportunities for law firm partners. Every day, our customers log onto our platform to see who to contact, why now, and what to say.

news.titleEn: What Do Lawyers Actually Want from Legal Technology?
news.titleZh: 律师究竟想从法律技术中获得什么？
news.summaryZh:
律师对法律技术的核心诉求并非最新AI模型或复杂功能，而是信任、易用性和切实节省时间。律师在赶截止日期、回应客户、谈判交易或准备听证时，只关心工具能否更快、更好、更低风险地完成工作。律师不问工具是否最先进，而问能否更好服务客户、降低风险、节省时间并融入现有工作方式。Spencer Harris则希望获得定制化体验，对声称“无所不能”的平台持怀疑态度，认为最成功的产品是能极好解决特定问题的工具。

简单不等于功能少，而是减少认知负担和摩擦。Delchin称最佳工具应直观到“融入背景”，在正确时间提供正确信息。Harris强调透明度，要求工具展示功能、答案来源并证明可靠性，直接链接源材料可建立可信度。生成式AI方面，行业已从早期兴奋转向实际用例和成本效益分析，Delchin指出组织日益权衡效率收益与AI工具成本，尤其是基于消费的定价模式；Harris称律师开始问“这值得吗”。两人一致认为律师需要可信的“副驾驶”而非自动驾驶，专业和道德义务仍要求律师行使独立判断。当前AI能力如起草、摘要、信息检索和文档分析将成标准配置，但持久采用取决于专注、可靠且真正节省时间的工具。

What Do Lawyers Actually Want from Legal Technology?

By

Virginia Ong

posted

08-10-2026 14:06

Like

Please enjoy this blog authored by Virginia Ong, Legal Innovation Manager, Greenberg Traurig.

In my work as a legal innovator at a large law firm, I spend a lot of time testing new technology. The field is full of conversations about AI, automation, integrations, workflows, and transformation. Legal technology professionals can easily get excited about new features and trends. Most lawyers don't. That's not a criticism. In fact, it's probably the reason many lawyers continue to be successful despite the endless stream of technology being introduced into the profession.

When a lawyer is racing to meet deadline, respond to a client, negotiate a deal, or prepare for a hearing, they are not thinking about whether a tool has the latest AI model or the most sophisticated feature set. They are thinking: “Will this tool help me complete my work faster, better, and with less risk?”

I have seen legal technology from both sides. I practiced as an attorney before moving into legal innovation, where I now evaluate tools, support adoption, and see what happens after the demonstration. One thing is clear: excitement may open the door, but a tool lasts only if it solves a real problem.

To understand what lawyers want from legal technology in the age of AI, I spoke with two attorneys who have practiced in different environments. Both focused less on features and more on three priorities: trust, usability, and meaningful time savings.

Relevance Over Novelty

Steve Delchin, attorney and legal ethics innovator, put it simply: lawyers are not asking, "What is the most advanced tool available?" They are asking, "Will this help me serve my clients better, reduce risk, save time, and fit into the way I already work?"

His observation captures one of the biggest misconceptions in legal technology. It is easy to assume adoption is driven by innovation when in reality, it is usually driven by relevance. Lawyers generally are not looking for technology for technology's sake. They are looking for solutions to specific problems.

Spencer Harris, who recently moved from private practice to an in-house role, wants a tailored experience. He noted that lawyers remain skeptical of platforms that claim to "do it all." Some of the most popular legal tools have unremarkable interfaces and aging technology yet survive because they solve one problem exceptionally well. As Harris explained, "Lawyers are looking for a tool that will solve a specific problem in a specialized practice, first and foremost." The industry often rewards larger feature sets, but the most successful product may be the one that does one thing extremely well.

Less Friction

The same principle applies when lawyers say technology should be "simple." The word is common in legal innovation but rarely defined. Both conversations made clear that simplicity does not mean fewer capabilities. It means less friction.

Delchin described simplicity as “reducing cognitive load.” Lawyers already manage complex facts, legal authorities, deadlines, business needs, and client expectations. They do not need software with a steep learning curve. The best tools, he explained, are intuitive enough to "fade into the background." They provide the right information at the right time, letting lawyers focus on legal judgment rather than the technology.

Harris approached the question from a different angle, focusing on transparency. As he put it, "Lawyers have no tolerance for a tool that hides the ball. Show me the features, show me where the answers are coming from, and prove that the answers are reliable. Links that go directly to source material are amazing and build credibility..."

That point matters for legal technology vendors and innovation teams. Lawyers do not just want answers. They want confidence. If a research tool provides a conclusion but requires ten minutes of source hunting and citation checking, it may save time on one task while creating work elsewhere. This tension is especially visible with generative AI.

From AI Excitement to Practical Value

The legal profession's relationship with AI has changed quickly. Early conversations centered on curiosity and excitement. Today, they are more practical and focused on specific use cases.

I have watched that shift firsthand. The first wave focused on what generative AI might make possible. Then came the harder phase: getting lawyers to use the tools consistently. Now the market is asking a more grounded question: which tool is best for this task?

Delchin noted that organizations are increasingly weighing efficiency gains against the cost of AI tools, especially as more vendors adopt consumption-based pricing. The conversation is no longer solely about capability. It is now about economics, governance, and measurable value.

Harris observed a similar shift, noting that some of the early optimism has given way to more rigorous cost-benefit analysis. His summary was refreshingly direct: “…lawyers are starting to ask whether the juice is worth the squeeze." That question may ultimately determine which AI tools survive because while many products can generate excitement, far fewer generate lasting adoption.

Actual Time Savings

Every legal innovation professional has seen an impressive demonstration. The AI drafts a memo in seconds, summarizes thousands of pages, and answers questions instantly. The audience approves. Six months later, nobody is using it.

In my work, what happens between the demonstration and sustained adoption is often the most revealing part of an evaluation. Lawyers return to a tool when it clearly improves a task they already need to complete, not simply because the underlying technology is impressive.

As Delchin observed, if a lawyer spends ten minutes using an AI tool and twenty minutes checking its work, the promised efficiency gains evaporate. The tools that become indispensable are the ones that save real time, fit naturally into existing workflows, and eliminate effort rather than merely shifting it elsewhere.

Harris highlighted another often-overlooked challenge: voice and tone. Many AI-generated outputs still require translation before a lawyer feels comfortable using them. Some are overly verbose. Others are too simplistic. Some sound authoritative without actually sounding like a lawyer. At a certain point, “translating” the output becomes more cumbersome than creating the work from scratch.

Tech as a Trusted Copil ot

One theme ran through both interviews: preserving lawyer judgment. Despite headlines about AI replacing lawyers, Delchin and Harris agreed on what practitioners want. They want assistance, not replacement.

Delchin argued that lawyers need a trusted “copilot”, not an autopilot. Professional and ethical obligations still require lawyers to exercise independent judgment, and the most successful technologies will be the ones that support that responsibility rather than attempt to bypass it.

Harris echoed the same idea. Regardless of how advanced technology becomes, lawyers still need to understand the substance of the work product. Whether standing in court, negotiating a transaction, advising a board, or counseling a client, human understanding remains essential. Technology may accelerate that understanding, but it cannot eliminate the need for it.

What Will Matter Next

Both attorneys expect many current AI capabilities to become standard. Drafting, summarization, information retrieval, and document analysis will become expected rather than differentiating features. The same three priorities will remain: tools lawyers can trust, that fit their work, and that save meaningful time.

From where I sit, this is the direction the market is already taking. Broad AI platforms may remain useful, but lasting adoption will increasingly depend on focused tools that fit a defined use case, produce reliable work, and make the lawyer's job easier.

Which brings us back to the original question: what do lawyers actually want from legal technology?

The answer is simpler than the legal innovation field sometimes makes it. Lawyers do not want another platform, dashboard, login, workflow, or AI assistant. They want fewer obstacles between themselves and the work that matters. They want technology they can trust, that fits their work, and that saves time without creating new tasks. The real measure is not how quickly a tool produces an answer, but how quickly a lawyer can use it with confidence. A tool that drafts in seconds but requires extensive checking has merely shifted the work from creation to verification. That hidden burden often separates an impressive demonstration from a tool lawyers adopt. Lawyers do not need the fanciest tool. They need one they will use. And if someone can finally solve time entry capture along the way, lawyers everywhere may give a standing ovation.

research.titleEn: Temporal Misgrounding in Legal RAG: A Versioned-Corpus Benchmark for French Tax Law
research.titleZh: 法律RAG中的时间错位：法国税法版本化语料库基准
research.abstractEn: We identify and quantify temporal misgrounding: the systematic retrieval and citation of the currently in-force version of a legal article when the applicable version is an earlier or future one. Standard legal RAG treats the corpus as static; we argue legal question answering is a temporally-indexed retrieval problem. We introduce FiscalQA Pro, pairing a versioned corpus of 32,436 article-versions of the French tax code (93 years, 1938-2031) with an all-model-hard temporal-reasoning track: 209 scored, expert-reviewed questions across 33 CGI articles (221 released; twelve flagged out of the answerable scope). At selection time, no evaluated model recovered its date-applicable answer closed-book in any of four sampling draws, and the currently in-force text lacks the gold value for all but one of the scored questions. Answers are scored deterministically via atomic ground-truth "nuggets" (regex and numeric-with-tolerance), never LLM-as-judge: an LLM judge would inherit the temporal bias it is meant to score. Across eleven models (five frontier closed-API systems plus Gemini 2.5 Pro as a substitute entry, and five open-weight), parametric knowledge yields 3.0% mean strict accuracy and RAG over a static current-version corpus 2.7%. Static RAG retrieves the date-applicable version 0% of the time, confidently citing a real but inapplicable version. Our end-to-end retriever over a multi-version index, with no oracle, reaches 98.3% mean strict; an oracle-article ablation reaches 99.1%, locating the residual gap in first-stage recall, not version selection. We additionally release a version-aware jurisprudence dataset of 69,208 citation links, together with the corpus, benchmark, model responses, and pipeline code.
research.abstractZh: 我们识别并量化了时间错位：即当适用版本是早期或未来版本时，系统性地检索并引用法律条款的现行有效版本。标准法律RAG将语料库视为静态的；我们认为法律问答是一个时间索引的检索问题。我们引入了FiscalQA Pro，将法国税法（93年，1938-2031年）的32,436个条款版本的版本化语料库与一个全模型困难的时间推理轨道配对：209个经过评分、专家审查的问题，涵盖33个CGI条款（共发布221个；其中12个被标记为超出可回答范围）。在选择时，没有任何评估模型在四次抽样中闭卷恢复其日期适用答案，并且对于所有评分问题，现行有效文本除一个外均缺乏黄金值。答案通过原子地面真值“金块”（正则表达式和数值容差）确定性评分，绝不使用LLM作为评判者：LLM评判者将继承其旨在评分的时间偏差。在十一个模型中（五个前沿闭源API系统加上Gemini 2.5 Pro作为替代条目，以及五个开放权重模型），参数知识产生3.0%的平均严格准确率，而静态当前版本语料库上的RAG为2.7%。静态RAG在0%的情况下检索到日期适用版本，自信地引用了一个真实但不适用的版本。我们的端到端检索器在多版本索引上，没有oracle，达到98.3%的平均严格准确率；oracle文章消融达到99.1%，将剩余差距定位在第一阶段召回，而非版本选择。我们还发布了一个版本感知的判例数据集，包含69,208个引用链接，以及语料库、基准、模型响应和管道代码。

research.titleEn: LexKairos: Benchmarking Legal Temporal Capabilities in LLMs
research.titleZh: LexKairos：法律大语言模型时间能力基准测试
research.abstractEn: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of legal tasks. In legal practice, time is a critical concept that governs the validity of statutes, the progression of legal cases, and the enforcement of procedural deadlines. However, legal temporal capabilities remain underexplored in existing legal AI benchmarks. To address this gap, we propose LexKairos, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the temporal capabilities of LLMs in the Chinese legal context across three dimensions: statutory temporal knowledge, case temporal modeling, and statute-case temporal reasoning. LexKairos comprises nine sub-tasks drawn from real-world Chinese judicial cases and statutes. We conduct systematic evaluations of eight LLMs under multiple inference settings, including vanilla, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), and thinking modes. Our results show that Gemini-3-Flash achieves the strongest overall performance, yet even the best-performing model exhibits notable limitations on tasks demanding precise time-sensitive statutory metadata recall or complex reasoning in time limits, indicating that legal temporal knowledge and reasoning remain open challenges for current LLMs. Data and code are available at https://github.com/thunlp/LexKairos.
research.abstractZh: 大型语言模型（LLMs）在法律领域的多种任务中展现了强大的性能。在法律实践中，时间是关键概念，它支配着法规的有效性、法律案件的进展以及程序性截止日期的执行。然而，现有的法律AI基准测试对法律时间能力的探索仍然不足。为解决这一空白，我们提出了LexKairos，一个全面的基准测试，用于评估LLMs在中国法律语境下的时间能力，涵盖三个维度：法规时间知识、案件时间建模以及法规-案件时间推理。LexKairos包含九个从真实中国司法案件和法规中提取的子任务。我们在多种推理设置下对八个LLM进行了系统评估，包括普通模式、思维链（CoT）和思考模式。我们的结果显示，Gemini-3-Flash在整体性能上表现最强，然而即使是最佳模型在需要精确时间敏感的法规元数据回忆或时间限制复杂推理的任务上仍表现出显著局限性，这表明法律时间知识和推理对当前LLMs仍是开放挑战。数据和代码可在https://github.com/thunlp/LexKairos获取。

news.titleEn: Chancery Addresses AI Hallucinations in Court Filings
news.titleZh: 衡平法院处理法庭文件中的人工智能幻觉问题
news.summaryZh: 特拉华州衡平法院近期的一项裁决就法庭文件中的人工智能幻觉所引发的问题提供了警示。在Leiske诉Kidd案（C.A. No. 2025-0426-CDW (LWW)，特拉华州衡平法院，2026年7月1日）中，法院处理了一份包含人工智能幻觉的法庭文件，并分析了潜在后果。该简短文章有意不披露涉事律师或律师事务所的身份，而是提供该裁决的要点及若干启示，这些内容对所有使用人工智能或遇到其他方使用人工智能的诉讼律师均具有相关性。尽管衡平法院还有其他裁决涉及人工智能幻觉，且法院引用了全国其他处理该问题的案例，但这份letter ruling就问题发生时如何应对以及如何避免问题提供了值得注意的指导。案件背景涉及一起由衡平法院治安法官裁决的预付款诉讼，该法官裁定了预付款。随后，副大法官审查此事，以决定对治安法官关于预付款最终报告的异议——而对该博客文章而言更重要的是，处理了人工智能问题。要点与启示：如果发现提交给法院的文件存在错误，无论是否基于生成式人工智能或其他原因，律师必须立即采取行动。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! A recent Delaware Court of Chancery decision provides a cautionary tale about the issues raised by AI hallucinations in a court filing. In Leiske v. Kidd, C.A. No. 2025-0426-CDW (LWW) (Del. Ch. July 1, 2026), the court addressed a court filing with AI hallucinations and analyzed potential consequences. Noteworthiness of This Case This short post intentionally does not identify the lawyers or the law firm involved, but instead provides highlights and a few takeaways from this ruling that have relevance to all litigators who use AI, or who encounter its use by other parties. Although there are other Chancery decisions that address AI hallucinations, and the court cites to other cases around the country that have dealt with the issue, this letter ruling provides noteworthy guidance about how to address this problem when it happens, and how to avoid the problem. Brief Background The background of this case involved an advancement suit that was decided by a Magistrate Judge in Chancery who awarded advancement. The Vice Chancellor then reviewed this matter to decide exceptions to the Magistrate’s final report on advancement–and more importantly for this blog post addressed the AI issues. Highlights Takeaways If a document filed with the court is found to contain errors, whether based on GenAI or other reasons, the lawyer must immediately: Postscript Bonus Supplement

research.titleEn: PROSLEX: A Novel Dataset for Expert-Annotated Legal Statute Prediction for Indian Judiciary
research.titleZh: PROSLEX：一个用于印度司法专家标注法律条文预测的新数据集
research.abstractEn: Legal Statute Prediction (LSP) involves automatically identifying relevant legal statutes given factual descriptions in legal documents, typically framed as a multi-label classification task within natural language processing and information retrieval research. While recent advances have begun incorporating Large Language Models (LLMs) for statute prediction, current approaches primarily focus on accuracy metrics without addressing the critical need for legal reasoning, a fundamental requirement in judicial contexts where decisions must be explainable and justifiable. To address this research gap, we present PROSLEX (PRediction Of Statutes and LEgal eXplanation), a comprehensive dataset comprising 1,623 expert-annotated legal documents from the Indian context. Each document is paired with statute predictions and detailed explanations, totaling 7,450 explanations, capturing the underlying legal reasoning. Using this dataset, we systematically evaluate various prompting strategies, including zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and tree-of-thoughts approaches, to generate both statute predictions and their corresponding legal rationales. Our evaluation framework measures not only predictive performance but also the coherence and legal validity of generated explanations, positioning PROSLEX as a benchmark for developing explainable AI systems that can support legal practitioners while advancing research in interpretable legal NLP. To ensure reproducibility, we have made our PROSLEX dataset and model code available on GitHub: https://github.com/subinay494/Legal_Statute_Prediction_Explanation.
research.abstractZh: 法律条文预测（LSP）涉及根据法律文件中的事实描述自动识别相关法律条文，通常在自然语言处理和信息检索研究中被构建为多标签分类任务。尽管最近的进展已开始将大型语言模型（LLM）用于条文预测，但当前方法主要关注准确性指标，而没有解决法律推理这一关键需求，而在司法背景下，决策必须是可解释和可论证的。为了解决这一研究空白，我们提出了PROSLEX（法律条文预测与法律解释），这是一个包含来自印度背景的1,623份专家标注法律文件的综合数据集。每份文件都配有条文预测和详细解释，总计7,450条解释，捕捉了潜在的法律推理。利用该数据集，我们系统地评估了各种提示策略，包括零样本、少样本、思维链和思维树方法，以生成条文预测及其相应的法律理由。我们的评估框架不仅衡量预测性能，还衡量生成解释的连贯性和法律有效性，将PROSLEX定位为开发可解释AI系统的基准，该系统可以支持法律从业者，同时推进可解释法律NLP的研究。为确保可重复性，我们已在GitHub上公开了PROSLEX数据集和模型代码：https://github.com/subinay494/Legal_Statute_Prediction_Explanation。

news.titleEn: What is conversational AI for business? Definition and how it works
news.titleZh: 什么是面向企业的对话式AI？定义及工作原理
news.summaryZh:
对话式AI是能够理解人类语言并自然回应的技术，利用自然语言处理（NLP）和机器学习解读用户意图、进行真正的双向对话，并在每次交互中持续改进。它不同于仅能遵循预设规则和关键词的规则型聊天机器人，通过NLP、对话管理和上下文保留三种机制运行，可在毫秒级内完成处理。常见商业用途包括支持分流、潜在客户资格筛选和预约安排，覆盖短信、电子邮件和社交渠道。麦肯锡2025年调查显示，88%的组织已在至少一个业务职能中使用AI。

对话式AI通过NLP将消息拆解为意图和实体，依托大语言模型处理未见过的表述；对话管理决定下一步回应或转接人工；上下文保留使系统记住对话及客户历史，连接CRM后更为强大。Salesforce研究显示，45%的消费者在存在明确人工升级路径时更愿意使用AI代理。评估平台时应关注NLP质量与多渠道支持、人工交接与监督模式、CRM集成深度、合规与安全认证（如SOC 2 Type 2、TCPA、A2P 10DLC、HIPAA及BAA）、团队协作、分析功能。Heymarket的AI代理以监督模式运行，原生集成Salesforce和HubSpot。建议先选择一个高流量、低复杂度的工作流进行30天试点，衡量解决率和升级率。
news.bodyHtml:
Conversational AI is technology that understands human language and responds to it naturally. It uses natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning to interpret what a person means, hold a genuine two-way conversation, and improve with every interaction.

Picture a clinic’s front desk on a Monday morning: 40 texts to reschedule appointments and a weekend of unanswered messages before the first patient walks in. Conversational AI handles that routine volume automatically, freeing your team for the conversations that need real human judgment.

Key takeaways about conversational AI

  • Conversational AI is software that uses NLP and machine learning to hold natural, two-way conversations, interpreting intent and retaining context instead of following a script.
  • It differs from a rule-based chatbot, which can only follow preset rules and keywords.
  • It works through three mechanisms: NLP, dialogue management, and context retention.
  • Common business uses include support triage, lead qualification, and appointment scheduling across SMS, email, and social channels.

This guide covers what conversational AI is, a breakdown of how the technology works, real business examples, and the features to evaluate when you or your team are comparing platforms.

What is conversational AI?

Conversational AI is a category of software that understands, processes, and responds to human language in an organic way. Rather than matching keywords to canned replies, it interprets what your customer is really saying. Whether they type “reschedule my delivery” or “can we push my order back a few days”, conversational AI responds appropriately in real time.

Conversational AI powers the automated side of business communication: answering questions, qualifying leads, booking appointments, and routing conversations over SMS, email, webchat, and social messaging. It’s the technology behind conversational messaging, where businesses and customers exchange messages the way people naturally text.

Adoption reflects how mainstream the technology has become. According to McKinsey’s State of AI research from their 2025 survey, 88% of organizations now use AI in at least one business function. For IT and operations leaders, that means the evaluation question has shifted from whether to use conversational AI to where it fits in your communication stack.

How does conversational AI work?

How conversational AI works is by interpreting a message with natural language processing, deciding how to respond through dialogue management, and remembering the conversation through context retention. These three mechanisms run together in milliseconds, which is why a well-built system feels like texting a knowledgeable colleague rather than filling out a form.

Natural language processing (NLP)

Natural language processing is the mechanism that lets software understand human language, including slang, typos, and ambiguity. NLP breaks a message down into intent (what the person wants) and entities (the specific details, like a date or order number).

Modern NLP is built on large language models, which is why current conversational AI can handle phrasing it has never seen before. When your customer writes “my thing never showed up”, it gets routed to order tracking without ever using the words “delivery” or “shipment.”

Dialogue management

Dialogue management is the decision-making layer that determines what the system says or does next. Once NLP identifies the intent, dialogue management chooses the response: answer the question, ask a clarifying follow-up, complete an action like booking a time slot, or route the conversation to a person.

This is where business rules live. A well-configured system knows which questions it can answer confidently and which ones should go straight to your team.

Context retention

Context retention is the system’s memory of the conversation so far—and, in business settings, of the customer’s history. It’s what allows your customer to say “actually, make it Thursday instead” without repeating everything they said two messages ago.

Context retention becomes far more powerful when it’s connected to your CRM. A system that can see a contact’s past orders, appointments, and previous conversations responds like someone who knows the customer, because functionally it does.

What’s the difference between conversational AI vs. chatbots?

The difference is that traditional chatbots follow pre-written scripts, while conversational AI understands language and generates responses dynamically. A rule-based chatbot is a decision tree with a chat window on top. Conversational AI interprets meaning, so it can handle questions through AI texting or messaging that your team never explicitly anticipated.

Rule-based chatbot Conversational AI
How it responds Follows a fixed script or decision tree Interprets intent and generates responses
Handles unexpected phrasing No–falls back to “I didn’t understand” Yes–NLP interprets meaning, not keywords
Remembers context Rarely, and only within one session Retains conversation and customer history
Improves over time Only when someone rewrites the script Learns from interactions and feedback
Best suited for Simple, predictable FAQs Multi-step conversations and real workflows
Human handoff Often a dead end Escalates with full conversation context

The right choice depends on the work you need the conversation to do. A rule-based chatbot remains a reasonable fit for a narrow set of predictable, high-volume questions to do with store hours and tracking links. Conversational AI earns its place when conversations branch: multi-step scheduling, lead qualification, and support that draws on customer history.

What is an example of conversational AI?

Common examples of conversational AI in business include AI agents that triage support, follow up with leads, and schedule appointments, over channels customers already use, like SMS and email. The strongest implementations are for omnichannel messaging: the same AI works across any channel, and every conversation lands in one platform where your team can see it.

research.titleEn: China RealDID: Verifiable Credentials Anchored in Legal Identity
research.titleZh: 中国RealDID：锚定法律身份的可验证凭证
research.abstractEn: Verifiable credentials (VCs) and decentralized identifiers (DIDs) enable selective disclosure but lack legal anchoring: without a trusted identity root, verifiers cannot distinguish a genuine holder from a fabricated identity. State identity systems provide biometric-grounded verification but impose three costs: verifiers must collect subjects' full personally identifiable information, infrastructure concentrates on a single API, and the state observes every transaction. We present China RealDID, a three-layer architecture -- CTID (centralized legal identity), RealDID (decentralized anchor on an open permissioned blockchain), and VCs with SD-JWT-based selective disclosure -- evaluated against five adversary classes and six security goals. The central mechanism is a content-blind government relay: the state authenticates participants and counter-signs every credential but cannot read the payload, encrypted by the issuer to the holder's public key. We describe the VC lifecycle, triple-signature chain, open template registry, and the architecture's metadata-level privacy limits, including the credential graph at the relay and presentation linkability from single-DID reuse. The design yields an asymmetric, state-bounded trust model: the state cannot impersonate or read contents; the user cannot fabricate identity or evade metadata observation. We analyze alignment with China's Personal Information Protection Law and the EU's GDPR, including the tension between immutable registries and erasure rights, and discuss generalizability through cross-border deployments with Singapore and Hong Kong.
research.abstractZh: 可验证凭证（VC）和去中心化标识符（DID）支持选择性披露，但缺乏法律锚定：没有可信的身份根，验证者无法区分真实持有者与伪造身份。国家身份系统提供基于生物识别的验证，但带来三项成本：验证者必须收集主体的完整个人身份信息，基础设施集中于单一API，且国家观察每笔交易。我们提出中国RealDID，一个三层架构——CTID（中心化法律身份）、RealDID（开放许可区块链上的去中心化锚点）以及基于SD-JWT选择性披露的VC——针对五类对手和六个安全目标进行评估。核心机制是内容盲化的政府中继：国家验证参与者并对每份凭证进行副署，但无法读取由签发者用持有者公钥加密的负载。我们描述了VC生命周期、三重签名链、开放模板注册表以及架构的元数据级隐私限制，包括中继处的凭证图和单一DID重用导致的呈现可链接性。该设计产生了一种不对称、国家受限的信任模型：国家无法冒充或读取内容；用户无法伪造身份或逃避元数据观察。我们分析了与中国《个人信息保护法》和欧盟GDPR的一致性，包括不可变注册表与删除权之间的张力，并通过与新加坡和香港的跨境部署讨论其通用性。

DOJ’s Willow Bridge Deal Signals More Aggressive Antitrust Review of Rental Pricing Software

by Bruno Queiroz

The Justice Department’s proposed settlement with Willow Bridge Property Company LLC marks another important step in the government’s expanding antitrust challenge to rent-setting tools and shared market data in multifamily housing. The case, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina, fits into a broader enforcement push targeting allegations that landlords used common pricing software and competitively sensitive information to coordinate rents.

While the specific terms of the proposed resolution will matter, the headline takeaway is already clear: DOJ is not treating rental algorithms as a niche issue. Instead, it is continuing to test the theory that a landlord’s participation in shared pricing systems can cross the line from lawful benchmarking into unlawful coordination, particularly where rivals exchange nonpublic data or rely on common recommendations to set prices.

That is significant because the government appears focused not just on software vendors, but also on the property owners and managers who use these tools. For in-house counsel and compliance teams, that raises immediate questions about antitrust risk in everyday revenue-management practices: What data is being shared? Is it historical, aggregated, or current and property-specific? How much discretion do managers retain when software generates pricing recommendations? And how are those recommendations documented, reviewed, and implemented?

The Willow Bridge settlement also lands against the backdrop of sprawling private litigation over similar allegations. Practitioners tracking the issue will likely also be watching IN RE: Realpage, Inc., Rental Software Antitrust Litigation (No. II) , where many of the core themes—shared data, algorithmic recommendations, and alleged market-wide effects on rents—are being tested in multidistrict proceedings. The DOJ’s continued activity may shape how courts and private plaintiffs frame these cases going forward.

For litigators, the enforcement action is a reminder that antitrust claims involving algorithms will turn on old competition-law principles applied to new technology. Expect close scrutiny of agreement allegations, information-exchange theories, market structure, and the role of software outputs in actual pricing decisions. Discovery fights over data inputs, internal communications, and vendor relationships are likely to remain central.

For businesses, the practical message is equally direct: use of algorithmic pricing tools does not insulate conduct from antitrust review. Companies in rental housing—and in other sectors using similar software—should revisit vendor contracts, data-sharing practices, governance around automated recommendations, and internal antitrust training. DOJ’s Willow Bridge resolution suggests regulators intend to keep pressing this theory, and companies relying on revenue-management software should assume that enforcement scrutiny is not going away.

news.titleEn: Anthropic hires Robert Mahari as head of Claude for Legal
news.titleZh: Anthropic聘请Robert Mahari担任Claude for Legal负责人
news.summaryZh: Anthropic已聘请Robert Mahari担任Claude for Legal负责人，帮助律师事务所、内部法务团队和法律科技公司“从产品走向市场推广”，显示其进一步加码法律领域。此次招聘距Claude for Legal推出约三个月，该产品含20个MCP连接器，可将Claude与律所软件相连。Mahari拥有哈佛法学院和MIT媒体实验室联合JD-PhD学位，研究法律人工智能，曾任斯坦福CodeX法律信息学中心副主任。近十年来一直将AI融入法律学习与实践，曾努力说服MIT媒体实验室和哈佛法学院设立AI与法律交叉的JD-PhD项目，说服律师相信技术将很快深刻影响实践，并说服计算机科学同行法律并不枯燥。他说Anthropic无人需要被说服，自Mark Pike、Eleanor Dorfman及团队推出Claude for Legal起便已清晰，此后遇到的每个人都认为AI将从根本上改变法律实践，律师应获得真正关注特权、保密和准确性的工具，法律教育和司法公正应处于转型核心。Pike称对Mahari的加入非常兴奋，自己依赖Claude完成法律工作，期待合作让每个法律团队获得同样工具，并赞赏Mahari能向非技术受众解释技术概念，也能向研究和产品团队解释法律工作，这正是当下所需技能。此次招聘的重点在于将产品能力转化为实际采用。
news.bodyHtml:
Anthropic has hired Robert Mahari as head of Claude for Legal, helping law firms, in-house teams and legal tech companies move “from product to GTM,” in a move that signals the frontier AI provider is putting further weight behind its push into the legal sector.

The hire comes around three months after Anthropic launched Claude for Legal, with 20 MCP connectors linking Claude to the software that law firms run on.

Advertisement

Mahari holds a JD-PhD from Harvard Law School and the MIT Media Lab focused on legal artificial intelligence and has served as associate director of Stanford’s CodeX Center for Legal Informatics. Announcing his move on LinkedIn, Mahari, who has spent much of his career at the intersection of AI and legal practice, said: “For almost a decade, I’ve been weaving AI into the study and practice of law. A surprising amount of my energy went into being convincing: convincing MIT Media Lab and Harvard Law School that the intersection of AI and law merits a JD-PhD program (thank you Alex ‘Sandy’ Pentland and David Wilkins for helping make the case!), convincing lawyers that this technology will have a profound impact on practice sooner than later, and convincing my computer science colleagues that law is not as boring as it sounds.

“No one at Anthropic needed to be convinced. This first became clear to me when Mark Pike, Eleanor Dorfman, and their team launched Claude for Legal. Since then, everyone I met at Anthropic sees that AI will change legal practice at its core. That lawyers deserve tools built with real care for privilege, confidentiality, and getting things right. And that legal education and access to justice belong at the center of this transformation. I can’t wait to work with these incredible people to reimagine the legal profession.”

Advertisement

Commenting on the hire Pike, who is associate general counsel, said: “Anthropic just hired Robert Mahari and I’m beyond excited. I rely on Claude to do my best legal work, and I can’t wait to collaborate with Robert to make sure every legal team out there has access to these same amazing tools.”

Pike added: “When Robert’s start was announced internally, I wrote that I was in awe of his ability to explain technical concepts to non-technical audiences (many of us lawyers!) in a very accessible way. It goes both ways, too: he’s just as good at explaining the work legal pros are doing to our Research and Product teams. That’s exactly the skill this moment demands. The tech is moving fast, and the profession deserves someone who can meet practitioners where they are.”

What’s interesting about the hire is the focus now on translating product capability into adoption.

news.bodyText:
By JT Consulting & Media

In a technology landscape overflowing with buzzword-heavy press releases and armchair futurists, JT Consulting & Media operates in a tier of its own.

For over a decade, we have operated at the absolute center of global disruption. We don’t merely report on the future from the sidelines; we sit in the green rooms, boardrooms, and keynote stages with the architects who are actively code-writing, policy-making, and financing it.

At its core, JT Consulting & Media powers two distinct yet deeply synergetic global functions:

High-Stakes Media & Intellectual Dialogue: We host unfiltered, candid conversations with the world’s most impactful innovators. We interrogate technology not just as software, but through its philosophical, geopolitical, personal, and professional impact on human civilization. Simultaneously, we deliver authoritative, on-the-ground recaps and podcasts from the world’s elite summits, from Davos and World Bank Week to flagship AI and Blockchain gatherings, alongside academic centers like MIT, Stanford, and Harvard.

Strategic Advisory & Frontier Education: Backed by more than ten years of executive education across AI, blockchain, cybersecurity, digital transformation, and digital assets, we consult for governments, enterprise leaders, and institutional titans. Today, we specialize in the absolute bleeding edge of autonomous architecture: Agentic AI converged with Stablecoins , the non-negotiable payment rails for autonomous software agents.

Here is an insider look into how both pillars are fundamentally reshaping how the global elite navigate what comes next.

Function I: The Global Stage & Unfiltered Dialogues

Technology doesn’t exist in a vacuum. A breakthrough in autonomous code in Silicon Valley instantly reverberates across global supply chains, international law, and state sovereignty. That is why our media operation, highlighted by the hit video podcast series Tech Snippets Today , rejects superficial product demos in favor of frank, high-level truth-telling.

We bring together world leaders, grandmasters, policy architects, and tech founders to wrestle with the existential and practical questions of our era.

High-Impact Luminaries Featured on Our Platform

Garry Kasparov | Chess Grandmaster & Chairman of the Human Rights Foundation

The Intersection of Decentralization & Liberty: Caught up in the green room at Consensus to dissect how open digital assets and cryptographic tools act as vital shields for personal freedom against rising authoritarian regimes globally.

Frank McCourt | Founder, Project Liberty & Executive Chairman, McCourt Global

Redesigning the Internet: Unpacking the philosophical and technical imperative to rebuild the web’s core infrastructure, shifting data control away from Big Tech monopolies back to individuals.

Dante Disparte | Chief Strategy Officer & Head of Global Policy, Circle

The Future of Global Reserve Currency: Exploring how dollar-backed stablecoins are quietly modernizing global remittance rails, cross-border settlement, and sovereign financial stability.

Dr. Kristin Gilkes | Global Innovation & Quantum Leader, EY (Ernst & Young)

The Next Frontier—Quantum Computing & Enterprise Strategy: Strategic analysis on the convergence of AI, quantum mechanics, and enterprise risk management, assessing how institutions must prepare today for post-quantum cryptography and computational shifts.

Prof. Beth Simone Noveck | Chief AI Strategist (State of NJ), Former White House Advisor

Rebooting Democratic Institutions: Examining how AI can repair public trust, modernize governance, and streamline state-level legislative workflows without sacrificing democratic integrity.

Sandeep Nailwal | Co-Founder, Polygon

Scaling Global Web3 Infrastructure: Deep dives into zero-knowledge rollups, institutional asset tokenization, and scaling public blockchains for mass international adoption.

Dana Maor | Senior Partner & Global Head of People & Organizational Performance, McKinsey & Company

Human Capital in the Age of Synthetic Intelligence: Strategic analysis on how global enterprises must restructure workforce psychology and leadership when AI agents become team members.

Austin Lin | Vice President of Product Management, Cisco

Inside the AI Playbook & Enterprise Networks: A deep dive into the underlying architecture required for autonomous systems, exploring how AgenticOps, Meraki platforms, and enterprise cloud infrastructure must evolve to handle real-time machine-to-machine traffic safely and seamlessly.

On the Ground: Global Summits & Academic Halls

Beyond individual sit-downs, JT Consulting & Media serves as the primary intelligence dispatch from the world’s most critical convenings:

Davos (World Economic Forum): In-depth recaps and panel leadership untangling macroeconomic shifts, AI governance, and global monetary policy.

World Bank & IMF Week: Keynotes and broadcasts breaking down digital financial inclusion, sovereign debt tokenization, and emerging market technology infrastructure.

Elite University Circuits (MIT, Stanford, Harvard): Deep-dive lectures and research roundtables dissecting machine learning models, neuro-linguistic AI limits, and cryptographic engineering.

Premier Tech Convergences: Live broadcasts from ETHConf NYC, Consensus, Token2049, and the Dubai World Government Summit.

Function II: A Decade of Executive Advisory & The Agentic AI x Stablecoin Frontier

While our media operation captures the global conversation, our consulting arm actively builds the strategic blueprints.

For over 10 years, JT Consulting & Media has educated, advised, and transformed Fortune 500 C-suites, legal titans, financial institutions, and government bodies on the practical implementation of AI, blockchain, and digital assets.

We don’t teach theory from a textbook. We translate complex technical breakthroughs into defensible market advantages and regulatory strategies.

The Core Paradigm: Agentic AI Meets Autonomous Payment Rails

The era of simple generative chatbots answering prompts is fading fast. We have entered the era of Agentic AI , autonomous software agents capable of planning, executing multi-step workflows, negotiating contracts, and interacting with software APIs independently.

However, autonomous agents face a structural brick wall in traditional finance: AI agents cannot open bank accounts, sign credit card forms, or undergo legacy manual KYC delays.

This is where JT Consulting & Media’s primary advisory focus resides: The convergence of Agentic AI and Stablecoins.

Machine-to-Machine Micro-Transactions: Enabling AI agents to autonomously buy API access, purchase compute time, pay for proprietary data feeds, and execute supply-chain orders in real-time fractions of a cent.

Programmable Escrow & Smart Contracts: Constructing autonomous payment rails where an AI agent only releases funds via stablecoins upon verified algorithmic completion of a task.

Borderless Agent Economics: Establishing instant, 24/7/365 settlement layers that allow software agents operating in different continents to transact without legacy banking friction.

Global Keynotes & Advisory Topics

From delivering command performances before Royal Family members and ministers at the Dubai World Government Summit to keynoting international legal and corporate conferences, our advisory footprint spans:

Autonomous Enterprise Architecture: Moving organizations from passive copilots to fully integrated AgenticOps systems.

LegalTech & Algorithmic Jurisprudence: Preparing global law firms and corporate legal departments for AI-driven contract negotiation, superjustice, and digital asset custody frameworks.

Real-World Asset (RWA) Tokenization: Guiding financial institutions through the digitization of private equity, real estate, treasury bills, and credit markets on blockchain rails.

Geopolitics & Tech Sovereignty: Advising public sector leaders on national AI infrastructure, data sovereignty, and foreign policy amidst technological decoupling.

The Standard of Excellence

Whether we are breaking down complex geopolitical shifts on a podcast recording, decoding neural network mechanics at Harvard, or designing the stablecoin payment architecture for autonomous AI workforces, JT Consulting & Media remains the definitive bridge between today’s reality and tomorrow’s market dominance.

We don’t predict the future, though our CEO tries. We consult the people who build it, educate the executives who lead it, and map the rails that power it.

news.titleEn: Startup Corner: Lawdie, the AI back office for law firms
news.titleZh: 创业角：Lawdie，律所的AI后台
news.summaryZh: Lawdie由首席执行官Sanay Shajith和首席技术官Meeth Naik于2025年创立，目标是成为律所的AI驱动后台，自动化计费、案件管理、文档生成和文件路由等运营任务，其理念是法律AI的未来不仅在于帮助律师执业，还在于消除阻碍执业的运营负担。Lawdie定位为律所的代理式后台，将工作流代理接入Filevine、Tabs3、Aderant、iManage、Outlook等标准法律技术栈，处理通常消耗员工和助理时间的重复性运营工作。触发方式有两种：自主工作流监控事件（如新案件开启、案卷记录、提交截止日期）并在无人工干预下行动；按需工作流通过每家律所的专用电子邮件地址触发，律师只需放入相关文件或转发邮件，解析和路由由系统内部处理。由于涉及敏感的客户和财务数据，Lawdie运行完整的SOC 2和HIPAA合规，并为AI代理本身投保。目标客户是拥有20名以上律师的律所，服务所有业务领域。增长策略聚焦于打造优质产品以推动有机推荐，并积极参与活动尤其是CLE。Lawdie已进入AmLaw 200，一家律所已追回超过25万美元收入，并与GA Bar及Berkeley Center of Law & Business建立关键合作。公司于今年夏初以1000万美元估值完成首轮风险融资，正筹备新一轮融资以支持强劲增长。市场关键挑战是采购时间线和信任，律所对AI接近客户数据和计费持谨慎态度，Lawdie通过清晰的部署手册和行业标准合规及AI代理保险来应对。联合创始人中学时曾同在一个舞蹈队，后在大学重聚。Lawdie的创立源于一位单亲母亲无法获得法律帮助，这让他们意识到司法救济是系统性问题，律所被运营开销淹没，导致法律服务缓慢、昂。
news.bodyHtml:
Founded in 2025 by CEO Sanay Shajith and CTO Meeth Naik, Lawdie is aiming to become the AI-powered back office for law firms. The startup automates operational tasks ranging from billing and matter management to document generation and file routing. Lawdie is betting that the future of legal AI lies not just in helping lawyers practise law, but in removing the operational burden that gets in the way.

How would you describe your company to a friend?

Lawdie is the AI back office for law firms. Billing, matter management, routine document generation, file routing, and general operational stuff that eats a firm’s time. We automate it. Every firm gets a custom email address with all their workflows baked in. Need something done? Send an email describing it, and the right workflow fires. No prompt engineering, no new tool to learn, just email like you already do. That handles the on-demand stuff. Everything else runs invisibly in the background, no email needed at all. We built it with the mission of giving lawyers their time back, recuperating money that slips through the cracks and cutting the non billable hours nobody wants to do.

Advertisement
And to a techy?

Lawdie is an agentic back office for law firms. A set of workflow agents wired into the standard legal stack, for example Filevine, Tabs3, Aderant, iManage, Outlook, and it handles the repetitive operational work that normally eats staff and associate time. Triggering works two ways. Autonomous workflows watch for events, a new matter opened, docket entry, a filing deadline, and act without a human in the loop. On-demand workflows fire from a dedicated email address per firm. No natural language request needed, attorneys just drop the relevant files in or forward an email, and we handle parsing and routing internally. Since we’re touching sensitive client and financial data, we run full SOC 2 & HIPAA compliance and carry dedicated insurance on the AI agents themselves.

When were you founded?

2025

Advertisement
By who?

Sanay Shajith (CEO) and Meeth Naik (CTO)

Who are your key managers/senior execs?

N/A

Who are your target clients?

Law firms with north of 20 attorneys. We serve all practice areas, from IP boutiques to general litigation to personal injury, the platform’s built to handle the operational back office regardless of specialty.

What is your plan (growth strategy)?

Our growth strategy really comes down to two things working together. First and foremost, we’re focused on just building a genuinely good product, that’s what drives most of our growth organically, since happy users end up referring us to their friends and colleagues at other firms. On top of that, we lean heavily into events, especially CLEs, since they’re a great way to build trust and get in front of attorneys directly.

Key achievements?

We’re in the AmLaw 200, a firm has recuperated over a quarter million in revenue, and we secured key partnerships with the GA Bar & Berkeley Center of Law & Business.

Have you received investment?

Yes. We raised our first venture round at the beginning of this summer at a $10M valuation. We’re gearing up to raise another round shortly to support our strong growth.

Have there been any key changes in direction since you were founded?

No.

What are the key challenges in your market?

Key challenges in the market come down to procurement timeline and trust, and those two go hand in hand. Firms are naturally cautious about letting an AI system near client data and billing, so trust is really the bottleneck, not interest in the product. We tackle that by coming in with a clear playbook from day one, exactly what we need from the firm, exactly how the rollout works, so there’s minimal guesswork and minimal lift on their end. The less work it takes for them to say yes, the faster procurement moves. On the trust side, we back that up with substance. We carry the industry standard compliances firms expect, and we’ve gone further and insured our AI agents themselves, so there’s real peace of mind if something goes wrong.

Tell us something people don’t already know about the company?

The co-founders were actually on the same dance team back in middle school, then reconnected years later in college. Lawdie also started because a single mother needed help finding legal assistance and couldn’t get it. That’s what made us realize access to justice isn’t just an individual problem, it’s a systems problem. Law firms are buried in operational overhead, and that overhead is exactly what keeps legal help slow, expensive, and out of reach for people who need it. So we built the back office that frees firms up to actually practice law

news.summaryZh: NetDocuments近期宣布进军原告胜诉酬金律师市场，这一举措本身引人关注，但其发展路径更值得借鉴。据其新闻稿，NetDocuments现推出医疗时间线应用，可总结并提取医疗记录中的关键事件，生成结构化备忘录以供时间顺序审查。此外，其需求生成器应用能够从医疗记录和案件文件中提取事实、因果关系证据及分项损害赔偿，用于起草人身伤害、就业和保险恶意索赔案件的需求函。NetDocuments还推出了专家证人档案构建器应用，可从简历、庭审记录和已发表作品中构建结构化专家证人档案，提取资历、先前意见和案件历史，并声称该工具可标记证词不一致之处，为交叉询问提供素材。这些新工具旨在提升原告律师处理案件时的效率，尤其是在医疗记录分析、损害赔偿计算和专家证人准备方面。NetDocuments的此次扩展表明其从传统文档管理向更专业的法律工作流程工具转型，利用人工智能技术辅助律师进行案件评估和文书准备。尽管这些应用的具体技术细节未完全披露，但其功能设计明显针对原告律师的常见痛点，如大量医疗记录的整理和需求函的起草。NetDocuments的举措反映了法律科技行业对特定执业领域定制化解决方案的日益重视。
news.bodyText:
NetDocuments

NetDocuments  recently announced its venture into the plaintiffs’ contingency fee lawyer’s market. That fact in and of itself is interesting. But how it got there is perhaps even more so and a good lesson.

According to its press release, NetDocuments is now offering a  Medical Chronology app which it says can summarize and extract key events from medical records into a structured memo for chronological review. Secondly, it has announced a  Demand Generator app  that, according to NetDocuments, can extract facts, causation evidence, and itemized damages from medical records and case documents to prepare demand letters for personal injury, employment, and insurance bad faith matters.

Finally, it is now offering an  Expert Witness Profile Builder app   which it says can   build structured expert witness profiles from CVs, transcripts, and published works, pulling credentials, prior opinions, and case histories. NetDocuments says the tool can flag testimony inconsistencies and supply cross-examination fodder.

news.titleEn: Early Signals: How a Debt Collection Agency Uses Trellis to Spot Litigation Risk Before It Escalates
news.titleZh: 早期信号：一家债务催收机构如何利用Trellis在诉讼风险升级前识别它
news.summaryZh: 一家债务催收机构的诉讼合规主管负责诉讼风险、监管合规与债务回收，需预判可能波及本机构的诉讼。他过去依赖联邦法院动态、外部律师和行业出版物监测风险，但无法看到州初审法院的案件，只能在诉讼形成势头后才察觉，应对空间受限。Trellis弥补了这一缺口。Trellis不收集也不提供非公开信息，无需以隐私换取可见性。当新的州初审法院立案符合其监测条件时，他会收到聚焦快照，包括原告姓名、立案地点和一般法律理论。他与Trellis客户成功经理合作，围绕重大诉讼风险构建查询，重点监测FDCPA、TCPA和FCRA三类索赔，并针对高频立案律师设置跨州查询，同时关注重复出现的原告，将信息与内部记录交叉比对，以便在争议升级前调整催收活动。Trellis在构建查询方面发挥了关键作用，明确需求有助于创建过滤器和查询。Trellis的常见问题说明，其可搜索州初审法院记录并发送警报，帮助合规团队监测特定律师、律所、原告、法规和司法管辖区，识别重复原告或模仿性索赔，且无需共享非公开客户或账户数据。
news.bodyText:
A single lawsuit reveals little on its own. It’s the next few cases, as the same names and claims begin to resurface, that make a filing matter. Litigation risk takes shape in that accumulation—in how quickly actions stack up and spread from one trial court to another.

One litigation compliance executive at a debt collection agency came to Trellis with exactly that problem. His role spans litigation risk, regulatory compliance, and debt recovery, requiring him to look beyond the actions already facing his organization and anticipate what might reach it next.

Today, he uses Trellis to identify new claims, track the people driving them, and act on potential risks earlier. This is how he built an early-warning system for litigation—one designed to catch isolated cases before they start stacking up.

The missing layer

Much of his work requires close coordination with outside counsel to investigate lawsuits and regulatory complaints. That involvement gives him a direct view into how the two converge.

“[R]egulatory complaints and lawsuits aren’t tremendously different from one another,” he observes. “Staying involved in both of those is very helpful.”

To do this, he used to rely on the same channels used by many other compliance leaders. He tracked federal court activity, leaned on outside counsel, and followed industry publications to understand litigation risk and identify new developments.

“At the federal level, we could monitor,” he recalls. “We could see cases at the federal level. Our attorneys could see them [there too].”

But, when it came to monitoring the state trial courts, he lacked the same visibility. Without that visibility, he could see claims once they had gained momentum, but rarely as they were first taking form. That gap in coverage shaped what could come next, narrowing the moves he could make in response.

Visibility without compromise

Litigation can spread quickly. A successful claim against one large collections agency often leads to copycat complaints. Once a specific legal theory gains traction, filings begin to cluster around the same allegations, sometimes spreading across multiple jurisdictions. Before Trellis, he couldn’t see those patterns developing at the state trial court level.

“Trellis closed that gap.”

Early visibility, however, couldn’t come at the expense of privacy. Several of the case-monitoring solutions he considered required access to sensitive internal data. For him, that was a nonstarter. He liked that Trellis took a different approach.

“One of the advantages of Trellis is that they’re not collecting non-public information, and they’re not providing non-public information,” he says. With Trellis, he doesn’t have to trade privacy for visibility.

Early signals in motion

From there, Trellis alerts drive the workflow.

When a new state trial court filing matches his monitoring criteria, he receives a focused snapshot—who filed the case, where, and under what general legal theories. The goal isn’t deep docket research. It’s early visibility into the claims and people shaping the litigation landscape at any given moment.

To keep these alerts focused, he worked with a Trellis customer success manager to build queries around the most significant litigation risks. His queries start with the claims themselves. “[Trellis] was instrumental in building these queries,” he says. “Once we knew what the specific law was that they were citing, we were able to create a query related to that unique claim.”

In his industry, that means monitoring the ‘big three’: FDCPA, TCPA, and FCRA claims. “Looking for the lawsuits that are filed with those kinds of claims is a start.” From there, he shifts his focus accordingly. Some attorneys file at high volume, and he monitors their activity across jurisdictions. “We have a query set up with Trellis so that we can see all of the cases [these attorneys are] filing within certain states,” he says.

He also watches for plaintiffs who appear repeatedly in different lawsuits. “What I get on almost every case is the first and last name of the plaintiff and the county and state where [the case] was filed,” he explains. He cross-references those details with internal records. When a match appears, he can review and adjust collections activity before the dispute escalates.

Clarity and connection at Trellis

“There are so many things that we do to mitigate lawsuits,” he reflects. “It would be impossible to determine how many lawsuits we’ve prevented. I have no idea how to gauge that.” With Trellis, what matters to him isn’t a number. It’s the shift in how he works.

“Know what you want,” he says to anyone thinking about adopting a legal analytics platform. “There’s no shortage of data out there. All of it,” he says, “is useful, but it’s not all useful to everyone.” It’s the sorting that matters. “Being able to articulate to Trellis exactly what I wanted helped them create filters, create queries—do what needed to be done so that I could get [the information] I wanted.”

That’s the principle guiding the way Trellis works with its customers.

“There’s got to be a connection.”

FAQ

How can a debt collection agency monitor new FDCPA, TCPA, and FCRA lawsuits in state courts? +

A debt collection agency can create searches for lawsuits that reference the FDCPA, TCPA, FCRA, or related claim language, then receive alerts when matching cases appear in covered state courts. Searches can also focus on particular jurisdictions, attorneys, firms, or parties. Trellis helps compliance teams build targeted searches across state trial court records, reducing the need to check individual court systems manually.

How can a debt collection agency identify emerging litigation risks before it gets sued? +

The agency can monitor newly filed cases involving similar companies, collection practices, statutes, plaintiffs, and attorneys. A single case may reveal little, but repeated allegations or filings can indicate that a legal theory is gaining traction. Trellis gives compliance teams earlier visibility into these state court patterns, allowing them to investigate relevant accounts or practices before the same type of claim reaches their organization.

What litigation risks can debt collection agencies miss by monitoring only federal court cases? +

Federal monitoring does not capture lawsuits filed and litigated solely in state trial courts. As a result, an agency may miss local claim patterns, active plaintiffs’ attorneys, repeat plaintiffs, or legal theories developing across particular counties and states. Trellis fills that visibility gap by making covered state trial court records searchable and alerting teams to relevant filings that would not appear on a federal docket.

How can a compliance team track lawsuits filed by a specific attorney or law firm across multiple states? +

A compliance team can create a search using the attorney’s or firm’s name and narrow it by jurisdiction, claim type, statute, or other case details. Because names may vary between court records, the search may need to account for spelling and firm-name variations. Trellis allows teams to configure attorney- and firm-focused searches across covered state courts and receive alerts when new matching lawsuits are filed.

How can a debt collection agency identify repeat plaintiffs or copycat claims across jurisdictions? +

Teams can compare new cases for recurring plaintiff names, attorneys, allegations, statutes, complaint language, and filing locations. Repetition across several cases may indicate coordinated activity, a high-frequency filer, or a claim being replicated in new jurisdictions. Trellis helps surface these connections across covered state trial courts, giving agencies a way to investigate patterns that would be difficult to recognize from isolated dockets.

How can a debt collection agency tell whether a new legal claim is becoming a broader industry trend? +

The agency should look for multiple lawsuits presenting similar allegations, citing the same law, or being filed by the same attorneys against comparable companies. Filing frequency and geographic spread can help distinguish an isolated claim from a developing trend. Trellis enables compliance teams to monitor distinctive claim language, statutes, parties, and attorneys across state courts so they can see when a theory begins appearing in additional cases or jurisdictions.

How can compliance teams monitor state court lawsuits that outside counsel and federal monitoring may not catch? +

Compliance teams need a centralized view of state trial court filings rather than relying only on federal dockets or updates about matters already assigned to outside counsel. Broader monitoring can reveal relevant cases before the organization becomes directly involved. Trellis supplements those existing resources with searchable state trial court data and configurable alerts, helping internal teams watch the wider litigation landscape while outside counsel focuses on specific matters.

Can a debt collection agency monitor lawsuits filed against other companies in its industry? +

Yes. Public court records can be searched for cases involving selected companies, types of defendants, legal claims, attorneys, or collection practices. Monitoring these cases can reveal risks affecting the wider industry without relying on access to another company’s private information. Trellis helps agencies follow relevant state court litigation involving peer organizations and identify claims or filing patterns that may eventually affect their own operations.

What information is included in a new-lawsuit alert? +

A new-lawsuit alert may include the case name, parties, filing date, case number, court, county, state, attorneys, law firms, and available information about the claims involved. The exact details depend on what the source court makes publicly available. Trellis provides a focused snapshot of a matching state trial court case, helping compliance teams determine whether the filing warrants additional research or an internal account review.

Can a debt collection agency monitor new lawsuits without sharing non-public customer or account data? +

Yes. An agency can monitor information available in public court records without uploading customer files, account histories, collection notes, or other internal data. Its team can compare relevant filing details with company records inside its own environment. Trellis uses public state trial court information to support lawsuit monitoring, allowing agencies to gain early visibility without providing Trellis with non-public customer or account data.

How can compliance teams identify patterns across consumer complaints and debt collection lawsuits? +

Teams can compare the allegations, practices, statutes, locations, and parties appearing in their complaint data with patterns found in newly filed lawsuits. Similarities may indicate that a recurring complaint issue is developing into litigation risk. Trellis supplies the state court side of that analysis by helping teams monitor relevant lawsuits, while the company keeps and reviews its consumer complaint and account information within its own internal systems.

What should a debt collection agency look for in a litigation-monitoring platform? +

An agency should evaluate state court coverage, search flexibility, alert quality, public-record sourcing, privacy practices, and the ability to monitor statutes, attorneys, firms, parties, and jurisdictions. It should also consider whether the provider can help turn the agency’s risk priorities into focused searches. Trellis combines state trial court data with configurable alerts and customer support that can help compliance teams build queries around their most significant litigation concerns.

research.titleEn: Protecting patient privacy in clinical foundation models: Technical and legal perspectives
research.titleZh: 保护临床基础模型中的患者隐私：技术与法律视角
research.abstractEn: Clinical foundation models trained on large-scale patient data are increasingly used for decision support, screening, and public health. As deployment expands, privacy risk increasingly arises from model-mediated leakage, yet its prevalence and severity remain poorly quantified. Models can disclose sensitive training artifacts, enabling patient re-identification in ways not captured by data-handling controls alone. Existing frameworks, including HIPAA and GDPR, offer limited guidance for such indirect threats. We propose a practical framework for assessing privacy risk in clinical foundation models and illustrate realistic leakage scenarios across deployment settings, map them to legal regimes, and outline complementary technical and legal mitigations. Our analysis provides a context-aware risk assessment grounded in realistic usage to preserve the value of medical foundation models while rigorously safeguarding patient privacy.
research.abstractZh: 基于大规模患者数据训练的临床基础模型越来越多地用于决策支持、筛查和公共卫生。随着部署的扩展，隐私风险日益源于模型介导的泄露，但其普遍性和严重性仍缺乏量化。模型可能泄露敏感的训练工件，使患者能够以数据处理控制无法捕获的方式被重新识别。现有框架，包括HIPAA和GDPR，对此类间接威胁提供的指导有限。我们提出了一个评估临床基础模型中隐私风险的实用框架，并说明了跨部署设置的真实泄露场景，将其映射到法律体系，并概述了互补的技术和法律缓解措施。我们的分析提供了基于实际使用的情境感知风险评估，以在严格保护患者隐私的同时保持医学基础模型的价值。

research.titleEn: Rhetorical-Role-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Legal Question Answering over Indian Supreme Court Judgments
research.titleZh: 面向印度最高法院判决的法律问答的修辞角色感知检索增强生成
research.abstractEn: This research paper proposes a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework that is specific to the legal field in order to assist interactive retrieval and reason about judgments from the Supreme Court of India. The solution uses an enhanced version of RAG framework which consists of rhetorically based chunking, fusion-based retrieval, and cross encoder reranking methods to increase the relevancy of the information retrieved. In order to improve conversations, the proposed framework uses chat history along with query classification and rewriting in order to understand user intention from successive queries. Additionally, there are features that take into account structural aspects of legal documents, such as isolated names of judges that could have an impact on retrieval quality. The evaluation was done using the DeepEval framework and demonstrated strong performance on metrics including contextual recall and answer relevancy, which proves that the framework is very effective in dealing with legal question-answering tasks that require a lot of context. The results emphasize the importance of domain specific enhancements in developing legal AI systems that are both reliable and explainable.
research.abstractZh: 本研究论文提出了一种针对法律领域的检索增强生成（RAG）框架，以协助对印度最高法院判决的交互式检索和推理。该解决方案使用增强版的RAG框架，包括基于修辞的分块、融合检索和交叉编码器重排序方法，以提高检索信息的相关性。为了改善对话，所提出的框架使用聊天历史以及查询分类和重写，以理解连续查询中的用户意图。此外，还有考虑法律文档结构方面的功能，例如可能影响检索质量的孤立法官姓名。评估使用DeepEval框架进行，并在上下文召回率和答案相关性等指标上表现出强劲性能，这证明该框架在处理需要大量上下文的法律问答任务方面非常有效。结果强调了领域特定增强在开发既可靠又可解释的法律AI系统中的重要性。

news.titleEn: Legal IT Insider Report: Beyond the perimeter – Security and risk in the age of legal AI
news.titleZh: Legal IT Insider报告：超越边界——法律AI时代的安全与风险
news.summaryZh: Legal IT Insider即将发布一份报告，探讨随着生成式AI融入日常法律工作，律师事务所的安全基础正在被重新定义。传统的基于边界的安全模型因云平台和混合办公已承受压力，而生成式AI则彻底改变了这一格局。最显著的变化并非技术层面，而是组织层面：律师既是最大的风险来源，也是最重要的安全控制环节。报告审视了实际风险所在，包括影子AI使用、提示词驱动的数据泄露、特权侵蚀、跨境数据暴露以及AI特定的事件响应。报告还针对法律实践的具体方面，如特权、保密性、监管风险和客户信任，指出在AI不再是可选项、环境无法完全控制、韧性比预防更重要的背景下，这些方面需要重新考量。该报告由首席分析师Neil Cameron撰写，将于今年十月发布，读者可注册后直接接收报告。此外，报告还提供广告合作机会，有意者可联系指定邮箱。

In a forthcoming report from Legal IT Insider, we examine how the security foundations of the law firm are being re‑written as AI becomes embedded in everyday legal work. Traditional perimeter‑based security models were already under strain from cloud platforms and hybrid working; generative AI has finished the job. The report argues that the most significant shift is not technical but organisational: lawyers are now both the greatest source of risk and the most important security control.

Advertisement

We look at where the real risk now sits – from shadow AI use and prompt‑driven data leakage, to privilege erosion, cross‑border data exposure and AI‑specific incident response.

And we examine the specifics of legal practice – privilege, confidentiality, regulatory exposure, client trust – for a world in which AI is no longer optional, the environment cannot be fully controlled, and resilience matters more than prevention.

Advertisement

Written by our lead analyst Neil Cameron, we will be publishing the report in October this year. You can sign up and receive the report straight to your inbox HERE.
