news.titleEn: Beyond the Technology: Protecting Value in AI Contracts
news.titleZh: 超越技术本身：在AI合同中保护价值
news.summaryZh:
AI正日益嵌入组织各环节，组织对其投入巨大且高度依赖。但最有价值的往往不是技术本身，而是流入和流出AI系统的数据、专有技术、商业智能和输出。许多AI系统仍沿用为传统软件或SaaS设计的合同框架采购，导致组织忽视影响AI投资价值的关键条款。审查和谈判AI合同时需特别关注以下领域。

首先是AI生成输出的所有权：许多组织误以为付费并提供提示即自动拥有输出，但实际上所有权和使用权由合同决定，客户可能仅获有限使用权。传统软件和SaaS合同的知识产权条款采用二元方法，难以适用涉及输入、输出、提示、训练等多方面的AI系统，每一方面都需单独考虑所有权和使用权。即使所有权归客户，也需了解供应商是否保留限制商业利用的权利，这在AI内容构成产品、服务或知识产权战略一部分时尤为重要；修改、衍生作品和未来发展相关权利可能比原始输出更有价值。其次是合规保障：很少有供应商愿无条件保证输出正确合法，而监管机构明确不接受以AI为不合规借口。客户必须考虑供应商为减轻误导、不正确或不合规输出风险所采取措施的合同保障，例如AI代理是否经过训练以尊重相关地区强制性消费者保护法，用于整理客户评论的系统是否理解评论须真实不误导的规则。同样重要的是审计措施（由客户和/或供应商）以识别此类输出，以及相应的纠正措施。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! AI is increasingly being embedded across almost every part of an organisation. From software development and customer service to marketing and product innovation, organisations are investing heavily in, and becoming heavily reliant on, AI tools and systems. But as AI adoption grows, so does a familiar pattern: the most valuable assets are often not the technology itself rather the real value lies in the underlying data, know-how, business intelligence and outputs that flow into and from AI systems. However, many AI systems are still being procured using contractual frameworks designed for traditional software or SaaS. As a result, organisations can overlook provisions or issues that have a significant impact on the value they ultimately derive from their AI investments. In that context, key areas that deserve particular attention when reviewing and negotiating AI contracts include: One of the first questions any organisation looking to procure an AI system will ask is: who owns the AI-generated output? It is also one of the most misunderstood. Many organisations will assume that because they pay for the service and provide the prompts, they automatically own everything the AI produces. In practice though, ownership and usage rights are determined by the underlying contract. Depending on the supplier’s terms, a customer may receive anything from full ownership to a limited right to use the output. Intellectual property ownership provisions in traditional software and SaaS contracts are not always an easy fit in this context as those usually reflect a binary approach that the supplier owns their software, which is then used by a customer under license. As such they fail to address the nuances of AI system use, which often involve multiple strands (input, output, prompts, training etc.) each of which require separate contractual consideration as to ownership and usage rights. Even where ownership sits with the customer, it is important to understand whether the supplier retains any rights that could restrict commercial exploitation. This becomes particularly important where AI-generated content forms part of a product, service or wider intellectual property strategy. It is also worth looking beyond the initial output. Rights relating to modifications, derivative works and future developments can ultimately become more valuable than the original AI-generated material. Very few AI suppliers will be willing to provide unconditional guarantees that the outputs provided by their system are correct, legally compliant etc. On the flip side, every regulator has made clear that it will not accept use of AI as an excuse for non-compliance. It is therefore critical for customers to consider what contractual comfort is provided as to the measures a supplier has put in place to mitigate the risk of misleading, incorrect or non-compliant output as far as is reasonably possible – for example, if an AI powered agent is being procured to interact with consumers, has that been trained to respect mandatory consumer protection laws in the territories in which the relevant consumers are based? If an AI system will be used to collate and summarise customer reviews, has that been trained to understand the rules on ensuring those are genuine and not misleading? Equally important to consider is what audit measures will be put in place (whether by the customer and/or supplier) to identify misleading, incorrect or non-compliant output and what corrective measures will be undertaken where that is identified.

news.titleEn: Beyond the Data, Part I: Using AI Tools to Turn Workforce Data Into Preventive Compliance
news.titleZh: 超越数据之外，第一部分：利用AI工具将劳动力数据转化为预防性合规
news.summaryZh: 雇主面临的挑战并非收集劳动力数据，多数雇主已在薪资、考勤、排班和HRIS系统中拥有这些数据，真正的挑战是在工资与工时争议发生前将数据转化为决策。AI辅助的劳动力分析以及对报告生成和审查方式的简单调整，可帮助雇主持续监控数据并更早纠正问题，从而降低加州及其他地区的工资与工时风险。本文开启“超越数据之外”系列，探讨如何将现有数据转化为预防性合规计划，并引入五阶段框架。过去二十年，雇主大力推动职场数字化，但数据用途仍局限于处理薪资、满足基本报告要求和诉讼时重建历史情况。这一局面正在改变：AI工具可持续分析已有数据或生成新报告，雇主也可仅通过改变审视现有报告的方式，将数据变为早期预警系统。多数报告只回答交易层面问题，如昨天谁错过用餐时间、上一周期谁应获补偿金；更有用的问题是哪些主管的违规呈上升趋势、哪些地点补偿金风险过高。AI的“模式识别”可大规模回答此类问题，但让分析师审查六个月趋势数据也能部分实现，技术只是加速工作，并非启动前提。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The challenge for employers has never been collecting workforce data. Most employers already have that data in their payroll, timekeeping, scheduling, and human resource information systems (HRIS). The challenge is turning that data into a decision before a wage-and-hour dispute forces the issue. Artificial intelligence (AI)–assisted workforce analytics and simpler changes to how reports are generated and reviewed can both help employers continuously monitor that data and correct issues earlier, reducing wage-and-hour exposure in California and beyond. This article opens a new series, “Beyond the Data,” on turning existing workforce data into a preventive compliance program. It also introduces a simple, five-stage framework that the rest of the series will build on. Quick Hits You Already Built This Over the past two decades, employers have invested heavily in digitizing the workplace: electronic time clocks, cloud-based payroll systems, scheduling software, and HRIS platforms. For most, the practical use of that data has remained narrow: process payroll, satisfy basic reporting requirements, and, when litigation arises, reconstruct what happened months or years earlier. That is starting to change—sometimes through AI tools that make it practical to continuously analyze data already in these systems or to generate new reports from the same dataset, and sometimes simply because someone decides to look at an existing report differently. Either path moves the data toward an early-warning system, and this series will cover both. The Opportunity: Different Questions, Same Data Whether an employer uses an off-the-shelf timekeeping and payroll platform, a customized internal system, or some mix of the two, most already generate substantial reporting built mainly to answer transaction-level questions: Who missed a meal period yesterday? Who was owed a premium last pay period? The more useful question is often different: Which supervisors show a rising trend in late or missed meal periods? Which locations carry disproportionate premium exposure once staffing and overtime are accounted for? AI tools, using a technique often called “pattern recognition,” can help answer questions like these at scale, but an employer can also get partway there simply by asking an analyst to review six months of trend data instead of one pay period at a time. The technology accelerates the work, no matter how sophisticated the business is; it isn’t a prerequisite for starting it. Five Stages, One Direction

research.titleEn: Legal aid eligibility and court outcomes: a design-based double-machine-learning approach
research.titleZh: 法律援助资格与法院结果：一种基于设计的双机器学习方法
research.abstractEn: Equality before the law is a human right, and access to high-quality legal aid for indigent defendants is essential to enforce it. In a context where all defendants have access to a lawyer, I study the impact of denying legal aid on court outcomes. I combine double machine learning and a new administrative dataset linking aid to court outcomes in New South Wales, Australia, to learn the assignment function, whose inputs are known. I find that applicants who fail the means test and hire private lawyers are 10 percentage points less likely to be incarcerated than if they passed and relied on legal aid. Given an average incarceration length of nearly four years, this gap is significant. However, I find evidence suggesting that they spend more time in jail if they are incarcerated. A government preference for broad access to aid over allocated time per case could explain this pattern.   Keywords: Indigent Defense, Crime, Criminal Justice.   JEL: I30, K14, H44.
research.abstractZh: 法律面前人人平等是一项人权，而贫困被告获得高质量的法律援助对于执行这一权利至关重要。在所有被告都能获得律师的背景下，我研究了拒绝法律援助对法院结果的影响。我将双机器学习与澳大利亚新南威尔士州将援助与法院结果联系起来的新行政数据集相结合，以学习分配函数，其输入是已知的。我发现，未通过经济状况调查并聘请私人律师的申请人，其被监禁的可能性比通过调查并依赖法律援助的申请人低10个百分点。鉴于平均监禁时间接近四年，这一差距是显著的。然而，有证据表明，如果他们被监禁，他们会在监狱中度过更多时间。政府倾向于广泛获得援助而非每个案件分配的时间，这可能解释这种模式。

news.titleEn: Universal Migrator helps closing startups offboard customers and reduce legal risk
news.titleZh: Universal Migrator帮助关闭中的初创公司完成客户迁移并降低法律风险
news.summaryZh:
关闭管理不善会带来重大风险：客户可能声称无法访问数据、未获合理机会取回数据，或收到的导出数据不完整、不可用。虽然技术无法消除法律风险，但记录有序的客户迁移流程可证明公司已采取合理措施保护客户并履行义务。Universal Migrator帮助初创公司在系统停用前提取客户数据，以结构化、可访问的格式交付信息，在适当情况下支持迁移至替代平台，在整个客户群中建立一致流程，减少对不断缩减的内部工程团队的依赖，并记录为返还或转移客户信息所采取的步骤，从而帮助创始人、投资者和清算团队在关闭公司时不留未解决的数据问题。

随着初创公司接近关闭，员工可能离职、基础设施可能缩减，工程资源日益有限，构建自定义导出工具会消耗剩余团队用于安全、计费、供应商终止、合规等关闭职责的时间。Universal Migrator让公司依赖迁移专家和成熟工具，而非从头创建新的客户迁移系统，使流程更高效、客户体验更好。该平台支持涉及170多个法律和商业应用的迁移，包括实践管理、文档管理、CRM、计费、会计及相关系统，广泛的连接器库可支持客户导出数据以妥善保存或直接转移到另一应用等关闭场景。对于准备关闭的初创公司，Universal Migrator提供了一种实用方式，将客户迁移作为负责任关闭流程的一部分，帮助保护客户关系、减少潜在纠纷，并让创始人更加安心。
news.bodyHtml:
A poorly managed shutdown can create significant risk. Customers may claim that they lost access to data, were not given a reasonable opportunity to retrieve it, or received exports that were incomplete or unusable.

While no technology can eliminate legal risk, a documented and organized offboarding process can demonstrate that a company took reasonable steps to protect its customers and fulfill its obligations.

Universal Migrator helps startups:

  • Extract customer data before systems are decommissioned.
  • Deliver information in structured, accessible formats.
  • Support migrations into replacement platforms when appropriate.
  • Create a consistent process across the entire customer base.
  • Reduce dependence on a shrinking internal engineering team.
  • Document the steps taken to return or transfer customer information.

This can help founders, investors, and wind-down teams close the company without leaving unresolved data issues behind.

Keeping Engineers Focused on the Wind-Down

As a startup approaches closure, employees may leave, infrastructure may be reduced, and engineering resources may become increasingly limited. Building and supporting custom export tools can consume time that the remaining team needs for security, billing, vendor termination, compliance, and other shutdown responsibilities.

Universal Migrator allows the company to rely on migration specialists and proven tooling rather than creating a new offboarding system from scratch.

The result is a more efficient process for the startup and a better experience for customers who need access to their information.

Support for More Than 170 Applications

Universal Migrator supports migrations involving more than 170 legal and business applications, including practice management, document management, CRM, billing, accounting, and related systems.

That broad connector library allows Universal Migrator to support a range of shutdown scenarios, whether customers need their data exported for safekeeping or transferred directly into another application.

About Universal Migrator

Universal Migrator is a migration platform built for consultants, technology professionals, and software companies that need to move customer data between business applications.

Its growing library of connectors and migration tools helps teams accelerate conversions, improve repeatability, and reduce the manual work involved in extracting, transforming, and transferring complex data.

For startups preparing to close, Universal Migrator provides a practical way to make customer offboarding part of a responsible wind-down—helping protect customer relationships, reduce potential disputes, and give founders greater peace of mind.

news.summaryZh: LexisNexis Legal & Professional宣布在纽约市开设客户创新实验室，该实验室约一个半月前已实际开放。法律专业人士、LexisNexis工程师及包括OpenAI和亚马逊云科技在内的AI技术合作伙伴在此并肩工作，设计、原型化和测试新的法律AI能力，有时一小时内多次迭代。实验室提供了一种法律AI构建和交付的新模式：不再内部开发后让客户验证，而是让客户参与工作会话，工程师实时针对其痛点构建。通过质量、准确性和安全标准的原型可进入LexisNexis代理平台，或为客户定制，或在Lexis+ with Protégé中扩展。实验室将了解问题的人与能构建解决方案的人之间的距离缩短，同一房间使技术专家真正理解问题，加速响应市场。传统方法每次迭代需数周或数月，实验室将循环缩短至几分钟。Dickason称上周看到解决方案在一小时内因客户反馈更改四次。约20人的实验室团队向约4000人的工程组织移交原型，功能级功能从原型到上线产品可不到一个月。实验室已产出原型和设计，正推进为Lexis+ with Protégé能力，包括：客户管理的Protégé Vault用于多媒体材料，允许存储和分析文档、视频、音频和图像，可上传两小时视频证词并询问证人何时表现惊讶及当时讨论内容，发现可追溯至时间戳和源材料；Protégé Workrooms，安全共享空间，团队可与外部律师、客户、专家等授权参与者汇集文档、分析、技能和AI辅助工作，受权限和访问控制管理；LexisNexis开发的法律AI模型，利用公司内容和专业知识专为法律工作构建。
news.bodyHtml:
LexisNexis Legal & Professional today announced the opening of its Customer Innovation Lab in New York City, a physical space where legal professionals, LexisNexis engineers, and AI technology partners including OpenAI and Amazon Web Services work side by side to design, prototype and test new legal AI capabilities – sometimes iterating on an idea multiple times within a single hour.

The company says the lab – which actually opened about 1.5 months ago – offers a new model for how legal AI gets built and shipped. Rather than developing AI capabilities internally and asking customers to validate them after the fact, the lab brings customers into a working session, where LexisNexis engineers build against their specific pain points in real time.

Prototypes that clear the company’s standards for quality, accuracy and security can advance into development as capabilities within the LexisNexis agentic platform, either customized for the customer or scaled across Lexis+ with Protégé.

“For me, the biggest thing is we’re collapsing the distance between the people who know what the problem is and the people who can build the solution,” Greg Dickason, chief technology officer of LexisNexis Legal & Professional, told me in an interview for my LawNext podcast, which will air later this week.

“Putting them in the same room means that our technologists really understand the problems, which means that our ability to respond very quickly to where the market’s going is hyper-accelerated.”

A Different Approach to Customer Input

Over the years, I have sat through any number of company briefings – including by LexisNexis – in which executives told me that customer involvement was a core tenet of how the company develops products. So I asked Dickason to explain what is actually different with the lab.

His answer, in a nutshell, was cycle time. The traditional approach – which involves interviewing customers, going and building something, bringing it back for feedback, and then repeating the process – could take weeks or months per iteration, he said. In the lab, that loop collapses to minutes.

“Literally in the session in the lab, the customers are telling us their problem. We’ve already got the first solution, because we’ve listened and we’ve already pulled that together. We show that to the customer. They say to us, ‘Yeah, but it would work slightly better if this happened or that happened.’ And then we tweak it live in the lab,” Dickason said.

Just last week, he said, he saw a solution get changed four times in one hour as a result of customer feedback.

The idea is for everyone to be hands-on in real time, Dickason said. While one or two LexisNexis staff talk with the customer, engineers sit alongside, listening and coding, often using agentic coding tools such as Claude Code integrated into the LexisNexis product. At some point, they turn their laptops around and ask, “Is this what you meant?”

Dickason said the lab has been quietly operating for about a month and a half ahead of today’s launch, with the company using that time to refine its working cadence, including how a lab team of roughly 20 people hands off prototypes to an engineering organization of some 4,000.

For functionality-level features, he said, the path from lab prototype to live product “can be less than a month.” 

Already Out of the Lab

The lab has already produced prototypes and designs that LexisNexis says are advancing into Lexis+ with Protégé capabilities, including:

  • A customer-managed Protégé Vault for multimedia materials, allowing legal professionals to store and analyze documents, video, audio and images together. Using this tool, Dickason told me, a customer could upload a two-hour video deposition and ask when the witness showed surprise and what was being discussed at that moment, with findings traced to timestamps and source materials.
  • Protégé Workrooms, secure shared spaces where teams can bring together documents, analyses, skills and AI-assisted work on a matter with outside counsel, clients, experts and other authorized participants, governed by permissions and access controls.
  • LexisNexis-developed legal AI models, purpose-built for legal work using the company’s content and expertise.

The vault work, Dickason said, originated from a gap the company had heard about from customers, then took shape when customers came into the lab and described the actual queries they would run. He said that one of LexisNexis’s core technology providers, which he declined to name, was in the room with the customers, helping define what was technically possible. 

Drafting As A Priority

LexisNexis says that the lab’s current top priority is legal drafting. The company cites research showing lawyers spend 40 to 60 percent of their time drafting and reviewing documents, more than on any other task.

Existing tools, Dickason said, get lawyers only 80 or 90 percent of the way there, leaving hours of work to reach a final product. The gaps he identified included conforming drafts to a firm’s own style, precedents and playbooks; flagging risk against a customer’s own standards; carrying context across related documents so a primary document and its supporting materials line up; verification of citations surfaced directly in the draft; and layering in litigation and judicial analytics.

Frontier Models, For Now

With Thomson Reuters recently announcing that its own proprietary model will begin replacing general-purpose models for certain tasks, I asked Dickason whether LexisNexis sees itself heading the same direction.

“Never say never,” he said, but for now the company’s view is that frontier models — he specifically mentioned Claude Opus 5 — combined with LexisNexis’s knowledge graph, retrieval infrastructure and prompting deliver state-of-the-art results.

The company has evaluated models continuously since its work with Amazon on Bedrock more than three years ago, he said, and already uses fine-tuned models for certain parts of the legal workflow.

“We’re going to make sure the highest quality is for us the number one bar,” he said.

Dickason also sees an agent-driven future in which AI agents increasingly act on behalf of lawyers — “disintermediating the user,” as he put it — and said LexisNexis is working on agent-to-agent and MCP interfaces to participate in that ecosystem.

Notably, he does not want third-party agents browsing raw content inside Lexis+ with Protégé, arguing that raw retrieval without the company’s grounding and tuning “generally doesn’t work.”

Who Gets In

Participation is open to “effectively anybody,” Dickason said, from CIOs and partners to junior associates, small firms, solos, and even judges, and whether or not they are current customers.

LexisNexis owns the IP in what comes out of the lab, which participants acknowledge before joining. Dickason said the lab is also set up for a separate track in which large firms building their own internal AI platforms can explore how LexisNexis might plug in.

Now that the lab has launched as an ongoing operation in New York, LexisNexis plans to expand it globally as well as to conduct on-site lab sessions at ILTACON and at customer locations. Firms and legal departments can learn more at www.lexisnexis.com/lab.

My full interview with Dickason will air later this week on LawNext.

news.bodyHtml:
LexisNexis Legal & Professional today (4 August) announced the opening of its Customer Innovation Lab in New York City – describing it as a new model for how legal AI gets built and shipped.  

Within the Lab, legal professionals, LexisNexis engineers, and AI collaborators like OpenAI and Amazon Web Services will “build side by side”, solving workflow pain points with prototypes “in hours”. 

Advertisement

The Lab launches with around 30 people, made up of engineers, AR scientists and productivity UX specialists, of which 20 are fully dedicated to the Lab. They have been hired in as well as moved internally, with the anticipation that LexisNexis will also cycle through its other 4,000 engineers and technologists.  

Speaking to Legal IT Insider about the Lab, LexisNexis executive vice president and chief technology officer Greg Dickason said that it is a reflection of the speed of change, observing: “What was done in months and years in the past is now being done in weeks.” 

Advertisement

With model providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI releasing models every six weeks to eight weeks, Dickason observed that “what we’re really seeing is that our customers are struggling with how do they absorb all of this AI, not just from the model providers, but also across the board from all the different vendors out there.” 

The idea of the Lab is to bring LexisNexis engineers closer to the customer, with “none of this middle layer.” It is hoped that this will help customers to get a handle on how to cut through the noise as well as help to build products live. 

Dickason says: “We did one this week, which I was pretty excited about. The customer gave us feedback, we iterated, they gave us more feedback, reiterated, and essentially in one hour, we had changed the product three times.  

“For me, that’s the real sort of signal of how the Lab can work, is that we can [not only] understand customer problems, but put them right with the people who can build the solution, which is the engineers.” 

Much of the development will focus on legal AI assistant LexisNexis Protégé, and asked how LexisNexis will streamline customer demands, Dickason said that “when you get that feedback from one customer, that doesn’t immediately become a product. It gives us really good ideas as to where we should be going. And then we can test it with a second set of customers and a third set. But very quickly, within a week or so, we would have tested it with, say, 10 or 20 different customers and got real ideas to what’s going to make a difference for them.” 

He adds: “The Lab’s really helping us crystallise what’s most important.”  

 LexisNexis via the Lab is already engaging with associates and CIOs and technology leaders. It is already working with a few of the Am Law top 50 firms and a couple of the Am Law top 10 firms. 

Examples of ideas that have come to fruition include an advanced, customer-managed Protégé Vault for analysing complex multimedia materials. Legal professionals will be able to store and analyse documents, videos, images, audio files, and other matter materials. A lawyer could, for example, analyse a two-hour deposition in minutes with Protégé, pinpoint the exact moments when key facts emerge, and trace findings directly to the timestamps and source materials. 

Interestingly, as we enter a period in which a lot of the largest law firms are looking at leveraging their own ecosystem rather than buying a product off the shelf, and even training their own models, Dickason says the Lab helps “because it helps them conceptualise.”

“I see it as educational,” he says. “So it’s not just about coming and us getting all the benefit of it. It’s also for them to get other benefits to come in, understand how we think about fine tuning, where we see fine tuning models make sense and where you should still be using foundation models. We use a blend of models across all the major vendors, but also fine tune our own. And I think it really comes down to what’s the right use case for your particular need , what you need to do.”  

While the Lab is currently a physical space in New York, LexisNexis will also be looking at rolling out in other major centers around the world.  

Dickason says: “I think you get so much more when people are in one room and they can actually see and interact. You get far more when people can see the response. And say ‘okay, that worked. That didn’t work.’ You don’t get that over Teams, et cetera.”  

“Congratulations to LexisNexis on the launch of its Customer Innovation Lab,” said Scott Liska, VP AWSI, Amazon Web Services in a statement. “Bringing trusted AI into professional work requires both rapid innovation and a strong technology foundation. We look forward to continuing our collaboration with LexisNexis as it advances secure, authoritative AI capabilities for legal professionals.”  

At the time of publishing, LexisNexis was looking for a director of software innovation, if you think that has your name on it, you can take a look at that role here: https://www.builtinnyc.com/job/director-software-engineering-customer-innovation-lab/9690097

news.summaryZh: LawSHIFT于7月1日推出迷你书《预受理问题：当受伤者寻找答案时，人身伤害律师缺席对话》，由Nick Kringas和Lydia Flocchini合著。书中将“预受理问题™”定义为受伤者在与法律顾问交谈前，试图了解发生了什么、自身权利及下一步行动的阶段。随着人们使用消费者AI平台提出法律问题、评估潜在索赔并决定信任哪些律师，AI在这一窗口期的影响力日益增强。人身伤害律所数十年来在搜索、电话或表单提交后竞争可见度，但最重要的决定越来越多地在受理前、律师与受伤者交谈前就已形成；第一次法律对话不再总是与律师进行，而越来越多是与AI进行。行业大量投资于改善受理后的流程，却较少关注人们仍在理解自身处境并决定信任谁的时期。LawSHIFT确立了“Pre-Intake AI for PI™”类别，并开发“AI for PI Index™”，追踪领先AI平台在美国数百个市场中如何解释、引用和推荐人身伤害律所。基于256个市场超过1500家律所的数据，覆盖约20000家律所，公司每周发布洞察，研究AI如何重塑法律可见度、权威和客户获取。客户旅程已经改变，律所声誉过去存在于市场中，现在还必须对机器可读，权威必须转化为AI能识别、信任和推荐的信号，这是新法律推荐经济的开始；AI不会取代人身伤害律师，但日益塑造受伤者的信念、提出的问题以及首先考虑的律师。该书现已在LawSHIFT的Substack上发布。LawSHIFT成立于2013年，总部纽约，拥有超过50年人身伤害营销、法律技术、类别设计和增长策略的综合经验，其技术包括AI for PI Index™、CASETIMATOR™和专有AI Authority Protocol™。
news.bodyHtml:
New mini-book examines how AI is influencing injured people before they ever speak with an attorney

NEW YORK — July 2026 — LawSHIFT, the Pre-Intake AI for PI™ company, announced the launch of The Pre-Intake Problem: When Injured People Are Searching for Answers, Personal Injury Attorneys Are Missing From the Conversation. This new mini-book co-authored by Nick Kringas and Lydia Flocchini examines how artificial intelligence is changing the earliest stage of the legal client journey.

Published July 1, the book defines the Pre-Intake Problem™ as the period when injured people are trying to understand what happened, what their rights may be, and what to do next before speaking with legal counsel. LawSHIFT argues that AI is becoming increasingly influential during this window as people use consumer AI platforms to ask legal questions, evaluate potential claims, and decide which attorneys they may trust.

“Personal injury firms have spent decades competing for visibility after someone searches, calls, or fills out a form,” said Nick Kringas, Founder and CEO of LawSHIFT. “The most important decisions are increasingly being shaped before intake and before a lawyer ever speaks with the injured person. That is the pre-intake problem.”

Law firms have traditionally built client acquisition strategies around referrals, advertising, reputation, and search visibility. Those channels remain important, but LawSHIFT believes the client journey is being rerouted as injured people increasingly seek AI-generated guidance before contacting a firm.

“The first legal conversation is no longer always with a lawyer. Increasingly, it is with AI,” Kringas said. “The legal industry has invested heavily in improving intake once someone reaches a firm, while paying far less attention to the period when that person is still trying to understand their situation and decide whom to trust.”

LawSHIFT was built around the question of what happens before an injured person ever calls an attorney. The company has established Pre-Intake AI for PI™ as a category focused on that previously difficult-to-measure stage and has developed the AI for PI Index™, an ongoing research initiative tracking how leading AI platforms interpret, cite, and recommend personal injury firms across hundreds of U.S. markets. Drawing on data from more than 1,500 firms across 256 markets, with visibility into approximately 20,000 firms, the company publishes weekly insights examining how AI is reshaping legal visibility, authority, and client acquisition.

 

Lydia Flocchini, Partner and Legal Category Designer at LawSHIFT, said, “The client journey has already changed. A law firm’s reputation used to live in the market. Now it must also be legible to machines. Authority has to be translated into signals AI can recognize, trust, and recommend. This is the beginning of a new legal referral economy.”

“AI is not replacing personal injury attorneys, but it is increasingly shaping what injured people believe, which questions they ask, and which attorneys they consider first,” Flocchini said. “Our mission is to help close the distance between that early search for answers and trusted legal counsel.”

The Pre-Intake Problem: When Injured People Are Searching for Answers, Personal Injury Attorneys Are Missing From the Conversation is available now on LawSHIFT’s Substack.

 

About LawSHIFT

LawSHIFT is the Pre-Intake AI for PI™ company, building AI systems, visibility infrastructure, and pre-intake tools for the personal injury legal market. Founded in 2013 and headquartered in New York, the company brings together more than 50 years of combined experience across personal injury marketing, legal technology, category design, and growth strategy. LawSHIFT’s technology includes the AI for PI Index™, CASETIMATOR™, and its proprietary AI Authority Protocol™, all developed around its mission to help injured people move from early questions and AI-assisted research toward trusted legal counsel.

Media Contact
Name: Lydia Flocchini
Email: lydia@lawshift.ai

news.titleEn: Federal magistrate judge treats LinkedIn’s Relativity aiR workflow as TAR
news.titleZh: 联邦治安法官将LinkedIn的Relativity aiR工作流程视为技术辅助审查
news.summaryZh: 在Schulte诉LinkedIn公司案中，美国加利福尼亚北区联邦治安法官Laurel Beeler签署了一项12页的命令，驳回了原告针对LinkedIn的Relativity aiR工作流程提出的全部三项要求。法官将该工具视为技术辅助审查的一种形式，并依据双方已有的证据开示协议进行处理。该命令于2026年6月30日签署，次日录入案件目录。它不构成对其他法院有约束力的先例，仅基于特定案件记录解决了一项协议争议，而非普遍认可生成式人工智能审查。评论认为此案的克制态度是新闻点。退休的美国治安法官Andrew Peck及其DLA Piper同事Reema Holz将Schulte案描述为第一个接受生成式人工智能在证据开示中做出最终响应性判断的联邦决定。该案本身是一起反垄断集体诉讼，而非技术争议。原告于2022年1月起诉LinkedIn，指控其垄断专业社交网络市场并向高级订阅用户超额收费。命令还一并解决了另外两项未引发评论的请求，即拒绝将内部律师添加为保管人以及拒绝提供短信的要求。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: A federal magistrate judge has given litigators their first close look at how a court handles generative artificial intelligence making final responsiveness calls, and the answer required no new law. In Schulte v. LinkedIn Corp., the court denied three plaintiff demands aimed at LinkedIn’s Relativity aiR workflow and treated the tool as a form of technology-assisted review under the case’s existing ESI order. The order is nonprecedential and tied to its record, which is exactly why the commentary matters: retired Magistrate Judge Andrew Peck, whose Da Silva Moore opinion opened the TAR era, describes it with DLA Piper colleague Reema Holz as the first federal decision to accept generative AI in that role.

Compliance, security and information governance teams should note what mattered: custodial volume materially influenced the proportionality decision, disclosure obligations began and ended with the protocol, and validation metrics were not compelled absent a specific deficiency. Watch the search-string conference the order required, the diverging AI confidentiality rulings, and the protocol language crossing your desk this quarter.

The rules held. The expectations moved.

Industry News – Artificial Intelligence Beat

Federal magistrate judge treats LinkedIn’s Relativity aiR workflow as TAR

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

A federal magistrate judge has looked at LinkedIn’s plan to let a generative artificial intelligence tool make final responsiveness calls and found nothing that required new rules.

In a 12-page order in Schulte v. LinkedIn Corp., U.S. Magistrate Judge Laurel Beeler of the Northern District of California denied all three plaintiff demands aimed at the Relativity aiR workflow, treating the tool as a form of technology-assisted review, or TAR, under the discovery protocol the parties already had.

Beeler signed the order June 30, 2026, and it entered the docket the next day. It creates no precedent that binds another court, and it resolves one protocol fight on one record rather than blessing generative AI review at large. What it does is meet a closely watched test with the machinery that already exists: reasonableness, proportionality and the disfavored status of discovery on discovery.

The commentary treated that restraint as the news. Retired U.S. Magistrate Judge Andrew Peck, who wrote the 2012 opinion in Da Silva Moore v. Publicis Groupe that first approved technology-assisted review, and his DLA Piper colleague Reema Holz describe Schulte as the first federal decision to accept generative AI making the final responsiveness call in discovery. At least eight law firms and eDiscovery providers published analyses within a month of the order.

The underlying case is an antitrust class action, not a technology dispute. Todd Crowder, Kevin Schulte and Garrick Vance sued LinkedIn in January 2022, alleging the company monopolized the professional social networking market and overcharged Premium subscribers. The operative complaint, as the discovery order summarizes it, alleges LinkedIn offered potential rivals access to its private user data through application programming interfaces unavailable to others, on the condition that they not compete with LinkedIn, and tied its user data to parent company Microsoft’s Azure cloud product. U.S. District Judge Haywood S. Gilliam Jr. dismissed an earlier version of the complaint with leave to amend in 2023, then allowed the amended complaint to proceed in March 2024. A proposed class settlement failed to win preliminary approval in 2025, Reuters reported, returning the parties to litigation and to the custodial document discovery that produced this dispute in case number 22-cv-00237. Court records opened the matter as Crowder v. LinkedIn Corporation; the discovery order and the commentary around it carry Schulte’s name. The order itself resolved three discovery letter briefs at once, and the two that drew no commentary, a denied request to add an in-house attorney as a custodian and a denied demand for text message production, are a reminder that the aiR fight was one dispute among several.

news.titleEn: When 'Agentic AI' Meets Data Protection Laws: A Fundamental Mismatch?
news.titleZh: 当“代理式AI”遇上数据保护法：根本性错配？
news.summaryZh: 代理式AI是自主、目标导向的系统，能追求开放式目标、自行创建工作流并在有限人类监督下实时适应，已在金融、医疗、物流和机器人等行业获得关注，主要AI开发商提供预构建工作流模板以加速这一转变。该技术对现代隐私与数据保护法构成根本性挑战，后者依赖同意、目的限制以及个人与非个人数据区分等假设。文章主张代理式AI要求重新思考隐私法，并邀请政策制定者、监管机构与科技公司考虑数据保护规则应如何为日益自主的AI系统演进。代理式AI违背GDPR和CCPA等法规的基本假设，体现在两个系统性挑战：个人与非个人数据的刚性二分法在AI介导的交互中瓦解；同意与目的限制等核心原则在自主代理流动、不确定的意图无法事前确定时功能上过时。GDPR建立在“同意与控制”框架上，依赖静态数据处理模型，要求控制者在收集时明确阐述具体目的，但该假设在AI时代不再成立。自主系统缺乏固定操作路径，使传统目的限制规则失去意义；AI代理遵循开放式目标并动态生成中间步骤、工作流和数据收集策略，其实际意图与行动轨迹无法事前知晓或预测。代理式爬虫基于广泛目标自主导航，动态决定路径，控制者无法事前知晓是否会摄取个人数据。AI代理持续重新利用数据，例如从健身追踪器生物识别数据推断心理健康状况，可能构成GDPR旨在防止的未经授权“进一步处理”。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Agentic AI represents a seismic shift toward autonomous, goal-directed systems that can pursue open-ended objectives, create their own workflows, and adapt in real time with limited human oversight. This development poses fundamental challenges to modern privacy and data protection laws, which depend on assumptions about consent, purpose limitation, and the distinction between personal and non-personal data. This post argues that agentic AI requires a rethinking of privacy law and invites policymakers, regulators, and technology companies to consider how data protection rules should evolve for a world of increasingly autonomous AI systems. Modern agentic AI introduces a distinct paradigm shift in data protection. Agentic AI refers to autonomous, goal-seeking systems capable of pursuing open-ended objectives and adapting continuously without persistent human direction. From a cognitive perspective, AI agents are capable of learning dynamically from their environment, revising their own goals, and making decisions with minimal human oversight and control. Adaptive AI agents are already gaining traction across sectors as diverse as finance, healthcare, logistics, and robotics. To accelerate this transition, major AI developers are providing pre-built workflow templates that automate complex sequences or empower users to build custom-designed agentic architectures. However, the rise of agentic AI reveals a profound and growing mismatch between the realities of machine autonomy and the well-established legal frameworks designed to govern digital systems and protect personal privacy. Crucially, agentic AI defies the foundational assumptions underpinning data protection regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). This tension is best illustrated by two systemic challenges. First, the rigid dichotomy between personal and non-personal data (a distinction central to regulatory scope) collapses within context-hungry, AI-mediated interactions. Second, core principles governing data processing, such as consent and purpose limitation, become functionally obsolete when the fluid, indeterminate, and unpredictable intent of an autonomous agent cannot be determined ex ante. Europe’s flagship data protection regulation, the GDPR, is built on an ambition to restrain the unchecked exploitation of data. The EU aimed to empower individual consumers and curb the surveillance-capitalism models that defined the commercialized Internet. The GDPR mandates a lawful basis for processing personal data while establishing robust safeguards for data subjects such as explicit consent, lawful basis, and purpose limitation. Under this “consent and control” framework, data subjects “relinquish” absolute privacy in exchange for an enforceable regime of “data protection.” This framework relies on a fundamentally static model of data processing, wherein a human data controller pre-determines what data is collected, how it will be utilized, and when it will be deleted. As such, the GDPR operates on the assumption that controllers can clearly articulate these discrete purposes to data subjects at the point of data collection. That assumption no longer holds in the age of AI. Agentic AI systems undermine these well-established legal principles. First, autonomous systems lack a fixed, pre-programmed operational path, rendering traditional purpose-limitation rules meaningless. AI agents follow open-ended objectives and dynamically generate their own intermediary steps, workflows, and data-gathering strategies. Simply put, the actual intent and action trajectory of an AI agent cannot be known or predicted ex ante, and this characteristic of the technology is by design. This systemic unpredictability of intent can be illustrated by modern automated web intelligence, or data scraping, practices. Unlike legacy scrapers that execute deterministic scripts targeting specific data fields, an agentic crawler operates autonomously in a browser based on broad goals, such as “map regional market sentiment” or “find the top 10 trending items on Amazon.” It independently navigates the web, uses adaptive machine learning to overcome operational frictions, and dynamically decides which pathways or unindexed forums to harvest. Because its retrieval logic evolves in real time, the controller cannot know ex ante whether it will ingest personal data or cross-reference anonymous profiles. In this setting, ex ante declarations of data access intent risk becoming a legal fiction because the agent itself determines relevance and collection scope mid-execution. Second, AI agents continuously repurpose data. Their core utility lies in reapplying ingested knowledge across fluid, evolving contexts. For example, an agent with access to an individual’s biometric data from a fitness tracker might begin by monitoring step counts, but later infer a user’s mental health status, burnout levels, or cardiac conditions. Neither the developer nor the user could have predicted this outcome ex ante. Although such synthesis may be an engineering breakthrough, it may constitute an unauthorized “further processing” the GDPR was designed to prevent. Because an autonomous agent reasons non-linearly and in real time, it cannot pause mid-execution to conduct an Article 6(4) compatibility assessment before shifting the purpose of its processing.
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要讨论代理式AI对数据保护法（如GDPR和CCPA）的挑战，属于法律与AI交叉领域，核心关注法律框架如何适应AI技术，因此高度相关。

news.titleEn: Alabama State Bar Issues AI Ethics Guidance for Lawyers: Key Questions and Practical Answers
news.titleZh: 阿拉巴马州律师协会发布律师AI伦理指南：关键问题与实践解答
news.summaryZh:
阿拉巴马州律师协会加入越来越多提供律师使用人工智能正式指导的司法管辖区行列。第2026-01号正式意见《人工智能使用：现行职业行为规则下的最佳实践》并未创设新的伦理义务，而是解释《职业行为规则》下的长期义务在律师于执业中使用生成式AI和新兴代理式AI工具时如何适用。该意见认识到AI已迅速从实验性技术转变为日常工具，用于起草文件、总结证据、开展研究、分析合同及与客户沟通。阿拉巴马州律师协会未等待纪律问题出现，而是主动解释现行职业行为规则如何管辖这些技术。

该意见强调AI不产生新的伦理义务，而是“重新语境化”现有义务，包括胜任、保密、监督、沟通、坦诚和合理费用。意见承认AI有潜力提高效率、降低成本并扩大法律服务获取。阿拉巴马州承认AI正成为现代法律实践的普通组成部分，律师应理解其益处与局限。随着AI更深入融入法律教育与实践，技术胜任日益包括理解AI工具。意见始终回归一个核心原则：律师对最终工作成果负责，即使AI协助创建。实际期望包括：胜任代理现在包括理解AI如何运作，以充分认识其能力与风险。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The Alabama State Bar has joined a growing number of jurisdictions providing formal guidance on lawyers’ use of artificial intelligence. Formal Opinion 2026-01, Artificial Intelligence Use: Best Practices Under Existing Professional Conduct Rules, does not create new ethical obligations. Instead, it explains how longstanding duties under the Rules of Professional Conduct apply when lawyers use generative AI and emerging agentic AI tools in practice. Below are answers to some of the most important questions for law firms and legal departments. The opinion recognizes that AI has rapidly moved from an experimental technology to an everyday tool used to draft documents, summarize evidence, conduct research, analyze contracts, and communicate with clients. Rather than waiting for disciplinary issues to arise, the Alabama State Bar sought to explain how existing professional conduct rules govern these technologies. Importantly, the opinion emphasizes that AI does not create new ethical duties. Instead, it “recontextualizes” existing duties—including competence, confidentiality, supervision, communication, candor, and reasonable fees—in light of AI-assisted legal practice. No. To the contrary, the opinion recognizes AI’s potential to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and expand access to legal services. Alabama acknowledges that AI is becoming an ordinary component of modern legal practice and that lawyers should understand both its benefits and its limitations. The opinion also notes that as AI becomes more integrated into legal education and practice, technological competence increasingly includes understanding AI tools. The opinion consistently returns to one central principle: Lawyers remain responsible for the final work product—even when AI assisted in creating it. research.titleEn: LegalPincite: Multi-level Legal Information Retrieval Dataset
research.titleZh: LegalPincite：多层级法律信息检索数据集
research.abstractEn: A common task in legal Information Retrieval (IR) is to find relevant legal sources from case-law collections. While legal practice often requires pinpoint citations (pincites) to specific case paragraphs, most existing public legal IR datasets lack paragraph-level citation annotations. Yet, publicly available datasets with such information contain data leakage in the query text and exclude paragraphs that are neither citing nor cited from the corpora, creating an unrealistic and oversimplified retrieval setting, potentially leading to inflated performance. To address these limitations, we contribute a large-scale legal IR dataset constructed from Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) judgments. The dataset contains: (i) masked case/paragraph queries, with removed citation information; (ii) a corpus that includes all paragraphs; and (iii) case- and paragraph-level ground-truth citations, with partial human expert validation. Our dataset supports both the development and rigorous evaluation of legal IR methods, at multiple query-document levels (case-to-case, paragraph-to-case, and paragraph-to-paragraph retrieval). Link to dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/theresiavr/legalpincite
research.abstractZh: 法律信息检索（IR）中的一个常见任务是从判例法集合中查找相关的法律来源。虽然法律实践通常需要针对特定案件段落的精确引用（pincites），但大多数现有的公开法律IR数据集缺乏段落级别的引用标注。然而，具有此类信息的公开数据集在查询文本中存在数据泄漏，并且从语料库中排除了既未引用也未引用的段落，从而造成不现实且过度简化的检索环境，可能导致性能虚高。为解决这些局限性，我们构建了一个基于欧盟法院（CJEU）判决的大规模法律IR数据集。该数据集包含：（i）掩码的案件/段落查询，移除了引用信息；（ii）包含所有段落的语料库；以及（iii）案件级和段落级的地面真值引用，并经过部分人类专家验证。我们的数据集支持法律IR方法在多个查询-文档层级（案件到案件、段落到案件、段落到段落检索）上的开发和严格评估。数据集链接：https://huggingface.co/datasets/theresiavr/legalpincite

news.titleEn: New Site From Suffolk Law Dean Andrew Perlman Catalogs AI Policies at 128 Law Schools
news.titleZh: 萨福克法学院院长安德鲁·珀尔曼推出新网站，收录128所法学院的AI政策
news.summaryZh: 萨福克大学法学院院长安德鲁·珀尔曼推出网站“AI in Legal Education: Law School Policy Archive”，收录196所美国法学院中128所的公开AI政策、教学策略和课程项目，按八个主题分类，数据源自各校公开文件。每条记录链接至原始来源，如学生手册、荣誉准则、院长备忘录等，并标注状态（生效、临时、试点、拟议、指南或已完成/有限）。数据集可下载为电子表格，珀尔曼邀请读者提交政策、更正和遗漏。网站方法部分说明，广泛使用ChatGPT Sites进行研究和构建，ChatGPT定位许多公开来源、组织主题类别并帮助起草摘要；珀尔曼未手动审查或独立确认每条参考或摘要，读者应查阅链接的原始来源。学校未出现在某主题中不意味着没有政策，受大学范围AI规则约束的学校可能完全不出现；清单排除通用大学政策、个人教学大纲、仅招生规则和期刊政策。下载的数据截至2026年8月2日，包含128所法学院的279条主题记录，涵盖八个主题：可选AI课程与机会66所；提交和评分作业中的AI使用58所；教师教学指导与支持37所；强制AI课程与素养26所；课程级AI政策披露20所；用于学习和研究的AI 16所；将课程材料上传至AI 3所。关于提交和评分作业，58所中多数默认禁止AI，除非教师明确书面授权，各校将未经授权使用视为作弊、抄袭或“未经授权协助”，但基本规则一致，斯坦福、西北、弗吉尼亚、密歇根（2026-27拟议）、北卡罗来纳、威斯康星等数十所学校均要求教师选择加入。
news.bodyHtml:
When law school AI policies have made news, it has usually been because they were controversial. UC Berkeley School of Law’s restrictive policy, which I wrote about in May, drew national attention for barring generative AI from nearly every stage of producing graded work.

But a new website launched by Andrew Perlman, dean of Suffolk University Law School, reveals how widespread and varied these policies have become. The site, AI in Legal Education: Law School Policy Archive, catalogs public AI policies, teaching strategies, and curricular programs from 128 of the 196 U.S. law schools, organized into eight topic areas and derived from the schools’ own published documents.

For each school, the archive links to the underlying source, including student handbooks, honor codes, dean’s memoranda, strategy statements and program pages. Each source is also labeled by its status: in effect, interim, pilot, proposed, guidance, or completed/limited.

The full dataset is downloadable as a spreadsheet, and Perlman invites readers to submit policies, corrections and omissions.

Perlman, long one of legal education’s most prominent voices on innovation and technology, is transparent about the site’s scope and limitations – and about how he built it.

Andrew Perlman

The site’s methodology section says that ChatGPT Sites was used extensively to research and construct the archive, with ChatGPT locating many of the public sources, organizing them into topic categories, and helping draft the summaries

Perlman, the site says, has not manually reviewed or independently confirmed every reference or summary, and readers should consult the linked original sources.

It is, in other words, an AI-assembled archive documenting how law schools regulate AI.

The site notes that a school’s absence from a topic does not mean it lacks a policy, and schools governed by university-wide AI rules may not appear at all.

The inventory excludes generic university policies, individual syllabi, admissions-only rules, and journal policies.

What the Data Shows

The site makes all of the underlying data downloadable. So, in keeping with the meta-ness of an AI-generated inventory of AI policies, I downloaded the data and asked AI to help me analyze it. Since Perlman used ChatGPT to create the site, I enlisted its competitor Claude to evaluate it.

The spreadsheet I downloaded, current as of Aug. 2, 2026, contains 279 topic records spanning eight subjects at 128 law schools.  Here is how the subjects break down, showing the number of schools catalogued in each:

  • Optional AI curriculum and opportunities: 66.
  • AI use in submitted and graded work: 58.
  • AI use on exams: 53.
  • Faculty teaching guidance and support: 37.
  • Mandatory AI curriculum and literacy: 26.
  • Course-level AI policy disclosure: 20.
  • AI use for studying and learning: 16.
  • Uploading course materials to AI: 3.

Several findings jump out.

  1. Prohibition is the default.

With regard to AI use for submitted and graded work, of the 58 schools catalogued, the majority prohibit AI by default unless the instructor expressly authorizes it, usually in writing.

The ways they do this vary. Some schools treat unauthorized AI use as cheating, others as plagiarism, others as “unauthorized assistance.” But the basic rule is remarkably consistent, with schools such as Stanford, Northwestern, Virginia, Michigan (proposed for 2026-27), North Carolina, Wisconsin, and dozens of others all requiring some version of instructor opt-in.

The same is true for exams, with nearly all 53 catalogued schools prohibiting AI use during an examination absent instructor permission. Columbia’s rule is typical: Students must not prompt or engage with AI during an exam, and every word of the answer must be the student’s own.

Considered in this context, Berkeley’s policy – which generated headlines and criticism (including from me) looks less like an outlier. Its basic structure, a default prohibition from which instructors can deviate in writing, is the majority approach.

That said, Berkeley’s policy is still unique for its breadth, in that it enumerates prohibited AI use at every stage from conceptualizing to editing, limits permitted research use to identifying sources, and bars students from uploading any course materials into AI systems.

On that last point, Berkeley has little company. Only three schools in Perlman’s inventory have rules on uploading course materials to AI: Berkeley, St. Mary’s and Suffolk itself, where Perlman’s own July 27 memo proposes prohibiting students from uploading class recordings or other students’ identifiable contributions to third-party AI services without permission.

  1. Mandatory AI instruction is spreading.

Notably, even as law schools are restricting AI use, they are mandating its training. Twenty-six schools have mandatory AI curriculum or literacy requirements, and the list is growing semester by semester. For example:

  • Case Western Reserve requires all first-year students to complete its Introduction to AI and the Law certification, launched in February 2025 and described by the school as the first required legal-AI certification of its kind nationally.
  • Mississippi College adopted the same certification requirement for its 1Ls beginning this past spring.
  • UC Law San Francisco will require every J.D. student, starting with the Class of 2029, to complete an AI-enabled lawyering lab.
  • UNLV’s Boyd School of Law adds a required course in responsible AI use this fall.
  • Texas maps AI learning objectives across all three years of its J.D. program.
  • Ohio State runs a mandatory three-part AI workshop series for all 1Ls.
  • Penn, Santa Clara, DePaul, George Washington, Albany, and others embed required AI instruction in their first-year skills sequences.

With regard to optional training, the numbers are even larger. Sixty-six schools offer elective AI courses, certificates, concentrations, clinics or labs.

Drake and Rutgers offer AI law certificates. St. Thomas (Minnesota) offers a 12-credit AI concentration. Emory launches an AI and the Law concentration this academic year. Boston University debuts an AI for Law Practice certificate this fall.

Taken together, the data suggests law schools are converging on a common approach, which is to restrict AI in graded work and exams, but teach it everywhere else.

  1. Assessment is changing.

Some of the more interesting entries in Perlman’s inventory are not about whether students may use AI, but how schools are redesigning assessment because of it:

  • The University of Texas reports the near-elimination of take-home exams, a sharp increase in secure in-class exams, and growing interest in class participation, live presentations and even oral exams.
  • Chicago is piloting device-free classrooms and no-access exam conditions across all of its required first-year courses for 2026-27.
  • Suffolk’s memo proposes interim requirements for secure summative assessments in foundational courses.

These moves echo the broader trend I noted in May, when Princeton reinstated universal in-person proctoring for the first time in 133 years.

  1. Syllabus disclosure of AI.

According to Perlman’s inventory, 20 schools have rules requiring instructors to disclose their course-level AI policies in writing, typically in the syllabus.

Wisconsin, for example, requires every faculty member to establish and clearly communicate a course AI policy. Suffolk’s interim measure for 2026-27 would require every syllabus to state what AI use is permitted, prohibited and conditional.

For law students, that means they will now have to be prepared to navigate a patchwork of instructor-by-instructor rules on using AI.

The Bottom Line

In compiling this inventory, Perlman is careful to note that he is dean of one of the schools represented, and the archive is comparative, not a ranking. He is equally careful about the archive’s provenance, disclosing that it was constructed using AI and inviting corrections. A school can even request that its entry be removed or linked rather than hosted.

Those caveats aside, the site clearly addresses a gap in understanding how legal education is responding to AI, providing greater detail than had been available through scattered news stories or high-level surveys.

For law schools that have policies, let us hope they will support and contribute to this effort. For those that are in the process of drafting or revising their own policies, this may now be the first place to look.

news.titleEn: As AI Legal Research Tools Race to Give Answers, This New Product Gives Only Cases — And That’s the Point
news.titleZh: 当AI法律研究工具竞相给出答案时，这款新产品只提供案例——而这正是其用意
news.summaryZh: 诉讼技术公司Align发布Align Research，接收自然语言研究问题，运行数小时后返回相关法院判决并高亮关键段落，不提供备忘录、摘要或答案，公司称其“检索而非生成”。设计既为应对生成式AI的幻觉问题，也为回归诉讼律师最常需要的任务：不是“回答问题”，而是“给我案例”。多数AI法律研究产品采用相反模式，提问后返回经过研究和验证的答案。他在LinkedIn列出理念，包括“不要委托你应该学习的内容”和“AI应该展示而非告知”。该产品是代理式流水线：模型分别分析问题、决定搜索、阅读分类案例、判断相关性并决定高亮段落，完成后邮件通知用户。案例以活页夹格式显示，高亮可点击，可下载PDF。产品仅返回实际判决并高亮相关文本，最坏是遗漏或高亮不准，但不会捏造引证。目前无法对话式跟进，需运行新任务或下载到其他AI工具分析。覆盖美国联邦和州判例法，来自CourtListener数据库，Align正构建自有数据库并计划回馈。定价无订阅，免费层每月三次且不过期，之后每任务100美元。Align自筹资金，每次搜索消耗真实AI代币成本，认为按任务定价是行业必然趋势，当前无限订阅反映供应商补贴代币以建立用户基础，律所会将费用转嫁客户。他并非针对Westlaw或Lexis，但认为该工具可在寻找初始案例集方面节省大量时间和律师工时。
news.bodyHtml:
At a time when virtually every major AI legal research product is moving toward delivering a single, synthesized answer to your research question, a new product launching today is based on the premise that many litigators want something that sounds almost old school – just the cases.

Align Research, released to general availability this morning by the litigation technology company Align, takes a research question in plain language, goes off for a few hours, and comes back with a set of relevant court opinions, with the key passages highlighted, and nothing else.

There is no memo, no summary, no answer. As the company’s press release puts it, the product “retrieves rather than generates.”

Align founder and CEO Sam Davidoff, a former litigation partner at Williams & Connolly, said the product’s design is in part an answer to the hallucination problem that has plagued the use of generative AI in law, and in part a return to what he believes is the actual task litigators most often want done.

“It’s not telling you anything, it’s just showing you,” Davidoff told me in an interview about the launch on my LawNext PR podcast. “If all the AI is doing is essentially pointing you to pre-existing things, as opposed to writing some narrative for you, it actually can’t hallucinate. It could miss something, it could highlight something that you don’t agree with, but it can’t make something up.”

‘Get Me the Cases’

Davidoff said he had long resisted entering the legal research market, which he considered well saturated. What changed his mind was a gap he perceived in the current crop of AI research tools, rooted in his own years of practice.

The research task he most often performed as an associate, and most often assigned as a partner, was not, “Answer this question,” he said, but, “Get me the cases. Find me every district court that has ever ruled this way on a motion to dismiss.”

Most AI legal research products these days are built around the opposite model, where you ask a question and get back a researched and validated answer. “That’s a little different than what, at least a lot of times, litigators want,” Davidoff said.

When I observed that this sounds, in a way, old school – closer to how we used to do research – he readily agreed. “There’s no secret where I get my ideas from. I was practicing law and this is how we used to do it, and there’s a little part of me that says, ‘Hey, some of our old tricks still kind of work.’”

In a LinkedIn post ahead of today’s launch, Davidoff listed some of the ideas that went into the product relating to the proper division of labor between lawyers and AI. Among them are, “Don’t delegate what you should learn,” and, “AI should show, not tell.”

Give the AI the uninteresting work of churning through thousands of cases, he said, and keep the interesting work of reading and analyzing the few dozen that matter for the lawyer to do.

“If you give to AI the job of actually reading the cases and distilling the final analysis, it means you’re not doing it,” he told me. “That’s both sometimes the fun of being a lawyer, but also sometimes the strategic advantage of being a lawyer – that I’ve read the cases and I see a new angle for how we could argue this in front of this judge.”

How It Works

As Davidoff describes it, Align Research is an agentic pipeline. One model analyzes the question and breaks out the legal research issues. Another decides what searches to run. Others read the retrieved cases, classify them, make relevance decisions, and determine whether more searching is needed. A final stage decides which passages to highlight.

That is why a research job in Align can run for a few hours before returning a result. Rather than work like a chatbot, Davidoff said, the product works more like a researcher on your staff. You submit a question, go do other work, and the system emails you when the results are ready.

The cases then appear on the website in a binder-like format, with highlights you can click through, and can be downloaded as PDFs.

For now, a user has no ability to follow-up in a conversational way with a research result. If the results raise a new question, you run another job. Alternatively, Davidoff suggested, you can download the cases and load them into some other AI tool for further interrogation.

Coverage spans U.S. federal and state case law, drawn from the Free Law Project’s CourtListener database. Align is building out additional case law databases of its own, but Davidoff said the company intends to contribute those cases back to the CourtListener opinion database, reflecting his view that the underlying case law corpus should not be the differentiator among legal tech companies.

Another way Align Research departs from the market norm is pricing. There is no subscription. A free tier provides three research jobs per month, with no expiration. Beyond that, the company charges a flat $100 per job.

Part of the rationale for that is practical. Align is bootstrapped and self-funded, Davidoff said, and every search costs the company real money in AI tokens.

But he also believes that per-job pricing is an inevitability for the industry at large, arguing that the all-you-can-eat subscription pricing now common in legal AI reflects vendors subsidizing token costs to build user bases.

“I don’t think it can last,” he said. “These token costs are real. The amount of money that every legal tech AI provider has to pay to Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini – that’s real money and it’s per token.”

He sees law firms passing this fee through to their clients. The math should be easy to explain to them, he said. A research task that once consumed a couple of associate hours at a couple hundred dollars or more per hour becomes a $100 flat fee.

多数律所将AI采用视为一次采购，但成为AI原生律所并非单一事件，而是一段漫长旅程，多数律所仅处于起点。法律行业正同时朝两个方向发展：律师个人持续使用ChatGPT、Claude等AI工具，律所则在平台层面重建标准化数据基础。目前几乎所有人只关注其中一个维度，同时聚焦两者的律所将获得真正的AI优势。随着个人AI使用普及与平台围绕AI重建，日常法律工作开始转变，常规打字和研究由工具处理，律师得以将更多时间用于咨询客户、行使判断和建立关系。

AI需要上下文才能有用，上下文要求访问律所全部数据。外挂式工具通常连接单一系统，只做好一件窄事；原生AI层位于完整实践管理系统之上，无论用户在哪工作，AI都能看到事项、客户历史和律所政策。原生AI在规模应用下可将不可计费时间推向零，并提升每个计费小时的价值，使律所更盈利、客户法律服务更便宜。原生还关乎安全：通过AI原生层使用ChatGPT等工具，可继承相同的治理和护栏，避免野蛮生长。中型律所通常无法像大所那样大量投资工具和人才，雇佣一人领导AI战略很脆弱，应通过平台合作伙伴而非内部招聘。投资AI原生工具的中型律所可为新律师提供更好日常工作、更少琐碎工作、现代工具和生活质量差异，从而吸引人才。律所需先整合数据、上云并结构化，但不要一次解决所有问题，先选一个对工作者影响最大的问题解决，早期胜利建立势头。这一切需要领导层自上而下真正推动。
news.bodyHtml:
Most firms talk about AI adoption like it’s a purchase. Buy the tool, turn it on, done. I push back on that idea every chance I get. Becoming an AI-native law firm isn’t a single event. It’s a longer journey, and most firms are only at the start of it. 

Actionstep’s Chief Product Officer, Triona Buckley covered the shift from the practice of law to the business of law in an earlier piece, “AI for Law Firms: Myths and Realities Explained.” Something law firms need to keep in mind over the next few years, is why the difference between bolted on AI and native AI matters so much, and why mid-market firms may be better positioned for this shift than people assume. 

Becoming AI native is a journey, not a purchase 

The legal industry heading toward two things happening at once. On one side, lawyers will keep using AI tools personally, the same way people across every industry now lean on tools like ChatGPT and Claude for their own work. On the other side, firms will be retooling at the platform level, building the standardized data foundation that AI needs to be useful. 

Right now, almost everyone is focused on only one of those two dimensions, either the personal productivity side or the platform side, rarely both. The firms that focus on both will have the real AI advantage. As individual AI use becomes more common in law firms, and firms rebuild their platforms around AI at the same time, those two threads start to come together, and the day-to-day work of a lawyer begins to shift. Routine typing and research get handled by the tools, which frees lawyers to spend more of their time advising clients, exercising judgment, and building relationships. That shift undercuts the doom and gloom predictions about law firms disappearing. Five years from now, those predictions will look less like a real outcome and more like a trivia question nobody thought to ask twice. 

The difference between bolted on AI and native AI 

One of the points we keep coming back to is that AI needs context to be useful, and context requires access to the firm’s full data, not just one part of it. A bolted-on tool typically connects to a single system and does one narrow thing well. A native AI layer sits on top of the complete practice management system, so AI has visibility into a matter, a client’s history, and firm policy no matter where someone is working. 

That difference has a direct financial effect. When AI operates with complete context, it can recommend or even execute work based on what’s worked for the firm in the past, or how the firm set up work to get done, then explain its reasoning for review. My honest expectation is that, done at scale, native AI pushes the unbillable hour toward zero and increases the value of each billable hour. Firms get more done per hour of work. If that plays out the way I think it will, it’s a rare case where both sides win: firms get more profitable, and legal services get less expensive for clients. 

Native also matters for a reason that has nothing to do with productivity: safety. One of the advantages of a native AI layer is that you can use AI against it from outside the system too. Someone can go use a tool like ChatGPT, and if it’s working through an AI-native layer, it inherits the same governance and guardrails Triona talked about, so your people can use these tools safely rather than operating in the wild west. That’s a big part of why AI needs to be built in at the base level of the platform, not added on the side. A bolt-on might let you do one thing well, but it also leaves you exposed everywhere it doesn’t reach, and stuck in your old ways everywhere else. 

Why mid-market firms need a partner, not a hire 

Large firms can often brute force their way into AI adoption by investing heavily in tools and specialized talent. Mid-market firms usually can’t. Hiring one person to lead an AI strategy is fragile. If that person leaves, the firm is back to square one. 

The path forward for mid-market firms is to run through platform partners rather than internal hires. A modern, AI-capable platform can carry more of that weight than a solo internal expert ever could, and a growing network of consultants is already emerging to help mid-market firms put these tools to work.This shouldn’t be thought of as a disadvantage. It’s simply a different, and often easier, path than the one larger law firms are on. 

There’s also an upside here that doesn’t get enough attention and that’s talent. A mid-market firm that invests in AI-native tools now and can offer new associates a genuinely better day-to-day with less of the mundane work, access to modern tools, and a real quality-of-life difference. It is going to look progressive to the next generation of graduates. That gives mid-market firms a real shot at attracting talent away from big firms, where the tooling and the competition for attention can be a lot less favorable. 

Start with one problem, not everything at once 

Firms need their data consolidated, cloud-based, and structured well enough for AI to come in and use it properly, and no matter which AI tool firms adopt, a patchwork of disconnected, on-premises tools will hold them back from becoming AI-native. 

So first, get your data house in order first because there’s no way around it. 

But don’t try to fix all of it at once. Pick one problem that would make the biggest difference to the people doing the work and solve that first. The early win builds momentum, and the next opportunity tends to become obvious. 

None of this happens without leadership driving it from the top, with real commitment, not as a side project for whoever happens to be curious. 

That same thinking shapes how we build AI into the Actionstep platform. We’re not interested in sprinkling in isolated features. We’re building one layer that connects the work a firm has already done to the work still ahead of it, all within Actionstep so firms don’t have to choose between moving fast and moving carefully. 

See what’s possible when AI works with your firm’s expert judgment, not in place of it. Talk to our team to learn how Actionstep can help you prepare for the future of law. 

The post The Difference Between Using AI and Becoming an AI-Native Law Firm  appeared first on Actionstep.

news.bodyHtml:
What distinguishes Firm AI from generic AI?

Nikolaus Grefe

Generic large language models (LLMs) — even frontier models like Fable 5, GPT 5.6, and Kimi K3 — struggle to make sense of a firm’s complex data model.  

For example, let’s say Claude is connected to your system of record through an MCP server. If you ask it to find all deals with a margin above 18%, it doesn’t know if you’re referring to EBITDA, free cash flow, or gross profit. As a result, it guesses.   

Or suppose you work at a private equity firm and need a report summarizing your team’s engagements across company types like LPs, advisors, and portfolio companies. However, your firm’s data model only has a data object called “interaction,” and a company object with categories. Generic LLMs would not understand your prompts. They simply lack the context to understand what these data objects mean and how they relate to one another, so it will likely require multiple rounds of prompting to produce the right output. 

Professionals don’t have time for trial and error. Senior partners in particular expect their firm’s AI to provide the same level of accuracy they’d get from their analysts.  

Firm AI, on the other hand, understands a firm’s data, unique terminology, compliance rules, and ways of working. It uses a semantic layer — including the firm’s ontology, nomenclature, and acronyms — to translate what prompts actually mean, so the LLM can produce accurate, reliable, and consistent outputs.
