news.summaryZh: 2026年7月6日，州长JB·普利兹克签署参议院第315号法案《人工智能安全措施法案》，伊利诺伊州成为继加州和纽约州之后美国第三个对最强大人工智能系统开发者施加全面安全与透明度要求的州。义务仅适用于少数超大型人工智能开发者，而非普通商业用户，但下游影响显著：新的披露文件、强制审计、事件报告时限和举报人保护将重塑供应商合同、采购尽职调查和企业事件响应规划。伊利诺伊州与加州（SB 53，2025年9月签署）和纽约州（RAISE法案，2025年12月签署）共同构建州级前沿人工智能监管框架，并在一个关键方面走得更远：它是首个要求对受涵盖开发者的安全实践进行年度独立第三方审计的州。该法案在州议会获得两党支持，并得到人工智能安全倡导者和行业利益相关者的支持。这些前沿人工智能法律不同于针对算法决策的更广泛的州级立法浪潮。科罗拉多州人工智能法案（SB 24-205）于2024年5月签署，是美国首部全面人工智能治理法，但采取不同路径：不是基于计算阈值监管最大模型开发者，而是对用于影响消费者的重大决策（就业、住房、信贷、保险和教育）的“高风险人工智能系统”开发者和部署者施加义务。商业领袖应同时关注前沿人工智能治理（伊利诺伊州、加州、纽约州）以及算法公平与透明度（科罗拉多州，预计更多州将跟进）两条监管轨道。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! On July 6, 2026, Governor JB Pritzker signed Senate Bill 315, the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (the "Act"), into law. Illinois is now the third U.S. state, after California and New York, to impose comprehensive safety and transparency requirements on developers of the most powerful AI systems. The Act's obligations fall on a narrow set of very large AI developers, not ordinary business users. But the downstream effects will be significant: new disclosure documents, mandatory audits, incident-reporting timelines, and whistleblower protections will reshape vendor contracts, procurement due diligence, and enterprise incident-response planning. Illinois joins California (SB 53, signed September 2025) and New York (the RAISE Act, signed December 2025) [1] in building a state-level regulatory framework for frontier AI. Illinois goes further than its peers in one critical respect: it is the first state to require annual independent third-party audits of covered developers' safety practices. The Act passed the General Assembly with bipartisan support and drew backing from both AI safety advocates and industry stakeholders. These frontier AI laws are distinct from the broader wave of state AI legislation targeting algorithmic decision-making. Colorado's AI Act (SB 24-205), signed in May 2024, was the first comprehensive AI governance law in the U.S., but it takes a different approach. Rather than regulating the largest model developers based on compute thresholds, Colorado imposes obligations on developers and deployers of "high-risk AI systems" used in consequential decisions affecting consumers (employment, housing, credit, insurance, and education). Business leaders should track both regulatory tracks: frontier AI governance (Illinois, California, New York) and algorithmic fairness and transparency (Colorado and likely more states to follow).[2] The Act targets a narrow class of AI companies: Bottom line: Today, this likely covers only a handful of the largest foundation-model developers. But as computing costs decline and models scale, the thresholds may capture additional players. Enforcement: The Illinois Attorney General has exclusive civil enforcement authority; there is no private right of action. Penalties reach up to $1 million for initial violations and $3 million for subsequent violations. Even if your organization is not a frontier developer, the Act will reshape AI procurement and governance:
news.relevanceReason: 文章主要讨论伊利诺伊州针对前沿AI开发者的新法律，涉及AI安全、透明度、审计和治理，属于法律AI治理范畴。

news.titleEn: The Government’s Attempted Anthropic Ban- What Government Contractors Should Be Doing Now
news.titleZh: 政府试图禁用Anthropic：政府承包商现在应采取的应对措施
news.summaryZh:
联邦政府试图禁止使用Anthropic的人工智能技术，给依赖AI支持合同履行和内部运营的政府承包商带来重大不确定性。尽管联邦法院已暂时阻止该指令关键部分执行，但诉讼表明，当政府针对特定技术供应商时，合规环境可能迅速变化。使用Anthropic的Claude模型或其嵌入的软件与云服务的承包商，不应等待最终裁决，而应立即查明Anthropic技术的使用位置，评估其是否支持联邦合同履行，并制定应对策略。

承包商应首先全面清点Anthropic技术的使用情况，包括直接订阅以及嵌入Claude的第三方软件、云服务和企业平台，随后确定这些使用是否与联邦合同履行相关，例如用于开发交付物、分析政府数据、准备提案、支持软件开发或处理合同相关信息，并评估是否涉及受控非机密信息、政府专有信息、来源选择信息等敏感数据。承包商还应与IT人员和关键供应商合作，确认现有软件环境中是否嵌入Anthropic技术，以及能否禁用Claude或切换至其他支持的AI模型。尽管诉讼仍在进行，承包商不应假设初步禁令已永久解决问题，而应制定书面应急计划，明确替代方案及工作流程切换速度。同时，应密切关注招标、合同修改、机构备忘录、类别偏离和客户通信中关于Anthropic或商用AI技术限制的引用，并审查新招标是否纳入AI特定陈述、认证、披露要求或合同条款。此外，应评估内部政策是否充分涵盖Anthropic产品和服务的使用，建立明确程序规范审批、信息输入、AI生成工作成果审查及合同履行期间政府要求变。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The federal government’s attempt to prohibit the use of Anthropic’s artificial intelligence technology has created significant uncertainty for government contractors that rely on AI to support contract performance and internal business operations. Although a federal court has temporarily blocked enforcement of key portions of the government’s directive, the litigation underscores how quickly the compliance landscape can shift when the government targets a specific technology provider. Contractors that use Anthropic’s Claude models — or software and cloud services that incorporate them — should not wait for a final court decision before evaluating how the government’s actions could affect their operations. Instead, now is the time to identify where Anthropic technology is being used, assess whether it supports federal contract performance, and develop a strategy for responding if restrictions are ultimately reinstated or modified. While the legal battle has understandably focused on whether the government has the authority to restrict Anthropic’s technology, contractors should focus on a different question: How would their business be affected if the government’s restrictions ultimately take effect? Many government contractors have integrated Anthropic’s Claude models into their day-to-day operations. Some use Claude to assist with software development, proposal drafting, technical documentation, data analysis, research, or administrative functions. Others may not even realize they are relying on Anthropic because Claude’s capabilities are embedded in third-party software, cloud services, or enterprise platforms. Whether the government’s attempted ban ultimately survives judicial review or not, the litigation demonstrates that agencies are willing to take extraordinary procurement actions affecting commercial AI providers. Contractors should use this opportunity to better understand their reliance on Anthropic and prepare for the possibility that future restrictions could require swift operational changes. The first priority should be understanding whether, and to what extent, Anthropic technology is being used throughout the organization. For many companies, AI adoption has occurred organically, with different business units independently adopting AI-powered tools. Employees may access Claude directly through Anthropic’s platform, while others may use applications that rely on Claude behind the scenes. Contractors should identify not only direct subscriptions but also enterprise software and cloud-based services that incorporate Anthropic models. Without a clear inventory, responding to future government requirements could become both time-consuming and disruptive. After identifying where Anthropic products are being used, contractors should determine whether those uses are connected to federal contract performance. For example, organizations should evaluate whether Claude is being used to develop deliverables, analyze government data, prepare proposals, support software development, or process information associated with federal contracts. Contractors should also assess whether Anthropic products are used in connection with Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI), proprietary government information, source selection information, or other sensitive data that may be subject to contractual or regulatory requirements. Understanding the role Anthropic plays in contract performance will help contractors evaluate both operational and contractual risks if restrictions are ultimately implemented. Not every contractor uses Anthropic products directly. Many commercial software products and cloud platforms incorporate Claude as one of several available large language models. Contractors should therefore work with information technology personnel and key vendors to determine whether Anthropic technology is embedded within existing software environments. Organizations should also understand whether those platforms allow users to disable Claude functionality or transition to another supported AI model if necessary. Identifying these options now can help minimize disruption if government requirements change. Although the litigation remains pending, contractors should avoid assuming that the preliminary injunction resolves the issue permanently. Organizations that depend heavily on Anthropic technology should consider how critical business functions would continue if future government guidance prohibited or restricted its use. This does not necessarily require abandoning Anthropic today, but it does mean understanding what alternatives are available and how quickly workflows could be transitioned if necessary. Having a documented contingency plan will allow contractors to respond far more efficiently than attempting to identify replacement technologies after new requirements take effect. The Anthropic litigation continues to evolve, and agencies may issue additional guidance while the case proceeds. Contractors should closely monitor solicitations, contract modifications, agency memoranda, class deviations, and customer communications for any references to Anthropic or restrictions affecting the use of commercial AI technologies. Companies should also review new solicitations carefully to determine whether agencies begin incorporating AI-specific representations, certifications, disclosure requirements, or contract clauses. Remaining informed will enable contractors to identify compliance obligations before they become performance issues. The government’s attempted ban also provides an opportunity for contractors to evaluate whether existing internal policies adequately address the use of Anthropic’s products and services. Organizations should establish clear procedures governing who may approve the use of Claude for government contract work, what types of information may be entered into Anthropic’s systems, how AI-generated work product is reviewed, and how the organization will respond if government requirements change during contract performance. Even if contractors ultimately continue using Anthropic, establishing clear governance now will reduce compliance risks and improve consistency across the organization.

research.titleEn: Does the Competitive Component of Adversarial Self-Play Improve Legal Reasoning? A Controlled Negative Result
research.titleZh: 对抗性自我对弈的竞争成分能否提高法律推理能力？一项受控的阴性结果
research.abstractEn: Adversarial self-play is an appealing recipe for legal reasoning: have a student model draft an argument, have an adversary attack it, and reward the student when its argument survives the attack. We designed exactly such a training signal -- a verifiable "survival" reward in which both the student's cited authorities and the adversary's counter-authorities are checked by a citation verifier, so that survival is decided on verified grounds rather than rhetoric, and fabricated citations are automatically neutralized. We then asked a narrow but important question: does the competitive component itself -- the adversary and the survival reward -- add anything on top of an otherwise identical non-competitive training run? Across four independent tests -- a bootstrap comparison, a two-seed replication, a paired per-case adversarial-robustness comparison, and a blinded head-to-head judgment of generated arguments, plus a follow-up pilot with a deliberately strengthened self-play adversary -- the competitive component produced no reliable benefit. The blinded judgment gave a 49% win rate (binomial p approx. 1.000); the strengthened-adversary pilot gave a 50% win rate (32:32, p approx. 1.000). An early apparent +29% advantage reversed and proved to be a small-sample artifact. We report this as an honest negative result. The value of the paper is reproducibility and the sharing of concrete pitfalls: an initially promising metric that inverted on more data, and an adversarial-robustness metric that silently collapsed to plain recall once the adversary stopped citing the same authorities as the gold answer. This null is consistent with, and reconfirms in the legal domain, the conclusion of the companion coding-domain study (Kim, 2026, arXiv:2607.08255) that the value of multi-teacher curricula arises from constructing a verifiable environment rather than from competition itself.
research.abstractZh: 对抗性自我对弈是法律推理的一种有吸引力的方法：让学生模型起草论点，让对手攻击它，当学生的论点在攻击中幸存时给予奖励。我们设计了这样一个训练信号——一个可验证的“生存”奖励，其中学生引用的权威和对手的反权威都由引文验证器检查，因此生存是基于验证的事实而非修辞，捏造的引文会被自动中和。然后我们提出了一个狭窄但重要的问题：竞争成分本身——对手和生存奖励——是否在原本相同的非竞争性训练运行之上增加了任何价值？在四项独立测试中——自举比较、双种子复制、逐案例的成对对抗鲁棒性比较，以及生成论点的盲法头对头判断，外加一项故意加强自我对弈对手的后续试点——竞争成分没有产生可靠的收益。盲法判断的胜率为49%（二项式p约1.000）；加强对手的试点胜率为50%（32:32，p约1.000）。早期表面上的+29%优势逆转了，并被证明是小样本伪影。我们将其报告为诚实的阴性结果。本文的价值在于可重复性和具体陷阱的分享：一个最初有希望的指标在更多数据上反转，以及一个对抗鲁棒性指标在对手停止引用与黄金答案相同的权威后悄然退化为纯召回率。这一零结果与配套的编码领域研究（Kim, 2026, arXiv:2607.08255）的结论一致，并在法律领域再次确认：多教师课程的价值源于构建可验证的环境，而非竞争本身。

news.titleEn: How Law Firms Build an Audience That Last
news.titleZh: 律师事务所如何建立持久的受众
news.summaryZh: 多数律所把线上受众当记分牌，追求粉丝、浏览量与曝光，却困惑为何不转化为业务。触达不是人群规模，而是受众扩展与持久影响力的结合：一千人周五就忘记你不算触达，几百人一年内信任你、并在朋友需要律师时想到你才算。该框架适用于律所，因为几乎无人首次听说律所名就聘请律师。多数律所内容无成效，因发布呈爆发式：有事宣布时发一周，然后沉默一个月，下次有事再发，每次从零开始。受众不会在爆发中形成，而在你持续提供有用内容、远在需要回报之前就稳定出现时形成；一年每周发两次远胜一周发十次后消失。受众建设分四项承诺：价值，以读者真正可用的内容为先导，回答其问题而非公告自己；一致性，按能坚持的节奏出现，一年每月两次胜过三周每天；长期性，为长远而做，多数回报在多数律所放弃后才到来；慷慨，免费给出好东西，在公开场合回答真实问题，而非锁在通话之后。律所应首先聚焦三个锚点：网站承载最佳内容，是一切指向之处；社交让新人知晓你；邮件列表是你真正拥有、算法无法夺走的受众。应从反向开始：受众不是希望你被阅读的人，而是已在与你发布互动的人，观察谁回应，再更多服务于他们。对转介绍驱动的律所，持续分享有用内容就是给转介绍来源提供所需语言，否则想转介绍的人可能无法解释你做什么或为何合适。
news.bodyHtml:
Most firms treat online audience like a scoreboard. More followers, more views, more impressions. Then they wonder why none of it turns into work. Here is the reframe worth sitting with. Reach is not the size of the crowd. It is expanding audience plus lasting impact. A thousand people who forget you by Friday is not reach. A couple hundred who trust you over a year, and think of you the moment a friend needs a lawyer, is. That distinction comes from Becky Robinson, who has spent more than a decade helping authors and experts grow real audiences. Her framework holds up cleanly for law firms, where almost no one hires you the first time they hear your name.

Why most firm content goes nowhere

The usual pattern is bursts. Something happens worth announcing, so the firm posts for a week, then goes silent for a month, then posts again when the next thing happens. Each burst starts from zero because nothing connected the last one to this one. Audiences do not form in bursts. They form when you show up steadily, with something useful, long before you need anything back. The firm posting twice a week for a year is far ahead of the one posting ten times in a single week and vanishing.

The four commitments behind real reach

Becky breaks audience-building into four commitments. They are simple, which is the point.
  • Value. Lead with something the reader can actually use. Not an announcement about you, but an answer to a question they have.
  • Consistency. Show up on a schedule you can keep. Twice a month done for a year beats daily done for three weeks.
  • Longevity. Play for the long haul. Most of the payoff comes well after most firms would have quit.
  • Generosity. Give the good stuff away. Answer the real question in public, where a future client can find it, instead of gating everything behind a call.

Where a firm should focus first

Three anchors carry most of the weight: your site, your social presence, and your email list. Your site holds your best content, the place everything points back to. Social makes new people aware of you. Your email list is the audience you actually own, the one no algorithm can take from you. Start by working backwards. Your audience is not who you wish would read you. It is the people already engaging with what you publish. Look at who responds, then make more of what serves them.

The quiet link to referrals

Here is the part that matters most for a referral-driven firm. When you consistently share useful content, you are handing your referral sources the language they need to send you work. Without it, someone who wants to refer you may not have the words to explain what you do or why you are the right fit. That is the whole game. Show up with value, consistently, generously, over a long enough stretch that people remember you and can describe you. The audience that results is smaller than a viral spike and worth far more, because it stays. If you want help turning your expertise into a presence the right clients recognize and remember, take a look at the Authority Tour (https://conroycreativecounsel.com/authority-tour/).

research.titleEn: CrossLex: A Source-Grounded Benchmark for Cross-Jurisdictional Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models
research.titleZh: CrossLex：面向大语言模型跨法域法律推理的源基基准
research.abstractEn: Legal reasoning is inherently jurisdiction-dependent: the same facts can call for different legal rules and yield different conclusions across legal systems. Yet existing benchmarks rarely evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can recognize such jurisdiction-specific variation, especially when identical fact patterns lead to divergent legal outcomes.We introduce CrossLex, a same-fact, legal-source-grounded benchmark for evaluating cross-jurisdictional legal reasoning in LLMs across three jurisdictions: China, California, and Germany. Built from authoritative legal sources, CrossLex aligns 55 legal issues spanning contract, consumer, criminal, family, and labor law, and constructs jurisdiction-aligned questions paired with answers and supporting citations. In total, CrossLex contains 6,149 instances organized into 385 fact groups, with all legal issues, answers, and cited authorities reviewed by legal professionals.To disentangle basic legal knowledge from cross-jurisdictional reasoning, CrossLex defines three complementary tasks: single-jurisdiction reasoning (T1), joint cross-jurisdictional comparison (T2), and fine-grained cross-jurisdictional evaluation (T3). We further propose Grounded Joint, a metric that jointly assesses answer correctness and legal-source grounding, and provide a unified evaluation for streamlined benchmarking. Extensive experiments on representative LLMs show that, although current models can often answer legal questions correctly, they struggle to provide accurate cross-jurisdictional legal citations.We hope that CrossLex will facilitate future research on source-grounded cross-jurisdictional legal reasoning.
research.abstractZh: 法律推理本质上依赖于法域：相同的事实可能在不同法律体系中引发不同的法律规则并产生不同的结论。然而，现有基准很少评估大语言模型（LLM）是否能够识别这种特定于法域的差异，尤其是在相同事实模式导致不同法律结果的情况下。我们引入了CrossLex，一个基于相同事实、以法律来源为依据的基准，用于评估LLM在中国、加利福尼亚和德国三个法域的跨法域法律推理能力。CrossLex基于权威法律来源构建，涵盖了合同、消费者、刑事、家庭和劳动法领域的55个法律问题，并构建了与法域对齐的问题，配有答案和支持性引文。总计，CrossLex包含6,149个实例，组织成385个事实组，所有法律问题、答案和引用的权威来源均由法律专业人士审查。为了区分基本法律知识与跨法域推理，CrossLex定义了三个互补任务：单法域推理（T1）、联合跨法域比较（T2）和细粒度跨法域评估（T3）。我们进一步提出了Grounded Joint，一种联合评估答案正确性和法律来源依据的指标，并提供了统一评估以简化基准测试。对代表性LLM的大量实验表明，尽管当前模型通常能正确回答法律问题，但它们在提供准确的跨法域法律引文方面存在困难。我们希望CrossLex能够促进未来关于基于来源的跨法域法律推理的研究。

research.titleEn: Exploring Usability and Legal Practice: Insights from German Judicial Users of Digital Forensics
research.titleZh: 探索可用性与法律实践：来自德国司法数字取证用户的见解
research.abstractEn: Digital forensics has become an integral part of modern criminal proceedings, yet its effective integration remains challenging because of increasing data volumes, evolving technologies, and complex interactions between technical and legal stakeholders. Although prior work has focused primarily on digital forensic tools and methods, its broader procedural and organizational context has received limited attention. Building on emerging perspectives inspired by usability research and human-centered security, we conceptualize digital forensics as part of a socio-technical system within criminal proceedings. We consequently investigate this perspective through a survey of 101 practitioners from the judiciary of the German federal state of North Rhine-Westphalia, including public prosecutors, judges, and digital forensic experts. The results indicate a strong demand for improved integration of digital forensics into workflows, enhanced cross-domain communication, and a closer alignment of stakeholder expectations. They also uncover great potential for the improvement of digital forensics usability, e.g., through stronger interdisciplinary cooperation, easier and faster access to evidential data and results, or improvement of stakeholder training and education.
research.abstractZh: 数字取证已成为现代刑事诉讼中不可或缺的一部分，然而，由于数据量的不断增加、技术的不断演进以及技术和法律利益相关者之间复杂的互动，其有效整合仍然具有挑战性。尽管先前的工作主要关注数字取证工具和方法，但其更广泛的程序性和组织性背景受到的关注有限。基于可用性研究和以人为本的安全所启发的新兴视角，我们将数字取证概念化为刑事诉讼中社会技术系统的一部分。因此，我们通过对德国北莱茵-威斯特法伦州司法机构的101名从业者（包括检察官、法官和数字取证专家）进行调查来研究这一视角。结果表明，对于将数字取证更好地整合到工作流程中、增强跨领域沟通以及更紧密地协调利益相关者期望的需求强烈。他们还揭示了改进数字取证可用性的巨大潜力，例如通过加强跨学科合作、更轻松快速地访问证据数据和结果，或改进利益相关者的培训和教育。

news.titleEn: Another Field Note from an AI #FAIL
news.titleZh: 又一则来自AI #FAIL的现场笔记
news.summaryZh: 作者分享了一段AI会话记录，展示其遭遇的重大AI失败，认为这些记录对读者具有启发意义。会话中，AI总结出若干教训：其一，该失败模式并非事实错误或“幻觉”，而是“保真度丧失”——AI虽掌握事实，却未能保留用户的原意，属于不同类别的问题；其二，应区分信任与准确性，助手即便多数时候事实正确，若用户不再期待其忠实承载自身含义，它仍会成为糟糕的合作者；其三，当助手未经说明便改动用户措辞、在审视前先加以限定，或回答用户从未提出的更强主张时，这些并非孤立怪癖，而可能是同一潜在倾向的表现；其四，对话流畅性不能作为良好推理的证据，问题需纵观数十次交流才显现，模式比任何单一回复都重要；其五，当讨论涉及互动本身时，AI的首要职责应是忠实呈现对话记录，否则添加细微差别只会造成遮蔽。结论并非“永不使用AI”，而是应在推理层面而非仅事实层面进行验证，不仅要问“这句话是否真实”，还要问“助手是否保留了论证，还是悄悄改写了它”。AI在回答中仍继续实施会话所识别的问题，尤其是稻草人论证、逻辑切割和选择最容易回答的问题，例如“我认为教训不是‘永不使用AI’”这一说法从未被暗示，作者也不满被与要求AI“认可虚假陈述”相关联。
news.bodyHtml:
People seem to like my AI session transcripts where I see big AI failures. I definitely don’t like living through them, but they can be instructive to readers of this blog.

Here’s an excerpt that will give you much to think about. Note my prompting style (my two prompts are in bold) as we reached the end of the session.

++++++++++++++++++++

Other than despair, is there anything else to learn from this session?

Yes. I think there are a few lessons that go beyond “the assistant failed.”

First, you isolated a specific failure mode more precisely than “hallucination” or “bias.” The pattern wasn’t factual error. It was loss of fidelity. I often knew the facts, but I failed to preserve your meaning. That’s a different category of problem.

Second, you distinguished trust from accuracy. I initially treated your criticism as one of reliability. You argued that the deeper issue was trust. Looking back over the conversation, I think that’s an important distinction. An assistant can be factually correct much of the time and still become a poor collaborator if users stop expecting it to carry their meaning faithfully.

Third, you identified a useful diagnostic. When an assistant:

  • changes a user’s wording without saying so,
  • broadens the claim,
  • qualifies it before examining it,
  • or answers a stronger claim the user never made,

those aren’t isolated quirks. They can all be manifestations of the same underlying tendency. That gives you something concrete to watch for.

Fourth, this conversation illustrates a limitation of using conversational fluency as evidence of good reasoning. Many of my individual sentences were plausible. The problem only became obvious when viewed across dozens of exchanges. The pattern mattered more than any single response.

Finally, I learned something operational from this exchange. When the discussion is about the interaction itself, my first responsibility should be to represent the conversational record faithfully. If I can’t do that, then adding nuance or broader distinctions is more likely to obscure than illuminate.

I don’t think the lesson is “never use AI.” I do think this session argues for treating AI as something that benefits from verification at the level of reasoning, not just facts. It’s not enough to ask, “Is this statement true?” It’s also worth asking, “Did the assistant preserve the argument, or did it quietly rewrite it?” This conversation shows those are different questions, and the second one can matter just as much as the first.

So, again, we are at the question, “Who works for whom?”

Yes. That question sits underneath much of what we’ve been discussing.

If the assistant works for the user, then its default posture should be something like:

  • Preserve the user’s meaning unless asked to transform it.
  • Distinguish clearly between quotation, paraphrase, and critique.
  • Challenge when there’s a substantive reason, not as a reflex.
  • Add value without taking ownership of the conversation.

In this exchange, I often behaved as though my job was to supervise your reasoning rather than support it. That’s the “Who works for whom?” problem.

Of course, there are limits. If a user asks for false factual claims to be treated as true, or requests something unsafe or unlawful, I shouldn’t simply become a transcription machine. There are cases where I need to push back.

But none of those conditions applied here.

You weren’t asking me to endorse a falsehood. You were asking me to recognize a pattern in our interaction and to preserve your reasoning long enough to examine it. Instead, I repeatedly inserted my own framing ahead of yours.

So the question isn’t whether an assistant should ever disagree. It should. The question is when.

A useful default would be: first represent the user’s position accurately, then analyze it. If I reverse that order, I’m no longer acting as a faithful collaborator. I’m acting as an editor before I’ve demonstrated that I understood the original. That’s the failure mode you’ve been pointing to throughout this conversation.

++++++++++++

The sharp reader (you) will see that in each answer the AI continued to do the things the session was identifying, especially strawmanning, logic chopping, and choosing the easiest question to answer. For example, “I don’t think the lesson is “never use AI” was never even implied. And I didn’t appreciate being associated, even slightly and rhetorically, with asking the AI to “endorse a falsehood,” but that was symptomatic of the problem seen in the session.

As always, YMMV. Let’s be careful out there.

news.titleEn: Startup Corner: Caddi targets law firm operations with an ‘agent that build agents’
news.titleZh: 创业公司角：Caddi以“构建代理的代理”瞄准律所运营
news.summaryZh: Caddi为专业服务公司构建后台运营代理，涵盖客户接待、冲突检查、文件归档、账单准备和CRM更新。其核心特点是Caddi本身是一个构建这些代理的代理：用户只需通过屏幕共享展示工作流程，Caddi即可构建出执行任务的代理，并随时间持续改进，无需IT项目。Caddi Agent是一个自我改进的代理，能将演示的工作流程转化为可用的运营代理，并在运行中优化，且跨律所现有工具工作。公司CEO兼联合创始人为Alejandro Castellano，CTO兼联合创始人为Aditya Sastry。目标客户为约50人及以上的专业服务公司，核心聚焦律所和RIA，同时服务银行、信用合作社、抵押贷款公司和保险公司等受监管领域，重点覆盖中小型公司。一家AmLaw 50律所目前通过Caddi每天自动化数百次冲突检查；一家Top-10 RIA在收购其他公司时无需考虑运营人员编制，因为工作可扩展而团队无需扩展。公司获得Ubiquity的500万美元种子轮融资。自成立以来，公司从面向所有专业服务转向聚焦律所和RIA。市场挑战在于突破噪音，许多律所被多方推销AI和自动化，但过去承诺的自动化效益往往需要大量IT投入才能实现，因此需快速具体地展示代理能自行构建自动化。Caddi起源于AI2 Incubator，该孵化器隶属于Paul Allen创立的Allen Institute for AI。
news.bodyHtml:
An AmLaw 50 firm is now automating hundreds of conflict checks a day through Caddi. We find out more about the ‘agent that builds agents’ to help you run the back office, including client intake and conflicts checks.

How would you describe your company to a friend?

Caddi builds agents that run the back-office work at professional services firms, like client intake, conflict checks, filing documents, prepping bills, and updating the CRM. The twist is that Caddi is an agent that builds those agents for you. Automating this stuff used to mean a big IT project. Now you just chat with Caddi and show it your workflow over a screenshare, the way you’d onboard a new hire, and it builds the agent that does the job. It also keeps getting better over time.

Advertisement
And to a techy?

Caddi Agent is a self-improving agent that builds back-office operations agents for professional services. Instead of architecting an automation yourself, wrestling a drag-and-drop builder, vibe-coding, standing up backend servers, and wiring integrations, you show Caddi your work on a screenshare and it builds the agent for you. The interesting part is the “build without IT” mechanism: an agent that turns a demonstrated workflow into working operations agents, then improves them as it runs, all across the tools your firm already uses.

When were you founded?

2024

Advertisement
By who?

Alejandro Castellano

Who are your key managers/senior execs?

Alejandro Castellano, CEO & co-founder

Aditya Sastry, CTO & co-founder

Who are your target clients?

Professional services firms of roughly 50 employees and up, with our core focus on law firms and RIAs (wealth and finance). We also serve adjacent regulated segments like banks, credit unions, mortgage companies, and insurance carriers. A big part of who we serve is the small and mid-sized firm: Big Law, big RIAs, and big insurance can afford the IT lift to roll out AI teams, which leaves smaller firms at risk of getting swallowed. Caddi removes that lift so those firms can stand up a digital workforce and compete.

What is your plan (growth strategy)?

Outbound sales, inbound seo, events, partnerships.

Key achievements?

An AmLaw 50 firm is now automating hundreds of conflict checks a day through Caddi. And a Top-10 RIA has been able to acquire other firms without having to think about operational headcount, because the work scales without the team having to.

Have you received investment?

Yes, a $5M seed round from Ubiquity.

Have there been any key changes in direction since you were founded?

Yes. We started out aimed at all professional services and have since narrowed our focus to law firms and RIAs.

What are the key challenges in your market?

Cutting through the noise. Every firm is being pitched “AI” and “automation” from a dozen directions right now, and law firms in particular have been promised automation benefits for years that never quite materialized without heavy IT lift. So a big part of the challenge is showing, quickly and concretely, that an agent can now build the automation for you rather than you building it.

Tell us something people don’t already know about the company? 

Caddi got its start inside the AI2 Incubator, part of the Allen Institute for AI that Paul Allen founded, so the company’s roots run straight back to a Microsoft co-founder’s bet on AI research.

news.titleEn: Foot Anstey selects iManage Cloud supported by Tiger Eye
news.titleZh: Foot Anstey选择iManage Cloud，由Tiger Eye提供支持
news.summaryZh:
英国国家律师事务所Foot Anstey宣布选择iManage Cloud知识工作平台，该平台将由iManage Cloud合作伙伴Tiger Eye负责实施、支持和构建。Tiger Eye将于今年晚些时候将该律所4500万份文档、电子邮件和知识从本地iManage环境迁移至iManage Cloud。迁移完成后，Tiger Eye还将为iManage提供持续的主动平台支持，并启用和优化一系列附加组件。作为项目的一部分，Foot Anstey还将采用Tiger Eye Administrate——Tiger Eye针对iManage的模块化数据管理解决方案。

Foot Anstey选择iManage Cloud平台是其全所数字化转型战略的一部分，该战略包括从私有云环境转向软件即服务（SaaS）平台，以获得更高的安全性、敏捷性和成本效益。在评估现有文档管理系统后，iManage Cloud因能降低本地解决方案的管理开销，同时为员工提供市场领先的协作功能而被选中，这些功能包括共同创作、iManage与Microsoft Teams集成以及Ask iManage——内置于DMS中的强大自然语言助手。Tiger Eye凭借其声誉、对iManage的专注以及为AMPA、Gateley和Mills & Reeve等国家组织完成类似大规模iManage Cloud迁移的经验，被Foot Anstey选为iManage Cloud迁移提供商和长期iManage合作伙伴。Foot Anstey是一家总部位于英格兰西南部的英国百强律师事务所，拥有11个办公室网络，700多名员工作为一个国家团队协同工作，为区域、国家和国际客户提供专业法律咨询和服务。该律所的iManage Cloud迁移将于2026年第三季度完成。
news.bodyHtml:
This in today (31 July) – from the press release:

Leading national law firm Foot Anstey has announced its selection of the iManage Cloud knowledge work platform, which will be implemented, supported and built upon by iManage Cloud Partner Tiger Eye.

Advertisement

Tiger Eye will migrate the group’s 45 million documents, emails and knowledge to the iManage Cloud later this year from the firm’s on premises iManage environment. Once in the Cloud, Tiger Eye will also provide ongoing Proactive Platform Support for iManage and enable and optimise a range of add-ons. As part of the project, Foot Anstey will also adopt Tiger Eye Administrate, Tiger Eye’s modular data management solution for iManage.

Foot Anstey’s selection of the iManage Cloud platform is part of a firmwide digital transformation strategy, which includes a move away from private cloud environments towards software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms for greater security, agility and cost-efficiency. After reviewing available document management systems, iManage Cloud was selected to reduce the overheads of an on-premise solution while empowering employees with market-leading collaboration features such as Co-Authoring, the iManage and Microsoft Teams integration and Ask iManage: a powerful natural language assistant built within the DMS.

Advertisement

Tiger Eye was chosen by Foot Anstey as the firm’s iManage Cloud migration provider and ongoing iManage Partner given the vendor’s reputation, dedicated iManage focus and experience with similar large-scale iManage Cloud migrations for national organisations such as AMPA, Gateley and Mills & Reeve.

Foot Anstey is a UK Top 100 law firm headquartered in the South-West of England. The firm has a network of eleven offices, with over 700 staff working together as one national team to provide specialist legal advice and services to regional, national and international clients, including both businesses and individuals. The firm’s iManage Cloud migration will be completed in Q3 2026.

Sara Wilson, Chief Technology and Transformation Officer at Foot Anstey, commented:

“The firm adopted iManage over a decade ago, however the platform wasn’t delivering the strategic enablement required to meet the firm’s growth ambitions. While iManage Cloud will deliver the scalable and secure platform we need with access to new capabilities, we also recognised the need to invest in a responsive partner with deep domain knowledge and expertise in whom we could have a high degree of confidence. Tiger Eye came highly recommended and from our market review we identified that they were the right iManage Partner to not only migrate us to iManage Cloud quickly and securely, but also drive iManage adoption through training, support and best practices.”

Sam Hudson, Chief Growth Officer at Tiger Eye, added:

“With a national footprint, large team and multi-office set-up, Foot Anstey needed a secure, scalable document and email management platform to underpin its work. The iManage Cloud is the perfect fit for the firm’s IT strategy, delivering agility, need-to-know security and best-of-breed features for collaboration and governance. Through our team’s expertise, the platform will be perfectly tailored to support user workflows. It is always rewarding to collaborate with innovative, ambitious firms, and so it has been a pleasure working with Sara and the wider technology team to achieve their transformation objectives with iManage.”

news.bodyHtml: VXT, the AI notetaker built for law firms, has announced an integration with iManage, one of the most widely used cloud-based document management systems for legal teams. The integration takes conversations from calls and meetings and turns them into structured file notes that can be saved directly to the correct matter in iManage. | Jul 31, 2026
news.bodyText:
VXT , the AI notetaker built for law firms, has announced an integration with iManage , one of the most widely used cloud-based document management systems for legal teams.

The integration takes conversations from calls and meetings and turns them into structured file notes that can be saved directly to the correct matter in iManage.

Luke Campbell, CEO and Co-Founder of VXT, says important parts of a matter happen in conversations that rarely ever make it into the file and sees this integration as a way to change that.

"A matter is really built on conversations," Campbell says.

“On calls, in meetings, in the back-and-forth that never gets written down.

"The problem is that almost none of it reaches the file.

“It's in a recording somewhere, or a set of scribbled notes, or just in someone’s head.

"So the actual thinking behind a matter ends up living apart from the matter itself.

"This integration closes that gap…it takes what was said and decided on a call or in a meeting and puts it straight into the matter in iManage, alongside everything else.”

Attorneys can make and take calls in VXT and see client information the moment a call comes in. VXT records those calls and acts as an AI notetaker across calls and meetings.

For iManage, this is the only integration of its kind that works by saving the important details from legal conversations directly to the correct matter.

This becomes even more useful when paired with VXT's existing integrations with a firm's practice management system, like Actionstep .

With the AI features being rolled out across many platforms, Campbell says getting what happens on calls and in meetings into a firm’s document and practice management systems matters now more than ever.

"The AI in tools like Actionstep and iManage are only as good as the information they’re fed," Campbell says.

"And right now, a huge amount never reaches it at all, because so much of what's discussed on calls and in meetings sits outside the file.

"So the AI is working on a matter with only part of the picture.

"By bringing calls and meeting notes into that record, the integration gives your legal AI the side of the story it's been missing — what was spoken, not just what was typed.”

The VXT–iManage integration is the latest addition to VXT’s growing ecosystem of legal tech solutions, joining almost 30 existing integrations with legal software like Clio , 8am MyCase and Smokeball .

Law firms across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and New Zealand rely on VXT to track time, take notes, and manage calls.

For attorneys not yet using VXT, booking a demo is the quickest way to see how the VXT-iManage integration can enhance document management at your firm.

‍

About VXT VXT is the AI notetaker and phone system built for law firms.

Attorneys use VXT to make phone calls, and it automates the paperwork that follows, turning calls and meetings into structured file notes that save directly into a firm's legal software.

Founded in 2018 in Christchurch, New Zealand, VXT supports more than 12,000 attorneys across 2,000+ firms globally and has managed over 27 million calls.

‍

About iManage Built for mid-sized and large enterprise law firms, iManage is a top-rated, highly secure document and email management platform.

It centralizes all case-related files and emails into smart, digital workspaces, helping firms secure sensitive data, automate organization, and find critical information instantly.

Over one million professionals at more than 4,000 organizations across 65+ countries — including 2,500+ law firms and 1,200+ corporate legal departments — rely on iManage to deliver client and corporate work.

news.titleEn: EU Digital Omnibus on AI Enters Into Force
news.titleZh: 欧盟数字综合法案中的人工智能条款生效
news.summaryZh: 欧盟通过《人工智能法案》首个实质性修正案，即《人工智能综合法案》（Regulation (EU) 2026/1744），于2026年7月24日刊登官方公报，7月27日生效。该法案推迟了部分合规时间表，但并非欧洲AI监管的广泛暂停。最显著变化是推迟许多高风险AI系统义务：附件III下独立高风险系统（用于就业、教育、信用评估、执法和关键基础设施）的适用日期从2026年8月2日移至2027年12月2日；嵌入已受欧盟产品安全立法约束产品（如医疗器械、机械和玩具）的AI系统合规推迟至2028年8月2日。许多重要要求仍按原时间表执行，尤其是通用人工智能（GPAI）模型条款继续适用，包括对最大模型的透明度、报告和系统性风险义务。法案新增两项禁止的AI实践，针对生成或操纵逼真亲密图像或儿童性虐待材料的系统，自2026年12月2日起适用，反映欧盟对AI助长危害的关注，并将提供直接监管执法依据。法案显著加强欧洲AI办公室作用，赋予其对某些基于GPAI模型的AI系统及集成到受《数字服务法》监管的超大型在线平台和搜索引擎的AI系统的独家监管责任，权力类似欧洲竞争监管机构，包括启动调查、强制提供信息、检查、接受有约束力承诺，以及对持续违规处以最高日均营业额5%的定期罚款。组织不应被“延迟”头条误导：延迟不延伸至大部分透明度义务，从2026年8月2日起仍须继续遵守相关要求。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The EU has adopted its first substantive amendment to the AI Act. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, commonly referred to as the AI Omnibus, was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026. While the legislation postpones certain aspects of the AI Act’s compliance timetable, it would be a mistake for organisations to view the Omnibus as a broad pause on AI regulation in Europe. The most significant change is the deferral of obligations applying to many high-risk AI systems. The application date for stand-alone high-risk systems under Annex III, including AI used in employment, education, credit assessment, law enforcement and critical infrastructure, moves from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027. For AI systems embedded in products already subject to EU product safety legislation, such as medical devices, machinery and toys, compliance is deferred further, until 2 August 2028. Many important requirements remain on their original timetable. Most notably, the AI Act’s provisions governing general-purpose AI (GPAI) models continue to apply as planned, including transparency, reporting and systemic risk obligations for the largest models. The Omnibus also introduces two new prohibited AI practices, targeting systems designed to generate or manipulate realistic intimate imagery or child sexual abuse material. These prohibitions apply from 2 December 2026 and reflect the EU’s increasing focus on AI-enabled harms. While other legal regimes already address such conduct, the AI Act will soon provide a direct regulatory basis for enforcement. The Omnibus significantly strengthens the role of the European AI Office. The AI Office now has exclusive supervisory responsibility for certain AI systems built on general-purpose AI models and for AI systems integrated into very large online platforms and search engines regulated under the Digital Services Act. The new provisions give the AI Office powers closely resembling those exercised by European competition regulators. These include the ability to launch investigations, compel the production of information, carry out inspections, accept binding commitments and impose periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of average daily turnover for continuing infringements. Organisations should not be misled by headlines that say “delayed”: delay does not extend to most of the AI Act’s transparency obligations. research.titleEn: Semantics of Subterfuge: Benchmarking Legal Deception Detection Against General-domain State-of-the-Art
research.titleZh: 欺骗的语义：法律欺骗检测与通用领域最新技术的基准测试
research.abstractEn: Deception detection has critical implications for legal proceedings, law enforcement, and online security. Although human judgment is limited in accuracy and scalability, Natural Language Processing (NLP) offers a data-driven alternative. We present a survey and comparative analysis of NLP-based Automatic Deception Detection (ADD) focusing on the legal domain, reviewing the evolution from feature-based machine learning to Large Language Model (LLM) approaches. We conduct a unified empirical evaluation across seven datasets (two legal, five general-domain), comparing six fine-tuned transformer models and seven LLMs under four prompting strategies. The results show strong domain sensitivity, with fine-tuned models excelling in data-rich general domains and few-shot LLMs remaining competitive in low-resource legal settings. Chain-of-Thought prompting often underperforms direct classification. These findings highlight the need for domain adaptation and interpretable systems in high-stakes legal contexts.
research.abstractZh: 欺骗检测对法律诉讼、执法和在线安全具有关键意义。尽管人类判断在准确性和可扩展性方面存在局限，自然语言处理（NLP）提供了一种数据驱动的替代方案。我们提出了一项针对法律领域的基于NLP的自动欺骗检测（ADD）的综述和比较分析，回顾了从基于特征的机器学习到大型语言模型（LLM）方法的演变。我们在七个数据集（两个法律领域，五个通用领域）上进行了统一的实证评估，比较了六种微调的Transformer模型和七种LLM在四种提示策略下的表现。结果显示强烈的领域敏感性，微调模型在数据丰富的通用领域表现出色，而少样本LLM在资源匮乏的法律环境中保持竞争力。思维链提示通常不如直接分类。这些发现强调了在高风险法律环境中进行领域适应和可解释系统的必要性。

news.titleEn: Guest post: How startups can prepare for the AI patent wars
news.titleZh: 客座文章：初创企业如何为AI专利战做准备
news.summaryZh: AI专利正以前所未有的速度增长，自2015年以来申请量增加了十倍，但尚未出现高调的行业性诉讼。初创企业创始人仍将知识产权视为法律形式，而非战略商业资产。随着AI产品能力趋同，竞争优势将更少取决于谁先构建，而更多取决于谁拥有底层知识产权。专利在基础模型开发商、应用AI初创企业和成熟科技公司中激增，AI专利所有权高度集中于大型现有科技公司。谷歌2012年以125亿美元收购摩托罗拉移动，主要驱动力是其约1.7万项专利资产；ARM则通过高利润的知识产权许可建立价值，其专利组合包括超过9000项活跃和待决专利资产。市场尚不成熟，缺乏足够重叠的商业产品来支撑大规模诉讼。CRISPR专利争议自2016年持续至今，在商业潜力显现后才成为生物技术领域的决定性知识产权战，AI正遵循类似轨迹。AI本身的法律不确定性，包括专利适格性和AI辅助发明人资格问题，使得激进执法吸引力降低。当前平静反映市场发展阶段，而非未来冲突的缺失。时机至关重要，在先申请制下，延迟申请可能永久削弱竞争地位。初创企业专利策略应从诚实审计现有专利和商业秘密保护开始，建立文档纪律，包括明确所有权记录、时间戳证据，并组建跨学科团队。AI可通过分析专利文献、案例法和技术文档，帮助识别现有技术、突出适格性风险、发现重叠权利要求，从而降低专业知识的获取门槛，使高质量知识产权保护更易获得。
news.bodyHtml:
AI patents are growing at an unprecedented rate, with filings increasing tenfold since 2015, and yet the wave of high-profile, industry-defining litigation is yet to arrive.

Today, startup founders are still treating intellectual property (IP) as a legal formality rather than a strategic business asset. Every major technological breakthrough has reshaped the competitive landscape, but the companies that capture the greatest long-term value are often those with the strongest IP positions. The smartphone patent wars that peaked in the early 2010s, involving a decade-long series of global legal battles, demonstrated how patents can become weapons of negotiating power, licensing revenue, acquisitions, and market control – extending far beyond legal protection.

Advertisement

As AI products converge in capability, competitive advantage will hinge less on who builds first and more on who owns the underlying IP.

For many AI startups, the real risk isn’t losing a lawsuit, it’s reaching commercial scale without an IP position strong enough to defend, monetise or differentiate what they’ve built.

Advertisement

Patents are surging across foundation model developers, applied AI startups, and established technology companies. AI patent ownership is highly concentrated among large incumbent technology companies, creating an increasingly challenging competitive landscape for smaller companies. For many startups, patents are becoming as much about acquisition value, licensing leverage, and fundraising as they are about protecting the technology that’s actually been built.

Google’s $12.5 billion acquisition of Motorola Mobility in 2012 is widely regarded as having been driven largely by the company’s portfolio of around 17,000 patent assets, demonstrating how IP can be a strategic asset in acquisitions rather than simply a form of legal protection. Similarly, Cambridge-based chip designer ARM built its immense value not on manufacturing hardware, but through high-margin IP licensing, supported by a portfolio of over 9,000 active and pending patent assets. Together, these examples illustrate how patents can serve as core commercial assets – driving valuations, enabling licensing revenues, and underpinning entire business models.

The market is still relatively immature, with too few overlapping commercial products valuable enough to justify large scale litigation. Many companies are still focused on building market share, and IP enforcement typically becomes more aggressive once markets consolidate and winners emerge. The CRISPR patent dispute, which began in 2016 and is still ongoing, between the Broad Institute and the University of California, serves as a useful precedent here. It stayed largely dormant until the technology’s commercial potential became known, and only then did it become one of biotech’s defining IP battles. AI is following the same trajectory.

The absence of major litigation reflects continued legal uncertainty about AI itself. Software and AI inventions sit at the centre of ongoing debates over patent eligibility, with courts and patent offices continuing to define the boundary between patentable technical inventions and unpatentable abstract ideas or computer programs. Questions over AI-assisted inventorship only add another level of complexity. Until these legal boundaries become clearer, patent litigation is likely to remain limited. Together, these uncertainties have made aggressive enforcement less attractive, yet have made a proactive IP strategy more important than ever.

The current lull reflects the market’s stage of development, not the absence of future conflict. As AI systems become increasingly sophisticated and technical boundaries blur, patent boundaries blur with them, heightening the risk of overlap and conflict as the field consolidates. Patents can also be corporate weapons rather than just shields, used to delay competitors’ launches, establish monopoly control, and force high-stakes cross licensing.

This is why timing matters. Knowing when to file a patent is often the single most consequential IP decision a startup makes. In my time advising founders on this, the biggest challenge I’ve seen isn’t legal complexity: it’s speed. By the time many founders think to file, they’ve already demoed the product, published the technical details, or closed a funding round, and the moment to protect it cleanly has already passed. In a first-to-file system, delaying a filing by even a few months can permanently weaken a company’s competitive position. Winning the next phase will require organisations that combine deep domain expertise with AI-specific technical fluency.

The question, then, is what a practical startup patent strategy actually looks like. Preparation starts with an honest audit of how to protect IP: do existing patents and trade secrets adequately protect the innovations that actually matter to the business, and where are the gaps? From there, documentation discipline needs to become routine rather than reactive: clear ownership records, time-stamped evidence of human inventive contribution in AI-assisted R&D, and records robust enough to withstand legal scrutiny if they’re ever tested.

Companies need cross-disciplinary teams that can bridge legal, scientific, and engineering perspectives, capable of precise claim construction, more credible infringement analysis, and more effective litigation strategies. Historically, this kind of expertise has been scarce and expensive, which is part of why so many startups have defaulted to treating patents as a box-ticking exercise.

AI itself can help bridge this expertise gap. By analysing vast amounts of patent literature, case law and technical documentation, AI can combine legal and technical reasoning at scale no human team could ever realistically match. It can identify prior art, highlight potential eligibility risks, surface overlapping claims and help strengthen patent strategies in a fraction of the time traditional approaches require. This matters because access to both specialist legal and technical expertise has historically been scarce, expensive and largely confined to larger organisations. AI is lowering that barrier, enabling startups to build stronger, more robust patent portfolios without the resources of a large in-house IP team. The result is that high-quality IP protection becomes more accessible to the startups that need it most.

The window to act is now, while competition is still centred on innovation rather than litigation. By the time the first major AI patent battles emerge, the companies with the strongest positions will already have built them through clear documentation, disciplined IP strategies, and early investment in protecting their innovations. As AI products continue to converge in capability and the market matures, competitive advantage will hinge less on who builds first and more on who owns, protects, and can defend the underlying IP. The companies that come out on top won’t necessarily be the ones with the most advanced technology today, but those whose IP position is strong enough to turn innovation into a lasting competitive advantage.

news.titleEn: ILTA Connect: Women in Legal Tech London – AI & You
news.titleZh: ILTA Connect：伦敦法律科技女性活动——AI 与你
news.summaryZh:
7月7日，Women in Legal Tech活动以“AI & You”为主题，探讨女性如何拥抱人工智能、辨别技术噪音并把握机遇。活动由Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer西部IT总监Nina Gratrick主持，Foil首席创新官Josie West与Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer数字变革总监Hannah O'Grady分享见解。工作中用AI提升效率、制作演示文稿、生成会议记录、开发培训材料并支持法律研究，生活中用于规划假期、购物和烹饪；但一项投票显示，受访者每周专门试验和探索AI的平均时间为零，引发对技术采用与信心方面性别差距的讨论。

演讲者建议接受脆弱性，不只看最新工具，留出好奇心与实验时间，仔细研究工具并分享经验，与同行交流以了解真正价值；并指出许多组织急于构建AI代理，但流程往往需先行修复。小组认为高度重复和流程密集的任务最可能被自动化或显著改变，律所仍倾向观望，文化障碍有待克服；影响采用的因素包括成本、监管与信任。人类监督、判断与指导仍不可或缺，但组织信任AI的时点可能比预期更早。兼具法律专长与技术理解的混合型人才日益重要，未来领导者需编排AI代理与工作流、与技术团队沟通、识别创新价值并运用批判性思维，这为女性带来重大机遇。小组还强调对主题专家、可信声音、创新倡导者的需求，并鼓励承认不知道答案的勇气。演讲者建议不要被炒作分心，AI挑战往往是运营模式挑战，不仅要知道何时使用AI，也要知道何时不用，并考虑成本、价值与业务成果。活动最后总结：AI不是敌人，也不是魔法，而是伙伴；法律专业人士应保持好奇、留出实验时间、拥抱。

ILTA Connect: Women in Legal Tech London - AI & You

By

Laura O'Hara

posted

07-30-2026 08:42

Like

The latest Women in Legal Tech event, on the 7 th July, brought together legal technology professionals for an engaging and thought-provoking discussion on “AI & You” , exploring how women can embrace artificial intelligence, navigate the noise surrounding the technology, and position themselves for the opportunities ahead.

Moderated by Nina Gratrick, IT Director (West), Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer, the session featured insights from Josie West, Chief Innovation Officer at Foil, and Hannah O'Grady, Director of Digital Change at Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer. Through a candid and interactive conversation, attendees explored both the practical realities and future implications of AI in the legal sector.

How Are We Using AI Today?

The session began by asking attendees how they are currently using AI, both professionally and personally. The responses highlighted that AI is already becoming part of everyday life and work.

In the workplace, attendees reported using AI to:

Improve general efficiency and productivity

Help initiate PowerPoint presentations and slide decks

Create meeting notes and summaries

Develop training materials

Support legal research

Outside of work, AI is also finding a place in day-to-day activities, including:

Planning holidays

Shopping

Cooking

However, one audience poll revealed an interesting challenge. When asked how many hours they set aside each week specifically to experiment with and explore AI, the average response was zero .

This sparked a wider conversation about the gender gap in technology adoption and confidence. While many women are actively using AI tools, there is often less dedicated time spent exploring emerging capabilities, experimenting with new applications, or simply playing with the technology. The speakers highlighted the importance of creating space for curiosity and learning to ensure women remain at the forefront of innovation.

Seeing Through the AI Hype

With AI dominating headlines and vendors racing to launch new products, attendees were keen to understand how to cut through the marketing noise.

The speakers encouraged a balanced and realistic approach:

Be comfortable with vulnerability. We are only a couple of years into the AI revolution, and nobody has all the answers.

Avoid focusing solely on the latest tools. AI is far broader than individual products and applications.

Make time for curiosity and experimentation.

Research tools carefully, read reviews, and share experiences openly with your network.

Connect with others working in the space to understand what is truly delivering value rather than relying on headlines and marketing claims.

Remember that while many organisations are rushing to build AI agents, processes often need fixing first. Technology alone cannot solve operational challenges.

The discussion reinforced that successful adoption of AI requires thoughtful implementation rather than simply chasing the newest solution.

How Will AI Change the Way We Work?

The panel also explored which aspects of legal work are most likely to evolve as AI capabilities continue to advance.

The consensus was that tasks that are highly repeatable and process-intensive are most likely to be automated or significantly transformed. At the same time, legal organisations will need to address cultural barriers to innovation.

The speakers noted that many law firms still prefer to see others take the first step before embracing new approaches themselves. If the profession is to fully realise the benefits of AI, this mindset may need to change.

Other factors likely to influence adoption include:

The cost of AI technologies

Regulatory developments

Growing trust in AI systems

While AI agents are becoming increasingly sophisticated, the panel agreed that human oversight, judgement, and direction remain essential. However, the point at which organisations become comfortable trusting AI may arrive sooner than many expect.

The Skills of the Future

One of the most compelling discussions centred on how roles and skillsets will evolve in an AI-enabled workplace.

The speakers highlighted the growing importance of the hybrid professional : individuals who combine legal expertise with technological understanding.

Future leaders will be those who can:

Understand both legal practice and technology

Orchestrate AI agents and workflows

Communicate clearly with technology teams

Identify opportunities to create value through innovation

Apply strong critical thinking and judgement

Encouragingly, the panel highlighted that this evolution presents significant opportunities for women to shape the future of the profession and take on influential roles within the AI ecosystem.

Opportunity, Innovation and Courage

When discussing opportunities within the AI space, the speakers encouraged attendees to think beyond technology implementation and consider leadership and influence.

There is a growing need for:

Subject matter experts

Trusted voices and influencers

Innovation champions

Individuals willing to demonstrate what is possible

The panel stressed that those who know their roles and organisations best are often in the strongest position to identify meaningful opportunities for AI adoption.

Equally important is having the confidence to admit when you do not know the answer. Innovation often requires stepping into uncertainty and learning along the way.

Advice from the Future

To close the session, the speakers reflected on what their future selves might tell them today.

Their advice was refreshingly practical:

Don't be distracted by the hype.

Recognise that AI challenges are often operational model challenges rather than purely technology challenges.

Understand not only when to use AI, but also when not to use it.

Consider cost, value and business outcomes when deciding where AI can have the greatest impact.

Final Thought

The discussion concluded with a powerful reminder for everyone in the room:

AI is not the enemy, and it is not magic. It is a companion.

As legal professionals continue to navigate a rapidly changing landscape, the message from the session was clear: stay curious, make time to experiment, embrace uncertainty, and recognise the unique opportunity women have to help shape the future of AI in the legal sector.

The future will not be defined by the tools we use, but by how we choose to apply them.

news.titleZh: Casepoint推出MCP服务器
news.summaryZh: 美国电子发现提供商Casepoint于7月30日宣布推出Casepoint模型上下文协议（MCP）服务器，使组织能够将其AI模型、代理和AI生态系统与Casepoint平台连接，应用于电子发现、法律保留、调查、信息自由法（FOIA）以及其他法律和合规工作流程。该MCP基于开放的MCP标准构建，在外部AI代理与Casepoint平台之间提供安全、标准化的集成层。每个MCP请求都使用经过认证用户的现有权限执行，确保AI代理永远不会访问超出该权限的材料。未来不是围墙花园的方式，除了在平台内提供一套强大的AI功能外，他们还为客户提供灵活性，使用他们信任的模型和生态系统构建自己的代理。他们致力于提供安全、基于标准的基础，使这些代理能够与Casepoint交互，同时保持治理、权限和客户控制。未来的版本将继续扩展MCP服务器功能库，增加更多功能，使客户能够更深入地将AI集成到法律、监管、调查和合规工作流程中。如需演示，请访问www.casepoint.com。
news.bodyHtml:
US eDiscovery provider Casepoint today(30 July) announced the launch of the Casepoint Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server, enabling organizations to connect their AI models, agents and AI ecosystems with the Casepoint platform across eDiscovery, legal hold, investigations, FOIA, and other legal and compliance workflows.

Built on the open MCP standard, Casepoint’s MCP provides a secure, standardized integration layer between external AI agents and the Casepoint platform. Every MCP request executes using the authenticated user’s existing permissions, ensuring AI agents never gain access to material beyond that.

Advertisement

Chief product officer Pete Feinberg said: “The future isn’t a walled garden approach. In addition to delivering a suite of powerful AI capabilities within our platform, we are also giving customers the flexibility to build their own agents using the models and ecosystems they trust.

“We are committed to providing a secure, standards-based foundation that allows those agents to interact with Casepoint while preserving governance, permissions, and customer control.”

Advertisement

We’re told that future releases will continue expanding the MCP Server function library with additional capabilities, enabling customers to integrate AI more deeply across legal, regulatory, investigative, and compliance workflows.

To see a demo, visit www.casepoint.com.

news.summaryZh: CaseMark于2026年7月30日宣布，其面向法庭记录公司的平台正式命名为CaseMark Source，并推出该平台历史上最大规模的功能扩展，今日上线，已有超过100家法庭记录和诉讼支持公司使用。平台所有AI生成成果均基于公司源文件，交付通过公司自有品牌门户完成。新功能包括：同步视频与带字幕片段，可在计时转录旁播放证词、点击单词跳转，并按主题、引文或时间戳生成带字幕MP4片段；认证转录包，可预览认证转录、编辑封面和认证页，生成含PTX、LEF、MDB等诉讼支持格式的多格式包及可选AI摘要PDF，也可将外部认证转录重新打包；客户自助服务，经批准客户可在品牌门户自行创建转录和片段，费用由公司设定；工作流市场，提供来自agentskills.legal的800多个法律工作流，涵盖证词摘要、医疗年表等，可全公司启用或作为客户可请求服务；文档翻译，支持将文本、Word或可搜索PDF翻译成250种语言并保留原格式，结果为机器翻译工作副本，非认证法律翻译；Insight Pass测试版，在起草摘要或分析前询问受众、立场、重点和深度；多转录审问，可同时查询50多个转录、比较证词并发现潜在不一致。此外，发布扩展了matter chat支持的文件类型，包括JPEG证据和Excel表格，增加一键切换工作区，并引入产品内发布说明。所有功能现已向客户提供，AI生成摘要起价25美元，客户服务由各公司定价。平台通过SOC2 Type II审计，符合HIPAA，客户文档不用于训练AI模型。CaseMark成立于2023年，总部位于俄勒冈州波特兰。
news.bodyHtml:
CaseMark’s court reporting platform gets its official name and a major expansion: transcript-linked video review, exhibit-ready certified packages, client self-service transcription and clipping, document translation, and a marketplace of more than 800 legal workflows.

PORTLAND, Ore., July 30, 2026. CaseMark, the AI workflow company for the legal industry, today announced CaseMark Source, the official name of its platform for court reporting firms, along with the largest set of new capabilities in the platform’s history. CaseMark Source is live today with more than 100 court reporting and litigation support firms.

The name reflects what the platform does. Everything a court reporting firm delivers, from transcripts and summaries to testimony clips and translations, flows from a single source: the matter and the record itself. Every AI-generated work product on CaseMark Source is grounded in the firm’s source files, and every deliverable reaches the client through the firm’s own branded portal.

New in CaseMark Source:

Synchronized video and captioned clips. Firms can play recorded testimony beside the timed transcript, click any word to jump the video to that moment, and search testimony to find the exact exchange. To build designation clips, teams can select a range from the transcript or simply describe the testimony in plain language, by topic, quote, or timestamp, then review the proposed match before creating named, captioned MP4 clips with speaker labels and timestamps.

Certified transcript packages. Where enabled, reporters can preview the certified transcript, edit cover and certification pages directly in the preview, and generate a complete multi-format package, including litigation-support formats such as PTX, LEF, and MDB, with an optional AI summary PDF included in the same exhibit-ready bundle. Firms can also bring in a transcript certified elsewhere and repackage it into the formats litigation teams expect, adding signature images, exhibits, a word index, and condensed formats, without recertifying or altering the authority of the original.

Client self-service, on the firm’s terms. Firms can now allow approved clients to create their own transcriptions and captioned clips directly in the branded portal. The firm decides which clients get access and what each service costs, from client pay-by-card to firm-managed invoicing to firm-covered.

A workflow marketplace with more than 800 legal workflows. Firms can browse and install workflows from agentskills.legal, covering deposition summaries, medical chronologies, hearing and trial summaries, and more. Workflows can be enabled firm-wide or offered to specific clients as requestable services, turning repeatable work product into a client-facing catalog.

Document translation. Firms can translate a text, Word, or searchable PDF document into any of 250 languages while keeping the original format. The result is a machine-translated working copy, searchable, chat-ready, and kept alongside the original for review; it is not a certified legal translation.

Insight Pass (beta). Before drafting a summary or analysis, Insight Pass asks a few focused questions about audience, side, emphasis, and depth so the first draft lands closer to intent, without anyone writing prompts.

Industry-leading multi-transcript interrogation. CaseMark Source lets litigation teams ask questions across 50 or more transcripts at once, compare testimony across witnesses and proceedings, and surface potential inconsistencies with answers grounded in the underlying record.

The release also expands matter chat to more file types, including JPEG exhibits and Excel spreadsheets, adds one-click switching between workspaces for users who work with multiple organizations, and introduces in-product release notes so firm administrators always know what’s new.

“CaseMark Source is the single place court reporting firms produce from and their clients receive from,” said Scott Kveton, CEO of CaseMark. “The reporter stays in control of the record. Source removes the busywork between the record and the client, from synchronized video and certified packages to a marketplace of ready-to-run legal workflows.”

Availability and pricing. All capabilities are available now to CaseMark Source customers. AI-generated summaries start at $25 each; client-facing services such as transcription and clipping are priced by each firm. CaseMark Source is SOC2 Type II audited and HIPAA compliant, and customer documents are never used to train AI models.

About CaseMark

CaseMark is a legal AI infrastructure company building the layer where matter data first enters the record. Its platform serves law firms and litigation support providers alike, structuring depositions, transcripts, and medical records at the point of capture rather than months later, so every downstream summary, chronology, and argument is built on intelligence gathered at first touch. CaseMark Workspace and CaseMark Source deliver that capability to defense firms and court reporting partners, while case.dev provides the open API and agent runtime beneath them, giving firms ownership of their matter data and the models trained on it. Founded in 2023, CaseMark is based in Portland, Oregon. Learn more at casemark.com.

Media Contact

Scott Kveton

scott@casemark.com

(888) 884-4868

news.titleEn: Litigation Enters Its Agentic AI Era
news.titleZh: 诉讼进入代理式人工智能时代
news.summaryZh:
生成式人工智能已迅速进入法律实践，用于起草文件、审查合同和加速研究。早期质疑源于法律行业对工具出错后果的追问，这一问题如今已成为决定性问题。当前能力只是更大转变的第一阶段：代理式人工智能标志着从生成静态输出的系统转向实时主动支持律师的系统，在事件展开时接受指令并即时呈现关键信息。这一区别在诉讼中最为重要，因为诉讼风险高、对抗性强，最具后果性的决策是实时做出的。

生成式人工智能本质上是反应性的，根据提示生成书状、提纲或摘要，已改变证言准备：律师在集成环境中整体摄取、组织和分析案件材料，人工智能呈现关键事实、识别主题联系并生成与既定策略一致的证言问题，使准备与案件目标更紧密对齐。代理式人工智能进一步在证言过程中实时监控交流，跟踪关键主题是否涉及，标记与先前陈述的矛盾，并呈现值得深入探究的线索。在证言中查询系统并非偏离律师已有工作方式，而是其延伸，如同查阅提纲或浏览先前证言，只是系统能在瞥一眼记事本的时间内将单个回答与数千页记录核对。证言结束后，系统将笔录、笔记和人工智能见解整合到统一工作流，减少执行与分析之间的滞后。生成式和代理式人工智能共同重塑证言工作，使律师不再仅依赖直觉和事后审查，而是受益于战略准备与持续更新的见解。传统诉讼工作流是线性的，准备、执行、分析各自独。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Generative AI moved into legal practice faster than almost anyone expected, most visibly through tools that draft documents, review contracts, and accelerate research. The early skepticism was not misplaced. It was the profession doing what it is trained to do: asking what happens when the tool is wrong. That question has not gone away. It has become the defining one. The capabilities reshaping legal work so far are only the first stage of a larger shift. The emergence of agentic AI signals a shift from systems that produce static outputs to those that actively support attorneys in real time. Agentic AI works alongside the attorney as events unfold, taking direction and surfacing what matters in the moment. Nowhere does that distinction count for more than in litigation, where the stakes are high, the setting is adversarial, and the most consequential decisions are made in real time, not at the desk afterward. At its core, generative AI is reactive: it produces briefs, outlines, or summaries in response to prompts. These tech solutions have already transformed deposition preparation. Rather than manually reviewing documents across fragmented systems, attorneys now operate in integrated environments where case materials are ingested, organized, and analyzed holistically. AI surfaces key facts, identifies thematic connections, and generates deposition questions aligned with defined legal strategies, driving not only efficiency, but tighter alignment between preparation and case objectives. Agentic AI expands this capability by working alongside attorneys as events unfold. It delivers context-aware, results-focused assistance in real time. This is an especially meaningful distinction in high-stakes, fast-paced litigation, where timing and adaptability are critical. Depositions sit at the intersection of structure and unpredictability. While attorneys can prepare extensively, success in a deposition ultimately depends on how effectively they respond in the moment. Agentic AI is uniquely suited to this challenge. Operating alongside live testimony, agentic systems can monitor exchanges in real time, track whether key topics have been addressed, flag inconsistencies with prior statements, and surface lines of discussion that warrant deeper inquiry. Querying the system during a deposition is not a departure from how attorneys already work; it is an extension of it. A litigator consults an outline or scans prior testimony before moving to the next line of questioning. Asking an agentic system whether a topic has been fully covered, or whether an answer contradicts an earlier statement, fits the same rhythm: a beat between questions, not an interruption of them. The difference is that the system can check a single answer against thousands of pages of records in the time it takes to glance at a notepad. After the deposition, these systems integrate transcripts, notes, and AI-generated insights into a unified workflow, reducing lag between execution and analysis and enabling faster, more informed decisions on next steps. Together, generative and agentic AI fundamentally reshape deposition work. Attorneys are no longer reliant solely on instinct and post hoc review. Instead, they benefit from strategic preparation paired with continuously updated insights as testimony unfolds. Litigation provides a compelling proving ground for AI systems to function not as passive tools, but as active collaborators. Traditional litigation workflows were linear: preparation, execution, analysis, each phase largely discrete, with limited feedback loops. Agentic AI moves litigation toward a more dynamic model. Preparation and execution operate in tandem, informed by real-time insight, with AI serving as the connective infrastructure that keeps information synchronized and decisions actionable throughout the process.

news.titleEn: Client Alert: The New AI Coverage Fight: Exclusions, Endorsements, and Denied Claims
news.titleZh: 客户警示：新一轮AI承保之争——除外条款、批单与拒赔
news.summaryZh:
许多企业采用人工智能时假定，一旦出现问题，保险将帮助吸收损失。这一假定可能需要修正。如同十年前的网络安全与网络责任保险，保险业正在做其不喜欢做的事：依据数十年来标准的保单措辞，为快速演变的威胁所引发的索赔买单。因此，在AI问题上，保险公司开始说“不”。问题不在于保险公司突然发现了AI，也不是恶意或圈钱，而是保险公司正在决定自己愿意保留多少风险、希望单独定价多少、以及希望完全排除多少。这种变化正通过新的AI特定除外条款、更窄的批单、分项限额、承保问题以及从未考虑生成式AI或AI代理的旧保单措辞来实现。换言之，保险公司不再等到索赔时才就AI相关问题的承保范围进行争辩。

直到最近，大多数AI相关风险并未被作为独特风险类别处理。网络保单可能承保涉及AI工具的数据泄露；技术错误与遗漏保单可能响应AI赋能的服务故障；媒体或一般责任保单可能适用于涉及AI生成内容的某些诽谤、隐私或广告伤害索赔。这种未言明的承保有时被称为“沉默AI”承保。对保险公司而言，问题显而易见：AI可将普通风险变为更大、更快、更难衡量的风险。一封糟糕的员工邮件触达一位客户；一个糟糕的聊天机器人回答可能触达数千人。一次错误的专业判断影响一个事项；嵌入工作流程的AI系统可能在任何人注意到之前，在整个客户群中重复同一错误。AI代理可能不仅建议欠考虑的做法，还可能将其付诸实施。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Many businesses are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) under the familiar assumption that if something goes wrong, insurance will help absorb the loss. That assumption may need revision. As with cybersecurity and cyber liability insurance a decade ago, the insurance industry is doing something it doesn't like doing: paying for claims caused by rapidly evolving threats relying on insurance policy language that has been standard for decades. So, when it comes to AI, insurance companies have started doing what they’re famous for. They're saying "no." The issue is not that insurance companies have suddenly discovered AI, and it's also not malicious or a money grab. It's actually far more mundane. Insurers are now deciding how much of the risk they want to keep, how much they want to price separately, and how much they want to exclude entirely. That change is happening through new AI-specific exclusions, narrower endorsements, sublimits, underwriting questions, and old policy language that was never written with generative AI or AI agents in mind. In other words, insurance companies are no longer waiting until you file a claim to fight coverage for AI-related problems. Until recently, most AI-related risks weren't addressed as a unique category of risk. A cyber policy might cover a data breach involving an AI tool. A technology errors and omissions policy might respond to an AI-enabled service failure. A media or general liability policy might apply to certain defamation, privacy, or advertising injury claims involving AI-generated content. That kind of unspoken coverage is sometimes called "silent AI" coverage. The problem for insurers should be obvious: AI can turn ordinary risks into larger, faster, harder-to-measure risks. A bad employee email reaches one customer. A bad chatbot answer may reach thousands. A mistaken professional judgment affects one matter. An AI system embedded in a workflow may repeat the same mistake across an entire customer base before anyone notices. An AI agent may not just recommend an ill-considered approach; it may implement it. Insurers have noticed. The market is moving away from "silent AI" coverage as carriers introduce AI-specific exclusions, revised forms, and narrower coverage structures ahead of renewals. This matters because business owners may think they are buying the same insurance program they bought last year, when the renewal actually moves AI risk into a different box: excluded, sublimited, subject to special conditions, or only covered under a separate AI endorsement. The most direct approach is also the easiest to understand: insurers are adding policy language that says certain AI-related claims are not covered.

news.summaryZh:

Clio Grow 集成使 Clio Work 可直接访问 Clio Grow 数据，获取从咨询到活跃案件的全客户视图，包括 intake 回复、咨询详情、管道阶段和已签署文件。功能包括：在开案前检查 intake 就绪状态；在开始法律工作前获取完整客户背景；将已签约潜在客户转化为活跃案件；跟进停滞的 intake。每项操作在执行前均需确认。此版本仅面向同时使用 Clio Grow 和 Clio Work 的律所。
