news.titleEn: No Single AI Rulebook but Plenty of Investigators
news.titleZh: 没有统一的人工智能规则手册，但调查者众多
news.summaryZh: 联邦政府将人工智能领导地位列为国家优先事项，白宫呼吁建立负担最小的国家框架、加强网络安全、扩大公私合作并减少州法律障碍。司法部成立人工智能诉讼工作组，挑战其认为干扰国家政策的州法律，并已介入挑战科罗拉多州算法决策监管的诉讼。但亲创新议程不等于没有执法风险：在全面框架尚未确定之际，联邦机构、州检察长和国会委员会正依据现有权力审查人工智能产品、数据实践、安全措施和公开陈述，形成专门规则较少但多个调查者依据重叠甚至冲突法律理论评估公司的局面。司法部可依据国家安全、反垄断、民权和欺诈等广泛刑事与民事权力处理人工智能相关行为；2026年6月行政命令要求优先刑事执法打击利用人工智能未经授权访问系统、破坏系统、非法获取信息或助长其他犯罪的行为，并指示联邦政府与人工智能开发商就网络安全和先进模型安全部署开展合作。审查可能涉及人工智能欺诈、网络安全事件、敏感数据或技术滥用、外国风险、反竞争行为或对政府客户的陈述。联邦贸易委员会明确人工智能公司仍受《联邦贸易委员会法》禁止不公平或欺骗性行为约束，并于2026年7月1日提出政策声明，关注公司是否通过操纵系统行为、违背客观性和准确性合理预期来欺骗消费者，聚焦其关于模型设计目的和表现准确性的明示与暗示陈述。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The federal government has made American leadership in artificial intelligence a national priority. The White House has called for a minimally burdensome national framework, stronger cybersecurity, greater public-private cooperation, and fewer state law barriers to AI innovation. The Justice Department has also established an Artificial Intelligence Litigation Task Force to challenge certain state laws that it believes interfere with that national policy. But AI developers and startups should not mistake a pro-innovation agenda for an absence of enforcement risk. Even as policymakers debate the contours of a comprehensive national framework, federal agencies, state attorneys general, and congressional committees are applying existing authorities to AI products, data practices, security measures, and public representations. The result is an unusual environment: fewer settled AI-specific rules but multiple potential investigators evaluating companies under overlapping and sometimes conflicting legal theories. For AI companies, the immediate question is therefore not simply what AI law applies to them. It is also: How would their decisions, documentation, and internal controls withstand government scrutiny? The Department of Justice can address AI-related conduct through a broad range of criminal and civil authorities, including national security, antitrust, civil rights, and fraud laws. A June 2026 executive order specifically directs the Attorney General to prioritize criminal enforcement against individuals who use AI to gain unauthorized access to computer systems, damage systems, obtain information unlawfully, or further other crimes. The same order directs the federal government to work with AI developers on cybersecurity and the secure deployment of advanced models. Depending on a company’s technology and business model, DOJ scrutiny could involve AI-enabled fraud, cybersecurity incidents, misuse of sensitive data or technology, foreign exposure, anticompetitive conduct, or representations to government customers. Companies may also find themselves interacting with DOJ in a different capacity. The Department’s AI Litigation Task Force is responsible for challenging state AI laws that the Administration views as unconstitutional, federally preempted, or otherwise unlawful. DOJ has already moved to intervene in litigation challenging Colorado’s regulation of algorithmic decision making. This dual role makes the current environment especially complicated: DOJ may be an enforcement authority or an ally challenging state restrictions, depending on the issue. The Federal Trade Commission has made clear that AI companies remain subject to the FTC Act’s prohibition on unfair or deceptive conduct. On July 1, 2026, the FTC proposed a policy statement addressing whether AI companies may deceive consumers by manipulating system behavior contrary to reasonable expectations concerning objectivity and accuracy. The proposal focuses on the representations – express and implied – that companies make about what their models are designed to do and how accurately they perform. The broader lesson extends beyond the precise subject of the proposal. Statements in product materials, investor communications, terms of service, and public testimony can all become relevant in an investigation. Claims that a model is accurate, secure, unbiased, or suitable for a particular use should be supported by testing and internal documentation.

research.titleEn: LLM-Assisted Ontology Engineering and Construction of a French Legal Knowledge Graph
research.titleZh: 基于LLM辅助的本体工程与法语法律知识图谱构建
research.abstractEn: Maintenance regulations are complex legal texts that are difficult to exploit when addressing a specific case and challenging to integrate into operational systems. This paper presents a two-stage LLM-assisted workflow for French maintenance regulations: ontology engineering from a SEMLEG-based core ontology, followed by construction of an ontology-grounded French legal knowledge graph. The first stage consists in the open extraction of typed entities and triples from a stratified corpus sample, the normalization of labels through embedding-based fusion, and the induction of candidate object properties with their signature (domain and range). The second stage uses the resulting ontology to guide the closed extraction of triples and RDF graph construction over the full corpus. Experiments with GPT-4.1 and mistral-large-2512 show robust structured outputs, near-complete class alignment, and a substantial reduction of duplicated entities and predicates after fusion. Fewer than 20% of triples introduce unseen properties, while lower exact signature compliance reveals new domain-range combinations for existing predicates. These results point to predicate normalization and the validation of newly observed relation signatures as key refinement steps for industrial maintenance settings.
research.abstractZh: 维护法规是复杂的法律文本，在处理特定案例时难以利用，并且难以集成到操作系统中。本文提出了一种针对法语维护法规的两阶段LLM辅助工作流程：从基于SEMLEG的核心本体进行本体工程，然后构建基于本体的法语法律知识图谱。第一阶段包括从分层语料库样本中开放提取类型化实体和三元组，通过基于嵌入的融合进行标签归一化，以及归纳候选对象属性及其签名（定义域和值域）。第二阶段利用生成的本体指导全语料库上的封闭三元组提取和RDF图构建。使用GPT-4.1和mistral-large-2512的实验显示出稳健的结构化输出、近乎完整的类对齐，以及融合后重复实体和谓词的显著减少。少于20%的三元组引入了未见过的属性，而较低的精确签名符合性揭示了现有谓词的新定义域-值域组合。这些结果表明，谓词归一化和对新观察到的关系签名的验证是工业维护环境中的关键细化步骤。

research.titleEn: Do Small Models Use the Law You Give Them? Context-Injected Fine-Tuning for Legal QA in Bangladesh
research.titleZh: 小模型会使用你提供的法律吗？孟加拉国法律问答中的上下文注入微调
research.abstractEn: A small language model can receive the governing statutory provision and still answer incorrectly. We test whether fine-tuning on examples containing relevant law improves later use of retrieved law. We curate 2{,}165 bilingual QA records from six Bangladeshi acts and three schedules, then fine-tune Qwen3.5 at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B. Evaluation uses the 2022 and 2023 Bangladesh Bar Council exams in Bangla and machine-translated English, with no retrieval, BM25, or FAISS, scored by strict consistency over three seeded runs. At 0.8B, fine-tuning raises the 2022 English FAISS score from 2 to 34 of 100. Gains at 0.8B and 2B survive paired testing, but the 4B model has no detectable net gain: Bangla improves while several English conditions regress. Fine-tuning also reduces answers that drift from Bangla into mostly English from 44.0--53.2\% to 0.2--0.7\%, with adjusted $p<.001$ at every scale. Retrieval quality is therefore not the only bottleneck. Small bilingual legal models also differ in how they use supplied law and whether they answer in the requested language. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/momahadi/bangladesh-legal-qa-dataset.
research.abstractZh: 一个小型语言模型可以接收到适用的法定条款，但仍然会给出错误的答案。我们测试了在包含相关法律的示例上进行微调是否能改善后续对检索到的法律的使用。我们从六部孟加拉国法案和三个附表中整理了2,165条双语问答记录，然后对Qwen3.5的0.8B、2B和4B版本进行微调。评估使用2022年和2023年孟加拉国律师协会考试（孟加拉语和机器翻译的英语），不进行检索、BM25或FAISS，通过三次种子运行的严格一致性进行评分。在0.8B规模下，微调将2022年英语FAISS分数从2分提高到34分（满分100分）。0.8B和2B规模的提升在配对检验中仍然显著，但4B模型没有可检测到的净收益：孟加拉语有所改善，而几个英语条件则出现退步。微调还将从孟加拉语漂移到主要使用英语的答案比例从44.0%–53.2%降低到0.2%–0.7%，在每个规模下调整后的p<.001。因此，检索质量并不是唯一的瓶颈。小型双语法律模型在如何使用提供的法律以及是否以所要求的语言回答方面也存在差异。该数据集公开可用，网址为https://huggingface.co/datasets/momahadi/bangladesh-legal-qa-dataset。

news.titleEn: Alabama Bar Draws a Clear Ethics Line on Lawyers’ AI Use
news.titleZh: 阿拉巴马州律师协会就律师使用AI划定明确道德界限
news.summaryZh:
阿拉巴马州律师协会发布正式道德指导意见，明确AI对律所而言不仅是技术问题，更是职业责任问题。意见聚焦计费与客户沟通：警告律师不得就AI辅助完成的工作收取虚高费用，并应坦诚告知客户AI的使用方式。意见将AI定位为须在胜任、合理、诚实和监督等长期义务框架内使用的工具，而非禁止性工具。

该意见影响超出阿拉巴马州。律师协会意见常成为法院、纪律机构、职业责任保险商及律所风险委员会的实践路线图。在正式规则尚未完全跟上技术发展之际，道德指导意见正日益塑造评判律师的标准，等待上诉判决或纪律案例再行动的律所可能已经落后。对诉讼律师而言，若AI减少研究、起草或文件审查时间而时间记录未反映效率提升，传统计费小时模式将更难辩护；同时律师不能将判断外包给聊天机器人，人工审查仍不可或缺，尤其考虑到对虚构判例、不准确摘要和过度自信输出的持续担忧。对内部法律顾问，该意见强化了向外聘律所直接询问AI政策的必要性：使用哪些工具、如何保护机密信息、AI辅助工作如何审查及如何计费。合规与风险团队也应注意，正式指导意见可迅速影响内部培训、委托书、网络安全协议和记录管理实践；已允许使用AI的律所可能需要更精确的书面规则，涵盖披露、监督和计费纪律。更广泛的结论是，法律道德监管机构行动速度快于许多人的预期。阿拉巴马州的意见强调了一个简单而有力。

Alabama Bar Draws a Clear Ethics Line on Lawyers’ AI Use

by Bruno Queiroz

The Alabama State Bar has issued formal ethics guidance on lawyers’ use of artificial intelligence, offering one of the clearest signals yet that AI is no longer just a technology issue for law firms — it is a professional responsibility issue.

The opinion reportedly focuses on two especially sensitive areas: billing and client communication. Lawyers are warned not to charge inflated fees for work performed with the assistance of AI, and they are expected to be candid with clients about how AI is being used in legal services. That combination is important. It frames AI not as a prohibited tool, but as one that must be used within long-standing duties of competence, reasonableness, honesty, and supervision.

For legal professionals, the significance goes beyond Alabama. Bar opinions often become practical roadmaps for courts, disciplinary authorities, malpractice carriers, and law firm risk committees. In an area where formal rules have not fully caught up to the technology, ethics guidance is increasingly shaping the standards attorneys will be judged by. That means firms waiting for appellate decisions or disciplinary cases before acting may already be behind.

For litigators, the billing point is particularly consequential. If AI reduces the time required for research, drafting, or document review, the traditional billable-hour model becomes harder to defend if time entries do not reflect that efficiency. At the same time, lawyers cannot outsource judgment to a chatbot. Human review remains essential, especially given continuing concerns about hallucinated authorities, inaccurate summaries, and overconfident outputs.

For in-house counsel, the opinion reinforces the value of asking outside firms direct questions about AI policies: What tools are being used? How is confidential information protected? How is AI-assisted work reviewed? How is that work billed? Those questions are becoming part of ordinary vendor-management and outside-counsel oversight.

Compliance and risk teams should also take note. Formal bar guidance can quickly influence internal training, engagement letters, cybersecurity protocols, and records-management practices. Firms that already permit AI use may now need more precise written rules on disclosure, supervision, and billing discipline.

The broader takeaway is that legal ethics regulators are moving faster than many expected. Alabama’s opinion underscores a simple but powerful principle: AI may change how legal work is done, but it does not change the lawyer’s duty to deliver accurate work, charge fairly, and communicate honestly with the client.

DOJ Settlement With Willow Bridge Signals Continued Scrutiny of Rental Pricing Algorithms

by Bruno Queiroz

The Justice Department has proposed an antitrust settlement with Willow Bridge Property Company LLC, one of the country’s largest landlords, in a case that underscores a continuing enforcement priority: the use of pricing algorithms and shared competitively sensitive information in rental housing markets.

According to the government, the case centers on allegations that Willow Bridge participated in information sharing and coordination practices affecting apartment rents. While the proposed settlement still must proceed through the enforcement action in the Middle District of North Carolina, the announcement is notable because it reinforces the Antitrust Division’s position that algorithmic tools do not insulate market participants from traditional Section 1 scrutiny. For landlords, property managers, and software vendors, the message is straightforward: if technology facilitates unlawful coordination, enforcers will treat it like any other anticompetitive mechanism.

The matter also fits into a broader wave of litigation over rental pricing software, including the multidistrict proceeding IN RE: Realpage, Inc., Rental Software Antitrust Litigation (No. II) pending in the Middle District of Tennessee. That MDL has become a key forum for testing allegations that landlords and technology providers used shared data and algorithmic recommendations to push rents upward. The Willow Bridge settlement suggests the government intends to keep building parallel pressure through direct enforcement, not just private civil litigation.

For legal professionals, the significance goes beyond housing. Litigators should expect continued discovery battles over what counts as competitively sensitive data, how pricing recommendations are generated, and whether “recommended” prices are in practice followed closely enough to support an inference of agreement. In-house counsel and compliance teams should read this development as a prompt to revisit policies governing revenue management systems, benchmarking exchanges, and communications with third-party software providers.

Several practical questions now matter more than ever: What data is being shared with vendors or competitors? How granular and current is that data? Are algorithmic recommendations independently evaluated, or effectively adopted automatically? And are business teams trained to understand that antitrust risk can arise from digital coordination just as easily as from direct human communications?

The enforcement action against Willow Bridge will likely be watched closely by parties already tracking the RealPage litigation and related claims. For anyone advising clients in multifamily housing, platform-driven pricing, or data-intensive markets, this settlement is another sign that antitrust compliance programs need to account specifically for algorithmic decision-making—not just traditional competitor contacts.

news.summaryZh: Lexidesk是一家快速成长的法律AI初创公司，致力于解决中小型律所持续面临的挑战：获取并筛选新业务。该公司由Ivan Tryskyba于2025年6月创立，结合对话式AI、语音技术和法律专用接案工作流，全天候接听电话和网络咨询。公司瞄准人身伤害、家庭、移民、刑事辩护和遗产规划等高业务量领域，定位为专为法律服务打造的AI接待员，而非通用语音助手。其平台整合语音AI、电话基础设施和LLM驱动的资格筛选逻辑，并具备原生CRM集成和针对每家律所及业务领域调优的提示架构。公司已在美国和英国签约50多家律所，推出基于对话的定价模式，上线多个CRM市场集成，并推出外呼功能。公司从Caseguru（与Vadym Baranivsky共同创立的律师市场）转型至当前的AI接案方向。市场挑战包括：律所技术采用缓慢，对涉及客户沟通的技术持风险规避态度；信任和准确性（不产生幻觉法律建议、正确的范围/冲突检查）至关重要；市场充斥着不理解法律接案细微差别的通用AI语音代理。公司首名客户通过ChatGPT找到他们，现已成为公司顾问。
news.bodyHtml:
In this week’s Startup Corner is Lexidesk, a fast-growing legal AI startup tackling one of the most persistent challenges facing smaller law firms: capturing and qualifying new business. Founded in June 2025 by Ivan Tryskyba, Lexidesk combines conversational AI, voice technology and legal-specific intake workflows to answer calls and web enquiries around the clock.

Targeting high-volume practice areas such as personal injury, family, immigration, criminal defence and estate planning, the company is positioning itself as an AI receptionist built specifically for legal services rather than a general-purpose voice assistant. Having already signed more than 50 law firms across the UK and US, launched multiple CRM integrations and expanded into outbound calling, the bootstrapped startup is seeking to differentiate itself through deep legal intake expertise at a time when the market is becoming increasingly crowded with AI voice solutions.

Advertisement

We caught up with Tryskyba and CTO Vadim Baranivsky to hear their origin story, how the company pivoted, its strategy, and a fact no-one else knows.

How would you describe your company to a friend?

Lexidesk is an AI receptionist for law firms. It answers the phone and website chat 24/7, figures out if a caller has a real case, and books them straight into a consultation — so firms stop losing leads to voicemail.

Advertisement
And to a techy?

Lexidesk is a conversational AI intake platform combining voice AI, telephony infrastructure, and LLM-driven qualification logic, with native CRM integrations and a state-of-the-art prompt architecture tuned per firm and practice area.

When were you founded?

June 2025

By who?

Ivan Tryskyba 

Who are your key managers/senior execs?

Ivan Tryskyba CEO, Vadim Baranivsky CTO

Who are your target clients?

Small-to-mid-size US and UK law firms — personal injury, family, immigration, criminal defense, and estate planning practices — that get high call/lead volume and can’t staff round-the-clock intake.

What is your plan (growth strategy)?

Direct sales plus CRM marketplace distribution, content/SEO via our Knowledge Hub, and expanding product surface area (outbound calling, referral network, agent memory) to increase seat value and reduce churn.

Key achievements?

50+ law firm clients live across the US and UK; conversation-based pricing model shipped; multiple CRM marketplace integrations live; outbound calling feature launched.

Have you received investment?

We are bootstrapping

Have there been any key changes in direction since you were founded?

Pivoted from Caseguru (a lawyer marketplace, co-founded with Vadym Baranivsky) to Lexidesk’s current AI intake focus.

What are the key challenges in your market?

Law firms are slow tech adopters and risk-averse about anything touching client communication; trust and accuracy (no hallucinated legal advice, correct scope/conflict checks) are non-negotiable; and the market is getting noisy with general-purpose AI voice agents that don’t understand legal intake nuance.

Tell us something people don’t already know about the company?

Our first customer found us through ChatGPT — and is now an advisor to the company.

news.titleZh: 认识演讲者：法律AI演示日（2026年夏季）
news.summaryZh:
法律AI工具正从通用聊天机器人转向日益专业化的法律工作流程。2026年8月11日，National Law Review、WashU Law和Wickard将举办“法律AI演示日：2026年夏季”，这是一个免费的虚拟活动，九家法律科技公司将进行八分钟的快速演示。参与产品涵盖诉讼事实管理、自动计时、房地产尽职调查、发现工作流程、特权会议情报、小型律所事务管理、证券披露合规、司法案件准备和工伤赔偿辩护等多种用例。每家公司将展示其产品的实际运作，而非传统的演示或销售推介。

Mary Technology是一个AI驱动的事实管理平台，旨在帮助诉讼团队整理大量无序的案件记录。该平台审查案件文件，并将信息转换为结构化、可搜索且可验证的事实记录。提取的事实、人物和日期仍与底层源材料相关联，使律师能够构建时间线、进行事实分析并准备工作成果，同时不丢失证据链。PointOne将AI应用于律师计时、计费合规和律所分析，被动识别可计费工作并根据律师活动生成拟议时间条目，旨在减少重建时间的行政负担、提高计费准确性并帮助律所遵守客户计费要求。Orbital Tech为房地产律师和物业专业人士提供AI驱动的尽职调查工具。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Legal AI tools are moving beyond general-purpose chatbots and into increasingly specialized legal workflows. On August 11, 2026, the National Law Review, WashU Law, and Wickard will host Legal AI Demo Day: Summer 2026, a free virtual program featuring rapid, eight-minute demonstrations from nine legal technology companies. The participating products address a wide range of use cases, including litigation fact management, automated timekeeping, real estate due diligence, discovery workflows, privileged meeting intelligence, small-firm matter management, securities disclosure compliance, judicial case preparation, and workers’ compensation defense. Rather than relying on conventional presentations or sales pitches, each company will demonstrate its product in action. Below is a preview of the participating companies and the legal workflows their technologies are designed to support. Mary Technology is an AI-powered fact-management platform designed to help litigation teams organize large and disordered case records. The platform reviews case documents and converts the information into a structured, searchable, and verifiable factual record. Extracted facts, people, and dates remain linked to their underlying source materials, allowing lawyers to build chronologies, conduct factual analysis, and prepare legal work product without losing the evidentiary trail. Mary Technology is designed for matters in which lawyers must identify significant facts across thousands of documents and establish a reliable account of what occurred. PointOne applies AI to attorney timekeeping, billing compliance, and law-firm analytics. The platform passively identifies billable work and generates proposed time entries based on an attorney’s activity. It is intended to reduce the administrative burden associated with reconstructing time, improve billing accuracy, and help firms comply with client billing requirements. PointOne may be particularly relevant to law firms seeking to minimize lost time, improve realization, and obtain better visibility into how legal work is performed. Orbital Tech provides AI-powered due diligence tools for real estate lawyers and property professionals.

research.titleEn: Legal Nugget Extraction for Granular Retrieval over Long Jurisprudential Texts
research.titleZh: 面向长篇幅法学文本的细粒度检索的法律要点提取
research.abstractEn: Legal retrieval over jurisprudential collections is challenging because court decisions are long, heterogeneous documents whose relevant legal thesis may occupy only a small portion of the text. This paper asks whether legal nuggets, defined as short and self-contained legal theses extracted from source documents, can improve dense retrieval over Brazilian legal collections. We propose a pipeline that extracts nuggets from each document, indexes them with embeddings, retrieves nugget-level evidence, and aggregates the retrieved nuggets back to document-level rankings. We evaluate this approach on four Portuguese legal retrieval benchmarks from the JUA ecosystem, reporting NDCG@10, MAP@10, and MRR@10. Nugget retrieval substantially improves the two jurisprudential datasets: on JUA-Juris, NDCG@10 increases from 0.10265 to 0.20461, and on JurisTCU from 0.20898 to 0.32696. However, it underperforms full-document retrieval on NormasTCU and BR-TaxQA, and an embedding-model ablation shows that strong domain-adapted retrievers can remain better in the full-document setting. The results demonstrate that legal nuggets can be useful for jurisprudence search, especially when queries are formulated as legal theses, but they may not transfer equally well to other legal retrieval scenarios.
research.abstractZh: 法律检索在判例集合中具有挑战性，因为法院判决是长篇幅、异构的文档，其相关的法律论点可能仅占文本的一小部分。本文探讨了法律要点（定义为从源文档中提取的简短且自包含的法律论点）是否能够改进巴西法律集合的密集检索。我们提出了一种流水线，从每个文档中提取要点，用嵌入向量对其进行索引，检索要点级别的证据，并将检索到的要点聚合回文档级别的排名。我们在JUA生态系统的四个葡萄牙语法律检索基准上评估了该方法，报告了NDCG@10、MAP@10和MRR@10。要点检索显著改善了这两个判例数据集：在JUA-Juris上，NDCG@10从0.10265提高到0.20461；在JurisTCU上，从0.20898提高到0.32696。然而，在NormasTCU和BR-TaxQA上，其表现不如全文检索，并且嵌入模型消融实验表明，强大的领域自适应检索器在全文设置中可能仍然更好。结果表明，法律要点对于判例搜索可能是有用的，特别是当查询以法律论点的形式提出时，但它们可能无法同样地迁移到其他法律检索场景。

news.summaryZh: 法律AI公司Harvey于今日宣布，微软的企业、外部及法律事务部门（CELA）将采用Harvey平台，以支持其法律与合规运营。CELA是微软内部约2000人的部门，涵盖公司律师与合规专业人员。与此同时，Harvey也宣布将扩大自身对微软365及微软365 Copilot的内部使用，称此举可让其团队与众多客户使用同一可信平台。微软产品是律师工作的基础，感谢与微软团队的深厚关系，并称此次公告是双方持续关系中的下一步。很高兴扩大与Harvey的合作，作为将AI引入运营的更广泛努力的一部分，该合作将帮助团队更高效地工作，专注于复杂且高影响力的工作。此次公告是双方多年合作的最新进展。Harvey运行于微软Azure基础设施上，2024年12月双方宣布整合Harvey与SharePoint、Word及微软365 Copilot。2025年3月，Harvey将其法律智能直接构建为微软365 Copilot中的代理，并于6月扩展至Copilot Cowork。微软采用第三方法律AI可能暗示Copilot无法独立处理专业法律工作，但更准确的理解是，微软一直将Copilot定位为横向平台，旨在承载专业垂直代理，Harvey正是理想候选。因此，微软法务部部署Harvey并非否定Copilot，而是产品生态系统按预期整合的体现。Harvey自豪于拥有超过1000个内部法律团队使用其平台，并致力于支持法律团队的全面需求，同时与组织合作实现更广泛的业务目标。
news.bodyHtml:
Microsoft’s legal department is becoming a Harvey customer.

The legal AI company Harvey announced today that Microsoft’s Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) organization — the roughly 2,000-person unit that houses the company’s lawyers and compliance professionals — will use the Harvey platform to support its legal and compliance operations.

As part of the same announcement, Harvey said it will expand its own internal use of Microsoft 365 and Microsoft 365 Copilot, which the company said will put its teams “on the same trusted platform used by many of its customers.”

For Harvey, landing Microsoft’s legal department as a customer is a significant milestone, given that it is arguably one of the most closely watched in-house legal teams in the technology industry. However, as I discuss more below, it is not so much a customer win as it is a next step in an evolving relationship.

“Microsoft’s products are foundational to the work lawyers do, so we have always been grateful for our deep relationship with their team,” said Winston Weinberg, Harvey’s CEO, in a statement.

“Today’s announcement that Microsoft’s legal team will use Harvey’s platform and that Harvey associates will use more Microsoft products to support our global growth represents the next step in our ongoing relationship with their team, and we look forward to building on it.”

Antony Cook, corporate vice president and deputy general counsel at Microsoft, said the company is “pleased to expand our work with Harvey as part of our broader efforts to bring the benefits of AI into our operations,” adding that the collaboration “will help our teams work more efficiently and focus on the complex, high-impact work that matters most.”

A Developing Relationship

Today’s announcement is the latest step in a relationship that has been building for several years. Harvey runs on Microsoft’s Azure infrastructure, and in December 2024 the two companies announced integrations connecting Harvey with SharePoint, Word and Microsoft 365 Copilot.

In March, Harvey went further, building its legal intelligence directly into Microsoft 365 Copilot as an agent, and in June it extended that to Copilot Cowork.

Against that backdrop, today’s news is not so much a customer win as it is a next step in an expanding relationship, with Microsoft’s lawyers adopting Harvey, and Harvey standardizing on Microsoft.

Even so, some might read Microsoft’s adoption of a third-party legal AI as a tacit admission that Copilot alone cannot handle specialized legal work. After all, if Copilot fully met the needs of Microsoft’s own lawyers, then CELA presumably would not need Harvey.

But the reality is more nuanced. The fact of the matter is that Microsoft has consistently positioned Copilot as a horizontal platform designed to host specialized vertical agents, with Harvey as a perfect candidate.

For that reason, its legal department’s deployment of Harvey probably should not be seen as a repudiation of Copilot, but as a demonstration of this product ecosystem coming together as intended.

“Harvey is proud to have more than 1,000 in-house legal teams using our platform to make their work more effective and efficient,” said Katie Burke, chief operating officer at Harvey. “We are committed to supporting the comprehensive needs of legal teams while partnering with their organization to help achieve broader business goals.”

news.titleEn: Entegrata hires Simpson Thacher AI leader Andrew Baker to run AI enablement strategy
news.titleZh: Entegrata聘请盛德律师事务所AI负责人Andrew Baker负责AI赋能战略
news.summaryZh: Entegrata已聘请Andrew Baker担任首席AI与数据战略官。Baker来自Simpson Thacher & Bartlett，曾任应用AI总监，组建约20人专家团队，推动采用Harvey和DeepJudge等生成式AI平台，并亲身体验律所规模化扩展AI的机遇与局限。其过往职务包括Seyfarth Shaw全球法律产品与技术总监、Janders Dean法律转型总监、LexPredict服务全球主管副总裁及HBR高级总监。此次任命恰逢Entegrata计划在现有数据湖仓平台之上推出AI赋能层，重点不是创建另一个法律AI应用，而是帮助律所建立支持多种AI工具、模型和内部开发应用所需的数据基础。市场最大挑战已不再是AI工具短缺，律所需要的是所有工具之下的那一层，提供更多内容、上下文、成本控制和选择，使其能自由选择不同模型而不被单一供应商锁定。Entegrata的新产品旨在为律所知识提供单一事实来源，可置于Harvey、Legora、CoCounsel及未来AI应用之下，让律所在不丢失上下文、专业知识或数据控制权的情况下切换模型。经过两年密集实验，律所正将注意力转向技术底层，行业进入新阶段，数据就绪、治理和软件开发能力将与选择正确AI工具同等重要，市场将大幅转向定制开发和更多软件工程。许多领先律所正探索竞争优势是否来自构建专有工作流、产品和客户解决方案，而非部署与同行相同的AI平台。Entegrata的答案是提供Baldwin所说的“管道层”，使律所专注于构建产品和解决方案，而非花费数月组装数据基础设施，从而加速AI计划并保持对成本、治理和模型选择的控制。模型路由将日益重要，律所根据成本、能力和风险将任务导向不同AI模型。
news.bodyHtml:
Entegrata has hired Andrew Baker as chief AI & data strategy officer, bringing on board one of the legal sector’s most experienced AI practitioners as it expands its ambitions beyond just data infrastructure and into AI enablement.

Baker joins from Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, where he served as director of applied AI and built a team of around 20 specialists focused on the firm’s AI and innovation strategy. During his time at the Am Law 10 firm, Baker helped drive the adoption of leading generative AI platforms including Harvey and DeepJudge and gained firsthand experience of the opportunities and limitations firms face as they scale AI across the enterprise.

Advertisement

Baker’s roles over the years include global director for legal product and technology at Seyfarth Shaw, director of legal transformation at Janders Dean, VP and global head of services at LexPredict, and a senior director at HBR.

This latest appointment coincides with Entegrata’s plans to launch a new AI enablement layer built on top of its existing data lakehouse platform. Rather than creating another legal AI application, the company says its focus is on helping firms establish the data foundations required to support multiple AI tools, models and internally developed applications.

Advertisement

Speaking to Legal IT Insider, Entegrata founder and chief executive Tom Baldwin said the market’s biggest challenge is no longer a shortage of AI tools.

“Firms don’t need another AI tool,” he said. “It is the layer beneath all these tools that gives firms more content, context, cost control and choice. Firms want more freedom to pick different models and not be locked into any one vendor as the market changes.”

According to Baldwin, law firms are increasingly concerned about preserving institutional knowledge and maintaining flexibility as AI models evolve rapidly. Entegrata’s new offering is designed to provide a single source of truth for firm knowledge that can sit underneath platforms such as Harvey, Legora, CoCounsel and future AI applications, allowing firms to switch between models without losing context, expertise or control over their data.

For Baker, the move reflects a broader shift taking place across the legal sector. After two years of intense experimentation with generative AI, firms are now turning their attention to what sits underneath the technology.

Baker said. “The question is how do you begin to capitalise on what’s happening across different platforms and bring it together in the right way.”

He argues that the industry is entering a new phase where data readiness, governance and software development capability will become just as important as selecting the right AI tools.

“We’re expecting to see a big swing toward custom development and much more software engineering in the market,” Baker said. “Regardless of how that happens, you need the right kind of data layer below that to support more creative uses of generative AI.”

That view reflects a growing trend among leading firms, many of which are now exploring whether competitive advantage will come not from deploying the same AI platforms as their peers, but from building proprietary workflows, products and client-facing solutions on top of them.

While legal AI vendors continue to compete aggressively, firms are increasingly aware that today’s leading products may not be tomorrow’s winners.

Baker says: “The economics of building and supporting custom software development have changed dramatically,” he said. “Every firm is looking for an experience beyond the four corners of Harvey, beyond the four corners of Legora. Right now there is a bit of a sea of sameness.”

Firms are looking to create differentiated experiences, whether for internal knowledge delivery, client service, pricing innovation or entirely new product offerings. But doing so requires access to well-governed, structured and unstructured data that can be reused consistently across multiple AI systems.

Entegrata’s answer is to provide what Entegrata’s founder Tom Baldwin describes as the “plumbing layer”, enabling firms to focus on building products and solutions rather than spending months assembling data infrastructure. The company says this will help firms accelerate AI initiatives while retaining greater control over costs, governance and model selection.

One area likely to become increasingly important is model routing, where firms direct different tasks to different AI models according to cost, capability and risk. Baker argues that making those decisions effectively requires deep contextual understanding of firm data and workflows.

Looking ahead, Baker’s role will encompass product architecture, advising firms on AI team development and supporting broader data strategy initiatives. More fundamentally, however, his appointment signals Entegrata’s belief that the next phase of legal AI will be won not by the firms with the most tools, but by those with the strongest foundations.

news.titleEn: Microsoft’s Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs team selects Harvey
news.titleZh: 微软企业、外部及法律事务团队选择Harvey
news.summaryZh: 微软企业、外部及法律事务（CELA）团队已选择Harvey，用于其法律与合规业务，这对这家法律AI公司而言是一次重大胜利。Harvey已于今年集成至Microsoft 365 Copilot和Cowork，此次经遴选流程后获选，将支持广泛的工作流程。微软产品是律师工作的基础，今日公告意味着微软法律团队将使用Harvey平台，Harvey员工也将使用更多微软产品以支持全球增长，这是双方持续关系的下一步。与Harvey的合作是更广泛努力的一部分，旨在将AI益处引入运营，该协作将帮助团队更高效工作，专注于最重要、高影响力的复杂工作。Harvey今年早些时候宣布通过365集成扩展与微软的合作伙伴关系，并表示将在内部扩大使用Microsoft 365和Microsoft 365 Copilot。Harvey最接近的竞争对手Legora构建于Microsoft Azure之上，并大力投资微软集成，包括SharePoint、Microsoft 365集成及Microsoft Word插件。当Legal IT Insider询问是否存在遴选流程时，Harvey首席运营官凯蒂·伯克表示，任何Harvey部署都会有遴选流程，同时该公告建立在与微软更广泛协作的基础上，长期关系和深度技术集成奠定了坚实基础，而CELA决定使用Harvey反映了其对该平台的自身评估及其如何支持法律与合规团队。此次选择正值大型科技公司构建自有垂直工具和产品之际，风险在于微软最终可能向Harvey学习并构建自己的法律AI能力。但毫无疑问，这是一次重大胜利，使Harvey进入微软外部和内部运营体系。
news.bodyHtml:
Microsoft’s Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) team has selected Harvey for use across its legal and compliance operations, in a significant win for the legal AI company.

We’re told that Harvey, which is already integrated within Microsoft 365 Copilot and Cowork as of this year, was chosen following a selection process and will be used to support a broad range of workflows.

Advertisement

Winston Weinberg, co-founder and CEO of Harvey, said: “Microsoft’s products are foundational to the work lawyers do, so we have always been grateful for our deep relationship with their team. Today’s announcement that Microsoft’s legal team will use Harvey’s platform and that Harvey associates will use more Microsoft products to support our global growth represents the next step in our ongoing relationship with their team, and we look forward to building on it.”

Of the announcement, Antony Cook, corporate vice president and deputy general counsel at Microsoft, added that its work with Harvey is part of a broader efforts to bring the benefits of AI into its operations, observing that “this collaboration will help our teams work more efficiently and focus on the complex, high-impact work that matters most.”

Advertisement

Harvey announced earlier this year that it was extending its partnership with Microsoft with the 365 integration. It also said that Harvey will expand its use of Microsoft 365 and Microsoft 365 Copilot internally.

Harvey’s closest rival Legora is build on Microsoft Azure and has invested heavily in its Microsoft integrations, including SharePoint and Microsoft 365 integrations and a Microsoft Word add-in.

Asked by Legal IT Insider if there was a selection process, Katie Burke, chief operating officer of Harvey said: “There was a selection process, as you would expect with any deployment of Harvey. At the same time, this announcement builds on our broader collaboration with Microsoft. Our longstanding relationship and deep technical integrations created a strong foundation, while CELA’s decision to use Harvey reflects its own evaluation of the platform and how it can support its legal and compliance teams.”

The selection comes as large tech companies building their own vertical tools and products, with the risk, one would guess, that Microsoft will ultimately learn from Harvey and build its own legal AI capability. There can be no doubt, however, that it is a big win that puts Harvey within the body of Microsoft’s external and internal operations.

news.titleEn: Entegrata Hires Simpson Thacher AI Leader Andrew Baker To Head New AI Enablement Product Line
news.titleZh: Entegrata聘请盛信律师事务所AI负责人Andrew Baker，领导新AI赋能产品线
news.summaryZh: 法律数据公司Entegrata已聘请Andrew Baker担任其首任首席AI与数据战略官。Baker此前在Simpson Thacher & Bartlett领导应用AI与数据科学超过五年。他将负责开发一条专注于为律所提供AI赋能的新产品线。Entegrata的数据湖仓平台帮助律所将孤立数据整合为单一可信来源。签约前10家客户用了三年，而签约最近10家客户用了六个月，近期签约客户包括Cleary Gottlieb、Mayer Brown、Wilson Sonsini、Mintz、Kilpatrick Townsend和Winston Taylor等全球大型律所。Entegrata于2023年由Baldwin创立，去年获得450万美元种子轮融资。Baker的职责包括：架构新的AI赋能产品线；向正在建立应用AI团队的律所提供其经验作为服务；接管Baldwin此前领导的数据战略咨询工作。Baldwin将产品愿景概括为四个C：内容、上下文、成本控制和选择。公司正在构建法律数据本体论，基于已包含约5000个字段的模式，旨在捕捉律所内部关系网络，提供360度视图。公司不构建新的AI模型或产品，而是为现有工具（如Harvey、Legora和Deep Judge）提供更丰富的上下文和内容，并保留律所更换工具的灵活性。数据层已成为律所推进生成式AI部署的瓶颈，律所面临的挑战在于数据宽度，需要整合20到30个系统的数据。领先的法律AI平台虽有帮助，但存在硬边界，而Entegrata能更好地为分析、综合和创新准备数据结构。公司正为一家拥有2000名律师的律所构建AI工具，供三名高层领导使用，以回答战略方向性问题。Baker将于8月23日至27日在纳什维尔举行的ILTACON上与企业会面。
news.bodyHtml:
The legal data company Entegrata, whose data lakehouse platform helps law firms consolidate siloed data into a single source of truth, has hired Andrew Baker, who for more than five years led applied AI and data science at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, as its first chief AI and data strategy officer, where he will lead development of a new product line focused on AI enablement for law firms.

The appointment, announced today, comes at a time of rapid growth for the company, founder and CEO Tom Baldwin told me during an interview this week with him and Baker. “It took us three years to sign our first 10 customers,” Baldwin said. “It’s taken six months to sign the last 10.”

Among those recent signings are some of the largest firms in the world, including Cleary Gottlieb, Mayer Brown, Wilson Sonsini, Mintz, Kilpatrick Townsend, and Winston Taylor.

As I reported last year when Entegrata raised $4.5 million in seed funding, Baldwin — the former CIO or CKO at firms including Cadwalader, Reed Smith and Sheppard Mullin — founded the company in 2023 to address the fragmentation of law firm data across dozens of business systems, consolidating it within a purpose-built data lakehouse.

With Baker’s hire, the company is extending that mission from business intelligence into the data layer that underpins firm-wide AI.

A Reunion Two Decades in the Making

For Baldwin and Baker, the hire is something of a reunion. The two worked together at Reed Smith in the early 2010s, when Baldwin was running pricing, legal project management and other functions there and, as he tells it, went looking for “a unicorn in the form of a JD black belt” in process improvement, and found Baker’s profile on LinkedIn.

Baker later returned to Seyfarth Shaw, where he had previously worked, to help launch that firm’s innovation program. There, he founded what Entegrata says was the industry’s first legal technology innovations office and pioneered the legal solutions architect role.

He went on to co-lead the legal transformation and innovation practice at HBR Consulting (now Harbor) before joining Simpson Thacher, where he has spent the last five-and-a-half years advancing the firm’s use of data science and emerging technology. Along the way, he earned a master’s degree in applied data science.

“I’ve been hunkered down at this intersection of law, data, tech and strategy for quite some time,” Baker said.

So why leave what he called “probably one of the cooler jobs in a law firm that you could ask for” to join a vendor?

“It’s really about the opportunity to build something big and lasting in the industry,” Baker said. “I spent a lot of time in pretty much every vendor tool that’s out there, a lot of time working with teams to build custom solutions within our firm, and I feel like I have a pretty clear understanding of where the hard edges are on each of those. And we keep running into the same challenges over and over.”

Solving those challenges from inside a single firm is daunting, he said, but it is a different ballgame from the outside.

“When you think about where you want to put your time and energy if you’re doing technical work in a law firm, it’s not on the plumbing and the data ecosystem,” he said. “It’s building the cool, exciting, creative things.”

What ‘AI Enablement’ Means

In his new role, Baker will own Entegrata’s AI roadmap across engineering, product and customer experience, with his central focus on a new product line the company describes as AI enablement.

To date, Baker said, Entegrata has been adjacent to the AI story — its data could be put to creative use, but AI was one step removed from the core product.

“This next chapter in the book brings Entegrata straight to the coalface on everything AI-related,” he said. Whatever firms are pursuing — model routing, autonomous agents, custom development — “none of those can be executed very well without the right kind of content or context to make that happen.”

The goal, he said, is “providing a framework and layer to help people truly do that, and moving beyond theory into pragmatism.”

Baldwin says the product vision centers around what he calls the four Cs: content, context, cost control and choice. The idea is to give AI tools richer content and context drawn from across a firm’s systems, provide firms observability into AI costs, and preserve their ability to swap in new models and tools as the market shifts, without starting over each time.

“To be clear, we are not building yet another AI model or product,” Baldwin said. “We’re enabling deeper context and giving more content to the existing tools firms have” — he named Harvey, Legora and Deep Judge as examples — “and creating that downstream off-ramp to different tools as they become available.”

Central to the effort is an ontology for legal data that the company is currently building, layered on top of a schema that Baldwin said already contains some 5,000 fields. (When I wrote about the company last year, that schema had 3,500 fields.)

The ontology is designed to capture the full web of relationships within a firm — the “360-degree view” that connects a document to a timekeeper, the timekeeper to a matter, the matter to a client, and outward to industry, jurisdiction, judge and opposing counsel.

“You lose all of that context the minute you take a document out of the DMS and manually upload it into an AI tool,” Baldwin said. “We bring that all back and throw an ontology on top of it.”

He drew a comparison to the much-discussed partnership between Kirkland & Ellis and Palantir. “Long term, this is going to be an offering that’s going to feel very Kirkland-esque in terms of the capabilities, but at a fraction of the time and cost that it’ll take to implement something like Palantir.”

The Data Layer as the Bottleneck

Both men agree that the data layer has become the choke point for firms trying to move beyond their first wave of generative AI deployments.

In the early rush, Baldwin said, firms were under enormous pressure simply to get AI up and running, in part so they could say they were using it.

Now that firms have had time to settle into it, he said, the next stage of maturity is “moving beyond the disconnected download-documents-out-of-the-DM, upload-them-manually-into-an-AI-tool” workflow toward AI that can run on the firm’s full data estate. He said the last six firms Entegrata signed all characterized their moves as being about AI readiness and enablement.

The challenge for law firms, Baldwin said, differs from other industries. “The challenge isn’t in depth and speed. We don’t have petabytes of real-time streaming from one or two ERP sources. Our challenge is width. It’s stitching together data from 20 or 30 systems.”

Baker made a similar point about leading practice-of-law AI platforms. “The Harveys and Legoras of the world are fantastic for helping firms move quickly,” he said. “The challenge you run into is that they all have hard edges.” Firms whose practices do not fit neatly within those boundaries — or that want to rethink a practice’s economics or go-to-market approach — quickly find themselves breaking through them.

“Right now, there are a number of solutions that are focused on retrieval, and some of them do a really good job,” Baker said. “But that next hop over — how do we analyze, synthesize and create anew — it’s hard to get the data in the right structure for that. And we think we can do that in a way that others really can’t.”

As an example of what this can mean for customers, Baldwin said that for one of its largest customers, a 2,000-lawyer firm, Entegrata is building an AI tool for just three people in firm leadership designed to answer the questions that, as he put it, the people who sign everyone’s checks care about.

“It’s the opposite of, ‘I’m a third-year associate grinding through this asset purchase agreement draft,'” he said. “It’s, ‘I’m the chair of the firm and I want to know directionally where the firm’s headed.'”

Baker’s Remit

Baldwin described Baker’s mandate as spanning three buckets. First and foremost is architecting the new AI enablement product line. Second, with law firms increasingly hiring for net-new data and AI leadership roles, Baker will offer his playbook as a service to firms just standing up applied AI functions — drawing on his consulting experience at Harbor in making what works at one firm portable to many. Third, he will take over much of the data strategy engagement work that Baldwin has been leading himself.

“Andrew has lived this problem from inside one of the most prestigious firms on the planet, so he knows what it takes to make AI dependable across a real practice,” Baldwin said.

“His mandate is simple: prepare firm data and context so any model or tool it chooses actually delivers. That is the layer most of the industry is still missing, and it is what Andrew will build for our clients.”

Baker will be at ILTACON in Nashville, Aug. 23-27, where he hopes to meet with firms to discuss the intersection of data strategy and AI.

Crawl, Walk, Run: A Practical Way to Deploy Claude Enterprise in a Law Firm

By

Steven Combs

posted

07-23-2026 15:02

Like

A phased rollout should not postpone security. It should match capability, data access and monitoring to what the firm is prepared to govern.

Law firms tend to talk about enterprise AI rollouts as a yes or no decision. Either the tool is approved for everyone, or it stays blocked until every question has been answered.

Neither option works particularly well.

Waiting for a perfect control environment can stall a useful platform for months. Moving too quickly creates the opposite problem. The firm launches broadly, then learns that the product can reach more data, take more actions or produce less useful telemetry than anyone expected.

I think there is a better middle ground: crawl, walk, run.

Not as a project slogan. Most of us have seen enough of those. I mean three real control boundaries, where each phase defines who can use Claude, what it can do, what information it can reach and what evidence the security team will receive. Access expands only after the next set of controls is working.

Start with the boundary that matters most

Before getting into connectors, agents or prompt injection, ask a more basic question: Which Claude account are people using?

A firm can purchase Claude Enterprise and still have lawyers using personal Claude Pro accounts through a browser or desktop application. The enterprise agreement does not protect work performed outside the enterprise organization. That sounds obvious when written out, but it is easy to miss in practice.

This became more important when Anthropic's updated consumer Privacy Policy took effect on July 8, 2026. Anthropic says the policy applies to consumer services and does not govern content processed for Enterprise customers. The consumer policy also describes circumstances in which personal data may be shared with government authorities or law enforcement when Anthropic has a good faith belief that disclosure is reasonably necessary.

I wrote about the law firm confidentiality implications in The AI Confidentiality Risk in Your Firm's Claude Pro Account . The short version is that approving the vendor is not enough. The firm also needs to enforce the approved account and service tier.

Claude Enterprise does not make every confidentiality concern disappear. It puts the firm's use under a different commercial and administrative boundary. Governance still has to keep the work inside that boundary.

The first gate should be simple: Can the firm demonstrate that client work occurs only inside its approved Enterprise organization, or has it merely published a policy saying that it should?

Crawl: create a minimum viable secure pilot

The crawl phase needs to be useful. If the pilot is so restricted that nobody can perform real work, it will not teach the firm much. But it should still be narrow enough that a mistake has a limited consequence.

Start with named users, named use cases and named data exclusions. Avoid vague descriptions such as “general productivity.” What work is the group testing? What information may they use? What remains off limits?

A reasonable crawl phase will usually include:

Enterprise identities enforced through the firm's identity provider, with SSO and MFA.

A small, supervised pilot group using role based access instead of organization wide enablement.

Firm managed endpoints, standard user privileges, encryption, endpoint protection and managed application settings.

Web search, browser control, computer use, connectors, plugins and MCP servers disabled unless a specific pilot use case requires one of them.

File access limited to approved working folders, with high-sensitivity repositories kept out of scope unless their use has been expressly authorized.

An acceptable use rule that tells people what data is permitted, what is prohibited, when human review is required and where questions should go.

Chat feedback disabled if the firm does not want a reported conversation retained and potentially used for model improvement.

The pilot is not safer merely because it is small. It is safer because the firm knows who is participating, what Claude can reach and which capabilities have been withheld. There is a difference.

Training matters here too, although not the generic “use AI responsibly” presentation everyone forgets by the following week. Users need to understand the boundaries of this specific pilot and what to do when Claude requests access or takes an action they did not expect.

Walk: add enforcement and visibility before expanding

Suppose the pilot goes well. People find useful workflows, demand grows and other practice groups want access. This is usually where the pressure to move faster shows up.

The next question should not be how quickly the firm can assign more licenses. It should be whether the firm can govern a larger population that will receive less direct supervision.

The walk phase should add:

SCIM provisioning and deprovisioning so access follows the firm's identity lifecycle.

Tenant Restrictions, or comparable network enforcement, to reduce the use of personal Claude accounts from managed networks.

Group based roles that separate ordinary chat, Cowork, connectors, plugins and administrative functions.

OpenTelemetry routing from Cowork into the firm's monitoring environment.

Data loss prevention and endpoint controls appropriate to the information the group is allowed to use.

A connector review that covers authorization scopes, read and write capabilities, downstream data handling and revocation.

An incident process that identifies who can suspend access, preserve the evidence that is available, assess affected matters and involve legal or client stakeholders.

Here is the monitoring issue that can catch a team off guard. As of July 2026, Anthropic says Cowork activity is not captured in its audit logs, Compliance API or data exports. Team and Enterprise organizations can stream Cowork events through OpenTelemetry, but that is a separate implementation step.

In other words, buying Enterprise does not cause Cowork activity to appear in the firm's SIEM. Someone still has to configure the telemetry, route it, test it and decide which events matter. That last part takes some judgment. Collecting everything without a plan usually creates noise, not visibility.

If the firm is not ready to monitor Cowork, it can keep Cowork limited while expanding lower risk chat use. The product's capabilities do not all have to move at the same speed. I would argue that they should not.

Run: scale through a repeatable approval model

Run does not mean unrestricted. It means the firm has stopped treating every new AI request as a one time exception.

At this point there should be a repeatable way to introduce new users, data sources and agent capabilities without redesigning governance each time. That operating model will look different by firm, but it should cover a few basics:

Capability profiles by role or practice group instead of one global configuration.

A documented approval path for connectors, plugins, MCP servers, browser use, computer use and scheduled or remote tasks.

Least privilege connector permissions, with additional review and human approval for write actions or actions that create an external consequence.

Testing for prompt injection, unintended tool use, data leakage and failure modes in the firm's real workflows.

Security analytics that combine identity, endpoint, network, data and Cowork telemetry.

Measures for adoption, quality, exceptions, incidents and control effectiveness, not just licenses assigned or prompts submitted.

A recurring review of Anthropic's product changes, privacy terms, model specific retention requirements and new administrative controls.

This last item is easy to underestimate. Claude is changing quickly. A control review performed six months ago may no longer describe what users can do today. New capabilities can alter the data flow without anyone changing the original deployment plan.

The real gotcha in crawl, walk, run

A phased plan can create false comfort when deferred controls begin to look like completed controls. They are not the same thing.

A faster launch may be reasonable. Sometimes it is the right decision. But the firm needs to write down what it is accepting, assign an owner and tie the missing control to a clear gate before expansion.

I find it more useful to organize those decisions around four questions that apply to almost any enterprise AI deployment: Who can get in? What can the system do? What information can it reach? What evidence will the firm receive? In other words: Identity, Capability, Data and Visibility.

Control gate

Pilot boundary

Evidence before expansion

Identity

Access is limited to a named Enterprise pilot group. Personal consumer accounts may still bypass firm controls if tenant enforcement is not in place.

Identity lifecycle, tenant restrictions and detection of access outside the approved organization have been tested.

Capability

Connectors, plugins, browser control, computer use and other higher consequence actions remain disabled unless the pilot requires them.

Each new capability has an owner, defined permissions, a human approval model and a tested method for disabling it.

Data

High-sensitivity repositories remain outside the pilot boundary, which means some intended workflows cannot yet be tested.

Approved data classes, access paths, DLP controls and use case authorization have been defined and validated.

Visibility

Investigation may depend on supervision and endpoint evidence until Cowork telemetry is routed into the firm's monitoring environment.

OpenTelemetry has been validated end to end, useful alerts have been tested and response ownership is clear.

The point is not to create another spreadsheet that nobody opens. It is to keep the deferred risk visible. It should appear in the risk register, the rollout plan and the decision to enter the next phase.

If it disappears into a future state diagram, people will eventually forget that the risk was accepted rather than resolved. I have seen that happen more than once.

A better question for the steering committee

Is Claude Enterprise secure?

That question is too broad to be very useful. Security depends on the account, enabled capabilities, accessible data, endpoint, identity controls, monitoring and what the firm does when the tool behaves in an unexpected way.

I would ask this instead:

What can this group of users do with Claude today, what information can it reach, what evidence will we receive and what must be true before we allow more?

Crawl, walk, run works when each phase is a control boundary, not a date on a project plan. Start with the commercial boundary. Constrain capability and data. Add visibility before scale. Then require evidence before each expansion.

That approach lets a firm learn quickly without pretending that speed and governance are opposites.

news.titleEn: On a 100-document responsiveness test, model price did not predict accuracy
news.titleZh: 在100份文档响应性测试中，模型价格未能预测准确性
news.summaryZh: 一项新的九模型法律AI基准测试显示，价格最高的模型在准确性上排名倒数第二，而价格低68倍的模型在F1分数上仅落后领先者0.075。该结果来自DecoverAI于2026年6月发布的工作论文，这家位于加州圣马特奥的电子发现供应商指出，买家为最贵选项支付了“品牌溢价而非性能溢价”。Decover研究论文2026-02测试了来自阿里巴巴、DeepSeek、MiniMax、月之暗面和Anthropic的九个大语言模型，使用固定100份文档的响应性分类任务，其中27份为响应性文档，73份为非响应性文档。供应商对每个模型运行其两步生产流程，仅更换底层模型，并按2026年6月价格计量实际token使用成本。九个模型中八个的F1分数落在0.76至0.87的11分区间内，每文档成本从0.0012美元到0.0813美元不等。Qwen 3.6 Plus以0.868的F1分数领先，每文档成本0.0205美元。Anthropic的claude-opus-4-8是测试中最贵的模型，每文档成本0.0813美元，得分0.760，为倒数第二，低于成本低30倍的模型。DeepSeek V4 Pro的F1分数为0.815，精确率和召回率均为0.815，每文档成本0.0027美元，被论文指定为价值操作点。按10万份文档计算，价值选项（270美元）与最贵模型（8130美元）之间的差距为7860美元，相当于约52小时合同律师质量控制时间（每小时150美元）。审查架构而非模型能力决定了准确性上限，但其单一管道设计无法证明这一解释。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: A vendor benchmark landed in June with a finding built to unsettle procurement assumptions: the highest-cost model among nine tested for legal document classification finished second to last, while models costing a fraction of its price clustered near the top. DecoverAI’s working paper argues that review architecture, not model capability, sets the accuracy ceiling, an interpretation its single-pipeline design cannot prove, and two other provider studies offer related though limited support.

For cybersecurity, data privacy, regulatory compliance and eDiscovery professionals, the stakes are concrete. Inadvertent production of privileged material can implicate Federal Rule of Evidence 502, and amended Rule 26(f)(3)(D), effective Dec. 1, 2025, requires early views and proposals on privilege claim timing and method, which means model choice and validation evidence may surface in meet-and-confer sessions. The paper also leaves questions open, from its 100-document single-run sample and unpublished methodological details to the governance implications of routing privileged material to models from Chinese developers.

Watch for privilege-specific benchmarks, court scrutiny of AI-assisted privilege logs, and controlled validation runs to become standard requests in the year ahead.

Industry News – eDiscovery Beat

On a 100-document responsiveness test, model price did not predict accuracy

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

The highest-cost model tested in a new nine-model legal AI benchmark finished next to last. The cheapest one, priced 68 times lower, landed 0.075 behind the leader on the study’s F1 score.

Those results anchor a working paper published in June 2026 by DecoverAI, a San Mateo, California-based eDiscovery vendor, and they carry an uncomfortable message for legal teams that equate model price with review quality. On this test, the paper concludes, buyers of the top-priced option were “paying a premium for brand rather than performance.”

What the benchmark measured

Decover Research Working Paper 2026-02 tested nine large language models from Alibaba, DeepSeek, MiniMax, Moonshot AI and Anthropic on a fixed 100-document responsiveness classification task with a gold-labeled answer key of 27 responsive and 73 nonresponsive documents. The vendor ran its own two-step production pipeline for every model, changing only the model underneath, and metered cost from actual token usage at June 2026 prices.

Eight of the nine models landed inside an 11-point F1 band, from 0.76 to 0.87, across a per-document cost spread from $0.0012 to $0.0813. Qwen 3.6 Plus posted the best F1 score, 0.868, at $0.0205 per document. Anthropic’s claude-opus-4-8, the highest-cost model tested at $0.0813 per document, scored 0.760, second-lowest in the study and below models costing 30 times less. DeepSeek V4 Pro delivered an F1 of 0.815, with precision and recall balanced at 0.815 each, for $0.0027 per document, which the paper designates its value operating point.

At 100,000 documents, the paper calculates, the spread between that value option ($270) and the highest-cost model ($8,130) is $7,860, which it equates to roughly 52 hours of contract attorney quality control at $150 per hour.

news.titleEn: Beyond the billable hour: How Firm AI is transforming timekeeping and billing into a strategic advantage
news.titleZh: 超越计费工时：Firm AI如何将时间记录与计费转化为战略优势
news.summaryZh: 收入流失是律师事务所面临的重大难题，其最常见原因在于工作完成与时间记录之间的间隙。例如，合伙人计划周五记录工时，但因疲劳而推迟，最终难以准确回忆工作内容，导致时间被核减、发票因不准确被拒付、收款延迟，并引发客户计费准则违规和折扣。即使费率是每小时300美元，最终可能只能收回225美元。Firm AI作为专为法律行业设计的解决方案，能够自动记录律师的工作，无需律师手动录入时间条目。其关键在于理解外部法律顾问准则（OCGs）以及阶段、任务和活动（PTA）编码要求，将每项活动进行逻辑分组，并根据律所自身规则，以合规且以客户为中心的方式预先撰写描述和添加标签。律师只需审核每条记录并在必要时进行修正。通过这种方式，Firm AI帮助律所减少收入流失，提高计费准确性和收款效率，将时间记录和计费从繁琐事务转变为战略优势。
news.bodyHtml:
Revenue leakage is a huge problem for law firms. What’s the most common cause, and how can Firm AI help them address it?

KEN HOUSEMAN

Most revenue leakage happens in the moments between doing the work and recording the work. For example, a partner might plan to do their timecard on a Friday, then put it off because they’re tired. By the time they get around to it, they have trouble recalling everything they did. So time is written off, invoices are rejected for inaccuracy, and collections are delayed, which results in client billing guideline violations and discounts.

While your rate may be $300 per hour, at the end you may only collect $225 of that.

But with Firm AI built specifically for legal, lawyers won’t even have to record time entries, because their firm will have already recorded their efforts.

Here’s the key: Firm AI understands outside-council guidelines (OCGs) and what’s expected of phase, task, and activity (PTA) coding. It will take each activity, group it logically, then pre-narrate and pre-tag it in a compliant, client-centric manner based on the firm’s unique rules. So all each lawyer has to do is review each entry and correct it if needed.

news.titleEn: AI Agents A Top 2026 Cybersecurity Threat
news.titleZh: AI代理成为2026年首要网络安全威胁
news.summaryZh: 网络安全公司Forrester近日发布年度报告《2026年首要网络安全威胁》，列出了“组织需要规划的最关键风险”。报告基于近期趋势和观察，预测了组织在2026年将面临的首要威胁。2026年预计的五大威胁包括：上述威胁源于AI模型的广泛可及性，以及AI工具和AI代理能够摄取大量数据、从中学习并以空前的速度和规模运行。这些能力使得日益复杂的网络安全攻击得以自动化和扩展，导致影子AI超出组织的治理和可见范围，并加剧供应链风险。这些挑战共同引发重大合规问题，降低组织控制力，并增加整体网络安全暴露。报告概述了组织在2026年面临的最重大风险，包括AI带来的日益严峻的挑战，并强调实施稳健的AI治理计划作为关键战略优先事项的重要性。

news.titleEn: AI In the Dugout: MLB’s AI Crackdown Shows Why Guardrails Matter
news.titleZh: AI进入棒球休息区：MLB对AI的打击表明护栏为何重要
news.summaryZh: 美国职业棒球大联盟（MLB）限制休息区iPad功能，此举提醒人们AI治理已无处不在，甚至出现在职业棒球比赛现场。据报道，MLB在担心球队使用AI工具实时支持换人、投球呼叫等比赛策略决策后，禁用了自定义平板标签页。联盟的担忧似乎并非针对技术本身，而是关于在直播比赛中保持允许的数据访问与自动化战略建议之间的界限。体育一直随着分析、视频、球探系统和表现数据而发展，但AI改变了决策支持的速度、规模和性质。帮助球队在赛前查看视频的工具与实时推荐下一投球的工具感觉截然不同。一旦AI开始影响实时决策，联盟必须回答更棘手的问题：哪些工具是公平的？可接受的自动化水平是多少？谁对决策负责？当技术比规则手册发展更快时，规则如何跟上？这一教训远远超出棒球领域。采用AI的组织需要明确的使用场景边界，而不仅仅是广泛允许“使用技术”。MLB的打击表明治理必须具体：系统可以访问什么、何时可以使用、谁可以依赖它、哪些决策必须由人类主导。无论是在休息区、交易台、医院还是招聘场合，同样的原则适用：AI可能很强大，但如果没有周到的护栏，它可能迅速从有用的工具变成改变规则的力量。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Major League Baseball’s (MLB) move to restrict dugout iPad functionality is a reminder that AI governance is showing up everywhere, including in the middle of professional baseball games. According to reports, MLB disabled custom tablet tabs after concerns that teams were using AI-powered tools to support real-time decisions on substitutions, pitch calling, and other in-game strategy. The league’s concern appears less about technology generally, and more about preserving the line between permitted data access and automated strategic recommendations during live competition. That line matters. Sports have always evolved with analytics, video, scouting systems, and performance data, but AI changes the speed, scale, and nature of decision support. A tool that helps a team review video before a game feels very different from one that recommends the next pitch in real time. Once AI starts influencing live decisions, leagues must answer harder questions: What tools are fair? What level of automation is acceptable? Who is accountable for the decision? And how can rules keep pace when technology moves faster than the rulebook? The takeaway extends well beyond baseball. Organizations adopting AI need clear use-case boundaries, not just broad permission to “use technology.” MLB’s crackdown shows why governance must be specific: what the system can access, when it can be used, who can rely on it, and which decisions must remain human-led. Whether the setting is a dugout, a trading desk, a hospital, or a hiring situation, the same principle applies: AI may be powerful, but without thoughtful guardrails, it can quickly move from helpful tool to rule-changing force. news.titleEn: AI Legislation- 2026 Legislative Wrap-Up
news.titleZh: 人工智能立法——2026年立法总结
news.summaryZh: 随着2026年各州立法会议接近尾声，人工智能监管已从新兴领域转变为主流合规义务。在缺乏联邦综合性法规的情况下，各州监管理念差异显著：部分州颁布广泛的消费者透明度框架，要求将人工智能用于重大决策时进行披露；部分州聚焦医疗覆盖决定或就业筛选工具；少数州采用基于风险框架，对高风险应用施加更严格要求。这导致合规义务因司法管辖区、行业和用例而异，一家企业可能同时面临三套不同监管制度。Epstein Becker Green持续追踪各州已颁布的人工智能立法，将其分为综合、医疗保健与生命科学、就业三大领域，并在Trending Issues页面提供交互式地图。2026年，综合性法规继续扩展，对各行各业施加透明度、披露、风险评估和问责要求，加州、科罗拉多州和犹他州最为活跃。一个显著趋势是针对生成式人工智能和大语言模型的披露要求，触发条件为部署超过特定规模阈值。医疗保健仍是监管最活跃领域，立法重点集中在事先授权，多个州强化或澄清禁止仅以人工智能作为拒绝承保依据，要求人工审查并保留足以支持上诉的文件。第二波立法针对人工智能生成的患者通信，要求披露并确保患者能获得人工替代方案，加州、科罗拉多州和纽约州较活跃，此前未立法的小州也开始跟进。就业领域监管显著成熟，第一代披露要求已基本完成立法，2026年会期出现第二代要求：审计、报告和积极反歧视义务，要求雇主不仅披露人工智能使用，还要证。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! As 2026 state legislative sessions draw to a close, one theme dominates the policy landscape: artificial intelligence (AI) regulation is no longer an emerging frontier but a mainstream compliance obligation. Epstein Becker Green continuously tracks enacted state AI legislation, organizing laws across three policy domains (Omnibus (affecting every sector), Health Care and Life Sciences, and Employment) and makes its interactive map freely available on the firm’s Trending Issues page. With 2026 legislative sessions now closing across the country, this wrap-up provides a comprehensive overview of what was enacted, what patterns emerged, and what compliance obligations businesses should prioritize heading into the second half of the year. In the continued absence of a comprehensive federal AI statute, states have filled the void with laws reflecting sharply different regulatory philosophies. Some states have enacted broad consumer-facing transparency frameworks that require disclosure whenever AI is used in a consequential decision. Others have taken a targeted approach, focusing narrowly on health care coverage determinations or employment screening tools. A few states have adopted risk-based frameworks that impose more demanding obligations on higher-risk applications while permitting lighter-touch treatment of lower-stakes deployments. The result is a patchwork of compliance obligations that vary by jurisdiction, sector, and use case. A business that uses AI to screen job applicants, generate patient-facing communications, and make automated coverage determinations may face three distinct regulatory regimes simultaneously—potentially from the same state. This complexity is precisely what the Epstein Becker Green AI Enacted Bills Map is designed to navigate. Omnibus AI statutes continued to expand in 2026. These laws impose broad transparency, disclosure, risk assessment, and accountability requirements that apply across industries and use cases, often requiring businesses to notify consumers when AI or automated decision-making affects them, to document training data and model behavior, and to establish liability frameworks for AI-caused harm. California, Colorado, and Utah remain the most active states in this space, with new legislation refining and extending the frameworks those states established in prior sessions. A notable trend in 2026 is the emergence of requirements specifically targeting generative AI and large language models. Several states enacted or proposed disclosure requirements that are triggered by the deployment of generative AI systems above specified scale thresholds, a category of obligation that did not exist in most state frameworks even two years ago. Businesses using generative AI in consumer-facing applications should evaluate whether these new requirements apply to their deployments. Health care remained the most active arena for AI regulation in 2026, driven by persistent concerns that automated systems are influencing clinical and coverage decisions without adequate human oversight. The primary focus of enacted legislation in this category was prior authorization: multiple states strengthened or clarified prohibitions on AI serving as the sole basis for coverage denials, requiring human review of AI-assisted determinations and mandating documentation sufficient to support appeals. A second wave of health care AI legislation targeted AI-generated patient communications, requiring health care organizations to disclose when a communication was generated or substantially drafted by an AI system and to ensure that patients can access a human alternative. States active in this area include California, Colorado, and New York. Smaller states that had not previously enacted health care AI legislation began moving in this direction in 2026 as well, suggesting that the sector-specific frameworks pioneered by early-mover states are now being adopted more broadly. State regulation of AI in the employment context has matured significantly in 2026. The early generation of employment AI laws focused primarily on disclosure requirements—obligating employers to notify applicants and employees when automated decision-making tools were used in hiring or performance evaluation. That first wave is now largely enacted. The 2026 session has seen states move to a second generation of requirements: auditing, reporting, and affirmative anti-discrimination obligations that require employers not just to disclose AI use but to demonstrate that their AI systems do not produce discriminatory outcomes.

news.titleEn: Harvey Deepens Microsoft Relationship
news.titleZh: Harvey深化与微软的合作关系
news.summaryZh: Harvey通过向微软的企业、外部及法律事务（CELA）部门提供其法律AI平台，深化了与微软的合作；这家法律AI先驱企业则相应“扩大其在内部对Microsoft 365和Microsoft 365 Copilot的使用”。目前Copilot使用多个模型，已不再最初仅依赖OpenAI的ChatGPT大语言模型，现在还使用Anthropic的产品。值得注意的是，微软也在开发自己的“法律代理”，由前Robin AI团队成员组成。也就是说，CELA团队本可以使用许多“自有品牌”工具，但选择了Harvey。作为此次合作的一部分，CELA将使用Harvey AI平台支持其工作并提升团队运作方式。这反映出微软持续投资于应用AI以提高效率、简化工作流程并大规模实现高质量成果”。AL就几个方面询问了Harvey首席执行官Winston Weinberg，包括这一深化关系对他和公司意味着什么，以及这是如何发生的。微软CELA组织使用Harvey是双方长期关系中的重要一步，更广泛地表明全球领先法律团队正将AI作为其运作的核心部分。Harvey与微软多年来建立了牢固关系，此次公告反映了合作的下一篇章。与任何企业部署一样，CELA在决定使用Harvey之前也经过了全面评估。微软产品是律师工作的基础，Harvey一直感激与其团队的深厚关系。今天宣布微软法律团队将使用Harvey平台，且Harvey员工将使用更多微软产品以支持其全球增长，这代表着双方持续关系的下一步。我们很高兴扩大与Harvey的合作，作为我们将AI益处引入运营的更广泛努力的一部分。这一合作将帮助我们的团队更高效地工作，并专注于最重要的复杂、高影响力工作。
news.bodyText: Harvey has deepened its engagement with Microsoft, in this case via providing its legal AI platform to the tech giant’s Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) group; with the legal AI pioneer in turn ‘expanding its use of Microsoft 365 and Microsoft 365 Copilot internally’. At present Copilot uses multiple models, having moved beyond its initial reliance on OpenAI’s ChatGPT LLMs and now also uses Anthropic’s offerings. And it’s worth noting that Microsoft is also developing its own ‘Legal Agent’, staffed by former Robin AI team members. I.e. the CELA team possibly could have used a lot of their ‘own brand’ tools, but have chosen to use Harvey. The legal tech company said that ‘as part of this collaboration, CELA will use the Harvey AI platform to support its work and enhance how teams operate. This reflects Microsoft’s continued investment in applying AI to improve efficiency, streamline workflows, and enable high-quality outcomes at scale’. AL asked Winston Weinberg, CEO of Harvey, about a couple of aspects, including what the deepening relationship meant to him and the company; and also how this has come about: ‘It means a lot. Microsoft’s Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) organization using Harvey is an important step in our long-standing relationship with Microsoft. More broadly, it signals that the world’s leading legal teams are making AI a core part of how they operate.’ ‘We’ve built a strong relationship with Microsoft over many years, and this announcement reflects the next chapter in that collaboration. Like any enterprise deployment, CELA also went through a thorough evaluation process before deciding to use Harvey.’ Weinberg also added: ‘Microsoft’s products are foundational to the work lawyers do, so we have always been grateful for our deep relationship with their team. ‘Today’s announcement that Microsoft’s legal team will use Harvey’s platform and that Harvey associates will use more Microsoft products to support our global growth represents the next step in our ongoing relationship with their team, and we look forward to building on it.’ And Antony Cook, Corporate Vice President and Deputy General Counsel at Microsoft, said: ‘We’re pleased to expand our work with Harvey as part of our broader efforts to bring the benefits of AI into our operations. This collaboration will help our teams work more efficiently and focus on the complex, high-impact work that matters most.’ — Two Major Legal Innovators Conferences this November Come and join us in New York and London this November at Legal Innovators!

news.titleEn: The Innovators – ‘Press Conference’
news.titleZh: 创新者——‘新闻发布会’
news.summaryZh: 凯蒂站在管理合伙人办公室门外，蒂姆已让其他人离开，以便独自进行紧急头脑风暴。与此同时，其他人正紧张地站在目前无人发言的“卢比孔项目”新闻发布会后排，一边回避恼怒的记者关于何时开始的提问，一边担心是否会有律所的人登上讲台。律所创新主管凯蒂深呼吸，自问是否引发了这场危机，内心另一部分回答“是的，但你别无选择”。蒂莫西·马克斯叫她进去后，未等她坐下便表示，尽管他想为混乱负责，但并非他造成这场惨败，现在他们大约只有五分钟来挽救律所声誉，也包括他自己的声誉。凯蒂点头等待下文，但这位Smyth & Marmalade股权合伙人中的首席似乎无话可说。两人隔着大办公桌对视，时间在管理合伙人背后的时钟上痛苦地流逝。最终沉默难以忍受，凯蒂问“先生？我们该怎么办？”他笑着回答“我们？你要出去吸收毒箭，每一个尖刻的问题，你要把律所声誉从嘲笑中拯救出来——如果允许我这样比喻。”凯蒂问“我？”他回应“你是创新主管，不是吗？去创新一篇演讲。你显然擅长在最后一刻想出毁灭性的事情。你让我们陷入困境，你就带我们脱困。”凯蒂咽了咽口水，深刻不同意他对局势的看法，但确定关于责任的争论必须等待。她再次长吸一口气，瞬间意识到自己站在辞职与绝佳机会之间，她选择了后者。
news.bodyText: Katie stood outside the managing partner’s door like a naughty student. Tim had sent everyone else away so he could have a solitary, emergency brainstorm. Meanwhile, the others were now standing nervously at the back of the currently speakerless Project Rubicon press conference, wondering if anyone from the firm would ever take the podium, while deflecting questions from the annoyed journalists about when things would start. The firm’s head of innovation breathed in deeply, as she had been taught at yoga. ‘Did I cause this crisis?’ Katie asked herself. ‘Yes, you did. But you had no choice,’ replied another part of her. ‘You can come back in now,’ Timothy Marks intoned from within. When she had shut the door behind her, he began, not waiting for her to sit. Much as he wanted to take responsibility for this mess, he explained, he had not caused this fiasco. Right now they had about five minutes to save the firm’s reputation. His as well, he added. Katie nodded in agreement and waited for the next bit. But Smyth & Marmalade’s elected leader, this primus inter pares of the equity partners, seemed to have nothing else to say. They stared at each other across the huge desk. The seconds ticked painfully by on the clock behind the managing partner. Eventually the silence was too much. ‘Sir? What are we going to do?’ ‘We?’ he replied with a grin that she didn’t like very much. ‘You are going to go out there and you will absorb the poison. Every arrow. Every barbed question. You are going to talk the firm’s reputation out of the jaws of ridicule – if I am allowed such a metaphor.’ ‘Me?’ ‘You’re the head of innovation, aren’t you? Go and innovate a speech. You’re obviously brilliant at thinking up devastating things at the last minute. You got us into this predicament, you get us out of it.’ She gulped. Disagreed profoundly with his take on the situation, but ascertained an argument about blame would have to wait. Katie took another long, deep breath and in that instant realised she stood half-way between resignation and a fantastic opportunity. She chose the latter.
