news.titleEn: Osborne Clarke launches independent company for AI regulatory monitoring
news.titleZh: Osborne Clarke成立独立公司，专注AI监管监测
news.summaryZh: 国际律师事务所Osborne Clarke正在分拆成立一家独立公司，利用AI代理为法律与合规部门自动持续监测欧洲法规。该平台每日分析超过200个法律与监管来源，仅向每家公司推送与其业务相关的变更。传统上，此类监测任务消耗公司法务部门大量资源，且仍存在遗漏关键更新的风险。Osborne Clarke从其自身咨询业务中深知这一痛点，并作为独家合作伙伴，为产品提供监管专业知识。创始团队兼具法律与技术专长：首席执行官Alexander Lilienbeck是律师兼软件开发者，2025年被JUVE评为“德国十大法律科技新星”之一；首席技术官Christian Braun专攻AI与机器学习系统，此前创立过两家AI初创公司；Gereon Abendroth作为董事长兼总经理，为Justima带来超过20年经验。通过Justima，其正在积极塑造律所由AI驱动的转型。当许多律所仍主要将AI视为内部效率工具时，Osborne Clarke推向市场的解决方案同时为客户带来直接价值。AI正在改变法律市场，我们更愿意主动塑造这一变化，而非被动应对。Osborne Clarke在监管领域和AI工程方面均处于领先地位。通过Justima，我们将两者结合。对客户而言，这意味着：凡能用AI解决的问题，我们就用AI解决。需要判断、经验和解释时，我们的律师会介入。”在正式推出前，约60家合规领域公司已注册早期访问。用户包括Condor、Karlsberg Brewery、AUTODOC等公司，以及其他DAX-40和财富500强企业。
news.bodyHtml:
International law firm Osborne Clarke is spinning off an independent company that uses AI agents to automate the continuous monitoring of European regulation for legal and compliance departments. The platform analyses more than 200 legal and regulatory sources daily and delivers only business-relevant changes tailored to each company.

Traditionally, these monitoring tasks have consumed substantial resources within corporate legal departments while still carrying the risk of critical updates being overlooked. Osborne Clarke knows this pain point from its own advisory practice and  acts as exclusive partner providing the regulatory expertise behind the product.

Advertisement

The founding team combines legal and technical expertise: CEO Alexander Lilienbeck is a lawyer and software developer, recognised by JUVE in 2025 as one of the “Top 10 Legal Tech Rising Stars in Germany”. CTO Christian Braun specialises in AI and machine learning systems and has previously founded two AI Start-ups. As Chairman & Managing Director, Gereon Abendroth brings more than 20 years of experience to Justima.

With Justima, Osborne Clarke says that it is actively shaping the AI-driven transformation of the firm. While many law firms still regard AI primarily as an internal efficiency tool, Osborne Clarke is bringing to market a solution that delivers direct value to clients as well.

Advertisement

“AI is transforming the legal market and we prefer to actively shape this change rather than simply react to it. Osborne Clarke is a leader in the regulatory space and in AI engineering. With Justima, we bring both together. For clients, this means: wherever problems can be solved with AI, we solve them with AI. Our lawyers step in where judgement, experience and interpretation are required,” says Abendroth.

Prior to its official launch, approximately 60 companies from the compliance sector had registered for early access. Users include companies such as Condor, Karlsberg Brewery, AUTODOC and further DAX-40 and Fortune 500 companies.

news.titleEn: Report from the FT Innovative Lawyers Asia-Pacific Awards in Hong Kong
news.titleZh: 香港FT亚太创新律师大奖现场报道
news.summaryZh: 香港法律市场呈现近年少见的乐观与活跃，律所业务繁忙，IPO蓬勃发展，新AI工具持续引入。律所负责人、总法律顾问及创新主管上周齐聚香港参加FT亚太创新律师大奖，该奖项及报告由RSGI团队研究，覆盖法律咨询与业务全谱系创新，包括AI在律所及内部法律团队的最新应用。今年AI在法律领域的应用沿三个方向不均衡推进：技术本身飞速发展，个人能力建设速度差异巨大，组织投资于利用AI所需的基础与新商业模式，许多情况下个人快于组织。亚太领先律所正部署定制AI平台、代理工作流和专有数据基础设施，部分准备将工具商业化对外销售。澳大利亚律所或具澳大利亚传统的律所主导FT最具创新律所榜单。新近独立的Mallesons（从金杜分拆后）居首，正利用Harvey快速构建代理工作流，涵盖并排条款比较、合规清单审查、文件与条款清单对齐、ACCC合并通知及诉状矩阵，其74步《支付安全法》工作流将处理时间从数月缩短至数小时。Gilbert + Tobin总排名第二，其Lakehouse项目获认可，该云数据平台基于Microsoft Fabric，统一此前分散的案件、客户、财务和运营数据，实现近实时报告、简化交易数据捕获的AI工作流及代理冲突检查工作流。澳大利亚以外律所专职法律科技与创新资源较少，常由执业合伙人或业务负责人主导AI与技术创新。
news.bodyHtml:
By Yasmin Lambert

There is a buzz of optimism and activity in the Hong Kong legal market unlike recent years. Law firms are busy, IPOs are booming and new AI tools are being onboarded regularly.

Advertisement

Law firm leaders, general counsel and heads of innovation were in Hong Kong last week for the FT Innovative Lawyers Asia-Pacific Awards. The awards and report, researched by our team at RSGI, cover innovation across the spectrum of legal advice and business, including the latest applications of AI within law firms and in-house legal teams.

This year we saw AI applications in the law progress unevenly along three vectors. The technology itself is racing ahead; individuals are building new capability at vastly different rates; and organisations are investing in the foundations and new business models needed to leverage AI. In many cases, individuals are moving faster than their organisations.

Advertisement

Across the Asia-Pacific region, leading law firms are deploying custom-built AI platforms, agentic workflows and proprietary data infrastructure. And in several cases, preparing to commercialise those tools for sale to other firms and clients.

Australian law firms – or those like with legacy Australian roots – dominated the FT list of most innovative law firms in the region.

The newly independent Mallesons (following its demerger from Chinese firm King & Wood) topped the ranking. It is building agentic workflows using Harvey at a rapid pace. They include workflows for side-by-side provision comparisons, compliance checklist reviews, document and term sheet alignment, ACCC merger notifications and a pleadings matrix. Mallesons report that a 74-step Security of Payment Act (SOPA) workflow has reduced processing time from months to hours.

Gilbert + Tobin came in second overall and was recognised for innovations including its Lakehouse project. The cloud-based data platform is built on Microsoft Fabric and unifies matter, client, financial and operational data that had previously been fragmented across systems. It has enabled near real-time reporting, a streamlined AI workflow for capturing deal data, and an agentic conflict-check workflow.

Outside Australia, law firms have fewer dedicated legal technology and innovation resources. Here practising partners or other business leaders often led AI and technology innovations.

In Japan, Nagashima Ohno & Tsunematsu’s Ryuhei Itaya won the individual ‘Intrapreneur’ award for co-founding MNTSQ (pronounced like the name of the French philosopher Montesquieu). MNTSQ aggregates contract data and expertise from three of Japan’s four largest law firms – Nagashima, Nishimura & Asahi, and Mori Hamada & Matsumoto – to help corporate legal teams digitise their contracting processes. Itaya reports that approximately 35% of Japanese companies with revenues exceeding JPY 1 trillion have now adopted MNTSQ.

Data sovereignty concerns guide other approaches to using AI in Asia. In Singapore, Allen & Gledhill built A&GEL, a custom on-premises large language model platform built with Singapore’s Pand.ai. In Korea, law firm Yulchon developed AI solutions with a Korean legal tech company that deployed its own proprietary small language model rather than OpenAI, Gemini or Claude.

And for the first time, an Indian law firm – Khaitan & Co – received the equal highest digital score in the FT report, including for its proprietary AI tool, KAI.

Law firms across the Asia-Pacific region may be smaller than the leading firms in the UK or US, but many are nimble and ready to move quickly.

However, at a roundtable event for managing partners and innovation heads following the awards, one lawyer noted a topic missing from the coverage this year. Pointing over the jagged green mountains surrounding Hong Kong, he referenced the tech powerhouses and startup labs rapidly developing AI in Shenzhen, the Chinese tech hub just 20 minutes away by train. Perhaps there will be a Chinese legal AI story to cover in 2027.
news.bodyText:
There is a buzz of optimism and activity in the Hong Kong legal market unlike recent years. Law firms are busy, IPOs are booming and new AI tools are being onboarded regularly.

Law firm leaders, general counsel and heads of innovation were in Hong Kong last week for the FT Innovative Lawyers Asia-Pacific Awards. The awards and report, researched by our team at RSGI, cover innovation across the spectrum of legal advice and business, including the latest applications of AI within law firms and in-house legal teams.

This year we saw AI applications in the law progress unevenly along three vectors. The technology itself is racing ahead; individuals are building new capability at vastly different rates; and organisations are investing in the foundations and new business models needed to leverage AI. In many cases, individuals are moving faster than their organisations.

Across the Asia-Pacific region, leading law firms are deploying custom-built AI platforms, agentic workflows and proprietary data infrastructure. And in several cases, preparing to commercialise those tools for sale to other firms and clients.

Australian law firms – or those like with legacy Australian roots – dominated the FT list of most innovative law firms in the region.

The newly independent Mallesons (following its demerger from Chinese firm King & Wood) topped the ranking. It is building agentic workflows using Harvey at a rapid pace. They include workflows for side-by-side provision comparisons, compliance checklist reviews, document and term sheet alignment, ACCC merger notifications and a pleadings matrix. Mallesons report that a 74-step Security of Payment Act (SOPA) workflow has reduced processing time from months to hours.

Gilbert + Tobin came in second overall and was recognised for innovations including its Lakehouse project. The cloud-based data platform is built on Microsoft Fabric and unifies matter, client, financial and operational data that had previously been fragmented across systems. It has enabled near real-time reporting, a streamlined AI workflow for capturing deal data, and an agentic conflict-check workflow.

Outside Australia, law firms have fewer dedicated legal technology and innovation resources. Here practising partners or other business leaders often led AI and technology innovations.

In Japan, Nagashima Ohno & Tsunematsu’s Ryuhei Itaya won the individual ‘Intrapreneur’ award for co-founding MNTSQ (pronounced like the name of the French philosopher Montesquieu). MNTSQ aggregates contract data and expertise from three of Japan’s four largest law firms – Nagashima, Nishimura & Asahi, and Mori Hamada & Matsumoto – to help corporate legal teams digitise their contracting processes. Itaya reports that approximately 35% of Japanese companies with revenues exceeding JPY 1 trillion have now adopted MNTSQ.

Data sovereignty concerns guide other approaches to using AI in Asia. In Singapore, Allen & Gledhill built A&GEL, a custom on-premises large language model platform built with Singapore’s Pand.ai. In Korea, law firm Yulchon developed AI solutions with a Korean legal tech company that deployed its own proprietary small language model rather than OpenAI, Gemini or Claude.

And for the first time, an Indian law firm – Khaitan & Co – received the equal highest digital score in the FT report, including for its proprietary AI tool, KAI.

Law firms across the Asia-Pacific region may be smaller than the leading firms in the UK or US, but many are nimble and ready to move quickly.

However, at a roundtable event for managing partners and innovation heads following the awards, one lawyer noted a topic missing from the coverage this year. Pointing over the jagged green mountains surrounding Hong Kong, he referenced the tech powerhouses and startup labs rapidly developing AI in Shenzhen, the Chinese tech hub just 20 minutes away by train. Perhaps there will be a Chinese legal AI story to cover in 2027.

news.summaryZh: Litify宣布推出LitifyAI Time Capture，该原生功能通过与Billables AI的战略合作，自动将律师活动转化为合规、可审核的时间条目。Billables AI是一个AI驱动的法律运营平台，旨在消除专业服务人员的手动时间记录。该方案能实时自主识别并记录可计费活动，让计时人员专注于实质性法律工作。手动计时长期导致收入流失，许多律所高达30%的可计费工作未被记录。LitifyAI Time Capture持续分析律师已在使用的工具中的活动，包括Microsoft 365、Zoom、Adobe等，并生成符合客户计费要求的详细叙述，律师可在Litify内审核批准，无需中断工作流程。该方案以安全、被动的方式捕捉活动，无需手动输入或侵入性监控。该功能通过消除遗漏条目和重新分配时间两次防止收入流失，并与Billables AI合作确保时间在同一地点生成、审核和最终确定。将时间捕捉技术引入Litify平台，让律所无需改变律师习惯即可挽回流失收入。该方案可帮助法律团队挽回高达30%的可计费时间，减少高达90%的叙述起草时间，并改善对客户计费要求的合规性。条目从一开始就结构正确，减少冲销和返工。系统随时间适应个人工作模式和写作风格，内置审核层确保律师在最终确定前拥有完全控制权。此次发布反映了向自主生成和编排工作的代理解决方案的转变。Litify自2016年成立以来，已服务超过55,000名法律专业人员和450多家企业客户。
news.bodyHtml:
Powered by Billables AI, LitifyAI Time Capture autonomously captures billable activities and generates review-ready time entries, improving realization and eliminating manual timekeeping. 

 

NEW YORK, NY — May 19, 2026 – Litify, the AI-native Platform of Action for law firms and legal departments, today announced LitifyAI Time Capture, a new native capability that automatically converts attorney activity into compliant, review-ready time entries. Through a strategic partnership with Billables AI, an AI-powered legal operations platform that eliminates manual time tracking for professional service providers, the solution autonomously identifies and records billable activity in real time, freeing timekeepers to focus on substantive legal work.

Despite advancements in legal technology, manual timekeeping remains one of the most persistent sources of lost revenue. With LitifyAI Time Capture, attorneys no longer need to struggle with the manual task of reconstructing time entries long after the work is done. This outdated method often leads to missed entries, reduced realization, and unnecessary administrative strain. In many firms, it also results in up to 30% of billable work going unrecorded. This gap has driven the rise of platforms like Billables AI, which take a fundamentally different approach to timekeeping.  

Today, Litify and Billables AI are operationalizing that approach by capturing work as it happens and drafting complete entries in real time. The capability continuously analyzes activity across the tools attorneys already use, including Microsoft 365, Zoom, Adobe, and more. It then generates detailed narratives aligned to client billing requirements, allowing attorneys to review and approve time within Litify without interrupting their workflow. The solution captures activity securely and passively, without requiring manual entry or invasive monitoring. By shifting timekeeping from a manual, after-the-fact task to an automated, continuous process, firms can capture more of the work they are already doing and reduce administrative strain.  

“At Litify, we’re committed to delivering AI solutions that drive real impact for our clients, ” says Lauren Rothrock, Chief Product Officer at Litify. “Litify AI Time Capture helps our customers prevent lost revenue twice: First, by eradicating missed time entries. Second, by reallocating thousands of hours previously spent tracking time to revenue-driving activities, instead. Our partners at Billables AI share this vision to recapture revenue. Together, we built these tools to save time in a third way — by ensuring time is generated, reviewed, and finalized in the same place. This is another exciting step in our journey as the legal industry’s only AI-native platform of action. 

“Law firms are under real pressure to do more with the same teams, and manual timekeeping is one of the most fixable drains on that capacity,” said Arvind Sujeeth, Co-Founder and CEO of Billables AI. “Bringing our time capture technology into Litify’s platform gives firms a way to recover that lost revenue without asking attorneys to change a single habit.”

As firms face increasing pressure to operate more efficiently without expanding headcount, LitifyAI Time Capture delivers immediate financial and operational impact. It offers a practical path for legal teams to recover up to 30% more billable time, reduce narrative drafting time by up to 90%, and improve compliance with client billing requirements. Because entries are structured correctly from the start, firms also see fewer write-downs and less rework. 

 Over time, the system adapts to individual work patterns and writing styles, which produces entries that reflect how attorneys actually work and maintain consistency across the firm. A built-in review layer ensures the attorney retains full control before any entry is finalized. 

 This launch reflects a broader shift toward agentic solutions that generate and orchestrate work autonomously in the background, reinforcing Litify’s position as the Platform of Action that helps legal teams turn insight into execution and move work forward with greater speed, visibility, and intelligence.

 

About Litify

Unleash your team’s full potential.

 Litify is powering a new era for the legal industry. Since its inception in 2016, Litify has helped law firms and corporate legal departments turn operations into impact through its leading AI-native platform of action. With over 55K legal professionals and 450+ enterprise clients across plaintiff, insurance defense, immigration, and the Fortune 500 — the industry-leading solution combines trusted cloud-based technology, configurable and AI-native workflows, and powerful business analytics. Additional capabilities include matter and intake management, document generation, timekeeping and billing, legal hold and corporate eBilling, mobile, and more.

 By integrating next-generation AI actions and insights across the platform, Litify offers a future-ready solution that enhances strategic decision-making, increases client satisfaction, and enables every teammate to operate at their full potential.

 To learn more and request your personalized demo, visit www.litify.com.

 

About Billables AI

Billables AI is an AI-powered legal operations platform that eliminates manual time tracking for law firms and professional service providers. By automatically capturing time from everyday workflows across Microsoft, Google, Zoom, and more, Billables AI generates detailed, compliant time entries while surfacing the workflow intelligence firms need to optimize performance, increase realization, and make smarter business decisions. For more information, visit www.billables.ai.

news.titleEn: Claude for Legal and Access to Justice: The Good, the Bad, and the Unknown
news.titleZh: Claude在法律与司法公正领域的应用：好、坏与未知
news.summaryZh: Anthropic发布迄今最大规模法律领域推进，包括20多个MCP连接器、12个执业领域插件，以及与Microsoft Word、Outlook、Excel和PowerPoint的集成。公告还包含司法公正内容：将Justice Technology Association和Free Law Project列为司法公正合作伙伴，将Courtroom5、BoardWise、Descrybe和CourtListener作为连接器内置到Claude中，并通过Claude for Nonprofits项目向符合条件的法律援助诊所、公设辩护人和非营利法律服务团体提供折扣定价。JTA执行主任Maya Markovich称这是领先AI公司首次明确将司法公正列为基础支柱。MCP使AI能从权威数据库实时获取可靠数据，CourtListener的MCP免费，Courtroom5可将其案件评估、截止日期计算和程序指导工具接入聊天界面，BoardWise为持牌专业人士提供结构化帮助，Descrybe提供约3亿条美国结构化初级法律记录。但文章也提出担忧：幻觉风险依然存在，自诉当事人涉及的已记录幻觉事件多于持牌律师，2025年为304起对219起；Whiting诉Athens市案中第六巡回法院处以3万美元制裁；帮助的表象可能掩盖实质；无授权执业问题未解决；Claude Pro订阅每月20美元可能对部分自诉当事人构成负担。文章还提出开放问题：集成是否会被使用、结果是否改善、法院如何回应、Anthropic五年后的定位、法律援助资金前景。
news.bodyHtml:
Last week, when Anthropic released its biggest legal push to date — more than 20 MCP connectors, 12 practice-area plugins,a and integrations with Microsoft Word, Outlook, Excel and PowerPoint — much of the coverage focused on what the announcement means for law firms, in-house teams, and the legal tech ecosystem. That is where the bulk of the announcement was directed. It is also where the money is.

But a less talked about part of the announcement was something potentially more impactful – the access-to-justice component. Anthropic named the Justice Technology Association and the Free Law Project as access-to-justice partners. It put Courtroom5, BoardWise, Descrybe, and CourtListener inside Claude as connectors that anyone can turn on. It offered discounted pricing to qualifying legal aid clinics, public defenders, and nonprofit legal services groups through its Claude for Nonprofits program. And it framed all of this as “working to put legal help within reach of people who can’t currently access it.”

That is a remarkable commitment from a leading AI lab. JTA executive director Maya Markovich said as much when she called it “the first time that a leading AI company is explicitly naming access to justice as a foundational pillar.”

But promises are easy. Outcomes are hard. I have been writing about access to justice and legal tech long enough to have seen a lot of promising tools land in the laps of self-represented litigants without moving the needle. So, the question worth asking is not whether the new Claude integrations could help — undoubtedly, they could — but whether they actually will. And, if so, who are they likely to help, and do they pose any potential dangers to the people they are designed to serve?

Here are my initial thoughts on the good, the bad, and the unknown.

The Good

Begin with the size of the problem. The Legal Services Corporation’s most recent Justice Gap Study found that 92% of the civil legal problems substantially affecting low-income Americans got no help or inadequate help. Roughly three-quarters of low-income households experience at least one civil legal problem a year. And the problem is not confined to the poor: an LSC Harris Poll commissioned for the organization’s 50th anniversary found that 59% of all Americans who had a civil legal matter in the prior three years did not seek out a lawyer at all.

That is the backdrop against which to evaluate the access-to-justice piece of last week’s announcement. Even modest improvements matter, and there are several aspects of this news that seem promising in their potential impact.

First, MCP rewires the foundational layer to make AI more reliable in legal situations. MCP – short for Model Context Protocol, the open standard Anthropic developed and which has spread quickly across legal tech – lets an AI assistant pull reliable data from an authoritative database at the moment of the query, rather than relying solely on whatever the model absorbed during training. For a self-represented litigant, that distinction could be the difference between an AI confidently fabricating a case citation and an AI retrieving an actual opinion from CourtListener. Free Law Project itself put it well: “A response built on verified CourtListener data is categorically different from one built on even the best model alone.” That is not marketing hype. It is a qualitative improvement.

Second, the pricing makes these tools accessible. CourtListener’s MCP is free with a free CourtListener account. Anyone with an internet connection now has access to the same primary-law backbone – millions of federal and state opinions, PACER dockets, citation networks, oral arguments, judge profiles – that, until not so long ago, was effectively gated by pricey legal research subscriptions. Courtroom5, which serves the roughly three out of four civil cases involving a self-represented litigant, can now plug its case-assessment, deadline-calculation, and procedural-guidance tools directly into the chat interface that millions of people are already using. BoardWise gives licensed professionals facing state board matters something they almost never have – structured help. Descrybe offers access to some 300 million structured U.S. primary law records.

Third, that old saw of tech, that “infrastructure beats apps,” is, in this context, right on point. For most of the last decade, the tech response to the justice gap has been to build standalone self-help tools — court websites, forms portals, chatbots, plain-language guides. Courtroom5 argues persuasively that the problem has never been a shortage of legal information; it has been a shortage of structured preparation. Meeting people inside the AI tool they are already using, with a justice-tech tool plugged in behind it, is closer to where help is actually needed than a self-help website that not everyone will find.

Fourth, the legal aid sector is ready for this. In an Everlaw survey last year, in which this blog partnered along with NLADA and Paladin, 74% of legal aid organizations reported using AI in some form — roughly double the rate of the broader profession — and 88% said they believed AI could meaningfully help close the justice gap. As Scheree Gilchrist of Legal Aid of North Carolina put it, “We will never be able to ‘lawyer ourselves’ out of this access-to-justice crisis. AI is a force multiplier to scale our services.” A discounted-pricing program for nonprofit legal services is something that sector can benefit from enormously.

So the upside is clear. But is there also a downside?

The Bad (Potentially)

The most obvious hazard of putting a general-purpose AI assistant in front of someone who is about to file something in court is hallucination. The numbers on this are sobering. Damien Charlotin’s running database of court filings containing AI-fabricated citations passed 1,000 cases earlier this year and is climbing rapidly. Self-represented litigants account for more documented hallucination incidents than licensed attorneys — 304 versus 219 in 2025, according to an analysis of Charlotin’s database done by DISCO. The Sixth Circuit imposed $30,000 in sanctions in Whiting v. City of Athens in March. An assistant U.S. attorney was reportedly fired. State courts are amending local rules. Bar associations are rewriting ethics guidance.

Grounding AI in real legal data, as MCP does, helps with this. It does not eliminate it. A pro se litigant who asks Claude — even Claude with CourtListener attached — to “write me a brief in support of my motion to dismiss” is going to get a brief. Whether every proposition in that brief is supported, whether every citation is real and on point, whether the procedural arguments are even available in that jurisdiction at that stage — those are judgments that the litigant is now responsible for, but possibly not equipped to make.

Free Law Project, to its credit, says so explicitly: “The MCP server is infrastructure. It connects a powerful AI model to a high-quality legal data source. … Claude is not a lawyer. Nothing produced through this integration is legal advice, and human judgment remains essential, especially for high-stakes decisions.”

Good on them for saying that. But how many users will get that message?

The second concern is that the appearance of help can obscure the substance of help. There is documented evidence that Courtroom5’s structured-preparation model produces results — the company reports that 73% of members who resolve their cases win or settle, and over 90% in eviction proceedings. Those numbers come from a curated platform with a curriculum, peer community, and human coaching. It is not a generic AI chat. The risk in the new architecture is that a user finds the brand-name AI assistant first, asks it a legal question, gets a confident-sounding answer, and never makes it to the structured tools — whether they be Courtroom5 or a lawyer-for-the-day program at the courthouse — that might have produced a better outcome.

Third, none of this resolves the unauthorized-practice-of-law question, which has hung over AI legal help since DoNotPay’s “robot lawyer” era. Anthropic’s approach — partnering with justice-tech tools rather than holding itself out as a legal service — is a sensible one. But the line between “information” and “advice” is fuzzier in a long, personalized chat than it ever was in a self-help website. State bar regulators might have a thing or two to say about that. Will that produce sensible regulatory sandboxes — as Utah, Arizona, and others have experimented with — or a defensive crackdown that protects the guild more than the public?

Fourth, there is a minor but real affordability question. While the CourtListener piece is genuinely free, the Anthropic piece on top of it is not. Use of these MCPs requires a Claude Pro subscription. Access to Claude for Nonprofits requires qualifying as a nonprofit. Even though a Claude Pro subscription is just $20 a month, even that might be a stretch for a self-represented litigant in a foreclosure or custody case. And there is always the risk of a two-tiered AI justice system, with better-resourced organizations running on Claude Enterprise, while unrepresented litigants rely on the free tier of whatever chatbot a friend told them about — which may or may not be the one with the verified primary-law connector turned on.

The Unknown

Beyond the potential upsides and downsides, there are also several open questions, the answers to which remain to be seen.

Will the integrations be used? Anthropic put the tools in the directory. That does not mean self-represented litigants will find them, turn them on, or know to use the CourtListener connector instead of asking Claude cold. Discovery and onboarding are real problems. For legal aid organizations, there may be a bandwidth challenge in actually deploying these in their workflows. Even if the infrastructure is there, the human and institutional plumbing may not be.

Do outcomes improve? We do not yet have data on whether self-represented litigants using grounded, MCP-connected AI assistants do measurably better in court, or with other legal problems, than those using ungrounded chatbots, or those using nothing. We need these studies, ideally conducted as collaborations among the justice-tech sector, legal aid and the courts themselves. Until we have them, any claims around access to justice are largely just hypotheses.

How will courts respond? Some judges are already imposing standing orders requiring litigants to disclose AI use. Some are amending local rules. A handful are imposing hallucination-related sanctions on pro se litigants in addition to attorneys. Some are openly embracing AI use – and are even using it themselves. The judiciary’s posture toward AI-assisted self-representation will shape whether the new tools actually expand access or set up users for an even harder fall.

Where is Anthropic in five years? Anthropic is not a justice-tech company. It is a frontier AI lab with an aggressive growth trajectory – including, we now know, in BigLaw and corporate legal. Its access-to-justice partnerships are only a small piece of a much larger commercial strategy. Whether the public-service aspect remains a foundational pillar may depend on what the company’s growth looks like over the next few years, who at the company champions this work, and whether the justice-tech partners are able to do their parts to keep the commitments alive.

What happens to the legal aid funding picture? Even the most capable AI tools are not a substitute for human lawyers handling the most serious civil matters — domestic violence, eviction defense, immigration, disability benefits. LSC is requesting $2.1 billion for FY2027, an increase over current levels. If the political response to, “AI can help with the justice gap,” is, “We can therefore cut legal aid funding,” then an unintended consequence of all this technology could be even less access for low-income Americans. Needless to say, if legislators start pushing that argument, then the access-to-justice community needs to push back on it hard.

Where That Leaves Me

The bottom line is that the access-to-justice component of last week’s announcement is unquestionably substantive, and that the infrastructure — open protocols, primary law accessible for free, justice-tech tools as first-class citizens of the Claude ecosystem — is genuinely promising. Maya Markovich is right that this is the first time a leading AI company has named access to justice as a foundational pillar, and that is worth marking.

But infrastructure is not outcomes. The same technology that lets CourtListener feed Claude verified case law could also let a self-represented litigant produce a beautifully formatted brief riddled with errors no judge will excuse. The potential good and the potential bad both turn on the same infrastructure.

Going forward, what I would like to see are three things:

  • Data on outcomes for self-represented litigants using grounded AI versus everything else.
  • Serious and open-minded engagement from courts and bar regulators on what is permitted and what is not.
  • A sustained commitment from Anthropic to keep the access-to-justice partners on equal footing with the enterprise side of the house – and similar commitments from other major AI companies.

If those things happen, then we will someday look back on this announcement as the moment the access-to-justice talk in legal tech turned tangible. If they do not, then the announcement may just become a forgotten footnote in a much larger commercial story.

One thing for sure: That someday will be sooner rather than later.

I have been writing about access to justice and legal tech long enough to have seen a lot of promising tools land in the laps of self-represented litigants without moving the needle. So, the question worth asking is not whether the new Claude integrations could help — undoubtedly, they could — but whether they actually will. And, if so, who are they likely to help, and do they pose any potential dangers to the people they are designed to serve?

Here are my initial thoughts on the good, the bad, and the unknown.

Begin with the size of the problem. The Legal Services Corporation’s most recent Justice Gap Study found that 92% of the civil legal problems substantially affecting low-income Americans got no help or inadequate help. Roughly three-quarters of low-income households experience at least one civil legal problem a year. And the problem is not confined to the poor: an LSC Harris Poll commissioned for the organization’s 50th anniversary found that 59% of all Americans who had a civil legal matter in the prior three years did not seek out a lawyer at all.

That is the backdrop against which to evaluate the access-to-justice piece of last week’s announcement. Even modest improvements matter, and there are several aspects of this news that seem promising in their potential impact.

First, MCP rewires the foundational layer to make AI more reliable in legal situations. MCP – short for Model Context Protocol, the open standard Anthropic developed and which has spread quickly across legal tech – lets an AI assistant pull reliable data from an authoritative database at the moment of the query, rather than relying solely on whatever the model absorbed during training. For a self-represented litigant, that distinction could be the difference between an AI confidently fabricating a case citation and an AI retrieving an actual opinion from CourtListener. Free Law Project itself put it well: “A response built on verified CourtListener data is categorically different from one built on even the best model alone.” That is not marketing hype. It is a qualitative improvement.

Second, the pricing makes these tools accessible. CourtListener’s MCP is free with a free CourtListener account. Anyone with an internet connection now has access to the same primary-law backbone – millions of federal and state opinions, PACER dockets, citation networks, oral arguments, judge profiles – that, until not so long ago, was effectively gated by pricey legal research subscriptions. Courtroom5, which serves the roughly three out of four civil cases involving a self-represented litigant, can now plug its case-assessment, deadline-calculation, and procedural-guidance tools directly into the chat interface that millions of people are already using. BoardWise gives licensed professionals facing state board matters something they almost never have – structured help. Descrybe offers access to some 300 million structured U.S. primary law records .

Third, that old saw of tech, that “infrastructure beats apps,” is, in this context, right on point. For most of the last decade, the tech response to the justice gap has been to build standalone self-help tools — court websites, forms portals, chatbots, plain-language guides. Courtroom5 argues persuasively that the problem has never been a shortage of legal information; it has been a shortage of structured preparation. Meeting people inside the AI tool they are already using, with a justice-tech tool plugged in behind it, is closer to where help is actually needed than a self-help website that not everyone will find.

Fourth, the legal aid sector is ready for this. In an Everlaw survey last year , in which this blog partnered along with NLADA and Paladin, 74% of legal aid organizations reported using AI in some form — roughly double the rate of the broader profession — and 88% said they believed AI could meaningfully help close the justice gap. As Scheree Gilchrist of Legal Aid of North Carolina put it, “We will never be able to ‘lawyer ourselves’ out of this access-to-justice crisis. AI is a force multiplier to scale our services.” A discounted-pricing program for nonprofit legal services is something that sector can benefit from enormously.

So the upside is clear. But is there also a downside?

The most obvious hazard of putting a general-purpose AI assistant in front of someone who is about to file something in court is hallucination. The numbers on this are sobering. Damien Charlotin’s running database of court filings containing AI-fabricated citations passed 1,000 cases earlier this year and is climbing rapidly. Self-represented litigants account for more documented hallucination incidents than licensed attorneys — 304 versus 219 in 2025, according to an analysis of Charlotin’s database done by DISCO. The Sixth Circuit imposed $30,000 in sanctions in Whiting v. City of Athens in March. An assistant U.S. attorney was reportedly fired. State courts are amending local rules. Bar associations are rewriting ethics guidance.

Grounding AI in real legal data, as MCP does, helps with this. It does not eliminate it. A pro se litigant who asks Claude — even Claude with CourtListener attached — to “write me a brief in support of my motion to dismiss” is going to get a brief. Whether every proposition in that brief is supported, whether every citation is real and on point, whether the procedural arguments are even available in that jurisdiction at that stage — those are judgments that the litigant is now responsible for, but possibly not equipped to make.

Free Law Project, to its credit, says so explicitly: “The MCP server is infrastructure. It connects a powerful AI model to a high-quality legal data source. … Claude is not a lawyer. Nothing produced through this integration is legal advice, and human judgment remains essential, especially for high-stakes decisions.”

Good on them for saying that. But how many users will get that message?

The second concern is that the appearance of help can obscure the substance of help. There is documented evidence that Courtroom5’s structured-preparation model produces results — the company reports that 73% of members who resolve their cases win or settle , and over 90% in eviction proceedings. Those numbers come from a curated platform with a curriculum, peer community, and human coaching. It is not a generic AI chat. The risk in the new architecture is that a user finds the brand-name AI assistant first, asks it a legal question, gets a confident-sounding answer, and never makes it to the structured tools — whether they be Courtroom5 or a lawyer-for-the-day program at the courthouse — that might have produced a better outcome.

Third, none of this resolves the unauthorized-practice-of-law question, which has hung over AI legal help since DoNotPay’s “robot lawyer” era. Anthropic’s approach — partnering with justice-tech tools rather than holding itself out as a legal service — is a sensible one. But the line between “information” and “advice” is fuzzier in a long, personalized chat than it ever was in a self-help website. State bar regulators might have a thing or two to say about that. Will that produce sensible regulatory sandboxes — as Utah, Arizona, and others have experimented with — or a defensive crackdown that protects the guild more than the public?

Fourth, there is a minor but real affordability question. While the CourtListener piece is genuinely free, the Anthropic piece on top of it is not. Use of these MCPs requires a Claude Pro subscription. Access to Claude for Nonprofits requires qualifying as a nonprofit. Even though a Claude Pro subscription is just $20 a month, even that might be a stretch for a self-represented litigant in a foreclosure or custody case. And there is always the risk of a two-tiered AI justice system, with better-resourced organizations running on Claude Enterprise, while unrepresented litigants rely on the free tier of whatever chatbot a friend told them about — which may or may not be the one with the verified primary-law connector turned on.

Beyond the potential upsides and downsides, there are also several open questions, the answers to which remain to be seen.

Will the integrations be used? Anthropic put the tools in the directory. That does not mean self-represented litigants will find them, turn them on, or know to use the CourtListener connector instead of asking Claude cold. Discovery and onboarding are real problems. For legal aid organizations, there may be a bandwidth challenge in actually deploying these in their workflows. Even if the infrastructure is there, the human and institutional plumbing may not be.

Do outcomes improve? We do not yet have data on whether self-represented litigants using grounded, MCP-connected AI assistants do measurably better in court, or with other legal problems, than those using ungrounded chatbots, or those using nothing. We need these studies, ideally conducted as collaborations among the justice-tech sector, legal aid and the courts themselves. Until we have them, any claims around access to justice are largely just hypotheses.

How will courts respond? Some judges are already imposing standing orders requiring litigants to disclose AI use. Some are amending local rules. A handful are imposing hallucination-related sanctions on pro se litigants in addition to attorneys. Some are openly embracing AI use – and are even using it themselves. The judiciary’s posture toward AI-assisted self-representation will shape whether the new tools actually expand access or set up users for an even harder fall.

Where is Anthropic in five years? Anthropic is not a justice-tech company. It is a frontier AI lab with an aggressive growth trajectory – including, we now know, in BigLaw and corporate legal. Its access-to-justice partnerships are only a small piece of a much larger commercial strategy. Whether the public-service aspect remains a foundational pillar may depend on what the company’s growth looks like over the next few years, who at the company champions this work, and whether the justice-tech partners are able to do their parts to keep the commitments alive.

What happens to the legal aid funding picture? Even the most capable AI tools are not a substitute for human lawyers handling the most serious civil matters — domestic violence, eviction defense, immigration, disability benefits. LSC is requesting $2.1 billion for FY2027 , an increase over current levels. If the political response to, “AI can help with the justice gap,” is, “We can therefore cut legal aid funding,” then an unintended consequence of all this technology could be even less access for low-income Americans. Needless to say, if legislators start pushing that argument, then the access-to-justice community needs to push back on it hard.

The bottom line is that the access-to-justice component of last week’s announcement is unquestionably substantive, and that the infrastructure — open protocols, primary law accessible for free, justice-tech tools as first-class citizens of the Claude ecosystem — is genuinely promising. Maya Markovich is right that this is the first time a leading AI company has named access to justice as a foundational pillar, and that is worth marking.

But infrastructure is not outcomes. The same technology that lets CourtListener feed Claude verified case law could also let a self-represented litigant produce a beautifully formatted brief riddled with errors no judge will excuse. The potential good and the potential bad both turn on the same infrastructure.

Going forward, what I would like to see are three things:

Data on outcomes for self-represented litigants using grounded AI versus everything else.

Serious and open-minded engagement from courts and bar regulators on what is permitted and what is not.

A sustained commitment from Anthropic to keep the access-to-justice partners on equal footing with the enterprise side of the house – and similar commitments from other major AI companies.

If those things happen, then we will someday look back on this announcement as the moment the access-to-justice talk in legal tech turned tangible. If they do not, then the announcement may just become a forgotten footnote in a much larger commercial story.

One thing for sure: That someday will be sooner rather than later.

news.titleEn: Littler rolls out DepoSim after partnering on employment law capability
news.titleZh: Littler合作开发劳动法能力后全面推广DepoSim
news.summaryZh: AltaClaro于5月21日宣布，其AI驱动的取证模拟平台DepoSim已扩展至涵盖劳动法模拟机会。该新功能与全球最大的代表管理方的劳动与就业法律事务所Littler合作设计，Littler在推出后正于全所范围内推广DepoSim，以提升全球业务中的诉讼准备和取证准备能力。DepoSim为律师提供在真实模拟诉讼场景中实践口头取证的机会，通过结合人工智能与情景式学习，提供即时、可操作的反馈，帮助诉讼律师优化提问策略、改善证人控制并提升整体取证表现。该平台受到关注，因为律所正在考虑如何模拟传统法律培训，尤其是在初级工作日益由AI承担的情况下。新的劳动法模拟功能与Littler以及其他顶级律所劳动法业务组密切合作开发，这些律所是DepoSim的早期采用客户，其律师提供直接意见，确保案件档案和场景反映劳动诉讼实践的现实。这一创新、可扩展的平台旨在通过使用真实AI模拟的实践培训进一步加强律师发展，DepoSim使律师能够建立和完善实践技能，并战略性地应用于取证。DepoSim由AltaClaro与语言智能解决方案领导者Verbit合作开发，旨在紧密模拟现实世界的取证动态。
news.bodyHtml:
AltaClaro today (21 May) announced that DepoSim, its AI-powered deposition simulation platform, has expanded to include employment law simulation opportunities. This new offering was designed in partnership with Littler — the world’s largest employment and labor law practice representing management — which is rolling out DepoSim firmwide following the launch to enhance litigation readiness and deposition preparation across its global practice.

DepoSim provides attorneys with live, hands-on opportunities to practice conducting oral depositions in realistic, simulated litigation scenarios. By combining artificial intelligence with scenario-based learning, the platform delivers immediate, actionable feedback designed to help litigators refine questioning strategies, improve witness control and strengthen overall deposition performance. It is being eyed with interest as practices consider how to simulate traditional legal training, not least as junior work is increasingly undertaken by AI.

Advertisement

The new employment law simulation was developed in close collaboration with Littler, as well as the employment practice groups of other top firms in DepoSim’s early adopter client list, with the attorneys providing direct input to ensure the case files and scenarios reflect the realities of employment litigation practice.

“This innovative, scalable platform is designed to further strengthen attorney development through practical training using realistic AI-powered simulations,” said Littler’s executive director of wellness, engagement & development, Michelle Gomez. “DepoSim equips attorneys to build and refine practical skills and apply those skills strategically for depositions.”

Advertisement

DepoSim is developed by AltaClaro in partnership with Verbit, a leader in verbal intelligence solutions, and is designed to closely mirror real-world deposition dynamics.

news.titleEn: Harvey Announces Contract Review Product, Adoption Analytics Features
news.titleZh: Harvey发布合同审查产品与采用分析功能
news.summaryZh:
Harvey于周三宣布推出采用管理工具Command Center，周四宣布推出合同审查产品Contract Intelligence。Command Center与Haynes and Boone、Foley & Lardner、Clayton Utz、Rajah & Tann及Dentsu等设计合作伙伴共同开发。两款产品均已设立早期访问等候名单，预计今年第三季度全面上市。

Command Center是一款分析与咨询工具，旨在帮助客户优化Harvey部署，可回答用户关于平台在不同业务组和经验级别采用差异、最常用工作流和提示类型以及高活跃用户差异的自然语言问题。该工具利用来自1500多个Harvey部署的匿名聚合数据，让客户与同行组织进行基准比较，并提供推荐功能以识别同行已启用的功能并建议内部推广优先级，还设有发布板块展示新功能与产品更新。原始使用量不足以衡量采用成熟度，需关注功能利用率、工作流复杂性、参与一致性及跨业务组、产品领域和角色的采用模式。Contract Intelligence旨在协助内部团队处理 incoming 协议的接收与合同审查，提供AI驱动的工作流用于接收、分类和初步标记，并能从过往协议中提取后备立场和首选语言，同时自动更新剧本以反映客户谈判姿态变化。默认设置下剧本更新需批准，但客户可选择自动应用。该工具还提供合同趋势、异常条款、即将到来的义务及整个合同组合中谈判立场的洞察。开发该工具是回应客户反馈，即其合同工作流分散在过多不同平台，限制了速度和效率。目前Docusign、Spellbook、Luminance、Definely、LegalOn、Ironclad、Leah、Tonkean、Onit和Ivo等多家供应商提供合同智能、审查和管理工具。
news.bodyHtml:
The company announced Wednesday the release of adoption management tool Command Center, followed Thursday by the announcement of the launch of Contract Intelligence, a new contract review offering.

Command Center was developed with design partners from Haynes and Boone, Foley & Lardner, Clayton Utz, Rajah & Tann, and Dentsu. Harvey has created waitlists for early access to both products, with general availability expected in the third quarter of this year.

What It Is: Command Center is an analytics and advisory tool designed to help customers optimize their deployment of Harvey. The center is designed to answer users’ natural language questions about how adoption of the platform differs across practice groups and experience levels, what workflows and prompt types are most heavily used, and how the most engaged users differ from others. The new offering also uses anonymized, aggregated data from more than 1,500 Harvey deployments to allow customers to benchmark their usage against peer organizations.

Command Center also includes a recommendation capability designed to identify platform features peer organization have enabled and suggest priorities for internal rollouts. It also features a release section that highlights newly added features and product updates.

“Raw usage volume alone is not a sufficient measure of adoption maturity,” Harvey chief product officer Anique Drumright told Law.com in response to written questions. “We look at a broader set of signals including feature utilization, workflow sophistication, consistency of engagement, and adoption patterns across practice groups, product areas and roles to understand how deeply Harvey is being integrated into workflows.”

Contract Intelligence is designed to assist in-house teams with intake and contract review on incoming agreements. The tool will provide artificial intelligence-powered workflows for intake, triage and initial markups, and is built to surface fallback positions and preferred language from past agreements while automatically updating playbooks to reflect changes in customers’ negotiating postures. Playbook updates require approval under default settings, but they can be applied automatically at the preference of the customer.

Contract Intelligence also provides insight into contract trends, outlier clauses, impending obligations and negotiated positions across the breadth of an organization’s contract portfolio.

Why It’s Needed: Command Center is intended to help innovation, knowledge management and legal operations teams measure how their organizations are adopting Harvey and quantify the return on their investments in the platform.

“Most organizations today can see baseline usage activity, but those approaches fall short in helping them understand adoption quality, what’s driving value across teams and practice groups, and where they stand relative to peer organizations,” Drumright said.

Contract Intelligence is intended to automate routine contract workflows, allowing legal teams to save time and focus on larger strategic challenges. It is also intended to help teams manage risks by surfacing obligations and highlighting provisions that deviate from company norms and playbooks.

Drumright said Harvey developed the tool in response to feedback from customers that their contracting workflows were spread across too many disparate platforms, limiting the speed and efficiency of their work.

“Legal teams currently juggle contract intake, playbooks, review and negotiation knowledge across disconnected platforms,” she said. “Because so much valuable information is buried across these surfaces, we often hear that customers want a way to surface and learn from those insights.”

The Competition: A number of vendors offer contract intelligence, review and management tools, including Docusign, Spellbook, Luminance, Definely, LegalOn, Ironclad, Leah, Tonkean, Onit and Ivo.

news.titleEn: The Silent Revolution: Scaling the CIA’s AI Frontier
news.titleZh: 静默革命：拓展CIA的人工智能前沿
news.summaryZh:
在特别竞争研究项目（SCSP）峰会上，中央情报局（CIA）副局长迈克尔·埃利斯发表简报，将当前技术变革定性为堪比工业革命的全球性转型。CIA已跨越实验阶段，2025年管理了超过300个人工智能项目。人工智能竞赛”与“中国挑战”已被视为同一优先事项。中国计划在2030年前超越美国成为人工智能主导力量，其“举国”模式无视个人权利。美国的策略是“冲刺-马拉松”混合模式：短期塑造全球人工智能架构，长期确保民主价值观成为未来基础代码。

在操作层面，埃利斯勾勒了未来十年人工智能从工具转变为自主任务伙伴的路线图。两年内，每个分析平台都将内置机密生成式人工智能，用于起草判断和编辑。CIA已成功生成首份由人工智能撰写的情报报告，自动化代理正在扫描海量数据流，标记人类可能忽略的“自信错误”或异常模式。埃利斯宣布了CIA采购框架，利用独特法定权限大幅缩短采购时间，并设立企业合作办公室，向科技行业传递“CIA开放商业”的信号。2025年，CIA技术相关外国情报报告翻倍，新兴技术开源报告增至三倍。网络安全之战将是人工智能之战，不能允许单一公司的意愿剥夺CIA使用人工智能工具，也不应认为单一公司拥有显著优势。中国正积极“蒸馏”美国模型，逆向工程创新以支持其监控国家。最终，情报的未来不仅取决于谁拥有最好的间谍，还取决于谁拥有最好的权重、偏差和算力。
news.bodyText:
In the hushed, high-stakes corridors of the Special Competitive Studies Project (SCSP) summit, **Michael Ellis**, Deputy Director of the **Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)**, delivered a briefing that felt less like a standard government update and more like a tech keynote from the bleeding edge.

As a technologist, listening to Ellis, the youngest person to ever hold his office, was a revelation. We aren’t just watching the CIA _use_ AI; we are witnessing the agency’s transition into an **AI-native intelligence service**. From the “Corona” satellites of the 1950s to the LLMs of 2026, the blueprint remains the same: pairing clandestine mission requirements with the raw, iterative power of Silicon Valley.

**The Macro View: The Industrial Revolution of Intelligence**

Ellis framed the current shift as a “global technological transformation” on par with the Industrial Revolution. In the macro sense, the CIA has moved past the experimental phase. In 2025 alone, the agency managed over **300 AI projects**.

The most significant strategic takeaway? The “AI race” and the “China challenge” are now officially considered the same priority. Ellis was blunt: China aims to surpass the U.S. as the dominant AI power by 2030, leveraging a “whole country” approach that ignores individual rights to fuel its models. For the U.S., the strategy is a **“Sprint-Marathon” hybrid**: a sprint to mold the immediate global architecture of AI, and a marathon to ensure democratic values remain the foundational code of the future.

**The Micro View: AI Co-workers and the End of Red Tape**

On a granular level, the “future of work” at Langley looks remarkably like the most advanced dev shops in the private sector. Ellis detailed a roadmap where AI shifts from a tool to an **autonomous mission partner** within a decade.

**Key Operational Milestones:**

*   **AI Co-workers:** Within two years, every analytical platform will have classified Generative AI built-in to draft judgments and edit for tradecraft.
*   **The First AI-Generated Intel Report:** Ellis revealed that the CIA has already successfully produced its first-ever intelligence report generated by AI, a milestone for the Directorate of Operations.
*   **Triage Agents:** Automated agents are now scanning massive data streams to flag “confidently wrong” or outlier patterns that humans would miss, effectively acting as a first-line filter for human analysts.

**Notable Insights from Deputy Director Michael Ellis**

“The battle of cybersecurity will be a battle of artificial intelligence… Whoever designs and capitalizes on the best AI models will wield enormous power.”

“We cannot allow the whims of a single company to deprive CIA from using AI tools… we should not fall into the trap of thinking that a single company possesses a significant advantage over others.”

“China views AI dominance as a way to secure a technological economic advantage… It wants the world to operate on a Chinese developed architecture. We can’t let that happen.”

* * *

**The New Acquisition Framework: Speed as a Target**

Perhaps the most “clever” part of Ellis’s strategy is the administrative overhaul. He announced the **CIA Acquisition Framework**, which utilizes the agency’s unique statutory authorities to slash procurement timelines. The message to the tech industry was clear: **“CIA is open for business.”** By creating the **Office of Corporate Partnerships**, the agency is actively removing the “stovepipes” that once made government contracts a nightmare for startups. They aren’t just buying off-the-shelf software; they are inviting the private sector to solve “Hollywood-style” prototypes, customized AI solutions for the world’s most complex field operations.

**The Adversarial Pulse: Quantifying the Threat**

Directly addressing the competition, Ellis highlighted that China is aggressively “distilling” U.S. models, reverse-engineering our innovation to fuel their surveillance state. To counter this, the CIA hasn’t just increased its defense; it has increased its collection. In 2025, the agency **doubled its tech-related foreign intelligence reporting** and **tripled its open-source reporting** on emerging tech.

To put the scale of the challenge in perspective, consider the following data points on global AI adoption and demographics that influence the strategic landscape:

**Metric****Estimated Value (2025-2026)**
**Global AI Users**~800 Million (10% of world population)
**CIA AI Projects**300+ Active Initiatives
**China AI Dominance Goal**Year 2030
**U.S. Tech Intel Reporting**200% Increase (YoY)

**Final Takeaway**

Michael Ellis didn’t just give a speech; he provided a manifesto for **Assurance through Innovation**. The CIA is betting big on the idea that human judgment must guide AI, but AI must scale human judgment. As we look toward the next decade, the “human-in-the-loop” model is evolving into a “human-on-the-loop” model, where officers manage teams of AI agents to keep pace with an adversarial OODA loop that never sleeps.

The future of intelligence isn’t just about who has the best spies; it’s about who has the best weights, biases, and compute. And according to Ellis, Langley is running at full speed to ensure those weights lean toward freedom.

news.bodyHtml:
We sat down with Greg Sando, founder of WorkCloud, to learn how they help law firms of all shapes and sizes trade in outdated, manual processes for smarter, more scalable ways of working.

Can you briefly introduce your firm and the types of law firms you typically work with?

At WorkCloud, we focus on shaping processes into seamless, innovative digital solutions by leveraging best in class software such as Actionstep, smart integrations, and unparalleled implementation experience. Over the years we have refined our processes in having worked with law firms, ranging from sole practitioners to multi-office, multi-practice firms, community legal centres, government departments, accountants, and tax advisory firms.

How long have you been an Actionstep implementation partner, and what attracted you to the platform initially?

We have been involved in training and onboarding new Actionstep Consulting Partners over the past 14 years. We work with over 400 organizations and have supported implementations of Actionstep’s practice management platform for more than 400 law firm users to date. As WorkCloud’s founder, I was initially attracted to Actionstep’s intuitive interface, cloud-based technology, and the power that firms can harness using Actionstep’s customisable list views and workflows.

What are the most common operational or workflow issues you see in firms before implementation?

More firms than we’d like to acknowledge are mired in outdated, inefficient, admin heavy manual processes. This is particularly prevalent in client onboarding, information gathering, internal and external collaboration, document generation, time recording and billing, and internal reporting and performance tracking.

How do manual intake, data entry, or disconnected systems usually show up as pain points for law firms?

Aside from staff frustration, when manual tasks, data entry, and disconnection bubble up it often results in double or triple data entry into multiple systems (depending on your law firm’s tech stack), inconsistent documentation going out to clients, onerous and convoluted billing processes, and the loss of countless hours in billable time that hurt a law firm’s bottom line.

Migrating to new tech can feel overwhelming for many law firms, how do you help firms move from legacy or patchwork systems to Actionstep without disrupting daily work?

Understandably so! But it doesn’t need to feel that way when you have the right plan in place and do the upfront work first before switching. We use a range of project management methodologies to ensure a smooth and seamless transition for firms moving away from their outdated legacy systems to Actionstep’s modern solution. We adopt a personalised, consultative approach from kick-off all the way through a firm being up and running. This includes the initial scoping and discovery stages, project planning, user training, go-live, and support, ensuring minimal downtime and disruption to a law firm’s routine tasks and processes.

What does innovation mean to you in the context of legal technology and workflows?

It’s about understanding a firms goals and strategies, then working with them to create bespoke, creative solutions that adapt to how they work as a firm. In doing so, it is essential to encourage firms to embrace change management and technology not as a challenge or burden, but as an opportunity. When harnessed correctly, these tools can help tackle inefficiencies, reduce risk, and make the provision of legal services more accessible and scalable.

What excites you most about working with Actionstep’s platform and community of law firms?

We love partnering with firms that embrace innovation and sharing ideas on how these firms can best use Actionstep’s capabilities to align to their business goals and ambitions, today, tomorrow, and years out.

What would you say to a firm that feels “too busy” to modernize its operations?

It’s worth making the time now and getting the right software in place as this will ultimately save the firm time and money in the future. A firm should also consider the ‘hidden costs’ they are incurring in retaining outdated technology and ineDicient processes and the extent to which it will be more disruptive, expensive and difficult to change and ‘catch up’ to their competitors later.

What trends are you seeing in how modern law firms think about operations and technology?

Firms are increasingly looking to update and future proof their organizations across a full software tech stack. We’re seeing firms become increasingly eager to be ‘ahead of the curve’ when it comes to making use of intelligent, AI-powered tools, dynamic reporting, and the automation of routine administrative tasks. They’re embracing new, dynamic ways of working more collaboratively with their clients. More recently, there’s been a big wave of firms moving toward compliancy and being prepared for the upcoming AML/CTF mandate in Australia.

Ready to modernise your firm’s operations and unlock the full power of Actionstep?

WorkCloud’s team of implementation experts are here to help you make the switch — seamlessly, strategically, and with minimal disruption to your day-to-day. Get in touch with WorkCloud today to start your journey toward a smarter, more efficient practice.

news.bodyHtml:
Latest release adds AI work code prediction and one-click narrative compliance, plus more of the timekeeping flexibility professional services firms need to protect earned revenue and drive firmwide adoption.

PALO ALTO, Calif. — May 21, 2026 — Intapp (NASDAQ: INTA), the governed AI platform for professional firms in highly regulated industries, today announced the latest release of Intapp Time. The release introduces new AI capabilities and timekeeping experiences that make it even easier to capture every hour of work — AI work code prediction, configurable narrative tone and style enforcement, a new timeline view, and mobile timekeeping enhancements.

Intapp Time makes every engagement more profitable by capturing every hour worked, protecting revenue already earned, and generating insights to help firms continuously improve performance. Already trusted by the world’s leading professional services firms, Intapp Time provides engagement intelligence and revenue governance, helping drive $12 billion in incremental billings each year.

“Intapp Time helps the world’s leading firms operate more profitably, with total compliance and maximum flexibility for every professional,” said Ken Houseman, Vice President and General Manager of Time at Intapp. “Now we’re accelerating our AI roadmap to eliminate the moments where revenue leaks: the wrong code, the non-compliant narrative, the entry that never got recorded.”

Revenue leakage rarely occurs all at once. It happens in the moments between work and time capture — when entries are delayed, coded inconsistently, or returned during billing review due to incomplete narratives. Building on the reengineered web and mobile experiences released in August 2025 and February 2026, the new Intapp Time release applies AI directly within a firm’s existing time entry workflow to accurately capture more time faster.

“Our clients told us the most powerful place to apply AI is inside the workflow their people already use, not next to it,” explained Houseman. “That’s what this release delivers. Capturing every hour worked and protecting earned revenue is the foundation, not the ceiling.”

What’s new

Our latest Intapp Time release offers several new capabilities:

  • AI work code prediction: Protect revenue by eliminating the coding errors that result in downstream billing issues and write-downs. AI knows when phase, task, and activity codes are required and adds them based on the narrative and matter coding history weighted by recency. Rather than manually look up, enter, and second-guess every entry, timekeepers can simply review and accept them.
  • Configurable narrative tone and style enforcement: Effortlessly deliver consistent, scalable compliance with firm and client requirements. Administrators configure rules covering outside counsel guidelines, restricted terms, and block billing. AI then validates every narrative and recommends rewrites that timekeepers can accept with a single click at the point of time entry.
  • Timeline view: Eliminate revenue leakage caused by underreported or lost time. Intapp Time’s new chronological view lays out time entries throughout the workday alongside AI-captured activity. Timekeepers can then map activities to the gaps in their day, turning them into complete time entries with just a few clicks.
  • Mobile timekeeping enhancements: Capture work in the moments it’s most likely to be lost. On-the-go timekeepers can now start, stop, and switch timers in the Intapp mobile app using Siri voice commands, run timers in the background, and automatically sync offline activity when connectivity is restored.

Today’s release is another step in Intapp Time’s accelerating cadence of AI innovation, with each enhancement building on the last to help make every engagement more profitable. This summer, Intapp will share what’s next — including agentic AI workflows embedded in Intapp Time that further automate critical firm processes, reduce friction in day-to-day work, surface more engagement intelligence, and drive profitable compliant growth.

Availability

The latest capabilities in this release of Intapp Time are available now on Intapp Cloud Infrastructure. Learn more or request a demo at intapp.com/time-tracking, or contact your Intapp account team.

About Intapp

Intapp (NASDAQ: INTA) is the governed AI platform for professional firms in highly regulated industries. Intapp’s vertically tailored agentic solutions are built for the specialized workflows, complex relationship networks, and professional compliance requirements of accounting, consulting, investment banking, law, private capital, and real assets firms. By applying Firm AI to core processes and data, Intapp helps partners, dealmakers, and advisors drive firm growth, manage compliance, and improve profitability. Learn why the world’s top firms trust Intapp’s industry-specific enterprise solutions at intapp.com

news.titleEn: Justima Spins Out of Osborne Clarke
news.titleZh: Justima从Osborne Clarke分拆独立
news.summaryZh: 国际律师事务所Osborne Clarke完成其历史上首次分拆：德国监管监测平台Justima将独立运营。Osborne Clarke作为战略投资者持有Justima股份并保持多数股权，该投资通过其德国法律科技实体进行，以保持灵活性。Justima由Alexander Lilienbeck（CEO）和Christian Braun（CTO）创立，Gereon Abendroth任董事长兼总经理，他同时是Osborne Clarke合伙人及全球AI管理委员会主席。平台以AI代理每日分析超过200个法律与监管来源，向客户推送与业务相关的更新。分拆后核心团队为五人，两位联合创始人来自Osborne Clarke Solutions，另有两名新员工于2026年4月加入，并计划在2026年下半年进一步扩张。团队采用精简架构，由AI代理承担大量运营工作流，人员专注于工程、监管专业知识和客户关系等不可替代领域。Justima作为独立公司注册，拥有自身管理、基础设施和市场存在，独立进入市场，同时嵌入Osborne Clarke的监管与技术能力。产品为面向跨境欧洲监管监测的AI原生SaaS平台，是软件产品而非法律服务。分拆时机基于三点：平台已完成结构化验证，约30家企业用户已使用数月；欧洲监管复杂性持续增长，内部团队仍依赖碎片化提醒和手动监测，关键挑战在于识别对特定业务真正重要的信息；技术已就绪，Osborne Clarke在监管领域的布局与顶级AI工程团队相结合。公司认为应构建垂直AI系统，将领域专业知识工程化到产品中，而非在运行时提示通用模型。Justima处理高容量监测层，更早更清晰地呈现相关监管变化；法律建议仍由客户选择的律所另行处理。
news.bodyHtml:
In what is the first spin out in international law firm Osborne Clarke’s history, Justima, a Germany-based regulatory monitoring platform, is forming a separate business. The firm will retain an ownership share, they told Artificial Lawyer. (See AL interview below).

Using AI agents Justima continuously monitors hundreds of European and other international regulatory sources, delivering business-relevant updates to clients. It was created by Alexander Lilienbeck, CEO, and Christian Braun, CTO, and the management team is completed by Gereon Abendroth, Chairman & Managing Director, Partner at Osborne Clarke and Chair of the firm’s global AI Management Board, (pictured).

They explained that the platform analyses more than 200 legal and regulatory sources daily, and that such ‘monitoring tasks have consumed substantial resources within corporate legal departments while still carrying the risk of critical updates being overlooked’.

AL Interview

How many people in the spin-off?

Justima launches with a core team of five: co-founders Alexander Lilienbeck, CEO, and Christian Braun, CTO, both from Osborne Clarke Solutions; Gereon Abendroth as Chairman & Managing Director focusing on the strategic aspects; and two additional hires who joined in April 2026.

Further growth is planned for the second half of 2026. The lean team structure is a deliberate architectural choice: AI agents handle a wide range of operational workflows, allowing the human team to focus on areas where judgement is irreplaceable – e.g. engineering, regulatory expertise, and direct customer relationships.

What company structure will it have?

Justima is incorporated as a separate company, with its own management, infrastructure and market presence. 

Justima will go to market independently while being strategically embedded in Osborne Clarke’s broader regulatory and technology capabilities. The product is designed for cross-border European regulatory monitoring and is built as an AI-native SaaS platform. It is a software product, not a legal services offering.

Will OC still own part of it? 

Yes, Osborne Clarke holds a shareholding in Justima as a strategic investor and holds the majority. The investment is structured through Osborne Clarke’s German legal tech entity for the sake of agility. 

Why do this now? 

The timing reflects three things coming together: validation, market need and technology readiness.

First, Justima has completed a structured validation phase. Around 30 corporate users have been using the platform productively for  several months, allowing the team to test it against real regulatory workloads and refine the relevance logic with Osborne Clarke’s regulatory practice.

Second, the market need is clear. Regulatory complexity across Europe continues to grow, while many in-house teams still rely on fragmented alerts, newsletters and manual monitoring. The issue is no longer access to information; it is identifying what actually matters to a specific business.

Third, the technology is ready. Osborne Clarke was well placed to act on that moment: it combines a strong footprint and strategic focus in regulatory work with a top-tier AI engineering team experienced in regulated domains.

Now is the time to build a vertical AI system. We have seen major improvements with General-purpose legal AI systems and even Foundation model providers tipping into legal. The next step closes the gap between a general-purpose model and an enterprise workflow: AI systems integrated directly into the operational process, with domain expertise engineered into the product rather than prompted into a generalist model at runtime.

This is why Justima is built as vertical AI. A product engineered bottom-up for one task – regulatory monitoring for corporate compliance teams. From our perspective a generic assistant repurposed for the same problem will not get you there.

The broader principle is simple: Osborne Clarke does not believe clients should pay lawyer rates for work that software can do. They should get lawyers where lawyers add the most value: judgement, interpretation, risk and strategy.

That is exactly where Justima fits. It handles the high-volume monitoring layer and surfaces relevant regulatory change earlier and more clearly. Legal advice remains separate: if a client wants advice on interpretation, enforcement risk or implementation, that is handled by the law firm the client chooses, under a separate mandate. Justima is a software product, not a legal services provider.

Thanks and congrats!

news.titleZh: Harvey宣布面向内部律师推出合同智能产品
news.summaryZh:
继昨日双项发布后，Harvey宣布推出Contract Intelligence，专为内部律师打造。该产品设有早期访问等候名单，计划于第三季度全面开放。与Command Center项目一样，该产品是与客户共同设计，以满足其需求。

该平台功能包括：加速受理与合同审查，简化受理、分类和合同审查流程，使法律团队减少常规标记时间，投入更多战略工作；从更强立场谈判，从先前协议中提取后备立场、条款语言和谈判模式，并在新合同签署时自动更新操作手册；提供组合级可见性，展示合同趋势、谈判立场、异常条款和即将到来的义务，帮助团队管理风险并支持业务。

Harvey正大力进军内部法律市场，原因在于全球大公司的内部法律团队数量远超大型律所。内部团队会向外部律所施压，要求其使用相同的法律AI公司，因此赢得内部客户有助于转化律所客户。但许多内部团队缺乏内部法律技术支持，部署帮助的重担落在Harvey身上。

另讯，Legora宣布聘请Zeynep Inanoglu Ozdemir担任首席营销官，她此前在Atlassian担任CMO，更早前在Palo Alto Networks担任类似职务。Artificial Lawyer下周休假，周五将发布Wrap，6月1日前无常规新闻。Legal Innovators Europe会议将于6月24日至25日在巴黎举行。
news.bodyHtml:
After yesterday’s double reveal, Harvey is announcing the arrival of Contract Intelligence, which is especially made for inhouse lawyers. It has a waitlist for early access, with general availability in Q3.

As with the Command Center project it was co-designed with customers to give them what they want, the legal AI platform said.  

Here’s what it can do:

  • ‘Accelerate intake and contract reviews – Streamline intake, triage, and contract review workflows so legal teams can spend less time on routine markups and more time on strategic work.
  • Negotiate from stronger positions – Surface fallback positions, clause language, and negotiation patterns from prior agreements, while automatically updating playbooks as new contracts are signed.
  • Operate with portfolio-wide visibility – Provide visibility into contract trends, negotiated positions, outlier provisions, and upcoming obligations to help teams better manage risk and support the business.’

Is this a big deal?

Well, it’s got a distinctly modern CLM-ish feel to it. And that’s not an accident. Harvey is going very heavily into the inhouse world, just as several of its rivals are. Why? Because there are way more inhouse legal teams at large companies globally than there are Big Law firms.

Also there is an added bonus, as noted earlier today, (see AL story), inhouse teams clearly put pressure on their law firm advisers to use the same legal AI companies they use – at least where that is possible. So, an inhouse win can later help to convert a law firm win.

In short, building out an inhouse client base – which they’ve already done to a large extent – makes strategic and financial sense. The one drawback here is that many inhouse teams may not have much in the way of internal legal tech support, which puts the weight of deployment help very much onto Harvey.

—

P.S. in other Hargorasphere news, Legora has announced that it’s hired Zeynep Inanoglu Ozdemir as Chief Marketing Officer. Previously she was CMO at Atlassian, and was in a similar role before that at Palo Alto Networks. Congrats to her. Question: do you get to hang out with Jude Law if you’re their CMO?

–
