news.titleEn: Legora Launches aOS ‘Agentic Operating System’
news.titleZh: Legora推出aOS“代理式操作系统”
news.summaryZh: Legora推出名为aOS的代理式操作系统，称其标志着“代理式法律的开端”。该系统为专为法律团队构建的代理式操作系统，支持从案件受理到客户交付的复杂工作端到端执行。其核心是Legora Agent，可自主持续执行法律工作，包括研究、起草和事务性工作，使律师能够大规模审阅并专注于关键决策。这是他们三年来一直努力构建的成果。aOS的独特之处在于它是一个单一连接系统，促进法律工作的信息流、沟通和执行。该系统编排代理自主持续执行法律工作，从第一英里案件受理、研究、起草和审阅，到最后一英里客户交付。例如，一方在午夜发送合同红线，到律师次日早上坐下时，Legora Agent已审阅每处修改、标记需关注的问题并起草好回复。然而，律师是否大规模使用这些代理能力将决定其影响。如果律所和内部团队仅偶尔使用代理处理小任务，影响将微乎其微。许多律师面临的挑战是必须真正信任代理完成工作，这在多方面都很困难。但如果他们拥抱代理，新的法律代理黎明有望到来。Junestrand总结道，可能性的上限一直受限于人类能力，Legora aOS改变了这一点，它是使法律团队能够以以前不可能达到的规模、速度和质量运用机器智能的操作系统。
news.bodyHtml:
Legora has launched what it’s calling aOS, an agentic operating system, which they say marks the ‘dawn of Agentic Law’. Sounds great. What is it?

They explained that it’s ‘a purpose-built agentic operating system that enables legal teams to execute complex work end-to-end, from matter intake through to client delivery’.

The ‘Legora Agent’ – which is the active bit in the aOS – ‘drives autonomous legal execution, handling research, drafting, and busy work continuously so lawyers can review it at scale and focus on the decisions that matter’.

In short, as with several other companies, they are going all in on agents.

Max Junestrand, CEO and Co-Founder of Legora, commented: ‘It’s something we’ve been building toward for three years.’

But, you may then say: ‘But, we already have agents, and workflows and related capabilities, what’s different about this?’

Legora noted that what makes this launch stand out is that its ‘aOS’ is a ‘single connected system that facilitates the flow of information, communication, and execution of legal work’.

Maybe think of it as a rail network that sits next to other transport systems, i.e. it’s got its own infrastructure all around it.

Or, as they added: ‘The Legora aOS … orchestrates agents to perform legal work autonomously and continuously – from first-mile matter intake, through research, drafting, and review, to last-mile client delivery.

‘At the heart of the aOS is the Legora Agent – the engine that powers it all. A party sends a contract redline at midnight. By the time the lawyer sits down the next morning, the Legora Agent has already reviewed every change, flagged the issues that need attention, and drafted a response ready to send.’

You get the picture.

So, more than just another workflow, but an entire system working within Legora to support agentic activity, such as the example noted above.

Is this a big deal?

Well, it all depends on whether lawyers actually use these agentic opportunities at scale.

If firms and inhouse teams just dabble with them and send the occasional agent to do the occasional small task, then the impact – despite all the work Legora and others have put into agents – will be minimal.

The challenge for many lawyers with agents is that they really have to trust them to do the work. That’s hard for lawyers in multiple ways.

However, if they do embrace agents, then the hope of a new Legal Agentic Dawn could happen………

Or as Junestrand concluded: ‘The ceiling of what’s possible has always been limited by human capacity. The Legora aOS changes that. It is the operating system that enables legal teams to operate with machine intelligence at a scale, speed, and quality that simply wasn’t possible before.’

More about Legora here.

news.summaryZh: 内部法律部门的转型历来以合同为主线，CLM平台、起草自动化和结构化工作流重塑了法务运作。相比之下，诉讼因不可预测、依赖判断且需求多变，长期难以纳入平台或流程，争议解决职能大多保持被动、偶发，并高度依赖外部律师提供法律专业知识和运营基础设施。诉讼中机构知识庞大而脆弱，人员变动时极易丢失；接手活跃诉讼的内部律师常发现文件散落各处，大量时间用于重建背景，导致在知识不完整时做出战略决策。诉讼工作空间正是为解决这一运营缺口而设计，它将争议全生命周期集中一处，涵盖初始指示、建议链、披露材料、证人陈述、专家报告和通信，使新成员数小时而非数周内跟上进度，外部律师与内部团队使用相同材料，总法律顾问可查看所有活跃事项。总法律顾问的角色正因AI工具加速和预算限制而改变，越来越多地负责争议战略层、制定AI治理政策并监督技术部署。内部团队借助AI能吸收更多工作，但更重要的转变在于内外部律师的合作方式：大型复杂争议仍需外部律师的专业和资源深度，而共享可见性、更好沟通和战略对齐，使总法律顾问能减少外部支出，并创建内部与外部律师真正合作的诉讼职能。第一代诉讼技术聚焦电子取证，范围狭窄，未创建持续运营环境。重大商业争议涉及多年积累的庞大数据，人工审查不可行，抽样则带来风险。
news.bodyHtml:
By Eimear McCann, TrialView.

Historically, the transformation of in-house legal departments has been narrated as a contracts story. The rise of the CLM platform, the automation of routine drafting, the shift from email chains to structured workflows; each of these developments reshaped how corporate legal teams operate, proffering GCs with a new language for demonstrating efficiency and value. Contracts became a function you could manage, measure, and improve.

Litigation has historically been pinned down by a very different, embedded narrative, i.e., it is too unpredictable, too dependent on judgement and much too variable in its demands to fit neatly into a platform or a process. While the transactional side of in-house legal departments was being systematically rebuilt around technology, the disputes function largely continued as it always had, reactive, episodic, and heavily dependent on external counsel to provide not just the legal expertise but the operational infrastructure too.

The Operational Gap

The CLM market addressed both a tangible workflow and a data problem, there were too many contracts, moving through too many hands, with too little visibility. The solution, a structured platform managing the lifecycle from request to renewal, was relatively straightforward to implement.

Litigation, of course, presents a different set of challenges. Disputes are not linear, they escalate and de-escalate; key personnel change on both sides. External counsel, barristers, experts, witnesses, and in some cases litigation funders all need to interact with the same materials at different times, with different levels of access, across timelines that can span years. The institutional knowledge embedded in a piece of litigation is vast, fragile, and constantly at risk of being lost when people move on.

Ask any in-house lawyer who has taken over a live piece of litigation from a predecessor what the experience is like, and the answer will likely be the same:  files are inherited in various forms, whether scattered across email threads or lost in the vortex of shared folders.  So much time can be lost simply trying to reconstruct the context, ultimately resulting in strategic decisions being made in an incomplete universe of knowledge.

Such is the operational gap that a litigation workspace addresses. Representing much more than a document repository, a litigation workspace is a purpose-built environment, designed to hold the entire lifecycle of a dispute in one place, encompassing initial instructions, the advice chain, disclosure materials, witness statements, expert reports and correspondence. Critically, it is a place where new team members can get up to speed in hours rather than weeks, where external counsel and in-house teams work from the same materials, and where the GC has visibility across every active matter.

Collaboration is Changing

The role of the General Counsel (and the in-house function more generally) is changing in many ways, driven as much by the fast acceleration of AI tools as by the usual budgetary constraints. GCs are increasingly expected to own the strategic layer of disputes, set AI governance policy and take direct responsibility for how the technology is deployed and overseen within their organisations. This inevitably narrows the historic tech engagement gap between the corporates and law firms, and dynamics are tangibly shifting.

In-house teams can now absorb more work, largely due to AI tools; but the more consequential shift is not about who does the work, but rather about how in-house and external counsel work together. Large, complex disputes will continue to require the specialism and resource depth that only external counsel can provide; however, what is changing is the quality of the collaboration around those instructions. With shared visibility, better communication and a strategic alignment thanks to shared systems, the GC who gets this right will ultimately reduce external spend, whilst also helping to create a litigation function where in-house and external counsel operate as genuine partners.

From Workaround to Workflow

What is new is not the concept of a litigation workspace but rather the technology available to make it genuinely useful. The first generation of litigation technology focused on e-discovery, a valuable, but narrow offering. It addressed one stage of the lifecycle and did not create the continuous operational environment that in-house teams actually need.

A significant commercial dispute involves vast amounts of data, accumulated over many years. Human review becomes simply untenable. Moreover, sampling them creates risk. What AI makes possible is something qualitatively different, a system that processes the entire corpus, identifies inconsistencies between witness accounts and contemporaneous documents, builds a chronology linked directly to source material, and answers specific questions about the evidence in natural language, in seconds rather than days.

In-house teams have historically been consumers of analysis produced by external counsel. AI-powered litigation platforms change that, making it possible for in-house teams to interrogate their own evidence and engage external counsel as executors of a strategy they have helped to shape rather than as its sole architects.

One Space for Every Case

TrialView was ultimately built with this vision in mind, rooted in the conviction that every dispute deserves to be managed from a single, secure, intelligent workspace, from the first instruction to the final submission.

For in-house teams building a disputes function, TrialView can provide the operational foundation the function needs. Bundle creation is automated, with court-compliant output in minutes rather than days. AI-powered Case Intelligence processes the entire document corpus, building timelines, surfacing inconsistencies, and answering evidential questions with the accuracy that high-stakes litigation demands. The same platform manages case preparation and hosts the hearing itself, including evidence presentation, video conferencing, and integrated real-time transcription.

In-house counsel, external solicitors, barristers, experts, and witnesses work within the same secure workspace, with access controlled, communications captured, and institutional knowledge preserved regardless of who comes and goes on either side.

The tools are here, the appetite is growing, and AI has created something that did not previously exist: a common space for every case, every party, every stage. There has never been a better moment to move from reactive dispute management to something genuinely collaborative and strategic.

To learn more about how TrialView can help you, please see here.


–

About the Author: Eimear McCann is a former lawyer, and Commercial Director at TrialView, an award-winning AI platform designed to streamline dispute resolution processes. Eimear is also a visiting lecturer at BPP and sits on the Law Society Technology & Law Committee.

With shared visibility, better communication and a strategic alignment thanks to shared systems, the GC who gets this right will ultimately reduce external spend, whilst also helping to create a litigation function where in-house and external counsel operate as genuine partners.

What is new is not the concept of a litigation workspace but rather the technology available to make it genuinely useful. The first generation of litigation technology focused on e-discovery, a valuable, but narrow offering. It addressed one stage of the lifecycle and did not create the continuous operational environment that in-house teams actually need.

A significant commercial dispute involves vast amounts of data, accumulated over many years. Human review becomes simply untenable. Moreover, sampling them creates risk. What AI makes possible is something qualitatively different, a system that processes the entire corpus, identifies inconsistencies between witness accounts and contemporaneous documents, builds a chronology linked directly to source material, and answers specific questions about the evidence in natural language, in seconds rather than days.

In-house teams have historically been consumers of analysis produced by external counsel. AI-powered litigation platforms change that, making it possible for in-house teams to interrogate their own evidence and engage external counsel as executors of a strategy they have helped to shape rather than as its sole architects.

TrialView was ultimately built with this vision in mind, rooted in the conviction that every dispute deserves to be managed from a single, secure, intelligent workspace, from the first instruction to the final submission.

For in-house teams building a disputes function, TrialView can provide the operational foundation the function needs. Bundle creation is automated, with court-compliant output in minutes rather than days. AI-powered Case Intelligence processes the entire document corpus, building timelines, surfacing inconsistencies, and answering evidential questions with the accuracy that high-stakes litigation demands. The same platform manages case preparation and hosts the hearing itself, including evidence presentation, video conferencing, and integrated real-time transcription.

In-house counsel, external solicitors, barristers, experts, and witnesses work within the same secure workspace, with access controlled, communications captured, and institutional knowledge preserved regardless of who comes and goes on either side.

The tools are here, the appetite is growing, and AI has created something that did not previously exist: a common space for every case, every party, every stage. There has never been a better moment to move from reactive dispute management to something genuinely collaborative and strategic.

news.bodyHtml:
LexisNexis has expanded its Lexis+ AI platform with Protégé Work, along with a new definition of its LLM-based offering as the ‘foundational infrastructure for legal AI’, plus a raft of improved capabilities (see below).

In terms of ‘Work’, you can ‘select a skill directly or describe a legal goal in natural language. Protégé intelligently routes the request to the appropriate skill or workflow’.

I.e. this is not just a one-shot prompt on the side of one’s work, it’s a multi-faceted system that is wholly integrated into the LexisNexis experience.

As they explained: ‘Instead of generating a single response, Protégé presents a structured plan for the work, giving users visibility and control as it executes tasks and produces review-ready legal work product.

‘Skills support repeatable tasks such as contract comparison, complaint analysis, research synthesis, checklist generation, due diligence, compliance review and playbook-based review.

‘This allows legal teams to reuse proven workflows, apply firm and department standards consistently, and benefit from broader market innovation while keeping work grounded in authoritative LexisNexis content, firm knowledge and trusted workflow safeguards.’

Plus, they added that Lexis+ with Protégé incorporates LexisNexis-developed and Anthropic-powered skills.

They also underlined that LexisNexis is now looking at what their legal AI capabilities can do as foundational infrastructure. I.e. that, as noted, it’s not about dipping in and out occasionally into an LLM with a prompt, but rather having a new AI architecture running all the way through LexisNexis that connects to skills, their curated data, and workflows.

Sean Fitzpatrick, CEO, LexisNexis Global Legal, commented: ‘Legal AI must do more than produce plausible answers. It must produce work that lawyers can verify, defend and trust. Lexis+ with Protégé brings together the content foundation, workflow intelligence, security and model flexibility legal professionals need to use AI at scale without compromising the standards of the profession.’

As well as Work, they highlighted:

  • ‘Protégé Agentic Drafting, which helps lawyers and legal teams produce review-ready work product in minutes.
  • Outputs from Protégé Skills can be delivered in the formats legal teams already use every day. This includes Microsoft Word for drafts, Excel for review tables and structured findings, PowerPoint for client-ready summaries, and PDF for polished, ready-to-use work product.
  • Protégé Workrooms extends legal AI into secure collaboration. Law firms, corporate legal departments and counsel can work together in private, permission-aware spaces where documents, drafts, analysis and AI workflows are shared only as authorized.
  • Shepard’s Verify Trust Markers bring LexisNexis’s trusted citation authority directly into AI-assisted work. The capability identifies legal citations in AI-generated and attorney-drafted content, checks them against LexisNexis authoritative legal sources, and flags citations that cannot be verified as existing.
  • And a reimagined Protégé Vault gives legal professionals a secure intelligence layer for large, complex matters. Teams can analyze documents, PDFs, spreadsheets, images, audio, video and other matter materials in one workspace, with support for up to 100,000 documents per Vault. Outputs link back to source material including exact document passages, spreadsheet rows, images or timestamps so legal teams can verify findings and defend the work product that follows.
  • As well as Protégé BYOK, which gives enterprise and government customers additional control over sensitive information. With Bring Your Own Key encryption, customers can manage their own encryption keys through their chosen key management service and revoke access when required, supporting the data-control expectations of law firms, regulated industries and public-sector legal teams.’

All in all, not just new capabilities, but a larger reframing of what is now possible with their legal AI.

The battle to provide the most comprehensive – and super-useful – legal AI platform continues.

news.titleEn: Hallucinations, Inaccuracies, And The Erosion Of The Rule Of Law
news.titleZh: 幻觉、不准确与法治的侵蚀
news.summaryZh: 2026年5月7日，Stephen Embry在LegalTech Monitor发文指出，又有一家律师事务所因引用不存在的案例而被曝光，这次是世界上最具影响力的律所之一苏利文·克伦威尔律师事务所。该所出现了36处错误，用了三页篇幅来描述这些错误，其中包括从真实案例中捏造的段落。其AI政策未被遵守，并且该所曾设有专门旨在防止此类问题的培训。尽管业界持续讨论教育、政策和罚款，但这些措施似乎并未奏效。问题已不仅仅是律师的懒惰行为。当公众听说律师引用不存在的案例时，他们的第一反应往往是律师为了胜诉而捏造了这些案例。虽然事实并非如此，但这种即时反应本身就说明了问题的严重性。正如法官伯恩斯·阿尔达纳在最近一次美国律师协会会议上所言：“法院的合法性取决于公众的信任和信心。”因此，AI幻觉不仅仅是草率执业的问题，它们正在侵蚀法治本身以及公众对法律的信任。作者提出，我们究竟能做些什么？是加强处罚、律师纪律惩戒，还是更好的教育和意识提升？或许这三者都需要。该文同时发布在Above the Law平台上。
news.bodyText:
Hallucinations, Inaccuracies, And The Erosion Of The Rule Of Law

By Stephen Embry on May 7, 2026

Posted in Uncategorized

Another week. Another law firm caught citing cases that don’t exist. But this time it was Sullivan and Cromwell, one of the most influential firms in the world. 36 errors. Three pages to describe them. Fabricated passages from real cases. S&C said its AI policies weren’t followed. That it had training designed to prevent exactly this.

We can keep talking about education, policies, and fines. We’re doing all of that. But it doesn’t seem to be working. Moreover, it isn’t just a lazy lawyering problem anymore. When the public hears that lawyers are citing cases that don’t exist, their first instinct, as I discovered recently, is that the lawyer made them up to win. Of course,

that’s not what typicaly happened. But the fact that it’s the immediate reaction says something about where we are. As Judge Bernes Aldana put it at a recent ABA conference: “The legitimacy of our courts depends on the public’s trust and confidence.” That’s why AI hallucinations aren’t just a sloppy practice problem. They’re helping to erode of the rule of and trust in law itself.

What can we actually do about it? Stronger penalities? Bar discipline? Better education and awareness? Maybe all three.

My post  for Above the Law.

news.titleEn: Cybersecurity Update: Vibe Coding vs. Verified Code – Can AI Fix the Mess it Created… with Eran Kinsbruner
news.titleZh: 网络安全更新：氛围编程与验证代码——AI能否修复它自己造成的问题……与Eran Kinsbruner对话
news.summaryZh: 本期节目探讨了软件开发领域前所未有的速度差距：代码创建速度与安全保障速度之间的鸿沟正在急剧扩大。我们已进入“机器速度开发”时代，AI不再仅仅是辅助程序员，而是逐渐成为编程主体。然而，大型语言模型生成数百万行代码的同时，也在以“大气层级别”的规模继承和放大人类错误。传统的“扫描并修复”网络安全模式已不堪重负。节目聚焦防御领域的根本性转变：从静态安全工具转向自主的、智能体驱动的安全系统。讨论内容包括：如何利用AI防御其自身创造的风险、企业中“影子AI”的兴起，以及未来安全是否能够完全自愈，还是“人在回路”才是防止数字世界信任全面崩溃的关键。节目分为三个部分：首先设定网络安全格局的基线，然后深入探讨智能体安全领域，最后进行哲学与未来展望。
news.bodyText:
In the history of software development, we have never seen a gap widen as quickly as the one between the speed of creation and the speed of assurance. We have entered the era of ‘Machine-Speed Development,’ where AI isn’t just assisting coders—it’s becoming the coder. But as large language models churn out millions of lines of code, they are also inheriting and scaling human errors at an atmospheric level. The traditional ‘scan and fix’ model of cybersecurity is buckling under this weight.

Today, we are exploring a fundamental shift in the defensive landscape: the move from static security tools to autonomous, agentic security systems. We’re diving into how AI is being harnessed to defend against the very risks it creates, the rise of ‘Shadow AI’ in the enterprise, and whether we are approaching a future where security is entirely self-healing—or if the ‘human in the loop’ is the only thing keeping the digital world from a total trust collapse.

Today, we’ll start with level setting about the cybersecurity landscape, get into the agentic space , and finally a Philosophical & Future Outlook .

news.titleZh: 重新定义增长：受治理的AI对会计与咨询公司的意义
news.summaryZh:
AI正在加速业务拓展前端，其速度超出合规基础设施的设计承载能力。许多公司仍沿用为较慢节奏构建的风险流程，随着交易流加快，这些流程成为收入的制约因素。未实现现代化的公司常感到压力，为跟上节奏而走捷径，但往往恰好在错误会带来最高职业后果的环节走捷径。文中列出的三个连续摩擦点相互叠加，仅修复一个阶段无法缓解压力，瓶颈只会转移。

Intapp Intake在上游解决该问题，利用AI从共享文件中提取关键细节，预填请求并在提交前标记数据缺口，使合规团队收到完整、结构化的信息，减少延迟并加速收入实现。Intapp Conflicts自动化消耗分析师产能的预分析工作，包括构建搜索策略、建立公司树、匹配别名以及查询Intapp Data、Dun & Bradstreet和Moody’s等关联数据源。分析师不再需要花费数小时进行准备工作，有更多时间审查高风险命中，平台会自动升级这些命中以供专家判断。每个结果还可附带生成的分析与决策摘要，形成支持一致、可辩护决策的文档记录。最被低估的风险并非入职期间不完整的尽职调查，而是之后发生的事情。客户情况通过所有权转移、并购活动、制裁新增或负面媒体发生变化。公司常因监控是手动和周期性的而错过这些数据。代理式AI使投资组合层面的持续监控在操作上可行，这是手动流程无法做到的。
news.bodyHtml:
Compliance: Keeping pace with AI-powered growth

AI is accelerating the front end of business development faster than compliance infrastructure was designed to handle. Many firms are still operating with risk processes built for a slower pace — and as deal flow speeds up, those processes become a constraint on revenue.

Firms that haven’t modernized often feel pressured to cut corners so they can keep up — but often cut corners in the exact places where errors carry the highest professional consequences.

Intapp Intake addresses this problem upstream. Using AI, it extracts key details from shared files to pre-populate requests and flag data gaps before submission. Instead of incomplete submissions and multiple follow ups, compliance teams receive complete, structured information — reducing delays and accelerating time to revenue. 

Intapp Conflicts automates the pre-analysis work that consumes analyst capacity — from constructing search strategies and building corporate trees, to matching aliases and querying connected data sources like Intapp Data, Dun & Bradstreet, and Moody’s. Analysts no longer need to spend hours on preparation work, and they have more time to review high-risk hits — which the platform automatically escalates for expert judgement. Every outcome can also be accompanied by a generated summary of the analysis and decisions, creating a documented record that supports consistent, defensible decision-making. 

The most underestimated risk isn’t incomplete diligence during onboarding — it’s what happens after. Client circumstances change through ownership transfers, M&A activity, sanctions additions, or adverse media. Firms often miss this data because monitoring is manual and periodic. Agentic AI makes continuous monitoring operationally viable at the portfolio level in a way that manual processes can’t.

news.titleZh: AI定价会成为向客户转嫁的成本吗？
news.summaryZh:
在科罗拉多州举行的ILTA Evolve会议上，有人多次提及AI可能引发严重的价格上涨。当前定价模式不可持续，Anthropic、OpenAI、谷歌、微软乃至SAP等传统工作技术平台都在朝同一方向调整。触发因素相同：AI打破了按席位收费的经济模式。当价值来自软件访问时，按席位定价合理；当价值来自输出——如做出的决策、处理的文件、筛选的候选人等——供应商的成本不再是固定的，而是可变的，并随使用量扩展。代理工作负载每项任务消耗的token量是标准聊天交互的5到30倍。旧价格下的数学计算不再成立，Anthropic选择坦诚面对。

在Evolve会议上，有人随口提到或许可以借鉴旧的法律研究模式，即按小时收取研究数据库访问费，并将该时间转嫁给客户。考虑到律所的预算方式，这一思路越来越合理。律所缺乏为“未知”计算量做规划的能力。预计始终会有按席位许可，提供行政任务、起草邮件、安排会议等所需的计算量。但一旦涉及客户工作，代理工作流和深度研究就会在token费用上迅速累积。客户也开始期望律所投资AI，因为这能减少他们的总计费小时数。或许可以这样解决两个问题：通过AI减少律师计费小时，但客户需承担AI使用费用。目前按席位固定价格下，特定事项使用AI的成本为零，但这种情况不会持续，也不可能持续。法律市场是否会调整，将AI计算成本转嫁给客户？如果不这样做，律所又如何证明其未定义成本的合理性？

news.bodyText:
Artificial Intelligence | LawFirms

Will AI pricing become a charge-back cost to clients?

By Mike McBride

May 6, 2026 May 6, 2026

Reading Time: 2 minutes

I spent a good part of last week at the ILTA Evolve conference in Colorado, and I heard it mentioned a few times: the potential for very serious price increases.

I wrote last week that the current pricing models are not sustainable . The link from Ed Zitron provides the deep analysis that led him and me to that conclusion.

This week, I found this article – The Anthropic Pricing Shift Is a Signal, Not a Surprise

This isn’t an Anthropic-specific story. OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and even legacy Work Tech platforms like SAP are all moving in the same direction. The trigger is the same everywhere: AI broke per-seat economics. When value came from software access, per-seat pricing made sense. When value comes from outputs: decisions made, documents processed, candidates screened, and the like, the vendor’s cost is no longer fixed. It’s variable, and it scales with usage. Agentic workloads consume anywhere from 5 to 30 times more tokens per task than a standard chat interaction. The math didn’t work at the old price, and Anthropic made a choice: be honest about it.

I, sadly, don’t remember who said it at Evolve, or which session it was said in, but I heard someone almost offhandedly comment that maybe the model would be the old legal research model, where you got billed by the hour for access to the research database and bill that time back to the client.

The more I think about the way law firms budget, the more I think this makes sense.

We don’t have very much capacity to plan out for an “unknown” amount of compute power. I’m assuming there will always be a per-seat license that gives you the level of compute needed for administrative tasks, drafting emails, scheduling meetings, etc. It’s when you start getting into client work that agentic workflows and deep research really start to add up in token expenses. Those are also the areas where clients are starting to expect firms to invest in AI because it reduces their total billed hours.

Maybe we can solve both of those issues this way? We’ll bill you fewer attorney hours by leveraging AI, but you need to foot the bill for its use? Right now, with a set price per seat, the cost of using AI on a given matter is nothing, but it won’t remain that way. It can’t.

Will the legal market make this adjustment to billing back the cost of AI compute? If not, how do firms justify the undefined cost for your firm?

news.titleEn: Wolters Kluwer Launches Invoice Review AI Agent for In-House Teams
news.titleZh: 威科集团面向内部法务团队推出发票审核AI代理
news.summaryZh:
威科集团推出LegalVIEW BillAnalyzer发票审核代理，这是一款AI驱动的助手，支持企业法务团队管理账单发票并保持合规。该代理可执行的任务包括：根据内部法务计费要求自动调整发票、为调整提供解释，并生成调整摘要及成本驱动因素总结。公司已有十年AI驱动、专家主导的账单审核业务，由具有执业背景的律师借助较旧的机器学习AI为客户审核账单；公司认为应利用新兴技术构建代理式AI来自动化这一流程，大幅减少人工审核时间。

该AI代理的推出源于内部法务团队希望更轻松地跟踪和削减支出，并更快了解资金去向。当前企业法务市场有两大驱动因素：一是减少外部支出，二是时间分配问题。该代理基于OpenAI的GPT-5.4和GPT-5.4 mini大语言模型，以及十年发票审核数据和经验构建，可编排10个其他代理，根据用户请求完成更具体的任务。竞争方面，Onit和Oddr等法律科技公司也利用生成式AI进行发票管理，但LegalVIEW BillAnalyzer发票审核代理专注于自动化法务团队调整发票时的个性化需求和要求。竞争对手可能标记差异，但不会像LegalVIEW BillAnalyzer那样进行调整。
news.bodyText:
The announcement comes a little over a month after the company expanded the launch of Libra, its legal AI workspace, to the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary and Romania.

What It Is: The LegalVIEW BillAnalyzer Invoice Review Agent is an AI-powered assistant that supports corporate legal teams in managing billing invoices and maintaining compliance.

The agent can perform tasks including automatically adjusting invoices based on in-house legal billing requirements, providing explanations for adjustments and producing summaries of the adjustments made and cost drivers.

“We [already have] AI-fueled, expert-driven bill review; we have a business that we've had for 10 years where we have lawyers who have come out of practice and who review bills for our clients with some older, machine learning AI in the background,” Dean Sonderegger, senior vice president and general manager of Wolters Kluwer Enterprise Legal Management Solutions business told Law.com. “We looked at that combination of things; we said we should be able to take emerging technology and build agentic AI to automate this to substantially reduce the amount of time it takes people to do bill review.”

Why It’s Needed: Sonderegger said the AI agent came about from the company noticing that in-house legal teams want to more easily track and reduce spending and more quickly figure out what they’re spending money on.

“You see two drivers in the legal market for corporate legal right now. The first driver is that they obviously want to reduce spend, outside spend. ... The second thing is just an issue of time and what you spend your time on,” Sonderegger explained. "When you look at that and then you overlay the hopes of artificial intelligence as it changes our world, that it has the ability to automate things and give us more insight or make better decisions, hopefully, and when we thought about this, we said, ‘What is something that people spend a lot of time doing?’ That is the review of the invoices.”

Under the Hood: Wolters Kluwer’s invoice analyzing AI agent is built on OpenAI’s GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4 mini large language models and a decade’s worth of invoice review data and experiences that help in navigating the varying complexities of invoice adjustments. The agent orchestrates 10 other agents that can complete more specific tasks depending on the user’s request.

“ Certain types of line items will get certain types of agents because there's a lot of nuances. To give you an example, you could have one adjustment where a partner has done a paralegal task and you see this come through at the partner rate and so what you do at that point in time is you say, ‘OK, we're going to adjust that back down to a different rate from that from a rule.’ That's a very different situation than say I have a first-year associate billing, and we've said that's disallowed or there's things where there's approval required,” Sonderegger said.

Competition: While other legal tech companies like enterprise legal management and contract life cycle management company Onit and invoice management platform Oddr leverage generative AI to perform invoice management, the LegalVIEW BillAnalyzer Invoice Review Agent is focused on automating the individual needs and requirements legal teams have when it comes to adjusting their invoices.

“It's not just the review process; it's what are the rules, the exceptions—all those things—and how do I codify those? So that's a differentiation point because these things are quite complex and they tend to change over time,” Sonderegger said. He added that competitors might flag discrepancies but won’t make the adjustments in the way that LegalVIEW BillAnalyzer does.

news.titleEn: Perkins Coie Turns to AI Avatars to Train Lawyers on Soft Skills
news.titleZh: Perkins Coie借助AI虚拟形象培训律师软技能
news.summaryZh: Perkins Coie律师事务所采用Levra公司的生成式AI虚拟形象，帮助各级律师模拟与同事的对话，培养软技能，并提升客户服务质量。Levra成立于2022年，为各行业专业人士提供虚拟形象，模拟情感和社交智能场景，培养社交、协作、冲突解决和授权技能。双方合作创建核心技能培训路径，让律师在客户场景之外练习，以便在客户和内部困难场景中做好准备、懂得最佳沟通方式。律师掌握人际技能并感到自信后，会渗透到为客户提供建议和决策的方式中。客户希望律师是值得信赖的顾问并提供价值，满足这两点就能获得重复业务关系，进而构建职业生涯和律所。该所今年第一季度开始与Levra合作，测试中生成式AI虚拟形象方法效果良好，尤其因为视觉化和互动性。对高智商人群，内容和制作必须达到相应水平，最佳互动形式是模拟真实生活场景，如消息、邮件、WhatsApp交流或视频通话，其中视频通话最具互动性、最易用且收益最大。该技术提供安全空间，让用户舒适地失败、从错误中学习并保持信心。在律所追求完美的环境中，批评可能导致失去信心，而技术创造了绝对安全空间，难以在人类辅导中复制。意外结果是人们喜欢Levra，因为确信与虚拟形象的互动仅限彼此。今年，越来越多法律科技公司提供模拟培训工具。2月，AltaClaro和Verbit推出共同开发的AI驱动deposition模拟器DepoSim；Hotshot宣布与Legora合作，计划开发模拟事项，让用户在应用于真实客户事项前练习部署Legora。
news.bodyText:
The avatars are designed to help lawyers of all experience levels simulate conversations with colleagues to build their soft skills, an area that Perkins Coie managing partner Ian Bagshaw told Law.com can also improve client services.

Founded in 2022, Levra provides professionals across industries with avatars that act out training simulations focused on how to approach scenarios related to emotional and social intelligence to help develop networking, collaboration, conflict resolution and delegation skills.

“We're working with [Levra] in order to create a training pathway across core skills that allows our talent to practice, learn, practice outside of client situations so that when they're in client situations and when they're in difficult internal situations, they are prepared, they've seen it before, they understand how best to communicate,” Bagshaw said.

He added that when lawyers master these interpersonal skills and feel confident, it trickles down to how they will advise and make decisions involving clients.

“Clients want a trusted adviser as a lawyer, clients want value for money from that trusted adviser, and if you hit both of those metrics, you'll get a repeat business relationship,” Bagshaw said. “Repeat business relationships not only build careers, but build law firms.”

The firm began its relationship with Levra in the first quarter of this year. Bagshaw said the gen AI avatar method has worked well so far during its testing, specifically because it is visual and interactive.

“With highly intelligent people, the content has got to be at the right level, the production has to be at the right level that inspires confidence in the content, and you want it to be interactive and the best form of interaction is simulating a real life scenario,” Bagshaw said. “That could be like a message exchange, an email exchange, WhatsApp exchange, or it could be simulating a video call. The most interactive experience, the one that's easiest to use with maximum benefit is a video call. The use of an avatar is accelerating the experience and making it the easiest to use.”

Bagshaw explained that technology like the gen AI avatar provides a safe space for users to comfortably fail, learn from their mistakes and maintain confidence.

“The key thing is making it acceptable for people to fail as part of a learning experience and in a law firm environment, that's often when people crave perfection, any criticism can cause people to lose confidence, not want to attempt something that may risk them failing,” Bagshaw said. “Now, the use of technology creates an absolute safe space for people to experiment in these modules and that safe space. It's very hard to recreate it in any human coaching environment. One of the unexpected outcomes is people enjoy Levra because they feel totally confident that what's between them and the avatar stays between them.”

This year, a growing number of legal tech companies have begun providing simulation training tools for legal professionals performing different tasks.

In February, legal training provider AltaClaro and legal transcription provider Verbit launched their AI-powered deposition simulator DepoSim, which they developed together.

Also in February, legal training provider Hotshot announced its partnership with Stockholm-based legal AI company Legora and said it planned to develop simulated matters that will allow users to practice deploying Legora in workshops before applying it to live client matters.

news.titleZh: 马斯克与OpenAI和解努力失败，奥克兰高风险审判即将展开
news.summaryZh: 据报道，埃隆·马斯克在奥克兰预定审判前寻求与OpenAI达成和解，但努力失败，使这起备受关注的人工智能商业案件走向法庭对决。案件核心是马斯克对OpenAI的结构、使命及其与微软关系的指控，已成为人工智能企业如何从非营利组织演变为主导商业实体的代理之战。和解失败在法律上至少有两重意义：其一，表明双方在审判前认为存在重大诉讼风险，审前和解讨论往往反映对法官或陪审团如何认定争议事实、内部通信和治理决策的不确定性；其二，若案件推进，可能就信义义务、合同意图、慈善或非营利承诺，以及将使命驱动实体重组为营利企业的法律界限形成更完善的公开记录。对诉讼律师而言，此案提醒人们，高关注度技术纠纷正日益融合传统商业索赔与新颖的治理和公共利益论点。在此态势下审判可能就证据开示、内部战略文件的可采性及衡平救济的框架产生重要裁决，并预示法院如何处理创始人指控组织初衷被后续融资和战略合作稀释的纠纷。对内部法律顾问，尤其在人工智能、生物技术等使命敏感行业，该纠纷凸显精确起草组织文件和创始人协议的重要性。若公司以非营利、利润上限或混合结构起步，法律顾问应预期董事会权力、投资者权利、关联方安排和使命声明日后受到审查。合规与治理团队也应关注，OpenAI之争凸显公开信息、内部决策和实体结构如何在诉讼中交织。受监管或政治敏感行业的董。

Musk’s Failed OpenAI Settlement Push Sets Up High-Stakes Oakland Trial

by Bruno Queiroz

Elon Musk reportedly sought to settle his dispute with OpenAI before a scheduled trial in Oakland, but the effort failed, leaving one of the most closely watched AI-related business cases on course for a courtroom fight. The case centers on Musk’s claims over OpenAI’s structure, mission, and relationship with Microsoft, and it has become a proxy battle over how artificial intelligence ventures can evolve from nonprofit-rooted organizations into dominant commercial players.

That failed settlement attempt is legally significant for at least two reasons. First, it suggests the parties see meaningful litigation risk heading into trial. Settlement discussions on the eve of trial often signal uncertainty about how a judge or jury may receive contested facts, internal communications, and governance decisions. Second, if the case proceeds, it could produce a more developed public record on fiduciary duties, contractual intent, charitable or nonprofit commitments, and the legal limits of restructuring mission-driven entities into profit-seeking enterprises.

For litigators, the story is a reminder that high-profile technology disputes are increasingly blending traditional commercial claims with novel governance and public-interest arguments. A trial in this posture can generate important rulings on discovery, admissibility of internal strategy documents, and the framing of equitable relief. It may also offer a preview of how courts handle disputes where founders allege that an organization’s original purpose has been diluted by later financing and strategic partnerships.

For in-house counsel, especially in AI, biotech, and other mission-sensitive sectors, the dispute underscores the importance of drafting organizational documents and founder agreements with precision. If a company begins with a nonprofit, capped-profit, or hybrid structure, counsel should expect later scrutiny of board authority, investor rights, related-party arrangements, and mission statements. Language that once seemed aspirational can become central evidence when commercial priorities shift.

Compliance and governance teams should also be paying attention. The OpenAI fight highlights how public messaging, internal decision-making, and entity structure can become intertwined in litigation. Boards and executives operating in regulated or politically sensitive industries may want to revisit how they document strategic pivots, conflicts management, and oversight of affiliated entities.

More broadly, the failed settlement shows that AI litigation is moving beyond IP and employment disputes into the realm of control, purpose, and corporate legitimacy. If this case reaches trial, legal professionals across the technology sector will be watching closely—not just for the outcome, but for the roadmap it may provide on governing transformative companies under intense commercial pressure.

news.summaryZh: Artificial Lawyer采访了Moritz联合创始人Pamir Ehsas，其计划以NewMod、AI优先战略挑战大型律所的法律服务模式，并与数十位精英律师合作。Moritz最初向律所销售AI工具，后决定创立自己的法律业务以产生更大影响。其业务范围远超保密协议，旨在向价值链高端延伸。Moritz直接聘用经验丰富的律师，并拥有其他律师资源。在与大型企业客户合作时，他们深入业务了解需求。Y Combinator支持的Moritz（原Arcline）近期完成900万美元种子轮融资，投资方包括Reddit、Dropbox、HuggingFace等创始人。迄今已帮助100多家公司完成交易，合同总价值超23亿美元，平均周转时间仅四小时，且仅用数月。AL强调NewMod模式对AI时代至关重要：若全由人类律师完成工作，则难以固定收费、快速且保证质量、快速扩展。将AI置于律所核心，处理约80%实际工作，并由经验丰富的律师密切监督和质量检查，才能真正改变游戏规则。该模式价格仅为大型律所的一小部分。Moritz只是市场上众多NewMod之一，AL获悉另有四家正在组建团队。
news.bodyHtml:
In this Artificial Lawyer interview, we speak to Moritz co-founder, Pamir Ehsas, whose plan is to take the legal delivery fight to Big Law with a NewMod, AI-first strategy that includes working with dozens of elite lawyers.

We cover:

  • How it all got started, (hint: they initially sold AI tools to law firms, but decided that to make a real impact it was better to launch their own legal business.)
  • The work they cover, (it’s a lot more than just NDAs…)
  • How far up the value curve they want to go, (very high…!)
  • How they work with experienced lawyers, (they have hired some directly and also have a bench of others.)
  • And how they engage with large corporate clients, (they go into the business and understand their needs.)

To watch the video, please press Play. You can also go direct to the AL TV Channel.

And you may have seen yesterday, Y Combinator-backed Moritz, formerly Arcline, has just raised a $9m Seed round – including investment from founders from Reddit, Dropbox, HuggingFace and many more. So far they have helped over 100 companies close deals worth more than $2.3 billion in aggregate contract value, with an average turnaround of just four hours’ – and that’s just after a few months.

Now the battle really begins.

–

AL’s Big Picture Perspective

AL would like to underline why the NewMod approach is so central to our new AI era:

  • If human lawyers do all the work it’s hard to operate with a fixed fee.
  • If human lawyers do all the work it’s hard to go fast and still get quality.
  • If human lawyers do all the work it’s hard to scale quickly.

Placing AI at the heart of the firm, where it handles around 80% of the actual work, but under the close supervision and quality checking of experienced lawyers, means that – for once – you can actually change the game.

And the prices for this approach? A fraction of what Big Law charges.

Plus, Moritz is just one of many other NewMods in the market already – and many more are about to launch. AL knows of four others that are currently assembling their teams – right now.

More about Moritz here.

—

news.titleEn: Harvey Launches ‘Legal Agent Bench’
news.titleZh: Harvey推出“法律智能体基准”
news.summaryZh: Harvey推出开源基准Legal Agent Benchmark（LAB），获Nvidia、OpenAI、Anthropic、Mistral和DeepMind等支持，供所有人测试智能体。首版含24个法律实践领域的1200多项任务，由逾75000条专家编写的评分标准评估。每项任务配有专门评分标准，例如并购交易中智能体需在合成数据中查找关键条款、评估重要性并撰写报告。智能体主要涉及规划、交互和适应：分解并执行任务，与数据、工具、其他智能体及人类交互以寻求帮助和审查，并适应以获取更多信息；测试材料中还加入问题以检验智能体能否发现。LAB提供共享框架，供模型提供商、智能体构建者、研究人员和法律界衡量进展，以指令、客户事项和所需工作产品结构评估真实法律任务表现。Harvey希望各方运行基准、审计评分标准、改进测试框架、贡献新任务族，并定义法律智能体评估下一步应衡量什么。未来几周将推出排行榜。合作者包括LangChain、Fireworks AI、Baseten、Applied Compute、Mithril/Jared Quincy David、Stanford Liftlab、Trajectory、Moritz Hardt、Snorkel、Mercor、Irwan Bello和Kelvin Guu。Harvey正与基础模型实验室、推理提供商、Neo实验室和AI公司密切合作，评估最佳开源和闭源法律智能体，这些研究小组已为基准及其研究方向做出贡献。智能体将成为法律科技关键部分，正如编码智能体对工程产生重大影响，法律智能体也将如此；允许公开测试有助于增强对产品的信心，帮助律师开发用例并熟悉该方法。
news.bodyHtml:
Agents….they sound great, but do these autonomous programs actually do what you want? Are they accurate? Are they reliable? Enter Legal Agent Benchmark by Harvey, which launches with the support of a list of major names such as Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, and DeepMind.

Think of Harvey’s ‘Big Law Bench’ for testing AI outputs, now think of something made to measure the performance of agents. In a nutshell, that’s it.

So, how does ‘Legal Agent Bench’ (LAB) work?

First, it will be opensource and open for everyone to get their agents tested.

The first version of LAB includes more than 1,200 agent tasks across 24 legal practice areas, and is evaluated by over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria.

As Niko Grupen, Head of Applied Research at Harvey, told AL: ‘You can bring your agents [to the LAB] to solve tasks.’

Those tasks, each with a specially designed rubric – or as AL suggested ‘an agent assault course’ – test the agent and show how it performed. As Grupen explained, it could be an M&A deal, and the agent has to find key provisions in synthetic data, consider those provisions’ importance, and then write a report.

Grupen said it’s useful to think of agents as working across three main areas: planning, interacting, and adapting.

‘Agents will decompose a task, execute it, interact with data, tools, and also with other agents, and humans to ask for help and review. There is also adaptation where the agent may need to know more information,’ he said.

He noted that they have also added issues in the test material to see if the agents will spot them.

In short, imagine giving an associate a bunch of documents, some rules on how to work, and some specific instructions as well. Tell them who they can ask for help, and where they can look for more information, and then say: ‘Begin and tell me when you are done, or if you get stuck.’

He also noted that people can test out Harvey agents, or ones they’ve customized, and he underlined that they will welcome vibe-coders to test agents out on the open sourced LAB.

Therefore ‘LAB provides a shared framework for model providers, agent builders, researchers, and the legal community to measure and track progress. It evaluates agent performance on real-world legal tasks using a structure of instructions, client matters, and required work product,’ the company explained.

‘We want model providers, startups, researchers, legal AI companies, and law firms to run the benchmark, audit the rubrics, improve the harness, contribute new task families, and help define what legal agent evaluation should measure next’, added Harvey.

There will also be a leader board in the coming weeks, so that you can see which AI systems are best at supporting certain agentic tasks.

And in terms of fellow collaborators that are supporting the project, the list includes: LangChain, Fireworks AI, Baseten, Applied Compute, Mithril/Jared Quincy David, Stanford Liftlab, Trajectory, Moritz Hardt, Snorkel, Mercor, Irwan Bello, and Kelvin Guu.

Harvey added: ‘For the collaborators listed we are working closely with the foundation model labs, inference providers, Neo labs, and AI companies to evaluate the best open and closed source legal agents. These research groups have already made contributions to the benchmark and the research directions that it enables.’

Is this a big deal?

Yes, agents are going to become a key part of legal tech. The tech is improving and as Grupen told AL, where coding agents have massively improved and had a big impact on engineering, so too legal agents will have a big impact here.

Allowing public testing of agents like this encourages faith in such products and helps lawyers to develop use cases and build familiarity with this approach.

Great stuff.

—

news.titleEn: Press Release | ILTA Celebrates 16th Annual Distinguished Peer Awards
news.titleZh: 新闻稿 | ILTA 庆祝第16届年度杰出同行奖
news.summaryZh:
国际法律技术协会（ILTA）于2026年5月1日在科罗拉多州丹佛市盖洛德落基山度假会议中心举行的ILTA EVOLVE大会上，颁发了2026年ILTA杰出同行奖。该奖项已进入第16年，旨在表彰在全球法律技术社区中取得卓越成就、创新和领导力的个人与组织。颁奖典礼汇聚了来自世界各地的法律技术专业人士，并提供了直播选项。获奖者体现了推动法律创新的智慧、勇气和社区精神。

2026年杰出同行奖获奖者包括：终身成就奖授予曾任职于Litera的Sherry Kappel；年度创新领袖（ILTA会员）授予曾任职于贝克·麦坚时的Sarah Pullin；年度创新领袖（商业伙伴）授予Steno的Joe Stephens；年度变革项目奖授予Ballard Spahr LLP；年度解决方案提供商奖授予汤森路透；开拓者奖授予Womble Bond与汤森路透；最佳博客奖授予Jenner & Block LLP的Elizabeth Suehr；最佳商业伙伴文章奖授予iCompli by LegalRM的Peter Lamb。值得关注的青年专业人士包括TitanFile的Arman Afkhami、Legora的Cem Uçan、Intellek的Daryl Fitzpatrick、Tarter Krinsky & Drogin LLP的Deanna Dubinsky、Baker & Hostetler LLP的Elaine Dick、Ballard Spahr LLP的Ian Lopez、Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer LLP的Imare' Jordan、HaystackID的Michael Sarlo、Levenfeld Pearlstein的Priti Saraswat以及汤森路透的Samantha Delaney。此外，ILTA还表彰了2026年法律技术领域五位有影响力的女性：Lexlytic创始人Chioma Wilson-Dike、Connell Foley LLP网络安全合伙人兼主席Karen Painter Randall、Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman LLP首席信息官Kim A. Wismer、汤森路透Co-Counsel Legal产品负责人Rawia Ashraf以及Indian LegalTech Network首席执行官兼创始人Shreya Vajpei。

Industry Leaders Honored at ILTA EVOLVE 2026 in Denver, Colorado

(CHICAGO, IL) 5 May 2026 - The International Legal Technology Association (ILTA) proudly announces the winners of the 2026 ILTA Distinguished Peer Awards, presented on Friday, May 1, 2026, during the ILTA EVOLVE Conference at the Gaylord Rockies Resort and Convention Center in Denver, Colorado. Now in its 16th year, the Distinguished Peer Awards recognize individuals and organizations whose work exemplifies outstanding achievement, innovation, and leadership across the global legal technology community.

The awards ceremony brought together legal technology professionals from around the world to celebrate peers who have delivered exceptional business value and transformational impact. A live-streamed option was also available for those attending remotely.

"These honorees reflect the ingenuity, courage, and community spirit that power legal innovation. Each winner demonstrates what impact truly looks like in practice, and ILTA is proud to elevate their contributions before our global membership." Joy Heath Rush, CEO - ILTA

2026 DISTINGUISHED PEER AWARDS WINNERS

Lifetime Achievement Award

Recognizing individuals whose careers span decades of exceptional leadership, vision, and service to the legal technology community:

Sherry Kappel   – formerly of Litera

Innovative Leader of the Year -- ILTA Member

Honoring ILTA members who have maximized the value of innovative technology in support of legal professionals:

Sarah Pullin   – formerly of Baker McKenzie

Innovative Leader of the Year -- Business Partner

Recognizing business partners driving meaningful innovation across the legal ecosystem:

Joe Stephens   – Steno

Transformative Project of the Year

Awarded to law firms that successfully planned and implemented transformative initiatives:

Ballard Spahr LLP

Solution Provider of the Year

Recognizing business partners delivering exceptional innovation and advancement in legal technology solutions:

Thomson Reuters

Trailblazer Award

Celebrating collaborative innovation between ILTA members and business partners:

Womble Bond and Thomson Reuters

Best Blog

Annual award for the year, noting the best Blog in the ILTA collection:

Elizabeth Suehr   – Jenner & Block, LLP

Best BP Article

Annual award for the year, noting the best Partner-written article in ILTA Publications:

Peter Lamb   - iCompli by LegalRM

Young Professionals to Watch

Highlighting rising leaders who are shaping the future of legal technology:

Arman Afkhami   - Senior Account Executive, TitanFile

Cem Uçan   - Legal Engineer, Legora

Daryl Fitzpatrick   - Chief Revenue Officer, Intellek

Deanna Dubinsky   - Business Process Optimization & Employee Engagement Specialist, Tarter Krinsky & Drogin LLP

Elaine Dick   - Lead Practice Innovation Attorney, Baker & Hostetler LLP

Ian Lopez   - Manager Business Intelligence, Ballard Spahr LLP

Imare' Jordan   - Practice Data Analyst, Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer LLP

Michael Sarlo   - Chief Innovation Officer & President of Global Investigations & Cyber IR, HaystackID

Priti Saraswat   - Director of Knowledge and Innovation, Levenfeld Pearlstein

Samantha Delaney   - Senior Solutions Consultant, Thomson Reuters

2026 INFLUENTIAL WOMEN IN LEGAL TECH

ILTA also recognized five outstanding leaders as part of its 2026 Influential Women in Legal Tech program, honoring women whose mentorship, innovation, and impact are shaping the global legal technology ecosystem:

Chioma Wilson-Dike , Founder, Lexlytic

Karen Painter Randall , Partner / Chair, Cybersecurity, Connell Foley LLP

Kim A. Wismer , Chief Information Officer, Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman LLP

Rawia Ashraf, Head of Product, Co-Counsel Legal, Thomson Reuters

Shreya Vajpei, CEO & Founder, Indian LegalTech Network — A global community builder and founder, Vajpei is recognized for elevating visibility, capability, and collaboration across a fast-growing regional and international legal tech ecosystem.

To view the complete list of 2026 Distinguished Peer Award winners, visit awards.iltanet.org/winners-26.

For more information about ILTA membership, upcoming events, and programs, visit www.iltanet.org .

About ILTA

The International Legal Technology Association (ILTA) serves the professional needs of more than 27,000 international legal technology professionals and their organizations. Since its founding in 1980, the association's focus is to achieve results for our membership and the legal technology profession at large. Much of the value we provide as an association comes from coordinated efforts with our global volunteer membership teams.

news.titleEn: Market Intelligence: The eDiscovery software market from 2025 to 2030
news.titleZh: 市场情报：2025至2030年电子取证软件市场
news.summaryZh:
全球电子取证市场中，软件是到2030年增长最快的细分领域。经校准估算，软件支出将从2025年约66.7亿美元增至2030年约109.5亿美元，五年增幅约64%，复合年增长率10.41%，比整体市场高近三个百分点，比服务高4.66个百分点。2025年软件约占整体市场34%，以审查、处理和分析平台为主，采集软件及相邻能力重要性上升；云交付为新部署默认方式，本地软件主要在安全、主权或合同约束下保留。该基线反映自2012年14.2亿美元起约13年复合增长，绝对值接近五倍扩张，同期整体市场约四倍。

10.41%的增速源于AI辅助审查、AI驱动分析及新兴代理功能以软件而非专业服务交付，原按文件或小时计费的工作流转为SaaS订阅或AI推理计费。对网络安全、数据隐私、监管合规和电子取证专业人士有三点观察：软件供应商评估已延伸至AI治理、模型透明度、数据驻留和推理成本；托管审查等服务定价压力在结构上与软件优异表现相关，将持续至2030年后；软件吸收人工服务工作，正重塑采购和供应商关系格局。后续分析将审视部署、云构成和细分动态，最终形成2025至2030年电子取证市场综合报告。

Editor’s Note: Software is the segment of the worldwide eDiscovery market compounding fastest through 2030. Reconciled estimates highlight software spending growing from approximately $6.67 billion in 2025 to approximately $10.95 billion in 2030 – a 10.41 percent compound annual rate that exceeds the aggregate market CAGR by nearly three percentage points and the services CAGR by 4.66 percentage points. The pattern is concrete: AI-assisted capabilities embedded in core review, analytics, and processing workflows are reclassifying work that once flowed through services into software-driven channels, while subscription consumption and cloud-first procurement reduce friction across the entire buyer evaluation and deployment cycle.

The 10.41 percent software CAGR is not an abstract growth number. It is the direct result of AI-assisted review, AI-driven analytics, and emerging agentic features being delivered as software features rather than as professional-services engagements. The same review workflow that once generated services revenue at per-document or per-hour rates now generates software revenue at SaaS subscription or AI-inference rates. The work has expanded with data volumes; the channel through which it gets billed has steadily shifted toward software.

For cybersecurity, data privacy, regulatory compliance, and eDiscovery professionals, three observations follow. First, software vendor evaluation criteria now extend into AI governance, model transparency, data residency, and inference cost – dimensions that were peripheral a decade ago and central today. Second, services pricing pressure – particularly in managed review – is structurally tied to software’s outperformance, not cyclically driven, and will persist through 2030 and beyond. Third, the procurement and vendor relationship landscape itself is being remade as software absorbs work that human-driven services historically performed. Subsequent Market Intelligence analyses will examine the deployment, cloud composition, and segment-specific dynamics underneath the headline software CAGR, culminating in the consolidated 2025–2030 eDiscovery Marketplace Mashup.

Industry Research – eDiscovery Market Sizing Beat

Market Intelligence: The eDiscovery software market from 2025 to 2030

Reconciled estimates highlight worldwide software spending of $6.67 billion in 2025, climbing to $10.95 billion in 2030 – a 10.41 percent CAGR driven by AI-assisted capabilities, subscription consumption, and the steady reclassification of work from services into software

ComplexDiscovery Staff

Software is the segment of the worldwide eDiscovery market compounding fastest. Reconciled estimates place worldwide software spending at approximately $6.67 billion in 2025, climbing to approximately $10.95 billion in 2030 – a five-year increase of roughly 64 percent and a reconciled compound annual growth rate of 10.41 percent. The software CAGR exceeds the aggregate market CAGR by nearly three percentage points a year, and the services CAGR by 4.66 percentage points. The pattern is steady, the cause is concrete, and the gap is widening. Software is becoming a different category than it was even five years ago, and AI is the reason.

The 2025 software baseline

In 2025, reconciled estimates place worldwide eDiscovery software spending at approximately $6.67 billion – approximately 34 percent of the aggregate market. The segment is dominated by review, processing, and analytics platforms, with collection software and adjacent capabilities growing in importance. Cloud delivery is the default for new deployments; on-premise software persists primarily where security, sovereignty, or contractual constraints require it. The 2025 software baseline reflects approximately 13 years of compounding from a $1.42 billion starting point in 2012 – close to a fivefold expansion in absolute terms, against an aggregate market that expanded roughly fourfold over the same span.

news.titleZh: 同行正在厘清的风险——以及它对贵所意味着什么
news.summaryZh:
律所已熟知的OCG痛点十分具体：不合规工时记录导致的账单减记、推介发出后才浮现的市场限制，以及合伙人直到客户提出才重视的人员配置准则。这些并非边缘案例，而是多数律所仍被动应对的反复出现的摩擦点。AI限制是在此之上最新的一层，而多数律所对其中任何一项都没有指定负责人。

客户正将AI特定限制直接嵌入其OCG：哪些工具可用于其事项、AI辅助工作如何计费、需要何种披露。律所可能完全遵守两年前同意的所有条款，却仍不符合同一客户今天的期望，因为条款可能变更且无系统化追踪方式。AI层使一切叠加：问题不再仅是工时记录是否合规，还延伸至律师是否使用了客户禁止的工具、以客户不认可的费率、且未做客户要求的披露。风险迅速叠加：横向引进的律师带来受AI条款约束的客户关系，而律所的受理流程可能无法捕捉；效率举措也撞上同一堵墙。多数律所没有指定负责人。在圆桌讨论中，反应是认同而非怀疑。律所知道这是个问题，只是不知道这是谁的问题。
news.bodyHtml:
Your OCGs already contain AI obligations your firm may not be tracking

The OCG pain firms already know is concrete: billing write-downs from non-compliant time entries, marketing restrictions that surface only after a pitch has gone out, and staffing guidelines that partners ignore until a client raises it. These aren’t edge cases. They’re recurring friction points that most firms still manage reactively. AI restrictions are the newest layer on top of that problem, and most firms don’t have a designated owner for any of it.

Clients are now embedding AI-specific restrictions directly into their OCGs: which tools can be used on their matters, how AI-assisted work can be billed, and what disclosure is required. A firm can be fully compliant with everything it agreed to two years ago and still be out of compliance with what the same client expects today, because terms can change without any systematic way to track them.

The AI layer compounds all of it. The question is no longer just whether the time entry was compliant. It now extends to whether the attorney used a tool the client prohibits, at a rate the client doesn’t recognize, without the disclosure the client requires.

The exposure compounds quickly. Laterals bring client relationships governed by AI terms that your intake process may not capture. Efficiency initiatives run into the same wall. Most firms don’t have a designated owner for this. In roundtables, the reaction was recognition, not skepticism. Firms know this is a problem; they just don’t know whose problem it is.

news.titleEn: California Bar Proposes Rule Requiring Lawyers to Verify Every AI Output — and Five Other AI-Focused Ethics Changes
news.titleZh: 加州律师协会提议新规：律师须核实所有AI输出——以及其他五项以AI为核心的伦理修订
news.summaryZh:
加州律师协会职业责任与行为常设委员会（COPRAC）提出一揽子AI相关修订，涉及六项《职业行为规则》，首次将具体AI义务写入加州规则。修订由加州最高法院2025年8月22日信函启动，法院指示COPRAC考虑将2023年11月《生成式人工智能在法律实践中使用的实用指南》的指导原则纳入正式规则，并考虑针对“代理式AI”的指导。COPRAC于2026年3月13日批准提案并开启45天评论期，评论期已于5月4日结束。提案未单独起草AI规则，而是将新语言嵌入现有六项规则。

规则1.1新增两条评论：一条明确技术能力义务涵盖AI；另一条要求律师使用包括AI在内的技术时，必须独立审查、核实并对用于客户代理的任何输出行使专业判断。规则1.4新增评论5，规定当AI使用带来重大风险或实质性影响代理范围、成本、方式或决策时，律师须向客户传达足够信息以便其做出知情决定，且该义务持续评估。规则1.6新增评论2，将“披露”扩展至向AI工具暴露保密信息且存在被访问、保留或使用的重大风险。规则3.3新增评论3，要求律师在提交前核实引注的准确性和存在性，包括确保AI生成或辅助的引注未被伪造、误述或断章取义。规则5.1要求管理律师建立符合职业行为规则的AI使用程序。规则5.3将AI使用纳入对非律师人员的监督范围。提案未明确涉及代理式AI，但规则1.1的独立核实要求及规则5.1、5.3的监督义务直接适用于代理式工作流。COPRAC将审查公众意见并可能修改提案，加州最高法院对规则拥有最终权力，修订是否及何时生效尚不确定。
news.bodyHtml:
When using any technology — including AI — a lawyer “must independently review, verify, and exercise professional judgment regarding any output generated by the technology that is used in connection with representing a client.”

That language appears in a new comment to Rule 1.1 on competence proposed by the State Bar of California’s Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct (COPRAC) as part of a package of AI-related amendments to six of the state’s Rules of Professional Conduct.

The proposed changes would, for the first time, write specific AI obligations into California’s rules. The changes span the rules on competence, client communication, confidentiality, candor toward tribunals, and supervision of both lawyers and other staff.

Unfortunately, I am reporting this a bit late, as the public comment period on the proposals closed yesterday, May 4. But the rulemaking process is still in early stages and the amendments are far from final. For anyone tracking how bar regulators are treating AI in legal practice, these proposals are worth a close read regardless.

Initiated by Supreme Court

The rulemaking was set in motion by the California Supreme Court itself. In an Aug. 22, 2025, letter to the state bar’s interim executive director, the court’s clerk and executive officer directed COPRAC to consider whether the guiding principles from the bar’s November 2023 “Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law” should be incorporated into the formal rules.

The court also directed the bar to consider guidance specifically addressing “agentic AI” tools — systems that can plan and execute tasks with little or no human intervention.

COPRAC approved the proposed amendments at its March 13, 2026, meeting and opened the 45-day comment period. Rather than drafting a standalone AI rule, the committee wove new language into six existing rules, reflecting a view that AI sharpens existing ethical duties rather than creating entirely new ones.

Whereas California’s 2023 practical guidance was a “living document” with no binding authority, these proposed amendments would change that by making AI-specific obligations part of the enforceable rules.

Most states that have addressed AI in legal practice have done so through ethics opinions, which carry persuasive but not always disciplinary force. California’s approach, if finalized, would be more muscular.

I have tracked the adoption of the duty of technology competence across jurisdictions on a dedicated page on this blog. These proposals represent among the most detailed and comprehensive set of AI-specific rule amendments I have seen any state bar put forward.

Amendments to Rule 1.1, Competence

The existing rule requires lawyers to maintain learning and skill sufficient for competent representation. The proposed amendments add two new comments specific to AI.

The first simply extends the existing technology-competence language to make explicit that the duty to stay abreast of “the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology” includes artificial intelligence.

The second, and more consequential, comment states that when using technology, including AI, a lawyer “must independently review, verify, and exercise professional judgment regarding any output generated by the technology that is used in connection with representing a client.”

In other words, under this proposed change, the lawyer must personally and independently evaluate what AI tools produce before relying on it. There is no carve-out for routine tasks or low-stakes matters.

Amendments to Rule 1.4, Communication with Clients

A new Comment 5 to Rule 1.4 addresses when lawyers must disclose their use of AI to clients.

The proposed language provides that when a lawyer’s use of technology, including AI, “presents a significant risk or materially affects the scope, cost, manner, or decision-making process of representation,” the lawyer must communicate “sufficient information regarding the use of technology to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.”

The comment adds that lawyers must continue to evaluate their communication obligations throughout a representation based on “the novelty of the technology, risks associated with the use of the technology, scope of the representation, and sophistication of the client.”

Notably, this does not create a blanket disclosure requirement every time a lawyer uses AI. The trigger is a “significant risk” or “material” effect on the representation.

More routine use may not require affirmative disclosure, depending on the circumstances. But the obligation is ongoing — it must be reassessed as the representation evolves.

Amendments to Rule 1.6, Confidential Information of a Client

The confidentiality rule, which prohibits lawyers from revealing confidential client information, gets a new Comment 2 that expand sthe definition of “reveal” to encompass AI use.

Under the proposed language, “reveal” includes “exposing confidential information to technological systems, including artificial intelligence tools, where such exposure creates a material risk that the information may be accessed, retained, or used, whether by the technological system or another user of that technological system, in a manner inconsistent with the lawyer’s duty of confidentiality.”

This means that inputting client information into an AI tool — even if the lawyer never intends for anyone else to see it — can constitute a revelation of confidential information under the rules if there is a material risk the system or its other users could access, retain or use that data.

Lawyers using cloud-based AI tools with unclear or unfavorable data retention and training policies need to pay attention to this.

Amendments to Rule 3.3, Candor Toward the Tribunal

This amendment directly addresses the AI hallucination problem that has generated judicial sanctions and considerable alarm across the profession.

A new Comment 3 states that “a lawyer’s duty of candor towards the tribunal includes the obligation to verify the accuracy and existence of cited authorities, including ensuring no cited authority is fabricated, misstated, or taken out of context, before submission to a tribunal, including any cited authorities generated or assisted by artificial intelligence or other technological tools.”

The existing rule already prohibits knowingly misquoting authority or citing overruled decisions. The new comment makes explicit that AI-generated citations are not exempt from those obligations, and that the verification duty extends specifically to fabricated, misstated or decontextualized authority.

In the wake of now-notorious sanctions cases involving AI-hallucinated citations, this comment codifies what many courts have already been saying in their opinions.

Amendments to Rule 5.1, Responsibilities of Managerial and Supervisory Lawyers

The proposed amendment adds AI governance to the list of matters that managerial lawyers at law firms must address through internal policies and procedures.

The existing comment already refers to policies for conflicts, calendaring and client funds. The new language adds that managerial lawyers must make reasonable efforts to establish procedures “governing the use of artificial intelligence, in accordance with the Rules of Professional Conduct.”

Law firm leaders, practice group chairs and managing partners will need to ensure their firms have actual, functioning AI governance policies, not just aspirational statements, if this rule is finalized.

Amendments to Rule 5.3, Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistants

A corresponding amendment to the rule on supervising nonlawyer personnel adds AI to the scope of supervision.

The existing comment states that lawyers must give nonlawyer assistants “appropriate instruction and supervision concerning all ethical aspects of their employment.” The proposed amendment adds “including the use of technology in the provision of legal services, such as artificial intelligence.”

This extends the AI supervision obligation to paralegals, legal assistants, law clerks and any other staff who use AI tools in their work. Given that AI tools are proliferating throughout law firm operations at every level, this makes sense as a practical clarification.

The Takeaway

A few things stand out to me about California’s approach.

First, by embedding these obligations in the enforceable rules rather than guidance documents, these changes would underscore and make explicit ethical duties that are already implicit in the existing rules. While some might argue that modifications of the existing rules are unnecessary, there are plenty of lawyers out there who have been proving them wrong.

Second, the independent verification requirement in Rule 1.1 is worth emphasizing. It does not say lawyers should generally be careful with AI output. It says they must independently review, verify and exercise professional judgment regarding any output used in client representation. That is a strict standard, and one that cuts against any casual reliance on AI-generated work product.

Third, the confidentiality amendment’s expansion of “reveal” is practically significant. Lawyers accustomed to thinking of confidentiality as a disclosure-to-humans concept will need to rethink how they select and use AI tools in light of this definition.

Finally, while the proposals do not explicitly address agentic AI, as the court suggested in the letter that spurred these revisions, they do address them implicitly.

The independent verification requirement in Rule 1.1 and the supervisory obligations in Rules 5.1 and 5.3 are directly relevant to agentic workflows. If a lawyer deploys an AI agent that researches, drafts and revises a brief with limited oversight, these rules would squarely apply.

Although the comment period has closed, the rulemaking process continues. COPRAC will review public input and could modify the proposals before they advance. The California Supreme Court ultimately has authority over the Rules of Professional Conduct. Whether and when these amendments might take effect remains to be seen.

The proposed amendment adds AI governance to the list of matters that managerial lawyers at law firms must address through internal policies and procedures.

The existing comment already refers to policies for conflicts, calendaring and client funds. The new language adds that managerial lawyers must make reasonable efforts to establish procedures “governing the use of artificial intelligence, in accordance with the Rules of Professional Conduct.”

Law firm leaders, practice group chairs and managing partners will need to ensure their firms have actual, functioning AI governance policies, not just aspirational statements, if this rule is finalized.

Amendments to Rule 5.3, Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistants

A corresponding amendment to the rule on supervising nonlawyer personnel adds AI to the scope of supervision.

The existing comment states that lawyers must give nonlawyer assistants “appropriate instruction and supervision concerning all ethical aspects of their employment.” The proposed amendment adds “including the use of technology in the provision of legal services, such as artificial intelligence.”

This extends the AI supervision obligation to paralegals, legal assistants, law clerks and any other staff who use AI tools in their work. Given that AI tools are proliferating throughout law firm operations at every level, this makes sense as a practical clarification.

A few things stand out to me about California’s approach.

First, by embedding these obligations in the enforceable rules rather than guidance documents, these changes would underscore and make explicit ethical duties that are already implicit in the existing rules. While some might argue that modifications of the existing rules are unnecessary, there are plenty of lawyers out there who have been proving them wrong.

Second, the independent verification requirement in Rule 1.1 is worth emphasizing. It does not say lawyers should generally be careful with AI output. It says they must independently review, verify and exercise professional judgment regarding any output used in client representation. That is a strict standard, and one that cuts against any casual reliance on AI-generated work product.

Third, the confidentiality amendment’s expansion of “reveal” is practically significant. Lawyers accustomed to thinking of confidentiality as a disclosure-to-humans concept will need to rethink how they select and use AI tools in light of this definition.

Finally, while the proposals do not explicitly address agentic AI, as the court suggested in the letter that spurred these revisions, they do address them implicitly.

The independent verification requirement in Rule 1.1 and the supervisory obligations in Rules 5.1 and 5.3 are directly relevant to agentic workflows. If a lawyer deploys an AI agent that researches, drafts and revises a brief with limited oversight, these rules would squarely apply.

Although the comment period has closed, the rulemaking process continues. COPRAC will review public input and could modify the proposals before they advance. The California Supreme Court ultimately has authority over the Rules of Professional Conduct. Whether and when these amendments might take effect remains to be seen.

news.bodyText:
The new offerings are currently available in early access to select customers and will be rolled out to additional customers over the next few months.

The newly released agents cover practice areas including mergers and acquisitions, family law and capital markets, and they address specific tasks such as analyzing counterparty markups, comparing closing checklists against transaction documents and identifying issues in a variety of document types.

In a press release announcing the launch, Harvey said the new agents were built by lawyers and tested against internal benchmarks for accuracy and relevance. The ability to customize the agents through Agent Builder is intended to allow firms to ground the agents in their own data and fit them into their existing workflows.

“We wanted every organization globally to be able to chart its own path with agents in Harvey, so we have a deep bench of off-the-shelf agents to choose from and an intuitive agent builder that makes the process of building highly sophisticated agents seamless for law firms and in-house teams alike,” Harvey CEO Winston Weingberg said in the press release.

The new offerings follow several other agentic product launches from Harvey in the past year. The company launched Workflow Builder, a self-service tool for AI agent customization, in June 2025. The following month, Harvey and A&O Shearman introduced agentic tools they built together for use in specific practice areas, which A&O Shearman was allowed to license to clients and other law firms under a revenue sharing agreement .

Several other legal AI companies, including Legora , Clio and Leah (formerly ContractPodAi), have also released self-service agentic workflow offerings.

news.titleEn: Practice Management Platform Clio To Discontinue Its Longtime Integration with Payments Processor LawPay
