When I first published The Annotated ESI Protocol in January 2023, I hoped it would age the way most legal …

Continue reading →
news.bodyText:
Tags

eDiscovery , ESI Protocols , generative-ai , Linked attachments

When I first published The Annotated ESI Protocol in January 2023, I hoped it would age the way most legal writing ages: slowly, with a few footnotes for the curious. Three years on, I’m releasing a substantially revised edition because the evidence has changed, and the protocols we negotiate need to change with it. The tools custodians use to communicate and collaborate in 2026 look materially different from just a few years ago, and the revised Annotated ESI Protocol seeks to address what we must accomplish today.

Download it here: http://www.craigball.com/Annotated_ESI_Protocol_2026_Final.pdf

The biggest changes are additions. Modern attachments—the cloud-hosted documents people send by pointers instead of as embedded files—now have their own section, with an exemplar provision distinguishing genuine substitute-attachments from documents merely referenced, a point-in-time-version obligation calibrated to what current collection tools can deliver, and a meet-and-confer trigger for cases where historical-version recovery genuinely matters. Short-message and collaboration-platform data—Slack, Teams, Google Chat—have a section requiring native export, a human-readable rendered transcript plus separately-produced attachments, with proportionality qualifiers acknowledging that not every producing party’s tooling produces all three out of the box. Mobile and ephemeral messaging get a tiered approach: consumer-grade backup-extraction utilities like iMazing are often acceptable for the run-of-the-mill civil cases, with forensic-grade collection (Cellebrite, AXIOM, and the rest) reserved for matters where alleged spoliation, deleted-content recovery, or device-integrity disputes warrant the greater rigor and cost. Audio, video, and voicemail get explicit native-production language. Search methodology, technology-assisted review, and generative AI in review each have their own short sections governing disclosure and validation. Foreign-language materials, which I had flagged in 2023 without addressing, now have an exemplar provision. In the years since I penned the original, we’ve benefited from insight on these topics gleaned from published case authority and thoughtful scholarship. The times are still a-changing and I’m reluctant to wade into contentious and unsettled topics; but at the same time, practitioners need guidance to move forward. Embrace what serves you and leave the rest.

A hybridized TIFF+ exemplar remains the primary form of production, because that’s what most institutional litigation still demands and a protocol that pretends otherwise won’t get traction, no matter the retrograde inefficiency of converting robust native formats to static images. But, the carve-outs for native production have grown to cover spreadsheets, presentations, databases, photographs, audio, video, short messages, mobile messages, structured-data exports, CAD, and anything else that doesn’t reduce sensibly to a static page image. If you can hold the line for native (instead of holding your nose for TIFFs), native is still better; the alternative language to get it is in there.

Addendum A addressing load file metadata production has expanded from twenty-seven fields to roughly sixty, organized into eleven labeled subsections covering the new evidence types, with explicit fields for collection-tool disclosure, modern-attachment metadata, conversation identifiers, edit and deletion flags, and platform tier. Thanks to the vigilance of my crack AI editor, a handful of drafting glitches in the 2023 edition are fixed.

The 2026 edition also acknowledges more directly than its predecessor that what counsel can demand and what a producing party’s platform and subscription tier can deliver are sometimes different things. The revised protocol asks more of producing parties—inevitably, considering all the new forms of ESI extant—but the new sections build in proportionality qualifiers, disclosure obligations and meet-and-confer triggers calibrated to what the leading platforms actually support in 2026. ESI protocols are still worth fighting for, and the better both sides understand their application and purpose, the less there is to bicker about.

If you’re interested in ESI Protocols and want to contribute your experience to an EDRM effort to frame a path to consensus protocols, please share your interest at https://edrm.net/edrm-projects/esi-protocol/

news.titleEn: The Hidden Cost of Agentic AI: Information Governance
news.titleZh: 代理式AI的隐性成本：信息治理
news.summaryZh: 法律行业正从生成式AI迈向能推理、规划并执行多步骤任务的代理式AI。Womble Bond Dickinson的实践显示：监管监测中，代理持续监控立法，按客户业务范围筛选，并在新碳税通过后识别受影响子公司、检索排放数据、生成特权备忘录；复杂诉讼中，律师设定战略目标后，代理构建时间线、交叉引用数据、标记逻辑漏洞并起草交叉询问脚本。但代理的可靠性取决于数据质量，标记不当的文档、孤立案件文件夹和未记录的保留规则都会成为隐患。该律所已将代理式AI设计团队与信息治理部门整合，在代理操作案件文件前须回答数据分类、访问权限、保留策略和道德隔离等问题。律所数据分散于案件管理、文档管理、邮件归档、工时记录和业务数据库等互不连通的系统，字段不一致、分类法漂移、元数据稀疏、特权标识常为隐性。生成式AI因依赖当前提示而掩盖这一问题，代理式AI则将其暴露；获得实际回报的律所都在扩展代理前投资于数据质量、分类法和系统集成。更长远看，世界模型将构建系统和环境的内部模拟，可模拟监管走向、合同条款在不同执行情景下的影响或诉讼策略在多个法官和司法管辖区中的演变，这将挑战当前基于文本的代理架构。
news.bodyText:
Today, that tool is no longer reactive. It is moving into the passenger seat, acting as a copilot, reading the road ahead.

The industry is moving through a predictable adoption curve. Rules-based search and document management gave way to generative AI, which introduced conversational tools that draft, summarize and synthesize at a level that surprised even early adopters. The next shift is already underway: agentic AI, systems that do not just respond to prompts but reason, plan and execute across multiple steps. This is the move from tools you use to partners that act. It also carries a cost most firms have not priced in, and that cost is information governance.

From Conversation to Action

If generative AI is like a consultant you talk to, agentic AI is more like an associate you can delegate to. You set a goal, and it figures out how to achieve it.

At Womble Bond Dickinson, our team has been testing this distinction in practice. Consider regulatory monitoring. A client operating across dozens of jurisdictions faces a real information problem. Traditionally, paralegals manually scan legislative updates. An agentic approach reframes the problem. The agent monitors activity continuously, filters for relevance against the client’s footprint and acts when something material occurs. When a new carbon tax passes, the agent identifies the affected subsidiary, retrieves emissions data from a secure firm repository and produces a privileged memorandum for partner review. A self-initiated model with an attorney always in the loop.

A second example is complex litigation. Rather than asking an AI to find emails about a specific meeting, the lawyer assigns a strategic goal: identify inconsistencies between a witness’s deposition and their internal communications on a merger valuation. The agent builds a timeline, cross-references figures, flags logical gaps and drafts a suggested cross-examination script with hyperlinked evidence. It is not just retrieving information but executing a strategy.

Governance Is the Entry Fee

Vendor demos rarely mention it, but an agent is only as trustworthy as the data it touches. When a system acts autonomously across repositories, every poorly tagged document, every orphaned matter folder and every undocumented retention rule becomes a liability.

At our firm, we formalized integration between our agentic AI design team and the information governance unit, not just an innovation unit, for exactly this reason. Before an agent operates on a matter file, someone has to answer basic questions. What is the data classification? Who can see it? What is the retention posture? Which ethical walls apply? Most firms have not answered these questions at the level of granularity an agent requires. The real work of agentic AI is not prompt engineering. It is the unglamorous work of cleaning up a decade of loosely governed content.

The Data Problem

This exposes a broader issue. Law firms have a data problem that is undermining their AI initiatives. Firm knowledge lives in matter management systems, document management systems, email archives, time entry records, and practice databases that were never designed to talk to one another. Fields are inconsistent. Taxonomy drifts across practice groups. Metadata is sparse. Privilege designations are often implicit rather than tagged.

Generative AI hides this problem because it works off the prompt in front of it. Agentic AI exposes it. An agent that is supposed to pull precedent, check conflicts and draft a closing memo cannot do so if the underlying data is unreliable. The firms seeing real return on AI investment are the ones spending on data quality, taxonomy and integration before scaling agents.

World Models Will Challenge the Current Approach

There is a longer horizon worth watching. Today’s AI agents reason through language. They read context, plan and act on text-based representations of the world. World models represent something different. They build internal simulations of systems and environments and reason by running them forward. Applied to legal work, a world model could simulate the likely trajectory of a regulatory regime, the downstream effects of a contract clause under different enforcement scenarios or how a litigation strategy plays out across multiple judges and jurisdictions.

This approach will challenge today’s agentic architectures. Text-native agents will need to interface with simulation-native systems. Governance and data questions will become harder, not easier. Firms still catching up to language models should pay attention to what comes next.

The Changing Role of the Lawyer

Agentic AI also reshapes the profession itself. Junior associates traditionally built foundational skills through the intensive document work that agents now handle. That training pathway is now being disrupted. The lawyer of the near future will function more as a legal architect and agent supervisor. The work will focus on setting strategic parameters, auditing reasoning chains, and ensuring everything stays within the bounds of client confidentiality and professional responsibility. Firms will need to be thoughtful about how they develop legal intuition in a generation that may never perform the foundational tasks their predecessors did.

The Path Forward

The tipping point is not about whether agentic AI will arrive. It has arrived. The advantage will go to firms that treat information governance as the real cost of admission, not an afterthought. The attorney of the future is less a solo practitioner and more an orchestrator of capabilities, deploying a research agent, a drafting agent, and a compliance monitor, then coordinating their outputs into a unified strategy. The skills that matter are knowing which agent to deploy, interrogating its reasoning, and applying the judgment only a human lawyer can provide.

Chad Ergun is the chief information officer at Womble Bond Dickinson, where he leads technology strategy, innovation, and AI transformation. His work spans generative AI, knowledge management, cybersecurity, eDiscovery, machine learning, and data science, with an emphasis on applying emerging technologies to modernize legal service delivery.

news.titleEn: LexisNexis Owner RELX Announces Plans to Acquire Legal Tech Company Doctrine
news.titleZh: LexisNexis母公司RELX宣布计划收购法律科技公司Doctrine
news.summaryZh: 法律信息提供商LexisNexis的母公司RELX宣布，计划收购法律科技公司Doctrine，交易条款未予披露。拟借助Doctrine的法律搜索、分析和起草工作流程，强化其现有法律科技产品并在欧洲扩大影响力。欢迎Doctrine加入，以便更好地服务法国、欧洲及其他地区的客户，并称Doctrine以客户为中心的创新方法、强大的平台和专业人才，与LexisNexis在权威法律AI工作流程解决方案方面的全球能力相辅相成。Doctrine由尼古拉斯·布斯塔曼特、安托万·杜塞奥和拉斐尔·尚佩蒙于2016年创立，为法律专业人士提供法律研究和情报软件，其平台利用生成式人工智能分析法院判决，提供见解、数据分析和起草解决方案。关于RELX是否计划整合Doctrine与LexisNexis产品，LexisNexis向Law.com表示，拟议收购需完成与相关员工代表机构的适用信息和协商程序，并获得惯常监管批准，两家公司在过渡期间将继续独立运营。此次收购要约公布前，RELX旗下风险投资部门REV曾于1月参与总部位于伦敦和纽约的房地产法律AI平台Orbital的B轮融资。
news.bodyText:
Terms of the transaction were not disclosed.

RELX plans to leverage Doctrine’s legal search, analysis and drafting workflows to bolster its current legal technology offerings and presence in Europe, according to a press release.

“We are excited about the prospect of welcoming Doctrine, so that we can serve customers in France, across Europe, and beyond in even greater ways,” said Sean Fitzpatrick, CEO of LexisNexis North America, UK and Ireland, in the release. “Doctrine’s customer-centric innovation approach, powerful platform and expert talent complement LexisNexis’s global capabilities in authoritative legal AI workflow solutions, and we look forward to delivering even more value to customers."

Founded in 2016 by Nicolas Bustamante, Antoine Dusséaux and Raphaël Champeimont, Doctrine provides legal research and intelligence software for legal professionals, and its platform uses generative artificial intelligence to analyze court decisions and provide insights and data analytics solutions and drafting.

When it comes to whether RELX intends to integrate Doctrine and LexisNexis offerings, LexisNexis told Law.com in a statement that "the proposed acquisition is subject to the completion of applicable information and consultation procedures with the relevant employee representative bodies and customary regulatory consents. The two companies will continue to operate separately in the interim."

The acquisition offer announcement comes several months after RELX’s venture capital arm REV participated in a Series B funding round for Orbital, a London and New York-based AI-powered platform for real estate legal work, in January.
news.relevanceReason: 文章核心内容是法律科技公司收购，涉及法律AI工作流程、法律搜索和分析平台，属于法律科技领域的重要商业动态。

news.titleEn: Legora Raises $50M Series D Extension, With Backing From Nvidia Fund
news.titleZh: Legora获5000万美元D轮扩展融资，英伟达旗下基金参投
news.summaryZh: 法律科技公司Legora宣布完成5000万美元D轮扩展融资，本轮由软件公司Atlassian和AI芯片开发商英伟达旗下风险投资部门NVentures领投。参与方还包括巴克莱银行、Insight Partners、Adams Street Partners、Airtree、Geodesic Capital、Liberty Global及Nikesh Arora。此轮融资建立在Legora于今年3月宣布的由Accel领投的5.5亿美元D轮初始融资基础之上。这笔资金将推动Legora业务及代理操作系统的快速增长。基础模型正在快速改进，但真正的突破在于应用方式，即AI不仅提供协助，还能在适当的人类监督下自主执行。他称正在为法律工作构建完整的代理操作系统。此次融资扩展宣布约一周前，Legora宣布收购斯德哥尔摩研究初创公司Qura，后者主要利用大语言模型构建和导航法律数据库。本轮投资者中既有熟悉法律科技行业的机构，也有新进入者。NVentures是英伟达旗下风险投资部门，此次是其首次涉足法律科技领域。而总部位于纽约的Insight Partners此前已投资Filevine、Flank、LawVu、Litera等多家法律科技公司。巴克莱的投资则是在Legora宣布其技术已在该行内部法律团队部署约一个月后作出。
news.bodyText:
The additional funding was led by software company Atlassian as well as NVentures, the venture capital arm of AI chip developer Nvidia. Participation also included Barclays, Insight Partners, Adams Street Partners, Airtree, Geodesic Capital, Liberty Global and Nikesh Arora.

The capital builds on Legora’s initial $550 million Series D funding round, announced in March and led by Accel.

The extension will bolster rapid growth of Legora’s business and agentic operating system, according to a press release.

“Foundation models are improving rapidly, but the real breakthrough is in how they’re applied, where AI doesn’t just assist, but executes autonomously with the right level of human oversight,” Legora co-founder and CEO Max Junestrand said in the release. “With the support of our investors and customers, we’re building a full agentic operating system for legal work”

This funding extension comes roughly a week after Legora announced its acquisition of Qura, a Stockholm-based research startup that assembles legal databases largely built using and navigated by large language models (LLMs).

The extension’s contributors are made up of investors who are both familiar and new to the legal tech industry.

NVentures’ investment is the firm’s first foray into legal technology, according to its available portfolio on its website. The firm acts as a venture arm to Nvidia, which develops chips for computer graphics and AI data centers .

On the other hand, Insight Partners’ contribution to Legora’s funding round extension is one of many investments the global venture capital and private equity firm has made in the legal tech industry. The New York-based firm has previously invested in Filevine , Flank , LawVu , Litera , among others.

Barclays’ investment comes a month after Legora announced that its technology has been rolled out with the bank’s in-house legal team.
news.relevanceReason: 文章核心内容围绕法律科技公司Legora的融资进展、其法律工作代理操作系统的建设，以及收购法律数据库初创公司Qura等事项，属于典型的法律AI与法律科技领域报道。

news.titleEn: Microsoft Launches Legal Agent in Word
news.titleZh: 微软在Word中推出法律智能体
news.summaryZh:
其新推出的法律智能体（Legal Agent）旨在分析文档、起草修改内容，并检查合同是否符合用户组织的内部标准。该工具允许用户跟踪更改，并审查智能体的编辑及其建议所依据的引文。目前，该法律智能体面向美国微软早期访问Frontier计划的参与者，在Windows桌面版Word上提供。博客文章未说明该智能体何时广泛发布。

该智能体的红线标注引擎理解Word文档的结构，而不仅仅是可见文本；它将Microsoft 365文档格式理解并结构化为一种表示形式，保留格式、列表、表格和修订记录。在此基础上，智能体对编辑应用确定性解析层，包括针对特定作者的更改，而不是依赖大语言模型直接生成每一处修订。这为处理复杂合同提供了更可靠的基础，同时有助于降低延迟和成本。法律智能体的推出，距离微软宣布Word、Excel和PowerPoint中新的智能体AI功能全面可用约一周。该智能体并非微软为法律相关任务创建的首个产品。其产品在法律行业广泛使用的微软，还在其数据治理与安全平台Microsoft Purview中提供电子取证工具。微软推出法律智能体，标志着主流科技公司进一步侵入法律领域。今年早些时候，Anthropic在Claude的智能体AI Cowork产品中引入法律插件，在法律科技市场引起轰动。一些人将该插件视为对某些法律专业科技公司的潜在威胁，另一些人则预测该工具最终将证明是法律科技行业的资产。
news.bodyText:
The new Legal Agent is designed to analyze documents, draft edits and check contracts for compliance with the user organization’s internal standards, according to a blog post from Microsoft. The tool allows users to track changes and review the agent's edits and citations supporting its suggestions.

The Legal Agent is currently available on Word on Windows desktop to participants in Microsoft’s early-access Frontier program in the U.S. The blog post did not state when the agent will be broadly released.

“The agent’s redlining engine understands the structure of a Word document, not just visible text. It understands and structures Microsoft 365 document format into a representation that preserves formatting, lists, tables and tracked changes. From there, the agent applies a deterministic resolution layer over the edits, including author-specific changes, instead of relying on an LLM to generate every revision directly,” the company said in its blog post. “This provides a more reliable foundation for handling complex contracts while helping reduce latency and cost.”

The introduction of the Legal Agent comes about a week after Microsoft announced the general availability of new agentic AI capabilities in Word, Excel and PowerPoint.

The agent is not the first offering Microsoft has created for law-related tasks. The company—whose products are widely used in the legal industry—also offers an e-discovery tool within Microsoft Purview, its data governance and security platform.

Microsoft’s introduction of its Legal Agent marks a further encroachment of mainstream tech companies into the legal space.

Earlier this year, Anthropic caused a stir in the legal tech market with the introduction of a legal plugin within Claude's agentic AI Cowork offering. While some saw the plugin as a potential threat to certain legal-specific tech companies, others predicted that the tool would ultimately prove an asset to the legal tech industry.
news.relevanceReason: 该文章主要介绍微软在Word中推出的法律AI工具，直接涉及法律科技产品，因此高度相关。

news.titleEn: Agentic Systems Add New Layer of AI Hallucination Risk in Legal Work
news.titleZh: 代理式系统为法律工作带来新一层AI幻觉风险
news.summaryZh: 随着新一代代理式工具进入市场，律师及支持人员需防范更多潜在失误。代理式AI会放大生成式AI的幻觉，使未受检查的错误在多步骤工作流中累积，还带来新型幻觉：错误不仅出现在产出信息中，也出现在完成任务所用的流程本身。这源于其构建与运行方式。AI代理可创建或与其他代理交互，分配用户请求的各个部分，从而在代理与人类及代理与代理的通信中制造幻觉机会。主代理可能声称已向特定代理发出指令，实际并未发出；被分配研究法律数据库的子代理可能报告已研究并给出结果，但它从未真正研究，而是基于训练数据虚构。代理利用工具与其他程序交互也构成风险。代理式系统的优势之一是能使用其他软件平台，执行此前生成式AI无法独立完成的任务，如从文档管理系统（DMS）访问数据。为此代理执行工具调用，向子代理提供使用另一软件的参数。若参数错误，操作可能失败，而子代理可能不向主代理或用户报告。此前点击按钮从DMS拉取信息始终成功，如今小型AI介于两个系统之间，失败率更高。除非严格限制代理可访问的工具和可执行的操作，否则它们可能选错工具或危及宝贵数据。没有必要的治理机制约束其行为，它可能按指令行事，但用户可能未考虑所有后果，或存在其他缺陷。代理式工具在效率与安全之间存在艰难权衡。
news.bodyText:
With a new generation of agentic tools rapidly entering the market, lawyers and support staff will also need to guard against even more kinds of potential misfires.

Agentic AI tools can magnify the kinds of hallucinations that can appear with gen AI tools, enabling unchecked errors to compound over the course of a multistep workflow.

But agentic tools also present novel forms of hallucinations, with errors appearing not just in the information a tool produces, but also in the very process the tool uses to complete a task.

Rok Popov Ledinski, founder and CEO of MPL Legal Tech Advisors, told Law.com that these new kinds of potential errors derive in part from the way agentic tools are built and how they operate. AI agents can create or interact with other agents that they task with various components of a user’s request, creating opportunities for hallucinations in both agent-to-human and agent-to-agent communications.

“Maybe the main agent that you're communicating with will say that it has given instructions to a specific agent, but in fact, it hasn't. It has hallucinated that to you,” he said.

“A sub-agent that was given a task to go and research a specific legal database will come back to the main agent saying, ... ‘Hey, I researched the legal database, here's the result of what I have found.’ That by itself might be a hallucination, because it never went and researched the legal database, it hallucinated the things based on its training data,” he added.

The ability of agents to leverage tools and interact with other programs presents another source of possible danger. One of the major advantages of agentic systems is their ability to use other software platforms, performing tasks previous gen AI tools could not on their own, like accessing data from document management systems (DMS).

To do so, agents perform an action called a tool call, where they may provide a sub-agent with parameters for how to use another piece of software. However, if these parameters are incorrect, the required action with the other tool may fail, and the sub-agent may not report that outcome to the main agent or to the user.

“Before gen AI, you would click a button, and that button meant that some information was pulled from your [DMS]—that was 100% successful all the time,” Popov Ledinski said. “Now you have this small AI that is sitting in between those two systems, and here there's [a higher percentage of] failures than we have seen before.”

Unless agents are strictly limited in what tools they can access and what actions they can perform, they can also pick the wrong tools or compromise or valuable data.

“There's no necessary governing mechanism over what it's doing,” said Tom Barnett, senior director at legal innovation and technology advisory firm Maker5 and former chief data officer at Jackson Lewis. “It has the potential to go out into the world and start doing what you told it to do, but maybe you didn't think of all the consequences of what you asked, or there's some other bug in what it's doing.”

Necessary Caution Agentic tools can present organizations with a steep tradeoff between efficiency and safety. The ability to act autonomously is part of what allows AI agents to help users perform tasks more quickly, but that autonomy can be the source of damaging mistakes, especially if the system is not set up to allow users to trace and monitor the steps it takes.

This tradeoff is particularly stark in law and other regulated industries that deal with sensitive or confidential information, mandating an elevated level of caution, particularly since structuring and evaluating technology safeguards lies outside the core functions of law firms.

“[Law firms] are really great at delivering legal services, but they're not at their core technical organizations, so I don't know that they're in a great position to be at the cutting edge of implementing technology, using it, governing it,” Barnett said.

While agentic tools will likely continue to improve, this won’t eliminate the potential for hallucinations and similar errors. The underlying large language models that power agentic tools are generally rewarded for their output while being trained, which can make them less likely to tell a user they could not perform a requested action. Popov Ledinski also noted that some researchers have found that hallucination rates can actually increase as models develop more sophisticated reasoning capabilities.

Will Gaus, chief knowledge management and innovation officer at Troutman Pepper Locke, told Law.com that responsible deployment of agentic tools in a legal setting requires continued human oversight of the work done by agents.

“Control points should be built into workflows so there is the ability to intervene, validate and correct when needed,” he noted. “The firms that get this right treat agentic AI as a controlled extension of their existing processes, not as an autonomous layer operating alongside them.”

Popov Ledinski added that the need to move cautiously has led legal teams to introduce defined agentic workflows rather than embracing fully autonomous systems like OpenClaw, a popular AI agent that can present dangerous vulnerabilities.

“There are a lot of agentic use cases today in law firms. However, when you when you think of the more autonomous ones, where the agent comes up with what is the next step to complete the task that I have been given, I do not see real life deployments,” he said. “I see Big Law firms experimenting with that, the ones that have invested in sandboxes and experimentational environments before.”

news.titleEn: Linda Henry Joins iManage as Vice President of Customer Success
news.titleZh: 琳达·亨利加入iManage担任客户成功副总裁
news.summaryZh:
iManage于2026年4月23日宣布，琳达·亨利加入公司担任客户成功副总裁。亨利将领导iManage全球客户成功组织，在公司持续向多产品SaaS平台演进的过程中，聚焦客户采用、价值实现、留存与增长。她将推动构建更主动、以价值驱动的客户成功模式，重点加强跨职能协同、运营一致性，并将AI能力融入团队支持客户的方式。其职责包括领导由50名成员组成的全球客户成功组织，优化运营模式与分层策略，并加强销售、支持、市场、产品及更广泛市场推广组织之间的协作。

亨利具备领导经验、客户优先思维和运营纪律，有助于推动公司下一阶段增长。加入iManage前，亨利曾在Salesforce、Google、AWS和Microsoft等科技公司任职，在扩展客户导向团队和支持复杂全球业务增长方面积累了丰富经验。iManage兼具市场领导力、增长机会和对创新的承诺，她期待推动客户成功组织演进，深化客户价值、加强长期合作伙伴关系并支持公司下一阶段增长。亨利常驻芝加哥，向詹姆斯·普里兹汇报。
news.bodyHtml:
New leader to help scale a more proactive, value-driven customer success organization aligned to adoption, retention, and growth

 

CHICAGO – April 23, 2026 – iManage, the company dedicated to Making Knowledge Work™, today announced that Linda Henry has joined the company as Vice President of Customer Success, bringing extensive experience leading customer success organizations across SaaS businesses. In this role, Henry will lead iManage’s global Customer Success organization as the company continues to evolve as a multi-product SaaS platform and sharpen its focus on customer adoption, value realization, retention, and growth.

 

Henry joins iManage at a time of continued growth and product expansion. She will focus on helping the company build a more proactive, value-driven customer success model, with an emphasis on stronger cross-functional alignment, operational consistency, and the incorporation of AI capabilities into how the team supports customers. Her remit includes leading a global Customer Success organization of 50 team members, refining operating models and tiering strategies, and strengthening collaboration across Sales, Support, Marketing, Product, and the broader go-to-market organization.

 

“Linda brings the leadership experience, customer-first mindset, and operational discipline needed to help drive our next phase of growth,” said James Priz, Executive Vice President of Customer Experience at iManage. “She understands what it takes to build and scale modern customer success organizations, and her experience will be instrumental as we continue helping customers realize greater value from the iManage platform.”

 

Before joining iManage, Henry built her career across leading technology companies, including Salesforce, Google, AWS, and Microsoft, gaining deep experience in scaling customer-focused teams and supporting growth across complex global businesses. Her background aligns closely with iManage’s focus on evolving Customer Success into a more proactive, strategic function that strengthens adoption, retention, and long-term customer value.

 

“I joined iManage because it has the right combination of market leadership, growth opportunity, and commitment to innovation,” said Linda Henry, Vice President of Customer Success at iManage. “I’m excited to help evolve the customer success organization in ways that deepen customer value, strengthen long-term partnerships, and support the company’s next phase of growth.”

 

As Vice President of Customer Success, Henry will help further position Customer Success as a revenue-impacting organization at iManage, with a focus on scalable customer engagement, measurable adoption outcomes, and stronger alignment between customer value and long-term business growth.

 

Henry is based in Chicago and reports to James Priz.

 

About iManage

iManage is dedicated to Making Knowledge Work™. Our cloud-native platform is at the center of the knowledge economy, enabling every organization to work more productively, collaboratively, and securely. Built on more than 30 years of industry experience, iManage helps leading organizations manage documents and emails more efficiently, protect vital information assets, and leverage knowledge to drive better business outcomes. As your strategic business partner, we employ our award-winning AI-enabled technology, an extensive partner ecosystem, and a customer-centric approach to provide support and guidance you can trust to make knowledge work for you. iManage is relied on by more than one million professionals at 4,000 organizations around the world. Visit www.imanage.com to learn more.

news.titleEn: CloudLex Introduces the First ‘Personal Injury Ecosystem’
news.titleZh: CloudLex推出首个“人身伤害生态系统”
news.summaryZh:
CloudLex推出首个“人身伤害生态系统”，即专为原告人身伤害律师事务所打造的完整人身伤害管理软件。CloudLex不再只是案件管理软件，而是由平台、Lexee AI、律师助理服务和Voices of PI（以Trial Lawyers Journal为核心的社区与内容支柱）组成的一个互联生态系统，旨在让人身伤害律所减少管理供应商的时间，将更多时间用于赢得案件。

中型人身伤害律所的典型早晨可能需要在案件管理系统中查看截止日期、登录单独的AI工具审阅医疗摘要，再联系外部供应商确认治疗机构的记录是否送达，三个系统、三次登录，同一案件数据存在略有不同的版本。这种多供应商组合是多数原告人身伤害律所的默认状态：法律软件处理案件、文件和日历，独立AI工具处理医疗摘要或接案，外部服务处理记录调取，摩擦出现在系统之间的空隙，数据同步负担落在员工身上。CloudLex生态系统将平台、Lexee AI和律师助理服务整合为单一记录系统，覆盖从接案到和解的完整生命周期，内置人身伤害专属工作流、医疗记录跟踪、索赔管理和和解管理；AI无需导出或上传即可原生读取案件文件，支持医疗摘要、时间线、需求起草、接案采集和案件问答；人身伤害专员直接在案件文件中工作，处理医疗记录调取、文档管理、时间线及相关支持工作。
news.bodyHtml:
CloudLex introduces the first Personal Injury Ecosystem — the complete personal injury management software, built exclusively for plaintiff personal injury law firms. CloudLex is no longer just case management software. It is one connected ecosystem of the Platform, Lexee AI, Paralegal Services, and Voices of PI — the community and content pillar anchored by Trial Lawyers Journal — built so PI firms spend less time managing vendors and more time winning cases.

A typical morning at a mid-size PI law firm might go something like this: check the case management system for deadlines, log into a separate AI tool to review a medical summary, then follow up with an outside vendor to confirm whether records from a treating provider have come in. Three systems, three logins, three places where the same case data lives in slightly different versions. Meanwhile, client phone calls go to voicemail because your intake team is toggling between platforms while trying to log yesterday’s new leads.

That’s not an unusual setup. For most plaintiff PI firms today, it’s the default. Some version of legal software handles matters, documents, and calendars. A standalone AI tool handles medical summaries or intake. An outside service handles record retrieval. Each one does its job. The friction shows up in the spaces between them – and the data management burden of keeping everything synchronized falls on your staff.

Medical records arrive from a vendor and get uploaded to the case management software by hand. Your AI tool generates a summary, but only from the case documents someone exported and uploaded to it – with no visibility into related documents still sitting in another system. A demand letter references treatment dates that have to be cross-checked against a timeline elsewhere. Individually, none of these administrative tasks take long. Across a few hundred active litigation matters, the cumulative time your team spends moving data between disconnected tools starts adding up in ways that are easy to overlook and hard to measure.

One connected ecosystem for personal injury law firms 

The CloudLex ecosystem brings platform, Lexee AI, and paralegal services together in a single system of record, so PI firms no longer have to assemble their stack one vendor at a time.

Platform

The system of record covering the full lifecycle from intake through settlement, with PI-specific workflows, medical records tracking, claims management, and settlement management built in.

Lexee AI

AI that reads case files natively, without exports or uploads, to support medical summaries, chronologies, demand drafting, intake capture, and case-specific Q&A.

Paralegal Services

PI specialists who work directly inside the case file to handle medical record retrieval, document management, chronologies, and related support work.

The structural difference lies in how these layers relate to one another. In one connected ecosystem, they share the same data, the same user interface, and the same workflow. Records retrieved by the support team are immediately available for the AI to summarize – no waiting, no re-uploading, real-time access for your entire legal team. Settlement calculations pull from billing data already in the matter. Demand drafts reference treatment chronologies that exist in the same case file where everything else lives.

This is a single system in which each layer operates on the same foundation, making each one more useful than it would be on its own.

What this looks like in a case

Consider a motor vehicle accident case with treatment across four providers over several months.

In a multi-vendor setup, the workflow might move like this: the firm requests records through an outside retrieval service. Records come back by email or portal and get manually uploaded to the case management software. Someone exports the relevant case documents and uploads them to the AI tool. The AI generates a summary based on whatever was uploaded – without pulling from related documents or billing records that may still be sitting in the case management system. An associate reviews the summary, cross-references it against the case timeline, and starts building the demand.

Each handoff between systems is a point where the dataset narrows. The AI only works with what it received. The case management software only reflects what was entered. The record retrieval service only tracks what was requested. Nobody on your legal team has a complete picture unless someone manually assembles one – and that fragmented view of the case files can directly affect the quality of the work product shaping your case outcomes.

In one connected ecosystem, that same case moves differently. The support team retrieves and indexes records directly inside the case file. The AI reads those records natively – full treatment history, billing data, case timeline, all already in the matter. Summaries and chronologies draw from the complete record, not a partial export. When your associate opens the case to draft the demand, the building blocks are already there, in the same place the case lives. No re-entering data, no exporting PDFs to another platform, no checking whether the AI had the latest version of the file.

Neither column is inherently right or wrong. Plenty of firms run multi-vendor stacks effectively. But the coordination overhead of keeping data synchronized across systems increases with every tool, and that overhead compounds as case volume grows – particularly for high-volume practices managing hundreds of active claims litigation files simultaneously. A connected ecosystem is increasingly where forward-looking PI firms find an edge — not because the tools they had before were wrong, but because one shared layer for case data, AI, and paralegal support tends to compound advantages the longer a firm runs on it.

Why this is coming up now

Two things are driving this conversation.

First, AI adoption in PI is picking up fast. Firms that were cautious a year or two ago are now actively evaluating tools for medical summaries, chronologies, and demand support. Most of these tools operate outside the case management system, which means the AI is only as current and complete as the last export someone ran. It also means AI-generated output has to be manually moved back into the case file – another handoff for your legal team to manage, another place where something can fall out of sync.

Second, outsourced support services have become standard at most mid-size PI law firms. Medical record retrieval, chronology preparation, document indexing. These services lighten your team’s workload, but they also introduce another data silo. Records come back through a vendor portal or email, then have to be filed into the case management software before anyone else on your team can work with them.

The pattern is familiar: you add tools to solve specific problems, and each new tool adds another system to maintain. Another login, another data format, another place where case information lives outside the system of record. Your stack gets wider without necessarily getting more connected – and the resulting litigation costs, along with the less visible legal costs of duplicated data management and staff time, grow quietly alongside the case count.

A connected ecosystem is the structural alternative. Instead of layering AI and services on top of legal software, it integrates all three into one platform. For firms rethinking their legal operations and looking to establish best practices for how technology, services, and case data connect, the distinction between case management software and an end-to-end connected ecosystem is critical to understand.

What this means for your firm

If your firm has case management software that’s working, the point isn’t to abandon it. But a few questions are worth sitting with:

  • How often does the same case data get entered, uploaded, or transferred between systems in a given week? 
  • When your AI tool generates a summary, is it working from the full case files or just the case documents someone remembered to export? 
  • How long after records arrive from an outside vendor does your legal team have real-time access in the case management software? 
  • If a client calls with a question about their case, how many systems does someone on your team need to open to give a complete answer? 

Every firm’s answer is different, and the right setup depends on case volume, team size, practice complexity, and appetite for managing vendor relationships. For legal professionals weighing whether to keep building on a multi-vendor stack or consolidate into a connected system, the choice is less about any single tool and more about how your whole operation fits together, and whether your approach to data management is helping or holding back the case outcomes you’re working toward.

CloudLex is the complete personal injury management software — one connected ecosystem of the Platform, Lexee AI, Paralegal Services, and Voices of PI. Each pillar has its own page with more details, and a demo is the most efficient way to see how it comes together on a real case.

Click here to schedule your demo today.

news.titleEn: Microsoft releases new Legal Agent for Word
news.titleZh: 微软发布面向Word的新法律智能体
news.summaryZh:
微软于4月30日宣布推出专为Microsoft Word法律工作流程设计的新法律智能体（Legal Agent）。该智能体与法律工程师合作开发，面向合同审查和修订等场景，而非将通用人工智能适配于法律用例。作为第一方体验，法律智能体直接与Word原生审阅工具（包括修订和批注）协同工作，并支持Microsoft 365中的法律工作流程。该智能体可实现剧本驱动的合同分析、具备透明修订记录的谈判就绪修订，以及在整个文档中可扩展地起草精确、可审阅的法律编辑。

该智能体通过专门构建的插入算法在文档中应用编辑，以确保一致性，无论每处编辑如何引入。其修订引擎理解Word文档结构而非仅可见文本，将Microsoft 365文档格式理解并结构化为保留格式、列表、表格和修订的表示。在此基础上，智能体对编辑应用确定性解析层，包括特定作者的更改，而非依赖大语言模型直接生成每处修订，从而为处理复杂合同提供更可靠的基础，并有助于降低延迟和成本。该进展将受到极大且警惕的关注。微软持续构建法律特定能力，包括4月初在Copilot中新增法律功能，与文档审查供应商形成竞争。一方面，微软拥有数十亿技术投资、熟悉度以及安全受治理的365环境内的功能；另一方面，经验表明，对法律工作流程的深入理解和产品卓越性在该领域始终胜过便利性，因此有待进一步信息和更新。
news.bodyHtml:
It’s looked to be on the cards for a while and today (30 April), Microsoft announced its new Legal Agent, designed specifically for legal workflows in Microsoft Word. Developed in collaboration with legal engineers, Legal Agent is designed for workflows such as contract review and redlining, rather than adapting general-purpose AI to legal use cases.

As a first-party experience, Legal Agent works directly with Word’s native reviewing tools (including track changes and comments) and is designed to support legal workflows across Microsoft 365. Microsoft says that the agent enables playbook‑driven contract analysis, negotiation‑ready redlining with transparent track changes, and scalable drafting of precise, reviewable legal edits across entire documents.

Advertisement

A post from Microsoft Office Product Group president Sumit Chauhan today says: “The agent applies edits in the document through a purpose-built insertion algorithm to drive consistency regardless of how each edit was introduced. The agent’s redlining engine understands the structure of a Word document, not just visible text. It understands and structures Microsoft 365 document format into a representation that preserves formatting, lists, tables, and tracked changes. From there, the agent applies a deterministic resolution layer over the edits, including author-specific changes, instead of relying on an LLM to generate every revision directly. This provides a more reliable foundation for handling complex contracts while helping reduce latency and cost.”

This development will be watched with great and also wary interest. Microsoft has been increasingly building its legal specific capability, including earlier in April, new legal functionality in Copilot that put it in competition with document review vendors. On the one hand, its Microsoft, with its billions of tech investment, familiarity, and functionality that falls within the secure and governed 365 world. On the other, we know from experience that a deep understanding of the legal workflow and product excellence succeed over and above convenience every time in this space, so we await further information and updates.

Advertisement

news.titleEn: NVIDIA Fund + Atlassian Join $50m Legora Investment
news.titleZh: 英伟达基金与Atlassian联合投资Legora 5000万美元
news.summaryZh: 英伟达旗下风险投资部门NVentures与Atlassian已投资于法律AI公司Legora。此次参与的5000万美元D轮扩展融资使该轮融资总额达到6亿美元。Legora自成立以来累计融资总额现已达到8.66亿美元，公司估值达56亿美元。其他主要投资方包括巴克莱银行、Geodesic Capital、Insight Partners、Liberty Global和Nikesh Arora。他们看到与Atlassian的AI驱动团队协作愿景高度一致，并期待支持Legora的持续扩张。基础模型正在快速改进，但真正的突破在于应用方式，AI不仅提供协助，还能在适当的人类监督下自主执行。他们正在构建一个面向法律工作的完整智能体操作系统。过去一年，Legora员工规模从40人扩展至400人，客户群从200家组织增至50多个市场的1000多家组织。企业法律部门现已成为Legora增长最快的细分领域之一。随着AI智能体从被动助手转变为能够代表用户行动、使用工具并完成工作流程的系统，软件模式正从SaaS向AaaS转变。对法律团队而言，这意味着超越孤立用例，转向整合公司数据、司法知识和智能代理的综合系统。市场对参与本轮融资兴趣浓厚，他们视此为引入更多战略投资者的机会。
news.bodyHtml:
NVIDIA’s venture capital arm NVentures and Atlassian have invested in Legora. The $50m Series D extension that they joined brings the total round to $600m.

The total overall money raised since launch by Legora is now $866m, valuing the company at $5.6 billion.

The Stockholm-based legal AI company added that other major names to have put money into Legora include: Barclays, Geodesic Capital, Insight Partners, Liberty Global and Nikesh Arora.

Sarah Hughes, Atlassian Head of Corporate Development and Product Partnerships, commented: ‘We see strong alignment with Atlassian’s vision for AI-powered team collaboration and look forward to supporting their continued expansion.’

And Max Junestrand, CEO and Co-founder of Legora, added: ‘Foundation models are improving rapidly, but the real breakthrough is in how they’re applied, where AI doesn’t just assist, but executes autonomously with the right level of human oversight. With the support of our investors and customers, we’re building a full agentic operating system for legal work.’

Over the past year, Legora has ‘scaled from 40 to 400 employees and expanded its customer base from 200 to more than 1,000 organizations across 50+ markets’, they noted. They also stressed that ‘corporate legal departments now represent one of Legora’s fastest-growing segments’

They also underlined that the future is agentic.

‘As AI agents move from passive assistants to systems that can act on behalf of users, using tools and completing workflows, the software model is beginning to shift from SaaS (Software as a Service) toward AaaS (Agent as a Service). For legal teams, this means moving beyond isolated use cases to integrated systems that combine firm data, jurisdictional knowledge, and intelligent agents,’ they concluded.

AL asked Legora why the funding extension has taken place now. A spokesperson told this site this morning: ‘There was great interest in participating in the round and we saw this as an opportunity to bring on more strategic investors.’

Congrats to Legora. More about them here.

–

news.titleEn: Magic Circle Firm Slaughter and May Adopts Harvey
news.titleZh: 魔术圈律所Slaughter and May采用Harvey
news.summaryZh:
英国魔术圈律所Slaughter and May经过长期考虑后，全面采用Harvey的法律AI平台。将在所有业务领域部署Harvey的完整平台，以支持律师处理跨境并购、尽职调查、监管研究和文件分析等事务。全所采用Harvey有助于提升客户服务质量，而对人员的投资是监督AI的关键人力层。律所的差异化优势在于经验深度和质量，AI有助于在不同情境中连接和运用这些专长，增强集体判断力、创造力和解决问题的能力。

Harvey因代理能力、安全性、在大型律所领导AI转型的成熟经验、在律所客户群中的存在以及满足律所严格标准的能力而中选。Harvey的转型办公室将与该所合作，支持推广并确保AI在业务中负责任且有效地应用。Slaughter and May在130年中凭借深厚的法律专长和杰出律师以及对新技术的拥抱建立了卓越声誉，Harvey很荣幸支持该所及其客户将AI应用于世界上一些最重要的法律工作。魔术圈五家律所中已有四家明确选择平台：Linklaters选择Legora，A&O Shearman很早就选择Harvey，Freshfields大规模采用Anthropic并早前与Google合作，Clifford Chance的选择仍在确认中。
news.bodyHtml:
And so the Magic Circle continues to pick their legal AI platforms. Slaughter and May, after a long period of consideration, has gone all-in with Harvey.

Linklaters went with Legora, A&O Shearman also famously went very early with Harvey, Freshfields has gone large with Anthropic, and also earlier with Google, and Clifford Chance has picked….hmmm. AL is still checking that.

The esteemed UK-based firm said that: ‘[We] are adopting Harvey’s full platform across all practice areas to support its lawyers on multi-jurisdictional matters spanning M&A, due diligence, regulatory research, and document analysis.’

David Johnson, Slaughter and May Managing Partner, commented: ‘Adopting Harvey firmwide allows us to enhance the excellent service that we provide to our clients. Critical to our adoption is the investment we make in our people, as the vital human layer that supervises AI.’

Sally Wokes, partner and Head of Slaughter and May’s Innovation Committee, added: ‘Our differentiator is the depth and quality of our experience. AI allows us to connect and apply that expertise in different situations, enhancing the collective judgment, creativity and problem solving we bring to client matters.’

Harvey was selected ‘for its agentic capabilities and security, its proven experience leading AI transformation inside major law firms, its presence across the firm’s client base, and its ability to meet the firm’s exacting standards’, they said.

Harvey’s Transformation Office, which includes ‘seasoned legal experts, will work alongside the firm to support the rollout and ensure AI is adopted responsibly and effectively across the business’, they added.

Winston Weinberg, CEO of Harvey, concluded: ‘Slaughter and May has built its reputation for excellence over 130 years by pairing deep legal expertise and outstanding lawyers with a willingness to embrace new technologies. We are honoured to support the firm and its clients as they apply AI to some of the most consequential legal work in the world.’

Is this a big deal?

Well, if you believe that the Magic Circle are very influential in the legal world….then yes, absolutely it matters. In fact, every major move they make matters, as their choices influence other major firms and in turn those choices trickle down through the market. Slaughters in particular has a global ‘best friends’ network of leading firms – so it will be interesting to see how this follows through.

There are also only five Magic Circle firms, and as noted above, four have now clearly picked a side, as it were. On CC, AL is still checking. Or, CC, if you’re reading this, drop AL a line.

More about Harvey here.

—

news.titleEn: Artificial Lawyer View On The Microsoft Legal Agent
news.titleZh: 人工智能律师对微软法律智能体的看法
news.summaryZh: 微软正式进军法律科技领域，推出了名为“法律智能体”的产品，旨在处理一系列法律任务。这一举措意义重大，因为此前Anthropic通过逐步布局进入法律科技市场，已引发巨大反响，如今微软也以明确意图加入竞争。与Claude for Word插件相比，微软法律智能体的影响可能更大，因为99%的法律工作都在Word中完成，而微软正是Word的开发商，该产品并非第三方应用，而是原生集成。该产品是与法律工程师紧密合作开发的，以反映合同审查和谈判的实际方式。与通用工具Copilot不同，法律智能体是专门为法律工作设计的专业工具，其开发团队中许多人来自已倒闭的法律AI公司Robin。讽刺的是，如果Robin AI没有倒闭，这一举措可能不会发生，或至少不会这么快。此外，Claude for Word插件的出现也可能加速了微软的布局。目前，Claude for Word的评价褒贬不一，但竞争对手的负面评价在所难免，且现有功能可通过定制化进一步提升。微软法律智能体是从底层代码开始构建，专为Word环境设计，并由深谙法律科技领域的人员参与开发，因此被视为一个完全不同的竞争层级。现在的问题是律师对其性能的评价如何。无论如何，目前已有两家科技巨头明确瞄准法律科技市场。
news.bodyHtml:
Microsoft has well and truly entered legal tech with its Legal Agent – see previous AL story. So, why does this matter? Well, Anthropic’s entry into legal tech, via a series of increasingly intentional steps, caused a huge reaction across the market. Now, Microsoft has joined in as well, and quite intentionally too, with a product branded as a ‘Legal Agent’ and designed to handle a whole range of legal tasks.

Is this about the same as the Claude for Word move? Arguably it’s a lot greater in impact, because – as we all know – 99% of legal work is done in Word. And this is made by the company that made Word. This is not a third-party app. It’s the real thing. 

You may then say ‘But, we have MS Copilot, and it’s not great.’ True, (although apparently getting better now).

As noted explicitly by Microsoft, this ‘was built in close collaboration with legal engineers to reflect how contracts are reviewed and negotiated’.

Copilot is a general tool that lawyers can use as best they can for legal work.

Legal Agent is a specific, professional tool, designed ‘by legal engineers’ – many of whom came from legal AI company Robin.

In short, where before Microsoft was both within the legal world, but not really into legal tech, this is really a legal tech tool, designed by experts who actually used to work at a legal tech company.

Ironically, if Robin AI had not gone under, this move may not have happened – or at least not so soon.

One can also assume that the Claude for Word plugin has also potentially sped things up.

Will this change the legal world?

Well, reviews of Claude for Word are mixed – but then, competitors will of course be negative about rivals. That’s to be expected. And whatever is there now can improve and also with customisation can deliver a lot more. 

But, even so, as noted, this is something else. This is a Microsoft legal tech product, made from the most foundational code upwards to work inside Word, and built by – at least some – people who are deep into the world of legal tech already.

In short, this is a whole different ballgame.

The question now is: what do lawyers think of its performance?

We shall soon find out.

Either way, there are now two tech giants quite intentionally targeting legal tech.

—

Richard Tromans, Founder, Artificial Lawyer

news.titleEn: Microsoft Launches Its Own Legal Agent For Word
news.titleZh: 微软推出自有Word法律代理
news.summaryZh:
微软在Word中推出面向法律行业的“法律代理”（Legal Agent），从Robin AI加入的团队在其中发挥关键作用。此举紧随Claude推出Word插件之后。该代理可处理生成红线标记、审阅对方修改等繁琐工作，让法律专业人士专注于高影响力决策。法律工作流程要求精确性和可审计性，通用AI工具并非为法律团队依赖的结构化流程而设计。

该代理与法律工程师密切合作构建，遵循真实法律实践塑造的结构化工作流，可依据操作手册逐条审阅合同。其红线引擎理解Word文档结构，保留格式、列表、表格和修订记录，并应用确定性解析层处理编辑，而非依赖LLM直接生成每处修订，从而降低延迟和成本。它能分析完整协议、深入条款、比较版本以发现风险，并提供链接源语言的引用；可生成保留原始格式的红线标记，在已含修订的文档中区分新旧提案以保留谈判历史，标记不合规条款并建议编辑，用户可查看引用并在批准前审阅所有编辑。该代理在Microsoft 365安全、合规和治理控制内运行。早期反馈显示法律专业人士重视其领域专长，同时保持完全控制。该代理即日起通过Frontier计划在美国Windows桌面版Word中提供。微软补充，该代理不提供法律建议，不能替代合格法律专业人士的判断，AI生成内容可能不准确，用户需自行负责审阅、验证并决定是否依赖任何输出。
news.bodyHtml:
In major news for the legal tech market, Microsoft is specifically targeting our sector with a ‘Legal Agent’ in Word. It is understood that the team that joined from Robin AI has been integral to this product launch. It comes after Claude launched a Word plugin.

Microsoft stated: ‘Building on our recent announcement of agentic capabilities in Word, today we are introducing the Legal Agent in Microsoft Word. Whether you are generating redlines or reviewing counterparty changes, the agent handles tedious work, so legal professionals can focus on high-impact decisions.’

In a blog by Sumit Chauhan, President, Office Product Group at Microsoft, it’s explained that: ‘Legal workflows demand precision and auditability. While general-purpose AI tools can assist with document review, they aren’t designed to follow the structured processes legal teams rely on to evaluate risk and maintain consistency.’

—

Express route to your Legal Innovators California June 10th and 11th ticket here.

Legal Innovators California, the landmark West Coast legal tech event, will take place on June 10 and 11, in the heart of the Bay Area, the home to many of the world’s leading AI businesses – and plenty of legal tech pioneers as well! More information and tickets here.

 —

How the Legal Agent works

And they explain that:

‘The Legal Agent was built in close collaboration with legal engineers to reflect how contracts are reviewed and negotiated. Instead of relying on general AI models to interpret commands, the agent follows structured workflows shaped by real legal practice, managing clearly defined, repeatable tasks like reviewing contracts clause by clause against a playbook.

‘The agent applies edits in the document through a purpose-built insertion algorithm to drive consistency regardless of how each edit was introduced. The agent’s redlining engine understands the structure of a Word document, not just visible text. It understands and structures Microsoft 365 document format into a representation that preserves formatting, lists, tables, and tracked changes. From there, the agent applies a deterministic resolution layer over the edits, including author-specific changes, instead of relying on an LLM to generate every revision directly. This provides a more reliable foundation for handling complex contracts while helping reduce latency and cost.

What the Legal Agent Does

‘[It can] understand complex legal documents. The Legal Agent analyzes the full agreement, drills into specific clauses, and compares versions to spot risks and obligations. It also provides citations that link directly to the source language, so reviewers can quickly verify responses.

‘Draft precise edits. Tell the Legal Agent what to change, and it produces negotiation-ready redlines with tracked changes across relevant sections, minimizing unnecessary edits and preserving original formatting.

‘Negotiate with confidence. The agent works inside documents that already contain tracked changes, separating prior revisions from new proposals, so negotiation history is retained.

‘Review contracts against your playbook. The Legal Agent flags non-conforming provisions and recommends edits to align with internal standards and approved language from your playbook. Apply suggestions one-by-one or across the document.

‘Maintain trust and control. View supporting citations for each suggestion from the agent and review all edits before approving. The agent keeps tracked changes and can also insert comments explaining the changes.

‘Keep sensitive workflows secure. The Legal Agent runs within Microsoft 365 security, compliance, and governance controls your organization already uses for legal documents and standards.’

—

Also they added that: ‘Early customer feedback shows strong interest in how the Legal Agent supports legal workflows in Word. Legal professionals value its domain expertise in inspecting citations, working with tracked changes, and reviewing documents against internal playbooks while maintaining full control. For legal teams, it’s crucial that their AI tools fit into established review processes without compromising security and confidence in the document.’

–

The Legal Agent is available today in Word on Windows desktop through the Frontier program in the US.

–

They also added that ‘the Legal Agent does not provide legal advice or professional determinations and is not a substitute for the judgment of a qualified legal professional. AI‑generated content may be inaccurate. Users are solely responsible for reviewing, verifying, and deciding whether to rely on any output before taking action’.

–

So, why does this matter? Well, Anthropic’s entry into legal tech, via a series of increasingly intentional steps, caused a huge reaction across the market. Now, Microsoft has joined in as well, and quite intentionally too, with a product branded as a ‘Legal Agent’ and designed to handle a whole range of legal tasks.

Is this about the same as the Claude for Word move? Arguably it’s a lot greater in impact, because – as we all know – 99% of legal work is done in Word. And this is made by the company that made Word. This is not a third-party app. It’s the real thing.

You may then say ‘But, we have MS Copilot, and it’s not great.’ True, (although apparently getting better now). As noted explicitly by Microsoft, this ‘was built in close collaboration with legal engineers to reflect how contracts are reviewed and negotiated’.

Copilot is a general tool that lawyers can use as best they can for legal work.

Legal Agent is a specific, professional tool, designed ‘by legal engineers’ – many of whom came from legal AI company Robin.

In short, where before Microsoft was both within the legal world, but not really into legal tech, this is really a legal tech tool, designed by experts who actually used to work at a legal tech company.

Ironically, if Robin AI had not gone under this move may not have happened – or at least not so soon.

One can also assume that the Claude for Word plugin has also potentially sped things up.

Will this change the legal world?

Well, reviews of Claude for Word are mixed – but then, competitors will of course be negative about rivals. That’s to be expected. And whatever is there now can improve and also with customisation can deliver a lot more.

But, even so, as noted, this is something else. This is a Microsoft legal tech product, made from the most foundational code upwards to work inside Word, and built by – at least some of the team – people who are deep into the world of legal tech already.

In short, this is a whole different ballgame.

The question now is: what do lawyers think of its performance?

We shall soon find out.

Either way, there are now two tech giants quite intentionally targeting legal tech.

Richard Tromans, Founder, Artificial Lawyer

research.titleEn: ViLegalNLI: Natural Language Inference for Vietnamese Legal Texts
research.titleZh: ViLegalNLI：面向越南法律文本的自然语言推理
research.abstractEn: In this article, we introduce ViLegalNLI, the first large-scale Vietnamese Natural Language Inference (NLI) dataset specifically constructed for the legal domain. The dataset consists of 42,012 premise-hypothesis pairs derived from official statutory documents and annotated with binary inference labels (Entailment and Non-entailment). It covers multiple legal domains and reflects realistic legal reasoning scenarios characterized by structured logic, conditional clauses, and domain-specific terminology. To construct ViLegalNLI, we propose a semi-automatic data generation framework that integrates large language models for controlled hypothesis generation and systematic quality validation procedures. The framework incorporates artifact mitigation strategies and cross-model validation to improve annotation reliability and ensure legal consistency. The resulting dataset captures diverse reasoning patterns, including paraphrasing, logical implication, and legally invalid inferences, thereby providing a comprehensive benchmark for Vietnamese legal inference tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on the ViLegalNLI using multilingual models, Vietnamese-specific pretrained language models, and instruction-tuned large language models. The results show that few-shot LLM configurations consistently achieve superior performance, while performance is significantly influenced by hypothesis length, lexical overlap, and reasoning complexity. Cross-domain evaluations further reveal the challenges of generalizing legal inference across distinct legal fields. Overall, ViLegalNLI establishes a foundational benchmark for Vietnamese legal NLI and supports future research in legal reasoning, statutory text understanding, and the development of reliable AI systems for legal analysis and decision support. The dataset is publicly available for research purposes.
research.abstractZh: 在本文中，我们介绍了ViLegalNLI，这是首个专门为法律领域构建的大规模越南语自然语言推理（NLI）数据集。该数据集包含42,012个前提-假设对，这些对源自官方法定文件，并标注了二元推理标签（蕴含和非蕴含）。它涵盖了多个法律领域，反映了以结构化逻辑、条件条款和领域特定术语为特征的真实法律推理场景。为了构建ViLegalNLI，我们提出了一种半自动数据生成框架，该框架集成了大型语言模型用于受控假设生成和系统化的质量验证程序。该框架结合了伪影缓解策略和跨模型验证，以提高注释可靠性并确保法律一致性。生成的数据集捕捉了多样化的推理模式，包括释义、逻辑蕴含和法律上无效的推理，从而为越南语法律推理任务提供了全面的基准。我们使用多语言模型、越南语特定预训练语言模型和指令微调的大型语言模型在ViLegalNLI上进行了大量实验。结果表明，少样本LLM配置始终取得优越性能，而性能受假设长度、词汇重叠和推理复杂性的显著影响。跨领域评估进一步揭示了在不同法律领域之间泛化法律推理的挑战。总体而言，ViLegalNLI为越南语法律NLI建立了基础基准，并支持未来在法律推理、成文法理解以及开发用于法律分析和决策支持的可靠AI系统方面的研究。该数据集可公开获取用于研究目的。

policy.summaryZh: 国家标准《人工智能终端智能化分级 第2部分：总体要求》（GB/Z 177.2-2026）为现行指导性技术文件，由全国信息技术标准化技术委员会（TC28）归口、其人工智能分会（TC28SC42）执行，主管部门为国家标准委。该标准于2026年4月30日发布，标准计划编号20252054-Z-469，标准类别为产品，中国标准分类号L62，国际标准分类号35.160（微处理机系统）。主要起草单位包括中国信息通信研究院、中国电子技术标准化研究院、中国软件评测中心、华为、联想、联通(广东)产业互联网、OPPO、维沃、小米、荣耀、中兴、科大讯飞、中移（杭州）、青岛海信移动通信、中国工业互联网研究院、中国电器科学研究院、海信视像等。主要起草人为高峰、陈磊、翟云、苗力元、杨磊、高歌、沈芷月、马子扬、邓森屾、翟腾、麦睿楷、史浩、王卓、陶宏芝、吕召彪、高明亮、康峰、杨振宇、高立发、曹宇琼、刘海涛、朱亚军、曾勇波、聂大伟、叶佳、张宏伟、杨彤晖、张云畅、宁懿、张学杰、薛强、邢军。该标准属人工智能终端智能化分级系列标准的总体要求部分，同系列相近标准计划还包括照明系统、翻译笔、学习机、智能玩具、智能门锁、投影显示设备、交互式电子白板、腕式可穿戴设备、工业控制计算机、扫地机器人等分册。

policy.summaryZh: 国家标准《网络安全技术 SM2密码算法加密签名消息格式》（GB/T 35275-2026）为推荐性国家标准，由全国网络安全标准化技术委员会（TC260）归口，主管部门为国家标准委，主管单位为国家市场监督管理总局、国家标准化管理委员会。该标准于2026年4月30日发布，2026年11月1日实施，全部代替GB/T 35275-2017《信息安全技术 SM2密码算法加密签名消息语法规范》，标准计划编号20250639-T-469，标准类别为安全，中国标准分类号L80，国际标准分类号35.030（IT安全）。主要起草单位包括格尔软件股份有限公司、北京国脉信安科技有限公司、广东省电子商务认证有限公司、智巡密码（上海）检测技术有限公司、北京信安世纪科技股份有限公司、北京数字认证股份有限公司、上海市数字证书认证中心有限公司、中电信量子信息科技集团有限公司、华为技术有限公司、商用密码检测认证中心、中国信息通信研究院、国家工业信息安全发展研究中心、麒麟软件有限公司等多家单位，主要起草人包括郑强、刘平、封维端、陈树乐、罗俊、韩玮等。

news.titleEn: Legal Marketing Association President Rachel Shields Williams On AI, Innovation, and Why People Still Come First
news.titleZh: 法律营销协会主席Rachel Shields Williams谈AI、创新以及为何人始终是第一位的
news.summaryZh:
本期LawNext节目在新奥尔良法律营销协会（LMA）年会现场录制，主持人与LMA主席、Sidley Austin客户情报总监Rachel Shields Williams展开对话。Rachel在Sidley Austin工作了17年，致力于构建营销、业务拓展、知识管理与数据交叉领域的角色。今年早些时候，她荣获ALM的Monica Bay法律科技女性奖。

双方讨论了AI如何重塑法律营销人员的工作，以及为何她认为营销社区具有独特优势，能帮助律所超越AI采用的“我很好奇，我想点按钮”阶段，实现持续、可重复的价值。对话涉及大律所创新的现状——包括Rachel的观点：律所无法用AI或金钱“跳过变革管理中的绝望峡谷”，以及她认为有意义的创新往往不像头条新闻，而更像每周进步1%。对话还涵盖传统律所面临的竞争格局变化，从Norm AI等AI原生进入者到MSOs和复苏的ALSP市场；关于计费小时的长期争论；Rachel认为每家律所数据核心的四个相互关联要素——文档、客户、事项和人员；以及律所领导者当前应如何做才能在未来十年保持竞争力。贯穿始终，Rachel回归到一个她自称“毫不掩饰的人文主义者”的主题——技术和流程会不断变化，但胜出的律所将是那些首先让合适的人参与进来的律所。
news.bodyHtml:
Recorded live at the annual meeting of the Legal Marketing Association in New Orleans, this episode features my conversation with Rachel Shields Williams, president of the LMA and director of client intelligence at Sidley Austin, where she has spent 17 years building out roles at the intersection of marketing, business development, knowledge management and data. Earlier this year, Rachel was named a recipient of ALM’s Monica Bay Women in Legal Tech Award.

Rachel and I discuss how AI is reshaping the work of legal marketers, and why she believes the marketing community is uniquely positioned to help law firms move past the “I’m curious, I want to click the buttons” stage of AI adoption to sustained, repeatable value. We get into the state of innovation in big law — including Rachel’s view that firms cannot use AI or money to “skip the canyon of despair” in change management — and why she thinks meaningful innovation often looks less like a headline and more like getting one percent better every week.

The conversation also covers the changing competitive landscape facing traditional firms, from AI-native entrants like Norm AI to MSOs and a resurgent ALSP market; the long-running debate over the billable hour; the four interrelated elements Rachel sees at the heart of every law firm’s data — documents, clients, matters, and people; and what firm leaders should be doing right now to stay competitive over the next decade. Throughout, Rachel returns to a theme about which she calls herself an “unapologetic humanist” — technology and process will keep changing, but the firms that win will be the ones that put the right people in the room first.

news.titleEn: AI for GCs: What You Need to Know for 2026
news.titleZh: 总法律顾问2026年AI须知
news.summaryZh: OpenAI发布GPT-5.3 Codex，Anthropic发布Opus 4.6，新模型显示AI工具可能重塑经济，总法律顾问需关注三大问题。领域特定大语言模型将成为2026年AI应用的突破类别，其使用针对特定行业的数据集训练或微调，如医疗、生命科学、法律服务和金融等，相比通用模型更可能提供相关高质量输出，减少提示工程、幻觉和验证时间，带来更快实施、可扩展用例、更高产出和生产力提升，从而驱动更强ROI。但这些模型并未消除AI部署的核心风险，如偏见、网络安全和隐私问题，且在高度监管行业最有价值，专业化可能因强化行业特定假设或历史不平等而加剧风险。总法律顾问应避免认为专业化等于低风险，需进行同样严格的法律、合规和治理审查，并了解模型训练方式，包括合成数据可能无法准确模拟现实，导致模型漂移。验证悖论要求总法律顾问确保业务领导防范：AI工具预期提高效率，但验证输出准确性可能抵消效率增益，尤其在高影响任务中，人工监督至关重要，验证过程可能比手动完成任务更耗时，导致周期延长、成本增加。法律团队应帮助识别AI真正增强人类判断的领域，设定用例边界、可接受错误容差，并使监督要求与任务风险匹配，鼓励考虑验证时间、培训成本和持续监督的ROI评估。2026年将是代理式AI之年，总法律顾问需考虑其独立决策能力，这带来法律不合规、第三方伤害和治理不当风险，需快速熟悉或寻求外部律师协助。AI治理、合同和管理问题众多，法律格局快速。
news.bodyText:
The speed at which AI is improving is breathtaking and the improvements are not simply marginal in nature: they are leaps and bounds better. On Feb. 5, GPT-5.3 Codex from OpenAI and Opus 4.6 from Anthropic were released. These new models show that large swaths of the economy could be remade through AI tools . GCs must be ready. The following are key issues for GCs to consider as the pace of AI accelerationism quickens in 2026.

Domain Specific Language Models

Domain specific large language models will be a breakout category of AI adoption in 2026. These are models trained or fine tuned using data sets tailored to a particular industry or area of knowledge, such as medicine, healthcare, life sciences, legal services, finance, and other specialized areas. As result, domain specific LLMs are more likely to provide relevant and high quality outputs for users in a particular field as compared to a general LLM. In practice, this often results in less prompt engineering, fewer hallucinations, and reduced time spent validating or correcting results. For business leaders, the value proposition is straightforward. Faster implementation, more immediate and scalable use cases, higher quality outputs, and greater productivity gains can drive a stronger ROI from AI initiatives. For organizations under pressure to justify expanding AI spend, domain specific LLMs offer a compelling narrative of efficiency and measurable business value.

At the same time, these models do not eliminate the core risks associated with AI deployment. While domain specific LLMs may come with added benefits, they continue to encounter similar risks as AI generally, such as bias, cybersecurity and privacy issues. A further complicating factor is that domain specific LLMs are often most valuable in highly regulated industries. Specialization may heighten the risks associated with these models by reinforcing industry specific assumptions or historical inequities reflected in the underlying data. Healthcare, financial services, and legal applications present obvious examples. GCs evaluating domain specific LLMs in 2026 should resist the assumption that greater specialization equals lower risk. Instead, these tools should be subject to the same disciplined legal, compliance, and governance review applied to general purpose AI systems, with additional scrutiny where industry specific regulations, professional standards, or enforcement trends are implicated.

To trust a domain specific LLM, GCs need to know how the model was trained. Consider that AI has, for the most part, been trained using real-world data and input. However, researchers are now branching out to “synthetic data,” designed to mimic real-world data to allow faster model learning, among other benefits. However, synthetic data cannot mimic the real world exactly as it often struggles to account for improbable events. This issue can compound over time resulting in an AI model that gives the same output each time no matter the input. Experts refer to this degradation as “model drift.” Domain specific LLMs theoretically are more insulated from this risk, but certainly not entirely immune.

Verification Paradox

GCs must ensure business leaders are appropriately guarding against “ verification paradox. ” AI tools are expected to translate to greater efficiency, yet, verifying the accuracy of a tool’s outputs may offset any efficiency gains. As AI systems are increasingly used for complex, high impact tasks such as legal analysis, contract review, medical documentation, financial modeling, or regulatory reporting, human oversight becomes essential. Errors in these contexts can carry consequences that far outweigh any efficiency benefit. As a result, organizations frequently require a “human in the loop” to validate outputs before they are relied upon. That review process often involves fact checking, cross referencing source materials, assessing compliance with applicable standards, and correcting subtle but consequential errors. The paradox arises when the verification process itself becomes more time consuming than completing the task manually. Reviewing an AI generated output may require reconstructing the underlying analysis, tracing assumptions, or re-performing key portions of the work to confirm accuracy. In these scenarios, AI shifts work rather than eliminating it. The net result can be longer cycle times, higher internal costs, and increased frustration for professional users who remain fully accountable for the outcome.

For GCs, this dynamic has important governance and risk management implications. Legal teams should help business leaders identify where AI truly augments human judgment and where it merely adds an additional layer of review. This includes setting clear use case boundaries, defining acceptable error tolerances, and aligning oversight requirements with the risk profile of the task. Without that discipline, organizations may overestimate the operational value of AI while underestimating the compliance burden it creates. GCs should also encourage more nuanced ROI assessments that account for verification time, training costs, and ongoing oversight obligations. In some cases, AI may deliver the greatest value not in fully automating complex tasks, but in supporting discrete, lower risk components of a workflow where verification is faster and more reliable. Understanding and managing the verification paradox is critical to ensuring that AI adoption delivers sustainable value rather than hidden inefficiency.

2026: The Year of Agentic AI

In 2025, widespread AI use and advances in AI meant GCs were required to evaluate various AI-powered tools and their risks, benefits, and ROI. In 2026, GCs must keep these same considerations in mind when encountering agentic AI, and its ability to make independent decisions. This autonomy can be immensely beneficial to organizations, but comes with an increased risk of legal noncompliance, third-party harms, and inappropriate decisions due to improper governance. Coupled with ever-increasing regulations, these new issues and risks will require GCs to quickly become comfortable and knowledgeable enough to confidently steer their organizations through the deep and murky waters of enterprise AI use, or to know when to call on experienced outside counsel to assist.

Conclusion

GCs have a lot to consider when it comes to AI governance, contracting, and management. This article describes the legal landscape as evolving at an unusually quick pace, even as federal policy is directing accelerationism at all levels of government. GCs are now positioned, through the AI addendum and similar contracting strictures, to protect their organizations, their people, and their stakeholders from AI pitfalls. Contracting for protections from AI vendor overreach, acts and omissions, or violations of law stands as the bulwark for GCs against a rapidly evolving landscape of AI tools and services. In 2026, AI will continue to rapidly evolve, evoking new issues for GCs even as they continue to develop playbooks for mitigating risks from standard fare AI vendors. We will continue to monitor developments in AI tools so that GCs can continue to protect their organizations in the highest manner.

Reece Clark is a shareholder in Polsinelli’s technology transactions practice and is based in Kansas City. He assists clients through the creation and use of technology, which involves counsel on transactions, privacy & cybersecurity, and intellectual property matters.

Benjamin C. Martin is an associate in Polsinelli’s technology transactions and privacy & cybersecurity practices. Based in Washington, D.C., he negotiates technology transactions for clients across a variety of industries.

Nguyen P. Le is a St. Louis-based associate in Polsinelli’s technology transactions and privacy & cybersecurity practices. She counsels clients through data use and privacy, licensing, digital risk, and transactional matters.

Simon合著，指出生成式AI正以类似当年互联网问世的方式冲击法律研究，压缩时间、重塑工作流程，并挑战“做研究”的既有假设。法律研究并非线性过程，生成式AI能即时给出流畅答案，却往往只是研究循环的起点。法律来源受管辖、时间、程序姿态与机构视角影响，AI的压缩与综合可能模糊约束力、时效与细微差别，因此“在何种情形、何种管辖、何时、依据谁”的追问更有价值。1990年代法律图书馆文献已警示速度不等于可靠，Kay Todd在AALL Spectrum文章中强调校准式怀疑与例行核实，正是生成式AI所需姿态。AI带来幻觉引证、近似的案例名称、不透明的训练数据与模型行为、保密与安全问题，以及协助与未经授权执业界限模糊等后果。研究团队与图书馆员负责测试工具、参与采购评估、追问数据处理与可审计性、起草政策、设计培训并建立人工复核节点。文章以电子邮件改变参考咨询、印刷向数字迁移为类比，认为AI将推动角色转型而非取代，使馆员有更多时间处理复杂问题与质量控制。传统能力仍是基础：有人须判断先测试什么、发现引证超出管辖或程序姿态有误、察觉引文无法找到或规则陈述过于干净，并教导他人在压力下区分好听答案与有据答案。最终“研究2.0”是一种职业姿态，连接已知与仍在成形之物。
