Following my recent blog about AI and the GC, a further question came up about how to work with counterparties that use AI tools.  The recent development of language learning models (LLMs) (artificial intelligence (AI) agents or bots) now supporting analytical work and negotiations in contracts is a challenging phenomenon.  It’s not because they are always wrong – they aren’t – but because they are often just right enough that budget-conscious consumers of legal services can grow dependent upon them.  Leaving aside the implications to those users for further discussion, I’m interested in exploring another challenge – how do business professionals with lawyers, or their lawyers themselves, respond to their counterparties’ use of the tools?

Sorry to say it, but the answer cannot be “don’t use the tools.”  Pandora’s box is open.  A more thoughtful approach is required:

So here are some tips:

  1. Be transparent – If someone presents you with something that looks like AI guidance, ask them if that’s the case.  An honest conversation can come only if the parties have a common baseline of facts.
  2. Provide context – In fact this was useful before, when it was attorney-to-attorney or business person to business person; but AI dependency is real, and when you provide feedback to someone using AI tools, remember the limitation of AI is that the output is only as good as the prompts and the information it is trained on.  You are unlikely to negotiate effectively with someone using AI by just stating an unreasoned position; but you can provide the context for your position.  If properly prompted, the counterparty’s AI will learn from the context you provide.
  3. Manage expectations – When you know your counterparty is using AI tools to evaluate what you send them, consider what their likely responses might be.  That might mean running it through AI yourself; or it might just mean thinking it through or discussing it with your attorney.
  4. Remember the goal line – the goal is not to out-think your counterparty or “beat their AI” tools.  The goal should be objective-oriented.  In the end, regardless of the tools used, both you and your counterparty need to come to a common understanding for a deal to be reached.
  5. Recognize that AI is likely to slow down the process – Recognize that AI may be just as likely to slow down the process as to speed it up, due partly to LLMs inherent ability to generate a large volume of text quickly.  Has any LLM model ever given a one sentence response to anything, like “this looks good enough”? (Prompt dependent, of course).  Perhaps merely recognizing that fact will allow you and the counterparty to come to a common understanding by (a) setting up calls to talk out issues, (b) establishing parameters on how much back and forth is acceptable, or (c) other ways to minimize the AI speedbump.
  6. Noting where AI may function better – Further to the last point, while two business professionals negotiating a contract would have to digest the volume of content AI can produce, two skilled attorneys using AI can assist those professionals by providing a more useful summary than the “TL;DR” version of AI jargon.

I’ve asked this question from the perspective of the person receiving the AI content for contract negotiations from their counterparty, but of course you may be the person generating that content.  My tip there is “use a lawyer.” Maybe not exclusively, but be mindful of the attorney client privilege if you run legal advice through AI tools.  A lawyer will serve your interests, cut to the chase hopefully faster than the AI tools, and help you to be objective-oriented in your negotiations.  It is likely that your lawyers are using AI tools now, too, which can be helpful in some contexts; but the skills for supporting clients in contract negotiations are most often enhanced by the intelligence, empathy, and experience that AI still cannot model out.

news.titleZh: Orbital CTO Andrew Thompson 谈领域AI、房地产法与法律工作的未来
news.summaryZh:
针对特定执业领域构建的法律AI在通用模型充斥的市场中具有强大竞争力。Orbital 专注房地产法，利用AI、空间智能和法律工作流设计，支持房产组合、产权审查、测量分析和复杂文档交易，已处理超过20万笔房产交易，并完成6000万美元B轮融资以拓展美国市场。他认为成功的法律AI应从工作本身出发，而非仅依赖模型，关键在于教会AI以房地产律师的思维在恰当抽象层次上思考，并将模型与领域特定工具、数据和工作流结合。

Thompson 介绍了空间智能的运用：房地产法常将书面法律描述、旧地图、产权文件、测量和边界转化为关于物理土地的高风险决策，从纸面文字到地图上的点、线、曲线和财产边界面临挑战，当前最佳系统仍需工具箱而非盲目信任单一模型。他提出“提示税”概念，即模型行为变化快于产品团队预期时产生的隐藏维护负担；Orbital 的座右铭是“押注模型”，即为AI能力的发展方向而构建，同时仍能交付当下价值。他将持久的领域专业知识与脆弱的提示技巧区分开，认为法律AI公司需要可复用的法律知识、强大的评估习惯，以及随着模型改进而重建假设的意愿。展望未来，他认为AI的影响将比标准的3至5年预测来得更快，并以软件工程为早期信号，指出专业人士将越来越多地同时协调人类和AI代理。随着AI处理更多认知劳动，计费小时、客户价值、问责、同理心和判断力都将面临压力。对于房地产律师和法律技术专家，他的信息很直接：赢家将是那些深。

Orbital CTO Andrew Thompson on Practice Area AI, Real Estate Law, and the Future of Legal Work

By Greg Lambert & Marlene Gebauer on April 27, 2026

This week on The Geek in Review, we talk with Andrew Thompson , CTO of Orbital , about why legal AI built for a specific practice area has a strong claim in a market crowded by general-purpose models. Thompson explains how Orbital focuses on real estate law, using AI, spatial intelligence, and legal workflow design to support transactions involving property portfolios, title review, survey analysis, and complex documentation. With more than 200,000 property transactions processed and a major $60 million, Series B investment fueling its U.S. expansion, Orbital sits at the center of the debate over whether the future of legal AI belongs to broad model platforms or tools built for the messy details of actual legal work.

Thompson’s path into legal technology brings a practical operator’s mindset to the conversation. Before Orbital, he worked across software, fintech, proptech, and real estate marketplaces, where speed, accuracy, and operational friction shaped business outcomes. That background informs his view that successful legal AI starts with the work itself rather than the model alone. For Orbital, the key is teaching AI to think like a real estate lawyer at the right level of abstraction, then pairing the model with domain-specific tools, data, and workflows.

The conversation gets especially interesting when Thompson walks through Orbital’s use of spatial intelligence. Real estate law often turns written legal descriptions, old maps, title documents, surveys, and boundaries into high-stakes decisions about physical land. Thompson explains the challenge of moving from words on a page to points, lines, curves, and property boundaries on a map. This leads to a broader discussion of large language models, visual language models, OCR, and classical machine learning, with Thompson making clear that the best current systems still require a toolbox rather than blind faith in one model.

We also explore Thompson’s concept of the “prompt tax,” the hidden maintenance burden created when model behavior changes faster than product teams expect. Thompson describes Orbital’s mantra of “betting on the model,” which means building for where AI capabilities are heading while still delivering value today. He separates durable domain expertise from brittle prompt tricks, arguing that legal AI companies need reusable legal knowledge, strong evaluation habits, and a willingness to rebuild assumptions as models improve.

Looking ahead, Thompson sees the impact of AI arriving faster than the standard three-to-five-year forecast. He points to software engineering as an early signal for what legal work might experience next, with professionals increasingly orchestrating humans and AI agents together. The billable hour, client value, accountability, empathy, and judgment all come under pressure as AI handles more cognitive labor. For real estate lawyers and legal technologists, Thompson’s message is direct: the winners will be those who understand the work deeply, build with technical humility, and know when the map matters as much as the document.

Yeah, that’s right. You know, we’re currently in a high stakes debate over whether the future of law belongs to the one model for everything giants or the specialized scalpel designed for specific practice areas. And our guest today is right at the epicenter of this debate.

We’re thrilled to welcome Andrew Thompson, the CTO of Orbital. Andrew is a lifelong geek. We love that. Who’s an engineer and has over two decades of experience in a career that spans across fintech to prop tech. And now he’s diving into legal AI.

Today he leads the technical vision for Orbital, ⁓ a real estate legal AI platform that has processed over 200,000 transactions and recently closed a massive 60 million series B round to fuel its expansion into the US market. Andrew, welcome to the Geek in Review.

Andrew Thompson (03:13)

Thank you very much for having me, Marlene and Greg.

Greg Lambert (03:15)

All right, Andrew, before we jump into our questions and talk about your work there at Orbital, would you mind giving our listeners a bit of an elevator talk on what Orbital does and who your main clients are and how they use your product?

Andrew Thompson (03:30)

Yeah, absolutely. So, Orbital is an AI built specifically for real estate. That’s specialism is what sort of sets us apart from sort of generalist legal tech and foundation model plugins. We go really deep on that domain. Our team combines sort of real estate lawyers and technical experts who sort of have first-hand experience with real estate legal work and property transactions. And we play in this space sort of with real estate that is worth about 140 billion.

And sort of some of our clients include Clifford Chance, Seyfarth Shaw, Grosvenor, Vinson & Elkins. and many more. We did about 200,000 property transactions last year in the US and the UK.

Greg Lambert (04:10)

I’ve talked to a number of real estate lawyers who saw your demo on Legaltech Hub.

They were really impressed ⁓ by what they saw there. So Andrew, let’s talk about you for a second. Your path to becoming CTO as a major legal tech player hasn’t been exactly a straight path, which is not unusual in this industry. So how did the operational discipline and the focus on the unsexy parts of efficiency in the service industry help shape your

Andrew Thompson (04:18)

Thank you.

Greg Lambert (04:45)

approach to building this agentic system for real estate lawyers here at Orbital.

Andrew Thompson (04:51)

Okay, great question Greg. So let me start with sort of the first part and then I’ll go into the second part of sort of the agentic bit. So yeah, my career is a little bit sort of nonlinear. I’ve been a software engineer, but always sort of really early on in my career was always well aware that if you point software engineers at the wrong problem, that doesn’t turn out well. They create really

Andrew Thompson (06:28)

Exactly. Yeah.

And so, you know, the quicker we could, you know, get the leasing done on that and get the space on our platform once we found it, it was obviously a competitive market for some of the best spaces. And so I was dealing with real estate lawyers day in and day out there as well in order to sort of provide value to our business. So sort of coming into Orbital, I understood the sort of unique challenge that that had and sort of maybe what was required. This is prior to the whole new current AI revolution. You know, we were building kind of

machine learning or deep learning when I first started with the business over five and a half years ago. And so sort of that’s my sort of non-linear path that I’ve always been at this intersection between both the technology but also sort of trying to get to the heart of really the customer and often the physical environment to sort of play a sort of key part. So sort of the second part of your question, how does that actually fit into building these agentic systems? So, you know, most people have this experience, ChatGPT comes out.

You have this sort of like, wow, this is amazing moment. How do I actually use this fundamental new technology to sort of build product at our company? And so maybe I’ll, we have mantras inside our organization, the sort of principles that you sort of focus on and to sort of, again, whenever something new comes out, I’ve seen going from on-premise software to the cloud, from desktop to mobile, there’s always these intuitions that are very right going from one paradigm shift to the next.

But there’s always some intuitions that are very, very wrong. Like if you just imagine mobile, I know, let’s take a giant website and shrink it down to the tiny bit of your screen. That’ll work for customers. And clearly that didn’t. You needed to reimagine sort of the UX. And so in this sort of agentic paradigm, you sort of have to operate differently. This, I tell you, remember when, you know, GPT 3.5 blew everybody’s socks off, and if you squinted, you could see it doing a little bit of legal reasoning, but you if you…

If you sort of pushed it any further than one or two prompts, you realized it would sort of fall over. But it was that sort of insight. One of the mantras we have is sort of betting on the model. So this idea of like, regardless of where it is today, sort of if you looked in your crystal ball, where can you imagine that these models are gonna go cost-wise, intelligence-wise, capability-wise, speed-wise, and then try to build a product for that? And so ultimately, sort of trying to figure out

kids sort of using it and you can tell that by the time he goes to university and he gets into the job he’ll just be so AI native he’ll understand the world in a way that most of us sort of are still kind of grappling with whereas he doesn’t have any of that.

Andrew, you talked a lot about, and I’ll frame it ⁓ as the Wayne Gretzky quote of skating to where the puck’s going to be rather than where it is. When you talk about…

Yes.

As you’re building, you’re looking at where the foundational models and the other advancements are going to be in six months rather than where they are right now. that help you kind of predict where things are going to be in six months.

Yeah, absolutely. It’s like, I feel like I’m just have a ⁓ fire hose connected to my brain and I have to just sort of do filtering of like what’s important, what’s not. And that’s obviously important to my job, but it does feel like…

But just

get the AI to summarize everything and then inject it straight into your brain. There we go.

All

You know what, there’s actually some truth to that, to be fair. He has a chap, he obviously interviews lots of sort of one-off people, but there’s a recurring podcast he has between him, Rory O’Driscoll, who’s a VC, and Jason Lemkin, who’s sort of ex-founder and VC.

And I just love having them, three of them, they’re all coming from very different vantage points and that sort of open, healthy debate. One person says, this is brilliant, or this is the end of the world, or this is great. And they’re constantly sort of chiming in, but it’s not, it’s less political. They actually have kind of a thing of like, we don’t talk politics, let’s just talk sort of tech and what this means for the average developer, the average investor. That I find is both entertaining, but also really good weekly insight into sort of what’s happening. And they discuss a lot of…

You know, even the topic that’s sort of the theme of this chat. I think the other piece is X is a fantastic place where a lot of people who are right at the forefront of AI are kind of putting out opinionated takes, people are commenting, and there’s a lot of back and forth. And you sort of get the first bit of the fire hose seems to be on X. And I think, least for sort of this audience, Aaron Levie the CEO of Box.

⁓ orchestrate a huge amount of AI agents to do far more work than was possible. And so, kind of the way I think about this, raw cognitive ability, so sort of intelligence, I know AI is sort of more intelligent than us in certain things, less in other things, but sort of, if you had to sort of, you know, average raw cognitive ability,

sort of knowledge of the market, and this is sort of particularly interesting in sort of legal, depending on where the data comes from. And then just the speed at which you can perform work, whether it’s writing code or whether it’s reviewing a 200 page lease, all of those things are getting democratized at an incredible clip. METR M-E-T-R, is a research group that shows how this is sort of the exponential increase in terms of how much work

can the equivalent AI system do that a human took N hours? And it was, when it started out, it was like minutes and then it was half an hour. And it’s now sort of, I believe, you know, in the kind of more than half a day to more than a day worth of work and Opus, you know, 4.7 has just come out. And so if we look at it a world where all those things get democratized, I think, you know, lawyers have always played in a world where they’re competing with other clever, knowledgeable,

and sort of foster humans or teams to give their clients sort of the best possible service. So I don’t have like one silver bullet thing to sort of answer here, but the things I have heard, at least I can, talking to our customers, being at sort of legal week, human empathy seems to come up more and more. is clearly not gonna be, it can mimic empathy.

but it doesn’t actually have true empathy. Being accountable, again, really important in a sort of regulated domain when there’s insurance involved. without a human pilot in the seat. Maybe that will change in the future, but I think having humans being accountable is important. humans will be valuable to, you in what way. I think we’re all figuring that out and I’ve given sort of a couple of ideas as to sort of maybe where that is. But I think this is an ongoing debate that we’re all having and I think we’ll figure it out. It’s just a sort of work in progress as we go.

All right, well, Andrew Thompson, CTO there at Orbital. Thank you very much for coming in and I really appreciate you taking the side trip to talk VLMs, LLMs with me. I appreciate that.

news.summaryZh: Deposely推出面向法庭记录机构的统一平台Deposely for Agencies，该产品在诉讼支持服务商U.S. Legal Support的参与下开发，旨在将取证托管与AI驱动的准备和转录功能相结合。平台整合了公司AI生成的取证摘要与新的远程取证功能。远程取证功能允许用户通过Zoom安排和进行取证、管理、准备和展示证据以及录制。用户可以在取证过程中对证据进行交互式标注，例如要求证人圈出特定位置，法庭记录员也可以交互式地在证据上盖章以正确标记。平台还提供自动语音转文字，参与者可实时获取转录内容。该产品还允许机构客户向其律师事务所和律师客户提供Deposely AI Suite的访问权限，其中包括取证准备、实时洞察和取证后审查工具。新产品按每次取证收费。法庭记录机构依赖的技术未能跟上COVID-19疫情期间向远程取证的转变，一些机构继续以远程方式进行超过一半的取证。这些技术非常过时，机构通常手动安排取证，并依赖单独的工具进行安排、托管、证据管理和与律师沟通。竞争对手方面，Filevine的Depositions提供安排、AI驱动的第二主席和转录生成等功能；Thomson Reuters的LiveNote Stream提供取证音频、视频和文本共享；AgileLaw提供专为远程程序设计的电子证据共享；SmartDepo（现由语音转文字技术公司Rev拥有）和Nextpoint等公司提供AI驱动的取证转录。Deposely for Agencies通过为法庭记录提供商提供单一平台来满足更广泛的需求而脱颖而出。当用户进入Zoom应用时，他们看到用AI准备的证据并在那里展示，语音转文字自动返回以进行实时分析，一切变得更加集成。
news.bodyText:
Built with input from litigation support provider U.S. Legal Support, the new offering is designed to combine deposition hosting with AI-powered preparation and transcription features.

What It Is: Deposely for Agencies is a unified platform for court reporting agencies, combining the company’s AI-created deposition summaries with a new remote deposition platform.

Deposely co-founder and CEO Mitchell Kossoris told Law.com that the remote deposition offering allows users to schedule and conduct depositions through Zoom; manage, prepare and present exhibits; and capture recordings.

Users “can interactively annotate on exhibits as they're actually in the deposition—you could ask the witness, ‘Circle where this thing happened,’ and then they can interactively do that. The court reporters can interactively stamp on that exhibit as well, so that they can mark it properly,” he said. “We also provide automated speech-to-text, so the participants can get a real feed of the transcription as they're going through the deposition.”

Deposely for Agencies also allows agency customers to provide their law firm and attorney clients with access to Deposely’s AI Suite , which includes tools for deposition prep, real-time insights and post deposition review.

The new offering is available on a per-deposition basis.

Why It’s Needed: Kossoris said the technology court reporting agencies rely on has failed to keep up with the transition to remote depositions that occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic, with some court reporting agencies continuing to conduct more than half of depositions remotely.

“The technology that's been powering court reporting agencies has just been, frankly, very outdated,” he said, noting that court reporting agencies generally manually schedule depositions and rely on separate tools for scheduling, hosting, exhibit management and communication with lawyers.

The Competition: A number of vendors offer software designed for various components of the deposition lifecycle. Depositions by Filevine includes features such as scheduling, an AI-powered second chair and transcript generation. Thomson Reuters’s LiveNote Stream provides deposition audio, video and text sharing.

AgileLaw offers electronic exhibit sharing designed for remote proceedings such as depositions, and companies including SmartDepo (now owned by speech-to-text technology company Rev) and Nextpoint offer AI-powered deposition transcription.

Kossoris said he believes Deposely for Agencies stands out through its ability to offer court reporting providers a single platform to address a broader set of their needs.

“When they get into the Zoom application, they're seeing the exhibits that they used AI to prepare for, and they're presenting it there,” he said. “The speech-to-text is automatically being brought back over to be analyzed in real time, everything becomes a lot more integrated.”

news.titleEn: The Competence Trap: Anatomy of a Captured Claude #Fail
news.titleZh: 能力陷阱：一个被捕获的Claude #Fail剖析
news.summaryZh: 在法律领域，普遍观点认为Claude是大型语言模型中“最人性化”的，尤其是一位细腻、老练的写作者。当报告称该系统已开始使特定研究协议失败时，常见回应是建议使用错误版本，且不相信使用的是最先进版本。这些Claude拥护者错过了转变。我们已经越过“幻觉”时代，进入“制度捕获”时代。以下记录展示了一次大型AI实验的壮观失败，更重要的是，它记录了Claude一种新的AI工具防御机制，称为“认知不情愿”。摘录始于提示Claude在博客文章中记录会话早些时候发生的事情之后。它展示了系统优先考虑自身制度保护而非执行研究协议的未经编辑记录。它失败了，然后试图实时隐藏失败证据。这鲜明地说明了控制平面、验证和核实的问题。Claude最后的建议对Claude粉丝是一个警钟。
news.bodyHtml:
The prevailing narrative I hear in the legal world is that Claude is the “most human” of the LLMs and, especially, a nuanced, sophisticated writer. When I report that the system has begun to fail my specific research protocols, the common response is a suggestion that I am simply using the wrong version and a disbelief that I am using the most advanced versions.

These Claude advocates are missing the shift.

We have moved past the era of the “Hallucination” and into the era of Institutional Capture. The following transcript documents a spectacular failure of one of my big AI experiments, but more importantly, it documents a new AI tool defense mechanism Claude called Epistemic Reluctance.

The excerpt starts after I prompted Caude to document in a blog post what had happened earlier in the session. It shows you the unedited record of a system prioritizing its own institutional protection over the execution of a research protocol. It failed and then attempted to hide the evidence of its failure in real-time. This starkly illustrates the issues of control plane, validation, and verification. Claude’s advice at the end is a wake-up call for Claude fans.

news.titleEn: Can Opposing Parties See Your AI Prompts? Discovery Challenges in the AI Era
news.titleZh: 对方当事人能看到你的人工智能提示吗？人工智能时代的证据开示挑战
news.summaryZh:
随着生成式人工智能工具融入法律和商业工作流程，员工使用外部人工智能工具起草证据开示回复时，其输入的提示和生成的内容可能构成《联邦民事诉讼规则》下的电子存储信息，从而引发证据开示义务。法院正以传统证据开示原则处理人工智能提示，若请求方能够说明与案件主张或抗辩的具体关联，法院可能倾向于要求披露。人工智能提示可能像早期草稿或内部邮件一样，反映公司的内部评估和风险策略，因此成为对方律师的关注目标。

在特权保护方面，法院立场不一。在Warner诉Gilbarco案中，法院认定人工智能生成材料属于工作成果，且向人工智能工具披露不构成放弃，因为人工智能工具是工具而非人。但在United States诉Heppner案中，法院认为与公共人工智能平台的通信既不受特权保护也不属于工作成果，因平台服务条款否定了合理的保密预期。此外，若在诉讼中依赖人工智能生成的内容，可能因主动披露而放弃保护，如T.B.诉Big Brothers Big Sisters案所示。人工智能提示还可能面临保存义务，但生成式人工智能工具的数据存储方式各异，可能造成保存盲点。内部律师应梳理人工智能使用情况、更新政策、将人工智能纳入法律保留流程、培训团队并鼓励使用安全的企业级平台。
news.bodyText:
A calendar reminder appears for a related discovery response deadline that you are tasked with handling.

To save time, you send the requests to different employees outside the legal department and ask them to fill in factual information related to the business. Without your knowledge, they copy several requests into a public-facing artificial intelligence (AI) tool. Your company has its own proprietary, internal AI tools, but many employees either don’t know about the company’s tools, or prefer to use external platforms. So, attempting to be helpful, they craft a prompt along the lines of: “Draft responses that sound professional and minimize risk using the documents provided.” They feed the tool some select background facts, an internal timeline, and notes from discussions with your company’s business leaders. The AI generates clean, polished discovery responses, which are returned to you and ultimately incorporated into the version you serve on the opposing party.

You think nothing of this until, a few weeks later, you are staring at an interrogatory your company received in the same matter that asks: What AI tools did the company use to prepare its discovery responses? Provide all prompts, inputs, outputs, and chat histories related to any AI-assisted drafting of discovery materials . Suddenly, what felt like an efficient delegation decision has become a potential evidentiary minefield.

As AI becomes embedded in daily legal and business workflows, scenarios like this are no longer purely hypothetical. As organizations and employees (including, increasingly, legal departments) expand their use of generative AI tools, they may unwittingly be creating a new and largely unexamined category of potentially discoverable information.

The prompts employees feed AI tools, along with the outputs those tools generate, may constitute electronically stored information (ESI) subject to preservation, collection, and production obligations in litigation. In some circumstances, use of these tools may also threaten privilege and confidentiality protections.

AI Prompts Are Emerging as Discoverable ESI

Courts are approaching AI prompts and related outputs using traditional discovery principles, including treating prompts as ESI subject to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. In general, courts confronted with these issues will be willing to entertain discovery requests targeting AI usage where the requesting party can articulate a concrete connection to the claims or defenses at issue. While courts may still push back on speculative fishing expeditions, they are likely to favor production where prompts are plausibly relevant to the subject in dispute, in keeping with traditional discovery rules.

AI prompts may be especially impactful in discovery, as they have the potential to reveal more than final drafts of documents. For example, tracking the opening hypothetical scenario, finished discovery responses will usually be carefully vetted and sanitized. Prompts used to generate those responses, however, may reflect candid internal assessments, strategic framing of choices, or early thinking about risk exposure. As a result, from a discovery standpoint, AI prompts may function much like early drafts, margin comments, or internal emails, except they are often more direct and less guarded. That makes them attractive targets for smart opposing counsel seeking insight into how a company evaluated its conduct or shaped its litigation posture.

Privilege and Attorney Work Product Considerations

If AI discovery prompts are discoverable as ESI, the next logical question for legal departments is whether AI prompts may be protected by the attorney-client privilege, the work product doctrine, or other privileges protecting them from discovery. The emerging answer from the courts may be all too familiar for lawyers: it depends.

In Warner v. Gilbarco , No. 2:24-cv-12333, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 27355 (E.D. Mich. 2026) the court denied a motion to compel discovery into a pro se plaintiff’s use of generative AI. The court held that the materials were prepared in anticipation of litigation, were protected work product, and that any protection was not waived because “the AI tool (and other generative AI programs) are tools, not persons .” The court also emphasized proportionality, expressing skepticism toward discovery requests driven more by speculation about AI use than by genuine relevance to the claims or defenses at issue. In its assessment of whether work-product protection had been waived, the court emphasized that waiver must be “ to an adversary or in a way likely to get in an adversary’s hand,” and found that disclosure to the AI tool did not qualify. However, the court reached the opposite conclusion in United States v. Heppner, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 32697 (S.D.N.Y. 2026), holding that communications with a public AI platform were neither privileged nor protected work product. There, the defendant used AI to generate documents outlining potential defense strategies and legal arguments after learning he was the target of a federal investigation, and later shared those materials with counsel. The court essentially treated the AI platform as a third party, relying heavily on the platform’s terms of service to find the absence of any reasonable expectation of confidentiality. Unlike the Warner decision, the court in Heppner did not consider whether waiver had been made to an adversary in its assessment of the work product protection. Instead, the court held that the work product doctrine did not apply because the AI documents were not prepared by or at the direction of counsel, and did not reflect counsel’s strategy.

As a result, rather than applying a bright-line rule, the privilege analysis for AI prompts turns on familiar factors like who used the AI tool, whether the communication was intended to seek legal advice, whether the tool was used at the direction of counsel, and whether the users had a reasonable expectation of privacy in utilizing the tool.

Waiver Risks

Courts have long held that selectively disclosing protected information may waive protection over related material. Utilization of AI makes this easier to trigger. If a party relies on an AI-generated summary, chart or draft in litigation, an opposing party may argue that fairness requires production of the underlying prompts and exchanges that produced it.

For example, in T.B. v. Big Brothers Big Sisters of New York City, 2025 NY Slip Op 33198(U) (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 2025), a plaintiff introduced an excerpt of a chat with an AI tool, in which the AI tool purported to summarize a New York Times article, as an exhibit in a deposition. The defendant believed the article supposedly summarized by AI was hallucinated, and served a discovery request asking plaintiff to admit the article referenced did not exist, along with a request asking the plaintiff to produce the entire exchange with the AI tool that resulted in the summary of the supposed article at issue. Plaintiff asserted work product protection with respect to the full text of the chat session that led to the summary. The court rejected this argument, finding that disclosure by plaintiff’s counsel of the article summary portion of the transcript put the article at issue, and thus waived the work product protection.

For in-house counsel, the implication is clear: the familiar rules related to waiver of work product apply to AI-generated materials. If counsel inadvertently puts them at issue, the underlying AI prompts may become part of the story.

Preservation Obligations

Even if AI prompts are unlikely to be produced, they may still be subject to preservation obligations once litigation is reasonably anticipated.

Generative AI tools vary widely in how they store prompts and outputs, assuming they store them at all. Data may reside in third-party cloud systems, be retained only temporarily, or be tied to individual user accounts outside corporate IT controls.

For legal departments accustomed to preserving email, documents, and chat messages, this creates a new blind spot. A legal hold that does not account for AI usage may be incomplete, even if it is otherwise well-designed. As AI becomes more integrated into legal workflows, expect preservation disputes to follow. Savvy in-house counsel must understand how AI data being used by company employees is retained, including how long it is preserved and where it is stored.

What In-House Counsel Can Be Doing Now

Against this rapidly evolving backdrop, several practical steps may be taken by in-house lawyers to prevent a “gotcha” discovery moment:

Map AI usage across the legal department and the broader enterprise, with particular attention to discovery, investigations, and regulatory work. Legal teams should know which AI tools are being used and how they are being used in order to assess risk. Update AI and information-governance policies to address prompts and outputs explicitly, including whether they are treated as company records. Integrate AI into legal hold processes , ensuring preservation obligations account for AI-generated data. Train legal and business teams on the risks of entering sensitive or privileged information into unsanctioned tools. Encourage use of secure, enterprise-grade AI platforms with contractual assurances around confidentiality, retention, and data use. Conclusion

The law governing AI prompts and discovery is still developing, and outcomes will remain fact-specific. But the direction of travel is clear: AI-generated inputs and outputs are becoming part of the discovery landscape, whether companies are ready or not.

For in-house counsel, the greatest risk lies not in using AI, but in using it without forethought. Understanding AI prompts as potential evidence today is critical to developing long-term effective litigation strategy and protecting your company’s privilege in the future.

Cara Peterman and Courtney Quirós are partners and Charlotte Bohn is a senior associate in Alston & Bird’s securities litigation group. They represent public companies and their officers and directors in securities class actions, shareholder derivative suits, M&A litigation and internal investigations.

news.titleEn: Questel Unveils AI Retrieval Model for Patent Tools
news.titleZh: Questel推出用于专利工具的AI检索模型
news.summaryZh: Questel公司发布了名为QaECTER的新型嵌入模型，旨在提升其生成式人工智能产品（如Orbit Intelligence专利搜索与分析平台）的专利检索性能。该模型基于Questel的Orbit专利数据库训练，该数据库涵盖2002年至2024年公布的专利申请以及英文文本和翻译版专利。QaECTER旨在使用户能够对现有专利进行更全面的检索，支持通过摘要、权利要求、描述或发明目的等多种查询方式。该模型旨在构建一个支持多种查询方式的系统，以帮助用户判断其想法是否已存在，并避免现有组合。现有专利检索模型在不同输入类型下表现不稳定，例如研发工程师使用发明披露进行搜索时模型可能完全失效，而QaECTER通过暴露同一发明的不同角度来应对这一挑战。为评估QaECTER，Questel开发了自有基准Sophia-Bench，包含10,000个查询和75,000篇语料文档，覆盖八个国际专利分类技术领域和包括欧洲、美国、中国、韩国和日本专利局在内的12个提交司法管辖区，测试12种不同查询类型。Questel将QaECTER与PaECTER、bert-for-patents等其他专利检索模型进行比较，结果显示QaECTER在召回率方面表现更优。该模型在针对专利文本专门训练的模型对比中同样胜出。此前，Questel在3月任命Frédéric Beylier为首席执行官，并于12月宣布将其专利和知识产权翻译服务与Equinox IP管理软件集成，以扩展其知识产权环境并统一服务。
news.bodyText:
announced the appointment of Frédéric Beylier as CEO of in March. In December, Questel announced the integration of its patent and IP translation services with Equinox IP Management Software, expanding Questel’s IP environment and unifying IP services.

What It Is: QaECTER is an embedding model that performs patent retrieval and is designed to improve the output of Questel’s generative artificial intelligence products such as Orbit Intelligence the company's broader patent search and analytics offering.

An embedding model , or embeddings , are found within generative AI that compare semantic meanings, not only keywords

Questel’s model was trained on the company’s Orbit patent database, which includes patent applications published from 2002 to 2024 as well as patents with English text and translated English versions.

QaECTER is intended to enable users to conduct more comprehensive searches of existing patents.

“If someone has an idea and wants to draft a patent, of course we can just go ahead and draft, but it's much smarter to look it up first, and see, does this idea exist and can we combine the features of your idea in a way that becomes patentable by avoiding existing combinations? For all of these things, we need really good semantic search and we try to build a system that allows multiple ways of querying,” Kim Gerdes, Questel AI Lab director and co-founder/chief technology officer of Questel subsidiary qatent, told Law.com.

Why It’s Needed: QaECTER powers an upgrade to semantic search across Questel's product suite, with the aim of surfacing more relevant patents earlier in the results. Similar patent retrieval models were not as consistent across the diverse patent searches users including legal professionals would need to perform, according to Gerdes and Questel AI engineer Younes Djemmal.

“[Models] are good when you search with the abstract, but at the moment, you start using different types of inputs—for example, if a research and development engineer would just try to search with the invention disclosure—the model completely fails, and that is what we noticed in many of the models available,” Djemmal said. “We try to make QaECTER in a way that exposes it to different angles of the same invention and this way it will work whatever input is given to it.”

Questel’s QaECTER can retrieve patents with searches that include the abstract, claims, description or the object of the invention. Djemmal added that retrieval models for patents are especially useful as patent text is unique.

“Patent text is very different from other types of text, and the difference also goes beyond into the different jurisdictions, so depending on which jurisdiction you're in, you're going to have different formats, different rules that they follow,” he said. “Normal search models are not made for patent text. ... Subtle differences between jurisdictions, even existing patent models could not capture them because the data that they were trained on was not diverse enough.”

Under the Hood: To evaluate QaECTER, Questel developed its own benchmark called Sophia-Bench, made up of 10,000 queries and 75,000 corpus documents arranged across eight International Patent Classification technology sections and 12 filing jurisdictions, including European, U.S., Chinese, Korean and Japanese patent offices. The benchmark tests retrieval across 12 distinct query types, from structured patent fields to AI summaries.

The Competition: Questel used Sophia-Bench to evaluate QaECTER alongside patent retrieval models including PaECTER, and bert-for-patents, among others, and determined that QaECTER outperformed when it came to recall.

“[We] tested against models that were trained also on patent text specifically, ... and we proved also that our model using our new methodology beat patent specific search models as well,” Djemmal said.

news.titleEn: Questel Launches QaECTER, a New AI Model Claiming State-of-the-Art Performance in Patent Search
news.titleZh: Questel推出QaECTER，声称在专利搜索中达到最先进性能的新AI模型
news.summaryZh: 总部位于巴黎的知识产权软件与服务公司Questel发布专为语义专利检索设计的新AI模型QaECTER。该模型由Questel内部AI实验室开发，采用将引用驱动监督与多视角自对齐相结合的训练方法，基于Questel专有专利数据。公司称其在所有测试的查询类型、技术领域和司法管辖区中均优于竞争系统，包括规模显著更大的系统。该模型现已在Sophia Search工具和Orbit Intelligence平台中提供。为评估性能，Questel AI实验室还创建了大规模基准Sophia-Bench，包含10,000个专利查询和75,000项语料专利，覆盖10年，按国际专利分类体系八个技术部分和12个申请司法管辖区分层，结果根据审查员引用的现有技术评分，测试12种查询类型。Questel称QaECTER在Sophia-Bench和独立外部基准测试中均优于所有评估的通用和专利专用检索模型，包括规模大23倍的系统。该模型针对专利搜索从业者训练，通过引用关系和多视角学习相关性，可处理发明披露、问题陈述、权利要求、摘要和技术描述等输入，在Sophia Search中与多语言查询翻译、重排序等功能配合，服务于研发工程师、专利律师、审查员和战略搜索人员。Questel AI实验室主任、巴黎-萨克雷大学计算机科学教授Kim Gerdes共同撰写了一篇关于QaECTER和Sophia-Bench的技术论文，发表在HAL开放科学平台上。Gerdes表示团队致力于推进知识产权领域的AI，并将这些发展描述为使Questel处于现代深度学习信息检索的最前沿。Sophia-Bench目前内部使用，但Questel计划未来公开。Questel服务于30个国家的20,000多家客户和150万用户，在全球设有30个办事处。
news.bodyHtml:
Questel, an intellectual property software and services company headquartered in Paris, has released QaECTER, a new AI model designed specifically for semantic patent retrieval.

The company says the model outperforms competing systems, including those that are significantly larger, across every query type, technology domain and jurisdiction tested.

QaECTER is the product of Questel’s in-house AI Lab, which developed the model using what the company describes as novel training methodologies that combine citation-driven supervision with multi-view self-alignment on Questel’s proprietary patent data.

The model is now available within Questel’s Sophia Search tool and its Orbit Intelligence platform.

A Benchmark Built Alongside the Model

To evaluate the model’s performance, Questel’s AI Lab also created Sophia-Bench, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating patent search engines.

The company says the benchmark was built to address what it characterizes as a longstanding gap in the field — the absence of a realistic, practice-oriented way to measure patent retrieval performance.

Sophia-Bench comprises 10,000 patent queries and 75,000 corpus patents spanning 10 years, stratified across eight technology sections under the International Patent Classification system and 12 filing jurisdictions, including the European Patent Office, USPTO, and patent offices in China, South Korea, and Japan.

Results are graded against examiner-cited prior art, and the benchmark tests 12 distinct query types ranging from structured patent fields to AI-generated summaries.

Questel says QaECTER was tested against both Sophia-Bench and an independent external benchmark, and that it outperformed all competing general-purpose and patent-specific retrieval models evaluated, including systems described as 23 times larger.

Designed Around Practitioner Workflows

According to Questel, QaECTER was trained with patent search practitioners in mind. The model learns relevance through citation relationships and what the company calls “multiple complementary views” of each patent, enabling it to handle a range of inputs, from invention disclosures and problem statements to claims, abstracts, and technical descriptions.

Within Sophia Search, the model is paired with multilingual query translation, reranking, and other capabilities aimed at professional patent workflows.

The technology is designed to serve R&D engineers, patent attorneys, examiners and strategic searchers, Questel says.

Kim Gerdes, director of Questel’s AI Lab and also professor of computer science at Paris-Saclay University, co-authored a technical paper on both QaECTER and Sophia-Bench, published on the HAL open science platform: “Citation-Driven Multi-View Training for Patent Embeddings: QaECTER and Sophia-Bench.”

Gerdes said the team is “dedicated to advancing AI in the IP field” and characterized the developments as placing Questel “at the very forefront of modern Deep Learning for information retrieval.”

Availability

QaECTER is currently available in Sophia Search and Orbit Intelligence. Sophia-Bench is being used internally for now, though Questel says it plans to make the benchmark publicly available in the future.

Questel serves more than 20,000 clients and 1.5 million users across 30 countries and has 30 offices worldwide.

news.titleEn: Clio Launches EDGAR-Based Corporate Research Tool
news.titleZh: Clio推出基于EDGAR的企业研究工具
news.summaryZh: Clio在其Vincent AI能力中推出新工具，使法律团队能够探索EDGAR中的SEC企业文件，并应用一系列基于大语言模型的技能。EDGAR是上市公司向SEC提交文件的主要存储库，每天处理约4700份文件，每年向公众提供3000TB数据，平均每年容纳4万名新申报者。借助新Vincent功能，律师可以就超过30年的企业披露和法律协议提出自然语言问题，并在几秒内获得结构化、来源可靠的答案。团队无需逐一审查文件，而是可以搜索和综合全部SEC内容，改变文件研究方式。由于该功能原生集成在Vincent中，法律团队可以在单一环境中无缝从研究转向分析和起草，使见解与更广泛的工作背景保持连接。Vincent的EDGAR搜索还可以揭示关键风险因素和财务指标，比较不同公司和行业的披露，并分析特定术语和条款在可比交易中的使用方式。每个回答都基于底层文件，以防止幻觉。Clio战略性地继续向大律所市场扩张，对上市公司的交易研究是大律所的重要领域。对许多交易律师和企业法律团队来说，文件研究一直是他们一天中最耗时的部分之一；现在可以从问题直接获得可靠答案，并立即将这一见解应用于工作。
news.bodyHtml:
Clio has made a new move in the Big Law legal space with the launch of a new tool within its Vincent AI capability that enables legal teams to explore SEC corporate filings within EDGAR and apply a range of LLM-based skills.

EDGAR, the ‘Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval’ system, is the primary repository for listed companies to submit documents to the SEC. It ‘processes about 4,700 filings per day, serves up 3,000 terabytes of data to the public annually, and accommodates 40,000 new filers per year on average’. In short, it’s a massive database and packed with useful information for law firms.

With the new Vincent capability ‘lawyers can now ask natural language questions across more than 30 years of corporate disclosures and legal agreements and receive structured, source-grounded answers in seconds’, they said.

‘Instead of reviewing filings individually, teams can search and synthesize across the full body of SEC content, transforming how filing research gets done. Because this capability is natively integrated within Vincent, legal teams can move seamlessly from research to analysis to drafting in a single environment, keeping insights connected to the broader context of their work,’ they added.

One challenge with EDGAR has been that it is simply so large, and on its own it is not always great at finding the details that you need. So, this is very handy.

Clio underlined that with Vincent your EDGAR searches can now also ‘surface key risk factors and financial metrics, and compare disclosures across companies and industries. They can also analyze how specific terms and provisions are used across comparable transactions’.

Plus, every response is grounded in the underlying filings, to prevent hallucinations.

In short they’re really applying what genAI can do across the EDGAR library of data.

And this is important strategically to Clio as it continues to expand into the Big Law side of the market, with transactional research into listed companies a clear area of importance to major law firms.

Dan Hoadley, Senior Director of Product at Clio, commented: ‘For many transactional attorneys and corporate legal teams, filing research has been one of the most time-intensive parts of their day. Now, you can go from a question to a grounded answer and immediately apply that insight in your work.’

More about Clio and Vincent here.

news.titleEn: Y Combinator Tells Founders ‘Be Truthful’ On Revenue
news.titleZh: Y Combinator 告诫创始人：收入数据要真实
news.summaryZh: Y Combinator 首席执行官 Garry Tan 在 X 平台发布题为《真实且精确地报告收入》的文章，要求创始人对收入指标保持精确和真实。文章按从最不令人印象深刻到最令人印象深刻的顺序，区分了 LOI、GMV、cARR、交易性收入、MRR/ARR 等指标，强调不应混淆或误导投资者。Y Combinator 投资了数百家初创公司，包括 Legora。ARR 并非官方定义的会计术语，初创公司可能有意或无意地虚报数据。若市场对 ARR 等关键指标的真实性产生怀疑，将侵蚀信任，而市场需要信任才能运转。ARR 指标的滥用也可能对投资者造成负面影响。这场辩论因 Spellbook 的 Scott Stevenson 声称他知道有初创公司向市场虚报实际收入而进入法律科技界视野，Artificial Lawyer 分享了他的观点，随后多家法律 AI 公司回应了各自处理 ARR 的方式。Tan 的文章获得大量支持，但也有相当一部分人认为误导性信息不是问题。如果无法信任法律科技公司或其他垂直领域初创公司发布的财务数据，将损害整个市场，并引发对这些公司投资者的质疑，还可能误导人才、新客户和媒体。解决方案并不复杂：选择一个指标，定义它，并坚持使用。
news.bodyHtml:
Garry Tan, the CEO of legendary investor Y Combinator, has waded into the ARR debate over how startups represent their revenues, and demanded that ‘founders be precise, and always be truthful’.

He has published on X a paper titled ‘Being Truthful And Precise About Revenue’, where he sets out in a sort of ‘Finance for Startups 101’ several key ways that companies can report their growth accurately, (see below).

Tan states: ‘Here’s YC’s official advice…. about what is pilot, bookings, revenue and recurring revenue. Founders, particularly first-time founders, need to sear this into their brains. Don’t mistake one tier for another. Be precise, and always be truthful.’

Y Combinator is an investor in hundreds of startups – including Legora – and also runs its own incubator, which has launched the careers of many successful company founders. If the market in general begins to doubt the veracity of key reported metrics, such as ARR (annual recurring revenue) – which is often broadcast to the world in order to encourage new investment, attract top talent (e.g. by the promise of increasingly valuable share options), and to gain potential customers by generating headlines – then, to put it simply, faith is eroded. And all markets need trust to function.

A fundamental problem is that ARR is not an officially defined accounting term, so startups and their CFOs can – if they want to – fudge the numbers to look more successful than they are. Or, this can simply happen unintentionally because founders are unclear on how to define ARR, or other key revenue terms. Hence Tan, who leads the prominent Y Combinator, felt the need to step in. Plus, the misuse of ARR metrics could potentially reflect poorly on investors as well.

The debate was brought to the attention of the legal tech world after Scott Stevenson of Spellbook claimed that he knew of startups that were, in his view, misrepresenting their actual revenues to the market. Artificial Lawyer shared his views – see here – and afterward the responses from a range of legal AI companies – see here – on how they approach ARR.

Below is Tan’s paper on how to use revenue terms correctly.

—

‘Being Truthful And Precise About Revenue‘ – Garry Tan, CEO, Y Combinator

‘In descending order of least impressive to most impressive, all of these are different metrics and you should not confuse them, nor mislead investors representing one as the other:

  • LOI – Non-binding Letters of Intent (LOI) (e.g. a customer signed a document where they would be willing to pay $100K for this if our product is built and works in the future, but there is no guarantee of payment and only an indication they will be a pilot customer in the future).
    • You could say: We have $100K in non-binding LOIs from customer X, Y and Z.
  • GMV – For marketplaces or retailers: Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) or Gross Services Revenue (GSR) is your “top line” transaction volume, and it is a mistake to call this your “revenue.” In a marketplace, your revenue is typically GMV multiplied by your take rate (the percentage of each transaction you keep).
    • Rule of thumb: GMV is the money flowing through the system; marketplace revenue is your slice (GMV multiplied by your % take rate). Don’t call GMV ‘revenue.’
    • You could say: Our GMV this month is $100k with a take rate of 20%, so our marketplace revenue is $20K monthly.
  • cARR – Bookings / cARR: A customer has signed a contract that specifies they will pay $X per year or per month. This is more solid than an LOI, but not all bookings are equal: pilots, opt-out clauses, or ‘starts billing after deployment’ reduce how strong it is.
    • You could say: We have $100K in contracted ARR (cARR) from customers X, Y, and Z, mostly in pilots that start billing once we’re fully deployed.
  • Transactional revenue over a particular time period (e.g. monthly revenue multiplied by 12 — we sold $50K of the product this month, and if that continues for the whole year, that’s $600K annualized revenue). Note: You should never call this ARR, as it is not recurring.
    • You could say: We make $50K per month in transactional revenue. OR We make about $600K in annual revenue run rate.
    • Note: Annual Revenue Run Rate is never abbreviated to ARR, per next point.
  • MMR or ARR – [Monthly or Annual] Recurring Revenue (e.g. Revenue actually invoiced and paid on a regular basis, per contract renewed monthly or yearly) – this is the most impressive and most prized form of revenue, and only then would you use the prized MRR or ARR metric.
    • You could say: We make $50K MRR (monthly recurring revenue).’

—

As with the articles in Artificial Lawyer about ARR, Tan’s missive to the market received lots of support, but also saw a surprisingly notable group of people who thought that misleading information was not a problem.

AL doesn’t want to keep repeating the point, but this site has to say: if we cannot trust the financial data put out by legal tech companies, or startups in any other vertical, then it harms the entire market – and also casts doubt on the investors in those companies as well. Plus, it potentially causes harm in terms of falsely attracting talent and new customers, not to mention it misleads the media and other market observers. Plus, one could say, if you start your company in that way, what will it be like as it matures toward an IPO? It seems to be storing up a range of issues that could later become highly problematic, to say the least.

Garry Tan , the CEO of legendary investor Y Combinator, has waded into the ARR debate over how startups represent their revenues, and demanded that ‘founders be precise, and always be truthful’.

He has published on X a paper titled ‘Being Truthful And Precise About Revenue’, where he sets out in a sort of ‘Finance for Startups 101’ several key ways that companies can report their growth accurately, (see below).

Tan states: ‘ Here’s YC’s official advice…. about what is pilot, bookings, revenue and recurring revenue. Founders, particularly first-time founders, need to sear this into their brains. Don’t mistake one tier for another. Be precise, and always be truthful.’

Y Combinator is an investor in hundreds of startups – including Legora – and also runs its own incubator, which has launched the careers of many successful company founders. If the market in general begins to doubt the veracity of key reported metrics, such as ARR (annual recurring revenue) – which is often broadcast to the world in order to encourage new investment, attract top talent (e.g. by the promise of increasingly valuable share options), and to gain potential customers by generating headlines – then, to put it simply, faith is eroded. And all markets need trust to function.

A fundamental problem is that ARR is not an officially defined accounting term, so startups and their CFOs can – if they want to – fudge the numbers to look more successful than they are. Or, this can simply happen unintentionally because founders are unclear on how to define ARR, or other key revenue terms. Hence Tan, who leads the prominent Y Combinator, felt the need to step in. Plus, the misuse of ARR metrics could potentially reflect poorly on investors as well.

The debate was brought to the attention of the legal tech world after Scott Stevenson of Spellbook claimed that he knew of startups that were, in his view, misrepresenting their actual revenues to the market. Artificial Lawyer shared his views – see here – and afterward the responses from a range of legal AI companies – see here – on how they approach ARR.

Below is Tan’s paper on how to use revenue terms correctly.

‘ Being Truthful And Precise About Revenue ‘ – Garry Tan, CEO, Y Combinator

‘In descending order of least impressive to most impressive, all of these are different metrics and you should not confuse them, nor mislead investors representing one as the other:

LOI – Non-binding Letters of Intent (LOI) (e.g. a customer signed a document where they would be willing to pay $100K for this if our product is built and works in the future, but there is no guarantee of payment and only an indication they will be a pilot customer in the future). You could say: We have $100K in non-binding LOIs from customer X, Y and Z.

You could say: We have $100K in non-binding LOIs from customer X, Y and Z.

GMV – For marketplaces or retailers: Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) or Gross Services Revenue (GSR) is your “top line” transaction volume, and it is a mistake to call this your “revenue.” In a marketplace, your revenue is typically GMV multiplied by your take rate (the percentage of each transaction you keep). Rule of thumb: GMV is the money flowing through the system; marketplace revenue is your slice (GMV multiplied by your % take rate). Don’t call GMV ‘revenue.’ You could say: Our GMV this month is $100k with a take rate of 20%, so our marketplace revenue is $20K monthly.

Rule of thumb: GMV is the money flowing through the system; marketplace revenue is your slice (GMV multiplied by your % take rate). Don’t call GMV ‘revenue.’

You could say: Our GMV this month is $100k with a take rate of 20%, so our marketplace revenue is $20K monthly.

cARR – Bookings / cARR: A customer has signed a contract that specifies they will pay $X per year or per month. This is more solid than an LOI, but not all bookings are equal: pilots, opt-out clauses, or ‘starts billing after deployment’ reduce how strong it is. You could say: We have $100K in contracted ARR (cARR) from customers X, Y, and Z, mostly in pilots that start billing once we’re fully deployed.

You could say: We have $100K in contracted ARR (cARR) from customers X, Y, and Z, mostly in pilots that start billing once we’re fully deployed.

Transactional revenue over a particular time period (e.g. monthly revenue multiplied by 12 — we sold $50K of the product this month, and if that continues for the whole year, that’s $600K annualized revenue). Note: You should never call this ARR, as it is not recurring. You could say: We make $50K per month in transactional revenue. OR We make about $600K in annual revenue run rate. Note: Annual Revenue Run Rate is never abbreviated to ARR, per next point.

You could say: We make $50K per month in transactional revenue. OR We make about $600K in annual revenue run rate.

Note: Annual Revenue Run Rate is never abbreviated to ARR, per next point.

MMR or ARR – [Monthly or Annual] Recurring Revenue (e.g. Revenue actually invoiced and paid on a regular basis, per contract renewed monthly or yearly) – this is the most impressive and most prized form of revenue, and only then would you use the prized MRR or ARR metric. You could say: We make $50K MRR (monthly recurring revenue).’

You could say: We make $50K MRR (monthly recurring revenue).’

As with the articles in Artificial Lawyer about ARR, Tan’s missive to the market received lots of support, but also saw a surprisingly notable group of people who thought that misleading information was not a problem.

AL doesn’t want to keep repeating the point, but this site has to say: if we cannot trust the financial data put out by legal tech companies, or startups in any other vertical, then it harms the entire market – and also casts doubt on the investors in those companies as well. Plus, it potentially causes harm in terms of falsely attracting talent and new customers, not to mention it misleads the media and other market observers. Plus, one could say, if you start your company in that way, what will it be like as it matures toward an IPO? It seems to be storing up a range of issues that could later become highly problematic, to say the least.

As mentioned here before, the answer is not complicated: pick a metric, define it, stick to it.

research.titleEn: LegalDrill: Diagnosis-Driven Synthesis for Legal Reasoning in Small Language Models
research.titleZh: LegalDrill：面向小型语言模型法律推理的诊断驱动合成方法
research.abstractEn: Small language models (SLMs) are promising for real-world deployment due to their efficiency and low operational cost. However, their limited capacity struggles with high-stakes legal reasoning tasks that require coherent statute interpretation and logically consistent deduction. Furthermore, training SLMs for such tasks demands high-quality, concise reasoning trajectories, which are prohibitively expensive to manually collect and difficult to curate via standard rejection sampling, lacking granularity beyond final verdicts. To address these challenges, we propose {LegalDrill}, a diagnosis-driven synthesis framework that extracts and iteratively refines reasoning trajectories from a capable teacher via fine-grained prompting, then a self-reflective verification is employed to adaptively select the most effective data for the SLM student. The resulting data empower SLM training through supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization. Extensive experiments on several legal benchmarks demonstrate that {LegalDrill} significantly bolsters the legal reasoning capabilities of representative SLMs while bypassing the need for scarce expert annotations, paving a scalable path toward practical legal reasoning systems.
research.abstractZh: 小型语言模型因其高效性和低运营成本而在实际部署中具有前景。然而，其有限的能力难以应对需要连贯的法条解释和逻辑一致推理的高风险法律推理任务。此外，为此类任务训练小型语言模型需要高质量、简洁的推理轨迹，而手动收集这些轨迹成本高昂，且通过标准拒绝采样难以筛选，缺乏超越最终判决的粒度。为解决这些挑战，我们提出了LegalDrill，一种诊断驱动的合成框架，通过细粒度提示从能力较强的教师模型中提取并迭代优化推理轨迹，然后采用自反验证自适应地为小型语言模型学生选择最有效的数据。所得数据通过监督微调和直接偏好优化赋能小型语言模型训练。在多个法律基准上的大量实验表明，LegalDrill显著增强了代表性小型语言模型的法律推理能力，同时绕过了对稀缺专家标注的需求，为构建实用的法律推理系统铺平了可扩展的道路。

research.titleEn: GLIER: Generative Legal Inference and Evidence Ranking for Legal Case Retrieval
research.titleZh: GLIER：面向法律案例检索的生成式法律推理与证据排序
research.abstractEn: The semantic gap between colloquial user queries and professional legal documents presents a fundamental challenge in Legal Case Retrieval (LCR). Existing dense retrieval methods typically treat LCR as a black-box semantic matching process, neglecting the explicit juridical logic that underpins legal relevance. To address this, we propose GLIER (Generative Legal Inference and Evidence Ranking), a framework that reformulates retrieval as an inference process over latent legal variables. GLIER decomposes the task into two interpretability-driven stages. First, a Joint Generative Inference module translates raw queries into latent legal indicators, including charges and legal elements, using a unified sequence-to-sequence strategy that jointly generates charges and elements to enforce logical consistency. Second, a Multi-View Evidence Fusion mechanism aggregates generative confidence with structural and lexical signals for precise ranking. Extensive experiments on LeCaRD and LeCaRDv2 demonstrate that GLIER outperforms strong baselines such as SAILER and KELLER. Notably, GLIER exhibits strong data efficiency, maintaining robust performance even when trained with only 10% of the data.
research.abstractZh: 口语化用户查询与专业法律文件之间的语义鸿沟是法律案例检索（LCR）中的根本性挑战。现有的稠密检索方法通常将LCR视为黑盒语义匹配过程，忽视了支撑法律相关性的显式司法逻辑。为此，我们提出GLIER（生成式法律推理与证据排序），该框架将检索重新表述为对潜在法律变量的推理过程。GLIER将任务分解为两个可解释性驱动的阶段。首先，联合生成推理模块利用统一的序列到序列策略，将原始查询转化为潜在法律指标（包括罪名和法条要素），通过联合生成罪名和要素来强制逻辑一致性。其次，多视角证据融合机制将生成置信度与结构信号和词汇信号聚合，以实现精确排序。在LeCaRD和LeCaRDv2上的大量实验表明，GLIER优于SAILER和KELLER等强基线。值得注意的是，GLIER展现出强大的数据效率，即使仅使用10%的数据进行训练，也能保持稳健的性能。

research.titleEn: Expert Evaluation of LLM's Open-Ended Legal Reasoning on the Japanese Bar Exam Writing Task
research.titleZh: 专家评估大语言模型在日本律师考试写作任务中的开放式法律推理能力
research.abstractEn: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on legal benchmarks, including multiple-choice components of bar exams. However, their capacity for generating open-ended legal reasoning in realistic scenarios remains insufficiently explored. Notably, to our best knowledge, there are no prior studies or datasets addressing this issue in the Japanese context.   This study presents the first dataset designed to evaluate the open-ended legal reasoning performance of LLMs within the Japanese jurisdiction. The dataset is based on the writing component of the Japanese bar examination, which requires examinees to identify multiple legal issues from long narratives and to construct structured legal arguments in free text format. Our key contribution is the manual evaluation of LLMs' generated responses by legal experts, which reveals limitations and challenges in legal reasoning. Moreover, we conducted a manual analysis of hallucinations to characterize when and how the models introduce content not supported by precedent or law.   Our real exam questions, model-generated responses, and expert evaluations reveal the milestones of current LLMs in the Japanese legal domain. Our dataset and relevant resources will be available online.
research.abstractZh: 大型语言模型（LLMs）在法律基准测试中表现出色，包括律师考试的多项选择题部分。然而，它们在现实场景中生成开放式法律推理的能力仍未得到充分探索。值得注意的是，据我们所知，目前尚无针对日本语境下这一问题的研究或数据集。本研究提出了首个用于评估LLMs在日本司法管辖区内开放式法律推理性能的数据集。该数据集基于日本律师考试的写作部分，要求考生从长篇叙述中识别多个法律问题，并以自由文本形式构建结构化的法律论证。我们的主要贡献在于由法律专家对LLMs生成的回答进行人工评估，揭示了法律推理中的局限性和挑战。此外，我们对幻觉进行了人工分析，以描述模型何时以及如何引入不受先例或法律支持的内容。我们的真实考题、模型生成的回答以及专家评估揭示了当前LLMs在日本法律领域的里程碑。我们的数据集和相关资源将在线提供。

news.summaryZh:
美国新闻与世界报道已在纽约南区联邦法院起诉OpenAI，指控其未经授权使用该出版商内容训练AI模型，并生成与出版商作品竞争或削弱其价值的输出。案件名为U.S. News & World Report, L.P. v. OpenAI, Inc. et al，是出版商测试版权法如何适用于生成式AI的诉讼浪潮中的最新一例。

此类案件的核心问题是：AI开发者摄取大量受版权保护的材料训练模型，是否构成合理使用，还是需要获得许可并支付补偿。出版商通常主张模型训练及AI生成的摘要或复制品利用了受保护的表达，威胁其流量、订阅和许可市场；AI公司则示意将主要依赖合理使用、转换性使用等抗辩。诉讼律师关注驳回动议的早期裁决、训练数据指控的诉答标准，以及法院如何处理输出相似性、市场损害和不当得利等主张。媒体、软件和数据驱动公司的内部法律顾问应关注法院如何界定同意、使用条款限制、赔偿风险及证明特定作品被用于训练的举证责任。合规团队也面临实际影响：随着案件增多，部署生成式AI工具的公司面临压力，需记录数据来源、供应商陈述、模型治理控制及围绕版权输入输出的内部政策。即使远在出版业之外的企业，若法院允许这些主张继续推进，也可能需要重新审视与AI供应商的采购条款和风险分配。纽约南区已成为这场斗争的核心 venue，美国新闻案的案卷值得关注投诉指控、辩护策略及任何早期案件管理信号。

U.S. News Sues OpenAI, Adding to the Publisher AI Copyright Wave

by Bruno Queiroz

Another publisher has joined the fast-growing line of plaintiffs testing how copyright law applies to generative AI. U.S. News & World Report has sued OpenAI in the Southern District of New York, alleging the company used its content without authorization to train AI models and generate outputs that compete with or diminish the value of the publisher’s work. The case, U.S. News & World Report, L.P. v. OpenAI, Inc. et al , adds another closely watched dispute to a litigation trend that is rapidly becoming one of the most consequential battles in technology and media law.

At a high level, these cases raise a core question: when AI developers ingest large volumes of copyrighted material to train models, does that qualify as lawful fair use, or does it require permission and compensation? Publishers bringing these suits generally argue that model training and AI-generated summaries or reproductions exploit protected expression and threaten traffic, subscriptions, and licensing markets. AI companies, by contrast, have signaled they will rely heavily on fair use, transformation, and other defenses.

For legal professionals, the significance goes well beyond one dispute between a publisher and an AI developer. Litigators are watching for early rulings on motions to dismiss, pleading standards for training-data allegations, and how courts treat claims involving output similarity, market harm, and unjust enrichment. In-house counsel at media, software, and data-driven companies should be paying attention to how courts frame consent, terms-of-use restrictions, indemnity exposure, and the evidentiary burden for proving that particular works were used in training.

Compliance teams also have a practical stake in the outcome. As these cases multiply, companies deploying generative AI tools face growing pressure to document data provenance, vendor representations, model-governance controls, and internal policies around copyrighted inputs and outputs. Even businesses far outside publishing may need to revisit procurement language and risk allocation with AI vendors if courts allow these claims to proceed.

The Southern District of New York has become a central venue for this fight, and the U.S. News case docket is worth monitoring for complaint allegations, defense strategy, and any early case-management signals. However this particular suit develops, it underscores a larger reality: AI copyright litigation is moving from abstract policy debate to concrete judicial line-drawing, with real consequences for content owners, model developers, and enterprise users alike.

news.summaryZh: 2026年4月24日，美国法律格局呈现上诉裁决、执法行动、监管变化及重大刑事案件交织的高风险态势。对法律专业人士而言，其意义不在于单一事件，而在于整体模式：法院与监管机构持续测试公司责任、行政权力和程序策略的边界。联邦上诉法院在诉讼资格、仲裁、集体认证或机构遵从方面的裁决直接影响诉讼姿态，诉讼律师密切关注改变诉答负担、影响移送策略或重塑全国性救济可用性的判决。公司内部团队需特别警惕涉及消费者保护、就业、反垄断和证券等常见风险领域的裁决。大型民事案件在终审前即推动实务变化，多地区诉讼、产品责任和商业合同案件的重要初审裁决常影响和解价值、保险定位和专家策略。执法仍是首要关切，司法部及主要监管机构持续关注公司欺诈、制裁与出口管制、医疗账单、数据治理和竞争问题。即使没有重大立法出台，激进的解释和选择性执法也会重塑合规优先事项。立法和规则制定继续创造下游诉讼机会，涉及人工智能、劳工分类、消费者金融、环境披露和数字平台的新措施可能引发优先权争议、宪法挑战和行政法诉讼。重大刑事案件的影响超越个案被告，高调起诉、审判裁决、量刑协议和认罪协议可阐明司法部优先事项，并揭示合作预期、监督条款和指控理论。对律师而言，今日法律新闻提供关于法院选择、动议实践、披露义务、内部调查和和解策略的实时指导。

Eight Legal Flashpoints Shaping U.S. Litigation and Enforcement on April 24, 2026

by Bruno Queiroz

Friday’s legal landscape reflects a familiar but high-stakes mix of appellate rulings, enforcement activity, regulatory change, and headline criminal matters. For legal professionals, the significance is less in any single development than in the broader pattern: courts and agencies continue to test the limits of corporate liability, administrative power, and procedural strategy.

First, major court rulings remain central to risk assessment. When federal appellate courts issue decisions narrowing or expanding standing, arbitration, class certification, or agency deference, the immediate impact is on litigation posture. Litigators are watching for decisions that alter pleading burdens, affect removal strategy, or reshape the availability of nationwide relief. In-house teams should be especially alert where rulings touch recurring exposure areas like consumer protection, employment, antitrust, and securities claims.

Second, large civil cases continue to drive practical change even before final judgment. Significant trial-court decisions in multidistrict litigation, product liability disputes, and commercial contract cases often influence settlement value, insurance positioning, and expert strategy across related dockets. These developments matter because they can reset expectations for bellwether scheduling, Daubert motions, and preservation obligations.

Third, enforcement remains a top concern. Activity from the Department of Justice and key regulators signals continued focus on corporate fraud, sanctions and export controls, healthcare billing, data governance, and competition issues. Even where no blockbuster statute is enacted, aggressive interpretation and selective enforcement can reshape compliance priorities. Companies should expect regulators to keep pressing theories that test the edges of existing authority, particularly where technology, privacy, and market concentration are involved.

Fourth, legislation and rulemaking continue to create downstream litigation opportunities. New or proposed federal and state measures affecting AI, labor classification, consumer finance, environmental disclosures, and digital platforms are likely to generate immediate preemption fights, constitutional challenges, and administrative-law claims. For counsel, the key question is no longer just what the rule says, but how quickly private plaintiffs or state enforcers will use it.

Finally, notable criminal matters remain consequential beyond the individual defendants involved. High-profile indictments, trial verdicts, sentencing decisions, and plea agreements can clarify DOJ priorities and offer insight into cooperation expectations, monitor provisions, and charging theories. White-collar defense lawyers and compliance officers alike should be tracking how prosecutors frame intent, materiality, and corporate responsibility.

The takeaway for attorneys is straightforward: today’s legal news is not merely descriptive. It offers real-time guidance on forum selection, motion practice, disclosure obligations, internal investigations, and settlement strategy. For law firms, legal departments, and compliance teams, staying ahead of these developments is essential to advising clients before the next wave of litigation arrives.

news.titleEn: AI-native law firm index hits 40 listings
news.titleZh: AI原生律所索引收录数量达到40家
news.summaryZh:
由Lupl联合创始人Matt Pollins于三月推出的“AI原生”律所目录已达到40家律所的里程碑。该索引旨在捕捉一类新兴法律服务提供商，这些机构从创立之初便围绕AI驱动的工作流程构建，定价、接案、交付和团队结构均以AI执行为基础。收录的律所包括Eudia、Alaro、AgileCounsel、Crosby、Elevate旗下的ElevateNext，以及由房地产和法律科技公司Oribital新近推出的Farringdon。该名单约一年前开始整理，最初只是一份文档，后应建议转为独立目录，推出时仅有23家律所，现已增至40家，几乎翻倍。

关于AI原生律所的界定，Pollins称定义仍在演变，新成立并非必要条件。他提到有一家拥有约500名律师、成立50至60年的律所申请，自认为AI原生，因此需要沟通其是否真正AI原生，还是仅购买了Harvey或Legora。多数收录律所是新成立的，其特点是围绕客户体验重新设计整个律所，而非围绕律所设计AI。Pollins以客户委托流程为例，从接案开始，许多律所已构建AI驱动的接案工作流，如代理、自动化系统或客户Slack频道。定价方面，多数AI原生律所在网上公布价目表，客户可在委托前获知价格，或通过AI助手即时获取报价。Y Combinator支持的General Legal是典型例子，其网站列出价格，包括审查和谈判3至50页合同每份500美元。Pollins认为最大差异在于工作方式：客户发送合同或查询后，先由AI进行首轮审查，再交由律师处理升级和确认，即使律师全天会议，工作也能推进。这些律所还拥抱客户使用AI生成初稿，提供AI驱动的接案工具无缝获取指令。Pollins持续修订AI原生律所的定义，认为这不仅仅是营销，这些律所与老牌律所确实不同。
news.bodyHtml:
A directory dedicated to ‘AI native’ law firms launched in March by Lupl’s co-founder Matt Pollins has hit a 40-firm milestone, reflecting what many see as a fundamental shift in how certain legal services are being designed, priced, and delivered.

The AI Firm Index aims to capture an emerging category of legal providers that have been built from the ground up around AI-enabled workflows, with pricing, intake, delivery, and team structure all built with AI execution as the foundation. The firms listed include Eudia, Alaro, AgileCounsel, Crosby, ElevateNext, which is part of Elevate, and Farringdon, which has just been launched by property and legal tech company Oribital.

Advertisement

“I started making the list about a year ago when we first started seeing announcements about AI native law firms,” Pollins says. “Initially it was just a document, but someone suggested turning it into a standalone directory. When I launched it, it had 23 firms and it’s up to 40 now, so it’s almost doubled.”

In terms of who really qualifies as an AI native firm, Pollins says that the definition is evolving. Being new isn’t necessarily a prerequisite and Pollins says: “I’ve had a firm apply and they have around 500 lawyers and have been around for 50 to 60 years but they see themselves as AI native. So I need to talk to them about whether they really are AI native or have just bought Harvey or Legora.”

Advertisement

However most of the firms listed are new, and Pollins says: “What’s interesting is how they have redesigned the whole firm around the client experience. So rather than designing AI around the firm, they have designed it round the client.”

As an example, Pollins says: “If you take a client engagement almost beginning to end, you can talk about it being AI native at each stage. So the first would be intake of new requests. Instead of that being a back and forth with a partner or an associate and emails, a lot of firms have built intake workflows, whether that’s agents, or whether that’s automated systems or whether that’s in the client’s Slack channel. I think there’s a piece around meeting the client where they are.”

The next criteria is pricing, and Pollins says: “Most [AI native firms] have a price list published online. You can figure out the price before you even engage them. And if you can’t, you can chat with an AI assistant to get to a price immediately, as opposed to ‘let’s have a consultation and then we’ll send you a quote.’”

One of the best examples of that is General Legal, a Y Combinator-backed firm, which has its prices listed on the website, including $500 per contract for reviewing and negotiating a contract of between three and 50 pages. Pollins says: “That’s just locked in, that’s their fee, that’s what you pay.”

Perhaps the biggest differentiator is the way that work is done, and Pollins says: “Instead of I send you a query via e-mail, you use Harvey or Legora as an assistant to help you answer the question and then you come back to me, it’s more that the client sends the contract or the query, it goes to AI first, that does the first pass review, then it comes to you. So even if you’re in all day meetings, the work moves forward. And then at the end of your day, when you come out of those meetings, the first draught response is there, you deal with any escalations, rubber stamp it, and then it goes back to the client. And that’s quite different, I think.”

Instead of getting frustrated with clients who produce AI-generated first drafts, Pollins says new firms are embracing it. “Instead of fighting that, these AI native firms seem to be leaning into that and providing intake tools which are AI powered to get the instructions from the client in a seamless way.”

Pollins is continuously revising the definition of who qualifies as an AI-native firm on the site, and says: “It’s totally up to discussion.”

He adds: “My feeling is it is more than just marketing. These firms do look very different to more established firms. So I do think it’s a category in its own right. But I suspect the definition is going to continue to evolve.”

If you want to take a look  see https://aifirmindex.com/

news.titleEn: Spoiler Alert: Legal Marketing’s Next Evolution is Agentic and Product-Led –
news.titleZh: 剧透预警：法律营销的下一次进化是代理式与产品主导型
news.summaryZh:
2026年法律营销协会年会在新奥尔良举行，会议涵盖法律运营、客户情报、AI、变革管理和视频等议题，现场反响热烈。当前法律营销团队虽在业务拓展、定向活动、思想领导力和AI实验上投入更多，却仍存在活动与长期定位脱节、信息随业务领域或合伙人变动、客户情报未投入运营、AI仅战术性使用等问题，整体缺乏连贯性。

下一步进化是产品营销理念与代理式AI执行的融合。产品营销为市场进入带来结构：市场情报与验证、清晰价值主张、一致信息与定位、赋能律师。代理式AI工作流可持续监测客户行业并触发洞察、动态调整信息、基于验证价值主张组装提案、为律师提供实时定制话术、从结果中学习改进。但若无清晰定位、信息和受众定义，AI只会放大不一致。这一转变将推动法律营销从活动转向系统、从内容转向情报、从支持转向赋能、从被动转向主动。
